Reduction of open-circuit losses
In order to study the non-radiative recombination behaviour in our
devices, we investigate the photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY)
and time-resolved photoluminescence (TRPL) on a series of perovskite
“half-stacks” and full devices. In Fig. 4a, the PLQY of the neat perovskite
ﬁlm of 0.7% is improved to 1% and 2% after GuaBr and ImBr treatments
respectively, indicating effective surface passivation. Most impor-
tantly, the large PLQY losses induced by the PCBM layer are strongly
reduced by either GuaBr or ImBr treatments, approaching similar
PLQY values of the neat perovskite on glass. Consistent with the device
VOCs, ImBr outperformed GuaBr. Contrary to 1.6 eV devices34, the
PTAA/PFN-P2/perovskite interface shows a signiﬁcant reduction of
PLQY, denoting strong interface recombination at the HTL/perovskite
interface. Consistent with the VOC of the full devices, the TEA-TFSI does
not show any signiﬁcant improvement. Importantly, as shown in
Figs. S30–31, all half-stack perovskite ﬁlms deposited on PTAA, present
a signiﬁcant degree of phase segregation and, therefore, the PLQY is
estimated by ﬁtting only the emission at 700 nm, as reported in a
recent study35. As such, the losses and QFLS calculated from half-stacks
on PTAA only represent an estimate of the non-radiative recombina-
tion losses. However, when the PTAA is replaced with the SAM, no
halide segregation is observed during the measurement (Fig. S30) and
the PLQY approaches that of neat perovskite on glass, denoting almost
complete elimination of the interface recombination induced by the
transport layers, consistent with previous ﬁndings for lower bandgap
perovskites2. This phenomenon has been previously associated with
more efﬁcient charge extraction by the SAM layers compared to PTAA,
which avoids a build-up of interfacial charge, responsible for phase
segregation2,36. The associated non-radiative energy losses are pre-
sented in Fig. 4b, calculated with respect to the thermodynamic limit
of the perovskite absorber as detailed in Figs. S32–S33. To check that
the nanoparticulate Al2O3 “wetting layer” is not inﬂuencing the
recombination at the SAM/perovskite interface, we investigate the
PLQY and non-radiative losses for a SAM/perovskite sample with and
without Al2O3 (Fig. S34). Given that the losses at the interfaces of the
two samples are the same, we can conclude that the additional Al2O3

mechanisms of this interface and therefore not changing our conclu-

large QFLS-VOC mismatch of almost 100 meV. With regard to the

The devices with TEA-TFSI show only a modest decrease of QFLS-VOC

Now the VOC losses are comparable to the one of narrower bandgap

Importantly, the experimental trend shown in Fig. 4c follows very
consistently what we predicted from drift-diffusion simulations in

the Br halide at the perovskite surface leads to the formation of a lower

The TRPL decays presented in Fig. 4d–f, consistently follow the
PLQY trends in Fig. 4a. Intensity dependent TRPL measurements for
each condition are reported in Fig. S35. The maximum differential
lifetime40, calculated in SI, of the neat perovskite of 1 μs is improved

Importantly, GuaBr and ImBr surface treatment signiﬁcantly increase
the lifetime of the perovskite/ETL stack, conﬁrming the effective
reduction of interface recombination. The best case is found for the
ImBr treatment, where the differential lifetime of the perovskite/ETL
stack (630 ns) approaches that of the neat (un-passivated) perovskite
ﬁlm (1 μs). Similarly, the short lifetime in contact with the PTAA
(70 ns) and the TEA-TFSI (70 ns) is dramatically enhanced using the
SAM HTM (800 ns). We acknowledge that due to halide segregation
in the PTAA and TEA-TFSI samples, these lifetimes might be inﬂu-

Reduction of short-circuit losses

To establish a physical model of the enhanced collection efﬁ-
ciency, we perform steady-state and time-dependent drift-diffusion
simulations implementing mobile ions on modelled PTAA, TEA-TFSI
and SAM devices. The reference PTAA device has been modelled fol-
lowing a combination of experimental results and theoretical models
previously published11,13,17. We modelled the TEA-TFSI device by adding
a 1 nm interlayer with high ionic density (1018cm−3) between the per-
ovskite and the HTL, where the ions (positive and negative) were
homogeneously distributed within this layer and ﬁxed in position so
that they do not displace when an electric ﬁeld is applied during
simulated operation. For the SAM device, we simulated the SAM by
using a 1 nm HTL, with the HOMO level set to align 0.1 eV shallower that
the VBM of the perovskite and with lower interface recombination
velocity (in comparison to PTAA/Perovskite). For all the models, we
allow a certain density of ions from within the perovskite absorber
layer to redistribute throughout the device layers under operation.
We also investigated allowing both negative and positive ions to
redistribute during measurements and found that in order to replicate
the current loss at short-circuit that we observe experimentally, we
need to allow only the positive ions to build up within the HTM layer.
The details of the simulations can be found in Supplementary Note 10.

Fig. 5d, these last two scenarios lead to a ﬁeld at the p-interface in
favour of hole extraction. We note that because of reduced interface
recombination, the very thin HTL case exhibits the largest JSC even if
the internal ﬁeld in this region is slightly lower compared to the ionic-
interlayer simulation. A schematic representation of the band diagram

between the reduced JSC decays and the voltage drop at the p-interface
indicates that the charge collection is strongly inﬂuenced by the
extraction efﬁciency in the proximity of the HTL interface rather than
in the perovskite bulk where the remaining ﬁeld is small in all condi-

besides promoting hole extraction, also repels electrons, which can
reduce non-radiative recombination of non-extracted carriers at short-
circuit conditions.
Impact of surface treatment on stability
Lastly, we investigate if there is any impact of the surface treatment
and the lower dimensional phases induced by the GuaBr or ImBr on the
stability of the perovskite ﬁlms and devices. In Fig. 6a–c, we present
the performance of devices over time, thermally stressed at 85 °C in N2
in the dark. The GuaBr devices show a faster degradation than the
“reference devices”, with average PCE reaching 80% of its peak (T80)
after ~480 h, as compared to a T80 lifetime of ~800 h of the SAM
reference devices. The ImBr devices exhibited the highest thermal
stability, reaching an average T80 of ~950 h. This effect is clearly visible
in Fig. 6e, where the VOC improvement of the ImBr device is maintained
for >1200 h, whereas the VOC of the GuaBr devices falls below the
reference cells after <200 h of thermal stress. We attribute these losses
to an increase of non-radiative recombination after degradation of the
perovskite absorber or interfaces. This GuaBr voltage loss is similar to
what has been previously observed with phenylethyl ammonium pas-
sivation in nip cells46. In Fig. 6d, we present the thermal stability of the
champion devices for each different treatment scenario for longer
times, and we ﬁnd that, in the best case, the SAM-ImBr treated device
retains 80% of its initial PCE for 3500 h.
As an alternative stress factor to temperature, water vapour and
oxygen in the atmosphere can also lead to the degradation of per-
ovskite ﬁlms, and different treatments to the perovskite surface may
have a positive or negative inﬂuence on this atmospheric stability. In
Fig. 6f–i, we show photographs and UV-Vis absorption spectra of
perovskite ﬁlms with and without surface modiﬁcation aged in air
under ambient light and 40–45% relative humidity. We observe that
the ﬁlms which have been treated with GuaBr undergo a relatively
rapid change in appearance, turning from dark brown/black to light
brown, and a reduction in the strength of the absorption onset after
only 3 days. In contrast, the ImBr treated ﬁlms exhibit a predominantly
unchanged absorption proﬁle and characteristic black perovskite ﬁlms
after 13–15 days, whereases the reference ﬁlms show a small change
over this timescale. We show further images of aged perovskite ﬁlms in
Fig. S42. It, therefore, appears that the GuaBr treatment results in a
deterioration of the ambient stability of the perovskite ﬁlms, whereas
the ImBr treatment results in a small improvement in the ambient

These results highlight that although in terms of device perfor-
mance the two different surface treatments exhibit comparably
beneﬁcial effects, only the ImBr treated devices retained their initial
improvement, enhancing the general stability of the perovskite
material. Possibly, the Gua+ cation can diffuse and incorporate in the
bulk 3D perovskite structure more easily than Im+, inducing addi-
tional degradation of the original perovskite phase. However, there
could be a number of different causes, which are important to reveal
in order to realise a generalisable strategy for passivation and long-
term stability enhancement of metal halide perovskite materials and
devices.
In conclusion, we have used a fundamental understanding of the
operational device physics of wide bandgap PSCs to identify key losses
in performance, and engineer improvement strategies to deliver
enhanced widegap perovskite thin-ﬁlms and solar cells. Speciﬁcally, we
have rationalized that using either very thin HTM layers (SAMs) or
introducing an ionic interlayer is important for reducing the short-
circuit current of pin perovskite solar cells. Introducing a surface
passivation layer, which results in the growth of a low dimensional top
layer, is important for reducing the voltage losses, eliminating the
discrepancy between QFLS and VOC, allowing access to the full
potential of the absorber material. As such, we demonstrated that the
major limitations of these devices are not related to the material itself
but mostly to the transport layers and interfaces. Our results highlight
how using optoelectronic modelling to guide device and interface
engineering can lead to successful optimization of widegap PSCs,
potentially leading to a more successful implementation in tandem
solar cells with higher efﬁciencies.

using Fourier transform photocurrent spectroscopy. Our custom-
built set up is based on a Bruker Vertex 80 v Fourier transform
interferometer. The solar cells were masked with a metal aperture
such that the whole active area was illuminated by a tungsten halo-
gen lamp47. To determine the EQE, the photocurrent spectrum of the
device under test was divided by that of a calibrated Si reference cell
(Newport) of a known EQE. The acquisition time for each photo-
current spectrum was ~60 s.
To determine the equivalent short-circuit current density under

Time-resolved photoluminescence measurements
Time-Correlated Single Photon Counting was carried out using a
398 nm pulsed laser (PicoHarp LDH-D-C405M) with a repetition rate of
0.125 MHz for isolated ﬁlms, and 2.5 MHz for those with transport
layers attached. Photoluminescence was collected using the same
monochromator, with a photon-counting detector (PDM series from
MPD). Timing is controlled electronically using a PicoHarp300 event
timer. PL decays were measured at the peak wavelengths of the PL
spectra.
Photoluminescence quantum yield
Excitation for the PL measurements was performed with a 532 nm CW
laser (ThorLabs DJ532-10) through an optical ﬁbre into an integrating
sphere. The intensity of the laser was adjusted to a 1 sun equivalent
intensity equal to 50 mW/cm2, calculated for the excitation wavelength
and the bandgap of the absorbing material. A second optical ﬁbre was
used from the output of the integrating sphere to an QEPro spectro-
meter. The system was calibrated by using a calibrated halogen lamp
with speciﬁed spectral irradiance, which was shone into to integrating
sphere. A spectral correction factor was established to match the
spectral output of the detector to the calibrated spectral irradiance of
the lamp.
X-Ray diffraction characterization
1D-XRD patterns were collected with a Panalytical X’Pert Pro X-ray
diffractometer in Bragg-Brentano geometry. The Cu source (K-α) was
operated at 40 kV and 40 mA, with 0.04 radian Soller slits and typically
120 mins collection time per sample. Grazing-incidence wide-angle
X-ray scattering (GIWAXS) data was acquired with a Rigaku SmartLab
diffractometer. In this setup, a 3 kW Cu source (operating at 40 kV,
45 mA) with CBO-f optics was incident on thin ﬁlms prepared as above.
Samples were mounted on a 2D-XRD attachment head, which incor-
porated a knife-edge to prevent air scatter and an aligned beam stop
for the direct beam. X-ray scattering was detected with a HyPix-3000
hybrid pixel-array 2D detector with a sample-to-detector distance of
65 mm. Sample widths were reduced to ~4 mm to minimise sample
footprint broadening. Data was collected at a grazing incidence angle
(αi) = of 1° and the detector goniometer arm was rotated through 2θ
angles from 0° to 40° in 1° steps. Detector images were resampled into
Q-space and combined together using scripts based on the PyFAI and
pygix libraries, which were also used for azimuthally integrated 1D
proﬁles48,49. For variable-angle GIWAXS measurements (αi = 0.2°−1.4°),
samples were measured using a different 2D-XRD aperture slit con-
ﬁguration with parallel-beam optics, a 1° in-plane parallel-slit colli-
mator, a 0.1 mm incident slit, and 10 mm length-limiting slit at a single
detector position, before processing as above. Powder XRD patterns
and structural illustrations were calculated and rendered using
VESTA50.
Scanning electron microscopy
An FEI Quanta 600 FEG scanning electron microscope was used to
investigate perovskite layer morphologies with different surface
treatments. The accelerating voltage was set to 5 kV and spot size was
ﬁxed at 2.5 (3.0 for cross-sectional images), with a typical working
distance of 5 mm and 30 μs dwell time for single pass image acquisi-
tion. Focusing and alignment were done away from imaged areas to
minimise electron beam–induced damage.
X-Ray photoelectron spectroscopy
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy measurements were carried out
using a Thermo Scientiﬁc K-alpha spectrometer and a mono-
chromated Al K-α X-ray source at a take-off angle of 90degrees. Core
level spectra were recorded with a pass energy of 20 eV from an ana-
lysis area of 300 um × 300 um. The ﬁtting procedure was carried out
using CasaXPS, the background of the spectra were ﬁtted using a
Shirley lineshape and the peaks were ﬁt using a mixture of Gaussian/
Lorentzian (Lorentzian = 20%) line shapes.
Current–voltage characteristic and JSC decay
Current density-voltage (J–V), maximum power point (MPP), and
transient open-circuit voltage and short-circuit current density mea-
surements were measured using a Keithley 2400 source measure unit
(SMU) in ambient air under both light (simulated AM1.5 G irradiance
generated by a Wavelabs SINUS-220 solar simulator) calibrated with a
certiﬁed KG3-ﬁltered reference diode (Fraunhofer) and dark. The
active area of the solar cell was masked with a black-anodised metal
aperture to either 0.25 or 1.00 cm2. The forward J–V scans were mea-
sured from forward bias to short-circuit and the reverse scans were
from short-circuit to forward bias, both at a scan rate of 0.3 Vs−1. Active
MPP tracking measurements using a gradient descent algorithm were
performed to obtain the steady-state power conversion efﬁciency. The
spectral mismatch factor was estimated to be 0.006 according to a
previously reported method [https://doi.org/10.1039/C2EE03429H],
and has been applied to calculate power conversion efﬁciencies. We
estimate the systematic error of this setup to be on the order of ±5%
(relative).
Photoluminescence quantum yield mapping
The illumination was provided by a ThorLabs M450LP1 LED collimated
by a Thorlabs SM2F lens. The emission was at 450 nm, well above the
bandgap of the tested samples. The Intensity was controlled by con-
trolling the power supplied to the LED. In order to determine the ‘1 sun’
illumination, the sample was shorted and the LED power tweaked till
the current readout was near the short circuit current measured on a
solar simulator. The biasing was done using a Keithley 2400. More
details are provided in Supporting Information.
Thermal stability
Thermal stability measurements were carried inside an oven kept in
the dark at 80˚C inside a glovebox under N2 atmosphere.

Concurrent Top and Buried Surface Optimization for Flexible 
Perovskite Solar Cells with High Efficiency and Stability
Chang Liu, Kaixin Huang, Bihua Hu, Yaru Li, Luozheng Zhang, Xianyong Zhou, 
Yanliang Liu, Zhixin Liu, Yifa Sheng, Shi Chen, Xingzhu Wang,* and Baomin Xu*
Although much progress is made toward enhancing the efficiency of 
perovskite solar cells (PSCs), their operational reliability, particularly their 
mechanical stability, which is a crucial factor for flexible PSCs (f-PCSs), has 
not attracted sufficient attention. The defects in the perovskite layer, espe-
cially on the top and the buried surface of the perovskite layer, can induce 
perovskite fracture, highly limiting the performance of f-PSCs. Herein, a novel 
multifunctional organic salt, metformin hydrochloride, which can passivate 
cationic and anionic defects, is incorporated on both the top and buried 
surfaces of perovskite layer to suppress defects. As a result, a power conver-
sion efficiency (PCE) of 24.40% for rigid PSCs and a PCE of 22.04% for f-PSCs 
are achieved. Simultaneously, the device can retain 90% and 80% of the 
initial efficiency after 1000 h of light illumination and 10 000 bending cycles, 
respectively, showing excellent operational stability. This study may provide 
a global way to design a passivation strategy and fabricate flexible perovskite 
solar cells with high efficiency and stability.

1. Introduction
The power conversion efficiency of perovskite solar cells (PSCs) 
based on metal-halide perovskite as a light-absorbing layer has 
rapidly increased from 3.8% to 25.7% in recent years, which is 
comparable with that of silicon solar cells.[1,2] The prospect of 
solution-processed, low-cost PSCs with excellent performance 
and their great influence on the global renewable energy market 
is promoting worldwide research efforts to improve PSCs.[3–5]

layers (ETLs).[16–23] Recently, the efficiency of f-PSCs reached 
22.44%, while the efficiency gap with rigid PSCs is still too 
large.[24] To reduce the efficiency gap, it is still necessary to 
develop new fabrication processes for flexible substrates and 
flexible devices. Regarding the second problem, some efforts 
have been made to enhance the flexibility and bending sta-
bility of f-PSCs by reducing mechanical damage.[25,26] There is 
a previous study that used a geometric engineering method to 
move the neutral axis during the bending process by reducing 
the thickness of the flexible polymer substrate, which results 
in the reduction of the tensile stress experienced by the perov-
skite film.[27] As a result, f-PSCs can achieve 17% efficiency and 
withstand 10 000 bending cycles. Engineering the perovskite 
film is another effective approach for enhancing the efficiency, 
stability, and bending-fatigue resistance of f-PSCs.[28–32] Due 
to their ionic nature, perovskites can present different defect 
states associated with I− anions, undercoordinated Pb2+ cations, 
halide vacancies, and organic cations (MA+/FA+), which usually 
accumulate on the surface and at the interface of the perovskite 
film.[33–35] Such defect states can result in nonradiative recombi-
nation and charge trapping, which is the main cause of hyster-
esis and reduces the performance of f-PSCs. With the effect of 
an external stressor, defect states may further cause ion migra-
tion and charge accumulation, leading to the destruction of the 
material lattice. Eventually, the defect states can lead to perfor-
mance losses and long-term device instability under real-time 
operation of f-PSCs.[36–39]
Recently, different defect passivation strategies have been 
reported to improve the stability of f-PSCs and reduce non-
radiative recombination.[39,40] Diverse metal cations (such as 
Cd2+, K+, Na+ and Rb+) were utilized to neutralize interstitial 
ions, negative PbI3− anti-sites and uncoordinated I− ions for 
passivating bulk defects. In addition, different anions (such as 
acetate [COO−] and thiocyanate [SCN−]) can be introduced to 
neutralize halide vacancies and interstitial Pb.[41] Additionally, 
several additives can be used to control the nucleation process 
of the perovskite film to obtain larger gains and reduced grain 
boundaries, which are associated with trap densities. In addi-
tion, ionic additives with functional groups were proposed to 
reduce the mobility of ions and defect number in the perov-
skite layer. Lewis-base additives such as thiophene, urea, caf-
feine, and poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) can passivate the 
uncoordinated Lewis-acid Pb2+ cations by donating electrons 
(from sulfur atoms, oxygen, and nitrogen, respectively).[42–46] 
In addition, Lewis-acid molecules such as zwitterions and 
[6,6]-phenyl-C61-butyric acid methyl ester (PCBM) have been 
developed to passivate I− defects.[47,48] On the other hand, var-
ious passivation strategies have been proposed to reduce the 
interface and surface defects in f-PSCs. Some additives, such 
as benzylamine, trioctylphosphine oxide (TOPO), and PMMA, 
are used to suppress phase segregation in the perovskite layer, 
leading to the reduction of surface defects.[45,49–51] To alleviate 
surface defects, building a 2D perovskite layer at the interface 
is also an effective strategy. In summary, adequate passivation 
strategies have been proposed to restrain the specific defects 
in perovskite films. Nonetheless, most of the early passiva-
tion research is based on experience. Therefore, it is still nec-
essary to gain a comprehensive understanding of the involved 
defects. Because perovskite is positively and negatively charged, 
the surface and interface of perovskite are strongly susceptible 
to ambient conditions and processing details. In most cases, 
uncoordinated Pb2+ ions tend to be featured on the surface of 
perovskite due to the volatile nature of halide and organic spe-
cies in perovskite.[52–55] Many relatively large organic molecules, 
such as butylammonium iodide (BAI) and phenethylammo-
nium iodide (PEAI), are known to form a 2D layer for passi-
vating defects. However, these highly positive molecules have 
difficulty effectively passivating the positively charged surface 
with uncoordinated Pb2+.[56–59] As a result, it is still necessary to 
find a suitable passivator to passivate different kinds of defects 
in perovskite. Moreover, although the defects on both the top 
and bottom surfaces of the perovskite layer are significantly 
detrimental to PSC performance, most researches have focused 
on passivating the defects on only one side surface. Therefore, 
it remains both urgent and challenging to develop an effective 
strategy to simultaneously decrease the number of defects on 
both the top and bottom surfaces of the perovskite layer.
In this work, we developed a universal passivation strategy 
for effectively passivating defects on both the top and buried 
surfaces of perovskite films. For this purpose, multifunctional 
passivating molecules with electron-rich and electron-poor 
domains are needed. Therefore, metformin hydrochloride 
(MFCl), which consists of negatively charged amine and imine 
groups and a positively charged ammonium head group, was 
proposed. This molecule can effectively passivate the defects on 
the buried surface of the perovskite layer when it was pre-depos-
ited between the ETL and the perovskite layer. Furthermore, 
it can further mitigate the defects on the top surface of the 
perovskite layer by introducing the molecules through a post-
treatment approach. This double-sided passivation strategy not 
only provides protection against the intrusion of environmental 
species but also retards the propensity for flexural fracture. 
Moreover, the passivation layers can enhance the photocarrier 
transport efficiency at the perovskite/ETL and perovskite/HTL 
interfaces. As a result, we achieved a high PCE of 24.40% and 
22.04% for rigid and flexible PSCs, respectively. Additionally, 
f-PSCs can maintain 90% of the initial PCE for 1000 h and 80% 
of the initial PCE after 10 000 bending cycles, showing excellent 
operational stability and mechanical durability, respectively.
2. Results and Discussion
As illustrated in Figure 1A, three kinds of passivating processes 
were investigated in this work. The SnO2 ETL was prepared by 
our previous work at low temperatures.[60] For the BSP case, 
MFCl was dissolved in dimethylformamide (DMF) and spun 
onto the SnO2 layer. Subsequentially, a perovskite layer was 
deposited on the SnO2 with MFCl. As perovskite, we utilized 
(FAPbI3)0.95(MAPbBr3)0.05 as a light absorption material due 
to its ideal band gap for fabricating high-efficiency f-PSCs. 
As shown in Figure S1 (Supporting Information), the average 
VOC of the f-PSCs improves from 1.06 to 1.15 V after the con-
centration of MFCl was increased to 1 mg mL−1. Considering 
the overall efficiency of the device, the optimal MFCl concen-
tration is 0.50 mg mL−1 for BSP, leading to an average VOC of 
1.13 V. The FF of the f-PSCs declined when the concentration of

BSP+TSP, respectively. All passivation methods increase the 
VOC without causing a decreased FF by using the optimal con-

improves from 1.06 to 1.12, 1.09, and 1.13  V after BSP, TSP, 
and BSP+TSP treatment, respectively (Figures  1B). As shown 
in the UV–vis absorption spectra (Figure S3, Supporting Infor-
mation), the perovskite films without and with passivation have 
similar band gaps of approximately 1.54  eV. Accordingly, the 
EQE spectra do not show considerable change with passiva-

resulted in a slightly increased series resistance (Rs) from 6.1 
to 7.4 Ω cm2 (Figure S4A, Supporting Information) due to the 
low conductivity of MFCl. The effect of increased Rs can be 
counterbalanced by an increased average shunt resistance (Rsh) 
from 1.8 to 5.5 kΩ cm2 revealing less charge recombination 
(Figure S4B, Supporting Information). Therefore, the passiva-
tion process did not show an obvious effect on the FF.
As shown in Figure  2A, the J–V curves of the champion 
device without passivation have a PCE of 20.01% with a VOC of 
1.086 V, an FF of 77.43%, and a JSC of 23.77 mA cm−2. Compared 
to the control device, the VOC of the best-performing BSP+TSP 
device exhibits an enhancement of 48  mV, achieving 1.134  V, 
leading to a PCE of 22.04%. The champion f-PSCs can achieve 
JSC values above 24.11 mA cm−2, which is consistent with the 
value of 23.56  mA cm−2 for integrated JSC derived from the 
external quantum efficiency (EQE) spectra (Figure 2B). This is 
one of the highest efficiencies reported for flexible single-junc-
tion PSCs.51 As shown in Figure S5 (Supporting Information), 
the certified efficiency can also achieve 20.35%. Additionally, 
the PSCs were fabricated on rigid ITO/glass substrates to dem-
onstrate the passivation effect. As shown in Figure 2C, we can 
see that the best-performing device has a JSC of 25.36 mA cm−2, 
VOC of 1.158 V, FF of 83.10%, resulting in a PCE of 24.40%. As 
we expected, rigid PSCs exhibit higher performance than their 
flexible counterparts, which can be attributed to the higher 
quality of the ITO conducting layer and better light transmis-
sion in the glass. As shown in Figure S6 (Supporting Informa-
tion), we compare the minimal achievable VOC losses calculated 
from the Shockley-Queisser limit condition for perovskite solar 
cells at 25 °C. As shown, for the best-performing device, the 
introduction of BSP+TSP reduces the VOC loss from 210 to 
150 mV.

index is a crucial factor for PSCs and is defined as [(PCEreverse-

decrease the average hysteresis index of devices with BSP, 
TSP, and BSP+TSP from 0.09 to 0.06, 0.08, and 0.04, respec-

help to anchor the PbI2.[61] Similarly, MF+ in MFCl can also act

To understand the mechanism of cationic and anionic defect 
passivation, we performed DFT calculations. Figure S10 (Sup-
porting Information) the electrostatic potential map (left) of 
the MF+ molecule. The molecule has various functional groups 
incorporating electron-rich amine and imine as well as electron-
poor ammonium groups. Because it is challenging to control 
the nature of surface defects of metal halide perovskites, multi-
functional molecules such as MFCl, incorporating electron-rich 
and electron-poor groups, are expected to be successful for full 
passivation of the surface defects. Otherwise, a highly electropo-

electron-poor (electron-rich) perovskite surface domain because

imine N atoms primarily interact with the electron-poor Pb 
surface atoms. As a result, the amine and imine groups in the 
molecule interact with the undercoordinated Pb atom, forming 
the strongest bond. The electron density differences also sug-
gest that one MF+ molecule can simultaneously passivate many 
surface dangling bonds. We also compare the results for MF+

effective for passivation of metal halide perovskite-dangling 
bonds than commonly used organic ammonium salts (such

The detailed procedure of PEACl passivation is mentioned in 
the experimental section. Figure S11 (Supporting Information) 
shows a comparison of the f-PSCs with MFCl and PEACl passi-
vation. It is noted that the BSP+TSP process is utilized for both 
passivation molecules. The devices are fabricated with the same 
methods and tested under identical conditions. The f-PSCs 
with PEACl passivation show slightly lower FF values of 77.98% 
than that (80.47%) of devices passivated with MFCl. In addition, 
the device with MFCl passivation exhibits a VOC of 1.14 V, which 
is higher than the VOC of 1.13 V for the device with PEAI pas-
sivation. As a result, MFCl passivation can lead to a higher effi-
ciency (21.95%) than PEACl passivation (21.05%). This result 
can be attributed to the multifunctional groups in the MFCl 
molecule, especially electron-rich imine nitrogens, and amines, 
which are not present in the PEACl molecule.
To investigate the impact of MFCl passivation on device sta-
bility, the stabilities of f-PSCs under different conditions were 
measured. As shown in Figure 3A, we record the evolution of 
maximum power point (MPP) tracking under 1-sun illumina-
tion for 200 s. The PCE of the device without MFCl passiva-
tion significantly decreases from 18.43% to 17.52% during the 
MPP tracking test. In contrast, the devices with MFCl pas-
sivation show a more stable power output. The remarkable 
PCE reduction in the devices without MFCl passivation can be 
attributed to the phase segregation of the perovskite induced 
by light illumination. To further investigate this, we tested the 
stability of the f-PSCs without encapsulation under continuous 
light illumination in an N2 atmosphere. Figure 3B shows that 
the device without MFCl passivation exhibits 40% degradation 
of its initial PCE for 600 h. However, the device with MFCl pas-
sivation retains 90% of its initial PCE after operation for 1000 h, 
showing much better light stability. Additionally, as shown in 
Figure 3C, the thermal stability of the f-PSCs was also meas-
ured by heating the devices without encapsulation at 85 °C 
in an N2 atmosphere. In accord with the results of the MPP 
tracking and light illumination measurements, the control 
device without MFCl passivation only retains 80% of its ini-
tial PCE for ∼50 h, while the device with MFCl passivation can 
retain 80% of its initial PCE after more than 200 h, indicating 
better thermal stability.
To further investigate the mechanical durability, a bending 
test of f-PSCs with and without MFCl passivation was per-
formed with a 5  mm radius for 10 000 cycles in ambient air. 
To reduce environmental effects, the 10 000-cycle bend test 
was processed rapidly within an hour. Figures 4A–C shows the 
photovoltaic parameters for a certain number of bending cycles. 
In summary, the f-PSCs with MFCl passivation can maintain 
80% of the initial PCE after 10 000 cycles, exhibiting excellent 
bending stability. As a comparison, the f-PSCs without MFCl 
passivation maintained only 34% of their original PCE. As 
shown in Figure 4D, it is noted that the f-PSCs without MFCl 
passivation rapidly lose FF after just 1000 cycles, which is most 
likely due to delamination cracks. After that, a fast decrease in 
FF appears up to approximately 5000 cycles with the accumula-
tion of continuous damage. In contrast, as shown in Figure 4C, 
the f-PSCs with MFCl passivation show a slow degradation rate 
of FF. We presumed that the defects on the buried and top 
surface of perovskite could accelerate the environmental deg-
radation of the perovskite films to PbI2, leading to easier crack 
and delamination under mechanical bend in these spots of 
degradation. As shown in Figure  4B,C, there is a decrease in 
VOC and FF after 10 000 cycles, leading to a slight decay of the 
PCE (Figure 4D). However, for the f-PSC without MFCl passiva-
tion, there is a steep decrease in all three parameters, including 
JSC, VOC, and FF, after 10 000 cycles, resulting in a signifi-
cantly reduced PCE. These results clearly indicate the crucial 
role of MFCl passivation in enhancing the bending stability of 
f-PSCs. As shown in Figure S12 (Supporting Information), the 
perovskite film with MFCl treatment after cyclic bend testing 
has not cracked. In addition, the cross-sectional morphology of 
f-PSC device W/ MFCl (Figure S13a,b, Supporting Information) 
does not exhibit obvious change after bending test. However, 
the f-PSC device W/O MFCl shows obvious prolific crack and

To further study the passivation effect of MFCl on the device 
stabilities, we extracted the density of trap states (nt) by con-
ducting space-charge limited current (SCLC) tests with the 
hole-only structure. As shown in Figure 5A, the lines present 
a linear response at a low bias voltage, revealing an ohmic-type 
response. The bias voltage above the kink point is defined as the 
trap-filled limit voltage (VTFL). At a higher bias voltage, the lines 
exhibit a nonlinear current increase, revealing that the trap sites 
are fully occupied. The trap density (Nt) can be calculated from 
the VTFL result using the equation Nt = 2εε0VTFT/eL2, where ε0 
is the vacuum permittivity, ε is the relative dielectric constant 
of perovskite, e is the electron charge and L is the thickness 
of the film. The trap densities of the perovskite layers without 
and with MFCl passivation are 3.57 × 1016 and 2.42 × 1016 cm−3, 
respectively. Because trapped charges play a critical role in the 
irreversible degradation of perovskites, the better operational 
stabilities of devices with MFCl passivation can be attributed 
to the low trap density. In this regard, previous literature has 
reported that local electric fields induced by trapped charges 
can trigger the beginning of irreversible decomposition at the 
beginning. It was demonstrated that irreversible degradation 
of perovskites along surfaces only occurs when both trapped 
charges and moisture simultaneously exist, despite the charge 
polarity.

recombination dynamics of the perovskite films, we meas-

were performed on perovskite films without and with MFCl 
passivation, as deposited on ITO/PET substrates and after cyclic 
bending tests in ambient air. As shown in Figure 5B, the results 
show that the PL of the as-deposited perovskite film with MFCl 
passivation is significantly higher than that of the film without 
MFCl passivation, which may result from the passivation effect 
of MFCl for the surface defects and the greatly decreased photo-

ginal reduction in the PL intensity of the film with MFCl passi-

attributed to the environmental and mechanical degradation of 
the perovskite film during the bending test, which is consistent 
with the results derived from Figures  3 and  4. From these 
results, the effective effect of MFCl passivation on improving 
the optoelectronic properties of perovskite films is demon-
strated. In addition, as shown in Figure 5C, the time-resolved

The improvement in steady-state PL intensities and TRPL life-
times reveals that MFCl passivation of the perovskite surface 
can suppress phase segregation due to a decreased number 
of surface defects. In line with our results, another report also 
demonstrated that carrier trapping and charge accumulation at 
defects on perovskite surfaces are the main drivers of photoin-
duced halide segregation.[50] Therefore, effective passivation of 
dangling bonds at the surface of perovskite film is a feasible 
way to reach phase stabilization of FAPbI3-based perovskites. 
Moreover, the density of halide vacancies can be reduced by 
employing excess halide, which is the major reason for halide 
segregation and migration. Therefore, the additional Cl- ions 
from the MFCl salt can also reduce the density of halide vacan-
cies and suppress phase segregation. To further study the effect 
of MFCl passivation on the density of defects, we measured 
thermal admittance spectroscopy (TAS). Figure S15 (Supporting 
Information) shows the values of the trap density of states 
(tDOS) calculated from the TAS analysis for the PSCs without 
and with MFCl treatment. Compared to the PSCs without 
MFCl treatment, the tDOS of the PSCs with MFCl treatment 
was reduced by almost two orders of magnitude. This result 
demonstrated that MFCl treatment has an effective passivation

3. Conclusion
In this work, we achieved simultaneous improvements in the 
efficiency, long-term stability, and bending reliability of f-PSCs 
by utilizing a double-side passivation strategy. A multifunc-
tional compound named MFCl was developed as a passivation 
material to reduce defects on both the buried and top surfaces 
of perovskite films. Because MFCl consists of both electron-
poor and electron-rich domains, it can effectively passivate the 
dangling bonds on the surface of perovskite and inhibit phase 
segregation without being limited by the compositional and 
electronic nature of perovskite. In addition, we demonstrated 
that these multifunctional materials can improve the passiva-
tion effect on defects in perovskites compared to common 
organic mono-cationic passivation materials. Taking advan-
tage of the passivation effect, the MFCl-passivated device can 
achieve a high efficiency of 24.40% for rigid perovskite solar 
cells and a high efficiency of 22.04% for flexible perovskite solar 
cells. Furthermore, MFCl passivation can significantly improve 
the long-term and bending stabilities of f-PSCs by effectively 
reducing phase segregation and ion migration. Moreover, the 
bending durability and operational stability of the f-PSCs were 
further enhanced by MFCl passivation. This work will pro-
vide guidance for designing an effective passivation strategy to 
simultaneously improve the efficiency and operational stability 
of f-PSCs.
4. Experimental Section
Materials: Formamidinium iodide (FAI), Methylammonium bromide 
(MABr), Methylamine hydrochloride (MACl), and 2,2″,7,7″-Tetrakis 
[N,N-di(4-methoxyphenyl) amino]-9,9′-spirobifluorene (Spiro-OMeTAD) 
were purchased from Advanced Election Technology Co., Ltd. lead 
(II) iodide (PbI2) and lead (II) bromide (PbBr2) were purchased from 
TCI Development Co., Ltd. Formamidinium lead iodide (FAPbI3) was 
synthesized by dissolving FAI and PbI2 in 2-methoxyethanol with stirring. 
The mixed solution was heated to 120 °C by oil bath method. And then 
the powder was precipitated by the retrograde method. After that, black 
FAPbI3 powder was filtered and then dried at 150 °C for 20 min.
Solar Cell Fabrication: ITO/glass and ITO/PEN substrates were etched 
using a laser-etching machine and then washed with cleaning detergent, 
Ultra-pure water, acetone, and ethanol. For the rigid substrate, a 2.5 wt. 
% SnO2 colloidal dispersion diluted by using deionized water was spin-
coated on the substrates at 3000 rpm for 30 s and then heated at 150 °C 
for 30  min. For the flexible substrate, the as-deposited SnO2 film was 
transferred to a 25 mL Teflon-lined stainless-steel autoclave with 10 mL 
of water and then heated to 100 °C for 1 h. All ETLs were then treated 
by UVO for 10 min and transferred to a glovebox. For BSP treatment, 
MFCl solution at different concentrations in DMF was added dropwise 
onto the SnO2 layer, spin-coated at 5000 rpm for 30 s, and then annealed 
at 100 °C for 5 min. FAPbI3 containing 5 mol% MAPbBr3 and 46 mol% 
MACl was dissolved in a mixture of DMSO and DMF (1:8 volume ratio) 
at 60 °C. To prepare the perovskite films, 50 µL of the above perovskite 
precursor was spread on ETL-coated conductive substrates, followed by 
a two-stage spin-coating process (1000 rpm for 5 s and 5000  rpm for 
20 s). During the second spin-coating stage, 1 mL of diethyl ether was 
dripped onto the spinning substrate 10 s prior to the end of the program. 
The films were then annealed at 120 °C for 30 min. For the TSP, the MFCl 
solution with different concentrations in isopropanol was dropped on 
the perovskite and spin-coated at 5000 rpm for 30 s, and the films were 
annealed at 100 °C for 5 min. The hole transport layer was spin-coated 
on the surface of the perovskite film at 3000 rpm for 30 s by using the 
Spiro-OMeTAD solution. The Spiro-OMeTAD solution was prepared by 
dissolving 72.3  mg of Spiro-MeOTAD, 35  µL of bis(trifluoromethane) 
sulfonamide lithium salt (Li-TFSi, 260  mg mL−1 in acetonitrile), and 
29  µL of 4-tert-butylpyridine (tBP) in 1  mL of chlorobenzene. Finally, 
a gold film with an 80-nm thickness was constructed on top of Spiro-
OMeTAD using thermal evaporation.
Characterization: The J–V characteristics of the PSC devices 
were measured by using a Keithley 2400 source meter under light 
illumination. The intensity of light was set at 100 mW cm−2 (AM 1.5 G) 
by a solar simulator (Newport, Oriel Sol3A Class AAA). A calibrated 
silicon cell certified by NREL was used as a reference cell. The step 
voltage was 0.02 V, and the delay time was set as 40 ms. A mask with 
an aperture of 0.09 cm2 was used to calibrate the active area. The film 
morphologies were measured using a scanning electron microscope 
(ZEISS Merlin). The optical properties of the films were measured by 
using UV–VIS spectroscopy (PerkinElmer LAMBDA 950). Steady-state 
photoluminescence (PL) and time-resolved photoluminescence (TRPL) 
spectra were measured using a commercial time-correlated single 
photon counting (TCSPC) setup (Edinburgh FLS 1000). Electrochemical 
impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was conducted using an electrochemical 
workstation (CH660).

Top and Buried Surface Optimization for Flexible \nPerovskite Solar Cells with High Efficiency and Stability\nChang Liu, Kaixin Huang, Bihua Hu, Yaru Li, Luozheng Zhang, Xianyong Zhou, \nYanliang Liu, Zhixin Liu, Yifa Sheng, Shi Chen, Xingzhu Wang,* and Baomin Xu*\nAlthough much progress is made toward enhancing the efficiency of \nperovskite solar cells (PSCs), their operational reliability, particularly their \nmechanical stability, which is a crucial factor for flexible PSCs (f-PCSs), has \nnot attracted sufficient attention. The defects in the perovskite layer, espe-\ncially on the top and the buried surface of the perovskite layer, can induce \nperovskite fracture, highly limiting the performance of f-PSCs. Herein, a novel \nmultifunctional organic salt, metformin hydrochloride, which can passivate \ncationic and anionic defects, is incorporated on both the top and buried \nsurfaces of perovskite layer to suppress defects. Regarding the second problem, some efforts \nhave been made to enhance the flexibility and bending sta-\nbility of f-PSCs by reducing mechanical damage.[25,26] There is \na previous study that used a geometric engineering method to \nmove the neutral axis during the bending process by reducing \nthe thickness of the flexible polymer substrate, which results \nin the reduction of the tensile stress experienced by the perov-\nskite film.[27] As a result, f-PSCs can achieve 17% efficiency and \nwithstand 10 000 bending cycles. Engineering the perovskite \nfilm is another effective approach for enhancing the efficiency, \nstability, and bending-fatigue resistance of f-PSCs.[28–32] Due \nto their ionic nature, perovskites can present different defect \nstates associated with I− anions, undercoordinated Pb2+ cations, \nhalide vacancies, and organic cations (MA+/FA+), which usually \naccumulate on the surface and at the interface of the perovskite \nfilm.[33–35] Such defect states can result in nonradiative recombi-\nnation and charge trapping, which is the main cause of hyster-\nesis and reduces the performance of f-PSCs. With the effect of \nan external stressor, defect states may further cause ion migra-\ntion and charge accumulation, leading to the destruction of the \nmaterial lattice. Eventually, the defect states can lead to perfor-\nmance losses and long-term device instability under real-time \noperation of f-PSCs.[36–39]\nRecently, different defect passivation strategies have been \nreported to improve the stability of f-PSCs and reduce non-\nradiative recombination.[39,40] Diverse metal cations (such as \nCd2+, K+, Na+ and Rb+) were utilized to neutralize interstitial \nions, negative PbI3− anti-sites and uncoordinated I− ions for \npassivating bulk defects. In addition, different anions (such as \nacetate [COO−] and thiocyanate [SCN−]) can be introduced to \nneutralize halide vacancies and interstitial Pb.[41] Additionally, \nseveral additives can be used to control the nucleation process \nof the perovskite film to obtain larger gains and reduced grain \nboundaries, which are associated with trap densities. In addi-\ntion, ionic additives with functional groups were proposed to \nreduce the mobility of ions and defect number in the perov-\nskite layer. Lewis-base additives such as thiophene, urea, caf-\nfeine, and poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) can passivate the \nuncoordinated Lewis-acid Pb2+ cations by donating electrons \n(from sulfur atoms, oxygen, and nitrogen, respectively).[42–46] \nIn addition, Lewis-acid molecules such as zwitterions and \n[6,6]-phenyl-C61-butyric acid methyl ester (PCBM) have been \ndeveloped to passivate I− defects.[47,48] On the other hand, var-\nious passivation strategies have been proposed to reduce the \ninterface and surface defects in f-PSCs. Some additives, such \nas benzylamine, trioctylphosphine oxide (TOPO), and PMMA, \nare used to suppress phase segregation in the perovskite layer, \nleading to the reduction of surface defects.[45,49–51] To alleviate \nsurface defects, building a 2D perovskite layer at the interface \nis also an effective strategy. In summary, adequate passivation \nstrategies have been proposed to restrain the specific defects \nin perovskite films. Nonetheless, most of the early passiva-\ntion research is based on experience. Therefore, it is still nec-\nessary to gain a comprehensive understanding of the involved \ndefects. Because perovskite is positively and negatively charged, \nthe surface and interface of perovskite are strongly susceptible \nto ambient conditions and processing details. In most cases, \nuncoordinated Pb2+ ions tend to be featured on the surface of \nperovskite due to the volatile nature of halide and organic spe-\ncies in perovskite.[52–55] Many relatively large organic molecules, \nsuch as butylammonium iodide (BAI) and phenethylammo-\nnium iodide (PEAI), are known to form a 2D layer for passi-\nvating defects. However, these highly positive molecules have \ndifficulty effectively passivating the positively charged surface \nwith uncoordinated Pb2+.[56–59] As a result, it is still necessary to \nfind a suitable passivator to passivate different kinds of defects \nin perovskite. Moreover, although the defects on both the top \nand bottom surfaces of the perovskite layer are significantly \ndetrimental to PSC performance, most researches have focused \non passivating the defects on only one side surface. Therefore, \nit remains both urgent and challenging to develop an effective \nstrategy to simultaneously decrease the number of defects on \nboth the top and bottom surfaces of the perovskite layer.\nIn this work, we developed a universal passivation strategy \nfor effectively passivating defects on both the top and buried \nsurfaces of perovskite films. For this purpose, multifunctional \npassivating molecules with electron-rich and electron-poor \ndomains are needed. Therefore, metformin hydrochloride \n(MFCl), which consists of negatively charged amine and imine \ngroups and a positively charged ammonium head group, was \nproposed. This molecule can effectively passivate the defects on \nthe buried surface of the perovskite layer when it was pre-depos-\nited between the ETL and the perovskite layer. Furthermore, \nit can further mitigate the defects on the top surface of the \nperovskite layer by introducing the molecules through a post-\ntreatment approach. This double-sided passivation strategy not \nonly provides protection against the intrusion of environmental \nspecies but also retards the propensity for flexural fracture. \nMoreover, the passivation layers can enhance the photocarrier \ntransport efficiency at the perovskite/ETL and perovskite/HTL \ninterfaces. As a result, we achieved a high PCE of 24.40% and \n22.04% for rigid and flexible PSCs, respectively. Additionally, \nf-PSCs can maintain 90% of the initial PCE for 1000\xa0h and 80% \nof the initial PCE after 10 000 bending cycles, showing excellent \noperational stability and mechanical durability, respectively.\n2. Conclusion\nIn this work, we achieved simultaneous improvements in the \nefficiency, long-term stability, and bending reliability of f-PSCs \nby utilizing a double-side passivation strategy. A multifunc-\ntional compound named MFCl was developed as a passivation \nmaterial to reduce defects on both the buried and top surfaces \nof perovskite films. Because MFCl consists of both electron-\npoor and electron-rich domains, it can effectively passivate the \ndangling bonds on the surface of perovskite and inhibit phase \nsegregation without being limited by the compositional and \nelectronic nature of perovskite. In addition, we demonstrated \nthat these multifunctional materials can improve the passiva-\ntion effect on defects in perovskites compared to common \norganic mono-cationic passivation materials. Taking advan-\ntage of the passivation effect, the MFCl-passivated device can \nachieve a high efficiency of 24.40% for rigid perovskite solar \ncells and a high efficiency of 22.04% for flexible perovskite solar \ncells. Furthermore, MFCl passivation can significantly improve \nthe long-term and bending stabilities of f-PSCs by effectively \nreducing phase segregation and ion migration. Moreover, the \nbending durability and operational stability of the f-PSCs were \nfurther enhanced by MFCl passivation. This work will pro-\nvide guidance for designing an effective passivation strategy to \nsimultaneously improve the efficiency and operational stability \nof f-PSCs.\n4. Experimental Section\nMaterials: Formamidinium iodide (FAI), Methylammonium bromide \n(MABr), Methylamine hydrochloride (MACl), and 2,2″,7,7″-Tetrakis \n[N,N-di(4-methoxyphenyl) amino]-9,9′-spirobifluorene (Spiro-OMeTAD) \nwere purchased from Advanced Election Technology Co., Ltd. lead \n(II) iodide (PbI2) and lead (II) bromide (PbBr2) were purchased from \nTCI Development Co., Ltd. Formamidinium lead iodide (FAPbI3) was \nsynthesized by dissolving FAI and PbI2 in 2-methoxyethanol with stirring. \nThe mixed solution was heated to 120 °C by oil bath method. And then \nthe powder was precipitated by the retrograde method. After that, black \nFAPbI3 powder was filtered and then dried at 150 °C for 20\xa0min.\nSolar Cell Fabrication: ITO/glass and ITO/PEN substrates were etched \nusing a laser-etching machine and then washed with cleaning detergent, \nUltra-pure water, acetone, and ethanol. For the rigid substrate, a 2.5\xa0wt. \n% SnO2 colloidal dispersion diluted by using deionized water was spin-\ncoated on the substrates at 3000\xa0rpm for 30 s and then heated at 150 °C \nfor 30\xa0 min. For the flexible substrate, the as-deposited SnO2 film was \ntransferred to a 25\xa0mL Teflon-lined stainless-steel autoclave with 10\xa0mL \nof water and then heated to 100 °C for 1\xa0h. All ETLs were then treated \nby UVO for 10\xa0min and transferred to a glovebox. For BSP treatment, \nMFCl solution at different concentrations in DMF was added dropwise \nonto the SnO2 layer, spin-coated at 5000\xa0rpm for 30 s, and then annealed \nat 100 °C for 5\xa0min. FAPbI3 containing 5 mol% MAPbBr3 and 46 mol% \nMACl was dissolved in a mixture of DMSO and DMF (1:8 volume ratio) \nat 60 °C. To prepare the perovskite films, 50\xa0µL of the above perovskite \nprecursor was spread on ETL-coated conductive substrates, followed by \na two-stage spin-coating process (1000\xa0rpm for 5 s and 5000\xa0 rpm for \n20 s). During the second spin-coating stage, 1\xa0mL of diethyl ether was \ndripped onto the spinning substrate 10 s prior to the end of the program. \nThe films were then annealed at 120 °C for 30\xa0min. For the TSP, the MFCl \nsolution with different concentrations in isopropanol was dropped on \nthe perovskite and spin-coated at 5000\xa0rpm for 30 s, and the films were \nannealed at 100 °C for 5\xa0min. The hole transport layer was spin-coated \non the surface of the perovskite film at 3000\xa0rpm for 30 s by using the \nSpiro-OMeTAD solution. The Spiro-OMeTAD solution was prepared by \ndissolving 72.3\xa0 mg of Spiro-MeOTAD, 35\xa0 µL of bis(trifluoromethane) \nsulfonamide lithium salt (Li-TFSi, 260\xa0 mg mL−1 in acetonitrile), and \n29\xa0 µL of 4-tert-butylpyridine (tBP) in 1\xa0 mL of chlorobenzene. Finally, \na gold film with an 80-nm thickness was constructed on top of Spiro-\nOMeTAD using thermal evaporation.\nCharacterization: The J–V characteristics of the PSC devices \nwere measured by using a Keithley 2400 source meter under light \nillumination. The intensity of light was set at 100\xa0mW cm−2 (AM 1.5 G) \nby a solar simulator (Newport, Oriel Sol3A Class AAA). A calibrated \nsilicon cell certified by NREL was used as a reference cell. The step \nvoltage was 0.02\xa0V, and the delay time was set as 40\xa0ms. A mask with \nan aperture of 0.09 cm2 was used to calibrate the active area. The film \nmorphologies were measured using a scanning electron microscope \n(ZEISS Merlin). The optical properties of the films were measured by \nusing UV–VIS spectroscopy (PerkinElmer LAMBDA 950). Steady-state \nphotoluminescence (PL) and time-resolved photoluminescence (TRPL) \nspectra were measured using a commercial time-correlated single \nphoton counting (TCSPC) setup (Edinburgh FLS 1000). Concurrent Top and Buried Surface Optimization for Flexible 
Perovskite Solar Cells with High Efficiency and Stability
Chang Liu, Kaixin Huang, Bihua Hu, Yaru Li, Luozheng Zhang, Xianyong Zhou, 
Yanliang Liu, Zhixin Liu, Yifa Sheng, Shi Chen, Xingzhu Wang,* and Baomin Xu*
Although much progress is made toward enhancing the efficiency of 
perovskite solar cells (PSCs), their operational reliability, particularly their 
mechanical stability, which is a crucial factor for flexible PSCs (f-PCSs), has 
not attracted sufficient attention. The defects in the perovskite layer, espe-
cially on the top and the buried surface of the perovskite layer, can induce 
perovskite fracture, highly limiting the performance of f-PSCs. Herein, a novel 
multifunctional organic salt, metformin hydrochloride, which can passivate 
cationic and anionic defects, is incorporated on both the top and buried 
surfaces of perovskite layer to suppress defects. As a result, a power conver-
sion efficiency (PCE) of 24.40% for rigid PSCs and a PCE of 22.04% for f-PSCs 
are achieved. Simultaneously, the device can retain 90% and 80% of the 
initial efficiency after 1000 h of light illumination and 10 000 bending cycles, 
respectively, showing excellent operational stability. This study may provide 
a global way to design a passivation strategy and fabricate flexible perovskite 
solar cells with high efficiency and stability.

1. Introduction
The power conversion efficiency of perovskite solar cells (PSCs) 
based on metal-halide perovskite as a light-absorbing layer has 
rapidly increased from 3.8% to 25.7% in recent years, which is 
comparable with that of silicon solar cells.[1,2] The prospect of 
solution-processed, low-cost PSCs with excellent performance 
and their great influence on the global renewable energy market 
is promoting worldwide research efforts to improve PSCs.[3–5] 
Compared with conventional photovoltaics (PVs), PSCs are 
much more versatile. Owing to their thin-film, lightweight

layers (ETLs).[16–23] Recently, the efficiency of f-PSCs reached 
22.44%, while the efficiency gap with rigid PSCs is still too 
large.[24] To reduce the efficiency gap, it is still necessary to 
develop new fabrication processes for flexible substrates and 
flexible devices. Regarding the second problem, some efforts 
have been made to enhance the flexibility and bending sta-
bility of f-PSCs by reducing mechanical damage.[25,26] There is 
a previous study that used a geometric engineering method to 
move the neutral axis during the bending process by reducing 
the thickness of the flexible polymer substrate, which results 
in the reduction of the tensile stress experienced by the perov-
skite film.[27] As a result, f-PSCs can achieve 17% efficiency and 
withstand 10 000 bending cycles. Engineering the perovskite 
film is another effective approach for enhancing the efficiency, 
stability, and bending-fatigue resistance of f-PSCs.[28–32] Due 
to their ionic nature, perovskites can present different defect 
states associated with I− anions, undercoordinated Pb2+ cations, 
halide vacancies, and organic cations (MA+/FA+), which usually 
accumulate on the surface and at the interface of the perovskite 
film.[33–35] Such defect states can result in nonradiative recombi-
nation and charge trapping, which is the main cause of hyster-
esis and reduces the performance of f-PSCs. With the effect of 
an external stressor, defect states may further cause ion migra-
tion and charge accumulation, leading to the destruction of the 
material lattice. Eventually, the defect states can lead to perfor-
mance losses and long-term device instability under real-time 
operation of f-PSCs.[36–39]
Recently, different defect passivation strategies have been 
reported to improve the stability of f-PSCs and reduce non-
radiative recombination.[39,40] Diverse metal cations (such as 
Cd2+, K+, Na+ and Rb+) were utilized to neutralize interstitial 
ions, negative PbI3− anti-sites and uncoordinated I− ions for 
passivating bulk defects. In addition, different anions (such as 
acetate [COO−] and thiocyanate [SCN−]) can be introduced to 
neutralize halide vacancies and interstitial Pb.[41] Additionally, 
several additives can be used to control the nucleation process 
of the perovskite film to obtain larger gains and reduced grain 
boundaries, which are associated with trap densities. In addi-
tion, ionic additives with functional groups were proposed to 
reduce the mobility of ions and defect number in the perov-
skite layer. Lewis-base additives such as thiophene, urea, caf-
feine, and poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) can passivate the 
uncoordinated Lewis-acid Pb2+ cations by donating electrons 
(from sulfur atoms, oxygen, and nitrogen, respectively).[42–46] 
In addition, Lewis-acid molecules such as zwitterions and 
[6,6]-phenyl-C61-butyric acid methyl ester (PCBM) have been 
developed to passivate I− defects.[47,48] On the other hand, var-
ious passivation strategies have been proposed to reduce the 
interface and surface defects in f-PSCs. Some additives, such 
as benzylamine, trioctylphosphine oxide (TOPO), and PMMA, 
are used to suppress phase segregation in the perovskite layer, 
leading to the reduction of surface defects.[45,49–51] To alleviate 
surface defects, building a 2D perovskite layer at the interface 
is also an effective strategy. In summary, adequate passivation 
strategies have been proposed to restrain the specific defects 
in perovskite films. Nonetheless, most of the early passiva-
tion research is based on experience. Therefore, it is still nec-
essary to gain a comprehensive understanding of the involved 
defects. Because perovskite is positively and negatively charged, 
the surface and interface of perovskite are strongly susceptible 
to ambient conditions and processing details. In most cases, 
uncoordinated Pb2+ ions tend to be featured on the surface of 
perovskite due to the volatile nature of halide and organic spe-
cies in perovskite.[52–55] Many relatively large organic molecules, 
such as butylammonium iodide (BAI) and phenethylammo-
nium iodide (PEAI), are known to form a 2D layer for passi-
vating defects. However, these highly positive molecules have 
difficulty effectively passivating the positively charged surface 
with uncoordinated Pb2+.[56–59] As a result, it is still necessary to 
find a suitable passivator to passivate different kinds of defects 
in perovskite. Moreover, although the defects on both the top 
and bottom surfaces of the perovskite layer are significantly 
detrimental to PSC performance, most researches have focused 
on passivating the defects on only one side surface. Therefore, 
it remains both urgent and challenging to develop an effective 
strategy to simultaneously decrease the number of defects on 
both the top and bottom surfaces of the perovskite layer.
In this work, we developed a universal passivation strategy 
for effectively passivating defects on both the top and buried 
surfaces of perovskite films. For this purpose, multifunctional 
passivating molecules with electron-rich and electron-poor 
domains are needed. Therefore, metformin hydrochloride 
(MFCl), which consists of negatively charged amine and imine 
groups and a positively charged ammonium head group, was 
proposed. This molecule can effectively passivate the defects on 
the buried surface of the perovskite layer when it was pre-depos-
ited between the ETL and the perovskite layer. Furthermore, 
it can further mitigate the defects on the top surface of the 
perovskite layer by introducing the molecules through a post-
treatment approach. This double-sided passivation strategy not 
only provides protection against the intrusion of environmental 
species but also retards the propensity for flexural fracture. 
Moreover, the passivation layers can enhance the photocarrier 
transport efficiency at the perovskite/ETL and perovskite/HTL 
interfaces. As a result, we achieved a high PCE of 24.40% and 
22.04% for rigid and flexible PSCs, respectively. Additionally, 
f-PSCs can maintain 90% of the initial PCE for 1000 h and 80% 
of the initial PCE after 10 000 bending cycles, showing excellent 
operational stability and mechanical durability, respectively.
2. Results and Discussion
As illustrated in Figure 1A, three kinds of passivating processes 
were investigated in this work. The SnO2 ETL was prepared by 
our previous work at low temperatures.[60] For the BSP case, 
MFCl was dissolved in dimethylformamide (DMF) and spun 
onto the SnO2 layer. Subsequentially, a perovskite layer was 
deposited on the SnO2 with MFCl. As perovskite, we utilized 
(FAPbI3)0.95(MAPbBr3)0.05 as a light absorption material due 
to its ideal band gap for fabricating high-efficiency f-PSCs. 
As shown in Figure S1 (Supporting Information), the average 
VOC of the f-PSCs improves from 1.06 to 1.15 V after the con-
centration of MFCl was increased to 1 mg mL−1. Considering 
the overall efficiency of the device, the optimal MFCl concen-
tration is 0.50 mg mL−1 for BSP, leading to an average VOC of 
1.13 V. The FF of the f-PSCs declined when the concentration of

centrations of MFCl were dissolved in isopropanol and then 
spin-coated on the surface of the perovskite film to passivate 
the top surface defects. After that, the device was annealed at 
100 °C for 5 min to remove the residual solvent. Although the 
VOC of the f-PSCs improved with increasing MFCl concentra-
tion, the FF of the devices began to decrease again when the 
concentration of MFCl exceeded 0.75 mg mL−1 (Figure S2, Sup-
porting Information). As a result, we found that 0.75 mg mL−1 
MFCl was most suitable for TSP. For the BSP+TSP case, we 
combine these two passivation processes to fabricate the PSC 
device. Figure  1B–E shows the main photovoltaic parameters 
for the performance of PSCs without and with BSP, TSP, and 
BSP+TSP, respectively. All passivation methods increase the 
VOC without causing a decreased FF by using the optimal con-
centrations of MFCl. The average VOC of the control f-PSCs 
improves from 1.06 to 1.12, 1.09, and 1.13  V after BSP, TSP, 
and BSP+TSP treatment, respectively (Figures  1B). As shown 
in the UV–vis absorption spectra (Figure S3, Supporting Infor-
mation), the perovskite films without and with passivation have 
similar band gaps of approximately 1.54  eV. Accordingly, the 
EQE spectra do not show considerable change with passiva-
tion (Figure 2F). On the other hand, the passivating treatments 
resulted in a slightly increased series resistance (Rs) from 6.1 
to 7.4 Ω cm2 (Figure S4A, Supporting Information) due to the 
low conductivity of MFCl. The effect of increased Rs can be 
counterbalanced by an increased average shunt resistance (Rsh) 
from 1.8 to 5.5 kΩ cm2 revealing less charge recombination 
(Figure S4B, Supporting Information). Therefore, the passiva-
tion process did not show an obvious effect on the FF.
As shown in Figure  2A, the J–V curves of the champion 
device without passivation have a PCE of 20.01% with a VOC of 
1.086 V, an FF of 77.43%, and a JSC of 23.77 mA cm−2. Compared 
to the control device, the VOC of the best-performing BSP+TSP 
device exhibits an enhancement of 48  mV, achieving 1.134  V, 
leading to a PCE of 22.04%. The champion f-PSCs can achieve 
JSC values above 24.11 mA cm−2, which is consistent with the 
value of 23.56  mA cm−2 for integrated JSC derived from the 
external quantum efficiency (EQE) spectra (Figure 2B). This is 
one of the highest efficiencies reported for flexible single-junc-
tion PSCs.51 As shown in Figure S5 (Supporting Information), 
the certified efficiency can also achieve 20.35%. Additionally, 
the PSCs were fabricated on rigid ITO/glass substrates to dem-
onstrate the passivation effect. As shown in Figure 2C, we can 
see that the best-performing device has a JSC of 25.36 mA cm−2, 
VOC of 1.158 V, FF of 83.10%, resulting in a PCE of 24.40%. As 
we expected, rigid PSCs exhibit higher performance than their 
flexible counterparts, which can be attributed to the higher 
quality of the ITO conducting layer and better light transmis-
sion in the glass. As shown in Figure S6 (Supporting Informa-
tion), we compare the minimal achievable VOC losses calculated 
from the Shockley-Queisser limit condition for perovskite solar 
cells at 25 °C. As shown, for the best-performing device, the 
introduction of BSP+TSP reduces the VOC loss from 210 to 
150 mV.
To prove the simultaneous anionic and cationic defect passi-
vation abilities of MFCl, we fabricated f-PSCs with Pb-deficient 
(FAI-rich) and I-deficient (PbI2-rich) surfaces. In detail, the 
perovskite films are overannealed to cause the volatilization of 
volatile halide and organic components, leading to I-defective 
surfaces with undercoordinated Pb2+ ions.[53] In addition, the

in Figure S7 (Supporting Information). From Figure S8 (Sup-

f-PSCs with the I-deficient surface increases from 1.08 to 1.13 V 
after the optimal TSP is processed. Therefore, the average PCE 
of the devices increases from 17.3% to 19.7%. Additionally, the 
f-PSCs with Pb-deficient surfaces exhibit a similar trend. The 
results further prove that the MFCl molecule with multifunc-
tional groups can effectively passivate the defects of perovskite 
surfaces with different ionic natures and chemical composi-

migration through surface passivation. In this work, MFCl can

dangling bonds on the surface of the perovskite film, resulting

help to anchor the PbI2.[61] Similarly, MF+ in MFCl can also act

To understand the mechanism of cationic and anionic defect 
passivation, we performed DFT calculations. Figure S10 (Sup-

the MF+ molecule. The molecule has various functional groups 
incorporating electron-rich amine and imine as well as electron-
poor ammonium groups. Because it is challenging to control 
the nature of surface defects of metal halide perovskites, multi-
functional molecules such as MFCl, incorporating electron-rich 
and electron-poor groups, are expected to be successful for full 
passivation of the surface defects. Otherwise, a highly electropo-

electron-poor (electron-rich) perovskite surface domain because 
of the unfavorable electrostatic interaction. The electron-defi-
cient NH3+ in MF+ group mostly interacts with the electronega-

imine N atoms primarily interact with the electron-poor Pb

electron-rich and electron-poor functional groups, are more 
effective for passivation of metal halide perovskite-dangling

as PEA+, butylammonium, allylammonium, and benzylam-

than that (80.47%) of devices passivated with MFCl. In addition,

is higher than the VOC of 1.13 V for the device with PEAI pas-

can be attributed to the multifunctional groups in the MFCl 
molecule, especially electron-rich imine nitrogens, and amines, 
which are not present in the PEACl molecule.
To investigate the impact of MFCl passivation on device sta-
bility, the stabilities of f-PSCs under different conditions were 
measured. As shown in Figure 3A, we record the evolution of 
maximum power point (MPP) tracking under 1-sun illumina-
tion for 200 s. The PCE of the device without MFCl passiva-
tion significantly decreases from 18.43% to 17.52% during the 
MPP tracking test. In contrast, the devices with MFCl pas-
sivation show a more stable power output. The remarkable 
PCE reduction in the devices without MFCl passivation can be 
attributed to the phase segregation of the perovskite induced 
by light illumination. To further investigate this, we tested the 
stability of the f-PSCs without encapsulation under continuous 
light illumination in an N2 atmosphere. Figure 3B shows that 
the device without MFCl passivation exhibits 40% degradation 
of its initial PCE for 600 h. However, the device with MFCl pas-
sivation retains 90% of its initial PCE after operation for 1000 h, 
showing much better light stability. Additionally, as shown in 
Figure 3C, the thermal stability of the f-PSCs was also meas-
ured by heating the devices without encapsulation at 85 °C 
in an N2 atmosphere. In accord with the results of the MPP 
tracking and light illumination measurements, the control 
device without MFCl passivation only retains 80% of its ini-
tial PCE for ∼50 h, while the device with MFCl passivation can 
retain 80% of its initial PCE after more than 200 h, indicating 
better thermal stability.
To further investigate the mechanical durability, a bending 
test of f-PSCs with and without MFCl passivation was per-
formed with a 5  mm radius for 10 000 cycles in ambient air. 
To reduce environmental effects, the 10 000-cycle bend test 
was processed rapidly within an hour. Figures 4A–C shows the 
photovoltaic parameters for a certain number of bending cycles. 
In summary, the f-PSCs with MFCl passivation can maintain 
80% of the initial PCE after 10 000 cycles, exhibiting excellent 
bending stability. As a comparison, the f-PSCs without MFCl 
passivation maintained only 34% of their original PCE. As 
shown in Figure 4D, it is noted that the f-PSCs without MFCl 
passivation rapidly lose FF after just 1000 cycles, which is most 
likely due to delamination cracks. After that, a fast decrease in 
FF appears up to approximately 5000 cycles with the accumula-
tion of continuous damage. In contrast, as shown in Figure 4C, 
the f-PSCs with MFCl passivation show a slow degradation rate 
of FF. We presumed that the defects on the buried and top 
surface of perovskite could accelerate the environmental deg-
radation of the perovskite films to PbI2, leading to easier crack 
and delamination under mechanical bend in these spots of 
degradation. As shown in Figure  4B,C, there is a decrease in

To further study the passivation effect of MFCl on the device 
stabilities, we extracted the density of trap states (nt) by con-
ducting space-charge limited current (SCLC) tests with the 
hole-only structure. As shown in Figure 5A, the lines present 
a linear response at a low bias voltage, revealing an ohmic-type 
response. The bias voltage above the kink point is defined as the 
trap-filled limit voltage (VTFL). At a higher bias voltage, the lines 
exhibit a nonlinear current increase, revealing that the trap sites 
are fully occupied. The trap density (Nt) can be calculated from 
the VTFL result using the equation Nt = 2εε0VTFT/eL2, where ε0 
is the vacuum permittivity, ε is the relative dielectric constant 
of perovskite, e is the electron charge and L is the thickness 
of the film. The trap densities of the perovskite layers without 
and with MFCl passivation are 3.57 × 1016 and 2.42 × 1016 cm−3, 
respectively. Because trapped charges play a critical role in the 
irreversible degradation of perovskites, the better operational 
stabilities of devices with MFCl passivation can be attributed 
to the low trap density. In this regard, previous literature has 
reported that local electric fields induced by trapped charges 
can trigger the beginning of irreversible decomposition at the 
beginning. It was demonstrated that irreversible degradation 
of perovskites along surfaces only occurs when both trapped 
charges and moisture simultaneously exist, despite the charge 
polarity.

times reveals that MFCl passivation of the perovskite surface 
can suppress phase segregation due to a decreased number 
of surface defects. In line with our results, another report also 
demonstrated that carrier trapping and charge accumulation at 
defects on perovskite surfaces are the main drivers of photoin-
duced halide segregation.[50] Therefore, effective passivation of 
dangling bonds at the surface of perovskite film is a feasible 
way to reach phase stabilization of FAPbI3-based perovskites. 
Moreover, the density of halide vacancies can be reduced by 
employing excess halide, which is the major reason for halide 
segregation and migration. Therefore, the additional Cl- ions 
from the MFCl salt can also reduce the density of halide vacan-
cies and suppress phase segregation. To further study the effect 
of MFCl passivation on the density of defects, we measured 
thermal admittance spectroscopy (TAS). Figure S15 (Supporting 
Information) shows the values of the trap density of states

and with MFCl treatment. Compared to the PSCs without 
MFCl treatment, the tDOS of the PSCs with MFCl treatment 
was reduced by almost two orders of magnitude. This result 
demonstrated that MFCl treatment has an effective passivation 
effect on deep trap states in perovskite films. The decreased 
trap states could be attributed to the lower concentration of 
defects on the buried and top surface of perovskite layer after 
MFCl treatment.
