3. Conclusion
In this work, we achieved simultaneous improvements in the 
efficiency, long-term stability, and bending reliability of f-PSCs 
by utilizing a double-side passivation strategy. A multifunc-
tional compound named MFCl was developed as a passivation 
material to reduce defects on both the buried and top surfaces 
of perovskite films. Because MFCl consists of both electron-
poor and electron-rich domains, it can effectively passivate the 
dangling bonds on the surface of perovskite and inhibit phase 
segregation without being limited by the compositional and 
electronic nature of perovskite. In addition, we demonstrated 
that these multifunctional materials can improve the passiva-
tion effect on defects in perovskites compared to common 
organic mono-cationic passivation materials. Taking advan-
tage of the passivation effect, the MFCl-passivated device can 
achieve a high efficiency of 24.40% for rigid perovskite solar 
cells and a high efficiency of 22.04% for flexible perovskite solar 
cells. Furthermore, MFCl passivation can significantly improve 
the long-term and bending stabilities of f-PSCs by effectively 
reducing phase segregation and ion migration. Moreover, the 
bending durability and operational stability of the f-PSCs were 
further enhanced by MFCl passivation. This work will pro-
vide guidance for designing an effective passivation strategy to 
simultaneously improve the efficiency and operational stability 
of f-PSCs.
4. Experimental Section
Materials: Formamidinium iodide (FAI), Methylammonium bromide 
(MABr), Methylamine hydrochloride (MACl), and 2,2″,7,7″-Tetrakis 
[N,N-di(4-methoxyphenyl) amino]-9,9′-spirobifluorene (Spiro-OMeTAD) 
were purchased from Advanced Election Technology Co., Ltd. lead 
(II) iodide (PbI2) and lead (II) bromide (PbBr2) were purchased from 
TCI Development Co., Ltd. Formamidinium lead iodide (FAPbI3) was 
synthesized by dissolving FAI and PbI2 in 2-methoxyethanol with stirring. 
The mixed solution was heated to 120 °C by oil bath method. And then 
the powder was precipitated by the retrograde method. After that, black 
FAPbI3 powder was filtered and then dried at 150 °C for 20 min.
Solar Cell Fabrication: ITO/glass and ITO/PEN substrates were etched 
using a laser-etching machine and then washed with cleaning detergent, 
Ultra-pure water, acetone, and ethanol. For the rigid substrate, a 2.5 wt. 
% SnO2 colloidal dispersion diluted by using deionized water was spin-
coated on the substrates at 3000 rpm for 30 s and then heated at 150 °C 
for 30  min. For the flexible substrate, the as-deposited SnO2 film was 
transferred to a 25 mL Teflon-lined stainless-steel autoclave with 10 mL 
of water and then heated to 100 °C for 1 h. All ETLs were then treated 
by UVO for 10 min and transferred to a glovebox. For BSP treatment, 
MFCl solution at different concentrations in DMF was added dropwise 
onto the SnO2 layer, spin-coated at 5000 rpm for 30 s, and then annealed 
at 100 °C for 5 min. FAPbI3 containing 5 mol% MAPbBr3 and 46 mol% 
MACl was dissolved in a mixture of DMSO and DMF (1:8 volume ratio) 
at 60 °C. To prepare the perovskite films, 50 µL of the above perovskite 
precursor was spread on ETL-coated conductive substrates, followed by 
a two-stage spin-coating process (1000 rpm for 5 s and 5000  rpm for 
20 s). During the second spin-coating stage, 1 mL of diethyl ether was 
dripped onto the spinning substrate 10 s prior to the end of the program. 
The films were then annealed at 120 °C for 30 min. For the TSP, the MFCl 
solution with different concentrations in isopropanol was dropped on 
the perovskite and spin-coated at 5000 rpm for 30 s, and the films were 
annealed at 100 °C for 5 min. The hole transport layer was spin-coated 
on the surface of the perovskite film at 3000 rpm for 30 s by using the 
Spiro-OMeTAD solution. The Spiro-OMeTAD solution was prepared by 
dissolving 72.3  mg of Spiro-MeOTAD, 35  µL of bis(trifluoromethane) 
sulfonamide lithium salt (Li-TFSi, 260  mg mL−1 in acetonitrile), and 
29  µL of 4-tert-butylpyridine (tBP) in 1  mL of chlorobenzene. Finally, 
a gold film with an 80-nm thickness was constructed on top of Spiro-
OMeTAD using thermal evaporation.
Characterization: The J–V characteristics of the PSC devices 
were measured by using a Keithley 2400 source meter under light 
illumination. The intensity of light was set at 100 mW cm−2 (AM 1.5 G) 
by a solar simulator (Newport, Oriel Sol3A Class AAA). A calibrated 
silicon cell certified by NREL was used as a reference cell. The step 
voltage was 0.02 V, and the delay time was set as 40 ms. A mask with 
an aperture of 0.09 cm2 was used to calibrate the active area. The film 
morphologies were measured using a scanning electron microscope 
(ZEISS Merlin). The optical properties of the films were measured by 
using UV–VIS spectroscopy (PerkinElmer LAMBDA 950). Steady-state 
photoluminescence (PL) and time-resolved photoluminescence (TRPL) 
spectra were measured using a commercial time-correlated single 
photon counting (TCSPC) setup (Edinburgh FLS 1000). Electrochemical 
impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was conducted using an electrochemical 
workstation (CH660).

Introduction \nOrganometal-halide perovskite solar cells (PSCs) have attracted \nconsiderable attention because of their remarkable power conver- \nsion eﬃciency (PCE), which can exceed 25.2% [1] . Such an out- \nstanding PCE is a consequence of their long charge-carrier diffu- \nsion length [ 2 , 3 ], low exciton binding energy [ 4 , 5 ], and good ab- \nsorption over the visible spectrum [6] . Despite these exceptional \nproperties and strengths, the commercialization of PSCs faces se- \nrious problems with respect to low-temperature solution process- \ning. In particular, PSCs with a planar device architecture typi- \ncally use TiO 2 as an electron-selective layer (ESL), which requires \nhigh-temperature annealing ( > 450 °C) for a long duration (1 −2 h) \n[7] . Furthermore, TiO 2 exhibits low electron mobility (0.1 −1 cm 2 \nV −1 S −1 ) and low conductivity (~1.1 × 10 −5 S cm −1 ), necessitat- \ning an additional mesoporous layer to compensate for the low \n∗Corresponding author. \nE-mail address: leemtx@konkuk.ac.kr (M.-J. Lee). \n1 These authors have contributed equally. \nmobility and conductivity by enhancing the surface area [8-10] . \nThe more serious issue with TiO 2 ESLs is that they exhibit pho- \ntocatalytic properties under UV illumination, which causes decom- \nposition of the perovskite materials and adversely affects device \nstability [11] . \nTo overcome the aforementioned shortcomings of TiO 2 , re- \nsearchers have extensively studied SnO 2 -based ESLs because of the \nhigh electron mobility, high electrical conductivity, wide bandgap \nrange (3.6–4.1 eV), and good photostability of SnO 2 [ 12 , 13 , 14 ]. Ke \net al. reported that the performance of SnO 2 -based PSCs depends \non the annealing temperature between 185 °C and 500 °C and con- \ncluded that low-temperature annealing leads to better surface cov- \nerage, a wider optical band gap, and greater electron mobility [15] . \nPark et al. also reported that Li-doped SnO 2 annealed at a low tem- \nperature (185 °C) exhibits much-improved performance [16] . De- \nspite the excellent characteristics and performance of SnO 2 pro- \ncessed at low temperatures, this approach is still problematic with \nrespect to commercialization because the extended annealing time \nof SnO 2 requires a long batch oven within the roll-to-roll setup \n[17] . Meanwhile, in the printed electronics industry, a damage-free \nhttps://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmst.2021.03.045 \n1005-0302/© 2021 Published by Elsevier Ltd on behalf of Chinese Society for Metals. \n\n\nK. Oh, K. Jung, J. Shin et al. \nJournal of Materials Science & Technology 92 (2021) 171–177 \nprocess known as intense pulsed light (IPL) has been used as a \nminimal-heat-exposure method to rapidly sinter nanoparticle thin \nﬁlms [18-20] . Because the IPL process involves irradiating the sur- \nface of an oxide thin ﬁlm with high-intensity pulsed light for a \nshort time, the total processing time is reduced to a few tens of \nseconds and substrate damage is minimized [21-23] . \nHere, the IPL irradiation of amorphous-SnO 2 ESLs is used \nto synthesize highly eﬃcient methylammonium lead iodide \n(MAPbI 3 )-based planar PSCs with improved performance. During \neach 2 ms pulse, 1.84 J cm −2 of energy is irradiated onto the sur- \nface of an amorphous-SnO 2 ﬁlm; the number of pulses is varied \nto optimize the ESL properties. The PSC with the highest PCE was \nobtained with an amorphous-SnO 2 ﬁlm subjected to 120 pulses \n(~220 J cm −2 ) of IPL within a few tens of seconds; a maximum PCE \nof 17.68% with an average and standard deviation of 15.58% ±0.85% \nwas achieved. Compared with PSCs based on nontreated SnO 2 \n(maximum PCE of 7.06% with 2.65% ±1.76%), the IPL treatment sub- \nstantially enhanced the photovoltaic properties. Notably, the IPL- \ntreated SnO 2 -based PSCs showed a PCE similar to that of devices \n(maximum PCE of 18.16%) with an SnO 2 ESL prepared by a gen- \neral heat-treatment process at 185 °C for 3 h. We found that the \nIPL treatment of the amorphous-SnO 2 substantially improved the \nshort-circuit current density ( J sc ) and open-circuit voltage ( V oc ) by \ndecreasing the number of hydroxyl ( −OH) species, which func- \ntion as defect/trap states. In addition, the irradiated SnO 2 ESLs ex- \nhibited enhanced conductivities and mobilities compared with the \nnontreated amorphous-SnO 2 . The results presented here show that \nthe IPL treatment can effectively control the ESL/perovskite inter- \nface over a short duration by regulating the inherent MAPbI 3 prop- \nerties such as stress and nucleation density, which makes this pro- \ncess very promising for the commercial high-throughput manufac- \nture of PSCs. \n2. Experimental \n2.1. Preparation of SnO 2 ESLs \nPSCs were fabricated on ﬂuorine-doped tin oxide (FTO)-coated \nglass substrates (Pilkington, Tec-8), which were patterned us- \ning Zn powder and a dilute HCl solution, followed by cleaning \nwith diluted Hellmanex, acetone, ethanol, and deionized water. \nAmorphous-SnO 2 was prepared as an ESL on the FTO glass by \nspin coating 0.1 M tin(II) chloride dihydrate solution in ethanol \n(Sigma-Aldrich) at 30 0 0 rpm for 30 s. After drying at 100 °C for \n1 min, the sample was instantly transferred to an IPL apparatus \n(HI-PULSE 15,0 0 0, PSTEK) for treatment using different ﬂash counts \ndelivering different amounts of energy. Fig. S1 shows a schematic \nof the IPL setup and the processing parameters corresponding to \nthe various IPL irradiation conditions. Table S1 shows the trans- \nferred energy values for each pulse time (1 and 2 ms), as mea- \nsured by a photosensor (Nova II, Ophir). From ten or more mea- \nsurements of each transferred energy value, 1.84 J cm −2 of en- \nergy per IPL pulse was conﬁrmed to be transferred to the SnO 2 \nsurface under the conditions used to conduct the experiment \n(60 0 V, 20 0 0 mA, 2 ms, 4 Hz). The SnO 2 ﬁlms were thereafter \nsubjected to an ultraviolet–ozone (UVO) treatment for as long as \n35 min. \n2.2. Synthesis of planar MAPbI 3 solar cells \nThe perovskite precursor solution (50 wt.%) was prepared by \ndissolving lead(II) iodide (PbI 2 ; TCI) and methylammonium iodide \n(MAI; GreatCell Solar) in 0.635 mL of dimethylformamide (DMF; \nSigma-Aldrich), to which 70 μL of dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO; \nSigma-Aldrich) was added to form the corresponding adducts \n[24] . The completely dissolved solution was spin-coated onto an \namorphous-SnO 2 ESL layer at 40 0 0 rpm for 25 s, and 0.5 mL of \ndiethyl ether (Sigma-Aldrich) was slowly dripped onto the sub- \nstrate before the surface became turbid as a result of the rapid \nvaporization of DMF. The sample was subsequently annealed at \n65 °C for 1 min and then at 100 °C for 2 min. A hole-selective \nlayer was then coated onto the perovskite layer by spin coating \n20 μL of a 2,2 ′ ,7,7 ′ -tetrakis[ N,N - di (4-methoxyphenyl)amino] −9,9 ′ - \nspirobiﬂuorene (spiroMeOTAD) solution (composed of 80 mg \nspiroMeOTAD (1-Material), 28.5 μL of 4–tert -butylpyridine, and 17.5 \nμL of lithium bis(triﬂuoromethanesulfonyl)imide (Li-TFSI, Sigma- \nAldrich) solution (520 mg Li-TSFI in 1 mL acetonitrile)), and 1 mL \nof chlorobenzene (Sigma-Aldrich) at 40 0 0 rpm for 30 s. The Au \nelectrode was evaporated under 10 −6 Torr using a thermal evapo- \nration system. \n2.3. Characterization \nThe crystal structures of the SnO 2 and perovskite ﬁlms were \ndetermined by X-ray diffraction (XRD, Rigaku SmartLab) analysis \nusing Cu K α radiation. The morphology of the synthesized ﬁlms \nwas examined by ﬁeld-emission scanning electron microscopy (FE- \nSEM) on an electron microscope (SU8010, Hitachi) with a resolu- \ntion of 5 kV and 15 kV. The contact angle of SnO 2 ﬁlms were mea- \nsured using a contact-angle measurement system (Phoenix 300 \nTouch, SEO, Korea). The photovoltaic (PV) properties of the as- \nsembled PSCs were determined under AM 1.5 simulated sunlight \nwith a power density of 100 mW cm −2 using a solar simula- \ntor (Polaronix K201, McScience, Korea) equipped with a 150 W \nxenon lamp and a Keithley 2401 source meter. The scan speed \nwas set to a constant of 0.1 V/s in this study. After the inten- \nsity was calibrated using a KIER-calibrated KG5-ﬁltered Si reference \ncell, all measurements were performed by masking the cells with \na metal aperture to deﬁne an active area of 0.09 cm 2 . An inci- \ndent photon-to-current conversion eﬃciency (IPCE) measurement \nsystem (HS Tech, Korea) was used to evaluate the external quan- \ntum eﬃciency (EQE). The UV–Vis absorption spectra of the SnO 2 \nﬁlms were recorded using a UV–Vis spectrometer (Optizen PoP). \nX-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, KBSI) and ultraviolet pho- \ntoelectron spectroscopy (UPS, KBSI) were carried out using an AXIS \nultra-delay line detector (Kratos, UK) equipped with a monochro- \nmatic Al K α (1486.6 eV) X-ray source or He-I gas (21.22 eV) UV \nsource. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS, Biologic SP- \n240) measurements were conducted in the dark. The surface con- \nductivity of the SnO 2 ﬁlms was measured by conductive atomic \nforce microscopy (C-AFM; Nanoscope V Multimode 8 atomic force \nmicroscope, KBSI). \n3. Results and discussion \nAmorphous SnO 2 ﬁlms were synthesized through a simple so- \nlution process using tin(II) chloride dihydrate in ethanol. Hereafter, \nthe amorphous-SnO 2 ﬁlms that were treated and not treated with \nIPL are denoted as I-SnO 2 and A-SnO 2 , respectively. Fig. 1 (a) shows \nthe XRD patterns of A-SnO 2 and I-SnO 2 , respectively, showing that \nno crystalline peaks were observed. XPS was used to characterize \nthe chemical bonding states of both amorphous ﬁlms (A-SnO 2 and \nI-SnO 2 ); the resultant spectra are shown in Fig. 1 (b) −(d). Fig. 1 (b) \nshows the XPS spectra of the Sn 3 d states in A-SnO 2 and I-SnO 2 . \nAccording to previous reports [ 25 , 26 ], the Sn 3 d XPS spectrum of \nSnO 2 ﬁlm shows peaks of Sn 3 d 5/2 and 3 d 3/2 at binding energy \n(BE) values of approximately 487 and 495 eV, respectively. The XPS \nspectrum of the A-SnO 2 ﬁlm, however, shows slight changes in the \nBE values of Sn 3 d 5/2 and 3 d 3/2 to 487.9 and 496.3 eV, respec- \ntively. By contrast, the Sn 3 d 5/2 and 3 d 3/2 BE values in the spec- \ntrum of the I-SnO 2 ﬁlms were 487.2 and 495 eV, respectively, sim- \nilar to the previously reported values. Such shifts in the BE \nvalues are attributed to changes in the electron interaction of Sn \nions in the I-SnO 2 ﬁlms [27] . According to previous reports [27- \n29] , the difference in the BE values between Sn 4 + and Sn 2 + ions \nis 0.7 eV. Thus, the BE shift of the Sn peaks in the spectrum of \nthe I-SnO 2 to lower BEs after the IPL treatment clearly suggests \nan increase in the amount of Sn 2 + ions [27] , which warrants fur- \nther study. Fig. 1 (c) and (d) shows the spectra of the O 1 s re- \ngion. After peak deconvolution, the main peak at 530.9 eV was at- \ntributed to O 1 s in SnO 2 and the peak at 531.8 eV was assigned \nto hydroxyl (–OH) groups. The intensity of the –OH peak in the \nspectrum of I-SnO 2 clearly decreased compared with that in the \nspectrum of A-SnO 2 , which means that the I-SnO 2 ﬁlms contain \nfewer –OH groups than the A-SnO 2 ﬁlms. According to previous \nreports [30] , the –OH groups in SnO 2 are associated with surface \noxygen vacancies, which can act as surface trap sites in metal oxide \nESLs. Therefore, we speculated that the IPL treatment of the amor- \nphous SnO 2 ﬁlms substantially reduced the number of surface –OH \ngroups acting as defect/trap states. \nTo further study the inﬂuence of the IPL treatment on the \namorphous-SnO 2 ESLs and on the resultant evolution of the \nMAPbI 3 ﬁlms deposited onto the treated ESLs, we conducted SEM \nobservations, contact-angle measurements, and grazing-incident \nXRD (GIXRD) analysis. Fig. S2 shows the contact angles of A-SnO 2 \nand I-SnO 2 surfaces, indicating that the I-SnO 2 surface has a lower \ncontact angle. Because a surface with a small contact angle has a \nhigh surface energy, the particle size of the network ﬁlm growing \non the surface tends to be uniform [ 31 , 32 ]. The nucleation den- \nsity during heterogeneous nucleation is known to be related to the \nGibbs free energy through the following equation: \x03G heterogeneous = \n\x03G homogeneou s × f (θ) , where f (θ) = ( 2 −3 cos θ + cos 3 θ) / 4 and θ\nis the contact angle of the precursor solution [33-35] . Thus, a small \ncontact angle can improve the nucleation process by reducing the \nGibbs free energy during heterogeneous nucleation ( G heterogeneous ). \nIn addition, a small contact angle provides a high surface energy, \nwhich can increase the grain size of the upper MAPbI 3 [36] . As \nshown in Fig. 2 (a, b) and Fig. S3, the MAPbI 3 ﬁlms grown on the \nI-SnO 2 ESL exhibited a more uniform microstructure with a grain \nsize (267 nm) larger than that of MAPbI 3 grown on the A-SnO 2 \nsamples (65 nm). \nWe conducted GIXRD analysis to investigate the internal stress \ndeveloped in the MAPbI 3 crystals during the densiﬁcation assisted \nby the increased surface energy. In GIXRD measurements, we var- \nied the incident angles from 1 to 3 ° to monitor the depth proﬁles \nof stress in the MAPbI 3 ﬁlms, as shown in Fig. 2 (c) −(f). The GIXRD \npatterns of A-SnO 2 and I-SnO 2 with different incident angles are \nshown in Fig. S4. The stress and crystallite size distribution in the \nﬁlms were characterized using the Halder–Wagner method, which \nis based on the equation ( β∗/δ) 2 = ( 1 /L )( β∗/ δ2 ) + ( ε S / 2 ) 2 , where \nβ∗= β cos θ/λ, δ = 2 sin θ/λ, β is the full-width at half-maximum \n(FWHM) of the XRD peak, θ is the Bragg angle, λ is 1.5406 ˚A, L is \nthe correlation length (corresponding to the crystalline ﬁlm), and \nεs is the stress parameter [ 37 , 38 ]. To obtain accurate values, we de- \ntermined the FWHM by ﬁtting the diffraction peaks with pseudo- \nVoigt functions. The plots of ( β∗/ δ2 ) corresponding to the peaks \nof MAPbI 3 ﬁlms on the A-SnO 2 and I-SnO 2 substrates are shown in \nFig. 2 (d) −(f). The detailed ﬁtting data are shown in Table 1 . With \nincreasing depth, the I-SnO 2 ﬁlms exhibit substantially smaller εs \nvalues (0.2115 (1 °), 0.1975 (2 °), and 0.2640 (3 °)) than the A-SnO 2 \nﬁlms (0.2435 (1 °), 0.2245 (2 °), and 0.3323 (3 °)). In addition, the I- \nSnO 2 ﬁlms exhibit a larger crystallite size than the A-SnO 2 ﬁlms, \nas indicated by the larger L value for the I-SnO 2 ﬁlms than for the \nA-SnO 2 ﬁlms. Therefore, we conclude that the IPL treatment of the \namorphous SnO 2 ESLs not only promotes nucleation of the over- \nlying perovskite ﬁlm but also reduces the stress in the obtained \nperovskite ﬁlms. \n173 \n\n\nK. Conclusions \nWe report in detail the inﬂuence of the IPL treatment on a \nsolution-processed amorphous SnO 2 ESL and on the photovoltaic \nperformance of an MAPbI 3 PSC based on the IPL-treated SnO 2 . \nThrough systematic investigations, we veriﬁed that the IPL treat- \nment not only reduces the number of –OH groups acting as de- \nfect/traps in SnO 2 ﬁlms but also facilitates the formation of dense \nand uniform MAPbI 3 ﬁlms by controlling the nucleation of the \nperovskite layer. In addition, the IPL treatment reduces the stress \nin the upper perovskite ﬁlm. Because of these effects, the PSCs \nbased on the IPL-treated SnO 2 achieved a PCE of 17.68%, whereas \nthose based on its nontreated counterpart exhibited a PCE of \n7.06%. The achieved PCE is comparable to the PCE (18.16%) of the \nperovskite solar cell based on high-temperature-processed SnO 2 . \nSuch a high eﬃciency is achieved through improved charge trans- \nport/extraction and recombination, which greatly increases the J sc \nand V oc . Because of the ultrafast processing time (a few tens of sec- \nonds) and the damage-free obtained ﬁlms, the IPL technique has a \nbright future. \nDeclaration of Competing Interest \nThe authors declare that they have no known competing ﬁnan- \ncial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to \ninﬂuence the work reported in this paper. \nAcknowledgments \nThis research was supported by Basic Science Research Program \nthrough the National Research Foundation of Korea (NRF) funded \nby the Ministry of Science and ICT (2020R1F1A10 686 64). a b s t r a c t 
Although perovskite solar cells (PSCs) have achieved a high power conversion eﬃciency (PCE) within a 
short period of development, the high-temperature sintering of the constituent electron-selective layers 
(ESLs) impedes the commercialization. In this report, we demonstrate the effectiveness of an intense- 
pulsed-light (IPL) treatment for the rapid and damage-free sintering of amorphous-SnO 2 ESLs for use 
in PSCs. The IPL treatment of amorphous-SnO 2 substantially reduced the amount of surface hydroxyl 
groups, modiﬁed the surface energy, and enabled the growth of a low-stress perovskite layer with large 
grain sizes, all of which enhanced the photovoltaic properties and led to the proper alignment of band 
structures for eﬃcient PSCs. Through comprehensive optimization of the IPL conditions, a PCE of 17.68% 
was achieved from the MAPbI 3 planar PSC based on an amorphous-SnO 2 IPL treated for a few tens of 
seconds, which was signiﬁcantly increased compared with a PCE (7.06%) of nontreated SnO 2 based coun- 
terpart. In addition, the PCE of the IPL-treated SnO 2 based PSC is comparable to the best PCE (18.16%) of 
PSCs fabricated with SnO 2 ESL annealed for three hours at 185 °C. Because of its ultrafast sintering time 
and tendency to not damage SnO 2 ESLs, the new IPL process is expected to open new opportunities for 
the commercialization of PSCs.

1. Introduction 
Organometal-halide perovskite solar cells (PSCs) have attracted 
considerable attention because of their remarkable power conver- 
sion eﬃciency (PCE), which can exceed 25.2% [1] . Such an out- 
standing PCE is a consequence of their long charge-carrier diffu- 
sion length [ 2 , 3 ], low exciton binding energy [ 4 , 5 ], and good ab- 
sorption over the visible spectrum [6] . Despite these exceptional 
properties and strengths, the commercialization of PSCs faces se- 
rious problems with respect to low-temperature solution process- 
ing. In particular, PSCs with a planar device architecture typi- 
cally use TiO 2 as an electron-selective layer (ESL), which requires 
high-temperature annealing ( > 450 °C) for a long duration (1 −2 h) 
[7] . Furthermore, TiO 2 exhibits low electron mobility (0.1 −1 cm 2 
V −1 S −1 ) and low conductivity (~1.1 × 10 −5 S cm −1 ), necessitat- 
ing an additional mesoporous layer to compensate for the low

The more serious issue with TiO 2 ESLs is that they exhibit pho- 
tocatalytic properties under UV illumination, which causes decom- 
position of the perovskite materials and adversely affects device 
stability [11] . 
To overcome the aforementioned shortcomings of TiO 2 , re- 
searchers have extensively studied SnO 2 -based ESLs because of the 
high electron mobility, high electrical conductivity, wide bandgap 
range (3.6–4.1 eV), and good photostability of SnO 2 [ 12 , 13 , 14 ]. Ke 
et al. reported that the performance of SnO 2 -based PSCs depends 
on the annealing temperature between 185 °C and 500 °C and con- 
cluded that low-temperature annealing leads to better surface cov- 
erage, a wider optical band gap, and greater electron mobility [15] . 
Park et al. also reported that Li-doped SnO 2 annealed at a low tem- 
perature (185 °C) exhibits much-improved performance [16] . De- 
spite the excellent characteristics and performance of SnO 2 pro- 
cessed at low temperatures, this approach is still problematic with 
respect to commercialization because the extended annealing time 
of SnO 2 requires a long batch oven within the roll-to-roll setup 
[17] . Meanwhile, in the printed electronics industry, a damage-free

process known as intense pulsed light (IPL) has been used as a 
minimal-heat-exposure method to rapidly sinter nanoparticle thin 
ﬁlms [18-20] . Because the IPL process involves irradiating the sur- 
face of an oxide thin ﬁlm with high-intensity pulsed light for a 
short time, the total processing time is reduced to a few tens of 
seconds and substrate damage is minimized [21-23] . 
Here, the IPL irradiation of amorphous-SnO 2 ESLs is used 
to synthesize highly eﬃcient methylammonium lead iodide 
(MAPbI 3 )-based planar PSCs with improved performance. During 
each 2 ms pulse, 1.84 J cm −2 of energy is irradiated onto the sur- 
face of an amorphous-SnO 2 ﬁlm; the number of pulses is varied 
to optimize the ESL properties. The PSC with the highest PCE was 
obtained with an amorphous-SnO 2 ﬁlm subjected to 120 pulses 
(~220 J cm −2 ) of IPL within a few tens of seconds; a maximum PCE 
of 17.68% with an average and standard deviation of 15.58% ±0.85% 
was achieved. Compared with PSCs based on nontreated SnO 2 
(maximum PCE of 7.06% with 2.65% ±1.76%), the IPL treatment sub- 
stantially enhanced the photovoltaic properties. Notably, the IPL- 
treated SnO 2 -based PSCs showed a PCE similar to that of devices 
(maximum PCE of 18.16%) with an SnO 2 ESL prepared by a gen- 
eral heat-treatment process at 185 °C for 3 h. We found that the 
IPL treatment of the amorphous-SnO 2 substantially improved the 
short-circuit current density ( J sc ) and open-circuit voltage ( V oc ) by 
decreasing the number of hydroxyl ( −OH) species, which func- 
tion as defect/trap states. In addition, the irradiated SnO 2 ESLs ex- 
hibited enhanced conductivities and mobilities compared with the 
nontreated amorphous-SnO 2 . The results presented here show that 
the IPL treatment can effectively control the ESL/perovskite inter- 
face over a short duration by regulating the inherent MAPbI 3 prop- 
erties such as stress and nucleation density, which makes this pro- 
cess very promising for the commercial high-throughput manufac- 
ture of PSCs. 
2. Experimental 
2.1. Preparation of SnO 2 ESLs 
PSCs were fabricated on ﬂuorine-doped tin oxide (FTO)-coated 
glass substrates (Pilkington, Tec-8), which were patterned us- 
ing Zn powder and a dilute HCl solution, followed by cleaning 
with diluted Hellmanex, acetone, ethanol, and deionized water. 
Amorphous-SnO 2 was prepared as an ESL on the FTO glass by 
spin coating 0.1 M tin(II) chloride dihydrate solution in ethanol 
(Sigma-Aldrich) at 30 0 0 rpm for 30 s. After drying at 100 °C for 
1 min, the sample was instantly transferred to an IPL apparatus 
(HI-PULSE 15,0 0 0, PSTEK) for treatment using different ﬂash counts 
delivering different amounts of energy. Fig. S1 shows a schematic 
of the IPL setup and the processing parameters corresponding to 
the various IPL irradiation conditions. Table S1 shows the trans- 
ferred energy values for each pulse time (1 and 2 ms), as mea- 
sured by a photosensor (Nova II, Ophir). From ten or more mea- 
surements of each transferred energy value, 1.84 J cm −2 of en- 
ergy per IPL pulse was conﬁrmed to be transferred to the SnO 2 
surface under the conditions used to conduct the experiment 
(60 0 V, 20 0 0 mA, 2 ms, 4 Hz). The SnO 2 ﬁlms were thereafter 
subjected to an ultraviolet–ozone (UVO) treatment for as long as 
35 min. 
2.2. Synthesis of planar MAPbI 3 solar cells 
The perovskite precursor solution (50 wt.%) was prepared by 
dissolving lead(II) iodide (PbI 2 ; TCI) and methylammonium iodide 
(MAI; GreatCell Solar) in 0.635 mL of dimethylformamide (DMF; 
Sigma-Aldrich), to which 70 μL of dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO; 
Sigma-Aldrich) was added to form the corresponding adducts 
[24] . The completely dissolved solution was spin-coated onto an 
amorphous-SnO 2 ESL layer at 40 0 0 rpm for 25 s, and 0.5 mL of 
diethyl ether (Sigma-Aldrich) was slowly dripped onto the sub- 
strate before the surface became turbid as a result of the rapid 
vaporization of DMF. The sample was subsequently annealed at 
65 °C for 1 min and then at 100 °C for 2 min. A hole-selective 
layer was then coated onto the perovskite layer by spin coating 
20 μL of a 2,2 ′ ,7,7 ′ -tetrakis[ N,N - di (4-methoxyphenyl)amino] −9,9 ′ - 
spirobiﬂuorene (spiroMeOTAD) solution (composed of 80 mg 
spiroMeOTAD (1-Material), 28.5 μL of 4–tert -butylpyridine, and 17.5 
μL of lithium bis(triﬂuoromethanesulfonyl)imide (Li-TFSI, Sigma- 
Aldrich) solution (520 mg Li-TSFI in 1 mL acetonitrile)), and 1 mL 
of chlorobenzene (Sigma-Aldrich) at 40 0 0 rpm for 30 s. The Au 
electrode was evaporated under 10 −6 Torr using a thermal evapo- 
ration system. 
2.3. Characterization 
The crystal structures of the SnO 2 and perovskite ﬁlms were 
determined by X-ray diffraction (XRD, Rigaku SmartLab) analysis 
using Cu K α radiation. The morphology of the synthesized ﬁlms 
was examined by ﬁeld-emission scanning electron microscopy (FE- 
SEM) on an electron microscope (SU8010, Hitachi) with a resolu- 
tion of 5 kV and 15 kV. The contact angle of SnO 2 ﬁlms were mea- 
sured using a contact-angle measurement system (Phoenix 300 
Touch, SEO, Korea). The photovoltaic (PV) properties of the as- 
sembled PSCs were determined under AM 1.5 simulated sunlight 
with a power density of 100 mW cm −2 using a solar simula- 
tor (Polaronix K201, McScience, Korea) equipped with a 150 W 
xenon lamp and a Keithley 2401 source meter. The scan speed 
was set to a constant of 0.1 V/s in this study. After the inten- 
sity was calibrated using a KIER-calibrated KG5-ﬁltered Si reference 
cell, all measurements were performed by masking the cells with 
a metal aperture to deﬁne an active area of 0.09 cm 2 . An inci- 
dent photon-to-current conversion eﬃciency (IPCE) measurement 
system (HS Tech, Korea) was used to evaluate the external quan- 
tum eﬃciency (EQE). The UV–Vis absorption spectra of the SnO 2 
ﬁlms were recorded using a UV–Vis spectrometer (Optizen PoP). 
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, KBSI) and ultraviolet pho- 
toelectron spectroscopy (UPS, KBSI) were carried out using an AXIS 
ultra-delay line detector (Kratos, UK) equipped with a monochro- 
matic Al K α (1486.6 eV) X-ray source or He-I gas (21.22 eV) UV 
source. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS, Biologic SP- 
240) measurements were conducted in the dark. The surface con- 
ductivity of the SnO 2 ﬁlms was measured by conductive atomic 
force microscopy (C-AFM; Nanoscope V Multimode 8 atomic force 
microscope, KBSI). 
3. Results and discussion 
Amorphous SnO 2 ﬁlms were synthesized through a simple so- 
lution process using tin(II) chloride dihydrate in ethanol. Hereafter, 
the amorphous-SnO 2 ﬁlms that were treated and not treated with 
IPL are denoted as I-SnO 2 and A-SnO 2 , respectively. Fig. 1 (a) shows 
the XRD patterns of A-SnO 2 and I-SnO 2 , respectively, showing that 
no crystalline peaks were observed. XPS was used to characterize 
the chemical bonding states of both amorphous ﬁlms (A-SnO 2 and 
I-SnO 2 ); the resultant spectra are shown in Fig. 1 (b) −(d). Fig. 1 (b) 
shows the XPS spectra of the Sn 3 d states in A-SnO 2 and I-SnO 2 . 
According to previous reports [ 25 , 26 ], the Sn 3 d XPS spectrum of 
SnO 2 ﬁlm shows peaks of Sn 3 d 5/2 and 3 d 3/2 at binding energy 
(BE) values of approximately 487 and 495 eV, respectively. The XPS 
spectrum of the A-SnO 2 ﬁlm, however, shows slight changes in the 
BE values of Sn 3 d 5/2 and 3 d 3/2 to 487.9 and 496.3 eV, respec- 
tively. By contrast, the Sn 3 d 5/2 and 3 d 3/2 BE values in the spec- 
trum of the I-SnO 2 ﬁlms were 487.2 and 495 eV, respectively, sim- 
ilar to the previously reported values. After the IPL irradiation, the

spectrum of I-SnO 2 clearly decreased compared with that in the 
spectrum of A-SnO 2 , which means that the I-SnO 2 ﬁlms contain 
fewer –OH groups than the A-SnO 2 ﬁlms. According to previous 
reports [30] , the –OH groups in SnO 2 are associated with surface 
oxygen vacancies, which can act as surface trap sites in metal oxide 
ESLs. Therefore, we speculated that the IPL treatment of the amor- 
phous SnO 2 ﬁlms substantially reduced the number of surface –OH 
groups acting as defect/trap states. 
To further study the inﬂuence of the IPL treatment on the 
amorphous-SnO 2 ESLs and on the resultant evolution of the 
MAPbI 3 ﬁlms deposited onto the treated ESLs, we conducted SEM 
observations, contact-angle measurements, and grazing-incident 
XRD (GIXRD) analysis. Fig. S2 shows the contact angles of A-SnO 2 
and I-SnO 2 surfaces, indicating that the I-SnO 2 surface has a lower 
contact angle. Because a surface with a small contact angle has a 
high surface energy, the particle size of the network ﬁlm growing 
on the surface tends to be uniform [ 31 , 32 ]. The nucleation den- 
sity during heterogeneous nucleation is known to be related to the 
Gibbs free energy through the following equation: G heterogeneous = 
G homogeneou s × f (θ) , where f (θ) = ( 2 −3 cos θ + cos 3 θ) / 4 and θ
is the contact angle of the precursor solution [33-35] . Thus, a small 
contact angle can improve the nucleation process by reducing the 
Gibbs free energy during heterogeneous nucleation ( G heterogeneous ). 
In addition, a small contact angle provides a high surface energy, 
which can increase the grain size of the upper MAPbI 3 [36] . As 
shown in Fig. 2 (a, b) and Fig. S3, the MAPbI 3 ﬁlms grown on the 
I-SnO 2 ESL exhibited a more uniform microstructure with a grain 
size (267 nm) larger than that of MAPbI 3 grown on the A-SnO 2 
samples (65 nm). 
We conducted GIXRD analysis to investigate the internal stress 
developed in the MAPbI 3 crystals during the densiﬁcation assisted 
by the increased surface energy. In GIXRD measurements, we var- 
ied the incident angles from 1 to 3 ° to monitor the depth proﬁles 
of stress in the MAPbI 3 ﬁlms, as shown in Fig. 2 (c) −(f). The GIXRD 
patterns of A-SnO 2 and I-SnO 2 with different incident angles are 
shown in Fig. S4. The stress and crystallite size distribution in the 
ﬁlms were characterized using the Halder–Wagner method, which 
is based on the equation ( β∗/δ) 2 = ( 1 /L )( β∗/ δ2 ) + ( ε S / 2 ) 2 , where 
β∗= β cos θ/λ, δ = 2 sin θ/λ, β is the full-width at half-maximum 
(FWHM) of the XRD peak, θ is the Bragg angle, λ is 1.5406 ˚A, L is 
the correlation length (corresponding to the crystalline ﬁlm), and 
εs is the stress parameter [ 37 , 38 ]. To obtain accurate values, we de- 
termined the FWHM by ﬁtting the diffraction peaks with pseudo- 
Voigt functions. The plots of ( β∗/ δ2 ) corresponding to the peaks 
of MAPbI 3 ﬁlms on the A-SnO 2 and I-SnO 2 substrates are shown in 
Fig. 2 (d) −(f). The detailed ﬁtting data are shown in Table 1 . With 
increasing depth, the I-SnO 2 ﬁlms exhibit substantially smaller εs 
values (0.2115 (1 °), 0.1975 (2 °), and 0.2640 (3 °)) than the A-SnO 2 
ﬁlms (0.2435 (1 °), 0.2245 (2 °), and 0.3323 (3 °)). In addition, the I- 
SnO 2 ﬁlms exhibit a larger crystallite size than the A-SnO 2 ﬁlms, 
as indicated by the larger L value for the I-SnO 2 ﬁlms than for the 
A-SnO 2 ﬁlms. Therefore, we conclude that the IPL treatment of the 
amorphous SnO 2 ESLs not only promotes nucleation of the over- 
lying perovskite ﬁlm but also reduces the stress in the obtained 
perovskite ﬁlms.

To assess the effect of the IPL treatment of the amorphous 
SnO 2 on the device properties, we fabricated MAPbI 3 -based pla- 
nar solar cells using a device architecture of FTO/ESL(I-SnO 2 /A- 
SnO 2 )/MAPbI 3 /spiroMeOTAD/Au, as shown in Fig. 3 (a, b). To opti- 
mize the number of IPL pulses for the SnO 2 ﬁlms, we character- 
ized the PV performance of 20 devices by varying the number of 
IPL treatment pulses. During each 2 ms pulse, 1.84 J cm −2 of en- 
ergy was irradiated onto the surface of amorphous-SnO 2 . To op- 
timize the IPL treatment, we varied the number of IPL pulses to 
as high as 140; the resultant PCEs and the corresponding PV pa- 
rameters are indicated in Fig. S5. As the number of IPL pulses was 
increased to 120, most of PV parameters improved. However, when 
the number of IPL pulses was 140, the PV parameters rapidly de- 
creased. Thus, we determined that the optimal IPL treatment was 
120 pulses. Fig. 3 (c) shows the current density −voltage (J −V) char- 
acteristics of I-SnO 2 -based devices treated under the optimized IPL 
conditions; the details of the PV parameters are summarized in the 
inset. The device based on the A-SnO 2 ESL showed a PCE of 7.06%, 
a short-circuit current density ( J sc ) of 13.20 mA cm −2 , an open- 
circuit voltage ( V oc ) of 0.952 V, and a ﬁll factor (FF) of 56.20%. In

lowest hysteresis index (HI) of 0.08, which is substantially lower 
than the HI of the A-SnO 2 -based device (0.73). The improved hys-

device are attributed to both the reduced defects/traps of I-SnO 2

pared these results with those for PSCs based on heat-treated SnO 2

vice based on the heat-treated ESL showed a best PCE of 18.16%, 
with a J sc of 22.12 mA cm −2 , V oc of 1.083 V, and FF of 75.85%,

to that of an SnO 2 ESL sintered at high temperature (185 °C, 3 h). 
To analyze the substantial inﬂuence of IPL-treated SnO 2 on the 
PV performance of devices, we used EIS to characterize the charge 
transport and recombination dynamics at the interfaces [ 10 , 40 ]. 
Fig. 4 (a) shows the Nyquist plot for the devices with A-SnO 2 - and 
I-SnO 2 -based ESLs, as measured at 0.8 V in the dark using an 
equivalent circuit (inset of Fig. 4 (a)). The Nyquist plot consists of 
two arcs or semicircles. The charge transfer resistance ( R tr ) was as- 
signed to the arc in the high-frequency region, and the recombina- 
tion resistance ( R rec ) was assigned to the arc in the low-frequency 
region [41] . The device with I-SnO 2 as the ESL exhibits a smaller 
R tr than that of the device with A-SnO 2 as the ESL, which indicates 
that I-SnO 2 exhibits better charge extraction than its counterpart 
( Fig. 4 (b)). In addition, the device with an I-SnO 2 ESL exhibits a 
larger R rec than the A-SnO 2 -based device, which means that the 
IPL treatment of SnO 2 ﬁlms greatly reduced the charge recombina- 
tion rate and increased the V oc ( Fig. 4 (c)) [42] . Because charge re- 
combination is closely related to the concentration of defects/traps 
in perovskite ﬁlms, we characterized the trap densities of the per- 
ovskite ﬁlm using the electron-only device conﬁguration shown in 
Fig. 4 (d). The trap densities can be calculated from the relation be- 
tween the trap-ﬁlled limited voltage ( V TFL ) and the trap density 
( N t ), N t = 2 ε ε 0 V TRL / e L 2 , where L is the ﬁlm thickness, ε is the di- 
electric constant of the perovskite layer, and ε0 is the dielectric 
constant of vacuum [43-45] . When calculated using the V TFL values 
( Fig. 4 (d)) of 0.42 V (I-SnO 2 ) and 0.95 V (A-SnO 2 ), the trap densi- 
ties were 5.62 × 10 15 and 1.25 × 10 16 cm −3 , respectively, which 
implies that I-SnO 2 contains fewer traps because of reduced stress 
in the perovskite ﬁlm. 
We carried out C-AFM using an FTO/ESL device structure to 
investigate the conductivity of the I-SnO 2 . Fig. 4 (e),(f) shows the 
C-AFM mapping images of the A-SnO 2 and I-SnO 2 ESLs, demon- 
strating that the I-SnO 2 ﬁlm exhibits higher conductivity than the 
A-SnO 2 ﬁlm. To further conﬁrm the increased conductivity of the 
I-SnO 2 ﬁlms, we performed I –V measurements in the dark using 
the electron-only device conﬁguration of FTO/ESLs/Au (Fig. S8). The 
conductivities of the I-SnO 2 and A-SnO 2 ESLs were calculated us- 
ing the equation σ = d/ AR , where σ is the direct-current conduc- 
tivity, A is the active area, R is the resistance, and d is the thick- 
ness of each ESL. The σ values of the I-SnO 2 and A-SnO 2 ESLs were 
found to be 8.2 × 10 −3 S cm −1 and 5.5 × 10 −3 S cm −1 , respec- 
tively, which means that the IPL treatment enhanced the carrier 
transport. The electron mobility of the ESL ﬁlms was obtained us- 
ing the Mott–Gurney equation, J = ( 9 / 8 ) ε 0 ε r μV 2 / d 3 , where J is the 
current density, ε 0 and ε r are the vacuum permittivity and relative 
permittivity values (13) of SnO 2 [46] , d is the thicknesses of the 
ESL (40 nm), V is the applied voltage, and μ is the electron mo- 
bility (Fig. S8). The electron mobility of I-SnO 2 was evaluated to 
be 8.2 × 10 −5 cm 2 V −1 S −1 , which is higher than the value for A- 
SnO 2 (7.3 × 10 −5 cm 2 V −1 S −1 ) for A-SnO 2 . These results demon- 
strate that the IPL treatment results in enhanced conductivity and 
mobility in the I-SnO 2 ﬁlm, consistent with the results of reduced 
–OH acting as defects/traps on the surface of SnO 2 . Because of 
these effects, PSCs based on I-SnO 2 exhibit excellent PV properties

4. Conclusions 
We report in detail the inﬂuence of the IPL treatment on a 
solution-processed amorphous SnO 2 ESL and on the photovoltaic 
performance of an MAPbI 3 PSC based on the IPL-treated SnO 2 . 
Through systematic investigations, we veriﬁed that the IPL treat- 
ment not only reduces the number of –OH groups acting as de- 
fect/traps in SnO 2 ﬁlms but also facilitates the formation of dense 
and uniform MAPbI 3 ﬁlms by controlling the nucleation of the 
perovskite layer. In addition, the IPL treatment reduces the stress 
in the upper perovskite ﬁlm. Because of these effects, the PSCs 
based on the IPL-treated SnO 2 achieved a PCE of 17.68%, whereas 
those based on its nontreated counterpart exhibited a PCE of 
7.06%. The achieved PCE is comparable to the PCE (18.16%) of the 
perovskite solar cell based on high-temperature-processed SnO 2 . 
Such a high eﬃciency is achieved through improved charge trans- 
port/extraction and recombination, which greatly increases the J sc 
and V oc . Because of the ultrafast processing time (a few tens of sec- 
onds) and the damage-free obtained ﬁlms, the IPL technique has a 
bright future.

Novel Intense-pulsed-light synthesis of amorphous SnO 2 
electron-selective layers for eﬃcient planar MAPbI 3 perovskite solar 
cells 
Kwonwoo Oh a , 1 , Kyungeun Jung b , 1 , Jaehak Shin c , Sunglim Ko c , Man-Jong Lee a , b , ∗
a Department of Chemistry, Konkuk University, Seoul 143-701, Republic of Korea 
b Department of Advanced Technology Fusion, Konkuk University, Seoul 143-701, Republic of Korea 
c Department of Mechanical Design and Production Engineering, Konkuk University, Seoul 146-701, Republic of Korea

Keywords: 
Perovskite solar cells

Amorphous SnO 2 
Electron-selective layer

a b s t r a c t 
Although perovskite solar cells (PSCs) have achieved a high power conversion eﬃciency (PCE) within a 
short period of development, the high-temperature sintering of the constituent electron-selective layers 
(ESLs) impedes the commercialization. In this report, we demonstrate the effectiveness of an intense- 
pulsed-light (IPL) treatment for the rapid and damage-free sintering of amorphous-SnO 2 ESLs for use 
in PSCs. The IPL treatment of amorphous-SnO 2 substantially reduced the amount of surface hydroxyl 
groups, modiﬁed the surface energy, and enabled the growth of a low-stress perovskite layer with large 
grain sizes, all of which enhanced the photovoltaic properties and led to the proper alignment of band 
structures for eﬃcient PSCs. Through comprehensive optimization of the IPL conditions, a PCE of 17.68% 
was achieved from the MAPbI 3 planar PSC based on an amorphous-SnO 2 IPL treated for a few tens of 
seconds, which was signiﬁcantly increased compared with a PCE (7.06%) of nontreated SnO 2 based coun- 
terpart. In addition, the PCE of the IPL-treated SnO 2 based PSC is comparable to the best PCE (18.16%) of 
PSCs fabricated with SnO 2 ESL annealed for three hours at 185 °C. Because of its ultrafast sintering time 
and tendency to not damage SnO 2 ESLs, the new IPL process is expected to open new opportunities for 
the commercialization of PSCs.

1. Introduction 
Organometal-halide perovskite solar cells (PSCs) have attracted 
considerable attention because of their remarkable power conver- 
sion eﬃciency (PCE), which can exceed 25.2% [1] . Such an out- 
standing PCE is a consequence of their long charge-carrier diffu- 
sion length [ 2 , 3 ], low exciton binding energy [ 4 , 5 ], and good ab- 
sorption over the visible spectrum [6] . Despite these exceptional 
properties and strengths, the commercialization of PSCs faces se- 
rious problems with respect to low-temperature solution process- 
ing. In particular, PSCs with a planar device architecture typi- 
cally use TiO 2 as an electron-selective layer (ESL), which requires 
high-temperature annealing ( > 450 °C) for a long duration (1 −2 h) 
[7] . Furthermore, TiO 2 exhibits low electron mobility (0.1 −1 cm 2 
V −1 S −1 ) and low conductivity (~1.1 × 10 −5 S cm −1 ), necessitat- 
ing an additional mesoporous layer to compensate for the low

E-mail address: leemtx@konkuk.ac.kr (M.-J. Lee). 
1 These authors have contributed equally. 
mobility and conductivity by enhancing the surface area [8-10] . 
The more serious issue with TiO 2 ESLs is that they exhibit pho- 
tocatalytic properties under UV illumination, which causes decom- 
position of the perovskite materials and adversely affects device 
stability [11] . 
To overcome the aforementioned shortcomings of TiO 2 , re- 
searchers have extensively studied SnO 2 -based ESLs because of the 
high electron mobility, high electrical conductivity, wide bandgap 
range (3.6–4.1 eV), and good photostability of SnO 2 [ 12 , 13 , 14 ]. Ke 
et al. reported that the performance of SnO 2 -based PSCs depends 
on the annealing temperature between 185 °C and 500 °C and con- 
cluded that low-temperature annealing leads to better surface cov- 
erage, a wider optical band gap, and greater electron mobility [15] . 
Park et al. also reported that Li-doped SnO 2 annealed at a low tem- 
perature (185 °C) exhibits much-improved performance [16] . De- 
spite the excellent characteristics and performance of SnO 2 pro- 
cessed at low temperatures, this approach is still problematic with 
respect to commercialization because the extended annealing time 
of SnO 2 requires a long batch oven within the roll-to-roll setup 
[17] . Meanwhile, in the printed electronics industry, a damage-free

1005-0302/© 2021 Published by Elsevier Ltd on behalf of Chinese Society for Metals. 


K. Oh, K. Jung, J. Shin et al. 
Journal of Materials Science & Technology 92 (2021) 171–177 
process known as intense pulsed light (IPL) has been used as a 
minimal-heat-exposure method to rapidly sinter nanoparticle thin 
ﬁlms [18-20] . Because the IPL process involves irradiating the sur- 
face of an oxide thin ﬁlm with high-intensity pulsed light for a 
short time, the total processing time is reduced to a few tens of 
seconds and substrate damage is minimized [21-23] . 
Here, the IPL irradiation of amorphous-SnO 2 ESLs is used 
to synthesize highly eﬃcient methylammonium lead iodide 
(MAPbI 3 )-based planar PSCs with improved performance. During 
each 2 ms pulse, 1.84 J cm −2 of energy is irradiated onto the sur- 
face of an amorphous-SnO 2 ﬁlm; the number of pulses is varied 
to optimize the ESL properties. The PSC with the highest PCE was 
obtained with an amorphous-SnO 2 ﬁlm subjected to 120 pulses 
(~220 J cm −2 ) of IPL within a few tens of seconds; a maximum PCE 
of 17.68% with an average and standard deviation of 15.58% ±0.85% 
was achieved. Compared with PSCs based on nontreated SnO 2 
(maximum PCE of 7.06% with 2.65% ±1.76%), the IPL treatment sub- 
stantially enhanced the photovoltaic properties. Notably, the IPL- 
treated SnO 2 -based PSCs showed a PCE similar to that of devices 
(maximum PCE of 18.16%) with an SnO 2 ESL prepared by a gen- 
eral heat-treatment process at 185 °C for 3 h. We found that the 
IPL treatment of the amorphous-SnO 2 substantially improved the 
short-circuit current density ( J sc ) and open-circuit voltage ( V oc ) by 
decreasing the number of hydroxyl ( −OH) species, which func- 
tion as defect/trap states. In addition, the irradiated SnO 2 ESLs ex- 
hibited enhanced conductivities and mobilities compared with the 
nontreated amorphous-SnO 2 . The results presented here show that 
the IPL treatment can effectively control the ESL/perovskite inter- 
face over a short duration by regulating the inherent MAPbI 3 prop- 
erties such as stress and nucleation density, which makes this pro- 
cess very promising for the commercial high-throughput manufac- 
ture of PSCs. 
2. Experimental 
2.1. Preparation of SnO 2 ESLs 
PSCs were fabricated on ﬂuorine-doped tin oxide (FTO)-coated 
glass substrates (Pilkington, Tec-8), which were patterned us- 
ing Zn powder and a dilute HCl solution, followed by cleaning 
with diluted Hellmanex, acetone, ethanol, and deionized water. 
Amorphous-SnO 2 was prepared as an ESL on the FTO glass by 
spin coating 0.1 M tin(II) chloride dihydrate solution in ethanol 
(Sigma-Aldrich) at 30 0 0 rpm for 30 s. After drying at 100 °C for 
1 min, the sample was instantly transferred to an IPL apparatus 
(HI-PULSE 15,0 0 0, PSTEK) for treatment using different ﬂash counts 
delivering different amounts of energy. Fig. S1 shows a schematic 
of the IPL setup and the processing parameters corresponding to 
the various IPL irradiation conditions. Table S1 shows the trans- 
ferred energy values for each pulse time (1 and 2 ms), as mea- 
sured by a photosensor (Nova II, Ophir). From ten or more mea- 
surements of each transferred energy value, 1.84 J cm −2 of en- 
ergy per IPL pulse was conﬁrmed to be transferred to the SnO 2 
surface under the conditions used to conduct the experiment 
(60 0 V, 20 0 0 mA, 2 ms, 4 Hz). The SnO 2 ﬁlms were thereafter 
subjected to an ultraviolet–ozone (UVO) treatment for as long as 
35 min. 
2.2. Synthesis of planar MAPbI 3 solar cells 
The perovskite precursor solution (50 wt.%) was prepared by 
dissolving lead(II) iodide (PbI 2 ; TCI) and methylammonium iodide 
(MAI; GreatCell Solar) in 0.635 mL of dimethylformamide (DMF; 
Sigma-Aldrich), to which 70 μL of dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO; 
Sigma-Aldrich) was added to form the corresponding adducts 
[24] . The completely dissolved solution was spin-coated onto an 
amorphous-SnO 2 ESL layer at 40 0 0 rpm for 25 s, and 0.5 mL of 
diethyl ether (Sigma-Aldrich) was slowly dripped onto the sub- 
strate before the surface became turbid as a result of the rapid 
vaporization of DMF. The sample was subsequently annealed at 
65 °C for 1 min and then at 100 °C for 2 min. A hole-selective 
layer was then coated onto the perovskite layer by spin coating 
20 μL of a 2,2 ′ ,7,7 ′ -tetrakis[ N,N - di (4-methoxyphenyl)amino] −9,9 ′ - 
spirobiﬂuorene (spiroMeOTAD) solution (composed of 80 mg 
spiroMeOTAD (1-Material), 28.5 μL of 4–tert -butylpyridine, and 17.5 
μL of lithium bis(triﬂuoromethanesulfonyl)imide (Li-TFSI, Sigma- 
Aldrich) solution (520 mg Li-TSFI in 1 mL acetonitrile)), and 1 mL 
of chlorobenzene (Sigma-Aldrich) at 40 0 0 rpm for 30 s. The Au 
electrode was evaporated under 10 −6 Torr using a thermal evapo- 
ration system. 
2.3. Characterization 
The crystal structures of the SnO 2 and perovskite ﬁlms were 
determined by X-ray diffraction (XRD, Rigaku SmartLab) analysis 
using Cu K α radiation. The morphology of the synthesized ﬁlms 
was examined by ﬁeld-emission scanning electron microscopy (FE- 
SEM) on an electron microscope (SU8010, Hitachi) with a resolu- 
tion of 5 kV and 15 kV. The contact angle of SnO 2 ﬁlms were mea- 
sured using a contact-angle measurement system (Phoenix 300 
Touch, SEO, Korea). The photovoltaic (PV) properties of the as- 
sembled PSCs were determined under AM 1.5 simulated sunlight 
with a power density of 100 mW cm −2 using a solar simula- 
tor (Polaronix K201, McScience, Korea) equipped with a 150 W 
xenon lamp and a Keithley 2401 source meter. The scan speed 
was set to a constant of 0.1 V/s in this study. After the inten- 
sity was calibrated using a KIER-calibrated KG5-ﬁltered Si reference 
cell, all measurements were performed by masking the cells with 
a metal aperture to deﬁne an active area of 0.09 cm 2 . An inci- 
dent photon-to-current conversion eﬃciency (IPCE) measurement 
system (HS Tech, Korea) was used to evaluate the external quan- 
tum eﬃciency (EQE). The UV–Vis absorption spectra of the SnO 2 
ﬁlms were recorded using a UV–Vis spectrometer (Optizen PoP). 
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, KBSI) and ultraviolet pho- 
toelectron spectroscopy (UPS, KBSI) were carried out using an AXIS 
ultra-delay line detector (Kratos, UK) equipped with a monochro- 
matic Al K α (1486.6 eV) X-ray source or He-I gas (21.22 eV) UV 
source. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS, Biologic SP- 
240) measurements were conducted in the dark. The surface con- 
ductivity of the SnO 2 ﬁlms was measured by conductive atomic 
force microscopy (C-AFM; Nanoscope V Multimode 8 atomic force 
microscope, KBSI). 
3. Results and discussion 
Amorphous SnO 2 ﬁlms were synthesized through a simple so- 
lution process using tin(II) chloride dihydrate in ethanol. Hereafter, 
the amorphous-SnO 2 ﬁlms that were treated and not treated with 
IPL are denoted as I-SnO 2 and A-SnO 2 , respectively. Fig. 1 (a) shows 
the XRD patterns of A-SnO 2 and I-SnO 2 , respectively, showing that 
no crystalline peaks were observed. XPS was used to characterize 
the chemical bonding states of both amorphous ﬁlms (A-SnO 2 and 
I-SnO 2 ); the resultant spectra are shown in Fig. 1 (b) −(d). Fig. 1 (b) 
shows the XPS spectra of the Sn 3 d states in A-SnO 2 and I-SnO 2 . 
According to previous reports [ 25 , 26 ], the Sn 3 d XPS spectrum of 
SnO 2 ﬁlm shows peaks of Sn 3 d 5/2 and 3 d 3/2 at binding energy 
(BE) values of approximately 487 and 495 eV, respectively. The XPS 
spectrum of the A-SnO 2 ﬁlm, however, shows slight changes in the 
BE values of Sn 3 d 5/2 and 3 d 3/2 to 487.9 and 496.3 eV, respec- 
tively. By contrast, the Sn 3 d 5/2 and 3 d 3/2 BE values in the spec- 
trum of the I-SnO 2 ﬁlms were 487.2 and 495 eV, respectively, sim- 
ilar to the previously reported values. After the IPL irradiation, the

Fig. 1. XRD patterns (a) and XPS spectra (Sn 3 d states) (b) of I-SnO 2 and A-SnO 2 ; (c, d) O 1s spectra (measured and ﬁtted) of I-SnO 2 and A-SnO 2 . 
BE values of the Sn 3 d 5/2 and 3 d 3/2 peaks in the spectrum of the 
I-SnO 2 ﬁlms were slightly shifted to lower values compared with 
those in the spectrum of the A-SnO 2 sample. Such shifts in the BE 
values are attributed to changes in the electron interaction of Sn 
ions in the I-SnO 2 ﬁlms [27] . According to previous reports [27- 
29] , the difference in the BE values between Sn 4 + and Sn 2 + ions 
is 0.7 eV. Thus, the BE shift of the Sn peaks in the spectrum of 
the I-SnO 2 to lower BEs after the IPL treatment clearly suggests 
an increase in the amount of Sn 2 + ions [27] , which warrants fur- 
ther study. Fig. 1 (c) and (d) shows the spectra of the O 1 s re- 
gion. After peak deconvolution, the main peak at 530.9 eV was at- 
tributed to O 1 s in SnO 2 and the peak at 531.8 eV was assigned 
to hydroxyl (–OH) groups. The intensity of the –OH peak in the 
spectrum of I-SnO 2 clearly decreased compared with that in the 
spectrum of A-SnO 2 , which means that the I-SnO 2 ﬁlms contain 
fewer –OH groups than the A-SnO 2 ﬁlms. According to previous 
reports [30] , the –OH groups in SnO 2 are associated with surface 
oxygen vacancies, which can act as surface trap sites in metal oxide 
ESLs. Therefore, we speculated that the IPL treatment of the amor- 
phous SnO 2 ﬁlms substantially reduced the number of surface –OH 
groups acting as defect/trap states. 
To further study the inﬂuence of the IPL treatment on the 
amorphous-SnO 2 ESLs and on the resultant evolution of the 
MAPbI 3 ﬁlms deposited onto the treated ESLs, we conducted SEM 
observations, contact-angle measurements, and grazing-incident 
XRD (GIXRD) analysis. Fig. S2 shows the contact angles of A-SnO 2 
and I-SnO 2 surfaces, indicating that the I-SnO 2 surface has a lower 
contact angle. Because a surface with a small contact angle has a 
high surface energy, the particle size of the network ﬁlm growing 
on the surface tends to be uniform [ 31 , 32 ]. The nucleation den- 
sity during heterogeneous nucleation is known to be related to the 
Gibbs free energy through the following equation: G heterogeneous = 
G homogeneou s × f (θ) , where f (θ) = ( 2 −3 cos θ + cos 3 θ) / 4 and θ
is the contact angle of the precursor solution [33-35] . Thus, a small 
contact angle can improve the nucleation process by reducing the 
Gibbs free energy during heterogeneous nucleation ( G heterogeneous ). 
In addition, a small contact angle provides a high surface energy, 
which can increase the grain size of the upper MAPbI 3 [36] . As 
shown in Fig. 2 (a, b) and Fig. S3, the MAPbI 3 ﬁlms grown on the 
I-SnO 2 ESL exhibited a more uniform microstructure with a grain 
size (267 nm) larger than that of MAPbI 3 grown on the A-SnO 2 
samples (65 nm). 
We conducted GIXRD analysis to investigate the internal stress 
developed in the MAPbI 3 crystals during the densiﬁcation assisted 
by the increased surface energy. In GIXRD measurements, we var- 
ied the incident angles from 1 to 3 ° to monitor the depth proﬁles 
of stress in the MAPbI 3 ﬁlms, as shown in Fig. 2 (c) −(f). The GIXRD 
patterns of A-SnO 2 and I-SnO 2 with different incident angles are 
shown in Fig. S4. The stress and crystallite size distribution in the 
ﬁlms were characterized using the Halder–Wagner method, which 
is based on the equation ( β∗/δ) 2 = ( 1 /L )( β∗/ δ2 ) + ( ε S / 2 ) 2 , where 
β∗= β cos θ/λ, δ = 2 sin θ/λ, β is the full-width at half-maximum 
(FWHM) of the XRD peak, θ is the Bragg angle, λ is 1.5406 ˚A, L is 
the correlation length (corresponding to the crystalline ﬁlm), and 
εs is the stress parameter [ 37 , 38 ]. To obtain accurate values, we de- 
termined the FWHM by ﬁtting the diffraction peaks with pseudo- 
Voigt functions. The plots of ( β∗/ δ2 ) corresponding to the peaks 
of MAPbI 3 ﬁlms on the A-SnO 2 and I-SnO 2 substrates are shown in 
Fig. 2 (d) −(f). The detailed ﬁtting data are shown in Table 1 . With 
increasing depth, the I-SnO 2 ﬁlms exhibit substantially smaller εs 
values (0.2115 (1 °), 0.1975 (2 °), and 0.2640 (3 °)) than the A-SnO 2 
ﬁlms (0.2435 (1 °), 0.2245 (2 °), and 0.3323 (3 °)). In addition, the I- 
SnO 2 ﬁlms exhibit a larger crystallite size than the A-SnO 2 ﬁlms, 
as indicated by the larger L value for the I-SnO 2 ﬁlms than for the 
A-SnO 2 ﬁlms. Therefore, we conclude that the IPL treatment of the 
amorphous SnO 2 ESLs not only promotes nucleation of the over- 
lying perovskite ﬁlm but also reduces the stress in the obtained 
perovskite ﬁlms.

To assess the effect of the IPL treatment of the amorphous 
SnO 2 on the device properties, we fabricated MAPbI 3 -based pla- 
nar solar cells using a device architecture of FTO/ESL(I-SnO 2 /A- 
SnO 2 )/MAPbI 3 /spiroMeOTAD/Au, as shown in Fig. 3 (a, b). To opti- 
mize the number of IPL pulses for the SnO 2 ﬁlms, we character- 
ized the PV performance of 20 devices by varying the number of 
IPL treatment pulses. During each 2 ms pulse, 1.84 J cm −2 of en- 
ergy was irradiated onto the surface of amorphous-SnO 2 . To op- 
timize the IPL treatment, we varied the number of IPL pulses to 
as high as 140; the resultant PCEs and the corresponding PV pa- 
rameters are indicated in Fig. S5. As the number of IPL pulses was 
increased to 120, most of PV parameters improved. However, when 
the number of IPL pulses was 140, the PV parameters rapidly de- 
creased. Thus, we determined that the optimal IPL treatment was 
120 pulses. Fig. 3 (c) shows the current density −voltage (J −V) char- 
acteristics of I-SnO 2 -based devices treated under the optimized IPL 
conditions; the details of the PV parameters are summarized in the 
inset. The device based on the A-SnO 2 ESL showed a PCE of 7.06%, 
a short-circuit current density ( J sc ) of 13.20 mA cm −2 , an open- 
circuit voltage ( V oc ) of 0.952 V, and a ﬁll factor (FF) of 56.20%. In

vice exhibits greater stability than the A-SnO 2 -based device. Fig. 
S6 shows the hysteresis behaviors of the devices fabricated with 
the A-SnO 2 and I-SnO 2 ESLs. In general, hysteresis originates from 
the trap states of charge carriers, ion charge carriers, ion migration, 
and ferroelectricity, all of which are related to the grain size and 
defect density [39] . The device with the I-SnO 2 ESL showed the 
lowest hysteresis index (HI) of 0.08, which is substantially lower 
than the HI of the A-SnO 2 -based device (0.73). The improved hys- 
teresis, high eﬃciency, and improved stability of the I-SnO 2 -based 
device are attributed to both the reduced defects/traps of I-SnO 2 
and the enhanced quality of the overlying MAPbI 3 ﬁlm, which ex- 
hibits fewer grain boundaries and less stress. Moreover, we com- 
pared these results with those for PSCs based on heat-treated SnO 2 
(185 °C for 3 h), as shown in Fig. 3 (f). In Fig S7 detailed compar- 
isons of the PV parameters and eﬃciencies are indicated. The de- 
vice based on the heat-treated ESL showed a best PCE of 18.16%, 
with a J sc of 22.12 mA cm −2 , V oc of 1.083 V, and FF of 75.85%, 
which is comparable to the performance of the I-SnO 2 -based de- 
vice subjected to the IPL treatment for only 30 s (220.8 J cm −2 ). On 
the basis of these results, we propose that an IPL process shorter 
than 30 s can result in an SnO 2 ESL with performance comparable 
to that of an SnO 2 ESL sintered at high temperature (185 °C, 3 h). 
To analyze the substantial inﬂuence of IPL-treated SnO 2 on the 
PV performance of devices, we used EIS to characterize the charge 
transport and recombination dynamics at the interfaces [ 10 , 40 ]. 
Fig. 4 (a) shows the Nyquist plot for the devices with A-SnO 2 - and 
I-SnO 2 -based ESLs, as measured at 0.8 V in the dark using an 
equivalent circuit (inset of Fig. 4 (a)). The Nyquist plot consists of 
two arcs or semicircles. The charge transfer resistance ( R tr ) was as- 
signed to the arc in the high-frequency region, and the recombina- 
tion resistance ( R rec ) was assigned to the arc in the low-frequency 
region [41] . The device with I-SnO 2 as the ESL exhibits a smaller 
R tr than that of the device with A-SnO 2 as the ESL, which indicates 
that I-SnO 2 exhibits better charge extraction than its counterpart 
( Fig. 4 (b)). In addition, the device with an I-SnO 2 ESL exhibits a 
larger R rec than the A-SnO 2 -based device, which means that the 
IPL treatment of SnO 2 ﬁlms greatly reduced the charge recombina- 
tion rate and increased the V oc ( Fig. 4 (c)) [42] . Because charge re- 
combination is closely related to the concentration of defects/traps 
in perovskite ﬁlms, we characterized the trap densities of the per- 
ovskite ﬁlm using the electron-only device conﬁguration shown in 
Fig. 4 (d). The trap densities can be calculated from the relation be- 
tween the trap-ﬁlled limited voltage ( V TFL ) and the trap density 
( N t ), N t = 2 ε ε 0 V TRL / e L 2 , where L is the ﬁlm thickness, ε is the di- 
electric constant of the perovskite layer, and ε0 is the dielectric 
constant of vacuum [43-45] . When calculated using the V TFL values 
( Fig. 4 (d)) of 0.42 V (I-SnO 2 ) and 0.95 V (A-SnO 2 ), the trap densi- 
ties were 5.62 × 10 15 and 1.25 × 10 16 cm −3 , respectively, which 
implies that I-SnO 2 contains fewer traps because of reduced stress 
in the perovskite ﬁlm. 
We carried out C-AFM using an FTO/ESL device structure to 
investigate the conductivity of the I-SnO 2 . Fig. 4 (e),(f) shows the 
C-AFM mapping images of the A-SnO 2 and I-SnO 2 ESLs, demon- 
strating that the I-SnO 2 ﬁlm exhibits higher conductivity than the 
A-SnO 2 ﬁlm. To further conﬁrm the increased conductivity of the 
I-SnO 2 ﬁlms, we performed I –V measurements in the dark using 
the electron-only device conﬁguration of FTO/ESLs/Au (Fig. S8). The 
conductivities of the I-SnO 2 and A-SnO 2 ESLs were calculated us- 
ing the equation σ = d/ AR , where σ is the direct-current conduc- 
tivity, A is the active area, R is the resistance, and d is the thick- 
ness of each ESL. The σ values of the I-SnO 2 and A-SnO 2 ESLs were 
found to be 8.2 × 10 −3 S cm −1 and 5.5 × 10 −3 S cm −1 , respec- 
tively, which means that the IPL treatment enhanced the carrier 
transport. The electron mobility of the ESL ﬁlms was obtained us- 
ing the Mott–Gurney equation, J = ( 9 / 8 ) ε 0 ε r μV 2 / d 3 , where J is the 
current density, ε 0 and ε r are the vacuum permittivity and relative 
permittivity values (13) of SnO 2 [46] , d is the thicknesses of the 
ESL (40 nm), V is the applied voltage, and μ is the electron mo- 
bility (Fig. S8). The electron mobility of I-SnO 2 was evaluated to 
be 8.2 × 10 −5 cm 2 V −1 S −1 , which is higher than the value for A- 
SnO 2 (7.3 × 10 −5 cm 2 V −1 S −1 ) for A-SnO 2 . These results demon- 
strate that the IPL treatment results in enhanced conductivity and 
mobility in the I-SnO 2 ﬁlm, consistent with the results of reduced 
–OH acting as defects/traps on the surface of SnO 2 . Because of 
these effects, PSCs based on I-SnO 2 exhibit excellent PV properties

For the complete analyses of the inﬂuence of the IPL treatment, 
we performed the UV–Vis spectroscopy and UPS to obtain the band 
offset in detail. The valence band maximum ( E VBM ), work function 
( 
), and conduction band minimum ( E CBM ) were evaluated using 
the UPS measurements. Fig. 5 (a) and (b) shows UPS spectra repre- 
senting the secondary electron cutoff energy ( E cutoff) and Fermi- 
edge ( E F,edge ) of the I-SnO 2 and A-SnO 2 ﬁlms, respectively. The 
Fermi levels ( E F ) and E VBM of the ESLs were calculated using the 
relations E F = E cutoff −21.22 eV, where 21.22 eV is the emission 
energy of He-I radiation, and E VBM = E F −E cutoff. The E CBM of the 
I-SnO 2 ESL was determined from the E F and E VBM to be −4.61 and 
−7.84 eV, respectively. The E CBM of the A-SnO 2 ESL was determined 
from the E F and E VBM to be −4.49 and −8.33 eV, respectively. In 
addition, the bandgaps of the I-SnO 2 and A-SnO 2 ESLs were esti- 
mated from the Tauc plots ( Fig. 5 (c)) and found to be same value 
(3.73 eV). From these data, the complete band offsets of the device 
diagram are shown in Fig. 5 (d). Notably, the E CBM of the I-SnO 2 is 
much closer to the E CBM of the MAPbI 3 , and the band alignment of 
the I-SnO 2 device is ideally tuned to the MAPbI 3 , promoting charge 
extraction from the ESL/perovskite interface. Thus, the ideal band 
offset between the interface of I-SnO 2 and MAPbI 3 can reduce the 
interface recombination probability, leading to enhanced PV prop- 
erties [ 41 , 47 , 48 ]. 
4. Conclusions 
We report in detail the inﬂuence of the IPL treatment on a 
solution-processed amorphous SnO 2 ESL and on the photovoltaic 
performance of an MAPbI 3 PSC based on the IPL-treated SnO 2 . 
Through systematic investigations, we veriﬁed that the IPL treat- 
ment not only reduces the number of –OH groups acting as de- 
fect/traps in SnO 2 ﬁlms but also facilitates the formation of dense 
and uniform MAPbI 3 ﬁlms by controlling the nucleation of the 
perovskite layer. In addition, the IPL treatment reduces the stress 
in the upper perovskite ﬁlm. Because of these effects, the PSCs 
based on the IPL-treated SnO 2 achieved a PCE of 17.68%, whereas 
those based on its nontreated counterpart exhibited a PCE of 
7.06%. The achieved PCE is comparable to the PCE (18.16%) of the 
perovskite solar cell based on high-temperature-processed SnO 2 . 
Such a high eﬃciency is achieved through improved charge trans- 
port/extraction and recombination, which greatly increases the J sc 
and V oc . Because of the ultrafast processing time (a few tens of sec- 
onds) and the damage-free obtained ﬁlms, the IPL technique has a 
bright future.

Perovskite Solar Cells: From Fabrication to Failure
Renita M. D’Souza and Timothy L. Kelly*
Cite This: ACS Appl. Electron. Mater. 2025, 7, 3621−3631

ABSTRACT: Over the past decade, there have been tremendous advances in the design
and fabrication of perovskite solar cells (PSCs). The unique optoelectronic properties of
lead halide perovskites have resulted in solution-processed solar cells with excellent
efficiencies, and significant advances have now been made in both lab-scale and large-area
devices. As the technology moves toward commercialization, it is increasingly important to
understand the stability of the devices under operationally relevant conditions. What is the
projected lifetime of a perovskite-based module? Which environmental factors (e.g.,
humidity, heat, light) are most pernicious? What is the precise mechanism of device failure?
To this end, both in situ and operando characterization techniques have proven to be useful
methods and have provided important information about perovskite crystallization,
degradation, and transformation processes. This spotlight article discusses recent advances
in PSCs from both a device fabrication and device failure perspective, highlighting our
research group’s contributions along the way.
KEYWORDS: lead halide perovskites, optoelectronic devices, operando, X-ray scattering, stability, device lifetime
■INTRODUCTION
Over the past decade, there has been tremendous advancement
in the power conversion efficiency (PCE) of perovskite solar
cells (PSCs). From the early report of Kojima et al. in 20091 to
today, PCEs have increased from a paltry 3.8%1 to a record
27.0%,2,3 with perovskite/silicon tandems even higher at
34.6%.3 Given the promising results achieved with labora-
tory-scale devices, the field has devoted significant efforts to
device scale-up; blade-coated and slot-die coated devices have
both become much more common,4 as has the roll-to-roll
processing of flexible devices.5 Given the numerous potential
benefits of perovskite technology −good performance, lower
production costs and embodied energies, and lightweight and
flexible modules −many companies are now attempting to
commercialize the technology.
In a typical PSC, the light-absorbing lead halide perovskite
(of general formula ABX3) is sandwiched between two charge
transport layers (CTLs). When illuminated, the photo-
generated electrons and holes are transported to their
respective electrodes via a p-type hole transport layer (HTL)
and n-type electron transport layer (ETL). In an ideal HTL,
the valence band maximum (EVB) is slightly higher than that of
the perovskite for efficient hole extraction, while the
conduction band minimum (ECB) is sufficiently high to block
the transport of electrons. The reverse is true for the ETL. The
two main PSC designs then depend on the relative ordering of
the CTLs, with regular devices featuring a n-i-p structure, and
inverted devices having a p-i-n design (Figure 1a,b). Early
reports almost universally used the regular (n-i-p) architec-
ture,6,7 where the ETL was deposited onto the substrate
electrode (typically a transparent conductive oxide, TCO,
Figure 1a). This was predominantly done for historical
reasons; in many ways, PSCs evolved from dye-sensitized
solar cells, and early designs featured the same mesoporous
TiO2 ETL and the same solid-state hole-transport material
(2,2,7,7′-tetra[N,N-bis(4-methoxyphenyl)amino]-9,9′-spirobi-
fluorene, Spiro-OMeTAD).1,8 Since then, the mesoporous
TiO2 layer has been largely replaced with compact, planar
alternatives.9,10 The relative instability of Spiro-OMeTAD,
related to its dopants, also led to a search for alternative HTLs.
The end result of this work has been a gradual shift toward
inverted (p-i-n) structures,11 with both NiOx
12 and carbazole-
based self-assembled monolayers (e.g., MeO-2PACz)13
becoming popular due to their high performance and
comparatively good stability.
In parallel with these advancements in device structure,
advancements in perovskite composition were also being
made. The prototypical lead halide perovskite is methyl-
ammonium lead iodide (MAPbI3), which was the composition
employed in many early studies.6,14,15 However, it was
apparent early on that this particular material was easily
degraded. Solid solutions of iodide and bromide anions were
initially found to improve stability.16 Subsequent work led to

and good stability.
As PSCs move into the later stages of commercialization, it
is increasingly important to understand the stability of the
devices under operationally relevant conditions. These
concerns were largely absent from the early perovskite
literature, which focused almost exclusively on efficiency;
however, in the past few years, lifetime and stability
measurements have moved to the forefront of the field. In
contrast to PCE measurements, which have highly stand-
ardized test protocols (i.e., 1 Sun, AM1.5G spectrum, 25 °C),
there were initially no standard test conditions for perovskite
stability. A consensus statement, published in 2020, recom-
mended using test protocols originally put forth at the
International Summit on Organic Solar Cells Stability
(ISOS).18 This more standardized approach has the potential
to greatly improve the rate of progress, as researchers can more
clearly benchmark how perovskite composition, the choice of
CTLs, and device architecture affect device stability. This is
greatly improving not just overall device lifetimes, but also our
understanding of how lead halide perovskites respond to a
variety of environmental stimuli (e.g., relative humidity, heat,
light, and oxygen) and of device failure mechanisms.
This spotlight article will focus on our research group’s
contributions to the development of PSCs. Our early
contributions to the field were primarily in the area of PSC
design. In more recent years, our emphasis has shifted toward
the characterization of lead halide perovskites and PSCs using
in situ and operando grazing-incidence wide-angle X-ray
scattering (GIWAXS) techniques, which has provided
important insights into perovskite degradation mechanisms.
■PEROVSKITE SOLAR CELL DESIGN
In 2014, when our research group first started working in this
area, PSCs still closely resembled dye-sensitized solar cells in
terms of their structure and design. As a result, most devices
still used a mesoporous TiO2 layer as the ETL. The downside
to this design is that a mesoporous TiO2 layer requires high-
temperature sintering at ∼500 °C, significantly increasing the
embodied energy of the device;19 such layers are also generally
incompatible with flexible (i.e., plastic) substrates. At this
point, our group reported the use of a ZnO nanoparticle film as
the ETL, which could be deposited entirely at room
temperature (Figure 2a).20 In a departure from the conven-
tional mesostructured devices of the time, the device also used
a planar heterojunction (with a ITO/ZnO/MAPbI3/Spiro-
OMeTAD/Ag structure), simplifying the overall fabrication
process. Part of the key to making this approach work was
using a two-step deposition procedure for the perovskite,
which had been reported earlier by Burshka et al.14 This
involved spin coating a layer of PbI2 onto the ZnO surface,
followed by immersion in a MAI solution. This allowed us to
circumvent the usual perovskite annealing step, which we later
found to work very poorly on ZnO substrates.21 The best PCE
for these devices was 15.7% (Figure 2b), which was among the
highest reported at the time, and was especially notable
considering the lack of mesoporous scaffold and any high-
temperature processing steps. The low-temperature processing
also enabled the fabrication of flexible devices with efficiencies

Having established that planar heterojunctions could be
used to produce highly efficient devices, we next set out to
understand how the thickness of the perovskite layer affected
the generation, transport, and collection of charge carriers.
This work used a more cost-effective HTL, poly(3-hexylth-
iophene-2,5-diyl) (P3HT), in a ITO/ZnO/MAPbI3/P3HT/
Ag device architecture.22 We found that the PbI2 deposition
method, whether spin-coated or thermally evaporated, had
only a minimal effect on device performance. Rather, the
thickness of the perovskite layer was the most significant factor
influencing the PCE. The thinnest devices (110 nm) showed
pinhole shorts and significant recombination at the ZnO
interface, leading to a low shunt resistance and a corresponding
loss in Voc (Figure 2c). As the film thickness increased from
110 to 330 nm, there was a marked improvement in both the
Voc and FF. This enhancement correlated with increases in the
shunt resistance, suggesting that the perovskite layer was now
thick enough to eliminate any short-circuit pathways, and the
PCE reached a maximum (11.3%) at 330 nm. As the thickness
increased beyond 400 nm, the series resistance also increased,
consistent with the increased distance over which charge
carriers have to travel prior to being collected at the electrodes.
By the time the thickness was >500 nm, the PCE was
extremely low, which clearly shows the limitations of the two-
step deposition method in a planar heterojunction config-
uration. Although many of the same principles apply, more
modern approaches produce PSCs with optimal thickness in
the range of 500 −700 nm.24 Higher quality perovskite films
can be made thicker without increasing the series resistance,
leading to higher overall PCEs.

PSCs on flexible substrates,20 we wanted to determine the
limitations of such devices. Depending on the intended
application, flexible cells might be coated in a roll-to-roll
fashion but then incorporated into a largely fixed installation;
however, in more mobile applications, they might also be
subjected to many repeated bending cycles during their
lifetime. The latter presents significant problems with
mechanical stability, as flexible devices are prone to issues
with either delamination or cracking when subjected to
repeated mechanical stress. In our study, we prepared PSCs
on a poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET) substrate coated with
a metallized indium oxide (M-In2O3) electrode.23 The devices
were wrapped around a cylinder of known curvature for up to
2000 cycles, and we tracked the changes in device performance
with repeated cycling. Device failure was determined to be due
to crack formation in the transparent conductive oxide (M-
In2O3) layer, with short-circuits occurring quite suddenly after
100 to 1100 bending cycles. On replacing the metal oxide with
