Additional work from our group reported unique behavior of
the planar heterojunctions prepared via the two-step
deposition method. In order to better understand the role of
the ZnO layer, we prepared PSCs both with and without the
ZnO ETL, using either a P3HT or Spiro-OMeTAD HTL.29
Surprisingly, the devices without the ZnO ETL performed
quite well; there was still a loss in PCE relative to the controls
with a ZnO ETL, however, the drop in performance was
relatively modest. The Voc of the ZnO-free devices was ∼1 V,
indicating a relative lack of charge carrier recombination at the
ITO contact. This behavior may be in part due to the unique
fabrication pathway of these devices. The initial PbI2 layer is
converted to MAPbI3 in a top-down manner, via diffusion and
intercalation of MAI into the PbI2 film. This often leaves a
small, residual amount of unreacted PbI2, presumably highly
localized at the interface with the ITO substrate. This
unreacted PbI2 may have been serving to block holes, leading
to the reasonable efficiencies that were observed. Notably, the
ZnO-free devices had a slightly improved stability, perhaps due
to eliminating the reactive ZnO/perovskite interface (see
below). Although other ETL-free designs have been reported
since (e.g., those that use modified TCOs30−32), ultimately
there is little to recommend such a design for practical
application; the ETL is a relatively simple and inexpensive
component, and there is little to be gained from its elimination.
■STABILITY OF LEAD HALIDE PEROVSKITES
Despite accommodating a wide variety of cell designs and
producing excellent PCEs, a fundamental issue with PSCs was
a lack of long-term stability. The prototypical lead halide
perovskite, MAPbI3, was identified early on as being easily
degraded under ambient laboratory conditions, and it was
assumed that this was the primary cause of cell failure. Early
work from our group by Yang et al. sought to better elucidate
the role of relative humidity (RH) in this degradation pathway
and to better quantify the rate at which the degradation
occurred.33 A custom-machined UV/vis cell allowed us to
monitor the UV/vis spectra of perovskite films as they were
degraded by an atmosphere of controlled RH (Figure 3a). The
high-energy absorption features below 500 nm and optical
band gap ca. 760 nm are hallmarks of MAPbI3. At high RHs
(80 −100%) the absorption features below 500 nm show
rapid decay and the band gap at 760 nm becomes much less
distinct. A corresponding increase in the background
absorbance (λ > 800 nm) is indicative of Mie scattering,
indicating that large crystallites are being formed within the
film as part of the decomposition process. Tracking the
absorption at 410 nm allowed us to compare degradation rates,
and it was found that the decomposition rate was highly
dependent on RH, with very high RH levels (80 −100%)
causing complete decomposition within 6 h, and lower RH
(e.g., 20%) causing only minimal degradation over the course
of several days (Figure 3a, inset).
We subsequently turned to in situ GIWAXS to identify the
structural changes occurring during this moisture-induced
degradation process.33 Although the data quality from these
experiments was modest, owing to very strong background
scattering from the amorphous glass substrate (q = 10−23
nm−1, or 1.0−2.3 Å−1), after 5 h of exposure to 80% RH, new
peaks become apparent in the GIWAXS pattern (Figure 3c) at
5 and 7 nm−1 (0.5 and 0.7 Å−1). From the 2D plot of the
azimuthally integrated linecuts (Figure 3d), this intermediate
starts to appear after ca. 2.5 h of exposure. This feature was
initially ascribed to the dihydrate phase MA4PbI6·2H2O
(Figure 3b), which contains isolated PbI6
4−octahedra;
however, other subsequent studies34 have confirmed this
intermediate phase to be the monohydrate, MAPbI3·H2O, a
1D structure of edge-sharing PbI6 octahedra.35 In either case,
these hydrated phases eventually lead to the irreversible
formation of hexagonal PbI2 (Figure 3b).
Although we identified key degradation mechanisms for
MAPbI3, the perovskite is never found by itself in a device; we
also needed to know how the choice of CTLs affected
perovskite stability. Expanding upon these early in situ UV/vis
results, Yang et al. showed how the choice of HTL (Spiro-
OMeTAD, poly[bis(4-phenyl)(2,4,6-trimethylphenyl)]amine
(PTAA), or P3HT) affects the moisture stability of MAPbI3
films.33 It was found that films coated with Spiro-OMeTAD
degraded relatively quickly, in part because of substantial
cracking of the Spiro-OMeTAD layer;33 in contrast, PTAA,
and especially P3HT, provided more conformal coverage of
the perovskite and acted as a barrier to moisture ingress.
Additional work focused on the effect of the ZnO ETL on the
thermal stability of MAPbI3 films.21 Early on, we found that
attempts to fabricate MAPbI3 films on top of ZnO via a one-
step deposition and annealing process always met with failure.
In this work, we found that the more basic nature of the ZnO
surface (compared to, e.g., TiO2) leads to proton-transfer
reactions at the interface, resulting in the deprotonation of the
MA cation, the loss of methylamine, and the formation of PbI2.
It was also found that the presence of surface hydroxyl groups
worsened the stability of the perovskite film. We subsequently
compared additional ETLs and mesoporous scaffolds −planar
TiO2, mesoporous TiO2, and mesoporous Al2O3 −to see how
they affected the perovskite degradation process at 93% RH.36
The mesoporous scaffolds did appear to protect the underlying
perovskite from moisture ingress, which in part explains the
better stability of early mesoporous designs compared to our
planar heterojunction based on ZnO. However, in a modern
context, such scaffolds add significantly to cell complexity and
embodied energy, and are simply unnecessary with the advent
of more stable perovskite compositions (see below).
With humidity having such a deleterious effect on perovskite
films, most of the research in this area focused on perovskite
degradation pathways. However, early work37 suggested that a
modest RH during fabrication could have a positive impact on
the growth of the perovskite film. Gangishetty et al. studied the
role of RH during the spin-coating process by placing the spin-
coated inside a glovebag of controlled RH.38 When the
perovskite films were deposited under dry conditions (RH ∼
1%), small crystallites with numerous grain boundaries were
observed, resulting in poor carrier transport and lower device
performance. With more water vapor present (RH ∼40%),
larger perovskite crystallites were observed with fewer grain
boundaries; this both increased device performance and
reduced the amount of hysteresis observed in the J−V curve.

Excessive moisture was, unsurprisingly, problematic, with the
devices fabricated at high humidities performing quite poorly.
However, with improvements in perovskite coating procedures,
including the use of antisolvents and/or air knives to induce
nucleation, and better optimized annealing procedures, it is
unlikely that elevated humidities have any continued benefit in
PSC fabrication.
Having determined how water vapor affects MAPbI3-based
devices, we next attempted to produce more moisture-resistant
PSCs. Motivated by our study on how HTLs can affect
perovskite stability,33 we attempted to produce more hydro-
phobic poly(3-alkylthiophene) HTLs.39 But although the
polymers were more hydrophobic, and did better protect the
underlying perovskite layer, the resulting devices performed
poorly, if they worked at all. Instead, Kundu et al. opted to use
a physical blend of P3HT and poly(methyl methacrylate)
(PMAA).40 The P3HT self-assembled into nanowires,
providing a percolation network for holes to migrate from
the perovskite layer to the electrode, while the PMMA matrix
proved to be an excellent encapsulant, leading to highly water-
resistant devices. However, while this approach addressed an
important challenge, the PSC performance was limited by the
use of P3HT as the HTL, and perovskite composition and film
quality ultimately advanced the field more than encapsulation-
based strategies.
More recently, motivated by reports of lead halide
perovskites being used as X-ray photodetectors,41 we turned
our attention to the issue of radiation tolerance in these
materials. Specifically, we wanted to understand whether either
perovskite composition or RH affected the rate of radiation-
induced damage.42 In situ GIWAXS was ideally suited to these
studies, as the synchrotron X-ray beam could be used to
simultaneously damage the sample and track the impact of that
beam damage on the perovskite lattice. We found that films of
various mixed-halide perovskites (MAPbI3−xBrx) experienced a
gradual reduction in long-range order with increasing radiation
dose (Figure 4a); however, this gradual vitrification process
was largely independent of perovskite composition. RH led to
a modest increase in the rate of beam damage, but the effect
was relatively small. Instead, we observed that when the
experiments were done under dry conditions, the (100) peak
of the perovskite shifted to larger q values and broadened
significantly (Figure 4b); the same effect was not observed at
higher RH. We hypothesized that this peak shift was due to the
formation of Schottky defects within the film, defects that were
better passivated when water vapor was present (Figure 4c).
■COMPOSITIONAL ENGINEERING
As discussed previously, MAPbI3 has many issues with stability,
not just with respect to humidity, but also heat, oxygen, and
light.43,44 At elevated temperature, there is a tetragonal-to-
cubic phase transition that occurs,45 while at more extreme
temperatures, the loss of volatile byproducts (e.g., methylamine
or iodine) can lead to irreversible degradation.46,47 Other
studies have pointed to the role of oxygen, which scavenges
photogenerated electrons. This leads to an excess of holes,
which can oxidize iodide and lead to either the loss of
molecular iodine or triiodide formation;48 triiodide anions, in
turn, have been shown to contribute to the degradation of the
organic cation.49 More recent work has further highlighted the

However, even relatively early on it was identified that by
making solid solutions with mixed anions (e.g., Br16), the
stability of the perovskite could be substantially improved. As
long as the various A-, B-, and X-site ions in the perovskite
lattice satisfy the Goldschmidt tolerance factor (i.e., fall in the
range of 0.8−1.0),51,52 a variety of perovskite compositions can
be prepared. We initially compared the influence of different
lattice substitutions (either FA or ethylammonium (EA) in the
A-site and either bromide or chloride in the B-site, Figure 5a)
on the stability of the perovskite with respect to either a 85%
RH environment or the photochemical stability in oxygen.53
We found that substitution of 20 mol % MA by FA to form the
mixed perovskite composition (MA0.8 FA0.2PbI3) led to greatly
improved stability in a humid atmosphere (85% RH, up to 100
h as measured by in situ UV/vis spectroscopy); in contrast,
other films (MA0.8 EA0.2PbI3, MAPbI3(Cl), MAPbI3−xBrx)
decomposed 4−6 times faster. More extensive replacement of
MA by FA (MA1−x FAxPbI3, x = 0.6) also led to improved
photochemical stability under 1 Sun irradiation in air, as
compared to samples with lower FA content (Figure 5b). The
improved moisture and photostability of MA1−x FAxPbI3 were
ascribed to the more delocalized positive charge on the FA
cation, which both reduces its ability to hydrogen bond with
water and increases its pKa.
As the field evolved, perovskite compositions converged
toward a fairly complex mixture of ions. A key report by Saliba
et al. showed that the addition of 5% CsI to FA0.83
MA0.17Pb(I0.83Br0.17)3 improved the device efficiency, stability,
and reproducibility,17 and the Cs0.05(FA0.83 MA0.17)0.95Pb-
(I0.83Br0.17)3, (triple cation) composition remains one of the
most widely used to this day. However, given the problems
associated with the MA cation,56 as well as the potential for
halide segregation into I-rich and Br-rich domains, we wanted
to determine whether the MABr and PbBr2 could be omitted
from the triple cation composition (Figure 5c). Our results
showed that this could be done with a small drop in
efficiency.54 The addition of guanidinium iodide and additional
lead iodide also led to a decrease in the trap state density, most
likely because of the additional salts passivating trap states at
grain boundaries, as the guanidinium is too large to be
incorporated into the lattice to any significant degree. As the
field has evolved, it has become clear that overly large cations
like EA and guanidinium do not effectively substitute into the
perovskite A-site, and therefore do not directly modulate the
perovskite stability; however, large cations like phenyl-
ethylammonium derivatives can induce the formation of
lower-dimensional phases that do significantly impact perov-

research. Comparing the relative stability of the various
perovskite formulations, the triple cation composition (Figure
5d, FCM-IB) was notably less photochemically stable than the
composition without either MA or bromide and with the
addition of guanidinium (Figure 5d, FCG-I). Presumably this

cation compared to MA. In a broad sense, the replacement of
MA with FA has been one of the most important develop-

efficiency, but also dramatically improved stability. Although
state-of-the-art devices often use the triple cation composition,
as we demonstrated here, complete removal of the MA cation

■OPERANDO GIWAXS
Although we used in situ GIWAXS quite successfully to
elucidate key perovskite degradation pathways, strictly in situ
experiments do not provide any information about device
performance. As a result, it becomes difficult to correlate the
structural changes observed by GIWAXS to changes in PCE.
Only by simultaneously tracking changes in both crystal
structure and efficiency can the two parameters be connected.
With this in mind, we have been continuing to develop fully
operando GIWAXS methods for the analysis of PSCs (Figure
6a). In these experiments, GIWAXS patterns are collected on
complete devices; through careful placement of electrical leads
(so as not to shadow the detector), J−V curves can
simultaneously be acquired. We first used these methods in
2018 in the study of ITO/ZnO/MAPbI3/P3HT/Ag PSCs.58
In these experiments, the devices were operated in an
atmosphere of 80% RH. Given that our previous in situ
GIWAXS experiments had revealed hydrate formation as a key
degradation mechanism in perovskite films (Figure 3),33 we
initially expected to see the devices fail because of moisture-
induced degradation. Instead, the corresponding I−V curves
and azimuthally integrated linecuts (Figure 6b) showed very
different trends. The scattering data showed little change in the
perovskite (110) peak intensity over the course of the
experiment, whereas the I−V curves revealed a dramatic loss
in PCE after only ca. 15 min. These data challenged our initial
assumptions about perovskite device failure mechanisms and
revealed that iodide migration to the silver electrode (followed
by corrosion at the interface) was in fact the primary reason for
the loss of PCE. Subsequent work has highlighted the
oxidation of PSC electrodes and the relative mobility of the
resulting metal cations,59,60 reinforcing the idea that even
noble metals are noninnocent in the local electrochemical
environment of an operating PSC. Moreover, under the
conditions of the experiment (constant illumination by a
halogen lamp), no hydrate phases or other intermediates were
observed. Subsequent experiments showed that the mono-
hydrate phase would form in the dark, but as soon as the
halogen lamp was turned on, the increase in temperature led to
water desorption and regeneration of the original perovskite
phase. This work highlighted the power of fully operando
GIWAXS methods; without being able to simultaneously track
changes in perovskite crystallinity and changes in device
performance, we would not have realized that the two
parameters were, in fact, decoupled in this instance.
Although our 2018 study58 provided important clues as to
the effect of mobile iodide ions and interfacial redox processes
on device performance, as was discussed previously, there have
been many subsequent advancements in both perovskite
composition (from MAPbI3 to Cs0.05(FA0.83MA0.17)0.95Pb-
(I0.83Br0.17)3) and device architecture made. This makes it an
open question whether the same failure pathways are operative
in more state-of-the-art devices. We therefore wanted to

Looking forward, we expect that operando X-ray scattering
methods will continue to be powerful tools in the analysis of
perovskite degradation mechanisms. The ability to temporally
correlate structural data with device efficiency, on a single
device, allows us to much more conclusively link changes in
device performance to things like phase transformations, defect
formation, and electrode corrosion. Having previously
identified the MA cation as a weak link in the perovskite
composition, one key question will be how MA-free devices
fare under conditions of elevated humidity. Another unknown
is the effect of temperature on defect formation and device
failure; we are currently working on improvements to our
operando sample holder that will allow for measurements at
elevated temperatures. Finally, these methods may allow us to
address lingering questions about how device lifetimes may be
correlated to device efficiencies; anecdotal reports suggest that
high efficiency devices often have improved lifetimes, perhaps

■CONCLUSIONS AND PERSPECTIVES
The field of PSCs has advanced tremendously over the past
decade. Our understanding of perovskite carrier dynamics and
photophysics has improved significantly, perovskite composi-
tions have evolved from MAPbI3 to complex mixtures of
cations and anions, and device designs and components have
all advanced as well. Today’s state-of-the-art devices, with
PCEs well in excess of 20%, would have been almost
unthinkable a decade ago, highlighting how much progress
has been made.
We have also significantly improved our understanding of
the complex chemistry of lead halide perovskites. It requires
relatively little energy to structurally deform a lead iodide
lattice, making it easy to accommodate water in the structure
(leading to the formation of hydrate phases), form defects, or
transition between polymorphs. In situ GIWAXS measure-
ments have helped elucidate many of these transformations,
and operando GIWAXS measurements are similarly helping to
correlate these structural changes to changes in device
performance. As a result, our understanding of device failure
mechanisms has improved. The best PSCs now have not just
excellent efficiency, but accelerated aging tests also project
quite reasonable device lifetimes. With that said, there is still
much work to be done to make sure that perovskite-based
modules are robust enough to survive outdoor use in a wide
variety of harsh environmental conditions. Passivating agents,
interfacial barrier layers, and of course encapsulants are all
promising strategies in this regard. Proper execution of these
stability and lifetime measurements, against a well-defined
standard, will be crucial in facilitating comparisons between
laboratories and advancing the field overall.
The field has also seen a significant paradigm shift in the past
few years as the efficiency of lab-scale (i.e., < 1 cm2) cells has
started to plateau. With performance and even stability no
longer being limiting factors for spin-coated devices, device
scale-up has been brought to the forefront. More scalable
coating techniques like slot-die coating, blade coating, and
even screen printing are increasingly being used for the
production of large-area devices.4,5 Here, much of the
knowledge gained from spin-coated PSCs cannot be directly
applied to these larger-area cells, as the film formation and
crystallization dynamics of these alternative coating methods
are radically different. As production scales up, confining the
fabrication process to a glovebox becomes significantly more
difficult, and fabricating devices under ambient conditions
becomes increasingly imperative. This creates additional
challenges, both in terms of performance and reproducibility.
However, if these challenges can be met, we will move
substantially closer to realizing the full potential of perovskite
materials for applications in energy, imaging, and optoelec-
tronics.

Mater. 2025, 7, 3621−3631\nRead Online\nACCESS\nMetrics & More\nArticle Recommendations\nABSTRACT: Over the past decade, there have been tremendous advances in the design\nand fabrication of perovskite solar cells (PSCs). The unique optoelectronic properties of\nlead halide perovskites have resulted in solution-processed solar cells with excellent\nefficiencies, and significant advances have now been made in both lab-scale and large-area\ndevices. As the technology moves toward commercialization, it is increasingly important to\nunderstand the stability of the devices under operationally relevant conditions. What is the\nprojected lifetime of a perovskite-based module? Which environmental factors (e.g.,\nhumidity, heat, light) are most pernicious? What is the precise mechanism of device failure?\nTo this end, both in situ and operando characterization techniques have proven to be useful\nmethods and have provided important information about perovskite crystallization,\ndegradation, and transformation processes. This spotlight article discusses recent advances\nin PSCs from both a device fabrication and device failure perspective, highlighting our\nresearch group’s contributions along the way.\nKEYWORDS: lead halide perovskites, optoelectronic devices, operando, X-ray scattering, stability, device lifetime\n■INTRODUCTION\nOver the past decade, there has been tremendous advancement\nin the power conversion efficiency (PCE) of perovskite solar\ncells (PSCs). From the early report of Kojima et al. in 20091 to\ntoday, PCEs have increased from a paltry 3.8%1 to a record\n27.0%,2,3 with perovskite/silicon tandems even higher at\n34.6%.3 Given the promising results achieved with labora-\ntory-scale devices, the field has devoted significant efforts to\ndevice scale-up; blade-coated and slot-die coated devices have\nboth become much more common,4 as has the roll-to-roll\nprocessing of flexible devices.5 Given the numerous potential\nbenefits of perovskite technology −good performance, lower\nproduction costs and embodied energies, and lightweight and\nflexible modules −many companies are now attempting to\ncommercialize the technology.\nIn a typical PSC, the light-absorbing lead halide perovskite\n(of general formula ABX3) is sandwiched between two charge\ntransport layers (CTLs). When illuminated, the photo-\ngenerated electrons and holes are transported to their\nrespective electrodes via a p-type hole transport layer (HTL)\nand n-type electron transport layer (ETL). In an ideal HTL,\nthe valence band maximum (EVB) is slightly higher than that of\nthe perovskite for efficient hole extraction, while the\nconduction band minimum (ECB) is sufficiently high to block\nthe transport of electrons. The reverse is true for the ETL. The\ntwo main PSC designs then depend on the relative ordering of\nthe CTLs, with regular devices featuring a n-i-p structure, and\ninverted devices having a p-i-n design (Figure 1a,b). Early\nreports almost universally used the regular (n-i-p) architec-\nture,6,7 where the ETL was deposited onto the substrate\nelectrode (typically a transparent conductive oxide, TCO,\nFigure 1a). This was predominantly done for historical\nreasons; in many ways, PSCs evolved from dye-sensitized\nsolar cells, and early designs featured the same mesoporous\nTiO2 ETL and the same solid-state hole-transport material\n(2,2,7,7′-tetra[N,N-bis(4-methoxyphenyl)amino]-9,9′-spirobi-\nfluorene, Spiro-OMeTAD).1,8 Since then, the mesoporous\nTiO2 layer has been largely replaced with compact, planar\nalternatives.9,10 The relative instability of Spiro-OMeTAD,\nrelated to its dopants, also led to a search for alternative HTLs.\nThe end result of this work has been a gradual shift toward\ninverted (p-i-n) structures,11 with both NiOx\n12 and carbazole-\nbased self-assembled monolayers (e.g., MeO-2PACz)13\nbecoming popular due to their high performance and\ncomparatively good stability.\nIn parallel with these advancements in device structure,\nadvancements in perovskite composition were also being\nmade. The prototypical lead halide perovskite is methyl-\nammonium lead iodide (MAPbI3), which was the composition\nemployed in many early studies.6,14,15 However, it was\napparent early on that this particular material was easily\ndegraded. The prototypical lead halide\nperovskite, MAPbI3, was identified early on as being easily\ndegraded under ambient laboratory conditions, and it was\nassumed that this was the primary cause of cell failure. Early\nwork from our group by Yang et al. sought to better elucidate\nthe role of relative humidity (RH) in this degradation pathway\nand to better quantify the rate at which the degradation\noccurred.33 A custom-machined UV/vis cell allowed us to\nmonitor the UV/vis spectra of perovskite films as they were\ndegraded by an atmosphere of controlled RH (Figure 3a). The\nhigh-energy absorption features below 500 nm and optical\nband gap ca. 760 nm are hallmarks of MAPbI3. At high RHs\n(80 −100%) the absorption features below 500 nm show\nrapid decay and the band gap at 760 nm becomes much less\ndistinct. A corresponding increase in the background\nabsorbance (λ > 800 nm) is indicative of Mie scattering,\nindicating that large crystallites are being formed within the\nfilm as part of the decomposition process. Tracking the\nabsorption at 410 nm allowed us to compare degradation rates,\nand it was found that the decomposition rate was highly\ndependent on RH, with very high RH levels (80 −100%)\ncausing complete decomposition within 6 h, and lower RH\n(e.g., 20%) causing only minimal degradation over the course\nof several days (Figure 3a, inset).\nWe subsequently turned to in situ GIWAXS to identify the\nstructural changes occurring during this moisture-induced\ndegradation process.33 Although the data quality from these\nexperiments was modest, owing to very strong background\nscattering from the amorphous glass substrate (q = 10−23\nnm−1, or 1.0−2.3 Å−1), after 5 h of exposure to 80% RH, new\npeaks become apparent in the GIWAXS pattern (Figure 3c) at\n5 and 7 nm−1 (0.5 and 0.7 Å−1). Expanding upon these early in situ UV/vis\nresults, Yang et al. showed how the choice of HTL (Spiro-\nOMeTAD, poly[bis(4-phenyl)(2,4,6-trimethylphenyl)]amine\n(PTAA), or P3HT) affects the moisture stability of MAPbI3\nfilms.33 It was found that films coated with Spiro-OMeTAD\ndegraded relatively quickly, in part because of substantial\ncracking of the Spiro-OMeTAD layer;33 in contrast, PTAA,\nand especially P3HT, provided more conformal coverage of\nthe perovskite and acted as a barrier to moisture ingress.\nAdditional work focused on the effect of the ZnO ETL on the\nthermal stability of MAPbI3 films.21 Early on, we found that\nattempts to fabricate MAPbI3 films on top of ZnO via a one-\nstep deposition and annealing process always met with failure.\nIn this work, we found that the more basic nature of the ZnO\nsurface (compared to, e.g., TiO2) leads to proton-transfer\nreactions at the interface, resulting in the deprotonation of the\nMA cation, the loss of methylamine, and the formation of PbI2.\nIt was also found that the presence of surface hydroxyl groups\nworsened the stability of the perovskite film. Instead, Kundu et al. opted to use\na physical blend of P3HT and poly(methyl methacrylate)\n(PMAA).40 The P3HT self-assembled into nanowires,\nproviding a percolation network for holes to migrate from\nthe perovskite layer to the electrode, while the PMMA matrix\nproved to be an excellent encapsulant, leading to highly water-\nresistant devices. However, while this approach addressed an\nimportant challenge, the PSC performance was limited by the\nuse of P3HT as the HTL, and perovskite composition and film\nquality ultimately advanced the field more than encapsulation-\nbased strategies.\nMore recently, motivated by reports of lead halide\nperovskites being used as X-ray photodetectors,41 we turned\nour attention to the issue of radiation tolerance in these\nmaterials. Specifically, we wanted to understand whether either\nperovskite composition or RH affected the rate of radiation-\ninduced damage.42 In situ GIWAXS was ideally suited to these\nstudies, as the synchrotron X-ray beam could be used to\nsimultaneously damage the sample and track the impact of that\nbeam damage on the perovskite lattice. A key report by Saliba\net al. showed that the addition of 5% CsI to FA0.83\nMA0.17Pb(I0.83Br0.17)3 improved the device efficiency, stability,\nand reproducibility,17 and the Cs0.05(FA0.83 MA0.17)0.95Pb-\n(I0.83Br0.17)3, (triple cation) composition remains one of the\nmost widely used to this day. Our results\nshowed that this could be done with a small drop in\nefficiency.54 The addition of guanidinium iodide and additional\nlead iodide also led to a decrease in the trap state density, most\nlikely because of the additional salts passivating trap states at\ngrain boundaries, as the guanidinium is too large to be\nincorporated into the lattice to any significant degree. As the\nfield has evolved, it has become clear that overly large cations\nlike EA and guanidinium do not effectively substitute into the\nperovskite A-site, and therefore do not directly modulate the\nperovskite stability; however, large cations like phenyl-\nethylammonium derivatives can induce the formation of\nlower-dimensional phases that do significantly impact perov-\nskite stability,57 and this continues to be an area of active\nresearch. Comparing the relative stability of the various\nperovskite formulations, the triple cation composition (Figure\n5d, FCM-IB) was notably less photochemically stable than the\ncomposition without either MA or bromide and with the\naddition of guanidinium (Figure 5d, FCG-I). Presumably this\nis because of the lower photochemical reactivity of the FA\ncation compared to MA. In a broad sense, the replacement of\nMA with FA has been one of the most important develop-\nments in PSCs, imparting the devices with not only better\nefficiency, but also dramatically improved stability. As a result, it becomes difficult to correlate the\nstructural changes observed by GIWAXS to changes in PCE.\nOnly by simultaneously tracking changes in both crystal\nstructure and efficiency can the two parameters be connected.\nWith this in mind, we have been continuing to develop fully\noperando GIWAXS methods for the analysis of PSCs (Figure\n6a). In these experiments, GIWAXS patterns are collected on\ncomplete devices; through careful placement of electrical leads\n(so as not to shadow the detector), J−V curves can\nsimultaneously be acquired. We first used these methods in\n2018 in the study of ITO/ZnO/MAPbI3/P3HT/Ag PSCs.58\nIn these experiments, the devices were operated in an\natmosphere of 80% RH. Given that our previous in situ\nGIWAXS experiments had revealed hydrate formation as a key\ndegradation mechanism in perovskite films (Figure 3),33 we\ninitially expected to see the devices fail because of moisture-\ninduced degradation. Instead, the corresponding I−V curves\nand azimuthally integrated linecuts (Figure 6b) showed very\ndifferent trends. The scattering data showed little change in the\nperovskite (110) peak intensity over the course of the\nexperiment, whereas the I−V curves revealed a dramatic loss\nin PCE after only ca. 15 min. These data challenged our initial\nassumptions about perovskite device failure mechanisms and\nrevealed that iodide migration to the silver electrode (followed\nby corrosion at the interface) was in fact the primary reason for\nthe loss of PCE. Subsequent work has highlighted the\noxidation of PSC electrodes and the relative mobility of the\nresulting metal cations,59,60 reinforcing the idea that even\nnoble metals are noninnocent in the local electrochemical\nenvironment of an operating PSC. Subsequent experiments showed that the mono-\nhydrate phase would form in the dark, but as soon as the\nhalogen lamp was turned on, the increase in temperature led to\nwater desorption and regeneration of the original perovskite\nphase. This work highlighted the power of fully operando\nGIWAXS methods; without being able to simultaneously track\nchanges in perovskite crystallinity and changes in device\nperformance, we would not have realized that the two\nparameters were, in fact, decoupled in this instance.\nAlthough our 2018 study58 provided important clues as to\nthe effect of mobile iodide ions and interfacial redox processes\non device performance, as was discussed previously, there have\nbeen many subsequent advancements in both perovskite\ncomposition (from MAPbI3 to Cs0.05(FA0.83MA0.17)0.95Pb-\n(I0.83Br0.17)3) and device architecture made. Since these operando methods provide\ncorrelated data on a single cell, they can potentially be used\nto tease out subtle differences in failure mechanisms on\notherwise nominally identical devices.\n■CONCLUSIONS AND PERSPECTIVES\nThe field of PSCs has advanced tremendously over the past\ndecade. Our understanding of perovskite carrier dynamics and\nphotophysics has improved significantly, perovskite composi-\ntions have evolved from MAPbI3 to complex mixtures of\ncations and anions, and device designs and components have\nall advanced as well. Today’s state-of-the-art devices, with\nPCEs well in excess of 20%, would have been almost\nunthinkable a decade ago, highlighting how much progress\nhas been made.\nWe have also significantly improved our understanding of\nthe complex chemistry of lead halide perovskites. It requires\nrelatively little energy to structurally deform a lead iodide\nlattice, making it easy to accommodate water in the structure\n(leading to the formation of hydrate phases), form defects, or\ntransition between polymorphs. In situ GIWAXS measure-\nments have helped elucidate many of these transformations,\nand operando GIWAXS measurements are similarly helping to\ncorrelate these structural changes to changes in device\nperformance. As a result, our understanding of device failure\nmechanisms has improved. The best PSCs now have not just\nexcellent efficiency, but accelerated aging tests also project\nquite reasonable device lifetimes. With that said, there is still\nmuch work to be done to make sure that perovskite-based\nmodules are robust enough to survive outdoor use in a wide\nvariety of harsh environmental conditions. Passivating agents,\ninterfacial barrier layers, and of course encapsulants are all\npromising strategies in this regard. Proper execution of these\nstability and lifetime measurements, against a well-defined\nstandard, will be crucial in facilitating comparisons between\nlaboratories and advancing the field overall.\nThe field has also seen a significant paradigm shift in the past\nfew years as the efficiency of lab-scale (i.e., < 1 cm2) cells has\nstarted to plateau. With performance and even stability no\nlonger being limiting factors for spin-coated devices, device\nscale-up has been brought to the forefront. More scalable\ncoating techniques like slot-die coating, blade coating, and\neven screen printing are increasingly being used for the\nproduction of large-area devices.4,5 Here, much of the\nknowledge gained from spin-coated PSCs cannot be directly\napplied to these larger-area cells, as the film formation and\ncrystallization dynamics of these alternative coating methods\nare radically different. As production scales up, confining the\nfabrication process to a glovebox becomes significantly more\ndifficult, and fabricating devices under ambient conditions\nbecomes increasingly imperative. This creates additional\nchallenges, both in terms of performance and reproducibility.\nHowever, if these challenges can be met, we will move\nsubstantially closer to realizing the full potential of perovskite\nmaterials for applications in energy, imaging, and optoelec-\ntronics.\n■AUTHOR INFORMATION\nCorresponding Author\nTimothy L. ABSTRACT: Over the past decade, there have been tremendous advances in the design
and fabrication of perovskite solar cells (PSCs). The unique optoelectronic properties of
lead halide perovskites have resulted in solution-processed solar cells with excellent
efficiencies, and significant advances have now been made in both lab-scale and large-area
devices. As the technology moves toward commercialization, it is increasingly important to
understand the stability of the devices under operationally relevant conditions. What is the
projected lifetime of a perovskite-based module? Which environmental factors (e.g.,
humidity, heat, light) are most pernicious? What is the precise mechanism of device failure?
To this end, both in situ and operando characterization techniques have proven to be useful
methods and have provided important information about perovskite crystallization,
degradation, and transformation processes. This spotlight article discusses recent advances
in PSCs from both a device fabrication and device failure perspective, highlighting our
research group’s contributions along the way.
KEYWORDS: lead halide perovskites, optoelectronic devices, operando, X-ray scattering, stability, device lifetime
■INTRODUCTION
Over the past decade, there has been tremendous advancement
in the power conversion efficiency (PCE) of perovskite solar
cells (PSCs). From the early report of Kojima et al. in 20091 to
today, PCEs have increased from a paltry 3.8%1 to a record
27.0%,2,3 with perovskite/silicon tandems even higher at
34.6%.3 Given the promising results achieved with labora-
tory-scale devices, the field has devoted significant efforts to
device scale-up; blade-coated and slot-die coated devices have
both become much more common,4 as has the roll-to-roll
processing of flexible devices.5 Given the numerous potential
benefits of perovskite technology −good performance, lower
production costs and embodied energies, and lightweight and
flexible modules −many companies are now attempting to
commercialize the technology.
In a typical PSC, the light-absorbing lead halide perovskite
(of general formula ABX3) is sandwiched between two charge
transport layers (CTLs). When illuminated, the photo-
generated electrons and holes are transported to their
respective electrodes via a p-type hole transport layer (HTL)
and n-type electron transport layer (ETL). In an ideal HTL,
the valence band maximum (EVB) is slightly higher than that of
the perovskite for efficient hole extraction, while the
conduction band minimum (ECB) is sufficiently high to block
the transport of electrons. The reverse is true for the ETL. The
two main PSC designs then depend on the relative ordering of
the CTLs, with regular devices featuring a n-i-p structure, and
inverted devices having a p-i-n design (Figure 1a,b). Early
reports almost universally used the regular (n-i-p) architec-
ture,6,7 where the ETL was deposited onto the substrate
electrode (typically a transparent conductive oxide, TCO,
Figure 1a). This was predominantly done for historical
reasons; in many ways, PSCs evolved from dye-sensitized
solar cells, and early designs featured the same mesoporous
TiO2 ETL and the same solid-state hole-transport material
(2,2,7,7′-tetra[N,N-bis(4-methoxyphenyl)amino]-9,9′-spirobi-
fluorene, Spiro-OMeTAD).1,8 Since then, the mesoporous
TiO2 layer has been largely replaced with compact, planar
alternatives.9,10 The relative instability of Spiro-OMeTAD,
related to its dopants, also led to a search for alternative HTLs.
The end result of this work has been a gradual shift toward
inverted (p-i-n) structures,11 with both NiOx
12 and carbazole-
based self-assembled monolayers (e.g., MeO-2PACz)13
becoming popular due to their high performance and
comparatively good stability.
In parallel with these advancements in device structure,
advancements in perovskite composition were also being
made. The prototypical lead halide perovskite is methyl-
ammonium lead iodide (MAPbI3), which was the composition
employed in many early studies.6,14,15 However, it was
apparent early on that this particular material was easily
degraded. Solid solutions of iodide and bromide anions were
initially found to improve stability.16 Subsequent work led to

the development of state-of-the-art compositions, which are a
complex mixture of MA, formamidinium (FA) and cesium A-
site cations, and iodide and bromide anions. The
Cs0.05(FA0.83MA0.17)0.95Pb(I0.83Br0.17)3 composition, originally
introduced by Saliba et al. in 2016,17 is now ubiquitous in the
PSC literature due to its combination of excellent performance
and good stability.
As PSCs move into the later stages of commercialization, it
is increasingly important to understand the stability of the
devices under operationally relevant conditions. These
concerns were largely absent from the early perovskite
literature, which focused almost exclusively on efficiency;
however, in the past few years, lifetime and stability
measurements have moved to the forefront of the field. In
contrast to PCE measurements, which have highly stand-
ardized test protocols (i.e., 1 Sun, AM1.5G spectrum, 25 °C),
there were initially no standard test conditions for perovskite
stability. A consensus statement, published in 2020, recom-
mended using test protocols originally put forth at the
International Summit on Organic Solar Cells Stability
(ISOS).18 This more standardized approach has the potential
to greatly improve the rate of progress, as researchers can more
clearly benchmark how perovskite composition, the choice of
CTLs, and device architecture affect device stability. This is
greatly improving not just overall device lifetimes, but also our
understanding of how lead halide perovskites respond to a
variety of environmental stimuli (e.g., relative humidity, heat,
light, and oxygen) and of device failure mechanisms.
This spotlight article will focus on our research group’s
contributions to the development of PSCs. Our early
contributions to the field were primarily in the area of PSC
design. In more recent years, our emphasis has shifted toward
the characterization of lead halide perovskites and PSCs using
in situ and operando grazing-incidence wide-angle X-ray
scattering (GIWAXS) techniques, which has provided
important insights into perovskite degradation mechanisms.
■PEROVSKITE SOLAR CELL DESIGN
In 2014, when our research group first started working in this
area, PSCs still closely resembled dye-sensitized solar cells in
terms of their structure and design. As a result, most devices
still used a mesoporous TiO2 layer as the ETL. The downside
to this design is that a mesoporous TiO2 layer requires high-
temperature sintering at ∼500 °C, significantly increasing the
embodied energy of the device;19 such layers are also generally
incompatible with flexible (i.e., plastic) substrates. At this
point, our group reported the use of a ZnO nanoparticle film as
the ETL, which could be deposited entirely at room
temperature (Figure 2a).20 In a departure from the conven-
tional mesostructured devices of the time, the device also used
a planar heterojunction (with a ITO/ZnO/MAPbI3/Spiro-
OMeTAD/Ag structure), simplifying the overall fabrication
process. Part of the key to making this approach work was
using a two-step deposition procedure for the perovskite,
which had been reported earlier by Burshka et al.14 This
involved spin coating a layer of PbI2 onto the ZnO surface,
followed by immersion in a MAI solution. This allowed us to
circumvent the usual perovskite annealing step, which we later
found to work very poorly on ZnO substrates.21 The best PCE
for these devices was 15.7% (Figure 2b), which was among the
highest reported at the time, and was especially notable
considering the lack of mesoporous scaffold and any high-
temperature processing steps. The low-temperature processing
also enabled the fabrication of flexible devices with efficiencies

of up to 10.2%. The shift away from mesoporous structures
was a significant advancement for the time, and planar
heterojunction designs are still found in state-of-the-art devices
today; however, with the advent of triple-cation composi-
tions,17 and the problems with interfacial surface chemistry on
ZnO surfaces,21 the two-step processing method has largely
been replaced by more conventional coating and annealing
approaches.
Having established that planar heterojunctions could be
used to produce highly efficient devices, we next set out to
understand how the thickness of the perovskite layer affected
the generation, transport, and collection of charge carriers.
This work used a more cost-effective HTL, poly(3-hexylth-
iophene-2,5-diyl) (P3HT), in a ITO/ZnO/MAPbI3/P3HT/
Ag device architecture.22 We found that the PbI2 deposition
method, whether spin-coated or thermally evaporated, had
only a minimal effect on device performance. Rather, the
thickness of the perovskite layer was the most significant factor
influencing the PCE. The thinnest devices (110 nm) showed
pinhole shorts and significant recombination at the ZnO
interface, leading to a low shunt resistance and a corresponding
loss in Voc (Figure 2c). As the film thickness increased from
110 to 330 nm, there was a marked improvement in both the
Voc and FF. This enhancement correlated with increases in the
shunt resistance, suggesting that the perovskite layer was now
thick enough to eliminate any short-circuit pathways, and the
PCE reached a maximum (11.3%) at 330 nm. As the thickness
increased beyond 400 nm, the series resistance also increased,
consistent with the increased distance over which charge
carriers have to travel prior to being collected at the electrodes.
By the time the thickness was >500 nm, the PCE was
extremely low, which clearly shows the limitations of the two-
step deposition method in a planar heterojunction config-
uration. Although many of the same principles apply, more
modern approaches produce PSCs with optimal thickness in
the range of 500 −700 nm.24 Higher quality perovskite films
can be made thicker without increasing the series resistance,
leading to higher overall PCEs.
Having previously shown that the low-temperature process-
ing of the ZnO and perovskite layers could be used to fabricate
PSCs on flexible substrates,20 we wanted to determine the
limitations of such devices. Depending on the intended
application, flexible cells might be coated in a roll-to-roll
fashion but then incorporated into a largely fixed installation;
however, in more mobile applications, they might also be
subjected to many repeated bending cycles during their
lifetime. The latter presents significant problems with
mechanical stability, as flexible devices are prone to issues
with either delamination or cracking when subjected to
repeated mechanical stress. In our study, we prepared PSCs
on a poly(ethylene terephthalate) (PET) substrate coated with
a metallized indium oxide (M-In2O3) electrode.23 The devices
were wrapped around a cylinder of known curvature for up to
2000 cycles, and we tracked the changes in device performance
with repeated cycling. Device failure was determined to be due
to crack formation in the transparent conductive oxide (M-
In2O3) layer, with short-circuits occurring quite suddenly after
100 to 1100 bending cycles. On replacing the metal oxide with

in performance, primarily driven by an increase in series
resistance. The HC-PEDOT:PSS electrode is clearly not
impervious to the effects of mechanical fatigue, but simply
degrades in a much more gradual way (and not by sudden
crack propagation). Work in this area has continued, with
other groups more successfully finding the intrinsic mechanical
limits of perovskite films,25,26 and efforts going into improving
mechanical stability (e.g., cross-linking oligomers at the
perovskite grain boundaries,27 using lamination protocols to
encapsulate flexible PSCs.28).
Additional work from our group reported unique behavior of
the planar heterojunctions prepared via the two-step
deposition method. In order to better understand the role of
the ZnO layer, we prepared PSCs both with and without the
ZnO ETL, using either a P3HT or Spiro-OMeTAD HTL.29
Surprisingly, the devices without the ZnO ETL performed
quite well; there was still a loss in PCE relative to the controls
with a ZnO ETL, however, the drop in performance was
relatively modest. The Voc of the ZnO-free devices was ∼1 V,
indicating a relative lack of charge carrier recombination at the
ITO contact. This behavior may be in part due to the unique
fabrication pathway of these devices. The initial PbI2 layer is
converted to MAPbI3 in a top-down manner, via diffusion and
intercalation of MAI into the PbI2 film. This often leaves a
small, residual amount of unreacted PbI2, presumably highly
localized at the interface with the ITO substrate. This
unreacted PbI2 may have been serving to block holes, leading
to the reasonable efficiencies that were observed. Notably, the
ZnO-free devices had a slightly improved stability, perhaps due
to eliminating the reactive ZnO/perovskite interface (see
below). Although other ETL-free designs have been reported
since (e.g., those that use modified TCOs30−32), ultimately
there is little to recommend such a design for practical
application; the ETL is a relatively simple and inexpensive
component, and there is little to be gained from its elimination.
■STABILITY OF LEAD HALIDE PEROVSKITES
Despite accommodating a wide variety of cell designs and
producing excellent PCEs, a fundamental issue with PSCs was
a lack of long-term stability. The prototypical lead halide
perovskite, MAPbI3, was identified early on as being easily
degraded under ambient laboratory conditions, and it was
assumed that this was the primary cause of cell failure. Early
work from our group by Yang et al. sought to better elucidate
the role of relative humidity (RH) in this degradation pathway
and to better quantify the rate at which the degradation
occurred.33 A custom-machined UV/vis cell allowed us to
monitor the UV/vis spectra of perovskite films as they were
degraded by an atmosphere of controlled RH (Figure 3a). The
high-energy absorption features below 500 nm and optical
band gap ca. 760 nm are hallmarks of MAPbI3. At high RHs
(80 −100%) the absorption features below 500 nm show
rapid decay and the band gap at 760 nm becomes much less
distinct. A corresponding increase in the background
absorbance (λ > 800 nm) is indicative of Mie scattering,
indicating that large crystallites are being formed within the
film as part of the decomposition process. Tracking the
absorption at 410 nm allowed us to compare degradation rates,
and it was found that the decomposition rate was highly
dependent on RH, with very high RH levels (80 −100%)
causing complete decomposition within 6 h, and lower RH
(e.g., 20%) causing only minimal degradation over the course
of several days (Figure 3a, inset).
We subsequently turned to in situ GIWAXS to identify the
structural changes occurring during this moisture-induced
degradation process.33 Although the data quality from these
experiments was modest, owing to very strong background
scattering from the amorphous glass substrate (q = 10−23
nm−1, or 1.0−2.3 Å−1), after 5 h of exposure to 80% RH, new
peaks become apparent in the GIWAXS pattern (Figure 3c) at
5 and 7 nm−1 (0.5 and 0.7 Å−1). From the 2D plot of the
azimuthally integrated linecuts (Figure 3d), this intermediate
starts to appear after ca. 2.5 h of exposure. This feature was
initially ascribed to the dihydrate phase MA4PbI6·2H2O
(Figure 3b), which contains isolated PbI6
4−octahedra;
however, other subsequent studies34 have confirmed this
intermediate phase to be the monohydrate, MAPbI3·H2O, a
1D structure of edge-sharing PbI6 octahedra.35 In either case,
these hydrated phases eventually lead to the irreversible
formation of hexagonal PbI2 (Figure 3b).
Although we identified key degradation mechanisms for
MAPbI3, the perovskite is never found by itself in a device; we
also needed to know how the choice of CTLs affected
perovskite stability. Expanding upon these early in situ UV/vis
results, Yang et al. showed how the choice of HTL (Spiro-
OMeTAD, poly[bis(4-phenyl)(2,4,6-trimethylphenyl)]amine
(PTAA), or P3HT) affects the moisture stability of MAPbI3
films.33 It was found that films coated with Spiro-OMeTAD
degraded relatively quickly, in part because of substantial
cracking of the Spiro-OMeTAD layer;33 in contrast, PTAA,
and especially P3HT, provided more conformal coverage of
the perovskite and acted as a barrier to moisture ingress.
Additional work focused on the effect of the ZnO ETL on the
thermal stability of MAPbI3 films.21 Early on, we found that
attempts to fabricate MAPbI3 films on top of ZnO via a one-
step deposition and annealing process always met with failure.
In this work, we found that the more basic nature of the ZnO
surface (compared to, e.g., TiO2) leads to proton-transfer
reactions at the interface, resulting in the deprotonation of the
MA cation, the loss of methylamine, and the formation of PbI2.
It was also found that the presence of surface hydroxyl groups
worsened the stability of the perovskite film. We subsequently
compared additional ETLs and mesoporous scaffolds −planar
TiO2, mesoporous TiO2, and mesoporous Al2O3 −to see how
they affected the perovskite degradation process at 93% RH.36
The mesoporous scaffolds did appear to protect the underlying
perovskite from moisture ingress, which in part explains the
better stability of early mesoporous designs compared to our
planar heterojunction based on ZnO. However, in a modern
context, such scaffolds add significantly to cell complexity and
embodied energy, and are simply unnecessary with the advent
of more stable perovskite compositions (see below).
With humidity having such a deleterious effect on perovskite
films, most of the research in this area focused on perovskite
degradation pathways. However, early work37 suggested that a
modest RH during fabrication could have a positive impact on
the growth of the perovskite film. Gangishetty et al. studied the
role of RH during the spin-coating process by placing the spin-
coated inside a glovebag of controlled RH.38 When the
perovskite films were deposited under dry conditions (RH ∼
1%), small crystallites with numerous grain boundaries were
observed, resulting in poor carrier transport and lower device
performance. With more water vapor present (RH ∼40%),
larger perovskite crystallites were observed with fewer grain
boundaries; this both increased device performance and
reduced the amount of hysteresis observed in the J−V curve.

Excessive moisture was, unsurprisingly, problematic, with the
devices fabricated at high humidities performing quite poorly.
However, with improvements in perovskite coating procedures,
including the use of antisolvents and/or air knives to induce
nucleation, and better optimized annealing procedures, it is
unlikely that elevated humidities have any continued benefit in
PSC fabrication.
Having determined how water vapor affects MAPbI3-based
devices, we next attempted to produce more moisture-resistant
PSCs. Motivated by our study on how HTLs can affect
perovskite stability,33 we attempted to produce more hydro-
phobic poly(3-alkylthiophene) HTLs.39 But although the
polymers were more hydrophobic, and did better protect the
underlying perovskite layer, the resulting devices performed
poorly, if they worked at all. Instead, Kundu et al. opted to use
a physical blend of P3HT and poly(methyl methacrylate)
(PMAA).40 The P3HT self-assembled into nanowires,
providing a percolation network for holes to migrate from
the perovskite layer to the electrode, while the PMMA matrix
proved to be an excellent encapsulant, leading to highly water-
resistant devices. However, while this approach addressed an
important challenge, the PSC performance was limited by the
use of P3HT as the HTL, and perovskite composition and film
quality ultimately advanced the field more than encapsulation-
based strategies.
More recently, motivated by reports of lead halide
perovskites being used as X-ray photodetectors,41 we turned
our attention to the issue of radiation tolerance in these
materials. Specifically, we wanted to understand whether either
perovskite composition or RH affected the rate of radiation-
induced damage.42 In situ GIWAXS was ideally suited to these
studies, as the synchrotron X-ray beam could be used to
simultaneously damage the sample and track the impact of that
beam damage on the perovskite lattice. We found that films of
various mixed-halide perovskites (MAPbI3−xBrx) experienced a
gradual reduction in long-range order with increasing radiation
dose (Figure 4a); however, this gradual vitrification process
was largely independent of perovskite composition. RH led to
a modest increase in the rate of beam damage, but the effect
was relatively small. Instead, we observed that when the
experiments were done under dry conditions, the (100) peak
of the perovskite shifted to larger q values and broadened
significantly (Figure 4b); the same effect was not observed at
higher RH. We hypothesized that this peak shift was due to the
formation of Schottky defects within the film, defects that were
better passivated when water vapor was present (Figure 4c).
■COMPOSITIONAL ENGINEERING
As discussed previously, MAPbI3 has many issues with stability,
not just with respect to humidity, but also heat, oxygen, and
light.43,44 At elevated temperature, there is a tetragonal-to-
cubic phase transition that occurs,45 while at more extreme
temperatures, the loss of volatile byproducts (e.g., methylamine
or iodine) can lead to irreversible degradation.46,47 Other
studies have pointed to the role of oxygen, which scavenges
photogenerated electrons. This leads to an excess of holes,
which can oxidize iodide and lead to either the loss of
molecular iodine or triiodide formation;48 triiodide anions, in
turn, have been shown to contribute to the degradation of the
organic cation.49 More recent work has further highlighted the

However, even relatively early on it was identified that by
making solid solutions with mixed anions (e.g., Br16), the
stability of the perovskite could be substantially improved. As
long as the various A-, B-, and X-site ions in the perovskite
lattice satisfy the Goldschmidt tolerance factor (i.e., fall in the
range of 0.8−1.0),51,52 a variety of perovskite compositions can
be prepared. We initially compared the influence of different
lattice substitutions (either FA or ethylammonium (EA) in the
A-site and either bromide or chloride in the B-site, Figure 5a)
on the stability of the perovskite with respect to either a 85%
RH environment or the photochemical stability in oxygen.53
We found that substitution of 20 mol % MA by FA to form the
mixed perovskite composition (MA0.8 FA0.2PbI3) led to greatly
improved stability in a humid atmosphere (85% RH, up to 100
h as measured by in situ UV/vis spectroscopy); in contrast,
other films (MA0.8 EA0.2PbI3, MAPbI3(Cl), MAPbI3−xBrx)
decomposed 4−6 times faster. More extensive replacement of
MA by FA (MA1−x FAxPbI3, x = 0.6) also led to improved
photochemical stability under 1 Sun irradiation in air, as
compared to samples with lower FA content (Figure 5b). The
improved moisture and photostability of MA1−x FAxPbI3 were
ascribed to the more delocalized positive charge on the FA
cation, which both reduces its ability to hydrogen bond with
water and increases its pKa.
As the field evolved, perovskite compositions converged
toward a fairly complex mixture of ions. A key report by Saliba
et al. showed that the addition of 5% CsI to FA0.83
MA0.17Pb(I0.83Br0.17)3 improved the device efficiency, stability,
and reproducibility,17 and the Cs0.05(FA0.83 MA0.17)0.95Pb-
(I0.83Br0.17)3, (triple cation) composition remains one of the
most widely used to this day. However, given the problems
associated with the MA cation,56 as well as the potential for
halide segregation into I-rich and Br-rich domains, we wanted
to determine whether the MABr and PbBr2 could be omitted
from the triple cation composition (Figure 5c). Our results
showed that this could be done with a small drop in
efficiency.54 The addition of guanidinium iodide and additional
lead iodide also led to a decrease in the trap state density, most
likely because of the additional salts passivating trap states at
grain boundaries, as the guanidinium is too large to be
incorporated into the lattice to any significant degree. As the
field has evolved, it has become clear that overly large cations
like EA and guanidinium do not effectively substitute into the
perovskite A-site, and therefore do not directly modulate the
perovskite stability; however, large cations like phenyl-
ethylammonium derivatives can induce the formation of
lower-dimensional phases that do significantly impact perov-
skite stability,57 and this continues to be an area of active
research. Comparing the relative stability of the various
perovskite formulations, the triple cation composition (Figure
5d, FCM-IB) was notably less photochemically stable than the
composition without either MA or bromide and with the
addition of guanidinium (Figure 5d, FCG-I). Presumably this
is because of the lower photochemical reactivity of the FA
cation compared to MA. In a broad sense, the replacement of
MA with FA has been one of the most important develop-
ments in PSCs, imparting the devices with not only better
efficiency, but also dramatically improved stability. Although
state-of-the-art devices often use the triple cation composition,
as we demonstrated here, complete removal of the MA cation

■OPERANDO GIWAXS
Although we used in situ GIWAXS quite successfully to
elucidate key perovskite degradation pathways, strictly in situ
experiments do not provide any information about device
performance. As a result, it becomes difficult to correlate the
structural changes observed by GIWAXS to changes in PCE.
Only by simultaneously tracking changes in both crystal
structure and efficiency can the two parameters be connected.
With this in mind, we have been continuing to develop fully
operando GIWAXS methods for the analysis of PSCs (Figure
6a). In these experiments, GIWAXS patterns are collected on
complete devices; through careful placement of electrical leads
(so as not to shadow the detector), J−V curves can
simultaneously be acquired. We first used these methods in
2018 in the study of ITO/ZnO/MAPbI3/P3HT/Ag PSCs.58
In these experiments, the devices were operated in an
atmosphere of 80% RH. Given that our previous in situ
GIWAXS experiments had revealed hydrate formation as a key
degradation mechanism in perovskite films (Figure 3),33 we
initially expected to see the devices fail because of moisture-
induced degradation. Instead, the corresponding I−V curves
and azimuthally integrated linecuts (Figure 6b) showed very
different trends. The scattering data showed little change in the
perovskite (110) peak intensity over the course of the
experiment, whereas the I−V curves revealed a dramatic loss
in PCE after only ca. 15 min. These data challenged our initial
assumptions about perovskite device failure mechanisms and
revealed that iodide migration to the silver electrode (followed
by corrosion at the interface) was in fact the primary reason for
the loss of PCE. Subsequent work has highlighted the
oxidation of PSC electrodes and the relative mobility of the
resulting metal cations,59,60 reinforcing the idea that even
noble metals are noninnocent in the local electrochemical
environment of an operating PSC. Moreover, under the
conditions of the experiment (constant illumination by a
halogen lamp), no hydrate phases or other intermediates were
observed. Subsequent experiments showed that the mono-
hydrate phase would form in the dark, but as soon as the
halogen lamp was turned on, the increase in temperature led to
water desorption and regeneration of the original perovskite
phase. This work highlighted the power of fully operando
GIWAXS methods; without being able to simultaneously track
changes in perovskite crystallinity and changes in device
performance, we would not have realized that the two
parameters were, in fact, decoupled in this instance.
Although our 2018 study58 provided important clues as to
the effect of mobile iodide ions and interfacial redox processes
on device performance, as was discussed previously, there have
been many subsequent advancements in both perovskite
composition (from MAPbI3 to Cs0.05(FA0.83MA0.17)0.95Pb-
(I0.83Br0.17)3) and device architecture made. This makes it an
open question whether the same failure pathways are operative
in more state-of-the-art devices. We therefore wanted to

Looking forward, we expect that operando X-ray scattering
methods will continue to be powerful tools in the analysis of
perovskite degradation mechanisms. The ability to temporally
correlate structural data with device efficiency, on a single
device, allows us to much more conclusively link changes in
device performance to things like phase transformations, defect
formation, and electrode corrosion. Having previously
identified the MA cation as a weak link in the perovskite
composition, one key question will be how MA-free devices
fare under conditions of elevated humidity. Another unknown
is the effect of temperature on defect formation and device
failure; we are currently working on improvements to our
operando sample holder that will allow for measurements at
elevated temperatures. Finally, these methods may allow us to
address lingering questions about how device lifetimes may be
correlated to device efficiencies; anecdotal reports suggest that
high efficiency devices often have improved lifetimes, perhaps

■CONCLUSIONS AND PERSPECTIVES
The field of PSCs has advanced tremendously over the past
decade. Our understanding of perovskite carrier dynamics and
photophysics has improved significantly, perovskite composi-
tions have evolved from MAPbI3 to complex mixtures of
cations and anions, and device designs and components have
all advanced as well. Today’s state-of-the-art devices, with
PCEs well in excess of 20%, would have been almost
unthinkable a decade ago, highlighting how much progress
has been made.
We have also significantly improved our understanding of
the complex chemistry of lead halide perovskites. It requires
relatively little energy to structurally deform a lead iodide
lattice, making it easy to accommodate water in the structure
(leading to the formation of hydrate phases), form defects, or
transition between polymorphs. In situ GIWAXS measure-
ments have helped elucidate many of these transformations,
and operando GIWAXS measurements are similarly helping to
correlate these structural changes to changes in device
performance. As a result, our understanding of device failure
mechanisms has improved. The best PSCs now have not just
excellent efficiency, but accelerated aging tests also project
quite reasonable device lifetimes. With that said, there is still
much work to be done to make sure that perovskite-based
modules are robust enough to survive outdoor use in a wide
variety of harsh environmental conditions. Passivating agents,
interfacial barrier layers, and of course encapsulants are all
promising strategies in this regard. Proper execution of these
stability and lifetime measurements, against a well-defined
standard, will be crucial in facilitating comparisons between
laboratories and advancing the field overall.
The field has also seen a significant paradigm shift in the past
few years as the efficiency of lab-scale (i.e., < 1 cm2) cells has
started to plateau. With performance and even stability no
longer being limiting factors for spin-coated devices, device
scale-up has been brought to the forefront. More scalable
coating techniques like slot-die coating, blade coating, and
even screen printing are increasingly being used for the
production of large-area devices.4,5 Here, much of the
knowledge gained from spin-coated PSCs cannot be directly
applied to these larger-area cells, as the film formation and
crystallization dynamics of these alternative coating methods
are radically different. As production scales up, confining the
fabrication process to a glovebox becomes significantly more
difficult, and fabricating devices under ambient conditions
becomes increasingly imperative. This creates additional
challenges, both in terms of performance and reproducibility.
However, if these challenges can be met, we will move
substantially closer to realizing the full potential of perovskite
materials for applications in energy, imaging, and optoelec-
tronics.
