Abstract 
A conceptually new carbon counter electrode for perovskite solar cell was demonstrated, which 
was fabricated on a separated substrate and then assembled with other components to complete 
a whole device, in contrast to conventional metal or carbon electrodes which are directly 
deposited on other component layers of the device. Power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 4.24% 
was achieved for perovskite solar cell with an optimized carbon electrode. The separation of 
preparation of electrode and device assembly provides much freedom for the choices of 
materials and preparation process to fabricate the device. 
Keywords 
Perovskite-based solar cell; Carbon materials; Counter electrode; Separated substrate; Energy 
storage and conversion 
1 Introduction 
Perovskite solar cells are currently believed to be the most promising alternatives to 
conventional photovoltaic devices due to the high efficiency and ease of preparation [1-4]. A 
typical perovskite solar cell is prepared by sequentially depositing component layers on a 
transparent substrate with the last step of device fabrication being thermal evaporation of Au or 
Ag metals under high vacuum conditions to form the counter electrode (CE). Undoubtedly, this 
high-cost metallic CE is not conducive for its large–scale application and commercialization. To 
date, several research groups have developed carbon CEs [5,6] to reduce the costs of perovskite 
solar cells and encouraging power conversion efficiencies have been achieved on such devices. 


2 
 
Both the metal and carbon CEs are deposited on other component layers of the device which 
have already been fabricated, then the compatibility of material and preparation process of CEs 
with other component layers imposes a rigorous restrict on the device fabrication. 
Inexpensive and abundant carbon materials have shown great potential in the alternative clean 
and sustainable energy technologies [5, 6]. Carbon materials have been investigated for the 
development of lithium-ion batteries, fuel cells, and dye-sensitized solar cells (DSSCs) [7]. 
Unfortunately, carbon materials are generally prepared with complicated processes, usually, in 
the presence of various metal catalysts [8, 9]. This restricts the practical application of carbon 
materials in photovoltaic devices.  
Herein, we demonstrated a conceptually new carbon counter electrode for perovskite solar cell. 
In contrast to conventional metal or carbon electrodes which are directly deposited on other 
component layers of the device, our proposed carbon electrodes are prepared on separated 
substrates and then assembled with other components to complete the device. Since the 
preparation of CE and the device assembly are decoupled, there is more freedom in the 
materials and processes used for the preparation of the device. A perovskite solar cell was 
prepared with the new type of carbon CE and a PCE of 4.24% was achieved under full sun 
illumination. We believe the idea of decoupling CE preparation and device assembly is promising 
and there is a large room for further improvements in device performance.  
2 Material and methods  
2.1 Device fabrication 
Fluorine-doped SnO2 (FTO) substrate was firstly etched using Zn powder and HCl (2 M) to form 
the desired electrode patterns. The resultant FTO substrates were ultrasonically cleaned with 
detergent, deionized water, acetone, ethanol, and 2-propanol, respectively. TiO2 compact layer 
was then deposited on the cleaned FTO substrate by spin-coating (solution-processing) it with a 
mildly acidic solution of titanium isopropoxide in ethanol solution at 2,000 rpm. for 60 s, before 
drying at 150 ° C for 10 min and then sintering at 500 °C for 30 min. The mesoporous TiO2 was 
deposited by spin coating at 2,000 rpm for 30 s using a commercial TiO2 paste diluted in ethanol 


3 
 
(2:7, weight ratio). These electrodes were sintered at 125 °C for 10 min, 325 °C for 15 min, 375 °C 
for 15 min, 450 °C for 20 min, and 500 °C for 15 min, respectively. PbI2 was dissolved in 
N,N-dimethylformamide at a concentration of 462 mg ml-1 under stirring at 75° C. The solution 
was kept at 75° C during the whole procedure. The mesoporous TiO2 films were then infiltrated 
with PbI2 by spin coating at 5500 rpm for 30 s and dried at 75° C for 30 min. After cooling to 
room temperature, the films were dipped in a solution of CH3NH3I in 2-propanol (10 mg ml-1) for 
20 s, rinsed with 2-propanol and dried at 75°C for 30 min. The hole transferring layer was 
prepared by spin-coating a solution containing 72.3 mg Spiro-MeOTAD, 28.8 μL 
4-tert-butylpyridine and 0.06 M lithium bis(trifluorome- thylsulfonyl)imide per mL of 
chlorobezene on the top of perovskite layer at 4,000 rpm for 45 s.  
A FTO glass was used as substrate to collect soot of a burning candle. The distance between FTO 
glass and the wick was 2 cm. The collecting time was controlled to adjust the thickness of the 
as-prepared carbon film. The collection time for counter electrode-1 (CE-1), CE-2 and CE-3 were 
10 s, 15 s and 20 s, respectively. The spongy carbon films on FTO substrates were then pressed 
on the spiro-OMeTAD layers of uncompleted devices, as illustrated in Fig. 1. A conventional 
device with evaporated Au as contact electrode (~60 nm) was deposited on the HTL using 
thermal evaporation at a pressure of 1 × 10–6 mbar. For the comparative devices fabricated using 
compressed Au CE, the Au layer was deposited on FTO glass substrate by magnetron sputtering 
and then pressed on the spiro-OMeTAD layers. 
2.2 Characterization 
The morphology of the soot deposited on FTO glass was observed with a field emission 
scanning electron microscope (FESEM, Hitachi S-4800). Energy dispersive X-ray spectrum (EDS) 
was collected to investigate the composition of the spongy film. The soot was characterized with 
a transmission electron microscope (TEM, FEI, Tecnai F20UT) operating at 200 KV. Raman 
spectrum was recorded with a Renishaw inVia Raman microscope. The as-prepared devices were 
measured under full sun illumination (AM 1.5, 100 mW cm-2) with a mask of 0.1 cm2 to define the 
active area.  


4 
 
3 Results and Discussion 
The preparation of carbon CEs was illustrated in Fig. 1. Field emission scanning electron 
microscope (FESEM) was used to characterize the morphology of the soot deposited on FTO 
glass. As revealed by SEM images (Fig.2a, b), a spongy film with a homogeneous thickness was 
deposited on FTO glass. The thickness of the film is approximately 27.5μm for the sample with 
the collecting time of 20 s (Fig.2c). SEM image of high magnification shows that the spongy film is 
composed of nanospheres of several tens nanometers. Energy dispersive X-ray spectrum (EDS) 
was collected to investigate the composition of the spongy film. According to the EDS spectrum 
as shown in Fig. 2(d), the dominant element is carbon, accompanied by Sn, Si and Ca which is 
ascribed to the FTO glass substrate, confirming that the spongy film is composed of carbon 
materials. The soot was also characterized with a transmission electron microscope (TEM). TEM 
images revealed that the soot was an aggregation of nanoparticles of several tens of nanometers 
(Fig. 2e), in agreement with the results obtained with SEM. Discontinuous, tanglesome lattice 
fringes approximately in parallel with the contours was observed for such nanoparticles with 
high resolution TEM characterization (Fig. 2f), indicating that they are graphitized disordered 
carbon materials of onion-like structure.  
 
Figure 1 Schematic illustration for the preparation of carbon counter electrode and 
device assembly 
Raman spectrum was presented in Fig. 3a. Two broad bands centered at around 1366 cm-1 and 
1595 cm-1 are observed, corresponding to the D-band caused by structural defects and the 
partially disordered structure of sp2 domains, and the G-band associated with the first-order 
scattering of the E2g vibrations observed for sp2 domains, respectively [10]. Both the band profile 


5 
 
and intensity ratio (IG/ID) suggest that the carbon materials prepared in this study are strongly 
disordered, in consistence with the TEM observations. 
 
Figure 2 SEM images (a, b, c), EDX spectrum (d), TEM images (e, f) of the soot of a 
burning candle deposited on the substrate 
 
Figure 3 (a) Raman spectrum of the soot of a burning candle deposited on the 
substrate; (b) J-V curves of perovskite solar cells with different carbon counter 
electrodes, measured under simulated sun light with intensity of 100 mW cm-2 (AM 
1.5G) 
Uncompleted perovskite solar cells with the structure of FTO/TiO2/CH3NH3PbI3/ spiro-OMeTAD 
were prepared using the method reported in literatures [3], and the spongy carbon films on FTO 
substrates were then pressed on the spiro-OMeTAD layers of uncompleted devices, as illustrated 
in Fig. 1. Three carbon counter electrodes with various thicknesses were used in device 


6 
 
fabrication, which were named as CE-1, CE-2 and CE-3, respectively. The thickness of each carbon 
counter electrode was determined by inspecting cross-sectional samples with SEM and reported 
in Table 1. Photocurrent density-voltage (J-V) curves of these devices were presented in Fig. 3b. 
The device with CE-2 exhibited the highest performance among three devices using carbon CEs. 
A conventional device with thermally evaporated Au as CE was also prepared and compared with 
ones with carbon CEs. The conventional device shows a PCE of 8.05% while the best performing 
device with carbon CE only gives a PCE of 4.24%. The series resistance of each device was 
estimated by evaluating the slope of J-V curves around open-circuit voltage. As expected, the 
conventional cell has the lowest series resistance and the performance of carbon CE based 
devices also varied consistently with the series resistance. Since the main difference among 
these devices lies in CEs, the variation of series resistance of the devices should be attributed to 
CEs. We suppose that contact resistance at the interfaces of spiro-OMeTAD/carbon and 
carbon/FTO dominates the series resistance of the device [3,5]. Therefore, the interface should 
be optimized to reduce the series resistance and improve the performance of the device. The 
spongy nature of the carbon film is crucial to enable the operation of the perovskite solar cells 
proposed in this study. When compressed by the FTO glass substrate and spiro-OMeTAD layer, 
the spongy carbon film deforms and a reliable electric contact between the carbon film and 
adjacent layers is resulted. For comparison, Au layer was deposited on FTO glass substrate by 
magnetron sputtering and applied as CE for perovskite solar cells. An insignificant PCE (~0.05%) 
as was observed, implying the device is non-functional. When the spongy carbon film is too thin, 
as in the case of CE-1, the deformation of the film under pressure is not sufficient to form well 
contacted interfaces between the carbon film and adjacent layer, resulting in a low efficiency of 
the device. When the spongy carbon film is too thick, as in the case of CE-3, charge carriers have 
a longer pathway through the disordered carbon material. Notwithstanding the good contact 
formed at the interfaces, an overly thick carbon film led to deteriorated device performance. FTO 
conducting glass substrates used to collect soot in this study may be replaced by other materials 
to further reduce the fabrication cost of perovskite solar cells. The substrate on which the spongy 


7 
 
carbon film is deposited can also be used in combination with edge sealants as a protective cover 
to prevent moisture from reaching the perovskite layer of the device, facilitating the practical 
application of perovskite solar cells.

4 Conclusions  
In conclusion, we have proposed a conceptually new counter electrode for perovskite-based 
solar cells. Different from the conventional counter electrodes which are fabricated directly on 
other component layers of a device, the new type of counter electrode is prepared on a 
separated substrate and then assembly with other components to complete the device. Spongy 
carbon film was prepared on FTO glass substrate with a facile and low-cost method and applied 
as the new type of counter electrode for a prototype device, which exhibited a power conversion 
efficiency of 4.24%. The idea of decoupling the preparation of counter electrodes and device 
assembly will enable new possibilities in choosing materials and processes to fabricate perovskite 
solar cells, and may be applied in other photovoltaic devices.

China \n*Corresponding authors: yinx@nanoctr.cn (Xiong YIN), mhe@nanoctr.cn (Meng HE) Tel.: \n86-10-8254-5555; xpzou2014@163.com (Xiaoping ZOU), Tel.: 86-10-64884673 \nAbstract \nA conceptually new carbon counter electrode for perovskite solar cell was demonstrated, which \nwas fabricated on a separated substrate and then assembled with other components to complete \na whole device, in contrast to conventional metal or carbon electrodes which are directly \ndeposited on other component layers of the device. Power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 4.24% \nwas achieved for perovskite solar cell with an optimized carbon electrode. The separation of \npreparation of electrode and device assembly provides much freedom for the choices of \nmaterials and preparation process to fabricate the device. \nKeywords \nPerovskite-based solar cell; Carbon materials; Counter electrode; Separated substrate; Energy \nstorage and conversion \n1 Introduction \nPerovskite solar cells are currently believed to be the most promising alternatives to \nconventional photovoltaic devices due to the high efficiency and ease of preparation [1-4]. A \ntypical perovskite solar cell is prepared by sequentially depositing component layers on a \ntransparent substrate with the last step of device fabrication being thermal evaporation of Au or \nAg metals under high vacuum conditions to form the counter electrode (CE). Undoubtedly, this \nhigh-cost metallic CE is not conducive for its large–scale application and commercialization. To \ndate, several research groups have developed carbon CEs [5,6] to reduce the costs of perovskite \nsolar cells and encouraging power conversion efficiencies have been achieved on such devices. \n\n\n2 \n \nBoth the metal and carbon CEs are deposited on other component layers of the device which \nhave already been fabricated, then the compatibility of material and preparation process of CEs \nwith other component layers imposes a rigorous restrict on the device fabrication. \nInexpensive and abundant carbon materials have shown great potential in the alternative clean \nand sustainable energy technologies [5, 6]. Carbon materials have been investigated for the \ndevelopment of lithium-ion batteries, fuel cells, and dye-sensitized solar cells (DSSCs) [7]. \nUnfortunately, carbon materials are generally prepared with complicated processes, usually, in \nthe presence of various metal catalysts [8, 9]. This restricts the practical application of carbon \nmaterials in photovoltaic devices.  \nHerein, we demonstrated a conceptually new carbon counter electrode for perovskite solar cell. \nIn contrast to conventional metal or carbon electrodes which are directly deposited on other \ncomponent layers of the device, our proposed carbon electrodes are prepared on separated \nsubstrates and then assembled with other components to complete the device. Since the \npreparation of CE and the device assembly are decoupled, there is more freedom in the \nmaterials and processes used for the preparation of the device. A perovskite solar cell was \nprepared with the new type of carbon CE and a PCE of 4.24% was achieved under full sun \nillumination. We believe the idea of decoupling CE preparation and device assembly is promising \nand there is a large room for further improvements in device performance.  \n2 Material and methods  \n2.1 Device fabrication \nFluorine-doped SnO2 (FTO) substrate was firstly etched using Zn powder and HCl (2 M) to form \nthe desired electrode patterns. The resultant FTO substrates were ultrasonically cleaned with \ndetergent, deionized water, acetone, ethanol, and 2-propanol, respectively. TiO2 compact layer \nwas then deposited on the cleaned FTO substrate by spin-coating (solution-processing) it with a \nmildly acidic solution of titanium isopropoxide in ethanol solution at 2,000 rpm. for 60 s, before \ndrying at 150 ° C for 10 min and then sintering at 500 °C for 30 min. The mesoporous TiO2 was \ndeposited by spin coating at 2,000 rpm for 30 s using a commercial TiO2 paste diluted in ethanol \n\n\n3 \n \n(2:7, weight ratio). These electrodes were sintered at 125 °C for 10 min, 325 °C for 15 min, 375 °C \nfor 15 min, 450 °C for 20 min, and 500 °C for 15 min, respectively. PbI2 was dissolved in \nN,N-dimethylformamide at a concentration of 462 mg ml-1 under stirring at 75° C. The solution \nwas kept at 75° C during the whole procedure. The mesoporous TiO2 films were then infiltrated \nwith PbI2 by spin coating at 5500 rpm for 30 s and dried at 75° C for 30 min. After cooling to \nroom temperature, the films were dipped in a solution of CH3NH3I in 2-propanol (10 mg ml-1) for \n20 s, rinsed with 2-propanol and dried at 75°C for 30 min. The hole transferring layer was \nprepared by spin-coating a solution containing 72.3 mg Spiro-MeOTAD, 28.8 μL \n4-tert-butylpyridine and 0.06 M lithium bis(trifluorome- thylsulfonyl)imide per mL of \nchlorobezene on the top of perovskite layer at 4,000 rpm for 45 s.  \nA FTO glass was used as substrate to collect soot of a burning candle. The distance between FTO \nglass and the wick was 2 cm. The collecting time was controlled to adjust the thickness of the \nas-prepared carbon film. The collection time for counter electrode-1 (CE-1), CE-2 and CE-3 were \n10 s, 15 s and 20 s, respectively. The spongy carbon films on FTO substrates were then pressed \non the spiro-OMeTAD layers of uncompleted devices, as illustrated in Fig. 1. A conventional \ndevice with evaporated Au as contact electrode (~60 nm) was deposited on the HTL using \nthermal evaporation at a pressure of 1 × 10–6 mbar. For the comparative devices fabricated using \ncompressed Au CE, the Au layer was deposited on FTO glass substrate by magnetron sputtering \nand then pressed on the spiro-OMeTAD layers. \n2.2 Characterization \nThe morphology of the soot deposited on FTO glass was observed with a field emission \nscanning electron microscope (FESEM, Hitachi S-4800). Energy dispersive X-ray spectrum (EDS) \nwas collected to investigate the composition of the spongy film. The soot was characterized with \na transmission electron microscope (TEM, FEI, Tecnai F20UT) operating at 200 KV. Raman \nspectrum was recorded with a Renishaw inVia Raman microscope. The as-prepared devices were \nmeasured under full sun illumination (AM 1.5, 100 mW cm-2) with a mask of 0.1 cm2 to define the \nactive area.  \n\n\n4 \n \n3 Results and Discussion \nThe preparation of carbon CEs was illustrated in Fig. 1. Field emission scanning electron \nmicroscope (FESEM) was used to characterize the morphology of the soot deposited on FTO \nglass. As revealed by SEM images (Fig.2a, b), a spongy film with a homogeneous thickness was \ndeposited on FTO glass. The thickness of the film is approximately 27.5μm for the sample with \nthe collecting time of 20 s (Fig.2c). SEM image of high magnification shows that the spongy film is \ncomposed of nanospheres of several tens nanometers. Energy dispersive X-ray spectrum (EDS) \nwas collected to investigate the composition of the spongy film. According to the EDS spectrum \nas shown in Fig. 2(d), the dominant element is carbon, accompanied by Sn, Si and Ca which is \nascribed to the FTO glass substrate, confirming that the spongy film is composed of carbon \nmaterials. The soot was also characterized with a transmission electron microscope (TEM). TEM \nimages revealed that the soot was an aggregation of nanoparticles of several tens of nanometers \n(Fig. 2e), in agreement with the results obtained with SEM. Discontinuous, tanglesome lattice \nfringes approximately in parallel with the contours was observed for such nanoparticles with \nhigh resolution TEM characterization (Fig. 2f), indicating that they are graphitized disordered \ncarbon materials of onion-like structure.  \n \nFigure 1 Schematic illustration for the preparation of carbon counter electrode and \ndevice assembly \nRaman spectrum was presented in Fig. 3a. Two broad bands centered at around 1366 cm-1 and \n1595 cm-1 are observed, corresponding to the D-band caused by structural defects and the \npartially disordered structure of sp2 domains, and the G-band associated with the first-order \nscattering of the E2g vibrations observed for sp2 domains, respectively [10]. Both the band profile \n\n\n5 \n \nand intensity ratio (IG/ID) suggest that the carbon materials prepared in this study are strongly \ndisordered, in consistence with the TEM observations. \n \nFigure 2 SEM images (a, b, c), EDX spectrum (d), TEM images (e, f) of the soot of a \nburning candle deposited on the substrate \n \nFigure 3 (a) Raman spectrum of the soot of a burning candle deposited on the \nsubstrate; (b) J-V curves of perovskite solar cells with different carbon counter \nelectrodes, measured under simulated sun light with intensity of 100 mW cm-2 (AM \n1.5G) \nUncompleted perovskite solar cells with the structure of FTO/TiO2/CH3NH3PbI3/ spiro-OMeTAD \nwere prepared using the method reported in literatures [3], and the spongy carbon films on FTO \nsubstrates were then pressed on the spiro-OMeTAD layers of uncompleted devices, as illustrated \nin Fig. 1. Three carbon counter electrodes with various thicknesses were used in device \n\n\n6 \n \nfabrication, which were named as CE-1, CE-2 and CE-3, respectively. The thickness of each carbon \ncounter electrode was determined by inspecting cross-sectional samples with SEM and reported \nin Table 1. Photocurrent density-voltage (J-V) curves of these devices were presented in Fig. 3b. \nThe device with CE-2 exhibited the highest performance among three devices using carbon CEs. \nA conventional device with thermally evaporated Au as CE was also prepared and compared with \nones with carbon CEs. The conventional device shows a PCE of 8.05% while the best performing \ndevice with carbon CE only gives a PCE of 4.24%. The series resistance of each device was \nestimated by evaluating the slope of J-V curves around open-circuit voltage. As expected, the \nconventional cell has the lowest series resistance and the performance of carbon CE based \ndevices also varied consistently with the series resistance. Since the main difference among \nthese devices lies in CEs, the variation of series resistance of the devices should be attributed to \nCEs. We suppose that contact resistance at the interfaces of spiro-OMeTAD/carbon and \ncarbon/FTO dominates the series resistance of the device [3,5]. Therefore, the interface should \nbe optimized to reduce the series resistance and improve the performance of the device. The \nspongy nature of the carbon film is crucial to enable the operation of the perovskite solar cells \nproposed in this study. When compressed by the FTO glass substrate and spiro-OMeTAD layer, \nthe spongy carbon film deforms and a reliable electric contact between the carbon film and \nadjacent layers is resulted. For comparison, Au layer was deposited on FTO glass substrate by \nmagnetron sputtering and applied as CE for perovskite solar cells. An insignificant PCE (~0.05%) \nas was observed, implying the device is non-functional. When the spongy carbon film is too thin, \nas in the case of CE-1, the deformation of the film under pressure is not sufficient to form well \ncontacted interfaces between the carbon film and adjacent layer, resulting in a low efficiency of \nthe device. When the spongy carbon film is too thick, as in the case of CE-3, charge carriers have \na longer pathway through the disordered carbon material. Notwithstanding the good contact \nformed at the interfaces, an overly thick carbon film led to deteriorated device performance. FTO \nconducting glass substrates used to collect soot in this study may be replaced by other materials \nto further reduce the fabrication cost of perovskite solar cells. The substrate on which the spongy \n\n\n7 \n \ncarbon film is deposited can also be used in combination with edge sealants as a protective cover \nto prevent moisture from reaching the perovskite layer of the device, facilitating the practical \napplication of perovskite solar cells. \nTable 1 Photovoltaic performances extracted from current-voltage measurements of perovskite \nsolar cells with different counter electrodes. \nDevices Thickness /μm Jsc a/ mA cm-2 \nVoc b / V \nFF c \nPCE d/ % Rs e/ Ω cm2 \nCE-1 \n16.5 \n8.60 \n0.80 \n0.43 \n2.96 \n43.6 \nCE-2 \n20.0 \n12.30 \n0.82 \n0.42 \n4.24 \n20.3 \nCE-3 \n27.5 \n8.23 \n0.82 \n0.42 \n2.83 \n30.4 \nAu \n0.06 \n16.88 \n0.90 \n0.53 \n8.05 \n12.3 \nAu/FTO \n0.2 \n0.28 \n0.75 \n0.23 \n0.05 \n2517.0 \na Jsc: Short-circuit photocurrent density, b Voc: Open-current voltage, c FF: Fill factor, d PCE: Power \nconversion efficiency, e Rs: Series resistance. \n4 Conclusions  \nIn conclusion, we have proposed a conceptually new counter electrode for perovskite-based \nsolar cells. Different from the conventional counter electrodes which are fabricated directly on \nother component layers of a device, the new type of counter electrode is prepared on a \nseparated substrate and then assembly with other components to complete the device. Spongy \ncarbon film was prepared on FTO glass substrate with a facile and low-cost method and applied \nas the new type of counter electrode for a prototype device, which exhibited a power conversion \nefficiency of 4.24%. The idea of decoupling the preparation of counter electrodes and device \nassembly will enable new possibilities in choosing materials and processes to fabricate perovskite \nsolar cells, and may be applied in other photovoltaic devices. \nAcknowledgments \nThis work was financially supported by CAS Key Lab of Nanosystem and Hierarchical Fabrication, \nthe National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant Nos. 91233201, 61376057, 21103032 \nand 51272049), the National High-Tech R&D Program of China (863, Grant No. 2011AA050527), \nthe Beijing Municipal Natural Science Foundation (Grant No. 3131001), the Scientific Research \nProject of Beijing Educational Committee (Grant No. KZ201211232040).  \nReferences \n\n\n8 \n \n[1] M.A. Green, A. Abstract 
A conceptually new carbon counter electrode for perovskite solar cell was demonstrated, which 
was fabricated on a separated substrate and then assembled with other components to complete 
a whole device, in contrast to conventional metal or carbon electrodes which are directly 
deposited on other component layers of the device. Power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 4.24% 
was achieved for perovskite solar cell with an optimized carbon electrode. The separation of 
preparation of electrode and device assembly provides much freedom for the choices of 
materials and preparation process to fabricate the device. 
Keywords 
Perovskite-based solar cell; Carbon materials; Counter electrode; Separated substrate; Energy 
storage and conversion 
1 Introduction 
Perovskite solar cells are currently believed to be the most promising alternatives to 
conventional photovoltaic devices due to the high efficiency and ease of preparation [1-4]. A 
typical perovskite solar cell is prepared by sequentially depositing component layers on a 
transparent substrate with the last step of device fabrication being thermal evaporation of Au or 
Ag metals under high vacuum conditions to form the counter electrode (CE). Undoubtedly, this 
high-cost metallic CE is not conducive for its large–scale application and commercialization. To 
date, several research groups have developed carbon CEs [5,6] to reduce the costs of perovskite 
solar cells and encouraging power conversion efficiencies have been achieved on such devices. 


2 
 
Both the metal and carbon CEs are deposited on other component layers of the device which 
have already been fabricated, then the compatibility of material and preparation process of CEs 
with other component layers imposes a rigorous restrict on the device fabrication. 
Inexpensive and abundant carbon materials have shown great potential in the alternative clean 
and sustainable energy technologies [5, 6]. Carbon materials have been investigated for the 
development of lithium-ion batteries, fuel cells, and dye-sensitized solar cells (DSSCs) [7]. 
Unfortunately, carbon materials are generally prepared with complicated processes, usually, in 
the presence of various metal catalysts [8, 9]. This restricts the practical application of carbon 
materials in photovoltaic devices.  
Herein, we demonstrated a conceptually new carbon counter electrode for perovskite solar cell. 
In contrast to conventional metal or carbon electrodes which are directly deposited on other 
component layers of the device, our proposed carbon electrodes are prepared on separated 
substrates and then assembled with other components to complete the device. Since the 
preparation of CE and the device assembly are decoupled, there is more freedom in the 
materials and processes used for the preparation of the device. A perovskite solar cell was 
prepared with the new type of carbon CE and a PCE of 4.24% was achieved under full sun 
illumination. We believe the idea of decoupling CE preparation and device assembly is promising 
and there is a large room for further improvements in device performance.  
2 Material and methods  
2.1 Device fabrication 
Fluorine-doped SnO2 (FTO) substrate was firstly etched using Zn powder and HCl (2 M) to form 
the desired electrode patterns. The resultant FTO substrates were ultrasonically cleaned with 
detergent, deionized water, acetone, ethanol, and 2-propanol, respectively. TiO2 compact layer 
was then deposited on the cleaned FTO substrate by spin-coating (solution-processing) it with a 
mildly acidic solution of titanium isopropoxide in ethanol solution at 2,000 rpm. for 60 s, before 
drying at 150 ° C for 10 min and then sintering at 500 °C for 30 min. The mesoporous TiO2 was 
deposited by spin coating at 2,000 rpm for 30 s using a commercial TiO2 paste diluted in ethanol 


3 
 
(2:7, weight ratio). These electrodes were sintered at 125 °C for 10 min, 325 °C for 15 min, 375 °C 
for 15 min, 450 °C for 20 min, and 500 °C for 15 min, respectively. PbI2 was dissolved in 
N,N-dimethylformamide at a concentration of 462 mg ml-1 under stirring at 75° C. The solution 
was kept at 75° C during the whole procedure. The mesoporous TiO2 films were then infiltrated 
with PbI2 by spin coating at 5500 rpm for 30 s and dried at 75° C for 30 min. After cooling to 
room temperature, the films were dipped in a solution of CH3NH3I in 2-propanol (10 mg ml-1) for 
20 s, rinsed with 2-propanol and dried at 75°C for 30 min. The hole transferring layer was 
prepared by spin-coating a solution containing 72.3 mg Spiro-MeOTAD, 28.8 μL 
4-tert-butylpyridine and 0.06 M lithium bis(trifluorome- thylsulfonyl)imide per mL of 
chlorobezene on the top of perovskite layer at 4,000 rpm for 45 s.  
A FTO glass was used as substrate to collect soot of a burning candle. The distance between FTO 
glass and the wick was 2 cm. The collecting time was controlled to adjust the thickness of the 
as-prepared carbon film. The collection time for counter electrode-1 (CE-1), CE-2 and CE-3 were 
10 s, 15 s and 20 s, respectively. The spongy carbon films on FTO substrates were then pressed 
on the spiro-OMeTAD layers of uncompleted devices, as illustrated in Fig. 1. A conventional 
device with evaporated Au as contact electrode (~60 nm) was deposited on the HTL using 
thermal evaporation at a pressure of 1 × 10–6 mbar. For the comparative devices fabricated using 
compressed Au CE, the Au layer was deposited on FTO glass substrate by magnetron sputtering 
and then pressed on the spiro-OMeTAD layers. 
2.2 Characterization 
The morphology of the soot deposited on FTO glass was observed with a field emission 
scanning electron microscope (FESEM, Hitachi S-4800). Energy dispersive X-ray spectrum (EDS) 
was collected to investigate the composition of the spongy film. The soot was characterized with 
a transmission electron microscope (TEM, FEI, Tecnai F20UT) operating at 200 KV. Raman 
spectrum was recorded with a Renishaw inVia Raman microscope. The as-prepared devices were 
measured under full sun illumination (AM 1.5, 100 mW cm-2) with a mask of 0.1 cm2 to define the 
active area.  


4 
 
3 Results and Discussion 
The preparation of carbon CEs was illustrated in Fig. 1. Field emission scanning electron 
microscope (FESEM) was used to characterize the morphology of the soot deposited on FTO 
glass. As revealed by SEM images (Fig.2a, b), a spongy film with a homogeneous thickness was 
deposited on FTO glass. The thickness of the film is approximately 27.5μm for the sample with 
the collecting time of 20 s (Fig.2c). SEM image of high magnification shows that the spongy film is 
composed of nanospheres of several tens nanometers. Energy dispersive X-ray spectrum (EDS) 
was collected to investigate the composition of the spongy film. According to the EDS spectrum 
as shown in Fig. 2(d), the dominant element is carbon, accompanied by Sn, Si and Ca which is 
ascribed to the FTO glass substrate, confirming that the spongy film is composed of carbon 
materials. The soot was also characterized with a transmission electron microscope (TEM). TEM 
images revealed that the soot was an aggregation of nanoparticles of several tens of nanometers 
(Fig. 2e), in agreement with the results obtained with SEM. Discontinuous, tanglesome lattice 
fringes approximately in parallel with the contours was observed for such nanoparticles with 
high resolution TEM characterization (Fig. 2f), indicating that they are graphitized disordered 
carbon materials of onion-like structure.

Raman spectrum was presented in Fig. 3a. Two broad bands centered at around 1366 cm-1 and 
1595 cm-1 are observed, corresponding to the D-band caused by structural defects and the 
partially disordered structure of sp2 domains, and the G-band associated with the first-order 
scattering of the E2g vibrations observed for sp2 domains, respectively [10]. Both the band profile 


5 
 
and intensity ratio (IG/ID) suggest that the carbon materials prepared in this study are strongly 
disordered, in consistence with the TEM observations.

Uncompleted perovskite solar cells with the structure of FTO/TiO2/CH3NH3PbI3/ spiro-OMeTAD 
were prepared using the method reported in literatures [3], and the spongy carbon films on FTO 
substrates were then pressed on the spiro-OMeTAD layers of uncompleted devices, as illustrated 
in Fig. 1. Three carbon counter electrodes with various thicknesses were used in device 


6 
 
fabrication, which were named as CE-1, CE-2 and CE-3, respectively. The thickness of each carbon 
counter electrode was determined by inspecting cross-sectional samples with SEM and reported 
in Table 1. Photocurrent density-voltage (J-V) curves of these devices were presented in Fig. 3b. 
The device with CE-2 exhibited the highest performance among three devices using carbon CEs. 
A conventional device with thermally evaporated Au as CE was also prepared and compared with 
ones with carbon CEs. The conventional device shows a PCE of 8.05% while the best performing 
device with carbon CE only gives a PCE of 4.24%. The series resistance of each device was 
estimated by evaluating the slope of J-V curves around open-circuit voltage. As expected, the 
conventional cell has the lowest series resistance and the performance of carbon CE based 
devices also varied consistently with the series resistance. Since the main difference among 
these devices lies in CEs, the variation of series resistance of the devices should be attributed to 
CEs. We suppose that contact resistance at the interfaces of spiro-OMeTAD/carbon and 
carbon/FTO dominates the series resistance of the device [3,5]. Therefore, the interface should 
be optimized to reduce the series resistance and improve the performance of the device. The 
spongy nature of the carbon film is crucial to enable the operation of the perovskite solar cells 
proposed in this study. When compressed by the FTO glass substrate and spiro-OMeTAD layer, 
the spongy carbon film deforms and a reliable electric contact between the carbon film and 
adjacent layers is resulted. For comparison, Au layer was deposited on FTO glass substrate by 
magnetron sputtering and applied as CE for perovskite solar cells. An insignificant PCE (~0.05%) 
as was observed, implying the device is non-functional. When the spongy carbon film is too thin, 
as in the case of CE-1, the deformation of the film under pressure is not sufficient to form well 
contacted interfaces between the carbon film and adjacent layer, resulting in a low efficiency of 
the device. When the spongy carbon film is too thick, as in the case of CE-3, charge carriers have 
a longer pathway through the disordered carbon material. Notwithstanding the good contact 
formed at the interfaces, an overly thick carbon film led to deteriorated device performance. FTO 
conducting glass substrates used to collect soot in this study may be replaced by other materials 
to further reduce the fabrication cost of perovskite solar cells. The substrate on which the spongy 


7 
 
carbon film is deposited can also be used in combination with edge sealants as a protective cover 
to prevent moisture from reaching the perovskite layer of the device, facilitating the practical 
application of perovskite solar cells.

4 Conclusions  
In conclusion, we have proposed a conceptually new counter electrode for perovskite-based 
solar cells. Different from the conventional counter electrodes which are fabricated directly on 
other component layers of a device, the new type of counter electrode is prepared on a 
separated substrate and then assembly with other components to complete the device. Spongy 
carbon film was prepared on FTO glass substrate with a facile and low-cost method and applied 
as the new type of counter electrode for a prototype device, which exhibited a power conversion 
efficiency of 4.24%. The idea of decoupling the preparation of counter electrodes and device 
assembly will enable new possibilities in choosing materials and processes to fabricate perovskite 
solar cells, and may be applied in other photovoltaic devices.

perovskite photovoltaic techniques \ndue to their potential to reach a much higher efficiency than \nthe detailed balanced efficiency limit of single-junction solar cells, \nwhich may contribute to a reduction of cost of photovoltaic systems1. \nCompared with single-junction perovskite modules, the application \ntandem structure, which has much smaller photocurrent but higher \nphotovoltage, can also reduce the cell-to-module efficiency derate2 \nand thus realize higher module efficiency for monolithically inter-\nconnected modules in series. After addressing the issues associated \nwith the low diffusion length in tin-containing Sn–Pb perovskites, \nthe efficiency of all-perovskite tandem cells quickly rose from \n10.4% (ref. 3) to 26.4% (ref. 4), which already surpassed that of \nsingle-junction perovskite cells5. However, compared with the fast \nprogress made on scaling up the single-junction perovskite modules \nin recent years, the upscaling of all-perovskite tandem modules is \nlagging behind mainly due to the challenges for the narrow bandgap \n(NBG) perovskite process in ambient conditions.\nWe identified the module-level fabrication of NBG perovskites \nand the subsequent laser scribing in air to be the bottlenecks that \nhinder the development of all-perovskite tandem solar mod-\nules. For lead-based perovskites, we have successfully developed \nthe gas-assisted blade-coating method to fabricate large-area \nsingle-junction perovskite modules with record efficiencies6–10. To \ncoat highly crystalline and compact films at high throughput, vola-\ntile solvents such as 2-methoxyethanol (boiling point of 124 °C) and \nacetonitrile (boiling point of 82 °C) were used to accelerate solvent \nevaporation during scalable coating6–10. However, such solvents do \nnot dissolve Cs-, Br- or Sn-based precursors well; those are needed \nto fabricate more efficient and stable wide bandgap (WBG) and \nNBG perovskite cells. Instead, common solvents such as dimeth-\nylformamide (DMF, boiling point of 153 °C) and dimethyl sulfox-\nide (DMSO, boiling point of 189 °C) are still the best for the WBG \nand NBG perovskite precursors. These non-volatile solvents do \nnot easily escape from the as-coated wet films even with the help \nof high-flow rate gas, mainly due to their high boiling points and \nstrong coordination to Pb2+ ions9. This challenge is even more \nsevere in NBG perovskites because its optimal thickness is generally \nlarger than that in single-junction perovskite devices, induced by \nthe low absorption coefficient of Sn–Pb perovskites in near-infrared \nrange11,12. Raising film annealing temperature cannot solve this \nproblem because the flowing of the precursor solution in a wet \nfilm right after coating drives the formation of large domains and \nnon-continuous films13. Consequently, it is much more challenging \nto deposit large-area, compact and smooth NBG perovskite films \nusing a scalable fabrication process.\nAnother obstacle is the oxidation of NBG perovskites due to \nair exposure in the following device-fabrication process steps after \nfilm deposition, including deposition of charge transport layers \nand laser scribing for module fabrication. Sn2+ in NBG perovskites \ncan be readily oxidized to Sn4+, which generates defects and excess \ndoping of NBG perovskites and thus reduces device efficiency. To \nthis end, reducing agents have been reported to prevent the oxida-\ntion of Sn2+, including metal Sn14,15, hydrazine16,17 and other Lewis \nbases12,18–20. However, most of them are aimed at removing Sn4+ in \nthe precursor solution or during film deposition. The oxidation of \nSn2+ during processes such as laser scribing for module fabrication \nhas not been investigated. Laser scribing is an essential step to cre-\nate monolithic interconnected modules. It is often conducted in air, \nexposing perovskites and scribed area to air21.\nHere we report the scalable fabrication of perovskite tandem \nmodules by blade coating. However, a 15 min air \nexposure could induce too much SnI4 or I2 so that the BHC in the \nfilm might not be enough to remove them, resulting in a shorter \ncarrier recombination lifetime of 828 ns even after storage.\nPerformance of all-perovskite tandem mini modules\nThe wide-bandgap perovskite has a composition of Cs0.25FA0.75Pb \n(I0.85Br0.15)3 with 5 mol% MAPbCl3 (ref. 49). The detailed discussion \nof the WBG junction can be found in Supplementary Note 5. The \ntandem cells and mini modules have a stacking of glass/ITO/PTAA/ \nCs0.25FA0.75Pb(I0.85Br0.15)3/C60/SnO2/Au/PEDOT:PSS/Cs0.2FA0.8Pb0.5 \nSn0.5I3/PCBM/C60/BCP/Cu, as shown in Fig. 4a, and the picture of \nan all-perovskite tandem photovoltaic mini module is shown in \nFig. 4b. We first went through the whole fabrication process using \nsmall area cells. The cross-section SEM image in Supplementary \nFig. 17 shows that the thicknesses of the blade-coated NBG and \nWBG films are 1,000 nm and 233 nm, respectively, which agree \nwith the targeted thicknesses. The 8 mm2 tandem solar cell showed \nan efficiency of 23.1% with VOC of 2.01 V, JSC of 14.8 mA cm−2 \nand FF of 77.5%. (Fig. 4c and Supplementary Table 6). The EQE \nspectra of the WBG and NBG junctions give an integrated JSC of \n14.7 mA cm−2 (Fig. 4d), which is well balanced and close to the \nJSC from the J–V measurement. In fabricating a mini module with \nan area of 10–20 cm2, the total scribing time for P2 and P3 lines \n(Fig. 4a) was around 20 min. The additional layers covering the \nNBG films should extend the operation window in air to be lon-\nger than the optimal 5 min shown above. The encapsulated mini \nmodules were stored in a glovebox for two days to reduce the \nSn4+ and iodine before measurement. Figure 4e (Supplementary \nTable 7) shows current–voltage (I–V) performance of a champion \nmini module with four subcells and an aperture area of 14.3 cm2, \ngiving an aperture PCE of 21.6% with negligible hysteresis. The \nstabilized photocurrent of the module at maximum power out-\nput point is shown as an inset of Fig. 4e, giving a stabilized PCE of \n21.5%. Each subcell in the mini module has a width of 0.65 cm, in \nwhich the dead area is 0.04 cm wide measured by optical microscopy \n(Supplementary Fig. 18), corresponding to a geometry filling factor \nof 93.8%. Therefore, the active area PCE of the tandem mini mod-\nule is 23.0%. Even though the module active area PCE is very close \nto that of small cell PCE of 23.0%, there was still a cell-to-module \nloss which was compensated by the anti-reflection layer on mod-\nules. The cell-to-module derate of only 6.5% (from 23.1% on small \ncells to 21.6% on modules) is much smaller than that of 18.2% on \nthe record-reported single-junction perovskite module10. The low \ncell-to-module derate attributed to lower photocurrent, and higher \nphotovoltage reduced the resistive loss by 66% based on our analy-\nsis shown in Supplementary Note 6. The average VOC for each sub-\ncell is 2.01 V, which is the same as that of the small devices. The no \nloss of VOC from cell-to-module transition indicates the 20 min air \nexposure during scribing, and other processes did not damage the \nNBG perovskite films. The reduced FF could stem from the large \nsubcell area, increasing the series resistance to 48.3 Ω cm2, which is \naround five times of the 8 mm2 small cells. The efficiency statistics of \n20 all-perovskite tandem mini modules are listed in Fig. 4f, showing \nthat the average aperture efficiency of the tandem modules reached \n20.5%. Supplementary Fig. 19 shows the long-term photo stability \nof the all-perovskite tandem solar module under 1 sun illumination. \nThe module retained ~90.0% of its initial PCE after 250 h.\nConclusions\nIn summary, we adopted a hot gas-assisted blade-coating strategy \nto deposit high-quality, large-area and thick NBG perovskite films \nto fabricate all-perovskite tandem modules. The reductant BHC \nprevented the formation of Sn4+ during film fabrication and also \nreduced the Sn4+ and iodine generated during air exposure. We \ndemonstrate a performance-enhancement mechanism on Sn–Pb \nperovskite solar cells resulting from a combination of oxidation, \nBHC in perovskites and a post-fabrication storage process that \nmakes modules efficient. The all-perovskite tandem mini modules \nhave been fabricated and achieved a PCE of 21.6% with an aperture \narea of 14.3 cm2.\nMethods\nMaterials. Lead iodide (PbI2, 99.999% trace metals), tin(ii) iodide (SnI2, \n99.999%), lead(ii) bromide (PbBr2, 99.999%), lead(ii) chloride (PbBr2, 99.999%), \ntin(ii) fluoride (SnF2, 99%), caesium iodide (CsI, 99.999%), Poly[bis(4-phenyl)\n(2,4,6-trimethylphenyl)amine] (PTAA), bathocuproine (BCP), anhydrous \nN,N-dimethylformamide (DMF, 99.8%), anhydrous dimethyl sulfoxide \n(DMSO, ≥ 99.9%), anhydrous acetonitrile (99.8%), anhydrous 2-Propanol \n(IPA, 99.5%), L-α-phosphatidylcholine (LP), propylhydrazine hydrochloride, \n(2-thienylmethyl)hydrazine hydrochloride, hydrazine monohydrochloride and \nanhydrous toluene (99.8%) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich and used without \nfurther purification. Methylammonium iodide, formamidinium iodide (FAI) and \nphenethylammonium iodide (PEAI) were purchased from Greatcell Solar. C60 and \n[6,6]-phenyl-C61-butyric acid methyl ester (PCBM) were purchased from Nano-C. \nPoly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene):poly(styrene sulfonate) PEDOT:PSS (Clevios P \nVP AI 4083) was purchased from Heraeus. Benzylhydrazine hydrochloride  \n(BHC, 95%) was purchased from AmBeed.\nPerovskite precursor solution preparation. For the WBG perovskite, 1.35 M Cs0.25\nFA0.75Pb(I0.85Br0.15)3 precursor solution was prepared in mixed solvents of DMF and \nDMSO with a volume ratio of 16:1. The molar ratios for CsI:FAI and PbI2:PbBr2 \nwere 0.25:0.75 and 0.775:0.225, respectively. The precursor solution was stirred \nat room temperature for 1 h. In addition, 5 mol% (relative to 1.35 M precursor \nsolution) MAPbCl3, 0.68 mg ml−1 PEAI, 0.68 mg ml−1 BHC, 0.17 mg ml−1 LP and \n0.17 mg ml−1 FAH2PO2 were added in the solution before blade coating.\nFor the NBG perovskite 2.4 M Cs0.2FA0.8Pb0.5Sn0.5I3 precursor solution was \nprepared in mixed solvents of DMF and DMSO with a volume ratio of 43:7. The \nmolar ratios for CsI:FAI and PbI2:SnI2 were 0.2:0.8 and 0.5:0.5, respectively. In \naddition, 10 mol% (relative to SnI2) SnF2 was added in the precursor solution. The \nprecursor solution was stirred at room temperature for 3 h. The additives 1 mg ml−1 \nPEAI and 1 mg ml−1 BHC were added into the precursor solution before blade \ncoating. In addition, 20 vol% (relative to precursor solution) acetonitrile was added \nbefore blade coating to dilute the solution.\nDevice fabrication. The commercial patterned ITO substrates were cleaned by \nultrasonication with deionized water, acetone and isopropanol sequentially. The \ndried substrate was then subjected to UV–ozone treatment for 15 min.\nSingle-junction WBG perovskite solar cell fabrication. PTAA (2 mg ml−1) dissolved \nin toluene was blade coated on the substrates without gas-assisted drying. The \ncoating was conducted in ambient air (20 ± 1 °C, 65 ± 5 RH%). The coating speed \nwas 20 mm s−1. The coating gap between the blade and substrates was 150 µm. \nSubsequently, the Cs0.25FA0.75Pb(I0.85Br0.15)3 (with 5 mol% MAPbCl3) precursor \nsolution was blade coated in a glovebox with room temperature N2 gas-assisted \ndrying. The coating speed was 20 mm s−1 with a coating gap of 215 µm. The \nas-coated films annealed on one hot plate at 130 °C for 10 s, then transferred \nto another hot plate with 100 °C to anneal another 15 min. The perovskite film \nthickness was around 230 nm. Finally, 25 nm C60, 6 nm BCP and 80 nm Cu were \nthermal evaporated subsequently onto the samples.\nSingle-junction NBG perovskite solar cell fabrication. Commercial PEDOT:PSS \nwas blade coated on the substrates heated to 70 °C. The coating was conducted \nin ambient air (20 ± 1 °C, 65 ± 5 RH%). The coating speed was 20 mm s−1 with \na coating gap of 200 µm. The blade-coated films annealed at 130 °C for 10 min. \nSubsequently, the Cs0.2FA0.8Pb0.5Sn0.5I3 precursor solution was blade coated in a \nglovebox under blowing N2 gas at 100 °C. The gas temperature was controlled by a \nproportional–integral–derivative controller through a thermocouple integrated on \nthe in-line heater. The coating speed was 25 mm s−1 with a coating gap of 275 µm. \nThe as-coated films annealed on one hot plate at 150 °C for 10 s, then transferred to \nNature Energy | VOL 7 | October 2022 | 923–931 | www.nature.com/natureenergy\n929\n\n\nArticles\nNature Energy\nanother hot plate with 100 °C to anneal another 7 min. The perovskite film thickness \nwas around 1,000 nm. Subsequently, the film surface was treated with BHC in a \nglovebox by spin coating a 1 mg ml−1 BHC solution in IPA at 5,000 r.p.m. for 25 s. \nPCBM dissolved in toluene (10 mg ml−1) was spin coated at 5,000 r.p.m. for 25 s. \nAfter annealing on a hot plate at 70 °C for 10 min, the samples were exposed in air \n(20 ± 1 °C, 65 ± 5 RH%) for 1 min, 5 min and 15 min, respectively. Finally, 25 nm C60, \n6 nm BCP and 80 nm Cu were subsequently thermally evaporated onto the samples.\nFabrication of tandem solar cells and modules. PTAA (2 mg ml−1) dissolved in \ntoluene was blade coated on the substrates without gas-assisted drying. The \ncoating was conducted in ambient air (20 ± 1 °C, 65 ± 5 RH%). The coating speed \nwas 20 mm s−1. The coating gap between the blade and substrates was 150 µm. \nSubsequently, the Cs0.25FA0.75Pb(I0.85Br0.15)3 (with 5 mol% MAPbCl3) precursor \nsolution was blade coated in a glovebox with room temperature N2 gas-assisted \ndrying. The coating speed was 20 mm s−1 with a coating gap of 215 µm. The \nas-coated films annealed on one hot plate at 130 °C for 10 s, then transferred to \nanother hot plate with 100 °C to anneal another 15 min. After thermal evaporation \nof 25 nm C60 on the WBG films, the samples were transferred to an atomic \nlayer deposition (Veeco Savannah S200) chamber to deposit 20 nm SnO2 using \nprecursors of tetrakis(dimethylamino) tin(iv) (99.9999%) and deionized water. \nSubsequently, 1 nm Au was thermally evaporated onto the samples. PEDOT:PSS \nwas blade coated onto the samples in ambient air (20 ± 1 °C, 65 ± 5 RH%) heated \nto 70 °C. The coating speed was 20 mm s−1 with a coating gap of 200 µm. The films \nannealed at 100 °C for 10 min in a glovebox. The Cs0.2FA0.8Pb0.5Sn0.5I3 precursor \nsolution was blade coated in a glovebox under blowing N2 gas at 100 °C. The coating \nspeed was 25 mm s−1 with a coating gap of 275 µm. The as-coated films annealed \non one hot plate at 150 °C for 10 s, then transferred to another hot plate with 100 °C \nto anneal another 7 min. Subsequently, the film surface was treated with BHC by \nspin coating a 1 mg ml−1 BHC solution in IPA at 5,000 r.p.m. for 25 s in a glovebox. \nPCBM dissolved in toluene (10 mg ml−1) was spin coated at 5,000 r.p.m. for 25 s in a \nglovebox. And samples annealed on a hot plate at 70 °C for 10 min. For small cells, \nthe samples were exposed in air (20 ± 1 °C, 65 ± 5 RH%) for 5 min before 25 nm C60, \n6 nm BCP and 80 nm Cu were subsequently thermally evaporated to complete the \nfabrication. For modules, 25 nm C60, 6 nm BCP and 20 nm Cu were subsequently \nthermally evaporated. The samples were then transferred to air (20 ± 1 °C, 65 ± 5 \nRH%) to laser scribe P2 lines. After scribing, another layer of 180 nm Cu was \ndeposited by thermal evaporation. The samples were scribed P3 lines with laser in \nair (20 ± 1 °C, 65 ± 5 RH%) to complete the module fabrication. All the devices were \nencapsulated in a glovebox with epoxy and glass on top. The devices were stored in \nthe glovebox before measurement. In addition, polydimethylsiloxane anti-reflection \nlayers were applied for J–V measurements.\nDevice characterizations. The current–voltage measurements were performed \nunder the simulated AM 1.5 G irradiation produced by a Xenon-lamp-based \nsolar simulator (Oriel 94043 A, Class AAA Solar Simulator). The light intensity \nwas calibrated using a silicon reference cell with a KG5 glass filter (Newport \n91150-KG5). The data were recorded by a Keithley 2400 Source-Meter. All the \nJ–V measurements were taken under 100 mW cm−2 illumination at a scan rate \nof 0.1 V s−1 with a delay time of 10 ms, and there was no preconditioning before \nmeasurements. EQE spectra were measured on a Newport quantum efficiency \nmeasurement kit by focusing a monochromatic beam from a Bruker Vertex 80 v \nFourier transform interferometer with tungsten lamp source onto the devices. \nThe photocurrent was recorded by a Stanford Research Systems SR570 current \npreamplifier. The calibration was done on a Newport silicon reference solar cell \nwith a known EQE. Blue (~470 nm) and infrared (~940 nm) light bias with an \nintensity of ~0.3 sun was applied to measure the EQE of the NBG and WBG \njunctions, respectively. Scanning electron microscope images were taken on \nFEI Helios 600 NanoLab DualBeam System operating at 5 kV. The XRD pattern \nwas obtained with a Rigaku sixth generation MiniFlex X-ray diffractometer. \nUltraviolet–visible–near-infrared absorbance was characterized by PerkinElmer \nLAMBDA 1050 spectrophotometers equipped with an integrating sphere. The \nhigh-resolution XPS measurements were conducted with a monochromatic Al Kα \nsource (1,486.6 eV). The samples were placed in an ultra-high vacuum analytical \nchamber under a base pressure of 1 × 10−10 Torr. The X-ray gun was running at \n10 kV and 20 mA with a spot size of 0.6 mm in diameter on the sample. Transient \nphotovoltage data was collected by an oscilloscope (DSO-X 3104 A, KEYSIGHT) \nwith internal impedance of 1 MΩ. The solar devices were applied a 1 sun light bias. \nA 337 nm laser pulse (Stanford Research Systems NL 100 nitrogen laser, frequency \nof 10 Hz and pulse width of <3.5 ns) hit on the device to trigger a photovoltage \nvariation (<5% of VOC) onto the VOC. DLCP was characterized using an Agilent \nE4980A precision inductance–capacitance–resistance (LCR) meter. The voltage \nwas scanning from 0 V to the VOC of the perovskite solar cells. The a.c. frequency \nwas set to be 1,000 kHz to characterize the doping level. For the long-term stability \nmeasurement, the devices that encapsulated with epoxy and glass were connected \nto resistors to operate at their maximum power point at the beginning of the \ntest. The devices were put in air (relative humidity of 30–65%) under constant \nillumination provided by a light-emitting diode (LED) light source with an \nintensity of 1 sun. The temperature of the devices was kept at ~30 °C. The devices \nwere scanned I–V curves every 48 h.\nReporting summary. T
andem perovskite solar cells have cut a fine figure in the 
rapid development of perovskite photovoltaic techniques 
due to their potential to reach a much higher efficiency than 
the detailed balanced efficiency limit of single-junction solar cells, 
which may contribute to a reduction of cost of photovoltaic systems1. 
Compared with single-junction perovskite modules, the application 
tandem structure, which has much smaller photocurrent but higher 
photovoltage, can also reduce the cell-to-module efficiency derate2 
and thus realize higher module efficiency for monolithically inter-
connected modules in series. After addressing the issues associated 
with the low diffusion length in tin-containing Sn–Pb perovskites, 
the efficiency of all-perovskite tandem cells quickly rose from 
10.4% (ref. 3) to 26.4% (ref. 4), which already surpassed that of 
single-junction perovskite cells5. However, compared with the fast 
progress made on scaling up the single-junction perovskite modules 
in recent years, the upscaling of all-perovskite tandem modules is 
lagging behind mainly due to the challenges for the narrow bandgap 
(NBG) perovskite process in ambient conditions.
We identified the module-level fabrication of NBG perovskites 
and the subsequent laser scribing in air to be the bottlenecks that 
hinder the development of all-perovskite tandem solar mod-
ules. For lead-based perovskites, we have successfully developed 
the gas-assisted blade-coating method to fabricate large-area 
single-junction perovskite modules with record efficiencies6–10. To 
coat highly crystalline and compact films at high throughput, vola-
tile solvents such as 2-methoxyethanol (boiling point of 124 °C) and 
acetonitrile (boiling point of 82 °C) were used to accelerate solvent 
evaporation during scalable coating6–10. However, such solvents do 
not dissolve Cs-, Br- or Sn-based precursors well; those are needed 
to fabricate more efficient and stable wide bandgap (WBG) and 
NBG perovskite cells. Instead, common solvents such as dimeth-
ylformamide (DMF, boiling point of 153 °C) and dimethyl sulfox-
ide (DMSO, boiling point of 189 °C) are still the best for the WBG 
and NBG perovskite precursors. These non-volatile solvents do 
not easily escape from the as-coated wet films even with the help 
of high-flow rate gas, mainly due to their high boiling points and 
strong coordination to Pb2+ ions9. This challenge is even more 
severe in NBG perovskites because its optimal thickness is generally 
larger than that in single-junction perovskite devices, induced by 
the low absorption coefficient of Sn–Pb perovskites in near-infrared 
range11,12. Raising film annealing temperature cannot solve this 
problem because the flowing of the precursor solution in a wet 
film right after coating drives the formation of large domains and 
non-continuous films13. Consequently, it is much more challenging 
to deposit large-area, compact and smooth NBG perovskite films 
using a scalable fabrication process.
Another obstacle is the oxidation of NBG perovskites due to 
air exposure in the following device-fabrication process steps after 
film deposition, including deposition of charge transport layers 
and laser scribing for module fabrication. Sn2+ in NBG perovskites 
can be readily oxidized to Sn4+, which generates defects and excess 
doping of NBG perovskites and thus reduces device efficiency. To 
this end, reducing agents have been reported to prevent the oxida-
tion of Sn2+, including metal Sn14,15, hydrazine16,17 and other Lewis 
bases12,18–20. However, most of them are aimed at removing Sn4+ in 
the precursor solution or during film deposition. The oxidation of 
Sn2+ during processes such as laser scribing for module fabrication 
has not been investigated. Laser scribing is an essential step to cre-
ate monolithic interconnected modules. It is often conducted in air, 
exposing perovskites and scribed area to air21.
Here we report the scalable fabrication of perovskite tandem 
modules by blade coating. A hot gas-assisted blade-coating system 
was developed to fabricate high-quality and thick NBG perovskite 
films. The hot gas accelerated the drying of the high boiling point 
solvents to solidify the as-coated film, preventing the microscale 
solution flows. In addition, a reducing agent benzylhydrazine hydro-
chloride (BHC) was introduced to prevent Sn2+ oxidation during 
film deposition and, more importantly, to withstand the air exposure 
during laser scribing. Surprisingly, air exposure of NBG perovskite 
films for a few minutes actually boosted the power conversion 
Efficient monolithic all-perovskite tandem solar 
modules with small cell-to-module derate
Xuezeng Dai   1, Shangshang Chen1, Haoyang Jiao1, Liang Zhao1, Ke Wang2, Zhenyi Ni1, Zhenhua Yu1, 
Bo Chen1, Yongli Gao2 and Jinsong Huang   1,3 ✉
All-perovskite tandem solar modules are promising to reduce the cost of photovoltaic systems with their high efficiency and 
solution fabrication, but their sensitivity to air still imposes a great challenge. Here a hot gas-assisted blading method is devel-
oped to accelerate the perovskite solidification, forming compact and thick narrow bandgap (NBG) perovskite films. Adding a 
reduction agent into NBG films followed by a short period of air exposure and a post-fabrication storage surprisingly increases 
carrier recombination lifetime and enables laser scribing in ambient conditions without obvious loss of device performance. This 
combination suppresses tin and iodide oxidation and forms a thin SnO2 layer on the NBG film surface. Monolithic all-perovskite 
tandem solar modules showed a champion efficiency of 21.6% with a 14.3 cm2 aperture area, corresponding to an active area 
efficiency of 23.0%. The very small cell-to-module derate of 6.5% demonstrates the advantage of a tandem monolithic struc-
ture for solar modules.

Blade coating high-quality NBG films
The NBG perovskite composition in this study is Cs0.2FA0.8Pb0.5Sn0.5I3 
which has a bandgap of 1.22 eV. The optimal thickness of this NBG 
perovskite for tandem devices was reported to be 1,000 nm (ref. 11). 
To fabricate such thick films by blade coating, the as-coated wet 
films also need to be thick enough, given that the NBG solution 
precursor concentration is not higher than that of lead perovskites. 
Figure 1 shows our blading system setup, photos of the films 
coated under different conditions and scanning electron micros-
copy (SEM) images of the perovskite films annealed after differ-
ent durations. In our initial trials, we applied our well-established 
room temperature (RT, 20 ± 1 °C) N2-assisted blade-coating 
method to coat the 1,000 nm thick NBG films6–9. However, the 
DMF/DMSO-based precursor solution dried much slower so that 
a large amount of precursor solution remained in the coated film 
(Fig. 1c). Post-annealing of such films at 100 °C drove the precur-
sor solution to flow, leaving non-continuous perovskite films with 
gaps between large domains, as shown in the SEM images in Fig. 1c 
and Supplementary Fig. 1. Such a domain structure growth has 
been observed in our previous study where the slow-drying ink was 
blade coated on heated substrates13. The flowing of precursor solu-
tion towards early nucleation sites forms such domain structures 
(not single crystalline). The domains were found to form within 1 s 
of annealing, and additional annealing did not change the domain 
structure anymore (Fig. 1c; 3 s–420 s). To address this issue, we 
accelerated the solvent evaporation during blading by raising the 
N2 temperature. Hot air-assisted drying was applied in spin coat-
ing22, spray coating23 and slot die coating24 of perovskites that are 
less sensitive to air. However, in those studies, hot air from hot guns 
had limited control of gas temperature and flow rate and could treat 
only small area films (< 1 cm2). The hot gas system developed by us 
has an in-line heater (Omega, AHPF-121) that transports heated 
gas to a wide gas knife (15 cm) to provide precise control of gas 
temperature and flow rate. To avoid oxidation of Sn perovskites, 
nitrogen was used as the working gas and was heated to 40 °C, 70 °C 
and 100 °C. The blade-coated film pictures and their SEM images 
are shown in Fig. 1d–f. With 40 °C N2, the as-coated film showed a 
grey colour, a sign of more efficient solvent removal during blading. 
However, the domain pattern still existed, though it became smaller. 
When N2 temperature was elevated to 70 °C, the film showed a 
light black colour without annealing, indicating most solvents had 
already evaporated. However, large pinholes were still observed 
in the whole film despite no domain pattern being captured after 
the annealing. Eventually, 100 °C N2 created a dark black film right 
after blading. X-ray diffraction (XRD) results in Supplementary 
Fig. 2 revealed that the as-coated film was already converted to 
the perovskite phase right after blading. SEM images (Fig. 1f) con-
firmed the formation of pinhole-free, compact perovskite films after 
annealing. The rapid solvent extraction assisted by hot gas quickly 
formed solid films, which prevents the particles from moving dur-
ing thermal annealing. The anti-solvent bathing25–27 is an alterna-
tive strategy to quickly remove the precursor solvents from films. 
However, such a strategy requires a relatively long bathing time, and 
there is also a strict requirement of bathing solvent. Superior to the 
anti-solvent method, the hot gas strategy is a physical approach that 
avoids using any solvent, making it much easier to integrate into the 
high-speed sheet-to-sheet or roll-to-roll manufacturing production 
lines. We also looked into whether tiny extra strain was introduced 
into the films by hot gas drying. As shown by the XRD patterns in 
Supplementary Fig. 3, there was no lattice constant change for the 
films made by hot gas drying. This can be explained by the follow-
ing grain-growth process during annealing releasing the possible 
strain in the perovskite films. We also evaluated the feasibility of 
coating NBG perovskite films using pre-heated substrates, and the 
discussion can be found in Supplementary Note 1, showing that 
using hot gas is a superior strategy for fabricating high-quality thick 
NBG perovskite films.
The generation of voids at the perovskite–substrate interfaces in 
bladed thick perovskites was previously observed; they are caused by 
the evaporation of trapped DMSO near the bottom of the perovskite 
films and downward growth of perovskite films due to initial evapo-
ration of solvents from the top surface28,29. Such voids could dra-
matically reduce device performance10,28. To find out whether these 
thick NBG perovskite films have voids, we conducted cross-section 
SEM measurement. The SEM images shown in Fig. 1g uncovered 
many voids generated at the bottom of the perovskite films made 
with 100 °C hot gas-assisted blading when DMSO/(Pb + Sn) molar 
ratio is 16%. To prevent the formation of the voids, we reduced the 
DMSO/(Pb + Sn) molar ratio to 8% and 4%. As shown in Fig. 1h, 
the 8% DMSO resulted in the formation of void-free films with 
large monolithic grains. However, 4% DMSO generated films with 
multi-layer small grains (Fig. 1i) that contain more grain boundar-
ies and thus more defects. By tuning the hot gas temperature and 
DMSO content in the precursor solution, we have successfully 
fabricated compact NBG perovskites over a large area using a scal-
able coating process. A high-quality blade-coated large-area NBG 
perovskite film is shown in Fig. 1b.
Improving NBG device performance by BHC
Suppressing the oxidation of Sn2+ in NBG perovskite in air is criti-
cal to achieve high performance devices. Therefore, we introduced 
a reductant BHC into the NBG film. Inspired by the excellent 
reduction function on preventing the generation of I2 in iodide 
perovskites7, we expect that BHC has the same function of reduc-
ing iodine generated during the operation of NBG perovskites. In 
addition, we verified its capability of reducing Sn4+ to Sn2+. A yellow 
NBG perovskite precursor solution was oxidized in the air until it 
turned into red, indicating the formation of a large amount of Sn4+ 
in solution16,30. As shown in Fig. 2a, after the BHC was added into 
the oxidized solution, the solution turned back into a yellow colour 
within 10 s, proving the capability of BHC to reduce Sn4+ to Sn2+ at 
room temperature. The product of BHC after the reducing reaction 
is phenyldiazomethane (Supplementary Scheme 1), which did not 
obviously harm the NBG perovskites within our testing time range.
We fabricated single-junction devices to evaluate the effect 
of BHC on NBG solar cell efficiency. The NBG single-junction 
perovskite solar cells had a structure of glass/indium tin oxide 
(ITO)/poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene):poly(styrene 
sulfonate)
(PEDOT:PSS)/Cs0.2FA0.8 Pb0.5Sn0.5I3/[6,6]-phenyl-C61-butyric acid 
methyl ester (PCBM)/fullerene (C60)/bathocuproine (BCP)/copper 
(Cu). As the perovskite film surface is most vulnerable to oxida-
tion, we treated the as-coated NBG perovskite surface using BHC 
dissolved in an orthogonal solvent of 2-propanol with a low con-
centration of 1 g l−1. Figure 2b (Supplementary Table 1) shows that 
BHC surface treatment clearly enhanced the efficiency of NBG 
solar cells. The open-circuit voltage (VOC) increased from 0.765 V to 
0.809 V, and the PCE went up from 17.0% to 18.6%. The enhance-
ment of short-circuit current (JSC) by BHC agrees with the higher 
external quantum efficiency (EQE) shown in Supplementary Fig. 5. 
The severe hysteresis disappeared after surface treatment. We fur-
ther added 0.4 g l−1 BHC into the precursor solution as an additive 
with an intention to reduce the pre-existing Sn4+ in raw precursor 
materials and the generated Sn4+ during film fabrication processes.

A surprising phenomenon was observed when we studied the 
aged NBG device performance, that is, we measured the device effi-
ciencies after storing the devices in the glovebox for a few days. After 
two days of storage, all devices showed increased efficiency (Fig. 2d  
and Table 1). Ageing-related efficiency enhancements from Pb 
perovskite solar cells were reported previously, which were attributed 
to several different mechanisms including strain relaxation31,32, defect 
self-annihilation33–36 or de-doping8 of perovskites. However, different 
from Pb perovskite solar cells, Sn–Pb perovskite devices showed the 
best efficiency gain by a combination of air exposure of perovskite 
films during fabrication and ageing of perovskite devices after fab-
rication. The devices with air-exposed films for 1 min and 5 min 
had efficiencies of 19.6% and 20.3%, respectively, which are much 
higher than that of the device without air exposure and comparable 
to the best spin coated NBG perovskite solar cells11,12,37. Even for the 
severely damaged device after 15 min air exposure, ageing recovered 
its VOC by 0.116 V and almost doubled its efficiency from 9.4% to 
15.2%. We speculate this phenomenon is caused by the BHC additive.

without BHC. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 8 and Supplementary 
Table 2, air exposure of NBG films without BHC caused a quick 
device degradation, and the ageing process did not recover the 
efficiencies. These results concluded that the reducing agent BHC

Performance of all-perovskite tandem mini modules
The wide-bandgap perovskite has a composition of Cs0.25FA0.75Pb 
(I0.85Br0.15)3 with 5 mol% MAPbCl3 (ref. 49). The detailed discussion 
of the WBG junction can be found in Supplementary Note 5. The 
tandem cells and mini modules have a stacking of glass/ITO/PTAA/ 
Cs0.25FA0.75Pb(I0.85Br0.15)3/C60/SnO2/Au/PEDOT:PSS/Cs0.2FA0.8Pb0.5 
Sn0.5I3/PCBM/C60/BCP/Cu, as shown in Fig. 4a, and the picture of 
an all-perovskite tandem photovoltaic mini module is shown in 
Fig. 4b. We first went through the whole fabrication process using 
small area cells. The cross-section SEM image in Supplementary 
Fig. 17 shows that the thicknesses of the blade-coated NBG and 
WBG films are 1,000 nm and 233 nm, respectively, which agree 
with the targeted thicknesses. The 8 mm2 tandem solar cell showed 
an efficiency of 23.1% with VOC of 2.01 V, JSC of 14.8 mA cm−2 
and FF of 77.5%. (Fig. 4c and Supplementary Table 6). The EQE 
spectra of the WBG and NBG junctions give an integrated JSC of 
14.7 mA cm−2 (Fig. 4d), which is well balanced and close to the 
JSC from the J–V measurement. In fabricating a mini module with 
an area of 10–20 cm2, the total scribing time for P2 and P3 lines 
(Fig. 4a) was around 20 min. The additional layers covering the 
NBG films should extend the operation window in air to be lon-
ger than the optimal 5 min shown above. The encapsulated mini 
modules were stored in a glovebox for two days to reduce the 
Sn4+ and iodine before measurement. Figure 4e (Supplementary 
Table 7) shows current–voltage (I–V) performance of a champion 
mini module with four subcells and an aperture area of 14.3 cm2, 
giving an aperture PCE of 21.6% with negligible hysteresis. The 
stabilized photocurrent of the module at maximum power out-
put point is shown as an inset of Fig. 4e, giving a stabilized PCE of 
21.5%. Each subcell in the mini module has a width of 0.65 cm, in 
which the dead area is 0.04 cm wide measured by optical microscopy 
(Supplementary Fig. 18), corresponding to a geometry filling factor 
of 93.8%. Therefore, the active area PCE of the tandem mini mod-
ule is 23.0%. Even though the module active area PCE is very close 
to that of small cell PCE of 23.0%, there was still a cell-to-module 
loss which was compensated by the anti-reflection layer on mod-
ules. The cell-to-module derate of only 6.5% (from 23.1% on small 
cells to 21.6% on modules) is much smaller than that of 18.2% on 
the record-reported single-junction perovskite module10. The low 
cell-to-module derate attributed to lower photocurrent, and higher 
photovoltage reduced the resistive loss by 66% based on our analy-
sis shown in Supplementary Note 6. The average VOC for each sub-
cell is 2.01 V, which is the same as that of the small devices. The no 
loss of VOC from cell-to-module transition indicates the 20 min air 
exposure during scribing, and other processes did not damage the 
NBG perovskite films. The reduced FF could stem from the large 
subcell area, increasing the series resistance to 48.3 Ω cm2, which is 
around five times of the 8 mm2 small cells. The efficiency statistics of 
20 all-perovskite tandem mini modules are listed in Fig. 4f, showing 
that the average aperture efficiency of the tandem modules reached 
20.5%. Supplementary Fig. 19 shows the long-term photo stability 
of the all-perovskite tandem solar module under 1 sun illumination. 
The module retained ~90.0% of its initial PCE after 250 h.
Conclusions
In summary, we adopted a hot gas-assisted blade-coating strategy 
to deposit high-quality, large-area and thick NBG perovskite films 
to fabricate all-perovskite tandem modules. The reductant BHC 
prevented the formation of Sn4+ during film fabrication and also 
reduced the Sn4+ and iodine generated during air exposure. We 
demonstrate a performance-enhancement mechanism on Sn–Pb 
perovskite solar cells resulting from a combination of oxidation, 
BHC in perovskites and a post-fabrication storage process that 
makes modules efficient. The all-perovskite tandem mini modules 
have been fabricated and achieved a PCE of 21.6% with an aperture 
area of 14.3 cm2.

(2,4,6-trimethylphenyl)amine] (PTAA), bathocuproine (BCP), anhydrous
