processing a thin layer of large cation on top of the 3D perovskite
ﬁlm, a mixed or layered multidimensional PSCs could be fabri-
cated which are stable and possess has both the environmentally
stable features and promising photovoltaic performance.[21–25]
However, only a handful of organic cation crystalize into 1D
perovskite structure. Bi et al. employed an aliphatic ﬂuorinated
additive 1,1,1-triﬂuoro-ethyl ammonium iodide (FEAI) in meth-
ylammonium lead iodide (MAPbI3) perovskite to improve the
environmental stability and PCE of the PSCs.[26] Fan et al. intro-
duced 2-(1H-pyrazol-1-yl) pyridine (PZPY) into 3D perovskite
which can not only produce a series of 1D or 1D D1 heterojunc-
tions, but also obtain a thermodynamic self-healing ability, and
improve the long-term stability.[27] Liu et al. constructed a lattice-
matched structure by incorporating 1D PbI2-bipydine (BPy)
perovskite into 3D perovskite to slow down ion migration with
enhanced stability of perovskite ﬁlm and device.[20] Yu et al. dem-
onstrated that the introduction of hydrazinium (HA) into forma-
midinium lead iodide (FAPbI3) perovskite can stabilize the α-
phase FAPbI3 by forming 1D/3D hybrid perovskite structure.[28]
In the work of Gao et al., thiazole ammonium iodide (TAI) was
applied to form a 1D passivation layer of TAPbI3 on the 3D perov-
skite ﬁlm and the corresponding device displayed higher PCE
and better long-term operational stability as compared to the ref-
erence device.[29] Similarly, Xu et al. employed a 1D PyPbI3 (Py:
pyrrolidine) perovskitoid layer on the 3D FAPbI3-based perov-
skite to stabilize the black perovskite phase and enhance the per-
formance of the achieved device.[30] Chen’s group introduced a
thin layer of 1D/3D heterostructure by in situ cross-linking of
polymerizable propargylammonium (PAþ) to facilitate the inter-
facial charge transport and release the residual tensile strain in
the perovskite ﬁlms.[31] Very recently, Bi et al. employed 2-dieth-
ylaminoethylchloride hydrochloride (DEAECCl) to prepare a
novel 1D perovskitoid, which can induce the growth of
1D@3D perovskite structure, leading to better crystallinity and
charge transport, and reduced remnant tensile strain in 3D
perovskite ﬁlm, thereby enhance the PCE and stability of the
devices.[9] However, steric hindrance induced by large organic
cation in 1D perovskite leads to poor and anisotropic charge con-
ductivity resulting lower PCE value. Thus, further research is
needed to explore new organic cation leading to 1D perovskite
structure which can be synchronized with 3D perovskite.
Typically, the conventional ammonium based organic cations
are easily decomposed due to the presence of N—H bonds, which
can be further hydrolyzed by water molecules in the air. To address
this stability issue, sulfonium-containing cations, such as including
trimethylsulfonium (Me3Sþ), trimethylsulfoxonium (Me3Sþ), and
butyldimethylsulfonium (BDMSþ), have been investigated and
these cations display great potential for constructing stable perov-
skite materials and related optoelectronic devices.[32] Among them,
it has been demonstrated that Me3SI, a novel sulfur-based cation,
could react with metal halide and form stable 1D perovskites
Me3SBX3 in or (Me3S)2BX3. Kaltzoglou and co-workers developed
Me3SPbI3 and investigated its structural and optoelectronic prop-
erties, which showed high stability under moist air conditions and
up to 200 C for the ﬁrst time.[33,34] Additionally, they also reported
the crystal structure and physical properties of (Me3S)2SnX6
(X ¼ Cl, Br, I) compounds as well as the application of
((CH3)3S)2SnI6 in dye-sensitized solar cells with enhanced perfor-
mance and stability.[21,35,36] Afterward, Hu et al. prepared 1D
Me3SPbI3 nanorod arrays and employed it for solar cells and photo-
detectors, which exhibited excellent stability over two months
under ambient conditions.[37] Inspired by this, we have synthesized
Me3SPbI3 nanoarray and fabricated PSCs device based on this
nanoarray shows, PCE over 2% and good long-term stability, which
is higher than the previously reported 1D perovskites based devi-
ces. Interestingly, after incorporating into 3D perovskites, the het-
erostructure
1D/3D
perovskites
exhibits
prolonged
photoluminescence lifetime and reduced charge recombination
compared with its 3D counterpart. Finally, an efﬁcient and stable
1D/3D device is realized, exhibiting a PCE of 22.06%, and main-
taining 97% of their initial efﬁciency after 1000 h storage in mois-
ture, illumination, and heat.
2. Results and Discussion
In this work, we successfully synthesized Me3SPbI3 nanoarrays
ﬁlm via a two-step aqueous phase approach for the ﬁrst time,
where the PbI2 solution was spin-coated on the ITO substrates
and then the substrates were immersed into the Me3SI aqueous
solution (1 mg mL1 in DI water) for various time at 60 C,
achieving
different
nanostructured
Me3SPbI3
nanoarrays.
These ﬁlms were characterized by XRD and SEM to study the
reaction mechanism between Me3SI and PbI2. From the SEM
image in Figure 1a, a layered PbI2 ﬁlm with some nano-sized
holes are deposited on the ITO, well agreed with the previous
reports.[37,38]
After
immersing
for
1 min,
an
uniform
Me3SPbI3 nanoarray is produced by the reaction of Me3SI and
PbI2, which can be clearly observed from Figure 1b. When we
prolonged the dipping time over 1 h, it randomly distributed
some large-size nanoparticles or hexagonal nanorods with length
of several micrometres (Figure 1c,d). All these results indicate a
good chemical stability of the Me3SPbI3 against water molecules.
Figure 1e shows the XRD patterns of the Me3SPbI3 nanoarrays
ﬁlms with various soaking time in aqueous solution with contin-
uous heating at 60 C. For the pure PbI2, only one main charac-
teristic peak located at 12.6 corresponding to (001) plane.[30]
After increasing of the dipping time, the peak of PbI2 gradually
weakened while some new peaks were observed at 10.6, 24.2,
and 31.2, corresponding to the (100), (201), and (202) reﬂections
of 1D Me3SPbI3, indicating the successful formation of hexago-
nal Me3SPbI3. The UV absorption and the steady-state PL spec-
trum are shown in Figure S1, Supporting Information, the
absorption peak ranges from 350 to 700 nm while a broad emis-
sion peak of Me3SPbI3 nanorod arrays is observed at about
520 nm perovskite with good crystallinity and purity.[30,32]
Meanwhile, we also measured XRD for the sampled prepared
at 25 C. However, we found that there was still a residual peak
for PbI2 after even 12 h dipping, suggesting a slow formation of
Me3SPbI3 nanoarrays as shown in Figure S2, Supporting
Information. In order to study the crystal phase of Me3SPbI3,
we prepared a needle-like 1D perovskite single crystal (SCs)
by following the antisolvent method as reported in our previous
work.[37] The well-deﬁned diffraction peaks (Figure 1f) suggested
a good crystallinity of the obtained Me3SPbI3 nanoarrays, which
can be indexed as the hexagonal crystal structure with space
group of P63mc (No.186) and lattice constants a ¼ b ¼ 9.615 Å,
c ¼ 7.950 Å, a ¼ b ¼ 90, c ¼ 120. As shown in Figure 1g,h,

low

of

To evaluate photovoltaic performance of the device with and
without 1D Me3SPbI3 incorporation, we assembled PSCs with
the structure of ITO/SnO2/3D or 1D/3D perovskite/ Spiro-
OMeTAD/Au (as shown in inset of Figure 4a). When the concen-
tration of Me3SI was 0.2 mg mL1, a maximum PCE of 22.07%

(Figure 4a), with an enhancement of Voc from 1.09 to 1.14 V, Jsc
from 24.14 to 24.64 mA cm2, FF from 76.30% to 78.57%; while
the J–V cure and the photovoltaic parameters with various adding
concentrations of Me3SI was presented in Figure S4 and

nal quantum efﬁciency (EQE) and the integrated current density

under

one) and high frequency (ﬁrst one) could be assigned to the

(electron or hole) selective layer and the perovskite light absorp-

device present larger R2 and lower R1, suggesting higher charge

value of PCE after 1000 h storage under ambient with 50% RH.
3. Conclusion
In summary, we have synthesized a sulfur-based 1D perovskite
Me3SPbI3 in aqueous medium and the PSCs fabricated with this
pure 1D Me3SPbI3 material exhibited excellent environmental
stability with a PCE of 2.08%. By applying this 1D Me3SPbI3 into
traditional 3D perovskite material, we successfully fabricated 1D/
3D heterostructure perovskite layer with remarkably improved
stability. The 1D Me3SPbI3 perovskite has passivated 3D perov-
skite surface. The champion device shows a PCE of 22.06%.
Importantly, it can maintain 97 % its initial PCE after storage
under ambient condition with 50% RH for over 1000 h.

layer\nAll-perovskite tandem devices are promising due to their high efficiency and low cost but their development is \nhindered by narrow-bandgap absorbers. Now, researchers combine two large organic cations to improve the \noptoelectronic quality of narrow-bandgap tin–lead perovskites, enabling single-junction and tandem cells with \nenhanced efficiency and stability.\nPengchen Zhu and Jia Zhu\nT\nwo-terminal all-perovskite tandem \nsolar cells have drawn researchers’ \nattention in recent years owing to \na low-cost solution processing and high \npower conversion efficiency (PCE). These \ndevices consist of two sub-cells with \ncomplementary light absorption: a front \nsub-cell based on a wide-bandgap (around \n1.75 eV) perovskite and a rear sub-cell based \non a narrow-bandgap (around 1.25 eV) \ntin–lead (Sn–Pb) perovskite. All-perovskite \ntandems are currently limited by the poor \nquality of the narrow-bandgap Sn–Pb mixed \nabsorber layer induced by p-type doping and \nuncontrollable crystallization1,2. The doping \neffect is a result of Sn2+ oxidation to Sn4+ \nduring the fabrication process. Sn4+ dopes \nthe Sn–Pb perovskite, leading to a high dark \ncarrier density. This is detrimental because a \nhigh dark carrier density will increase charge \nrecombination and shorten carrier diffusion \nlength, leading to larger current leakage \nand poorer device performance3,4. The fast \ncrystallization process of Sn-containing \nperovskites often leads to porous and \nnonuniform Sn–Pb films, which results in \ndevice shorting, inefficient charge transport, \nand undesirable carrier recombination3,4.\nNow, writing in Nature Energy, Kai Zhu \nand colleagues from National Renewable \nEnergy Laboratory, University of Colorado \nand University of Toledo report on two \nbulky organic cation additives to retard Sn2+ \noxidation, enabling low dark carrier density \nin Sn–Pb perovskite cells. The cations also \npassivate defects and assist the growth of the \nperovskite, improving the optoelectronic \nand structural quality of the layer. The \nall-perovskite tandem cell based on the \noptimized narrow-bandgap sub-cell achieves \na PCE of 25.5% and 1,500-h operational \nstability in inert atmosphere5.\nThe researchers introduce \nphenethylammonium (PEA+) and \nguanidinium (GA+) in the Sn–Pb perovskite \nprecursor solution, inducing the formation \nof a quasi-two-dimensional (quasi-2D) \nstructure in the 3D Sn–Pb perovskites. \nBy tuning the precursor’s mixture \nconcentrations and GA+/PEA+ ratios, they \nprimarily form a quasi-2D structure with \na (PEA)2GAPb2I7 composition and n-the \nnumber of inorganic perovskite layers \nbetween the bulky PEA+ spacers of 2 (Fig. \n1). Only a small number of structures with n \n= 1, such as (PEA)2PbI4 or (GA)2PbI4, while \nnone with n higher than 3, form, as they \nare unstable. The (PEA)2GAPb2I7 structure \nis key to the optoelectronic quality of the \nSn–Pb perovskites. It exhibits enhanced \nout-of-plane charge transport relative to the \npure components (PEA)2PbI4 or (GA)2PbI4, \nminimizing charge recombination and \nimproving charge extraction at the 3D/2D \npervskite interface.\nFurthermore, (PEA)2GAPb2I7 acts as a \nbarrier that prevents the diffusion of Sn out \nof the device and the ingress of oxygen into \nthe cell, effectively suppressing the oxidation \nof Sn2+. This leads to a dark carrier density \nof ~1.3 × 1014 cm–3, which is similar to that \nfor Pb-only perovskites and a reduction \nof more than two orders of magnitude \ncompared to the untreated sample. \nIn addition, the quasi-2D perovskites \npassivate defects at the perovskite surface \nand grain boundaries and help form a \nuniform film. The smoother and denser \nfilms with relatively large grains mainly \nresult from the coordination effect between \nSn2+ and additives, which promotes \nuniform nucleation and slows down the \ncrystallization process2,5. As a consequence, \nthe bulk carrier lifetime increases by almost \nan order of magnitude, up to ~9.2 μs, while \nthe surface recombination velocity decreases \nto ~1.4 cm s–1. All these improvements in \nthe optoelectronics and morphology of the \nSn–Pb perovskite are key to the efficiency \nand stability of solar cells.\nWhen employed in single-junction \nSn–Pb solar cells, the optimized Sn–Pb \nperovskite leads to a PCE of 22.1% and to \nan operational time of up to 1,830 hours. \nThe device is among the best-performing \nnarrow-bandgap solar cells reported \nso far. Zhu and colleagues also prepare \ntwo-terminal tandem cells coupling their \nnarrow-bandgap perovskite with a 1.75-eV \nwide-bandgap perovskite, which serves as \nITO/glass\n1.75-eV perovskite \n1.25-eV perovskite \nSelective\ncontacts\nTop electrode \nRecombination layer\n[PbI6]4–\nGA+\nMA+\n[SnI6]4–\nFA+\nQuasi-2D\n(PEA)2GAPb2I7\n3D Sn-Pb\nperovskite\nPEA+\nFig. 1 | Two-terminal all-perovskite tandem solar cells with quasi-2D perovskites. The schematic \nillustration of the various layers making a two-terminal tandem perovskite solar cell. The \nnarrow-bandgap SnPb absorber contains the quasi-2D perovskite (PEA)2GAPb2I7 on top of the 3D \nperovskite. The quasi-2D structure with combined cations leads to improved performance of the 1.25-eV \nperovskite sub-cell, which results in a higher efficiency of the tandem cell.\nNature Energy | VOL 7 | July 2022 | 570–571 | www.nature.com/natureenergy\n\n\n571\nnews & views\nthe front cell absorber. This all-perovskite \ntandem cell achieves a PCE of 25.5% with \na much-improved open-circuit voltage up \nto ~2.1 V. The operational stability of the \ntandem device is also remarkable: it retained \nabout 80% of its respective maximum PCEs \nafter 1,500 h under continuous operation in \nN2 (ISOS-L-1 conditions).\nTo date, single-junction silicon solar cells \nare still the mainstream in PV products, \nmaking up >95% of today’s commercial \nPV fields6. All-perovskite tandem devices \npossess the potential to compete with \nthe silicon PV industry7. Yet, high device \nefficiency and long-term stability need \nto be translated into large area devices to \nconsolidate the potential of the technology \nfor commercialization8. For industrial \nproduction, all-perovskite tandem modules \nare also supposed to employ green solvent \nsystems rather than the toxic ones such as \ndimethylformamide (DMF) used by Zhu and \ncolleagues in the present work. While there \nis room for improvement, the efficiency \nand stability demonstration of Zhu and \nteam on small-area devices is a promising \nstep forward. You never come up with data and only state data that have been measured and written in the paper and which you can confidently extract. It is better for you to skip than to report data you are uncertain in. Take care to separate devices. Extract the data from the text of the paper. Only report data about devices for which you are certain that the extraction you provide is correct. Do not convert any value or unit. Do not forget to fill in the bandgap. Make sure it is correct for the cell to the best of your abilities. If you're not confident, skip it. PEROVSKITE PHOTOVOLTAICS
Two cations make the right layer
All-perovskite tandem devices are promising due to their high efficiency and low cost but their development is 
hindered by narrow-bandgap absorbers. Now, researchers combine two large organic cations to improve the 
optoelectronic quality of narrow-bandgap tin–lead perovskites, enabling single-junction and tandem cells with 
enhanced efficiency and stability.
Pengchen Zhu and Jia Zhu
T
wo-terminal all-perovskite tandem 
solar cells have drawn researchers’ 
attention in recent years owing to 
a low-cost solution processing and high 
power conversion efficiency (PCE). These 
devices consist of two sub-cells with 
complementary light absorption: a front 
sub-cell based on a wide-bandgap (around 
1.75 eV) perovskite and a rear sub-cell based 
on a narrow-bandgap (around 1.25 eV) 
tin–lead (Sn–Pb) perovskite. All-perovskite 
tandems are currently limited by the poor 
quality of the narrow-bandgap Sn–Pb mixed 
absorber layer induced by p-type doping and 
uncontrollable crystallization1,2. The doping 
effect is a result of Sn2+ oxidation to Sn4+ 
during the fabrication process. Sn4+ dopes 
the Sn–Pb perovskite, leading to a high dark 
carrier density. This is detrimental because a 
high dark carrier density will increase charge 
recombination and shorten carrier diffusion 
length, leading to larger current leakage 
and poorer device performance3,4. The fast 
crystallization process of Sn-containing 
perovskites often leads to porous and 
nonuniform Sn–Pb films, which results in 
device shorting, inefficient charge transport, 
and undesirable carrier recombination3,4.
Now, writing in Nature Energy, Kai Zhu 
and colleagues from National Renewable 
Energy Laboratory, University of Colorado 
and University of Toledo report on two 
bulky organic cation additives to retard Sn2+ 
oxidation, enabling low dark carrier density 
in Sn–Pb perovskite cells. The cations also 
passivate defects and assist the growth of the 
perovskite, improving the optoelectronic 
and structural quality of the layer. The 
all-perovskite tandem cell based on the 
optimized narrow-bandgap sub-cell achieves 
a PCE of 25.5% and 1,500-h operational 
stability in inert atmosphere5.
The researchers introduce 
phenethylammonium (PEA+) and 
guanidinium (GA+) in the Sn–Pb perovskite 
precursor solution, inducing the formation 
of a quasi-two-dimensional (quasi-2D) 
structure in the 3D Sn–Pb perovskites. 
By tuning the precursor’s mixture 
concentrations and GA+/PEA+ ratios, they 
primarily form a quasi-2D structure with 
a (PEA)2GAPb2I7 composition and n-the 
number of inorganic perovskite layers 
between the bulky PEA+ spacers of 2 (Fig. 
1). Only a small number of structures with n 
= 1, such as (PEA)2PbI4 or (GA)2PbI4, while 
none with n higher than 3, form, as they 
are unstable. The (PEA)2GAPb2I7 structure 
is key to the optoelectronic quality of the 
Sn–Pb perovskites. It exhibits enhanced 
out-of-plane charge transport relative to the 
pure components (PEA)2PbI4 or (GA)2PbI4, 
minimizing charge recombination and 
improving charge extraction at the 3D/2D 
pervskite interface.
Furthermore, (PEA)2GAPb2I7 acts as a 
barrier that prevents the diffusion of Sn out 
of the device and the ingress of oxygen into 
the cell, effectively suppressing the oxidation 
of Sn2+. This leads to a dark carrier density 
of ~1.3 × 1014 cm–3, which is similar to that 
for Pb-only perovskites and a reduction 
of more than two orders of magnitude 
compared to the untreated sample. 
In addition, the quasi-2D perovskites 
passivate defects at the perovskite surface 
and grain boundaries and help form a 
uniform film. The smoother and denser 
films with relatively large grains mainly 
result from the coordination effect between 
Sn2+ and additives, which promotes 
uniform nucleation and slows down the 
crystallization process2,5. As a consequence, 
the bulk carrier lifetime increases by almost 
an order of magnitude, up to ~9.2 μs, while 
the surface recombination velocity decreases 
to ~1.4 cm s–1. All these improvements in 
the optoelectronics and morphology of the 
Sn–Pb perovskite are key to the efficiency 
and stability of solar cells.
When employed in single-junction 
Sn–Pb solar cells, the optimized Sn–Pb 
perovskite leads to a PCE of 22.1% and to 
an operational time of up to 1,830 hours. 
The device is among the best-performing 
narrow-bandgap solar cells reported 
so far. Zhu and colleagues also prepare 
two-terminal tandem cells coupling their 
narrow-bandgap perovskite with a 1.75-eV 
wide-bandgap perovskite, which serves as

tandem cell achieves a PCE of 25.5% with 
a much-improved open-circuit voltage up 
to ~2.1 V. The operational stability of the 
tandem device is also remarkable: it retained

To date, single-junction silicon solar cells 
are still the mainstream in PV products, 
making up >95% of today’s commercial 
PV fields6. All-perovskite tandem devices 
possess the potential to compete with 
the silicon PV industry7. Yet, high device 
efficiency and long-term stability need 
to be translated into large area devices to 
consolidate the potential of the technology 
for commercialization8. For industrial 
production, all-perovskite tandem modules 
are also supposed to employ green solvent 
systems rather than the toxic ones such as 
dimethylformamide (DMF) used by Zhu and 
colleagues in the present work. While there 
is room for improvement, the efficiency 
and stability demonstration of Zhu and 
team on small-area devices is a promising 
step forward. The findings can inspire the 
development of other additive engineering 
for producing high-quality narrow-bandgap 
Sn–Pb perovskites over large scales, thus 
accelerating the pace of commercialization 
of perovskite solar cells.

PEROVSKITE PHOTOVOLTAICS
Two cations make the right layer
All-perovskite tandem devices are promising due to their high efficiency and low cost but their development is 
hindered by narrow-bandgap absorbers. Now, researchers combine two large organic cations to improve the 
optoelectronic quality of narrow-bandgap tin–lead perovskites, enabling single-junction and tandem cells with 
enhanced efficiency and stability.
Pengchen Zhu and Jia Zhu
T
wo-terminal all-perovskite tandem 
solar cells have drawn researchers’ 
attention in recent years owing to 
a low-cost solution processing and high 
power conversion efficiency (PCE). These 
devices consist of two sub-cells with 
complementary light absorption: a front 
sub-cell based on a wide-bandgap (around 
1.75 eV) perovskite and a rear sub-cell based 
on a narrow-bandgap (around 1.25 eV) 
tin–lead (Sn–Pb) perovskite. All-perovskite 
tandems are currently limited by the poor 
quality of the narrow-bandgap Sn–Pb mixed 
absorber layer induced by p-type doping and 
uncontrollable crystallization1,2. The doping 
effect is a result of Sn2+ oxidation to Sn4+ 
during the fabrication process. Sn4+ dopes 
the Sn–Pb perovskite, leading to a high dark 
carrier density. This is detrimental because a 
high dark carrier density will increase charge 
recombination and shorten carrier diffusion 
length, leading to larger current leakage 
and poorer device performance3,4. The fast 
crystallization process of Sn-containing 
perovskites often leads to porous and 
nonuniform Sn–Pb films, which results in 
device shorting, inefficient charge transport, 
and undesirable carrier recombination3,4.
Now, writing in Nature Energy, Kai Zhu 
and colleagues from National Renewable 
Energy Laboratory, University of Colorado 
and University of Toledo report on two 
bulky organic cation additives to retard Sn2+ 
oxidation, enabling low dark carrier density 
in Sn–Pb perovskite cells. The cations also 
passivate defects and assist the growth of the 
perovskite, improving the optoelectronic 
and structural quality of the layer. The 
all-perovskite tandem cell based on the 
optimized narrow-bandgap sub-cell achieves 
a PCE of 25.5% and 1,500-h operational 
stability in inert atmosphere5.
The researchers introduce 
phenethylammonium (PEA+) and 
guanidinium (GA+) in the Sn–Pb perovskite 
precursor solution, inducing the formation 
of a quasi-two-dimensional (quasi-2D) 
structure in the 3D Sn–Pb perovskites. 
By tuning the precursor’s mixture 
concentrations and GA+/PEA+ ratios, they 
primarily form a quasi-2D structure with 
a (PEA)2GAPb2I7 composition and n-the 
number of inorganic perovskite layers 
between the bulky PEA+ spacers of 2 (Fig. 
1). Only a small number of structures with n 
= 1, such as (PEA)2PbI4 or (GA)2PbI4, while 
none with n higher than 3, form, as they 
are unstable. The (PEA)2GAPb2I7 structure 
is key to the optoelectronic quality of the 
Sn–Pb perovskites. It exhibits enhanced 
out-of-plane charge transport relative to the 
pure components (PEA)2PbI4 or (GA)2PbI4, 
minimizing charge recombination and 
improving charge extraction at the 3D/2D 
pervskite interface.
Furthermore, (PEA)2GAPb2I7 acts as a 
barrier that prevents the diffusion of Sn out 
of the device and the ingress of oxygen into 
the cell, effectively suppressing the oxidation 
of Sn2+. This leads to a dark carrier density 
of ~1.3 × 1014 cm–3, which is similar to that 
for Pb-only perovskites and a reduction 
of more than two orders of magnitude 
compared to the untreated sample. 
In addition, the quasi-2D perovskites 
passivate defects at the perovskite surface 
and grain boundaries and help form a 
uniform film. The smoother and denser 
films with relatively large grains mainly 
result from the coordination effect between 
Sn2+ and additives, which promotes 
uniform nucleation and slows down the 
crystallization process2,5. As a consequence, 
the bulk carrier lifetime increases by almost 
an order of magnitude, up to ~9.2 μs, while 
the surface recombination velocity decreases 
to ~1.4 cm s–1. All these improvements in 
the optoelectronics and morphology of the 
Sn–Pb perovskite are key to the efficiency 
and stability of solar cells.
When employed in single-junction 
Sn–Pb solar cells, the optimized Sn–Pb 
perovskite leads to a PCE of 22.1% and to 
an operational time of up to 1,830 hours. 
The device is among the best-performing 
narrow-bandgap solar cells reported 
so far. Zhu and colleagues also prepare 
two-terminal tandem cells coupling their 
narrow-bandgap perovskite with a 1.75-eV 
wide-bandgap perovskite, which serves as

tandem cell achieves a PCE of 25.5% with 
a much-improved open-circuit voltage up 
to ~2.1 V. The operational stability of the 
tandem device is also remarkable: it retained 
about 80% of its respective maximum PCEs 
after 1,500 h under continuous operation in 
N2 (ISOS-L-1 conditions).
To date, single-junction silicon solar cells 
are still the mainstream in PV products, 
making up >95% of today’s commercial 
PV fields6. All-perovskite tandem devices 
possess the potential to compete with 
the silicon PV industry7. Yet, high device 
efficiency and long-term stability need 
to be translated into large area devices to 
consolidate the potential of the technology 
for commercialization8. For industrial 
production, all-perovskite tandem modules 
are also supposed to employ green solvent 
systems rather than the toxic ones such as 
dimethylformamide (DMF) used by Zhu and 
colleagues in the present work. While there 
is room for improvement, the efficiency 
and stability demonstration of Zhu and 
team on small-area devices is a promising 
step forward. The findings can inspire the 
development of other additive engineering 
for producing high-quality narrow-bandgap 
Sn–Pb perovskites over large scales, thus 
accelerating the pace of commercialization 
of perovskite solar cells.

China\nA variety of dopant-free hole-transporting materials (HTMs) is developed \nto serve as alternatives to the typical dopant-treated ones; however, their \nphotovoltaic performance still falls far behind. In this work, the side chain \nof a polymeric HTM is engineered by partially introducing diethylene \nglycol (DEG) groups in order to simultaneously optimize the properties \nof both the bulk of the HTM layer and the HTM/perovskite interface. The \nintermolecular π–π stacking interaction in the HTM layer is unexpectedly \nweakened after the incorporation of DEG groups, whereas the lamellar \npacking interaction is strengthened. A doubled hole mobility is obtained \nwhen 3% of the DEG groups replace the original alkyl side chains, and a \nchampion power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 20.19% (certified: 20.10%) \nis then achieved, which is the first report of values over 20% for dopant-free \norganic HTMs. The device maintains 92.25% of its initial PCE after storing \nat ambient atmosphere for 30 d, which should be due to the enhanced \nhydrophobicity of the HTM film.\nyielded the highest PCE so far of 24.2%,[1] \nhowever, it requires doping treatment \nby oxidants to enhance its hole conduc-\ntivity, which always inevitably leads to the \nconsequences of long fabrication dura-\ntion and poor long-term stability for the \nPSC devices.[3–5] As a result, numerous \ndopant-free organic substitutes including \nsmall molecules[6–28] and polymers[29–44] \nhave been developed, and reports of PCE \nvalues of over 19%[29,31,45,46] have been fre-\nquently issued. Although PCEs of 20.5[47] \nand 23.3%[48] were also released, this high \nefficiency was obtained through optimizing \nthe ETM layer[47] or the perovskite layer,[48] \nwhile the HTM itself was earlier designed/\nemployed and reported with a PCE of only \n18.3[49] or 0.52%[50] at its first appearance. \nTherefore, strictly speaking there are no \ndopant-free organic HTMs reported yet to \npresent a PCE of over 20%.\nPreviously, designing of HTMs was mainly focused on the \nbulky properties of the HTM layer, especially the hole mobili-\nties, and consequently the well-known face-on molecular ori-\nentation where the plane of polymer’s main chain is parallel or \nintermolecular π–π stacking direction is perpendicular to the \nsubstrate was widely adopted as a criterion when one designs \nan HTM.[29,31–33,49] Later, the interfaces between the perovskite \nand HTM layer were paid attention to be modified by small \nmolecules[51–53] and polymers,[54,55] so that the defects on the \nsurface and/or in the bulk of the perovskite layer could be \npassivated, leading to an enhanced photovoltaic performance. \n1. Introduction\nPerovskite solar cells (PSCs), as one of the most promising alter-\nnatives to the conventional silicon-based solar cells, have achieved \ntremendous progress in the last decade since their advent, and a \npower conversion efficiency (PCE) of over 23.0% has been realized \nbased on the n-i-p type device configuration where n is composed \nof an electron-transporting material (ETM), i is the perovskite \nlayer, and p stands for a hole-transporting material (HTM) \nlayer.[1,2] As a classic and standard HTM, 2,2′,7,7′-tetrakis(N,N-\ndi-p-methoxyphenyl-amine)-9,9′-spirobifluorene (spiro-OMeTAD) \nSide-Chain Engineering on Dopant-Free Hole-Transporting \nPolymers toward Highly Efficient Perovskite Solar  \nCells (20.19%)\nLuozheng Zhang, Chang Liu, Xingzhu Wang, Yanqing Tian, Alex K. KGaA, Weinheim\nNowadays, researchers have gradually recognized that the \ninteraction between the perovskite layer and the HTM is also \nvery crucial, and this interaction now turns to be an important \ndesigning factor for the HTMs. Wang and co-workers[31] con-\nstructed a copolymer with carbazole and benzothiadiazole (BT), \nwhere the oxygen atoms in the side chain attached on BT units \nwere believed to bring about a defect-passivation effect, leading \nto a PCE of 19.1%. Park and co-workers[29] replaced the alkyl side \nchain with tetraethylene glycol (TEG) group on the BT units, \nand the resulting polymer yielded a higher hole mobility due \nto the increased π–π stacking and an improved contact with the \nperovskite layer owing to the lifted surface energy, giving a PCE \nof 19.8%. Besides this side-chain modification, very recently we \ndesigned a simple structured copolymer DTB with 2,5-dialkoxyl-\n1,4-phenylene unit and bithiophene unit, where an intensive \nexposure of its main chain to the perovskite layer was acquired, \nresulting in a superior passivation effect to the defects on the \nsurface of the perovskite, a higher extraction efficiency of photo-\ngenerated holes, and a comparable PCE of 19.68% compared \nwith the typical spiro-OMeTAD (19.81%).[45] Although the HTM/\nperovskite interface was optimized, the polymer itself owned a \nrelatively low hole mobility, limiting its further improvement. \nTherefore, it would be of great interest and a further advance \nin PCE could be expected if the bulky properties, especially the \nhole mobility, are simultaneously increased for our copolymers.\nTo this end, we tune the polarity of DTB polymer in this \nwork through the side-chain engineering and introduce dieth-\nylene glycol (DEG) groups to replace part of the alkyl groups \nin the side chains. Contrary to the previous reports,[29,56–59] \nhere the π–π stacking is unexpectedly weakened while the \nlamellar packing is strengthened after the introduction of DEG \ngroups. The properties of DTB polymers (noted as DTB(xDEG), \nScheme\xa01) do not monotonically vary with the percentage of the \nDEG group. When 3% of the alkyl side chains are substituted, \na synergistic effect between the bulky properties of the HTM \nlayer and the interfacial interaction of perovskite/HTM is real-\nized. Consequently, a nearly doubled hole mobility is achieved, \nand a champion PCE of 20.19% with a certified value of 20.10% \nis accomplished, which is the first one of over 20% reported \nfor dopant-free organic HTMs including small molecules and \npolymers. The champion device also holds a superior long-term \nstability to the rest where the PCE remains its initial 92.25% \nafter being kept in air for 30 d without any encapsulation.\n2. If the content of DEG groups further increases \nto 10%, the π–π stackings in both the edge-on and the face-\non arranging modes (as illustrated in Figure S6, Supporting \nInformation) are remarkably weakened, whereas the lamellar \npacking patterns in the edge-on mode are obviously strength-\nened. As observed from Figure S5a (Supporting Informa-\ntion), the diffraction peak for lamellar packing at around 4.6° \nshifts to a higher degree, indicating the decreased lamellar \ndistance. On the contrary, the peak for the π–π stacking at \naround 15.7° in Figure S5b (Supporting Information) moves \nto a lower degree, indicative of a larger π–π stacking spacing \n(summarized in Table S1, Supporting Information). This \nloosened π–π stacking interaction is opposite to the previous \nreports where the incorporation of ethylene glycol oligomers \ngenerally led to a closer π–π stacking,[56–60] and the tightened \nlamellar packing has seldom been reported. In order to unveil the underlying mech-\nanism and provide a strategy for the future improvement, \ninvestigation on the HTM/perovskite interface beside the \nHTM bulk is needed, and to this end, we conducted further \nexperiments based on photoluminescence (PL). The PL spectra \nwere recorded on the sample of FTO/c-TiO2/m-TiO2/perov-\nskite/HTM. As shown by the steady-state PL (SSPL) spectra \nin Figure\xa04a, the DTB(3%DEG) sample owns the highest PL \nintensity, revealing the charge transfer at its HTM/perovskite \ninterface is the poorest. The locations of PL peaks for the three \nsamples are also different, which are 766, 768, and 763\xa0 nm, \nrespectively. The redshift of PL peak signifies there are more \ndefects existing in the perovskite layer for the DTB(3%DEG) \nsample, whereas the blueshift for DTB(10%DEG) is just the \nopposite when compared with the DTB(0%DEG) one.[61] Fit-\nting the time-resolved PL (TRPL) spectra (Figure\xa04b) with the \nbicomponent decay model, we obtained the time constants for \nthe two decaying processes (Table S3, Supporting Informa-\ntion). The fast decay, which is believed to arise from the charge-\ntransfer at the HTM/perovskite interface, has a constant of \n1.44, 1.61, or 1.38\xa0 ns for the sample with x of 0, 3, or 10%, \nrespectively. The biggest value for the 3% sample suggests \nfree carriers in the sample cannot be taken away timely to \nquench the PL, consistent with the inference from SSRL. To \nknow the exact quantity and distribution of these defects in the \nperovskite layer, we turned to thermal admittance spectroscopy \n(TAS, Figure\xa0 4c). According to the literature,[61,62] the region \nwith energy lower than 0.40\xa0eV is the shallow trap state that \ncan be assigned to the defects in the bulk of the perovskite \nlayer, while the one over 0.40\xa0eV belongs to the deep trap state \nthat stems from the defects on the surface of the perovskite \nlayer. The specific concentrations of these defects are conse-\nquently calculated by integrating the TAS spectra. As summa-\nrized in Table S4 (Supporting Information), the defects in the \ndevice of DTB(3%DEG) touch the maximum concentrations \non all the three indexes, including shallow trap state, deep trap \nstate, and the sum, whereas those for DTB(10%DEG) are the \nlowest. As mentioned before, with the increased DEG content, \nthe crystallinity of HTM film and the concentration of hydro-\nphilic groups increase, leading to a maximum hydrophobicity \nwhen x\xa0= 3%. The perovskite layer is hydrophilic, and its inter-\naction with HTM layer should be quite similar to that of water. \nIn such condition, the DTB(3%DEG) is supposed to interact \npoorly with the perovskite layer, and the DTB(10%DEG) film \ninteracts strongly. Accordingly, the defects of the perovskite \nlayer could then be passivated by DTB(xDEG) to different \nextent, and it is also reasonable for DTB(3%DEG) to present \nthe strongest PL intensity, the longest time for the PL decay, \nand the moderate JSC value. Combining the results from PL \nand TAS analyses, we can infer that a better hydrophilicity \nwould be ideal if the HTMs want to passivate the defects more \neffectively in and extract the holes more efficiently from the \nperovskite layer, which could be another important factor for \ndesigning HTMs.\n3. A PCE of 20.19% with a certified value of 20.10% \nwas realized based on the DTB(3%DEG) polymer, which is \nthe first report of over 20% values for the dopant-free organic \nHTMs. The champion device also possessed a superior long-\nterm stability of keeping its initial 92.25% PCE after storing \nin air for 30 d due to its enhanced hydrophobicity. Our results \nfurther demonstrate that both the interface of HTM/perovskite \nand the bulk of HTM layer are of great significance, and a \nbetter ability of defect passivation and/or hole extraction for the \nHTMs may be realized if possessing a higher hydrophilicity. \nMoreover, the intermolecular interaction including the π–π \nstacking and lamellar packing ones should be delicately tailored \nwhen one designs HTMs, not just the π–π stacking interaction \nas regarded previously.\n4. Experimental Section\nFabrication of PSC Devices: A PSC device having the structure of FTO/\nc-TiO2/m-TiO2/Cs0.05FA0.81MA0.14PbI2.55Br0.45/HTL/Au was fabricated, \nwherein the FTO was the bottom layer. The process for fabricating the \noptoelectronic device is summarized as follows. FTO glasses (Nippon \nSheet Glass) were cleaned with detergent, deionized water, and acetone \nand sonicated with ethanol in an ultrasonic bath for 30\xa0min. After that, \nFTO glasses were treated in a UV cleaner for 30\xa0min. The cleaned FTO \nglasses were coated with titanium diisopropoxide bis(acetylacetonate) \n(0.15 m) in 1-butanol solution by the spin-coating method at 2000\xa0rpm \nfor 60 s, followed by heating at 125\xa0°C for 5\xa0min. The films were cooled \nto room temperature and a titanium diisopropoxide bis(acetylacetonate) \nsolution (0.15 m) in 1-butanol was spin-coated again to ensure a pinhole-\nfree dense TiO2 film is obtained. Then the substrates were calcinated in \na box furnace at 450\xa0°C for 30\xa0min. Mesoporous TiO2 (m-TiO2) layer was \ndeposited on the compact TiO2 (c-TiO2) layer by spin-coating the TiO2 \nethanol solution containing TiO2 (14.3 wt%) paste at 4000\xa0rpm for 20 s, \nwhich was then calcinated at 500\xa0°C for 0.5 h. The precursor solution \nof mixed perovskite consists of FAI (172\xa0 mg), PbI2 (507\xa0 mg), MABr \n(22.4\xa0mg), and PbBr2 (73.4\xa0mg) dissolved in 1\xa0mL mixed solvent of DMF \nand DMSO with a volume ratio of 9:1. Then, a stock solution of 1.5 m \nCsI in DMSO was added to the mixed perovskite precursor to obtain the \nCs0.05FA0.81MA0.14PbI2.55Br0.45 precursor solution. The perovskite films \nwere deposited onto the TiO2 substrates using a two-step spin-coating \nprocedure. The first step was 1000\xa0rpm for 10 s with an acceleration of \n500\xa0rpm s−1. The second step was 4000\xa0rpm for 35 s with a ramp-up \nof 2000\xa0rpm s−1. Chlorobenzene (around 100\xa0µL) was quickly dropped \non the spinning substrate during the second spin-coating step at 15 s \nbefore the end of the procedure. Afterward, the as-prepared films were \nheated at 100\xa0°C for ≈2 h until the color changed to dark red. The HTL \nwas prepared by spin-coating the dissolved polymer in chlorobenzene \n(30\xa0 mg mL−1) which was preheated at 60\xa0 °C. The HTM solution was \nspin-coated onto the perovskite layer at 4000\xa0 rpm for 30 s with a \nramp-up of 2000\xa0rpm s−1. Finally, a 100\xa0nm thick Au layer was thermally \nevaporated under vacuum of 4 × 10−5\xa0Torr at a rate of ≈0.05\xa0nm s−1 to \nfinish the device fabrication. The effective area of the obtained device \nwas 0.10 cm2.\nCharacterization of Perovskite Solar Cells: The J–V measurements of \nthe devices under AM1.5G solar 100\xa0 mW cm−2 simulator illumination \n(Enlitech Solar Simulator SS-F7-3A) were performed on a computer-\ncontrolled Keithley 2400 Source Measure Unit in air (60% humidity) \nat room temperature without encapsulation, with a sweep delay time \n100\xa0 ms. The light intensity was calibrated by a standard silicon solar \ncell 91150. The EQE was measured under ambient atmosphere at \nroom temperature using a DSR100UV-B spectrometer with a SR830 \nlock-in amplifier. The steady-state PCE was measured by monitoring \nphotocurrent with a bias voltage at the maximum power point. A xenon \nlamp was used as the light source.\nSupporting Information\nSupporting Information is available from the Wiley Online Library or \nfrom the author.\nAcknowledgements\nL.Z.Z. and C.L. contributed equally to this work. A variety of dopant-free hole-transporting materials (HTMs) is developed 
to serve as alternatives to the typical dopant-treated ones; however, their 
photovoltaic performance still falls far behind. In this work, the side chain 
of a polymeric HTM is engineered by partially introducing diethylene 
glycol (DEG) groups in order to simultaneously optimize the properties 
of both the bulk of the HTM layer and the HTM/perovskite interface. The 
intermolecular π–π stacking interaction in the HTM layer is unexpectedly 
weakened after the incorporation of DEG groups, whereas the lamellar 
packing interaction is strengthened. A doubled hole mobility is obtained 
when 3% of the DEG groups replace the original alkyl side chains, and a 
champion power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 20.19% (certified: 20.10%) 
is then achieved, which is the first report of values over 20% for dopant-free 
organic HTMs. The device maintains 92.25% of its initial PCE after storing 
at ambient atmosphere for 30 d, which should be due to the enhanced 
hydrophobicity of the HTM film.

however, it requires doping treatment 
by oxidants to enhance its hole conduc-
tivity, which always inevitably leads to the 
consequences of long fabrication dura-
tion and poor long-term stability for the 
PSC devices.[3–5] As a result, numerous 
dopant-free organic substitutes including 
small molecules[6–28] and polymers[29–44] 
have been developed, and reports of PCE 
values of over 19%[29,31,45,46] have been fre-
quently issued. Although PCEs of 20.5[47] 
and 23.3%[48] were also released, this high 
efficiency was obtained through optimizing 
the ETM layer[47] or the perovskite layer,[48] 
while the HTM itself was earlier designed/
employed and reported with a PCE of only 
18.3[49] or 0.52%[50] at its first appearance. 
Therefore, strictly speaking there are no 
dopant-free organic HTMs reported yet to 
present a PCE of over 20%.
Previously, designing of HTMs was mainly focused on the 
bulky properties of the HTM layer, especially the hole mobili-
ties, and consequently the well-known face-on molecular ori-
entation where the plane of polymer’s main chain is parallel or 
intermolecular π–π stacking direction is perpendicular to the 
substrate was widely adopted as a criterion when one designs 
an HTM.[29,31–33,49] Later, the interfaces between the perovskite 
and HTM layer were paid attention to be modified by small 
molecules[51–53] and polymers,[54,55] so that the defects on the 
surface and/or in the bulk of the perovskite layer could be 
passivated, leading to an enhanced photovoltaic performance. 
1. Introduction
Perovskite solar cells (PSCs), as one of the most promising alter-
natives to the conventional silicon-based solar cells, have achieved 
tremendous progress in the last decade since their advent, and a 
power conversion efficiency (PCE) of over 23.0% has been realized 
based on the n-i-p type device configuration where n is composed 
of an electron-transporting material (ETM), i is the perovskite 
layer, and p stands for a hole-transporting material (HTM) 
layer.[1,2] As a classic and standard HTM, 2,2′,7,7′-tetrakis(N,N-

Nowadays, researchers have gradually recognized that the 
interaction between the perovskite layer and the HTM is also 
very crucial, and this interaction now turns to be an important 
designing factor for the HTMs. Wang and co-workers[31] con-
structed a copolymer with carbazole and benzothiadiazole (BT), 
where the oxygen atoms in the side chain attached on BT units 
were believed to bring about a defect-passivation effect, leading 
to a PCE of 19.1%. Park and co-workers[29] replaced the alkyl side 
chain with tetraethylene glycol (TEG) group on the BT units, 
and the resulting polymer yielded a higher hole mobility due 
to the increased π–π stacking and an improved contact with the 
perovskite layer owing to the lifted surface energy, giving a PCE 
of 19.8%. Besides this side-chain modification, very recently we 
designed a simple structured copolymer DTB with 2,5-dialkoxyl-
1,4-phenylene unit and bithiophene unit, where an intensive 
exposure of its main chain to the perovskite layer was acquired, 
resulting in a superior passivation effect to the defects on the 
surface of the perovskite, a higher extraction efficiency of photo-
generated holes, and a comparable PCE of 19.68% compared 
with the typical spiro-OMeTAD (19.81%).[45] Although the HTM/
perovskite interface was optimized, the polymer itself owned a 
relatively low hole mobility, limiting its further improvement. 
Therefore, it would be of great interest and a further advance 
in PCE could be expected if the bulky properties, especially the 
hole mobility, are simultaneously increased for our copolymers.
To this end, we tune the polarity of DTB polymer in this 
work through the side-chain engineering and introduce dieth-
ylene glycol (DEG) groups to replace part of the alkyl groups 
in the side chains. Contrary to the previous reports,[29,56–59] 
here the π–π stacking is unexpectedly weakened while the 
lamellar packing is strengthened after the introduction of DEG 
groups. The properties of DTB polymers (noted as DTB(xDEG), 
Scheme 1) do not monotonically vary with the percentage of the 
DEG group. When 3% of the alkyl side chains are substituted, 
a synergistic effect between the bulky properties of the HTM 
layer and the interfacial interaction of perovskite/HTM is real-
ized. Consequently, a nearly doubled hole mobility is achieved, 
and a champion PCE of 20.19% with a certified value of 20.10% 
is accomplished, which is the first one of over 20% reported 
for dopant-free organic HTMs including small molecules and 
polymers. The champion device also holds a superior long-term 
stability to the rest where the PCE remains its initial 92.25% 
after being kept in air for 30 d without any encapsulation.
2. Results and Discussions
The molecular structures of DTB(xDEG) polymers are shown 
in Scheme  1. The synthetic procedures for monomers of

our previous work (Scheme S1, Supporting Information),[45] 
and the polymers with x values of 0, 3, and 10% were synthe-
sized. The absorption spectra of polymers in Figure 1a demo­
nstrate that the absorption band edges are almost the same 
and the optical bandgap energies are calculated to be 2.14 eV

542  nm which can be assigned to the intermolecular π–π

with the DEG amount, probably caused by the increased crys-
tallinity of the films. Through the cyclic voltammetry (CV) test 
(Figure S4, Supporting Information), the highest occupied 
molecular orbitals (HOMOs) of the polymers are determined 
to be −4.99, −4.97, and −4.94 eV when x increases from 0% to

3% and 10%. Combined with the bandgap values, the lowest 
unoccupied molecular orbitals (LUMOs) are obtained and sche-
matically illustrated in Figure 1b. As for the variation of HOMO 
levels, the DEG group is an electron-donating group, thus the 
electrons in the HOMO of polymers with DEG groups would be 
of higher energy than the ones for the pristine DTB(0%DEG), 
and as a result the HOMO level would rise after the introduc-
tion of DEG. The more DEG groups introduced, the higher the 
HOMO level of polymers goes. As suggested by Figure 1b, all 
the three polymers could not only effectively block the photo-
generated electrons in the perovskite from reaching the posi-
tive electrode (here is Au electrode) but also fluently extract the 
photogenerated holes due to their large HOMO offsets with the 
perovskite layer and freely pass these holes to the Au electrode 
due to the ohmic contact.
The molecular packing was examined by the grazing-
incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering (GIWAXS). As shown 
in Figure  2 and Figure S5 (Supporting Information), when 
3% of DEG groups are introduced to the polymer, the mole-
cular packing does not change apparently, but the diffraction 
intensity is improved, further demonstrating the increased 
crystallinity. If the content of DEG groups further increases 
to 10%, the π–π stackings in both the edge-on and the face-
on arranging modes (as illustrated in Figure S6, Supporting 
Information) are remarkably weakened, whereas the lamellar 
packing patterns in the edge-on mode are obviously strength-
ened. As observed from Figure S5a (Supporting Informa-
tion), the diffraction peak for lamellar packing at around 4.6° 
shifts to a higher degree, indicating the decreased lamellar 
distance. On the contrary, the peak for the π–π stacking at 
around 15.7° in Figure S5b (Supporting Information) moves 
to a lower degree, indicative of a larger π–π stacking spacing 
(summarized in Table S1, Supporting Information). This 
loosened π–π stacking interaction is opposite to the previous 
reports where the incorporation of ethylene glycol oligomers 
generally led to a closer π–π stacking,[56–60] and the tightened 
lamellar packing has seldom been reported. We suspect that 
the weakened π–π stacking is caused by the lowered sym-
metry of the random DTB(xDEG) copolymer in comparison 
to the previous alternating copolymers, and the lamellar dis-
tance is shortened due to the interdigitation of the side chains 
in neighboring layers (Figure S6a, Supporting Information) or 
stacks (Figure S6b, Supporting Information) stemming from 
the higher flexibility of oligo(ethylene glycol) chains compared 
with the alkyl chains.[58] It should be noticed that the lamellar 
packing patterns only exist in the edge-on mode for all the 
three samples, suggesting that the majority of these polymers 
adopt an edge-on arrangement in the solid state, which is con-
sistent with our previous observation.[45] The hole mobility was 
measured through the space-charge-limited-current (SCLC) 
method (Figure S7, Supporting Information), and the values 
for DTB(xDEG) are extracted to be 1.74 × 10−4, 3.22 × 10−4, 
and 2.02 × 10−4 cm2 V−1 s−1 for x is 0, 3, and 10%, respectively. 
Although the gradually weakened π–π stackings, especially 
those in the face-on mode, decrease the hole transportation, the 
lamellar packing interaction increases as the DEG percentage 
rises, which could engender the enhancement of hole mobility. 
As a consequence, the mobility touches its maximum around 
x = 3%, which is nearly as twice as that of without DEG groups.
To guarantee the long-term stability of PSC devices, the 
thermal stability of the polymers is of great importance and 
was tested by thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) and differen-
tial scanning calorimetry (DSC) (Figure S8, Supporting Infor-
mation). The polymers could stay stable up to over 375 °C and 
undergo no obvious phase transitions in the tested temperature

The photovoltaic performance of the three polymers is char-
acterized on the PSC devices with a configuration of FTO/c-
TiO2/m-TiO2/Cs0.05FA0.81MA0.14PbI2.55Br0.45/HTM/Au, 
where 
FTO stands for a layer of fluorine-doped tin oxide and c-TiO2/m-
TiO2 are the compact and mesoporous TiO2 layers. Figure  3a 
shows the current density–voltage (J–V) characteristics of the 
three optimized devices for the polymers. As summarized in 
Table 1, when x comes to 3%, a champion PCE of 20.19% is 
attained with an open-circuit voltage (VOC) of 1.14 V, a short-cir-
cuit current density (JSC) of 23.64 mA cm−2, and a fill factor (FF) 
of 75.08% (the certified PCE is 20.10%, Figure S9, Supporting 
Information). The distribution of all the four photovoltaic 
parameters can be found in Figure  3b,c and Table  1, where 
almost all of them catch its maximum at x = 3%. The stabilized 
PCE values measured at the biases of the maximum power 
points (MPPs) are 19.09, 19.90, and 16.71%, respectively (the 
biases are 0.85, 0.96, and 0.82 V, respectively), which are very 
close to these extracted from J–V characterization (Figure 3d). 
External quantum efficiencies (EQEs) of the devices were also 
recorded to verify the photovoltaic properties. As can be seen in 
Figure  3e, the polymers exhibit strong photoresponses across 
the range of 350–750  nm, revealing their high effectivity of 
being HTMs. The integrated current densities from these EQE 
charts are 24.81, 24.32, and 23.01  mA cm−2, respectively, and 
thus relative deviations of as low as 0.8, 2.9, and 2.2% in com-
parison to the corresponding JSC values are obtained, which 
are much lower than the generally acceptable deviation limit of 
5% and demonstrate the validity of our J–V measurement. The 
stability of PSCs at ambient atmosphere (room temperature 
and 20–30% relative humidity) was also tested. As described in 
Figure  3f, all the polymers could render their devices remain 
over 87% of the initial PCEs, and DTB(3%DEG) holds the best 
long-term stability, which may be ascribed to its better hydro-
phobicity. The PCE evolution under continuous 100 mW cm−2 
illumination also suggests that the PSCs based on DTB(xDEG) 
polymers own a good long-term stability (Figure S11, Sup-
porting Information).

mobility. The corresponding JSC of its device is also much 
higher than those for the reported dopant-free organic HTMs 
(Table S2, Supporting Information); however, it is still a little 
smaller than that of the control polymer without DEG groups, 
contradictory to the expectation of a larger JSC value from a 
higher hole mobility. In order to unveil the underlying mech-
anism and provide a strategy for the future improvement, 
investigation on the HTM/perovskite interface beside the 
HTM bulk is needed, and to this end, we conducted further 
experiments based on photoluminescence (PL). The PL spectra 
were recorded on the sample of FTO/c-TiO2/m-TiO2/perov-
skite/HTM. As shown by the steady-state PL (SSPL) spectra 
in Figure 4a, the DTB(3%DEG) sample owns the highest PL 
intensity, revealing the charge transfer at its HTM/perovskite 
interface is the poorest. The locations of PL peaks for the three 
samples are also different, which are 766, 768, and 763  nm, 
respectively. The redshift of PL peak signifies there are more 
defects existing in the perovskite layer for the DTB(3%DEG) 
sample, whereas the blueshift for DTB(10%DEG) is just the 
opposite when compared with the DTB(0%DEG) one.[61] Fit-
ting the time-resolved PL (TRPL) spectra (Figure 4b) with the 
bicomponent decay model, we obtained the time constants for 
the two decaying processes (Table S3, Supporting Informa-
tion). The fast decay, which is believed to arise from the charge-
transfer at the HTM/perovskite interface, has a constant of 
1.44, 1.61, or 1.38  ns for the sample with x of 0, 3, or 10%, 
respectively. The biggest value for the 3% sample suggests 
free carriers in the sample cannot be taken away timely to 
quench the PL, consistent with the inference from SSRL. To 
know the exact quantity and distribution of these defects in the 
perovskite layer, we turned to thermal admittance spectroscopy 
(TAS, Figure  4c). According to the literature,[61,62] the region 
with energy lower than 0.40 eV is the shallow trap state that 
can be assigned to the defects in the bulk of the perovskite 
layer, while the one over 0.40 eV belongs to the deep trap state 
that stems from the defects on the surface of the perovskite 
layer. The specific concentrations of these defects are conse-
quently calculated by integrating the TAS spectra. As summa-
rized in Table S4 (Supporting Information), the defects in the 
device of DTB(3%DEG) touch the maximum concentrations 
on all the three indexes, including shallow trap state, deep trap 
state, and the sum, whereas those for DTB(10%DEG) are the 
lowest. As mentioned before, with the increased DEG content, 
the crystallinity of HTM film and the concentration of hydro-
philic groups increase, leading to a maximum hydrophobicity 
when x = 3%. The perovskite layer is hydrophilic, and its inter-
action with HTM layer should be quite similar to that of water. 
In such condition, the DTB(3%DEG) is supposed to interact 
poorly with the perovskite layer, and the DTB(10%DEG) film 
interacts strongly. Accordingly, the defects of the perovskite 
layer could then be passivated by DTB(xDEG) to different 
extent, and it is also reasonable for DTB(3%DEG) to present 
the strongest PL intensity, the longest time for the PL decay, 
and the moderate JSC value. Combining the results from PL 
and TAS analyses, we can infer that a better hydrophilicity 
would be ideal if the HTMs want to passivate the defects more 
effectively in and extract the holes more efficiently from the 
perovskite layer, which could be another important factor for 
designing HTMs.
3. Conclusion
In summary, a highly efficient polymeric HTM was 
develo­ped through the incorporation of DEG polar group. 
With the increased DEG content, crystallinity of the polymer 
gradually increased, while the hydrophilicity, hole mobility, 
defect passivation ability, and photovoltaic performance varied

4. Experimental Section
Fabrication of PSC Devices: A PSC device having the structure of FTO/
c-TiO2/m-TiO2/Cs0.05FA0.81MA0.14PbI2.55Br0.45/HTL/Au was fabricated, 
wherein the FTO was the bottom layer. The process for fabricating the 
optoelectronic device is summarized as follows. FTO glasses (Nippon 
Sheet Glass) were cleaned with detergent, deionized water, and acetone 
and sonicated with ethanol in an ultrasonic bath for 30 min. After that, 
FTO glasses were treated in a UV cleaner for 30 min. The cleaned FTO 
glasses were coated with titanium diisopropoxide bis(acetylacetonate) 
(0.15 m) in 1-butanol solution by the spin-coating method at 2000 rpm 
for 60 s, followed by heating at 125 °C for 5 min. The films were cooled 
to room temperature and a titanium diisopropoxide bis(acetylacetonate) 
solution (0.15 m) in 1-butanol was spin-coated again to ensure a pinhole-
free dense TiO2 film is obtained. Then the substrates were calcinated in 
a box furnace at 450 °C for 30 min. Mesoporous TiO2 (m-TiO2) layer was 
deposited on the compact TiO2 (c-TiO2) layer by spin-coating the TiO2 
ethanol solution containing TiO2 (14.3 wt%) paste at 4000 rpm for 20 s, 
which was then calcinated at 500 °C for 0.5 h. The precursor solution 
of mixed perovskite consists of FAI (172  mg), PbI2 (507  mg), MABr 
(22.4 mg), and PbBr2 (73.4 mg) dissolved in 1 mL mixed solvent of DMF 
and DMSO with a volume ratio of 9:1. Then, a stock solution of 1.5 m 
CsI in DMSO was added to the mixed perovskite precursor to obtain the 
Cs0.05FA0.81MA0.14PbI2.55Br0.45 precursor solution. The perovskite films 
were deposited onto the TiO2 substrates using a two-step spin-coating 
procedure. The first step was 1000 rpm for 10 s with an acceleration of 
500 rpm s−1. The second step was 4000 rpm for 35 s with a ramp-up 
of 2000 rpm s−1. Chlorobenzene (around 100 µL) was quickly dropped 
on the spinning substrate during the second spin-coating step at 15 s 
before the end of the procedure. Afterward, the as-prepared films were 
heated at 100 °C for ≈2 h until the color changed to dark red. The HTL 
was prepared by spin-coating the dissolved polymer in chlorobenzene 
(30  mg mL−1) which was preheated at 60  °C. The HTM solution was 
spin-coated onto the perovskite layer at 4000  rpm for 30 s with a 
ramp-up of 2000 rpm s−1. Finally, a 100 nm thick Au layer was thermally 
evaporated under vacuum of 4 × 10−5 Torr at a rate of ≈0.05 nm s−1 to 
finish the device fabrication. The effective area of the obtained device 
was 0.10 cm2.
Characterization of Perovskite Solar Cells: The J–V measurements of 
the devices under AM1.5G solar 100  mW cm−2 simulator illumination 
(Enlitech Solar Simulator SS-F7-3A) were performed on a computer-
controlled Keithley 2400 Source Measure Unit in air (60% humidity) 
at room temperature without encapsulation, with a sweep delay time 
100  ms. The light intensity was calibrated by a standard silicon solar 
cell 91150. The EQE was measured under ambient atmosphere at 
room temperature using a DSR100UV-B spectrometer with a SR830 
lock-in amplifier. The steady-state PCE was measured by monitoring 
photocurrent with a bias voltage at the maximum power point. A xenon 
lamp was used as the light source.

A variety of dopant-free hole-transporting materials (HTMs) is developed 
to serve as alternatives to the typical dopant-treated ones; however, their 
photovoltaic performance still falls far behind. In this work, the side chain 
of a polymeric HTM is engineered by partially introducing diethylene 
glycol (DEG) groups in order to simultaneously optimize the properties 
of both the bulk of the HTM layer and the HTM/perovskite interface. The 
intermolecular π–π stacking interaction in the HTM layer is unexpectedly 
weakened after the incorporation of DEG groups, whereas the lamellar 
packing interaction is strengthened. A doubled hole mobility is obtained 
when 3% of the DEG groups replace the original alkyl side chains, and a 
champion power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 20.19% (certified: 20.10%) 
is then achieved, which is the first report of values over 20% for dopant-free 
organic HTMs. The device maintains 92.25% of its initial PCE after storing 
at ambient atmosphere for 30 d, which should be due to the enhanced 
hydrophobicity of the HTM film.

however, it requires doping treatment 
by oxidants to enhance its hole conduc-
tivity, which always inevitably leads to the 
consequences of long fabrication dura-
tion and poor long-term stability for the 
PSC devices.[3–5] As a result, numerous 
dopant-free organic substitutes including 
small molecules[6–28] and polymers[29–44] 
have been developed, and reports of PCE 
values of over 19%[29,31,45,46] have been fre-
quently issued. Although PCEs of 20.5[47] 
and 23.3%[48] were also released, this high 
efficiency was obtained through optimizing 
the ETM layer[47] or the perovskite layer,[48] 
while the HTM itself was earlier designed/
employed and reported with a PCE of only 
18.3[49] or 0.52%[50] at its first appearance. 
Therefore, strictly speaking there are no 
dopant-free organic HTMs reported yet to 
present a PCE of over 20%.
Previously, designing of HTMs was mainly focused on the 
bulky properties of the HTM layer, especially the hole mobili-
ties, and consequently the well-known face-on molecular ori-
entation where the plane of polymer’s main chain is parallel or 
intermolecular π–π stacking direction is perpendicular to the 
substrate was widely adopted as a criterion when one designs 
an HTM.[29,31–33,49] Later, the interfaces between the perovskite 
and HTM layer were paid attention to be modified by small 
molecules[51–53] and polymers,[54,55] so that the defects on the 
surface and/or in the bulk of the perovskite layer could be 
passivated, leading to an enhanced photovoltaic performance. 
1. Introduction
Perovskite solar cells (PSCs), as one of the most promising alter-
natives to the conventional silicon-based solar cells, have achieved 
tremendous progress in the last decade since their advent, and a 
power conversion efficiency (PCE) of over 23.0% has been realized 
based on the n-i-p type device configuration where n is composed 
of an electron-transporting material (ETM), i is the perovskite 
layer, and p stands for a hole-transporting material (HTM) 
layer.[1,2] As a classic and standard HTM, 2,2′,7,7′-tetrakis(N,N-
di-p-methoxyphenyl-amine)-9,9′-spirobifluorene (spiro-OMeTAD)

Nowadays, researchers have gradually recognized that the 
interaction between the perovskite layer and the HTM is also 
very crucial, and this interaction now turns to be an important 
designing factor for the HTMs. Wang and co-workers[31] con-
structed a copolymer with carbazole and benzothiadiazole (BT), 
where the oxygen atoms in the side chain attached on BT units 
were believed to bring about a defect-passivation effect, leading 
to a PCE of 19.1%. Park and co-workers[29] replaced the alkyl side 
chain with tetraethylene glycol (TEG) group on the BT units, 
and the resulting polymer yielded a higher hole mobility due 
to the increased π–π stacking and an improved contact with the 
perovskite layer owing to the lifted surface energy, giving a PCE 
of 19.8%. Besides this side-chain modification, very recently we 
designed a simple structured copolymer DTB with 2,5-dialkoxyl-
1,4-phenylene unit and bithiophene unit, where an intensive 
exposure of its main chain to the perovskite layer was acquired, 
resulting in a superior passivation effect to the defects on the 
surface of the perovskite, a higher extraction efficiency of photo-
generated holes, and a comparable PCE of 19.68% compared 
with the typical spiro-OMeTAD (19.81%).[45] Although the HTM/
perovskite interface was optimized, the polymer itself owned a 
relatively low hole mobility, limiting its further improvement. 
Therefore, it would be of great interest and a further advance 
in PCE could be expected if the bulky properties, especially the 
hole mobility, are simultaneously increased for our copolymers.
To this end, we tune the polarity of DTB polymer in this 
work through the side-chain engineering and introduce dieth-
ylene glycol (DEG) groups to replace part of the alkyl groups 
in the side chains. Contrary to the previous reports,[29,56–59] 
here the π–π stacking is unexpectedly weakened while the 
lamellar packing is strengthened after the introduction of DEG 
groups. The properties of DTB polymers (noted as DTB(xDEG), 
Scheme 1) do not monotonically vary with the percentage of the 
DEG group. When 3% of the alkyl side chains are substituted, 
a synergistic effect between the bulky properties of the HTM 
layer and the interfacial interaction of perovskite/HTM is real-
ized. Consequently, a nearly doubled hole mobility is achieved, 
and a champion PCE of 20.19% with a certified value of 20.10% 
is accomplished, which is the first one of over 20% reported 
for dopant-free organic HTMs including small molecules and 
polymers. The champion device also holds a superior long-term 
stability to the rest where the PCE remains its initial 92.25% 
after being kept in air for 30 d without any encapsulation.
2. Results and Discussions
The molecular structures of DTB(xDEG) polymers are shown 
in Scheme  1. The synthetic procedures for monomers of 
Ph(EH) and Ph(DEG) and polymers are similar to those in 
our previous work (Scheme S1, Supporting Information),[45] 
and the polymers with x values of 0, 3, and 10% were synthe-
sized. The absorption spectra of polymers in Figure 1a demo­
nstrate that the absorption band edges are almost the same 
and the optical bandgap energies are calculated to be 2.14 eV 
for the three polymers. The absorption shoulder at around 
542  nm which can be assigned to the intermolecular π–π 
stacking is moderated after the introduction of DEG groups, 
indicating that the DEG group forces the polymer turn to be 
a random packed copolymer and weaken the interchain π–π 
interaction. As presented in Figure S3 (Supporting Informa-
tion), the light absorption coefficient monotonically increases 
with the DEG amount, probably caused by the increased crys-
tallinity of the films. Through the cyclic voltammetry (CV) test 
(Figure S4, Supporting Information), the highest occupied 
molecular orbitals (HOMOs) of the polymers are determined 
to be −4.99, −4.97, and −4.94 eV when x increases from 0% to

3% and 10%. Combined with the bandgap values, the lowest 
unoccupied molecular orbitals (LUMOs) are obtained and sche-
matically illustrated in Figure 1b. As for the variation of HOMO 
levels, the DEG group is an electron-donating group, thus the 
electrons in the HOMO of polymers with DEG groups would be 
of higher energy than the ones for the pristine DTB(0%DEG), 
and as a result the HOMO level would rise after the introduc-
tion of DEG. The more DEG groups introduced, the higher the 
HOMO level of polymers goes. As suggested by Figure 1b, all 
the three polymers could not only effectively block the photo-
generated electrons in the perovskite from reaching the posi-
tive electrode (here is Au electrode) but also fluently extract the 
photogenerated holes due to their large HOMO offsets with the 
perovskite layer and freely pass these holes to the Au electrode 
due to the ohmic contact.
The molecular packing was examined by the grazing-
incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering (GIWAXS). As shown 
in Figure  2 and Figure S5 (Supporting Information), when 
3% of DEG groups are introduced to the polymer, the mole-
cular packing does not change apparently, but the diffraction 
intensity is improved, further demonstrating the increased 
crystallinity. If the content of DEG groups further increases 
to 10%, the π–π stackings in both the edge-on and the face-
on arranging modes (as illustrated in Figure S6, Supporting 
Information) are remarkably weakened, whereas the lamellar 
packing patterns in the edge-on mode are obviously strength-
ened. As observed from Figure S5a (Supporting Informa-
tion), the diffraction peak for lamellar packing at around 4.6° 
shifts to a higher degree, indicating the decreased lamellar 
distance. On the contrary, the peak for the π–π stacking at 
around 15.7° in Figure S5b (Supporting Information) moves 
to a lower degree, indicative of a larger π–π stacking spacing 
(summarized in Table S1, Supporting Information). This 
loosened π–π stacking interaction is opposite to the previous 
reports where the incorporation of ethylene glycol oligomers 
generally led to a closer π–π stacking,[56–60] and the tightened 
lamellar packing has seldom been reported. We suspect that 
the weakened π–π stacking is caused by the lowered sym-
metry of the random DTB(xDEG) copolymer in comparison 
to the previous alternating copolymers, and the lamellar dis-
tance is shortened due to the interdigitation of the side chains 
in neighboring layers (Figure S6a, Supporting Information) or 
stacks (Figure S6b, Supporting Information) stemming from 
the higher flexibility of oligo(ethylene glycol) chains compared 
with the alkyl chains.[58] It should be noticed that the lamellar 
packing patterns only exist in the edge-on mode for all the 
three samples, suggesting that the majority of these polymers 
adopt an edge-on arrangement in the solid state, which is con-
sistent with our previous observation.[45] The hole mobility was 
measured through the space-charge-limited-current (SCLC) 
method (Figure S7, Supporting Information), and the values 
for DTB(xDEG) are extracted to be 1.74 × 10−4, 3.22 × 10−4, 
and 2.02 × 10−4 cm2 V−1 s−1 for x is 0, 3, and 10%, respectively. 
Although the gradually weakened π–π stackings, especially 
those in the face-on mode, decrease the hole transportation, the 
lamellar packing interaction increases as the DEG percentage 
rises, which could engender the enhancement of hole mobility. 
As a consequence, the mobility touches its maximum around 
x = 3%, which is nearly as twice as that of without DEG groups.
To guarantee the long-term stability of PSC devices, the 
thermal stability of the polymers is of great importance and 
was tested by thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) and differen-
tial scanning calorimetry (DSC) (Figure S8, Supporting Infor-
mation). The polymers could stay stable up to over 375 °C and 
undergo no obvious phase transitions in the tested temperature

higher than those for the reported dopant-free organic HTMs 
(Table S2, Supporting Information); however, it is still a little 
smaller than that of the control polymer without DEG groups, 
contradictory to the expectation of a larger JSC value from a 
higher hole mobility. In order to unveil the underlying mech-
anism and provide a strategy for the future improvement, 
investigation on the HTM/perovskite interface beside the 
HTM bulk is needed, and to this end, we conducted further 
experiments based on photoluminescence (PL). The PL spectra 
were recorded on the sample of FTO/c-TiO2/m-TiO2/perov-
skite/HTM. As shown by the steady-state PL (SSPL) spectra 
in Figure 4a, the DTB(3%DEG) sample owns the highest PL 
intensity, revealing the charge transfer at its HTM/perovskite 
interface is the poorest. The locations of PL peaks for the three 
samples are also different, which are 766, 768, and 763  nm, 
respectively. The redshift of PL peak signifies there are more 
defects existing in the perovskite layer for the DTB(3%DEG) 
sample, whereas the blueshift for DTB(10%DEG) is just the 
opposite when compared with the DTB(0%DEG) one.[61] Fit-
ting the time-resolved PL (TRPL) spectra (Figure 4b) with the 
bicomponent decay model, we obtained the time constants for 
the two decaying processes (Table S3, Supporting Informa-
tion). The fast decay, which is believed to arise from the charge-
transfer at the HTM/perovskite interface, has a constant of 
1.44, 1.61, or 1.38  ns for the sample with x of 0, 3, or 10%, 
respectively. The biggest value for the 3% sample suggests 
free carriers in the sample cannot be taken away timely to 
quench the PL, consistent with the inference from SSRL. To 
know the exact quantity and distribution of these defects in the 
perovskite layer, we turned to thermal admittance spectroscopy 
(TAS, Figure  4c). According to the literature,[61,62] the region 
with energy lower than 0.40 eV is the shallow trap state that 
can be assigned to the defects in the bulk of the perovskite 
layer, while the one over 0.40 eV belongs to the deep trap state 
that stems from the defects on the surface of the perovskite 
layer. The specific concentrations of these defects are conse-
quently calculated by integrating the TAS spectra. As summa-
rized in Table S4 (Supporting Information), the defects in the 
device of DTB(3%DEG) touch the maximum concentrations 
on all the three indexes, including shallow trap state, deep trap 
state, and the sum, whereas those for DTB(10%DEG) are the 
lowest. As mentioned before, with the increased DEG content, 
the crystallinity of HTM film and the concentration of hydro-
philic groups increase, leading to a maximum hydrophobicity 
when x = 3%. The perovskite layer is hydrophilic, and its inter-
action with HTM layer should be quite similar to that of water. 
In such condition, the DTB(3%DEG) is supposed to interact 
poorly with the perovskite layer, and the DTB(10%DEG) film 
interacts strongly. Accordingly, the defects of the perovskite 
layer could then be passivated by DTB(xDEG) to different 
extent, and it is also reasonable for DTB(3%DEG) to present 
the strongest PL intensity, the longest time for the PL decay, 
and the moderate JSC value. Combining the results from PL 
and TAS analyses, we can infer that a better hydrophilicity 
would be ideal if the HTMs want to passivate the defects more 
effectively in and extract the holes more efficiently from the 
perovskite layer, which could be another important factor for 
designing HTMs.
3. Conclusion
In summary, a highly efficient polymeric HTM was 
develo­ped through the incorporation of DEG polar group. 
With the increased DEG content, crystallinity of the polymer 
gradually increased, while the hydrophilicity, hole mobility, 
defect passivation ability, and photovoltaic performance varied
