Research article 
Compact-porous hole-transport-layer for highly efficient near-infrared 
region transparent perovskite solar cells for tandem applications
Barkha Tyagi a, Neetesh Kumar a, Hock Beng Lee a, Young Min Song b, Sinyoung Cho c,  
Jong-Soo Lee c, Jae-Wook Kang a,⁎
a Department of Flexible and Printable Electronics, LANL-JBNU Engineering Institute-Korea, Jeonbuk National University, Jeonju 54896, Republic of Korea 
b School of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology, 123 Cheomdangwagi-ro, Buk-gu, Gwangju 61005, Republic 
of Korea 
c Department of Energy Science and Engineering, DGIST, Daegu 42988, Republic of Korea 
a r t i c l e  i n f o
Article history: 
Received 23 September 2022 
Received in revised form 10 May 2023 
Accepted 12 June 2023 
Available online 13 June 2023
Keywords: 
Energy band structure tailoring 
Semitransparent perovskite solar cells 
NIR-transparency 
Tandem solar cells 
Spray-coating
a b s t r a c t
Wide-bandgap perovskites solar cells (PSCs) are vital as top cells in perovskite-based tandem solar cells 
(TSCs). However, poor band alignment with the charge transport layer and unwanted parasitic absorption in 
the top semitransparent-PSC (ST-PSC) are major factors limiting the power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 
TSCs. Herein, we present a compact-porous nickel oxide (cp-NiOx) hole-transport layer (HTL) sequentially 
fabricated using a sol-gel suspension and colloidal suspension of highly crystalline NiOx. The cp-NiOx film 
exhibited enhanced transparency, mesoporous surface morphology, and better energy band alignment with 
a 1.68 eV perovskite film for fabricating highly near-infrared transparent (∼92 % (@800–1200 nm)) ST-PSCs. 
The best cell achieved a PCE of 15.9 %. In addition, a four-terminal perovskite/silicon TSC based on the cp- 
NiOx HTL achieved an outstanding PCE of ∼26.0 %. The tailored energy band structure and reduced parasitic 
absorption in the near-infrared region of the ST-PSCs based on the cp-NiOx HTL enabled fabrication of highly 
efficient inverted ST-PSCs for perovskite/silicon TSCs.

1. Introduction
Silicon solar cells (SiSCs) are the mainstream technology of 
photovoltaics with a recent record power conversion efficiency (PCE) 
of ∼26.81% by LONGI, which is very close to the Shockley-Queisser 
(S-Q) limit [1,2]. To date, achieving a PCE that can surpass the S-Q 
limit has not been viable in a single junction solar cell due to the 
absorption loss below the bandgap. To overcome this efficiency limit, 
tandem solar cell (TSC) structures have been considered a promising 
strategy. The simplest form of a tandem configuration is the in­
tegration of a wide-band-gap top cell with a narrow-band-gap 
bottom cell. The TSC structure allows high-energy photon to be 
harvested by the top-cell and allows the bottom cell to harvest the 
transmitted low-energy-photons. These tandem configurations re­
quire a highly near-infrared (NIR) transparent top cell. Organic-in­
organic halide-based perovskite materials offer excellent band-gap 
tunability which makes them ideal top cell candidates for tandem 
configurations [3–5]. Perovskite solar cells (PSCs) having an inverted 
structure offer excellent PCE and, device stability [6]. The inorganic 
hole-transport layer (HTL) in inverted PSCs is the key for high device 
stability. Herein, nickel oxide (NiOx) shows tremendous potential 
due to its low-cost, high hole mobility, energy bands well aligned 
with the perovskite layer, and superior stability [7]. Moreover, PSCs 
based on NiOx exhibited higher transmittance in the NIR region 
compared to PSCs consisting organic HTLs such as PEDOT:PSS and 
PTAA that makes them promising candidates for fabricating semi­
transparent-PSCs (ST-PSCs) for perovskite/silicon TSC applica­
tions [8].
Several reports demonstrated deposition of NiOx films for PSC 
application using different solution and non-solution-based techni­
ques possessing distinct morphologies, such as compact morpholo­
gies using the combustion [9], sputtering [10], and spray pyrolysis 
techniques [11] and nanostructured NiO morphologies using the 
conventional sol-gel [12], nanoparticle [13], and pulsed laser de­
position techniques [14]. However, most of the PSCs based on so­
lution processed NiOx HTLs yielded lower device performance than

expected and exhibited a particularly low open-circuit voltage (VOC). 
The low VOC of the PSCs could be ascribed to the existence of in­
terstitial defects on the surface of the NiOx films [15,16]. To realize 
highly efficient and stable ST-PSCs for perovskite/silicon TSCs, we 
need highly efficient NiOx HTL, which can yield a higher VOC. In 
general, solution processed NiOx suffers from poor surface 
morphologies and mismatched band alignment with the perovskite 
layer, which causes Voc loss in PSCs. Incorporating metals into the 
NiOx material can allow tuning of band-alignment, resulting in 
better hole extraction efficiency. Conversely, these metal dopants 
can cause parasitic optical absorption in ST-PSCs leading to trans­
mittance losses over wide spectral ranges causing photocurrent loss 
in the bottom cell in TSC [17]. Therefore, further research is required 
to develop an efficient NiOx HTL for ST-PSCs that can yield high PCEs 
as top cells and provide high NIR transmittance for bottom SiSC in 
TSCs. Several strategies have been adopted to minimize the optical 
losses in ST-PSCs; however, the ideal transparency to efficiency 
trade-off is far from being achieved [18–20]. One such strategy to 
overcome the conductivity issues and voltage loss in PSCs without 
doping the charge-transport layer (CTL) is by fabricating hybrid/bi­
layer CTLs [21–27]. These CTLs can enhance the optical and elec­
tronic properties of the PSC devices leading to enhanced in device 
performance [25]. “In recent years, multiple studies have shown the 
advantages of porous NiOx films as HTL in inverted perovskite solar 
cells (PSCs). For instance, in 2017, a Que’s group employed Ni(OH)2 
nanosheets to generate mesoporous structured NiOx films via high- 
temperature annealing (500 ºC) of the film and reached a peak 
power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 11.97 % for a MAPbI3 based PSC 
[28]. Further, Hong’s group, reported the application of p-type na­
noporous nickel oxide films as a HTL for fabricating the inverted 
PSCs and achieved PCE of 19.10 % for (FAPbI3)0.85(MAPbBr3)0.15 based 
perovskite absorber [29]. Later, Alex K-Y-Jen’s group developed a 
bilayer structure of NiOx nanoparticle-based mesoporous and NiOx 
blocking layers to enable efficient charge collection at the NiOx/ 
perovskite interface, with a outstanding PCE of 19.6 % for a MAPbI3 
based PSC [30]. However, most of these techniques for the fabrica­
tion porous NiOx involved high-temperature annealing or additional 
additives. In 2019, a low-temperature spray combustion method was 
reported to fabricate NiOx thin films, but the device performance 
remained relatively low (∼11.4 %) [31]. Recently, a compact-porous 
NiOx HTL was synthesized by using Pluronic P123 as the structure- 
directing agent and acetylacetone (AcAc) as the coordination agent 
[32]. This method achieved PCEs of 19.0 % and 21.4 % for PSCs with 
MAPbI3 and Cs0.05(MA0.15FA0.85)0.95Pb(I0.85Br0.15)3 perovskite com­
positions, respectively. However, reports on the suitability of porous 
NiOx films for wide bandgap applications are still limited.”
Here, we report an energy level engineered compact-porous NiOx 
(cp-NiOx) layer fabricated by two step spin- and spray-coating 
techniques with an enhanced electron blocking effect and high 
transmittance for highly efficient ST-PSCs and TSCs. The compact- 
NiOx (c-NiOx) HTL can enable efficient and selective collection of 
charges from the perovskite layer. The spray-deposition of high 
crystalline NiOx colloidal particles led to a mesoporous film which 
can be used to control the crystallization of the perovskite material 
and increase the contact area between HTL/perovskite interface. In 
general, the cp-NiOx film exhibited superior morphology, better 
energy level alignment with the perovskite, enhanced average 
transmittance, and suppressed recombination at the HTL/perovskite 
interface in comparison with the conventional c-NiOx HTL. An op­
timized cp-NiOx film thickness of ∼35 nm enhanced the VOC, sup­
pressed the hysteresis, and reduced optical losses in the NIR region 
in ST-PSCs leading to an outstanding NIR transmittance of ∼92 %, 
which is desirable for perovskite/silicon TSCs. The performance of 
the cp-NiOx HTL based ST-PSC and a 4T perovskite/silicon TSC 
yielded PCEs of ∼15.9 % and ∼26.0 %.
2. Experimental section
2.1. Materials
Formamidinium iodide (FAI, > 98 %), methylammonium bromide 
(MABr, > 98 %) and methylammonium chloride (MACl, > 99 %) were 
purchased from Greatcell Solar Ltd., Australia. Lead iodide (PbI2, 
99.99 %), lead bromide (PbBr2, 99.99 %), and PC60BM were purchased 
from Tokyo Chemical Industry Ltd., Japan. Nickel (II) acetate tetra­
hydrate ((NiOCOCH3)2.4 H2O), 98 %), cesium iodide (CsI, 99.99 %), 
dimethylformamide (DMF, anhydrous 99.8 %), dimethyl sulfoxide 
(DMSO, anhydrous 99.8 %), 2-propanol (IPA, anhydrous 99.5 %) 
chlorobenzene (CB, anhydrous 99.8 %) were purchased from Sigma 
Aldrich. Nickel oxide colloidal particles (NiO, 2.5 wt% in ethanol) and 
zinc oxide (ZnO, 2.5 wt% in 2-propanol) colloidal particles were 
purchased from Nano Clean Tech. An ITO sputter target (In2O3:SnO2 
=90:10 wt%, 99.99 %) was purchased from Dasom rms, Korea.
2.2. Compact-porous NiOx hole transport layer
Patterned ITO substrates (25 mm × 25 mm) were successively 
sonicated for 10 min in acetone and ethanol, followed by boiling in 
2-propanol for 5 min. After drying, the substrates were UV-Ozone 
treated for 15 min. The NiOx sol-gel precursor was prepared by 
dissolving 24 mg of (NiOCOCH3)2.4 H2O) in 1 mL of ethanol and 5 μL 
of ethanolamine mixed solvent. The NiOx precursor was spin-coated 
onto ITO substrates at 5000 rpm for 30 s, followed by annealing in 
air for at 350 °C for 30 min in ambient air. Subsequently, a NiOx 
colloidal suspension was prepared by diluting 1.0 mL of the as- 
bought NiOx colloidal particles (0.3 mg of NiOx) in a mixture of 5 mL 
of DI water and 5 mL of ethanol (EtOH). The NiOx colloidal suspen­
sion was loaded into the nozzle at a rate of 3.0 mL min−1 and was 
atomized using compressed N2 gas (1.5 kg cm−2). The spray nozzle 
was scanned at a speed of 1800 mm min−1 in a pre-programmed 
zigzag pattern in x- and y-directions with 2.0 cm spacing at a height 
of 20.0 cm above the substrates in ambient air without using a hot 
plate [36]. The samples were annealed on a hot plate at 350 °C for 
30 min in ambient air.
2.3. PSC and ST-PSC device fabrication
Opaque perovskite solar cells (PSCs) with a device architecture of 
glass/ITO/NiOx/perovskite/PC60BM/ZnO/Ag were fabricated. For ST- 
PSCs, the devices were fabricated by replacing the top Ag electrode 
with a-ITO TCE. The perovskite precursor solution with a composi­
tion of Cs0.25FA0.75PbI2.4Br0.6 was prepared by dissolving 387.24 mg 
of PbI2, 132.12 mg of PbBr2, 154.77 mg of FAI, and 77.94 mg of CsI in 
1 mL of DMF: DMSO (4:1 v/v) mixed solvent. The perovskite pre­
cursor was spin-coated onto the HTL-coated substrates in a two-step 
process, 1000 rpm for 8 s followed by 5000 rpm for 45 s inside an 
N2-filled glove box. During the 15 s interval in the second step, 
300 μL of CB was dropped onto the substrate. The samples were then 
annealed at 100 °C for 30 min. The PC60BM solution (20 mg/mL in 
CB) was first spin-coated onto the perovskite layer at 5000 rpm for 
40 s. Then, 100 μL of ZnO NPs solution was spin-cast at 2500 rpm for 
40 s, followed by annealing at 100 °C for 5 min. For opaque PSCs, 
100 nm Ag was deposited onto the device as top contact via thermal 
evaporation under high vacuum (∼2.0 × 10−6 torr) condition. For ST- 
PSC devices, an amorphous indium tin oxide (a-ITO) top transparent 
conducting electrode (TCE) was used to replace Ag electrode as top 
contact. The a-ITO TCE was fabricated by first depositing an ∼80 nm 
thick a-ITO film onto the devices using an ultra-high vacuum 
(∼1.0 × 10−7 torr) sputtering system (A-Tech System). The sputtering 
process was conducted at 100 W under Ar:O2 (40:0.2 sccm) flow rate 
at a working pressure of 1.0 × 10−3 Pa.
B. Tyagi, N. Kumar, H.B. Lee et al. 
Journal of Alloys and Compounds 960 (2023) 170970
2


2.4. Characterization
The structural phase and crystallographic changes of the per­
ovskite films were characterized via XRD (Bruker D8 Advance) using 
CuKα excitation. The surface morphology and topography of the 
perovskite films were characterized by FE-SEM (Hitachi SU-70) and 
AFM (Park Systems NX10). The TEM measurement of NiO colloidal 
particles was performed using a dark-field- scanning transmission 
electron microscope (JEM-2010, JEOL). All the previously mentioned 
research facilities are at the Center for University-wide Research 
Facilities (CURF) at Jeonbuk National University. A UV–vis spectro­
meter (PerkinElmer Lambda 750) and a PL spectrometer (Horiba 
FluroMAx-4) were used for optical absorption and steady-state PL 
measurements, respectively. XPS and UPS measurements were per­
formed using a Nexsa XPS system (ThermoFisher Scientific UK) 
system equipped with monochromatized Al K-alpha radiation at hυ 
= 1486.6 eV for XPS and 21.22 eV for UPS with a base pressure of 
∼2 × 10−7 Torr. The optical absorption and transmittance of the 
perovskite samples were measured using a UV–vis spectro­
photometer (PerkinElmer Lambda 750). J-V curves of the PSCs were 
measured using a Keithley 2400 source meter SMU instrument

3. Results and discussion
For the fabrication of ST-PSCs, we designed a cp-NiOx HTL scheme 
that consists of compact and mesoporous NiOx films. The HTLs were 
sequentially fabricated by sol-gel and spray deposition techniques 
using NiO precursor salt and crystalline NiOx colloidal particles, re­
spectively, as displayed in Fig. 1a. A device architecture of ITO/cp- 
NiOx/perovskite/PC60BM/ZnO NPs/a-ITO was fabricated for ST-PSC 
demonstration (Fig. 1a). A photo-stable cesium (Cs) and bromide (Br) 
rich perovskite composition of Cs0.25FA0.75PbI0.8Br0.2 used in this 
work has an optical Eg of ∼1.68 eV [33]. The NiOx colloidal particle 
spray-coating parameters were first optimized in terms of device 
performance. The optimum device performance was obtained for ∼6 
spray cycles (Fig. S1). Details of the fabrication process can be found 
in the experimental section.
For physical characterization of the cell structure, field-emission 
scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM) cross-sectional imaging was 
used as displayed in Fig. 1b. The cp-NiOx HTL between the indium tin 
oxide (ITO) and perovskite layers can be easily observed. The dense 
and uniform perovskite layer (∼500 nm) deposited on the cp-NiOx 
HTL was confirmed. Fig. 1c shows photocurrent density-voltage (J-V) 
curves for the c-NiOx and cp-NiOx HTL based ST-PSCs. The cp-NiOx 
HTL based ST-PSC shows an VOC of 1.10 V, a short-circuit (JSC) of 
18.56 mA/cm2, and a fill factor of 78.1 %, giving an overall PCE of 
15.95 % (Table 1), whereas the c-NiOx HTL based ST-PSC shows an 
overall PCE of 13.9 %, with a VOC of 1.04 V, a JSC of 18.2 mA/cm2, and a 
fill factor of 73.3 %. It is to be note that ST-PSC device based on p- 
NiOx showed similar performance of ∼14 % (Fig. S2). Additionally, 
the average PCE for 35 cells based on cp-NiOx HTL was 15.1%, which 
was higher than that of cells based on c-NiOx HTL (avg. PCE ∼ 13.2 %) 
as displayed in the histogram (inset of Fig. 1c). We observed that a 
higher VOC of 1.1 V was obtained using the cp-NiOx HTL, which led to 
the overall higher performance of the ST-PSC. A cp-NiOx HTL over an 
opaque PSC device was also investigated. The best PSC based on the 
cp-NiOx HTL yielded a PCE of ∼17.8 %, which was ∼10 % higher than 
the c-NiOx HTL based PSC (PCE ∼16.1 %) (Fig. S3). Moreover, the cp- 
NiOx HTL based PSC devices also demonstrated lower hysteresis in 
PSCs. The device parameters obtained in both in reverse- and for­
ward-scan directions are summarized in Table S1. The cp-NiOx HTL 
based device exhibited PCEs of ∼17.8 % and ∼16.8 % in reverse- and 
forward-scan directions, respectively, with a negligible hysteresis 
index (HI) of 0.059 compared to the c-NiOx HTL based device (HI 
∼0.093) (Fig. S3) as extracted from the PCE measured under the 
forward and reverse scan (Expression S1). This confirms that there is 
a reduced capacitive effect shown by the PSCs based on cp-NiOx HTL. 
High annealing temperatures (∼350 °C) can lead to sintering at the 
interface between the compact and mesoporous films and improve 
the charge transfer property at the interface of the sol-gel and col­
loidal suspension-based NiOx HTLs. The external quantum efficiency 
(EQE) spectra of the PSCs based on the NiOx HTL is displayed in Fig. 
S4. The integrated photocurrent density calculated using the EQE 
spectrum matched well with the JSC values obtained from the J-V 
measurements. The EQE spectra of the cp-NiOx HTL based PSCs 
showed a superior photon-to-current conversion efficiency com­
pared with the c-NiOx HTL based PSCs. The integrated JSC value de­
termined by the EQE data were 18.7 and 19.2 mA /cm2 for c-NiOx and 
cp-NiOx based devices, respectively. Therefore, the EQE enhance­
ment could be attributed to improved charge collection, confirming 
that the cp-NiOx HTL can lead to enhanced device performance.
To understand the better performance of the cp-NiOx HTL based 
ST-PSCs, we explored the optical and structural properties of the 
HTLs. Fig. 2a shows total transmittance spectra of the c-NiOx and cp- 
NiOx HTL deposited over ITO substrates. The c-NiOx and cp-NiOx 
films showed transmittances of ∼82 % and ∼83 % at 550 nm, re­
spectively. Interestingly, the c-NiOx and cp-NiOx films also showed 
average transmittances (AVTs) of ∼82 % and ∼83 % from 750 nm to 
1200 nm, respectively. Most importantly, the overall transmittance 
of the cp-NiOx was uncompromised by the increase in thickness after 
additional deposition of the NiOx colloidal particles. Rather, the cp- 
NiOx exhibited a significant enhancement (∼2.3 %) in its transmit­
tance spectrum in the visible region (380–750 nm) [34]. This is 
possibly because an increase in the NiOx film thickness enables 
stronger light propagation and photon oscillation [31]. Basically, the 
thickness of the cp-NiOx HTL increased consecutively with an

cp-NiOx films, respectively. The presence of the Ni3+ state in Ni2O3 is 
a result of the oxygen deficiency in NiO, indicating the presence of a 
Ni vacancy. The slightly higher Ni3+ ratio in the c-NiOx sample may 
contribute to the increase in the hole conductivity due to the in­
creased concentration of oxygen vacancies, which act as hole car­
riers. Therefore, the c-NiOx film improves its hole conductivity by 
increasing the concentration of Ni vacancies, which lead to an in­
crease in the Ni3+/Ni2+ ratio [39]. Therefore, we concluded that the p- 
type conductivity was higher for the c-NiOx film compared to the cp- 
NiOx film. However, it has also been demonstrated that Ni3+ surface 
species can result in the formation of the A-site cation-deficient 
perovskite at the NiOx/perovskite interface. This defective PbI2−xBrx- 
rich perovskite forms an energetic barrier limiting the efficient hole 
extraction process and increasing the recombination at the NiOx/ 
perovskite interface, resulting in VOC losses in PSCs [40]. The higher 
value of Ni3+/Ni2+ for the c-NiOx films suggests the possibility of 
higher defects buried under the c-NiOx/perovskite interface, which 
can lead to the lower VOC of the perovskite devices.

Transient photovoltage (TPV) measurements were conducted to 
better understand the quality of perovskite films (i.e., the charge 
trap-state densities) deposited on the cp-NiOx HTL, by studying the 
carrier recombination kinetics and carrier recombination lifetimes 
(τrec) of both the NiOx HTLs-based devices. The decay profiles of 
these devices are displayed in Fig. S15. The cp-NiOx HTL-based ST- 
PSCs exhibited longer decay profile (τrec of ∼2.39 μs measured at 1/e) 
compared to the c-NiOx, which had a comparatively shorter decay 
profile τrec of ∼1.38 μs (Table S5). This indicates that the cp-NiOx 
based PSC exhibits longer carrier lifetime, which might have resulted 
from the reduced trap density in the perovskite layer and the HTL/ 
perovskite interface [45]. Further, the charge dynamics of the PSCs 
based on NiOx HTLs is studied from the dark J-V characteristics hole- 
only devices by space charge limited current (SCLC) measurements. 
For this, hole-only devices having a device structure of ITO/NiOx/ 
perovskite/PTAA/a-ITO were fabricated. Typically, three regions are 
distinctly visible in dark J-V curves in a log-log representation, as 
shown Fig. S16. The low-bias region represents an ohmic contact 
with the electrode, while the current density increased abruptly 
with the increasing bias, corresponding to a trap-filled limit (TFL) 
current. The trap-filled limited voltage (VTFL) values for c-NiOx and 
cp-NiOx HTL were determined to be 0.72 V and 0.61 V, respectively. 
The trap density (Ntrap) was calculated using the Mott-Gurney re­
lation (Expression S4) are to be 5.7 × 1016 cm−3 and 4.8 × 1016 cm−3 
for c-NiOx and cp-NiOx HTL based hole only devices, respectively. 
The lower trap density in the cp-NiOx HTL based device can be as­
cribed to the higher crystallinity of the NiOx colloidal particles pre­
sent in contact with the perovskite layer. We further investigate the 
internal charge transfer dynamics of PSC devices using electro­
chemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) measurements performed 
under dark condition at a constant bias of 0.9 V. The Nyquist plots of 
the PSCs based on the c-NiOx and cp-NiOx HTLs are displayed in Fig. 
S17. The high frequency arc is associated with the charge transfer 
resistance (RCT), and the lower frequency arc is assigned to re­
combination resistance (RREC) at HTL/perovskite interface. The cp- 
NiOx based PSC shows the least resistance in charge transfer as 
confirmed by the radius of semicircle in the high frequency range. 
Moreover, the radius of semicircles in the low frequency region 
confirms that cp-NiOx/perovskite interface offers higher charge re­
combination resistance compared to the c-NiOx/perovskite interface. 
The values of RCT and RREC for each PSC were extracted by fitting 
their corresponding Nyquist curves using the circuit model depicted 
in the inset of Fig. S17. The extracted values of RREC for PSCs based on 
c-NiOx and cp-NiOx HTLs were ≈ 105 Ω and ≈ 243 Ω, respectively. All 
these characterizations have simultaneously confirmed that the cp- 
NiOx can extract charge better than the c-NiOx at the HTL/perovskite 
interface that led to better device performance.

The stability of the ST-PSCs is also a crucial factor from a com­
mercialization point of view. Therefore, the stability of ST-PSCs based 
on the c-NiOx and cp-NiOx HTLs was explored. In general, perovskite 
devices having ITO applied as top the electrode will have better 
stability and moisture resistance [46]. We simply dropped water 
over PSC devices with and without an a-ITO top electrode. The film 
without the a-ITO electrode immediately degraded as the water 
molecules easily reach the perovskite layer and irreversibly destroy 
it. In contrast, the PSC with a-ITO top electrode maintains its form 
(Fig. S20). The ambient stability was tested at room-temperature of 
∼25 °C and relative humidity (RH) of ∼20 % as displayed in Fig. 5c 
and photostability was measured under the 1 sun illumination. The 
ambient stability of ST-PSC cells based on the c-NiOx and cp-NiOx 
showed PCE retentions of ∼68 % and ∼77 % after 3500 h, respectively. 
Evidently, ST-PSCs based on cp-NiOx HTL demonstrated improved 
photostability, showing a PCE retention of >  80 % after 350 h of 
continuous illumination (100 mW/cm2) by a white LED. In contrast, 
ST-PSC based on the c-NiOx demonstrated a PCE retention of only 
70.68 % subjected to the same condition (Fig. 5d). The different de­
gradation rates of the ST-PSCs based on c-NiOx and cp-NiOx HTLs can 
possibly be explained using the XRD spectra (Fig. 2f) of the per­
ovskite films deposited over each HTL. After the ST-PSC devices are 
constantly illuminated from the bottom ITO side, the minor amount 
of unreacted PbI2 observed in the XRD spectrum of the perovskite 
film (Fig. 3g) deposited over the c-NiOx can accelerate the de­
gradation process [42].
4. Conclusion
This work demonstrated the fabrication of a dopant-free, highly 
transparent compact-porous-NiOx HTL for applications in ST-PSCs 
and perovskite/silicon TSCs. The cp-NiOx HTL was sequentially fab­
ricated by sol-gel and spray deposition techniques using NiOx pre­
cursor salt and highly crystalline NiOx

respectively. The cp-NiOx film demonstrated a mesoporous and pin- 
hole-free morphology, enhanced transmittance, better energy band 
alignment with perovskite layer, and control over the formation of 
the perovskite films. The device performance of ST-PSCs based on cp- 
NiOx HTL was investigated taking compact-NiOx HTL as a reference. 
The ST-PSCs based on cp-NiOx HTL demonstrated reduced charge 
recombination at the HTL/perovskite interface and higher NIR 
transmittance leading to the best PCE of 15.9 % and a PCE of ∼26.0 % 
when mechanically integrated with SiSC to form 4T perovskite/si­
licon TSCs. The ST-PSCs also demonstrated great PCE retention in 
ambient conditions and continuous light illumination. This work 
demonstrated the facile fabrication of highly transparent and effi­
cient cp-NiOx HTLs, which have the potential for fabricating highly 
efficient, and stable inverted ST-PSCs and perovskite/silicon TSCs.

Introduction\nThe global climate change and energy security crisis demands\nimmediate action, and renewable energy technologies are crucial\nto addressing these challenges.[1,2] Solar energy is one of the\nmost reliable and sustainable non-conventional energy sources\navailable.[3–5] There are a variety of evolving solar photovoltaic\ntechnologies, including traditional inorganic solar cells,[6,7]\norganic solar cells,[8,9] dye-sensitized solar cells,[10–12] and perov-\nskite solar cells (PSCs),[13–17] all of which have the potential to\nharness solar energy on a large scale. Among these promising\nnext-generation photovoltaic technologies,\nsolution-processed halide PSCs are emerg-\ning as one of the most promising photovol-\ntaic\ntechnology\nthat\ndelivers\nexcellent\npower conversion efﬁciency (PCE) over\n25.5%,[18–24]\napproaching\nthe\nsingle-\ncrystalline\nsilicon\nphotovoltaics\nperfor-\nmance. This could signiﬁcantly reduce the\nsolar panel production over power output\n(or dollar per watt) cost.[25,26] Their excel-\nlent performance is primarily due to the\nexceptional properties of perovskites, such\nas high absorption coefﬁcient, long carrier\ndiffusion lengths, low charge recombination\nrates, and defect tolerance. Furthermore,\nhole-transporting materials (HTMs)[27–36]\neffectively block electron movement, suppress charge recombi-\nnation, and inﬂuence the perovskite crystal growth during fabri-\ncation. These characteristics have a signiﬁcant impact on device\nperformance.[37–47] Further improvements in PSCs were antici-\npated by improving the quality of the perovskite layer and manip-\nulating the HTM properties.\nThe quality of the perovskite layer, such as good crystallinity,\ncompact and continued layer with pin-hole free thin ﬁlm, greatly\nimpacts the PSCs performance. Nie\nDepartment of Physics\nUniversity at Buffalo, The State University of New York\nBuffalo 14260, NY, USA\nThe hole-transporting material (HTM) in perovskite solar cells (PSCs) provides an\nideal interface with the perovskite layer for hole collection while inﬂuencing the\nperovskite crystalline structure and morphology. This article presents SIM and\nDIM, two new dopant-free imidazolium-based HTMs with charged units\naccompanied by counter ions that show the potential to function as ionic HTMs\nand ionic liquid additives and help improve the efﬁciency and stability of inverted\nPSCs. DIM-based PSCs demonstrates exceptional performance with a high-\npower conversion efﬁciency of 19.15%, attributed to improved passivation of\nperovskite interface defects. Furthermore, these new imidazolium salt-based\nHTMs can be manufactured economically, making them a viable option for mass\nproduction and PSC commercialization.\nRESEARCH ARTICLE\nwww.solar-rrl.com\nSol. RRL 2024, 8, 2300817\n2300817 (1 of 9)\n© 2023 Wiley-VCH GmbH\n\n\nperovskite absorber.[26–51] Along with these, advanced techniques\nsuch as tuning perovskite compositions, post-treatment, and the\nuse of additive engineering, including polymers, Lewis bases, and\nionic liquids, have been explored to optimize crystal orientation\nand surface passivation, which can simultaneously enhance the\nstability and efﬁciency of PSCs.[52–64] Among these techniques,\nthe ionic liquid-based adduct approach, which uses additives in\nthe perovskite precursor, is directly involved in the crystallization\nprocess and defect passivation.[55] However, using such dopants\nand additives is challenging as they may cause device instability,\npoor reproducibility, and reduced efﬁciency.[65,66]\nIncorporating charged moieties in the HTM design is seen as\nan effective way of bypassing the requirements of any additional\ndopant and compromising the stability of PSCs. However, there\nhas been little research into the ionic HTMs, particularly inverted\nPSCs.[67–73] Shang et al. reported a dopant-free neutral, nonhy-\ngroscopic benzo[1,2-b:4,5- b]dipyrrole HTM with two racemic\nalkanediylsulfonate anion side chains (BDPSOs).[69] The BDPSO-\nbased inverted devices demonstrated exceptional storage and\noperational stability. In our previous attempt to create ionic\nHTM, we also developed salt-based HTM AI110 for inverted\nPSC applications.[72] According to the previous ﬁndings, the pres-\nence of counter ions aids in the passivation of perovskite defects,\nwhich improves PCE performance.[72] Nevertheless, for the\naccomplishments of stable high-performing PSCs, new multi-\nfunctional designs with cost-effective production are required\nto guide the development of dopant-free HTMs. Imidazolium\nsalts are widely used as ionic liquids to optimize crystal orienta-\ntion and passivate defects in perovskites, using additive-assisted\ntechniques\nor\nsurface-antisolvent\nmethods.[74]\nDifferent\nimidazolium-based ionic liquids[75–81] were reported in the pio-\nneer works, promoting good quality perovskite layer formation.\nFurthermore, the ionic nature of HTM from imidazolium salt\ncan help passivate defects and achieve good hole mobility.\nAlso, the imidazolium unit has distinct physicochemical proper-\nties, high thermal stability, lower toxicity, and is simple to\nsynthesize, which can beneﬁt in developing low-cost, green,\nhigh-performing, and dopant-free HTM for PSCs.[82–86]\nHerein, we developed a novel imidazolium-based HTM\n(Figure 1) to evaluate its ability to function as an ionic HTM\nand an ionic liquid additive in PSC. SIM (Figure 1a) is the ﬁrst\nexample of such a design consisting of a single unit of imidazo-\nlium bromide salt combined with one 4-bromo-N,N-bis(4-\nmethoxyphenyl)aniline donor (ImOMeTPA). Our group previously\nshowed that giving HTMs an ionic character can help increase cell\nefﬁciency without using any dopant.[71] Present work validates the\ndesign of imidazole-based SIM HTM to achieve such an effect with\nno additional doping. This result is further enhanced by the design\nof DIM HTM (Figure 1b), which has a structure similar to SIM but\nboosts efﬁciency due to the presence of one additional ImOMeTPA\nunit. Furthermore, synthesizing these two HTMs is simple and\ninexpensive, decreasing the overall cost of PSC and making it com-\nmercially viable. Therefore, we believe utilizing the innovative\nHTM structure designs to fulﬁll the role of ionic liquids and dop-\nants in PSCs without compromising their stability and reproducibil-\nity can be an effective strategy for commercialization.\n2. Results and Discussion\nAs shown in Scheme 1, SIM and DIM HTMs were synthesized\nin two steps. First, using the Ullmann reaction, an OMeTPA\ndonor (1) was combined with imidazole (2) through SN2 reaction\nto\nproduce\nN-(4-(1H-imidazol-1-yl)phenyl)-4-methoxy-N-(4-\nmethoxyphenyl)aniline (3).[87] Second, imidazolium bromide\nsalts were formed by alkylating imidazolyl (3) with bromoethane\nand 1,2-dibromoethane to yield SIM and DIM HTMs, respec-\ntively.[88] Characterization of newly synthesized HTMs was com-\npleted using proton (1H) and carbon-13 (13C) nuclear magnetic\nresonance analysis. The 1H and 13C spectral patterns and relative\nintegrated values are consistent with the structures of SIM and\nDIM HTMs [see detail in experimental section in Supporting\nInformation (SI)]. We also performed the synthesis cost evalua-\ntion of new HTMs to investigate their potential application pros-\npects. Conclusion\nIn conclusion, we designed and synthesized two imidazolium-\nbased ionic compounds, SIM and DIM, and used them as\ndopant-free HTMs in inverted PSCs. The device performance\nwith these two HTMs yields high VOC of 1.06 and 1.08 V, respec-\ntively, which results in remarkable PCEs of 18.13% and 19.15%.\nComparatively, better PCE in DIM than SIM is primarily due to\nhigher JSC and VOC, which comes from better perovskite/HTM\ninterface and efﬁcient hole transport, as evidenced by SEM,\nAFM, TRPL, SCLC, and XPS studies. These ionic HTMs\nexhibit adequate wettability and desirable photophysical and elec-\ntrochemical properties, resulting in excellent ﬁlm formation even\nat low concentrations. Furthermore, these HTMs are produced\nwith simple synthesis, less hazardous chemicals that can lower\nthe mass production cost, promoting their usage in commercial-\nization. Our work opens a new perspective toward designing efﬁ-\ncient HTMs for the application in PSCs.\n4. Experimental Section\nDevice Fabrication and Characterizations: The ﬂuorine doped tin oxide\n(FTO) conducting glass substrates were ﬁrst cleaned in an ultrasonic\ncleaner using detergent, deionized water, acetone, and isopropanol\nsequentially for 15 min each. The cleaned substrates were then treated\nwith ultraviolet ozone (UV-ozone) for 15 min and transferred to a glove-\nbox. The solutions of SIM (1 mg mL\x011) and DIM (1 mg mL\x011) were pre-\npared using anhydrous chlorobenzene solvents inside the N2-ﬁlled\nglovebox. The solutions were spin coated on the FTO substrates at a rate\nof 3000 rpm for 30 s and then were annealed at 100 °C for 10 min. For\nHTM PEDOT:PSS, its stock solution was ﬁrst ﬁltered through a 0.22 μm\nPVDF and then spin coated on the FTO at 3500 rpm for 40 s and subse-\nquently heated at 120 °C for 20 min before transfer to glovebox. The solu-\ntion\nof\nmixed-cation\nmixed-halide\n(Cs0.05FA0.78MA0.17PbI2.53Br0.47)\nperovskites used was prepared by mixing MAI (34 mg), FAI (145 mg),\nCsI (16.8 mg), PbI2 (510 mg) and PbBr2 (71.3 mg) in 1 mL of DMF:\nDMSO (4:1) mix solvent and stirred at 70 °C inside the N2-ﬁlled glove\nbox. The perovksite thin ﬁlms were prepared with anti-sovlent process.\nGenerally, the prepared perovskite solution (80 μL) was then spin-coated\nin one step at 2700 rpm for 50 s. Chlorobenzene (200 μL) was dropped on\nthe perovskite layer in the last 3 s of the procedure. The resulting perov-\nskite ﬁlm turned transparent brown after applied anti-solvent, which\nturned darker after annealing at 100 °C for 1 h. After cooling down,\n50 μL of [6,6]-phenyl-C61-butyric acid methyl ester (PCBM, 20 mg mL\x011\nin chlorobenzene) ﬁltered through a 0.45 μm PTFE, was spin-coated at\n1000 rpm for 60 s and allowed to stand for 30 min to dry the solvent. A\n≈3 nm thick ﬁnishing bathocuproine (BCP) layer was vapor deposited\non the top of PCBM layer. Finally, a 100 nm thick Ag electrode was depos-\nited by thermal evaporation in a vacuum deposition chamber with pres-\nsure of 10\x017 torr. The J–V characteristics were measured with Keithley 2400\nmeasurement source units with the devices maintained at room temper-\nature. The photovoltaic testing was measured under a calibrated solar sim-\nulator (Class 3A, SS-F5-3A, Enli Technology) at 100 mW cm\x012. The light\nintensity was calibrated with a standard photovoltaic reference cell\n(SRC-2020 series, Enli Technology). The light intensity test were changed\nthrough the software (IVS-KA6000) from Enli Technology. The hole-transporting material (HTM) in perovskite solar cells (PSCs) provides an
ideal interface with the perovskite layer for hole collection while inﬂuencing the
perovskite crystalline structure and morphology. This article presents SIM and
DIM, two new dopant-free imidazolium-based HTMs with charged units
accompanied by counter ions that show the potential to function as ionic HTMs
and ionic liquid additives and help improve the efﬁciency and stability of inverted
PSCs. DIM-based PSCs demonstrates exceptional performance with a high-
power conversion efﬁciency of 19.15%, attributed to improved passivation of
perovskite interface defects. Furthermore, these new imidazolium salt-based
HTMs can be manufactured economically, making them a viable option for mass
production and PSC commercialization.

perovskite absorber.[26–51] Along with these, advanced techniques
such as tuning perovskite compositions, post-treatment, and the
use of additive engineering, including polymers, Lewis bases, and
ionic liquids, have been explored to optimize crystal orientation
and surface passivation, which can simultaneously enhance the
stability and efﬁciency of PSCs.[52–64] Among these techniques,
the ionic liquid-based adduct approach, which uses additives in
the perovskite precursor, is directly involved in the crystallization
process and defect passivation.[55] However, using such dopants
and additives is challenging as they may cause device instability,
poor reproducibility, and reduced efﬁciency.[65,66]
Incorporating charged moieties in the HTM design is seen as
an effective way of bypassing the requirements of any additional
dopant and compromising the stability of PSCs. However, there
has been little research into the ionic HTMs, particularly inverted
PSCs.[67–73] Shang et al. reported a dopant-free neutral, nonhy-
groscopic benzo[1,2-b:4,5- b]dipyrrole HTM with two racemic
alkanediylsulfonate anion side chains (BDPSOs).[69] The BDPSO-
based inverted devices demonstrated exceptional storage and
operational stability. In our previous attempt to create ionic
HTM, we also developed salt-based HTM AI110 for inverted
PSC applications.[72] According to the previous ﬁndings, the pres-
ence of counter ions aids in the passivation of perovskite defects,
which improves PCE performance.[72] Nevertheless, for the
accomplishments of stable high-performing PSCs, new multi-
functional designs with cost-effective production are required
to guide the development of dopant-free HTMs. Imidazolium
salts are widely used as ionic liquids to optimize crystal orienta-
tion and passivate defects in perovskites, using additive-assisted
techniques
or
surface-antisolvent
methods.[74]
Different
imidazolium-based ionic liquids[75–81] were reported in the pio-
neer works, promoting good quality perovskite layer formation.
Furthermore, the ionic nature of HTM from imidazolium salt
can help passivate defects and achieve good hole mobility.
Also, the imidazolium unit has distinct physicochemical proper-
ties, high thermal stability, lower toxicity, and is simple to
synthesize, which can beneﬁt in developing low-cost, green,
high-performing, and dopant-free HTM for PSCs.[82–86]
Herein, we developed a novel imidazolium-based HTM
(Figure 1) to evaluate its ability to function as an ionic HTM
and an ionic liquid additive in PSC. SIM (Figure 1a) is the ﬁrst
example of such a design consisting of a single unit of imidazo-
lium bromide salt combined with one 4-bromo-N,N-bis(4-
methoxyphenyl)aniline donor (ImOMeTPA). Our group previously
showed that giving HTMs an ionic character can help increase cell
efﬁciency without using any dopant.[71] Present work validates the
design of imidazole-based SIM HTM to achieve such an effect with
no additional doping. This result is further enhanced by the design
of DIM HTM (Figure 1b), which has a structure similar to SIM but
boosts efﬁciency due to the presence of one additional ImOMeTPA
unit. Furthermore, synthesizing these two HTMs is simple and
inexpensive, decreasing the overall cost of PSC and making it com-
mercially viable. Therefore, we believe utilizing the innovative
HTM structure designs to fulﬁll the role of ionic liquids and dop-
ants in PSCs without compromising their stability and reproducibil-
ity can be an effective strategy for commercialization.
2. Results and Discussion
As shown in Scheme 1, SIM and DIM HTMs were synthesized
in two steps. First, using the Ullmann reaction, an OMeTPA
donor (1) was combined with imidazole (2) through SN2 reaction
to
produce
N-(4-(1H-imidazol-1-yl)phenyl)-4-methoxy-N-(4-
methoxyphenyl)aniline (3).[87] Second, imidazolium bromide
salts were formed by alkylating imidazolyl (3) with bromoethane
and 1,2-dibromoethane to yield SIM and DIM HTMs, respec-
tively.[88] Characterization of newly synthesized HTMs was com-
pleted using proton (1H) and carbon-13 (13C) nuclear magnetic
resonance analysis. The 1H and 13C spectral patterns and relative
integrated values are consistent with the structures of SIM and
DIM HTMs [see detail in experimental section in Supporting
Information (SI)]. We also performed the synthesis cost evalua-
tion of new HTMs to investigate their potential application pros-
pects. The detailed calculation for synthesizing 1 g of SIM and
DIM is described in Table S1–S4, Supporting Information. As
a result, the new SIM and DIM HTMs afford a ﬁnal synthesis
cost of $8.88 g1 (Table S2, Supporting Information) and $4.73 g1
(Table S3, Supporting Information) in lab-scale, respectively.
Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) was used to evaluate the
thermal properties of SIM and DIM HTMs (Figure 2a and
Table 1). TGA data showed that the decomposition temperature
(Td) of SIM containing one unit of ImOMeTPA is 270 °C, while
DIM containing two units of ImOMeTPA has a higher Td of
300 °C. The absorption behaviours of SIM and DIM in dichloro-
methane (DCM) were recorded, and the resulting spectra and
values are shown in Figure 2b and Table 1. Due to their structural
similarities, both HTMs have two distinct peaks with maxima at
328 and 333 nm for SIM and DIM, respectively. The UV-Vis
absorption and transmission spectra of SIM and DIM thin ﬁlms
were also recorded and dispatched in Figure 2c. The absorption
maximum of SIM on ﬁlm appeared at 371 nm, while DIM was
shown at 342 nm. In an inverted PSC design, the HTM is located
beneath the perovskite layer (PV). Therefore, an HTM should
have optical transparency between the visible range to allow good
light-harvesting for the perovskite layer. SIM and DIM display a
similar transmittance range between 400 and 800 nm, and the

For efﬁcient hole transport and to prevent electron recombi-
nation, HTMs with well-matched energy levels to the valance
band of perovskite are critical for efﬁcient hole transport and
improved open-circuit voltage (VOC). We ﬁrst investigate the
highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) and the lowest
unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) of SIM and DIM using
cyclic voltammetry and UV-Vis absorption curves (Table 1). The
energy levels (Figure 2e) obtained for both imidazolium-based
HTMs are well aligned with perovskite energy bands and are
favorable for hole transport and electron blocking. SIM and
DIM HOMOs were found at 5.30 and 5.33 eV, respectively,
while LUMO was observed at 2.12 and 2.20 eV. From
Figure 3a, DIM has a much deeper HOMO than SIM and
PEDOT:PSS, which is recognized to help achieve the high
VOC of the solar cell.[89,90] To further investigate hole transport,
hole mobility measurements for SIM and DIM HTMs were per-
formed using FTO/HTMs/Au device structures and the space
charge limited current (SCLC) technique. The HTM SIM has
a hole mobility of 3.30  104 cm2 v1 s1, whereas the DIM has
a hole mobility of 3.72  104 cm2 v1 s1 (Figure 2f). The stan-
dard HTM PEDOT:PSS hole mobility used for comparison is
2.89  104 cm2 v1 s1. Therefore, the hole-mobility measure-
ments conﬁrm that the DIM is more efﬁcient HTM than SIM
and PEDOE:PSS for inverted PSCs.
Computational calculations were performed using density
functional theory (DFT) at the B3LYP/6-31G level to gain insights
into the energy level distribution and geometrical structures of
SIM and DIM. Visually represented by Figure 3a,b, the frontier
molecular orbitals of SIM and DIM, respectively, show that the
HOMOs of both HTMs have an electron density localized to the
OMeTPA electron donors. While the LUMO in SIM is located on
the imidazole unit and the phenyl of the OMeTPA, the LUMO in
DIM stretches across both the imidazoles and the phenyls of the
OMeTPAs. The dispersion of electron transfer plays a crucial role
in the HOMO-LUMO excitation, with DIM having a higher elec-
tron transfer distribution, it is accepted to have more efﬁcient
generation of charge carriers in PCS devices. In terms of dihedral
angles (Figure 3c), SIM has a dihedral angle of 179° between
OMeTPA and the connected imidazole ring, while DIM has a
dihedral angle of 177° for the two imidazole rings attached to
the alkyl chain. The similarity in the dihedral angles in SIM
and DIM depicts that the backbone of these HTL molecular units
remain mostly unaltered despite increased molecular length of
the later. These insights support the fact that DIM with a greater
number of imidazole and phenyl units has a greater electronic
delocalization in frontier molecular orbitals that can be beneﬁcial
for charge carrier dynamics. Furthermore, SIM has a larger
dipole moment of 11.6 Debye than DIM (3.21 Debye), which
might inﬂuence their solubility in organic solvents.[91,92]
In an inverted PSC, an HTM also inﬂuences the perovskite
ﬁlm morphology. To evaluate the capacity of these new
imidazolium-based ionic HTMs to promote ﬁlm formation,
we characterized the thin ﬁlm morphologies and materials qual-
ity via scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (Figure 4) and the
X-ray diffraction (XRD) pattern (Figure S1, Supporting Information)
of the perovskite ﬁlm on SIM, DIM, and PEDOT:PSS HTMs.
The surface and cross- sectional SEM images of perovskite ﬁlms
grown on SIM and DIM are shown in Figure 4a–d, respectively.

and provided in Figure S2a (Supporting Information). As

the morphology of the perovskite. Interestingly, the crystal grain
size in the perovskites layer on DIM HTM is larger than perov-
skite/SIM and perovsite/PEDOT:PSS HTMs. This could be due

Information). It is known that a non-wetting HTM promotes
grain boundary migration during grain growth, resulting in a
high-quality perovskite ﬁlm.[90–93] The wettability experiments
of SIM, DIM, and PEDOT:PSS show that the increased hydro-
phobicity of the DIM ﬁlm favors large grain size perovskite depo-
sition and full ﬁlm coverage in inverted PSCs. Atomic force
microscopy (AFM) tests of SIM, DIM, and PEDOT:PSS-based
ﬁlms, as shown in Figure 4e,f, and S2b, Supporting Information,
support the following. The root-mean-square roughness values
of DIM, SIM, and PEDOT:PSS are in increasing order of
5.99 < 7.32 < 7.46 nm. The signiﬁcantly lower surface rough-
ness of the DIM compared to SIM and PEDOT:PSS implies that
the DIM-based perovskite layer has superior continuity and ﬂat-
ness. In addition, the XRD patterns for perovskites coated on
HTMs studied in this work (Figure S1, Supporting Information)
show the characteristic diffraction peaks of the perovskite mate-
rial (13.91 and 28.11). However, compared to SIM and PEDOT:
PSS, the presence of sharp and intense peaks for perovskite
coated on DIM HTM indicates the formation of a ﬁlm with high
crystallinity. These results suggest that the imidazolium-based
HTMs (SIM and DIM) have good surface wettability, good ﬁlm
formation, and better crystallinity, with which good PSC perfor-
mance is expected.
We further performed the steady-state and transient photolu-
minescence (PL) spectra of the perovskites grown on the SIM,
DIM, PEDOT:PSS, and FTO glass were recorded to primarily
evaluate the hole-extraction behaviours. As shown in Figure 5a,
in the case of perovskite/FTO glass, a strong, steady PL peak of
perovskite is observed. In contrast, the perovskite/PEDOT:PSS
shows considerably decreased PL peak intensity, indicating the

efﬁciency than that of the PEDOT:PSS, with DIM having the
weakest PL peak intensity. This ﬁnding is supported by their
time-resolved PL (TRPL) spectra, shown in Figure 5b. The

3. Conclusion
In conclusion, we designed and synthesized two imidazolium-
based ionic compounds, SIM and DIM, and used them as
dopant-free HTMs in inverted PSCs. The device performance
with these two HTMs yields high VOC of 1.06 and 1.08 V, respec-
tively, which results in remarkable PCEs of 18.13% and 19.15%.
Comparatively, better PCE in DIM than SIM is primarily due to
higher JSC and VOC, which comes from better perovskite/HTM
interface and efﬁcient hole transport, as evidenced by SEM,
AFM, TRPL, SCLC, and XPS studies. These ionic HTMs
exhibit adequate wettability and desirable photophysical and elec-
trochemical properties, resulting in excellent ﬁlm formation even
at low concentrations. Furthermore, these HTMs are produced
with simple synthesis, less hazardous chemicals that can lower
the mass production cost, promoting their usage in commercial-
ization. Our work opens a new perspective toward designing efﬁ-
cient HTMs for the application in PSCs.
4. Experimental Section
Device Fabrication and Characterizations: The ﬂuorine doped tin oxide
(FTO) conducting glass substrates were ﬁrst cleaned in an ultrasonic
cleaner using detergent, deionized water, acetone, and isopropanol
sequentially for 15 min each. The cleaned substrates were then treated
with ultraviolet ozone (UV-ozone) for 15 min and transferred to a glove-
box. The solutions of SIM (1 mg mL1) and DIM (1 mg mL1) were pre-
pared using anhydrous chlorobenzene solvents inside the N2-ﬁlled
glovebox. The solutions were spin coated on the FTO substrates at a rate
of 3000 rpm for 30 s and then were annealed at 100 °C for 10 min. For
HTM PEDOT:PSS, its stock solution was ﬁrst ﬁltered through a 0.22 μm
PVDF and then spin coated on the FTO at 3500 rpm for 40 s and subse-
quently heated at 120 °C for 20 min before transfer to glovebox. The solu-
tion
of
mixed-cation
mixed-halide
(Cs0.05FA0.78MA0.17PbI2.53Br0.47)
perovskites used was prepared by mixing MAI (34 mg), FAI (145 mg),
CsI (16.8 mg), PbI2 (510 mg) and PbBr2 (71.3 mg) in 1 mL of DMF:
DMSO (4:1) mix solvent and stirred at 70 °C inside the N2-ﬁlled glove
box. The perovksite thin ﬁlms were prepared with anti-sovlent process.
Generally, the prepared perovskite solution (80 μL) was then spin-coated
in one step at 2700 rpm for 50 s. Chlorobenzene (200 μL) was dropped on
the perovskite layer in the last 3 s of the procedure. The resulting perov-
skite ﬁlm turned transparent brown after applied anti-solvent, which
turned darker after annealing at 100 °C for 1 h. After cooling down,
50 μL of [6,6]-phenyl-C61-butyric acid methyl ester (PCBM, 20 mg mL1
in chlorobenzene) ﬁltered through a 0.45 μm PTFE, was spin-coated at
1000 rpm for 60 s and allowed to stand for 30 min to dry the solvent. A
≈3 nm thick ﬁnishing bathocuproine (BCP) layer was vapor deposited
on the top of PCBM layer. Finally, a 100 nm thick Ag electrode was depos-
ited by thermal evaporation in a vacuum deposition chamber with pres-
sure of 107 torr. The J–V characteristics were measured with Keithley 2400
measurement source units with the devices maintained at room temper-
ature. The photovoltaic testing was measured under a calibrated solar sim-
ulator (Class 3A, SS-F5-3A, Enli Technology) at 100 mW cm2. The light
intensity was calibrated with a standard photovoltaic reference cell
(SRC-2020 series, Enli Technology). The light intensity test were changed
through the software (IVS-KA6000) from Enli Technology. The EQE spec-
trum was measured using a QE-R Model of Enli Technology.

1. Introduction
The global climate change and energy security crisis demands
immediate action, and renewable energy technologies are crucial
to addressing these challenges.[1,2] Solar energy is one of the
most reliable and sustainable non-conventional energy sources
available.[3–5] There are a variety of evolving solar photovoltaic
technologies, including traditional inorganic solar cells,[6,7]
organic solar cells,[8,9] dye-sensitized solar cells,[10–12] and perov-
skite solar cells (PSCs),[13–17] all of which have the potential to
harness solar energy on a large scale. Among these promising
next-generation photovoltaic technologies,
solution-processed halide PSCs are emerg-
ing as one of the most promising photovol-

lent performance is primarily due to the
exceptional properties of perovskites, such
as high absorption coefﬁcient, long carrier

The quality of the perovskite layer, such as good crystallinity,

The hole-transporting material (HTM) in perovskite solar cells (PSCs) provides an
ideal interface with the perovskite layer for hole collection while inﬂuencing the
perovskite crystalline structure and morphology. This article presents SIM and
DIM, two new dopant-free imidazolium-based HTMs with charged units
accompanied by counter ions that show the potential to function as ionic HTMs
and ionic liquid additives and help improve the efﬁciency and stability of inverted
PSCs. DIM-based PSCs demonstrates exceptional performance with a high-
power conversion efﬁciency of 19.15%, attributed to improved passivation of
perovskite interface defects. Furthermore, these new imidazolium salt-based
HTMs can be manufactured economically, making them a viable option for mass
production and PSC commercialization.

perovskite absorber.[26–51] Along with these, advanced techniques
such as tuning perovskite compositions, post-treatment, and the
use of additive engineering, including polymers, Lewis bases, and
ionic liquids, have been explored to optimize crystal orientation
and surface passivation, which can simultaneously enhance the
stability and efﬁciency of PSCs.[52–64] Among these techniques,
the ionic liquid-based adduct approach, which uses additives in
the perovskite precursor, is directly involved in the crystallization
process and defect passivation.[55] However, using such dopants
and additives is challenging as they may cause device instability,
poor reproducibility, and reduced efﬁciency.[65,66]
Incorporating charged moieties in the HTM design is seen as
an effective way of bypassing the requirements of any additional
dopant and compromising the stability of PSCs. However, there
has been little research into the ionic HTMs, particularly inverted
PSCs.[67–73] Shang et al. reported a dopant-free neutral, nonhy-
groscopic benzo[1,2-b:4,5- b]dipyrrole HTM with two racemic
alkanediylsulfonate anion side chains (BDPSOs).[69] The BDPSO-
based inverted devices demonstrated exceptional storage and
operational stability. In our previous attempt to create ionic
HTM, we also developed salt-based HTM AI110 for inverted
PSC applications.[72] According to the previous ﬁndings, the pres-
ence of counter ions aids in the passivation of perovskite defects,
which improves PCE performance.[72] Nevertheless, for the
accomplishments of stable high-performing PSCs, new multi-
functional designs with cost-effective production are required
to guide the development of dopant-free HTMs. Imidazolium
salts are widely used as ionic liquids to optimize crystal orienta-
tion and passivate defects in perovskites, using additive-assisted
techniques
or
surface-antisolvent
methods.[74]
Different
imidazolium-based ionic liquids[75–81] were reported in the pio-
neer works, promoting good quality perovskite layer formation.
Furthermore, the ionic nature of HTM from imidazolium salt
can help passivate defects and achieve good hole mobility.
Also, the imidazolium unit has distinct physicochemical proper-
ties, high thermal stability, lower toxicity, and is simple to
synthesize, which can beneﬁt in developing low-cost, green,
high-performing, and dopant-free HTM for PSCs.[82–86]
Herein, we developed a novel imidazolium-based HTM
(Figure 1) to evaluate its ability to function as an ionic HTM
and an ionic liquid additive in PSC. SIM (Figure 1a) is the ﬁrst
example of such a design consisting of a single unit of imidazo-
lium bromide salt combined with one 4-bromo-N,N-bis(4-
methoxyphenyl)aniline donor (ImOMeTPA). Our group previously
showed that giving HTMs an ionic character can help increase cell
efﬁciency without using any dopant.[71] Present work validates the
design of imidazole-based SIM HTM to achieve such an effect with
no additional doping. This result is further enhanced by the design
of DIM HTM (Figure 1b), which has a structure similar to SIM but
boosts efﬁciency due to the presence of one additional ImOMeTPA
unit. Furthermore, synthesizing these two HTMs is simple and
inexpensive, decreasing the overall cost of PSC and making it com-
mercially viable. Therefore, we believe utilizing the innovative
HTM structure designs to fulﬁll the role of ionic liquids and dop-
ants in PSCs without compromising their stability and reproducibil-
ity can be an effective strategy for commercialization.
2. Results and Discussion
As shown in Scheme 1, SIM and DIM HTMs were synthesized
in two steps. First, using the Ullmann reaction, an OMeTPA
donor (1) was combined with imidazole (2) through SN2 reaction
to
produce
N-(4-(1H-imidazol-1-yl)phenyl)-4-methoxy-N-(4-
methoxyphenyl)aniline (3).[87] Second, imidazolium bromide
salts were formed by alkylating imidazolyl (3) with bromoethane
and 1,2-dibromoethane to yield SIM and DIM HTMs, respec-
tively.[88] Characterization of newly synthesized HTMs was com-
pleted using proton (1H) and carbon-13 (13C) nuclear magnetic
resonance analysis. The 1H and 13C spectral patterns and relative
integrated values are consistent with the structures of SIM and
DIM HTMs [see detail in experimental section in Supporting
Information (SI)]. We also performed the synthesis cost evalua-
tion of new HTMs to investigate their potential application pros-
pects. The detailed calculation for synthesizing 1 g of SIM and
DIM is described in Table S1–S4, Supporting Information. As
a result, the new SIM and DIM HTMs afford a ﬁnal synthesis
cost of $8.88 g1 (Table S2, Supporting Information) and $4.73 g1
(Table S3, Supporting Information) in lab-scale, respectively.
Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) was used to evaluate the
thermal properties of SIM and DIM HTMs (Figure 2a and
Table 1). TGA data showed that the decomposition temperature
(Td) of SIM containing one unit of ImOMeTPA is 270 °C, while
DIM containing two units of ImOMeTPA has a higher Td of
300 °C. The absorption behaviours of SIM and DIM in dichloro-
methane (DCM) were recorded, and the resulting spectra and
values are shown in Figure 2b and Table 1. Due to their structural
similarities, both HTMs have two distinct peaks with maxima at
328 and 333 nm for SIM and DIM, respectively. The UV-Vis
absorption and transmission spectra of SIM and DIM thin ﬁlms
were also recorded and dispatched in Figure 2c. The absorption
maximum of SIM on ﬁlm appeared at 371 nm, while DIM was
shown at 342 nm. In an inverted PSC design, the HTM is located
beneath the perovskite layer (PV). Therefore, an HTM should
have optical transparency between the visible range to allow good
light-harvesting for the perovskite layer. SIM and DIM display a
similar transmittance range between 400 and 800 nm, and the

new HTMs may harvest photons more efﬁciently than conven-
tional PEDOT:PSS HTMs.
For efﬁcient hole transport and to prevent electron recombi-
nation, HTMs with well-matched energy levels to the valance
band of perovskite are critical for efﬁcient hole transport and
improved open-circuit voltage (VOC). We ﬁrst investigate the
highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) and the lowest
unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) of SIM and DIM using
cyclic voltammetry and UV-Vis absorption curves (Table 1). The
energy levels (Figure 2e) obtained for both imidazolium-based
HTMs are well aligned with perovskite energy bands and are
favorable for hole transport and electron blocking. SIM and
DIM HOMOs were found at 5.30 and 5.33 eV, respectively,
while LUMO was observed at 2.12 and 2.20 eV. From
Figure 3a, DIM has a much deeper HOMO than SIM and
PEDOT:PSS, which is recognized to help achieve the high
VOC of the solar cell.[89,90] To further investigate hole transport,
hole mobility measurements for SIM and DIM HTMs were per-
formed using FTO/HTMs/Au device structures and the space
charge limited current (SCLC) technique. The HTM SIM has
a hole mobility of 3.30  104 cm2 v1 s1, whereas the DIM has
a hole mobility of 3.72  104 cm2 v1 s1 (Figure 2f). The stan-
dard HTM PEDOT:PSS hole mobility used for comparison is
2.89  104 cm2 v1 s1. Therefore, the hole-mobility measure-
ments conﬁrm that the DIM is more efﬁcient HTM than SIM
and PEDOE:PSS for inverted PSCs.
Computational calculations were performed using density
functional theory (DFT) at the B3LYP/6-31G level to gain insights
into the energy level distribution and geometrical structures of
SIM and DIM. Visually represented by Figure 3a,b, the frontier
molecular orbitals of SIM and DIM, respectively, show that the
HOMOs of both HTMs have an electron density localized to the
OMeTPA electron donors. While the LUMO in SIM is located on
the imidazole unit and the phenyl of the OMeTPA, the LUMO in
DIM stretches across both the imidazoles and the phenyls of the
OMeTPAs. The dispersion of electron transfer plays a crucial role
in the HOMO-LUMO excitation, with DIM having a higher elec-
tron transfer distribution, it is accepted to have more efﬁcient
generation of charge carriers in PCS devices. In terms of dihedral
angles (Figure 3c), SIM has a dihedral angle of 179° between
OMeTPA and the connected imidazole ring, while DIM has a
dihedral angle of 177° for the two imidazole rings attached to
the alkyl chain. The similarity in the dihedral angles in SIM
and DIM depicts that the backbone of these HTL molecular units
remain mostly unaltered despite increased molecular length of
the later. These insights support the fact that DIM with a greater
number of imidazole and phenyl units has a greater electronic
delocalization in frontier molecular orbitals that can be beneﬁcial
for charge carrier dynamics. Furthermore, SIM has a larger
dipole moment of 11.6 Debye than DIM (3.21 Debye), which
might inﬂuence their solubility in organic solvents.[91,92]
In an inverted PSC, an HTM also inﬂuences the perovskite
ﬁlm morphology. To evaluate the capacity of these new
imidazolium-based ionic HTMs to promote ﬁlm formation,
we characterized the thin ﬁlm morphologies and materials qual-
ity via scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (Figure 4) and the
X-ray diffraction (XRD) pattern (Figure S1, Supporting Information)
of the perovskite ﬁlm on SIM, DIM, and PEDOT:PSS HTMs.
The surface and cross- sectional SEM images of perovskite ﬁlms
grown on SIM and DIM are shown in Figure 4a–d, respectively.
Figure 3. Calculation results of SIM and DIM based on the DFT. a) Appropriate highest occupied molecular orbital. b) Lowest unoccupied molecular
orbital, and c) Optimized molecular conﬁgurations of SIM and DIM obtained from DFT calculations.

For comparison, the SEM of PEDOT:PSS has also been recorded
and provided in Figure S2a (Supporting Information). As
expected, the perovskite layers are densely packed with no pin-
holes, indicating that the imidazolium-based HTMs contribute to
the morphology of the perovskite. Interestingly, the crystal grain
size in the perovskites layer on DIM HTM is larger than perov-
skite/SIM and perovsite/PEDOT:PSS HTMs. This could be due
to the difference in hydrophobicity between these HTMs, as
illustrated in the insets of Figure 4a,b, and S2a, Supporting
Information. SIM’s water contact angle of 24.5° (insets of
Figure 4a) is smaller than that of DIM (30.7°; insets of
Figure 4b), and both HTMs have better perovskite precursor wet-
tability than PEDOT:PSS (14.0°; insets of Figure S2a, Supporting
Information). It is known that a non-wetting HTM promotes
grain boundary migration during grain growth, resulting in a
high-quality perovskite ﬁlm.[90–93] The wettability experiments
of SIM, DIM, and PEDOT:PSS show that the increased hydro-
phobicity of the DIM ﬁlm favors large grain size perovskite depo-
sition and full ﬁlm coverage in inverted PSCs. Atomic force
microscopy (AFM) tests of SIM, DIM, and PEDOT:PSS-based
ﬁlms, as shown in Figure 4e,f, and S2b, Supporting Information,
support the following. The root-mean-square roughness values
of DIM, SIM, and PEDOT:PSS are in increasing order of
5.99 < 7.32 < 7.46 nm. The signiﬁcantly lower surface rough-
ness of the DIM compared to SIM and PEDOT:PSS implies that
the DIM-based perovskite layer has superior continuity and ﬂat-
ness. In addition, the XRD patterns for perovskites coated on
HTMs studied in this work (Figure S1, Supporting Information)
show the characteristic diffraction peaks of the perovskite mate-
rial (13.91 and 28.11). However, compared to SIM and PEDOT:
PSS, the presence of sharp and intense peaks for perovskite
coated on DIM HTM indicates the formation of a ﬁlm with high
crystallinity. These results suggest that the imidazolium-based
HTMs (SIM and DIM) have good surface wettability, good ﬁlm
formation, and better crystallinity, with which good PSC perfor-
mance is expected.
We further performed the steady-state and transient photolu-
minescence (PL) spectra of the perovskites grown on the SIM,
DIM, PEDOT:PSS, and FTO glass were recorded to primarily
evaluate the hole-extraction behaviours. As shown in Figure 5a,
in the case of perovskite/FTO glass, a strong, steady PL peak of
perovskite is observed. In contrast, the perovskite/PEDOT:PSS
shows considerably decreased PL peak intensity, indicating the
efﬁcient quenching (extraction) of the photogenerated carriers
by HTM. Notably, the SIM and DIM exhibit better hole extraction
efﬁciency than that of the PEDOT:PSS, with DIM having the
weakest PL peak intensity. This ﬁnding is supported by their
time-resolved PL (TRPL) spectra, shown in Figure 5b. The

3. Conclusion
In conclusion, we designed and synthesized two imidazolium-
based ionic compounds, SIM and DIM, and used them as
dopant-free HTMs in inverted PSCs. The device performance
with these two HTMs yields high VOC of 1.06 and 1.08 V, respec-
tively, which results in remarkable PCEs of 18.13% and 19.15%.
Comparatively, better PCE in DIM than SIM is primarily due to
higher JSC and VOC, which comes from better perovskite/HTM
interface and efﬁcient hole transport, as evidenced by SEM,
AFM, TRPL, SCLC, and XPS studies. These ionic HTMs
exhibit adequate wettability and desirable photophysical and elec-
trochemical properties, resulting in excellent ﬁlm formation even
at low concentrations. Furthermore, these HTMs are produced
with simple synthesis, less hazardous chemicals that can lower
the mass production cost, promoting their usage in commercial-
ization. Our work opens a new perspective toward designing efﬁ-
cient HTMs for the application in PSCs.
4. Experimental Section
Device Fabrication and Characterizations: The ﬂuorine doped tin oxide
(FTO) conducting glass substrates were ﬁrst cleaned in an ultrasonic
cleaner using detergent, deionized water, acetone, and isopropanol
sequentially for 15 min each. The cleaned substrates were then treated
with ultraviolet ozone (UV-ozone) for 15 min and transferred to a glove-
box. The solutions of SIM (1 mg mL1) and DIM (1 mg mL1) were pre-
pared using anhydrous chlorobenzene solvents inside the N2-ﬁlled
glovebox. The solutions were spin coated on the FTO substrates at a rate
of 3000 rpm for 30 s and then were annealed at 100 °C for 10 min. For
HTM PEDOT:PSS, its stock solution was ﬁrst ﬁltered through a 0.22 μm
PVDF and then spin coated on the FTO at 3500 rpm for 40 s and subse-
quently heated at 120 °C for 20 min before transfer to glovebox. The solu-
tion
of
mixed-cation
mixed-halide
(Cs0.05FA0.78MA0.17PbI2.53Br0.47)
perovskites used was prepared by mixing MAI (34 mg), FAI (145 mg),
CsI (16.8 mg), PbI2 (510 mg) and PbBr2 (71.3 mg) in 1 mL of DMF:
DMSO (4:1) mix solvent and stirred at 70 °C inside the N2-ﬁlled glove
box. The perovksite thin ﬁlms were prepared with anti-sovlent process.
Generally, the prepared perovskite solution (80 μL) was then spin-coated
in one step at 2700 rpm for 50 s. Chlorobenzene (200 μL) was dropped on
the perovskite layer in the last 3 s of the procedure. The resulting perov-
skite ﬁlm turned transparent brown after applied anti-solvent, which
turned darker after annealing at 100 °C for 1 h. After cooling down,
50 μL of [6,6]-phenyl-C61-butyric acid methyl ester (PCBM, 20 mg mL1
in chlorobenzene) ﬁltered through a 0.45 μm PTFE, was spin-coated at
1000 rpm for 60 s and allowed to stand for 30 min to dry the solvent. A
≈3 nm thick ﬁnishing bathocuproine (BCP) layer was vapor deposited
on the top of PCBM layer. Finally, a 100 nm thick Ag electrode was depos-
ited by thermal evaporation in a vacuum deposition chamber with pres-
sure of 107 torr. The J–V characteristics were measured with Keithley 2400
measurement source units with the devices maintained at room temper-
ature. The photovoltaic testing was measured under a calibrated solar sim-
ulator (Class 3A, SS-F5-3A, Enli Technology) at 100 mW cm2. The light
intensity was calibrated with a standard photovoltaic reference cell
(SRC-2020 series, Enli Technology). The light intensity test were changed
through the software (IVS-KA6000) from Enli Technology. The EQE spec-
trum was measured using a QE-R Model of Enli Technology.

Berry4,5,6,\nYanfa Yan2,3, Kai Zhu1*\nThe development of highly stable and efficient wide-bandgap (WBG) perovskite solar cells (PSCs) based\non bromine-iodine (Br–I) mixed-halide perovskite (with Br greater than 20%) is critical to create tandem\nsolar cells. However, issues with Br–I phase segregation under solar cell operational conditions (such as\nlight and heat) limit the device voltage and operational stability. This challenge is often exacerbated by\nthe ready defect formation associated with the rapid crystallization of Br-rich perovskite chemistry with\nantisolvent processes. We combined the rapid Br crystallization with a gentle gas-quench method to\nprepare highly textured columnar 1.75–electron volt Br–I mixed WBG perovskite films with reduced\ndefect density. With this approach, we obtained 1.75–electron volt WBG PSCs with greater than 20%\npower conversion efficiency, approximately 1.33-volt open-circuit voltage (Voc), and excellent operational\nstability (less than 5% degradation over 1100 hours of operation under 1.2 sun at 65°C). When further\nintegrated with 1.25–electron volt narrow-bandgap PSC, we obtained a 27.1% efficient, all-perovskite,\ntwo-terminal tandem device with a high Voc of 2.2 volts.\nT\nhe bandgap tunability of organic-inorganic\nhybrid perovskites makes them a suitable\ncandidate for applications in both single-\njunction and multijunction solar cells\n(1–3). Perovskite-based tandem solar cells\nhave demonstrated rapid improvements in\npower conversion efficiencies (PCEs) for mul-\ntiple tandem configurations (4–6). As the top\nsubcell for an efficient tandem device, the\nwide-bandgap (WBG) perovskite (about 1.7 eV\nor higher) harvests high-energy photons, con-\ntributes to high open-circuit voltage (Voc), and\nenables stable operation of the tandem stack\nby filtering harmful ultraviolet radiation from\nreaching the bottom cell (7).\nFor state-of-the-art perovskite tandem de-\nvices, WBG perovskites are normally based on\nbromine-iodine (Br–I) mixed halides with a\nrange of high Br contents (4, 5). In principle,\nadding more Br should make the perovskite\nabsorber more stable, given the strength of the\nlead (Pb)–Br bond relative to the Pb–I bond.\nThis effect is associated with the smaller radius\nof Br−(1.96 Å) compared with that of I−(2.20 Å)\nand the higher electronegativity of Br (3, 8, 9).\nHowever, perovskites with mixed halides are\nprone to phase segregation under operating\nconditions (exposure to light and heat) and\nlimit WBG perovskite solar cell (PSC) per-\nformance (10–12) by creating a large Voc deficit\nand poor operational stability in comparison\nwith those of mid-bandgap (~1.5 to 1.6 eV)\nperovskites (13, 14).\nA high Br content causes more rapid crystal-\nlization of the perovskite film that often creates\ndefects associated with structure and composi-\ntion nonuniformity and high density of grain\nboundaries (GBs) (15–17). Various strategies\nhave been proposed to mitigate these issues,\nsuch as composition engineering (18–22),\nadditive engineering (23–29), and interface\nengineering (30–34). Despite these efforts,\nthe stability of WBG PSCs is still inadequate,\nespecially for devices under illumination or\noperation at elevated temperatures (table S1).\nHere, we report a rational strategy to\ndrastically enhance 1.75-eV Br–I mixed WBG\nPSC operational stability with high PCE and\nlow Voc deficit. Our design strategy is based on\na few principles for Br–I mixed WBG perov-\nskite thin films: (i) Br–I phase segregation is\nthe main limitation on Br-rich WBG PSC per-\nformance (that is, operational stability and ef-\nficiency), (ii) Br–I phase segregation is facilitated\nby defective sites, and (iii) reducing the density\nof defective sites can suppress Br–I phase seg-\nregation. We hypothesized that a high-quality\nWBG perovskite thin film in which the bulk and\nsurface defects are minimized could suppress\nBr–I phase segregation in a device under oper-\national conditions.\nWe leveraged the rapid crystallization char-\nacteristics of Br−(relative to I−) by using a gas-\nquenching process that was amenable to the\nBr-rich WBG perovskite precursors. In com-\nparison with the conventional antisolvent ap-\nproach, the gentler gas-quench method first\nproduced a Br-rich surface layer that then\ninduced top-down columnar growth to form\na gradient structure, which had less Br in the\nbulk than in the near-surface region. The re-\nsulting WBG perovskite film had improved\nstructural and optoelectronic properties, such\nas larger grain size, fewer GBs, longer diffu-\nsion length, and reduced defect density. We\nachieved 1.75-eV WBG PSCs with >20% PCE,\n~1.33-V Voc, and excellent operational stability\n(retaining >95% maximum PCE over 1100 hours\nof operation under 1.2 sun at 65°C). When\ncoupling the 1.75-eV WBG PSC with the 1.25-eV\ntin (Sn)–Pb PSC, we obtained a 27.1% all-\nperovskite two-terminal tandem cell with a\nhigh Voc of 2.2 V.\nWBG PSC characteristics\nWe first illustrate the value of the gas-quench\nmethod for processing the high-Br-content\nperovskite to simultaneously achieve high\nPCE—especially high Voc—and excellent oper-\national device stability. In this study, the WBG\nperovskite is based on Cs0.3FA0.6DMA0.1Pb\n(I0.7Br0.3)3. We highlight the gas-quench\nmethod by comparing it with the conventional\nantisolvent approach (supplementary materials,\nmaterials and methods). We used nitrogen\n(N2) gas for most gas-quench studies unless\notherwise stated. In comparison with the\nantisolvent sample, the gas-quench sample\nexhibited a slight redshift of the absorption\nonset, corresponding to a 10- to 20-meV de-\ncrease in bandgap (fig. S1). We used a typical\ninverted (or p-i-n) device structure: glass/ITO/\nSAM/perovskite/LiF/C60/bathocuproine (BCP)/\nAg, where ITO is indium tin oxide, and SAM\ndenotes a self-assembled monolayer (LiF,\nlithium fluoride; Ag, silver). The\nhighest Voc values reached ~1.33 V, and fill\nfactor (FF) reached 85% (fig. S2), both of which\nare among the best reported for 1.75-eV WBG\nPSCs (35).
