Abstract 
Advancing lead halide perovskite solar cells to photovoltaic application requires reproducible 
and stable devices using low-cost fabricating techniques. Here a device structure is developed 
with organic network uniformly incorporated into the organic/inorganic hybrid perovskite 
film by one-step solution-processing strategy, which significantly improves the photovoltaic 
performance and long-term stability of planar type perovskite solar cells. The organic network 
is composed with PCBM and PEG. Therein, a long-chain insulating polymer PEG acts as a 
network to improve film morphology, as well as device stability. The fullerene derivative 
PCBM in the composite forms conducting channels to assist the charge transfer and transport 
in perovskite film. Besides, PCBM in perovskite film can passivate trap states on grain 
boundaries, so that the photocurrent hysteresis of the device is suppressed significantly. This 
organic composite network enhances the photovoltaic performance of perovskite solar cells 
with maximum power conversion efficiency of 17.1%, showing long duration at the 
maximum power point tracking up to ~170 min. This low-cost organic network demonstrates 


 
 
2 
 
a promising method for industry-scale fabrication of the organic/inorganic hybrid perovskite 
solar technology.  
 
Graphical Abstract 
PCBM/PEG polymer network perovskite solar cells are developed and show superior 
photovoltaic performance and longer continuous power output with suppressed hysteresis. 
The power conversion efficiency is 17% under standard 1.5 AM solar illumination and the 
maximum power point tracking maintains up to 170 min. 
 
  
 
Keywords: Perovskite solar cells, Suppressed hysteresis, Stability, Organic network, 
PCBM/PEG 
 
Introduction 
Lead halide perovskite, typically CH3NH3PbI3 (MAPbI3), has become the highlighted solar 
energy harvester, for high absorption coefficient, weak exciton binding energy, and long 
diffusion length [1-8]. Two types of device architectures, namely mesoporous scaffold and 


 
 
3 
 
planar heterojunction structures, are well developed [9-12]. For the former devices, the 
fabrication of inorganic metal oxide mesoporous scaffold shows good stability and relatively 
little hysteresis[13]. However, the fabrication process is complicated and needs sintering at 
high temperature above 450 oC [14-16]. Usually the interface between metal oxide and 
perovskite is not ideal, which contains charge traps for electron-hole recombination [17, 18]. 
The planar heterojunction perovskite solar cells (PSCs) are fabricated layer by layer with low-
cost solution process, while controlling the morphology and crystal quality of perovskite film 
is rather challenging due to the interrelationship between dewetting and crystallization process 
in preparing the film [19, 20]. A number of endeavors have been directed to solve these 
troubles, and the photovoltaic performance of perovskite solar cells has improved 
significantly in the past several years [21-23]. However, some crucial problems still remaine 
unsolved: the photocurrent hysteresis, and the decay of long-term output at maximum power 
point (MPP) [24-27]. Trap states on the surface and grain boundaries of perovskite layers 
would be one factor leading to hysteresis effects in perovskite solar cells [17]. C60 and its 
derivatives were often used to passivate the charge traps, by covering the interface between 
perovskite and charge collector materials [28], or filling the grain boundaries [29].  
Here we report a planar perovskite solar cell architecture based on a kind of organic 
network structure. Phenyl-C61-butyric acid methyl ester (PCBM) and polyethylene glycol 
(PEG), mixed in perovskite precursor solution, assemble the organic network simultaneously 
as the perovskite phase forms. PEG forms insulating networks in the  perovskite film after 
annealing[30]. PCBM plays another two important roles: 1) restrain the charge traps on grain 
boundaries and those induced by PEG; 2) provide conducting channels along grain boundaries 
for photo-generated electrons. The light-absorption layer is simply fabricated via a one-step 
process under mild temperature ~100oC. The novel architecture combines the merits of both 
the fast charge transfer of mesoporous scaffold and the ease of fabrication of planar 
heterojunction. The as-made devices demonstrate higher power conversion efficiency (PCE), 


 
 
4 
 
smaller hysteresis, and longer duration at MPP tracking, compared to the conventional planar 
heterojunction devices. The solar cells present maximum PCE of 17.1 % under standard 1.5 
AM solar illumination, and the continuous power output at mamximum power point (MPP) 
tracking maintains up to 170 min. 
Results and discussion 
Small hysteresis and high stability of perovskite solar cells with PCBM-PEG network 
The configuration of the planar perovskite solar cells with PCBM/PEG network is illustrated 
in Figure 1a. The fabrication of organic-network PSC is similar to that of planar 
heterojunction PSCs. The perovskite precursor solution is prepared by PbCl2 and CH3NH3I 
(MAI) at a 1:3 molar ratio in N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF). PCBM is dissolved in 
chlorobenzene, and added into the perovskite precursor solution followed by PEG (See 
methods for more details). The PCBM/PEG/perovskite blending solution is spin-coated on 
FTO/TiO2 substrate, followed by the thermal annealing at around 100°C to form the 
perovskite film with PCBM/PEG network. Finally the spiro-OMeTAD is spin-coated and 
gold electrode is evaporated on the films. 
Figure 1b demonstrates the cross section of scanning electron microscopy (SEM) image of 
the as-prepared solar cell. In order to reveal the function of PCBM/PEG network in PSCs, 
conventional planar heterojunction PSCs, and PSCs with PCBM are also prepared and the 
photovoltaic performances are presented in Figure 2a,b. For simplicity, conventional PSC, 
PSC with PCBM, PSC with PCBM/PEG network and PSC with PEG are labelled as Device 1, 
Device 2, Device 3 and Device 4, and the corresponding perovskite films are denoted as Film 
1, Film 2, Film 3, and Film 4, respectively.  Device/Film 1~4 will be labelled as no 
PCBM/PEG, +PCBM, +PCBM/PEG, +PEG in the figures, respectively. The fabrication 
difference among the four kinds of PSCs is the precursor solution. Their photovoltaic 
characteristics were carried out in glovebox under 100 mW/cm2 AM1.5 simulated sunlight. 


 
 
5 
 
The current-density-voltage (J-V) measurements demonstrate that Device 3 attains the highest 
PCE with suppressed hysteresis (Figure 2a). And the critical parameters of device 
performance are summarized in Table 1, including open circuit voltage (Voc), short circuit 
current density (Jsc), fill factor (FF) and PCE in forward and reverse scan. As shown in Figure 
2a and Table 1, Device 2 presents a much smaller hysteresis than Device 1, indicating that the 
photocurrent hysteresis is suppressed effectively by PCBM. It can be attributed to PCBM 
passivation of charge traps on perovskite grain boundaries [17]. PCBM plays the same role in 
Device 3 to decrease hysteresis. In addition, Voc and PCE of Device 3 is enhanced with 
introduce of PEG, due to the full coverage to reduce short-circuit risk, which will be 
demonstrated in later SEM characterization. Device 4 shows similar PCE to Device 3, but 
larger hysteresis than Device 3 without PCBM passivation. 
The real performance of PSCs cannot be estimated accurately according to J-V 
characteristics due to photocurrent hysteresis. Thus, we measured the long-term continuous 
output at MPP to simulate the actual working condition of solar cells. As is shown in Figure 
2b, from Device 1 to 4, the PCE is 9.6%, 12.8%, 13.9% and 12.5% in order during the first 
100 s, demonstrating that device performance is improved by using PCBM/PEG network. 
When the test duration was extended up to 10,000 s, the variance of steady-state PCE is 
observed. The output of Device 1 increased to 12.4% in the first ~20 s, but soon dropped to 
5% in the next 800 s. Device 2 reached its highest PCE in 12.8% after 40 s, and declined 
rapidly to a stage of 7.2% after 1200 s. It suggests that charge traps in perovskite film are 
passivated temporarily by PCBM, and the system becomes unstable under working condition 
after hundreds of seconds. We speculate that it is easy for PCBM located on perovskite grain 
boundaries to migrate under bias or light illumination, so the defect passivation cannot hold 
for a long time. Device 3 showed extremely stable PCE above 14% throughout the 10000 s 
test. Thus PCBM/PEG network ameliorates PSCs in long term output. It is inferred that 
PCBM is restrained by PEG networks and charge traps are filled up solidly. Device 4 also 


 
 
6 
 
showed stable PCE at the first 3000 s, but with slower light response and the PCE gradually 
declined in the later time without PCBM passivation. 
Furthermore, the influence of PCBM content on device’s performance when optimizing 
PCE is shown in Figure 2c,d. The results of Device 2 and Device 3 are similar, indicating that 
function of PEG is independent to that of PCBM. The device with low PCBM content in 
1.8‰ mole ratio to perovskite had large photocurrent hysteresis due to the charge traps which 
have not been passivated by PCBM. The device with higher PCBM content in 10.0‰ mole 
ratio to perovskite had lower Jsc and FF, because excess PCBM would introduce short circuit 
channels in contact with hole transport layer (HTM) above perovskite film. The optimized 
device with PCBM content in 5.4‰ mole ratio to perovskite had the highest PCE and smallest 
hysteresis compared to both former devices. More detailed optimization process is shown in 
Figure S1. The molecule weight of PEG has also been optimized, which is reported in our 
previous work [30], where PEG 20000 Da is found to facilitate the formation of three-
dimensional molecular network in the perovskite film, and result in good photovoltaic 
properties. Therefore, PEG molecule weight of 20000 Da is used in this work.  
Morphology characterization of perovskite film with PCBM/PEG network 
PEG in the perovskite precursor influences crystallization rate and film morphology 
significantly, which is confirmed by the SEM images (Figure 3). The quality of Film 2 is 
similar to that of Film 1, except a slight improvement of film coverage, which indicates that 
additional PCBM exerts little influence on the formation of perovskite film. The film has 
large pin holes leaving short-circuit risk there (Figure 3a-d). However, Film 3 covers the 
substrate fully and uniformly compared to Film 1/2 (Figure 3e,f). The crystallizing process 
can be controlled by using PEG in perovskite precursor due to the interaction between PEG 
and perovskite, which will be demonstrated below.  Introducing PEG improves the wetting 
properties of the precursor solution, thus improving the film morphology (ref. 30). Besides, 


 
 
7 
 
we conjecture that dewetting process can be greatly suppressed by the crosslinking effect of 
polymer chains between perovskite crystal grains, leading to the ultimate uniform perovskite 
film. Furthermore, due to the superior phase separation between PCBM/PEG and perovskite 
material, the PCBM/PEG composites should fill grain boundaries of perovskite film. Thus a 
high-quality film with few charge traps is obtained by introducing PCBM and PEG. 
Other characterization of perovskite film with PCBM/PEG network 
Energy dispersive X-ray spectra (EDS) measurements were carried out for Device 3 to detect 
the distribution of PCBM/PEG in perovskite film. Element oxygen (O) stands for PCBM and 
PEG, and element lead (Pb) stands for perovskite. The result is presented in Figure S2a-c, and 
it is proved that PCBM/PEG network is uniform in perovskite film. The film structure was 
further characterized by high resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM), which is 
shown in Figure S2d. From the image, perovskite is partly coated by organic molecule 
(amorphous phase), but the exposed area demonstrates a perfect crystal structure. This image 
proves directly that the organic network does not exist in the perovskite grains. Therefore, we 
infer that the PCBM/PEG network fills interstices between crystal domains. 
According to X-ray diffraction (XRD) spectra (Figure 4a), it is evidenced that the 
perovskite characteristic peaks of Film 3 are consistent with Film 1 and 2, demonstrating that 
the crystallization of perovskite is not influenced by PCBM and PEG. XRD data implies that 
PCBM and PEG have little impact on perovskite crystal lattice. 
We move on to characterize the difference of optical property for the three films. 
Firstly,light absorption spectra of different perovskite films present obvious difference in the 
short-wavelength region (Figure 4b). It is found that the light absorption below 650 nm is 
enhanced effectively by introducing PCBM/PEG composite. All the measured perovskite 
films arepossessed a similar thickness of ~300 nm. The increase of absorption can be partially 
attributed to the higher coverage of perovskite film with PCBM/PEG network. 


 
 
8 
 
Figure 4c shows the time-integrated photoluminescence (PL) spectra of Film 1~3. With 
PCBM mixed in the perovskite film, photo-generated carriers are extracted quickly by PCBM 
around them, causing a sharp decline of PL peak in Film 2 and 3. Moreover, time-resolved 
transient PL measurements were performed to detect the charge transfer of the perovskite film 
(Figure 4d). The Film 1, 2 and 3 were made by spin-coating their respective precursor 
solution on plasma-treated Al2O3/FTO glass substrate, followed by annealing at 100oC for 70 
min. The Al2O3 layer was deposited by atom-layer-deposition (ALD) to ensure good quality 
of substrate. The PL decay of Film 1 exhibits a time-constant of τ1=215 ns. This is consistent 
with the test results of ref. 28 [31]. The addition of PCBM and PCBM/PEG electron-
quenching layers around the perovskite crystals accelerate the PL decay process, with 
observed time constant of τ2 = 17 ns, τ3 = 15 ns, respectively, showing good ability of electron 
transfer of the organic network. 
To probe the interaction between perovskite and PCBM/PEG, we performed liquid-state  
1H proton nuclear magnetic resonance (1H NMR) measurements [32]. MAI is used to 
represent the functional group of MAPbI3 because it contains all the hydrogen part of MAPbI3. 
Figure 5a and b compares the proton NMR spectra of a neat MAI solution in deuterated 
chlorobenzene (PhCl-d5) with a small amount of deuterated N,N-dimethylformamide-d7 
(DMF-d7) to the signals of MAI-PCBM and MAI-PEG. In the 1H NMR spectra of MAI-
PCBM, the presence of PCBM induces an upfield chemical shift of Δδ ≈ −0.08 ppm for the –
CH3
+ protons of MAI compared to that in neat MAI solution (Figure 5a). And the spectra of 
MAI-PEG showed a strong upfield chemical shift of Δδ ≈ −1 ppm of NH3
+ on MA+ compared 
to that in neat MAI solution (Figure 5b). The results demonstrate that MA+ could be 
connected to PCBM and PEG according to hydrogen bonds as shown in the schematic of 
Figure 5c and d. More illustration and discussion regarding NMR is shown in Figure S3. The 
healing effect on charge traps in perovskite film can be explained partially by the connection 


 
 
9 
 
between MA+ and PCBM. And the bonding between MA+ and PEG would enforce the 
network.  
Impedance spectroscopy analysis of perovskite solar cells 
To extract the detailed information about the interface among different devices, impedance 
spectra (IS) were measured and analyzed. The devices were measured under 0.1 sun 
illumination with bias from 0 to 1 V, and equivalent circuit model (inset of Figure 6a) is used 
to identify the main recombination process in perovskite films [33]. The resistor-capacitor 
(RC) parallel circuit with Rfilm and Cfilm presents the total charge recombination. The 
corresponding time constant, τfilm of charge recombination, were extracted under various bias 
(Figure 6a). Under given applied voltage, τfilm increased as the sample altered from Device 1 
to 3. It indicates that the recombination induced by charge traps on grain boundaries is 
effectively suppressed by PCBM in perovskite film. On the other hand, the series resistance 
(Rseries) extracted from the equivalent circuit was at the highest value in Device 1, and at the 
lowest value in Device 3 (Figure 6b). The decrease of Rseries by using PCBM/PEG indicates 
that the conductive network forms in the perovskite film to offer the transport path to 
electrons. We further calculated the trap density of states (tDOS) and presented the NT(Eω) at 
zero-bias for devices with or without PCBM/PEG (Figure S4). With PCBM/PEG adding into 
perovskite, the tDOS decreased by nearly two orders of magnitude with the energy level 
above 0.34 eV, indicating the effective passivation of charge traps in perovskite by PCBM. 
Improved reproducibility and stability of perovskite solar cells with PCBM/PEG 
network 
More than 100 devices have been fabricated and measured to certify the reproducibility of the 
PSCs with or without PCBM/PEG network. Figure 7a shows the PCE distribution of Device 
1, 2, and 3, and their average value is 7.4%, 14.3%, and 16.1%, respectively. PCE of Device 3 
has smaller variance compared to Device 1 and 2, so PEG in perovskite film raises 
reproducibility of PSCs, which agrees to the good film quality mentioned above. 


 
 
10 
 
To further confirm the stability of the PSCs with PCBM/PEG network in ambient air, the 
performance of cells was characterized by J-V measurement, and stored in the dark at a 
humidity of ~50% without any sealing. Figure 7b shows the PCE evolution as a function of 
time of Device 1, 2 and 3. In contrast to the fast PCE decay from 14.5% to 3% ~ 4% within 
50 ~ 100 hours of devices without PEG, Device 3 maintains more than 85% of its initial PCE 
after a period of 1200 hours. This result well proves that PEG can protect perovskite film 
from moisture in the air and improve the stability of devices effectively. The protection of 
polymer to perovskite is similar to carbon nanotube/polymer composites enhancing the 
stability of perovskite solar cells [34]. 
Conclusion 
In summary, we proposed a planar perovskite solar cell architecture based on organic network 
via simple, low-cost process. The perovskite film quality and device performance can be 
improved effectively by introducing PCBM/PEG network. More importantly, the long-term 
continuous output of the device is much higher than that of conventional PSCs, which should 
be the foundation of industrial applications. Further investigation reveals that both PCBM and 
PEG play important roles in the PCBM/PEG network perovskite solar cells. PCBM has two 
functions here: passivate charge traps on grain boundaries, and form electron transporting 
channel to TiO2 compact layer. PEG plays the role in improving the morphology of perovskite 
thin film and protecting perovskite from moisture in air. This architecrure provides a solution 
to fabricate uniform perovskite layer and to heal the defects at the same time, by adjusting the 
recipe of the precursor. This recipe can be optimized by choosing other low-cost, more 
effective materials. The organic-network perovskite layer would also reinforces the 
architecture and improves strain tolerance, which might facilitate the production of flexible, 
wearable devices in the future. 
Experimental section  


 
 
11 
 
Device fabrication 
All of the chemicals were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich or J&K Scientific Ltd. unless 
expressly stated. CH3NH3I was purchased from Dyesol. A thin blocking-TiO2 layer is first 
deposited onto fluorine doped tin oxide (FTO) by spin coating titanium diisopropoxide 
bis(acetylacetonate) solution (75% in 2-propanol) diluted in ethanol (1:15, volume ratio) and 
annealed at 450oC for 30 min and then cooling to room temperature naturally. Before use, the 
substrate was preheated to 70°C.  
To get the perovskite solution, CH3NH3I and PbCl2 were dissolved in anhydrous N,N-
Dimethylformamide(DMF) at a 3:1 molar ratio with final concentrations of ~35 wt%. As 
PCBM has very low solubility in DMF, it was firstly dissolved in chlorobenzene at a 
concentration of 50 mg ml-1. For PCBM-perovskite film, PCBM/chlorobenzene solution (90 
l ml-1, 5.4‰ mole ratio to perovskite) was added into the perovskite solution. For 
PCBM/PEG network perovskite film, PEG (molecular weight: 20,000; 20 mg ml-1, 1.1‰ 
mole ratio to perovskite) was firstly added into the perovskite solution under stirring at 60°C 
for 12 h. Then PCBM/chlorobenzene solution was added in perovskite solution.   
Then the as-prepared perovskite solution was spin coated onto the TiO2 substrate to get ~ 
400 nm thick film. The spin coating speed is tuned to 4000 r.p.m for perovskite solution with 
PEG, and is 2500 r.p.m in control sample in order to get the same thickness of perovskite 
films. The film was dried at 50°C for 1 h, and annealed at 100°C for 90 min to form 
perovskite crystal. Then hole transporting materials (HTM) was deposited by spin coating the 
solution of HTM at 3,000 r.p.m. for 60 s. The HTM formulation was prepared by dissolving 
2,2',7,7'-Tetrakis(N,N-p-dimethoxy-phenylamino)-9,9'-spirobifluorene (spiro-MeOTAD, 73 
mg), 4-tert-butylpyridine (tBP, 29.5 μl) and a stock solution of lithium 
bis(trifluoromethylsulphonyl)imide(Li-TFSI, 520 mg ml-1) in acetonitrile (18.5 μl)  in 1 ml 
chlorobenzene. Finally, 80 nm of gold electrodes were deposited on top of the devices by 
evaporation at ~10-6 Torr.

Device characterization 
J-V Measurement.  
The current−voltage (J−V) characteristics were obtained using an Agilent B2900 Series 
precision source/measure unit, and the cell was illuminated by a solar simulator (Solar IV-
150A, Zolix) under AM1.5 irradiation (100 mW cm−2). For scan test, the J-V curves are tested 
from 1.5 V to -0.1 V and -0.1 V to 1.5 V with a scan velocity of 200 mV s-1. For steady-state 
test, the voltage is fixed on the maximum power point to test the current output for all the test 
time. The masked active area is 9 mm2. The scan test and MPP tracking test were taken in a 
glove box. For stability test, devices were put in the air and the relative humidity is around 
50%~60%. The devices were tested every 12 hours under AM1.5 light irradiation. The 
temperature is around 30oC. 
SEM & EDS.  
The surface morphology and EDS mapping of the perovskite film was characterized by SEM 
(Nano430, FEI). The electron beam is accelerated at 10 kV. Considering that oxygen element 
only exists in PEG and PCBM among the perovskite film, we detect it to stand for PEG and 
PCBM, to see if they distribute homogeneously in the film. 
X-ray diffraction measurement.  
X-ray powder diagrams were recorded on an X’PertMPD PRO from PANalytical equipped 
with a ceramic tube (Cu anode, λ=1.54060A), a secondary graphite (002) monochromator and 
a RTMS X’Celerator detector, and operated in BRAGG-BRENTANO geometry. The samples 
were mounted without further modification, and the automatic divergence slit and beam mask 
were adjusted to the dimensions of the thin films. A step size of 0.008 deg was chosen and an 
acquisition time of up to 7.5 min/deg.  
PL.  


 
 
13 
 
Steady-state photoluminescence spectra were measured using a green laser (514 nm in 
wavelength) guided by a micro-zone confocal Raman spectroscope (Renishaw inVia 
microRaman system) as the laser beam with a spot size diameter of 2 μm. The collected 
duration is ~10 ms. The time-resolved fluorescence spectra were recorded with a high 
resolution streak camera system (Hamamatsu C10910). We used an amplified mode-lock Ti: 
Sapphire femtosecond laser system (Legend, Coherent) and a two-stage optical parametric 
amplifier (OperA Solo, Coherent) to generatethe pump beam with a repetition rate of 1 KHz. 
All the samples were excited by 517 nm at room temperature with ~ 110 nJ cm-2. 
UV–vis.  
The absorbance of the perovskite films on compact TiO2-coated FTO glasses were measured 
on a Carry 300 Bio (Agilent Technologies). 
NMR.  
For NMR measurement, the samples were examined by Bruker 400 UltraShield using pulse 
signal. The MAI, PCBM, PCBM-MAI samples were prepared by dissolving MAI (0.03 mM), 
PCBM (0.03 mM), and MAI (0.02 mM) + PCBM (0.03 mM), in deuterated chlorobenzene 
(PhCl-d5, 500 l) and deuterated N,N-dimethylformamide-d7 (DMF-d7, 30 l) solution, 
respectively. The MAI, PEG, PEG-MAI samples were prepared by dissolving MAI (0.03 
mM), PEG (0.02 mM), and MAI (0.02 mM) + PEG (0.02 mM), in PhCl-d5 (500 l) and 
DMF-d7 (30 l) solution, respectively. 
IS.  
The impedance spectrum and cyclic voltammograms were measured using a 
potentiostat/galvanostat (SP-150, Bio-Logic, France). The frequency can be tuned from 0.1 
Hz to 1 MHz. And the voltage tuned from 0 V to 1.0 V.

Email address: zhaoqing@pku.edu.cn \n \nAbstract \nAdvancing lead halide perovskite solar cells to photovoltaic application requires reproducible \nand stable devices using low-cost fabricating techniques. Here a device structure is developed \nwith organic network uniformly incorporated into the organic/inorganic hybrid perovskite \nfilm by one-step solution-processing strategy, which significantly improves the photovoltaic \nperformance and long-term stability of planar type perovskite solar cells. The organic network \nis composed with PCBM and PEG. Therein, a long-chain insulating polymer PEG acts as a \nnetwork to improve film morphology, as well as device stability. The fullerene derivative \nPCBM in the composite forms conducting channels to assist the charge transfer and transport \nin perovskite film. Besides, PCBM in perovskite film can passivate trap states on grain \nboundaries, so that the photocurrent hysteresis of the device is suppressed significantly. This \norganic composite network enhances the photovoltaic performance of perovskite solar cells \nwith maximum power conversion efficiency of 17.1%, showing long duration at the \nmaximum power point tracking up to ~170 min. This low-cost organic network demonstrates \n\n\n \n \n2 \n \na promising method for industry-scale fabrication of the organic/inorganic hybrid perovskite \nsolar technology.  \n \nGraphical Abstract \nPCBM/PEG polymer network perovskite solar cells are developed and show superior \nphotovoltaic performance and longer continuous power output with suppressed hysteresis. \nThe power conversion efficiency is 17% under standard 1.5 AM solar illumination and the \nmaximum power point tracking maintains up to 170 min. \n \n  \n \nKeywords: Perovskite solar cells, Suppressed hysteresis, Stability, Organic network, \nPCBM/PEG \n \nIntroduction \nLead halide perovskite, typically CH3NH3PbI3 (MAPbI3), has become the highlighted solar \nenergy harvester, for high absorption coefficient, weak exciton binding energy, and long \ndiffusion length [1-8]. Two types of device architectures, namely mesoporous scaffold and \n\n\n \n \n3 \n \nplanar heterojunction structures, are well developed [9-12]. For the former devices, the \nfabrication of inorganic metal oxide mesoporous scaffold shows good stability and relatively \nlittle hysteresis[13]. However, the fabrication process is complicated and needs sintering at \nhigh temperature above 450 oC [14-16]. Usually the interface between metal oxide and \nperovskite is not ideal, which contains charge traps for electron-hole recombination [17, 18]. \nThe planar heterojunction perovskite solar cells (PSCs) are fabricated layer by layer with low-\ncost solution process, while controlling the morphology and crystal quality of perovskite film \nis rather challenging due to the interrelationship between dewetting and crystallization process \nin preparing the film [19, 20]. A number of endeavors have been directed to solve these \ntroubles, and the photovoltaic performance of perovskite solar cells has improved \nsignificantly in the past several years [21-23]. However, some crucial problems still remaine \nunsolved: the photocurrent hysteresis, and the decay of long-term output at maximum power \npoint (MPP) [24-27]. Trap states on the surface and grain boundaries of perovskite layers \nwould be one factor leading to hysteresis effects in perovskite solar cells [17]. C60 and its \nderivatives were often used to passivate the charge traps, by covering the interface between \nperovskite and charge collector materials [28], or filling the grain boundaries [29].  \nHere we report a planar perovskite solar cell architecture based on a kind of organic \nnetwork structure. Phenyl-C61-butyric acid methyl ester (PCBM) and polyethylene glycol \n(PEG), mixed in perovskite precursor solution, assemble the organic network simultaneously \nas the perovskite phase forms. PEG forms insulating networks in the  perovskite film after \nannealing[30]. PCBM plays another two important roles: 1) restrain the charge traps on grain \nboundaries and those induced by PEG; 2) provide conducting channels along grain boundaries \nfor photo-generated electrons. The light-absorption layer is simply fabricated via a one-step \nprocess under mild temperature ~100oC. The novel architecture combines the merits of both \nthe fast charge transfer of mesoporous scaffold and the ease of fabrication of planar \nheterojunction. The as-made devices demonstrate higher power conversion efficiency (PCE), \n\n\n \n \n4 \n \nsmaller hysteresis, and longer duration at MPP tracking, compared to the conventional planar \nheterojunction devices. The solar cells present maximum PCE of 17.1 % under standard 1.5 \nAM solar illumination, and the continuous power output at mamximum power point (MPP) \ntracking maintains up to 170 min. \nResults and discussion \nSmall hysteresis and high stability of perovskite solar cells with PCBM-PEG network \nThe configuration of the planar perovskite solar cells with PCBM/PEG network is illustrated \nin Figure 1a. The fabrication of organic-network PSC is similar to that of planar \nheterojunction PSCs. The perovskite precursor solution is prepared by PbCl2 and CH3NH3I \n(MAI) at a 1:3 molar ratio in N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF). PCBM is dissolved in \nchlorobenzene, and added into the perovskite precursor solution followed by PEG (See \nmethods for more details). The PCBM/PEG/perovskite blending solution is spin-coated on \nFTO/TiO2 substrate, followed by the thermal annealing at around 100°C to form the \nperovskite film with PCBM/PEG network. Finally the spiro-OMeTAD is spin-coated and \ngold electrode is evaporated on the films. \nFigure 1b demonstrates the cross section of scanning electron microscopy (SEM) image of \nthe as-prepared solar cell. In order to reveal the function of PCBM/PEG network in PSCs, \nconventional planar heterojunction PSCs, and PSCs with PCBM are also prepared and the \nphotovoltaic performances are presented in Figure 2a,b. For simplicity, conventional PSC, \nPSC with PCBM, PSC with PCBM/PEG network and PSC with PEG are labelled as Device 1, \nDevice 2, Device 3 and Device 4, and the corresponding perovskite films are denoted as Film \n1, Film 2, Film 3, and Film 4, respectively.  Device/Film 1~4 will be labelled as no \nPCBM/PEG, +PCBM, +PCBM/PEG, +PEG in the figures, respectively. The fabrication \ndifference among the four kinds of PSCs is the precursor solution. Their photovoltaic \ncharacteristics were carried out in glovebox under 100 mW/cm2 AM1.5 simulated sunlight. \n\n\n \n \n5 \n \nThe current-density-voltage (J-V) measurements demonstrate that Device 3 attains the highest \nPCE with suppressed hysteresis (Figure 2a). And the critical parameters of device \nperformance are summarized in Table 1, including open circuit voltage (Voc), short circuit \ncurrent density (Jsc), fill factor (FF) and PCE in forward and reverse scan. As shown in Figure \n2a and Table 1, Device 2 presents a much smaller hysteresis than Device 1, indicating that the \nphotocurrent hysteresis is suppressed effectively by PCBM. It can be attributed to PCBM \npassivation of charge traps on perovskite grain boundaries [17]. PCBM plays the same role in \nDevice 3 to decrease hysteresis. In addition, Voc and PCE of Device 3 is enhanced with \nintroduce of PEG, due to the full coverage to reduce short-circuit risk, which will be \ndemonstrated in later SEM characterization. Device 4 shows similar PCE to Device 3, but \nlarger hysteresis than Device 3 without PCBM passivation. \nThe real performance of PSCs cannot be estimated accurately according to J-V \ncharacteristics due to photocurrent hysteresis. Thus, we measured the long-term continuous \noutput at MPP to simulate the actual working condition of solar cells. As is shown in Figure \n2b, from Device 1 to 4, the PCE is 9.6%, 12.8%, 13.9% and 12.5% in order during the first \n100 s, demonstrating that device performance is improved by using PCBM/PEG network. \nWhen the test duration was extended up to 10,000 s, the variance of steady-state PCE is \nobserved. The output of Device 1 increased to 12.4% in the first ~20 s, but soon dropped to \n5% in the next 800 s. Device 2 reached its highest PCE in 12.8% after 40 s, and declined \nrapidly to a stage of 7.2% after 1200 s. It suggests that charge traps in perovskite film are \npassivated temporarily by PCBM, and the system becomes unstable under working condition \nafter hundreds of seconds. We speculate that it is easy for PCBM located on perovskite grain \nboundaries to migrate under bias or light illumination, so the defect passivation cannot hold \nfor a long time. Device 3 showed extremely stable PCE above 14% throughout the 10000 s \ntest. Thus PCBM/PEG network ameliorates PSCs in long term output. It is inferred that \nPCBM is restrained by PEG networks and charge traps are filled up solidly. Device 4 also \n\n\n \n \n6 \n \nshowed stable PCE at the first 3000 s, but with slower light response and the PCE gradually \ndeclined in the later time without PCBM passivation. \nFurthermore, the influence of PCBM content on device’s performance when optimizing \nPCE is shown in Figure 2c,d. The results of Device 2 and Device 3 are similar, indicating that \nfunction of PEG is independent to that of PCBM. The device with low PCBM content in \n1.8‰ mole ratio to perovskite had large photocurrent hysteresis due to the charge traps which \nhave not been passivated by PCBM. The device with higher PCBM content in 10.0‰ mole \nratio to perovskite had lower Jsc and FF, because excess PCBM would introduce short circuit \nchannels in contact with hole transport layer (HTM) above perovskite film. The optimized \ndevice with PCBM content in 5.4‰ mole ratio to perovskite had the highest PCE and smallest \nhysteresis compared to both former devices. More detailed optimization process is shown in \nFigure S1. The molecule weight of PEG has also been optimized, which is reported in our \nprevious work [30], where PEG 20000 Da is found to facilitate the formation of three-\ndimensional molecular network in the perovskite film, and result in good photovoltaic \nproperties. Therefore, PEG molecule weight of 20000 Da is used in this work.  \nMorphology characterization of perovskite film with PCBM/PEG network \nPEG in the perovskite precursor influences crystallization rate and film morphology \nsignificantly, which is confirmed by the SEM images (Figure 3). The quality of Film 2 is \nsimilar to that of Film 1, except a slight improvement of film coverage, which indicates that \nadditional PCBM exerts little influence on the formation of perovskite film. The film has \nlarge pin holes leaving short-circuit risk there (Figure 3a-d). However, Film 3 covers the \nsubstrate fully and uniformly compared to Film 1/2 (Figure 3e,f). The crystallizing process \ncan be controlled by using PEG in perovskite precursor due to the interaction between PEG \nand perovskite, which will be demonstrated below.  Introducing PEG improves the wetting \nproperties of the precursor solution, thus improving the film morphology (ref. 30). Besides, \n\n\n \n \n7 \n \nwe conjecture that dewetting process can be greatly suppressed by the crosslinking effect of \npolymer chains between perovskite crystal grains, leading to the ultimate uniform perovskite \nfilm. Furthermore, due to the superior phase separation between PCBM/PEG and perovskite \nmaterial, the PCBM/PEG composites should fill grain boundaries of perovskite film. Thus a \nhigh-quality film with few charge traps is obtained by introducing PCBM and PEG. \nOther characterization of perovskite film with PCBM/PEG network \nEnergy dispersive X-ray spectra (EDS) measurements were carried out for Device 3 to detect \nthe distribution of PCBM/PEG in perovskite film. Element oxygen (O) stands for PCBM and \nPEG, and element lead (Pb) stands for perovskite. The result is presented in Figure S2a-c, and \nit is proved that PCBM/PEG network is uniform in perovskite film. The film structure was \nfurther characterized by high resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM), which is \nshown in Figure S2d. From the image, perovskite is partly coated by organic molecule \n(amorphous phase), but the exposed area demonstrates a perfect crystal structure. This image \nproves directly that the organic network does not exist in the perovskite grains. Therefore, we \ninfer that the PCBM/PEG network fills interstices between crystal domains. \nAccording to X-ray diffraction (XRD) spectra (Figure 4a), it is evidenced that the \nperovskite characteristic peaks of Film 3 are consistent with Film 1 and 2, demonstrating that \nthe crystallization of perovskite is not influenced by PCBM and PEG. XRD data implies that \nPCBM and PEG have little impact on perovskite crystal lattice. \nWe move on to characterize the difference of optical property for the three films. \nFirstly,light absorption spectra of different perovskite films present obvious difference in the \nshort-wavelength region (Figure 4b). It is found that the light absorption below 650 nm is \nenhanced effectively by introducing PCBM/PEG composite. All the measured perovskite \nfilms arepossessed a similar thickness of ~300 nm. The increase of absorption can be partially \nattributed to the higher coverage of perovskite film with PCBM/PEG network. \n\n\n \n \n8 \n \nFigure 4c shows the time-integrated photoluminescence (PL) spectra of Film 1~3. With \nPCBM mixed in the perovskite film, photo-generated carriers are extracted quickly by PCBM \naround them, causing a sharp decline of PL peak in Film 2 and 3. Moreover, time-resolved \ntransient PL measurements were performed to detect the charge transfer of the perovskite film \n(Figure 4d). The Film 1, 2 and 3 were made by spin-coating their respective precursor \nsolution on plasma-treated Al2O3/FTO glass substrate, followed by annealing at 100oC for 70 \nmin. The Al2O3 layer was deposited by atom-layer-deposition (ALD) to ensure good quality \nof substrate. The PL decay of Film 1 exhibits a time-constant of τ1=215 ns. This is consistent \nwith the test results of ref. 28 [31]. The addition of PCBM and PCBM/PEG electron-\nquenching layers around the perovskite crystals accelerate the PL decay process, with \nobserved time constant of τ2 = 17 ns, τ3 = 15 ns, respectively, showing good ability of electron \ntransfer of the organic network. \nTo probe the interaction between perovskite and PCBM/PEG, we performed liquid-state  \n1H proton nuclear magnetic resonance (1H NMR) measurements [32]. MAI is used to \nrepresent the functional group of MAPbI3 because it contains all the hydrogen part of MAPbI3. \nFigure 5a and b compares the proton NMR spectra of a neat MAI solution in deuterated \nchlorobenzene (PhCl-d5) with a small amount of deuterated N,N-dimethylformamide-d7 \n(DMF-d7) to the signals of MAI-PCBM and MAI-PEG. In the 1H NMR spectra of MAI-\nPCBM, the presence of PCBM induces an upfield chemical shift of Δδ ≈ −0.08 ppm for the –\nCH3\n+ protons of MAI compared to that in neat MAI solution (Figure 5a). And the spectra of \nMAI-PEG showed a strong upfield chemical shift of Δδ ≈ −1 ppm of NH3\n+ on MA+ compared \nto that in neat MAI solution (Figure 5b). The results demonstrate that MA+ could be \nconnected to PCBM and PEG according to hydrogen bonds as shown in the schematic of \nFigure 5c and d. More illustration and discussion regarding NMR is shown in Figure S3. The \nhealing effect on charge traps in perovskite film can be explained partially by the connection \n\n\n \n \n9 \n \nbetween MA+ and PCBM. And the bonding between MA+ and PEG would enforce the \nnetwork.  \nImpedance spectroscopy analysis of perovskite solar cells \nTo extract the detailed information about the interface among different devices, impedance \nspectra (IS) were measured and analyzed. The devices were measured under 0.1 sun \nillumination with bias from 0 to 1 V, and equivalent circuit model (inset of Figure 6a) is used \nto identify the main recombination process in perovskite films [33]. The resistor-capacitor \n(RC) parallel circuit with Rfilm and Cfilm presents the total charge recombination. The \ncorresponding time constant, τfilm of charge recombination, were extracted under various bias \n(Figure 6a). Under given applied voltage, τfilm increased as the sample altered from Device 1 \nto 3. It indicates that the recombination induced by charge traps on grain boundaries is \neffectively suppressed by PCBM in perovskite film. On the other hand, the series resistance \n(Rseries) extracted from the equivalent circuit was at the highest value in Device 1, and at the \nlowest value in Device 3 (Figure 6b). The decrease of Rseries by using PCBM/PEG indicates \nthat the conductive network forms in the perovskite film to offer the transport path to \nelectrons. We further calculated the trap density of states (tDOS) and presented the NT(Eω) at \nzero-bias for devices with or without PCBM/PEG (Figure S4). With PCBM/PEG adding into \nperovskite, the tDOS decreased by nearly two orders of magnitude with the energy level \nabove 0.34 eV, indicating the effective passivation of charge traps in perovskite by PCBM. \nImproved reproducibility and stability of perovskite solar cells with PCBM/PEG \nnetwork \nMore than 100 devices have been fabricated and measured to certify the reproducibility of the \nPSCs with or without PCBM/PEG network. Figure 7a shows the PCE distribution of Device \n1, 2, and 3, and their average value is 7.4%, 14.3%, and 16.1%, respectively. PCE of Device 3 \nhas smaller variance compared to Device 1 and 2, so PEG in perovskite film raises \nreproducibility of PSCs, which agrees to the good film quality mentioned above. \n\n\n \n \n10 \n \nTo further confirm the stability of the PSCs with PCBM/PEG network in ambient air, the \nperformance of cells was characterized by J-V measurement, and stored in the dark at a \nhumidity of ~50% without any sealing. Figure 7b shows the PCE evolution as a function of \ntime of Device 1, 2 and 3. In contrast to the fast PCE decay from 14.5% to 3% ~ 4% within \n50 ~ 100 hours of devices without PEG, Device 3 maintains more than 85% of its initial PCE \nafter a period of 1200 hours. This result well proves that PEG can protect perovskite film \nfrom moisture in the air and improve the stability of devices effectively. The protection of \npolymer to perovskite is similar to carbon nanotube/polymer composites enhancing the \nstability of perovskite solar cells [34]. \nConclusion \nIn summary, we proposed a planar perovskite solar cell architecture based on organic network \nvia simple, low-cost process. The perovskite film quality and device performance can be \nimproved effectively by introducing PCBM/PEG network. More importantly, the long-term \ncontinuous output of the device is much higher than that of conventional PSCs, which should \nbe the foundation of industrial applications. Further investigation reveals that both PCBM and \nPEG play important roles in the PCBM/PEG network perovskite solar cells. PCBM has two \nfunctions here: passivate charge traps on grain boundaries, and form electron transporting \nchannel to TiO2 compact layer. PEG plays the role in improving the morphology of perovskite \nthin film and protecting perovskite from moisture in air. This architecrure provides a solution \nto fabricate uniform perovskite layer and to heal the defects at the same time, by adjusting the \nrecipe of the precursor. This recipe can be optimized by choosing other low-cost, more \neffective materials. The organic-network perovskite layer would also reinforces the \narchitecture and improves strain tolerance, which might facilitate the production of flexible, \nwearable devices in the future. \nExperimental section  \n\n\n \n \n11 \n \nDevice fabrication \nAll of the chemicals were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich or J&K Scientific Ltd. unless \nexpressly stated. CH3NH3I was purchased from Dyesol. A thin blocking-TiO2 layer is first \ndeposited onto fluorine doped tin oxide (FTO) by spin coating titanium diisopropoxide \nbis(acetylacetonate) solution (75% in 2-propanol) diluted in ethanol (1:15, volume ratio) and \nannealed at 450oC for 30 min and then cooling to room temperature naturally. Before use, the \nsubstrate was preheated to 70°C.  \nTo get the perovskite solution, CH3NH3I and PbCl2 were dissolved in anhydrous N,N-\nDimethylformamide(DMF) at a 3:1 molar ratio with final concentrations of ~35 wt%. As \nPCBM has very low solubility in DMF, it was firstly dissolved in chlorobenzene at a \nconcentration of 50 mg ml-1. For PCBM-perovskite film, PCBM/chlorobenzene solution (90 \nl ml-1, 5.4‰ mole ratio to perovskite) was added into the perovskite solution. For \nPCBM/PEG network perovskite film, PEG (molecular weight: 20,000; 20 mg ml-1, 1.1‰ \nmole ratio to perovskite) was firstly added into the perovskite solution under stirring at 60°C \nfor 12 h. Then PCBM/chlorobenzene solution was added in perovskite solution.   \nThen the as-prepared perovskite solution was spin coated onto the TiO2 substrate to get ~ \n400 nm thick film. The spin coating speed is tuned to 4000 r.p.m for perovskite solution with \nPEG, and is 2500 r.p.m in control sample in order to get the same thickness of perovskite \nfilms. The film was dried at 50°C for 1 h, and annealed at 100°C for 90 min to form \nperovskite crystal. Then hole transporting materials (HTM) was deposited by spin coating the \nsolution of HTM at 3,000 r.p.m. for 60 s. The HTM formulation was prepared by dissolving \n2,2\',7,7\'-Tetrakis(N,N-p-dimethoxy-phenylamino)-9,9\'-spirobifluorene (spiro-MeOTAD, 73 \nmg), 4-tert-butylpyridine (tBP, 29.5 μl) and a stock solution of lithium \nbis(trifluoromethylsulphonyl)imide(Li-TFSI, 520 mg ml-1) in acetonitrile (18.5 μl)  in 1 ml \nchlorobenzene. Finally, 80 nm of gold electrodes were deposited on top of the devices by \nevaporation at ~10-6 Torr. \n\n\n \n \n12 \n \nDevice characterization \nJ-V Measurement.  \nThe current−voltage (J−V) characteristics were obtained using an Agilent B2900 Series \nprecision source/measure unit, and the cell was illuminated by a solar simulator (Solar IV-\n150A, Zolix) under AM1.5 irradiation (100 mW cm−2). For scan test, the J-V curves are tested \nfrom 1.5 V to -0.1 V and -0.1 V to 1.5 V with a scan velocity of 200 mV s-1. For steady-state \ntest, the voltage is fixed on the maximum power point to test the current output for all the test \ntime. The masked active area is 9 mm2. The scan test and MPP tracking test were taken in a \nglove box. For stability test, devices were put in the air and the relative humidity is around \n50%~60%. The devices were tested every 12 hours under AM1.5 light irradiation. The \ntemperature is around 30oC. \nSEM & EDS.  \nThe surface morphology and EDS mapping of the perovskite film was characterized by SEM \n(Nano430, FEI). The electron beam is accelerated at 10 kV. Considering that oxygen element \nonly exists in PEG and PCBM among the perovskite film, we detect it to stand for PEG and \nPCBM, to see if they distribute homogeneously in the film. \nX-ray diffraction measurement.  \nX-ray powder diagrams were recorded on an X’PertMPD PRO from PANalytical equipped \nwith a ceramic tube (Cu anode, λ=1.54060A), a secondary graphite (002) monochromator and \na RTMS X’Celerator detector, and operated in BRAGG-BRENTANO geometry. The samples \nwere mounted without further modification, and the automatic divergence slit and beam mask \nwere adjusted to the dimensions of the thin films. A step size of 0.008 deg was chosen and an \nacquisition time of up to 7.5 min/deg.  \nPL.  \n\n\n \n \n13 \n \nSteady-state photoluminescence spectra were measured using a green laser (514 nm in \nwavelength) guided by a micro-zone confocal Raman spectroscope (Renishaw inVia \nmicroRaman system) as the laser beam with a spot size diameter of 2 μm. The collected \nduration is ~10 ms. The time-resolved fluorescence spectra were recorded with a high \nresolution streak camera system (Hamamatsu C10910). We used an amplified mode-lock Ti: \nSapphire femtosecond laser system (Legend, Coherent) and a two-stage optical parametric \namplifier (OperA Solo, Coherent) to generatethe pump beam with a repetition rate of 1 KHz. \nAll the samples were excited by 517 nm at room temperature with ~ 110 nJ cm-2. \nUV–vis.  \nThe absorbance of the perovskite films on compact TiO2-coated FTO glasses were measured \non a Carry 300 Bio (Agilent Technologies). \nNMR.  \nFor NMR measurement, the samples were examined by Bruker 400 UltraShield using pulse \nsignal. The MAI, PCBM, PCBM-MAI samples were prepared by dissolving MAI (0.03 mM), \nPCBM (0.03 mM), and MAI (0.02 mM) + PCBM (0.03 mM), in deuterated chlorobenzene \n(PhCl-d5, 500 l) and deuterated N,N-dimethylformamide-d7 (DMF-d7, 30 l) solution, \nrespectively. The MAI, PEG, PEG-MAI samples were prepared by dissolving MAI (0.03 \nmM), PEG (0.02 mM), and MAI (0.02 mM) + PEG (0.02 mM), in PhCl-d5 (500 l) and \nDMF-d7 (30 l) solution, respectively. \nIS.  \nThe impedance spectrum and cyclic voltammograms were measured using a \npotentiostat/galvanostat (SP-150, Bio-Logic, France). Suppressed hysteresis and improved stability in perovskite solar cells with 
conductive organic network 
Jing Weia,b, Heng Lia,b, Yicheng Zhaoa,b, Wenke Zhoua,b, Rui Fua,b, Yamin Leprince-Wangc, 
Dapeng Yua,b, Qing Zhaoa,b* 
aState Key Laboratory for Mesoscopic Physics and Electron Microscopy Laboratory, School 
of Physics, Peking University, 100871 Beijing, China 
bCollaborative Innovation Center of Quantum Matter, 100084 Beijing, China 
cUniversité Paris-Est, ESYCOM, UPEM, 5 bd. Descartes, F-77454 Marne-la-Vallée, France 
*Corresponding author. Tel./fax:+86 10 62753673. Email address: zhaoqing@pku.edu.cn 
 
Abstract 
Advancing lead halide perovskite solar cells to photovoltaic application requires reproducible 
and stable devices using low-cost fabricating techniques. Here a device structure is developed 
with organic network uniformly incorporated into the organic/inorganic hybrid perovskite 
film by one-step solution-processing strategy, which significantly improves the photovoltaic 
performance and long-term stability of planar type perovskite solar cells. The organic network 
is composed with PCBM and PEG. Therein, a long-chain insulating polymer PEG acts as a 
network to improve film morphology, as well as device stability. The fullerene derivative 
PCBM in the composite forms conducting channels to assist the charge transfer and transport 
in perovskite film. Besides, PCBM in perovskite film can passivate trap states on grain 
boundaries, so that the photocurrent hysteresis of the device is suppressed significantly. This 
organic composite network enhances the photovoltaic performance of perovskite solar cells 
with maximum power conversion efficiency of 17.1%, showing long duration at the 
maximum power point tracking up to ~170 min. This low-cost organic network demonstrates 


 
 
2 
 
a promising method for industry-scale fabrication of the organic/inorganic hybrid perovskite 
solar technology.  
 
Graphical Abstract 
PCBM/PEG polymer network perovskite solar cells are developed and show superior 
photovoltaic performance and longer continuous power output with suppressed hysteresis. 
The power conversion efficiency is 17% under standard 1.5 AM solar illumination and the 
maximum power point tracking maintains up to 170 min. 
 
  
 
Keywords: Perovskite solar cells, Suppressed hysteresis, Stability, Organic network, 
PCBM/PEG 
 
Introduction 
Lead halide perovskite, typically CH3NH3PbI3 (MAPbI3), has become the highlighted solar 
energy harvester, for high absorption coefficient, weak exciton binding energy, and long 
diffusion length [1-8]. Two types of device architectures, namely mesoporous scaffold and 


 
 
3 
 
planar heterojunction structures, are well developed [9-12]. For the former devices, the 
fabrication of inorganic metal oxide mesoporous scaffold shows good stability and relatively 
little hysteresis[13]. However, the fabrication process is complicated and needs sintering at 
high temperature above 450 oC [14-16]. Usually the interface between metal oxide and 
perovskite is not ideal, which contains charge traps for electron-hole recombination [17, 18]. 
The planar heterojunction perovskite solar cells (PSCs) are fabricated layer by layer with low-
cost solution process, while controlling the morphology and crystal quality of perovskite film 
is rather challenging due to the interrelationship between dewetting and crystallization process 
in preparing the film [19, 20]. A number of endeavors have been directed to solve these 
troubles, and the photovoltaic performance of perovskite solar cells has improved 
significantly in the past several years [21-23]. However, some crucial problems still remaine 
unsolved: the photocurrent hysteresis, and the decay of long-term output at maximum power 
point (MPP) [24-27]. Trap states on the surface and grain boundaries of perovskite layers 
would be one factor leading to hysteresis effects in perovskite solar cells [17]. C60 and its 
derivatives were often used to passivate the charge traps, by covering the interface between 
perovskite and charge collector materials [28], or filling the grain boundaries [29].  
Here we report a planar perovskite solar cell architecture based on a kind of organic 
network structure. Phenyl-C61-butyric acid methyl ester (PCBM) and polyethylene glycol 
(PEG), mixed in perovskite precursor solution, assemble the organic network simultaneously 
as the perovskite phase forms. PEG forms insulating networks in the  perovskite film after 
annealing[30]. PCBM plays another two important roles: 1) restrain the charge traps on grain 
boundaries and those induced by PEG; 2) provide conducting channels along grain boundaries 
for photo-generated electrons. The light-absorption layer is simply fabricated via a one-step 
process under mild temperature ~100oC. The novel architecture combines the merits of both 
the fast charge transfer of mesoporous scaffold and the ease of fabrication of planar 
heterojunction. The as-made devices demonstrate higher power conversion efficiency (PCE), 


 
 
4 
 
smaller hysteresis, and longer duration at MPP tracking, compared to the conventional planar 
heterojunction devices. The solar cells present maximum PCE of 17.1 % under standard 1.5 
AM solar illumination, and the continuous power output at mamximum power point (MPP) 
tracking maintains up to 170 min. 
Results and discussion 
Small hysteresis and high stability of perovskite solar cells with PCBM-PEG network 
The configuration of the planar perovskite solar cells with PCBM/PEG network is illustrated 
in Figure 1a. The fabrication of organic-network PSC is similar to that of planar 
heterojunction PSCs. The perovskite precursor solution is prepared by PbCl2 and CH3NH3I 
(MAI) at a 1:3 molar ratio in N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF). PCBM is dissolved in 
chlorobenzene, and added into the perovskite precursor solution followed by PEG (See 
methods for more details). The PCBM/PEG/perovskite blending solution is spin-coated on 
FTO/TiO2 substrate, followed by the thermal annealing at around 100°C to form the 
perovskite film with PCBM/PEG network. Finally the spiro-OMeTAD is spin-coated and 
gold electrode is evaporated on the films. 
Figure 1b demonstrates the cross section of scanning electron microscopy (SEM) image of 
the as-prepared solar cell. In order to reveal the function of PCBM/PEG network in PSCs, 
conventional planar heterojunction PSCs, and PSCs with PCBM are also prepared and the 
photovoltaic performances are presented in Figure 2a,b. For simplicity, conventional PSC, 
PSC with PCBM, PSC with PCBM/PEG network and PSC with PEG are labelled as Device 1, 
Device 2, Device 3 and Device 4, and the corresponding perovskite films are denoted as Film 
1, Film 2, Film 3, and Film 4, respectively.  Device/Film 1~4 will be labelled as no 
PCBM/PEG, +PCBM, +PCBM/PEG, +PEG in the figures, respectively. The fabrication 
difference among the four kinds of PSCs is the precursor solution. Their photovoltaic 
characteristics were carried out in glovebox under 100 mW/cm2 AM1.5 simulated sunlight. 


 
 
5 
 
The current-density-voltage (J-V) measurements demonstrate that Device 3 attains the highest 
PCE with suppressed hysteresis (Figure 2a). And the critical parameters of device 
performance are summarized in Table 1, including open circuit voltage (Voc), short circuit 
current density (Jsc), fill factor (FF) and PCE in forward and reverse scan. As shown in Figure 
2a and Table 1, Device 2 presents a much smaller hysteresis than Device 1, indicating that the 
photocurrent hysteresis is suppressed effectively by PCBM. It can be attributed to PCBM 
passivation of charge traps on perovskite grain boundaries [17]. PCBM plays the same role in 
Device 3 to decrease hysteresis. In addition, Voc and PCE of Device 3 is enhanced with 
introduce of PEG, due to the full coverage to reduce short-circuit risk, which will be 
demonstrated in later SEM characterization. Device 4 shows similar PCE to Device 3, but 
larger hysteresis than Device 3 without PCBM passivation. 
The real performance of PSCs cannot be estimated accurately according to J-V 
characteristics due to photocurrent hysteresis. Thus, we measured the long-term continuous 
output at MPP to simulate the actual working condition of solar cells. As is shown in Figure 
2b, from Device 1 to 4, the PCE is 9.6%, 12.8%, 13.9% and 12.5% in order during the first 
100 s, demonstrating that device performance is improved by using PCBM/PEG network. 
When the test duration was extended up to 10,000 s, the variance of steady-state PCE is 
observed. The output of Device 1 increased to 12.4% in the first ~20 s, but soon dropped to 
5% in the next 800 s. Device 2 reached its highest PCE in 12.8% after 40 s, and declined 
rapidly to a stage of 7.2% after 1200 s. It suggests that charge traps in perovskite film are 
passivated temporarily by PCBM, and the system becomes unstable under working condition 
after hundreds of seconds. We speculate that it is easy for PCBM located on perovskite grain 
boundaries to migrate under bias or light illumination, so the defect passivation cannot hold 
for a long time. Device 3 showed extremely stable PCE above 14% throughout the 10000 s 
test. Thus PCBM/PEG network ameliorates PSCs in long term output. It is inferred that 
PCBM is restrained by PEG networks and charge traps are filled up solidly. Device 4 also 


 
 
6 
 
showed stable PCE at the first 3000 s, but with slower light response and the PCE gradually 
declined in the later time without PCBM passivation. 
Furthermore, the influence of PCBM content on device’s performance when optimizing 
PCE is shown in Figure 2c,d. The results of Device 2 and Device 3 are similar, indicating that 
function of PEG is independent to that of PCBM. The device with low PCBM content in 
1.8‰ mole ratio to perovskite had large photocurrent hysteresis due to the charge traps which 
have not been passivated by PCBM. The device with higher PCBM content in 10.0‰ mole 
ratio to perovskite had lower Jsc and FF, because excess PCBM would introduce short circuit 
channels in contact with hole transport layer (HTM) above perovskite film. The optimized 
device with PCBM content in 5.4‰ mole ratio to perovskite had the highest PCE and smallest 
hysteresis compared to both former devices. More detailed optimization process is shown in 
Figure S1. The molecule weight of PEG has also been optimized, which is reported in our 
previous work [30], where PEG 20000 Da is found to facilitate the formation of three-
dimensional molecular network in the perovskite film, and result in good photovoltaic 
properties. Therefore, PEG molecule weight of 20000 Da is used in this work.  
Morphology characterization of perovskite film with PCBM/PEG network 
PEG in the perovskite precursor influences crystallization rate and film morphology 
significantly, which is confirmed by the SEM images (Figure 3). The quality of Film 2 is 
similar to that of Film 1, except a slight improvement of film coverage, which indicates that 
additional PCBM exerts little influence on the formation of perovskite film. The film has 
large pin holes leaving short-circuit risk there (Figure 3a-d). However, Film 3 covers the 
substrate fully and uniformly compared to Film 1/2 (Figure 3e,f). The crystallizing process 
can be controlled by using PEG in perovskite precursor due to the interaction between PEG 
and perovskite, which will be demonstrated below.  Introducing PEG improves the wetting 
properties of the precursor solution, thus improving the film morphology (ref. 30). Besides, 


 
 
7 
 
we conjecture that dewetting process can be greatly suppressed by the crosslinking effect of 
polymer chains between perovskite crystal grains, leading to the ultimate uniform perovskite 
film. Furthermore, due to the superior phase separation between PCBM/PEG and perovskite 
material, the PCBM/PEG composites should fill grain boundaries of perovskite film. Thus a 
high-quality film with few charge traps is obtained by introducing PCBM and PEG. 
Other characterization of perovskite film with PCBM/PEG network 
Energy dispersive X-ray spectra (EDS) measurements were carried out for Device 3 to detect 
the distribution of PCBM/PEG in perovskite film. Element oxygen (O) stands for PCBM and 
PEG, and element lead (Pb) stands for perovskite. The result is presented in Figure S2a-c, and 
it is proved that PCBM/PEG network is uniform in perovskite film. The film structure was 
further characterized by high resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM), which is 
shown in Figure S2d. From the image, perovskite is partly coated by organic molecule 
(amorphous phase), but the exposed area demonstrates a perfect crystal structure. This image 
proves directly that the organic network does not exist in the perovskite grains. Therefore, we 
infer that the PCBM/PEG network fills interstices between crystal domains. 
According to X-ray diffraction (XRD) spectra (Figure 4a), it is evidenced that the 
perovskite characteristic peaks of Film 3 are consistent with Film 1 and 2, demonstrating that 
the crystallization of perovskite is not influenced by PCBM and PEG. XRD data implies that 
PCBM and PEG have little impact on perovskite crystal lattice. 
We move on to characterize the difference of optical property for the three films. 
Firstly,light absorption spectra of different perovskite films present obvious difference in the 
short-wavelength region (Figure 4b). It is found that the light absorption below 650 nm is 
enhanced effectively by introducing PCBM/PEG composite. All the measured perovskite 
films arepossessed a similar thickness of ~300 nm. The increase of absorption can be partially 
attributed to the higher coverage of perovskite film with PCBM/PEG network. 


 
 
8 
 
Figure 4c shows the time-integrated photoluminescence (PL) spectra of Film 1~3. With 
PCBM mixed in the perovskite film, photo-generated carriers are extracted quickly by PCBM 
around them, causing a sharp decline of PL peak in Film 2 and 3. Moreover, time-resolved 
transient PL measurements were performed to detect the charge transfer of the perovskite film 
(Figure 4d). The Film 1, 2 and 3 were made by spin-coating their respective precursor 
solution on plasma-treated Al2O3/FTO glass substrate, followed by annealing at 100oC for 70 
min. The Al2O3 layer was deposited by atom-layer-deposition (ALD) to ensure good quality 
of substrate. The PL decay of Film 1 exhibits a time-constant of τ1=215 ns. This is consistent 
with the test results of ref. 28 [31]. The addition of PCBM and PCBM/PEG electron-
quenching layers around the perovskite crystals accelerate the PL decay process, with 
observed time constant of τ2 = 17 ns, τ3 = 15 ns, respectively, showing good ability of electron 
transfer of the organic network. 
To probe the interaction between perovskite and PCBM/PEG, we performed liquid-state  
1H proton nuclear magnetic resonance (1H NMR) measurements [32]. MAI is used to 
represent the functional group of MAPbI3 because it contains all the hydrogen part of MAPbI3. 
Figure 5a and b compares the proton NMR spectra of a neat MAI solution in deuterated 
chlorobenzene (PhCl-d5) with a small amount of deuterated N,N-dimethylformamide-d7 
(DMF-d7) to the signals of MAI-PCBM and MAI-PEG. In the 1H NMR spectra of MAI-
PCBM, the presence of PCBM induces an upfield chemical shift of Δδ ≈ −0.08 ppm for the –
CH3
+ protons of MAI compared to that in neat MAI solution (Figure 5a). And the spectra of 
MAI-PEG showed a strong upfield chemical shift of Δδ ≈ −1 ppm of NH3
+ on MA+ compared 
to that in neat MAI solution (Figure 5b). The results demonstrate that MA+ could be 
connected to PCBM and PEG according to hydrogen bonds as shown in the schematic of 
Figure 5c and d. More illustration and discussion regarding NMR is shown in Figure S3. The 
healing effect on charge traps in perovskite film can be explained partially by the connection 


 
 
9 
 
between MA+ and PCBM. And the bonding between MA+ and PEG would enforce the 
network.  
Impedance spectroscopy analysis of perovskite solar cells 
To extract the detailed information about the interface among different devices, impedance 
spectra (IS) were measured and analyzed. The devices were measured under 0.1 sun 
illumination with bias from 0 to 1 V, and equivalent circuit model (inset of Figure 6a) is used 
to identify the main recombination process in perovskite films [33]. The resistor-capacitor 
(RC) parallel circuit with Rfilm and Cfilm presents the total charge recombination. The 
corresponding time constant, τfilm of charge recombination, were extracted under various bias 
(Figure 6a). Under given applied voltage, τfilm increased as the sample altered from Device 1 
to 3. It indicates that the recombination induced by charge traps on grain boundaries is 
effectively suppressed by PCBM in perovskite film. On the other hand, the series resistance 
(Rseries) extracted from the equivalent circuit was at the highest value in Device 1, and at the 
lowest value in Device 3 (Figure 6b). The decrease of Rseries by using PCBM/PEG indicates 
that the conductive network forms in the perovskite film to offer the transport path to 
electrons. We further calculated the trap density of states (tDOS) and presented the NT(Eω) at 
zero-bias for devices with or without PCBM/PEG (Figure S4). With PCBM/PEG adding into 
perovskite, the tDOS decreased by nearly two orders of magnitude with the energy level 
above 0.34 eV, indicating the effective passivation of charge traps in perovskite by PCBM. 
Improved reproducibility and stability of perovskite solar cells with PCBM/PEG 
network 
More than 100 devices have been fabricated and measured to certify the reproducibility of the 
PSCs with or without PCBM/PEG network. Figure 7a shows the PCE distribution of Device 
1, 2, and 3, and their average value is 7.4%, 14.3%, and 16.1%, respectively. PCE of Device 3 
has smaller variance compared to Device 1 and 2, so PEG in perovskite film raises 
reproducibility of PSCs, which agrees to the good film quality mentioned above. 


 
 
10 
 
To further confirm the stability of the PSCs with PCBM/PEG network in ambient air, the 
performance of cells was characterized by J-V measurement, and stored in the dark at a 
humidity of ~50% without any sealing. Figure 7b shows the PCE evolution as a function of 
time of Device 1, 2 and 3. In contrast to the fast PCE decay from 14.5% to 3% ~ 4% within 
50 ~ 100 hours of devices without PEG, Device 3 maintains more than 85% of its initial PCE 
after a period of 1200 hours. This result well proves that PEG can protect perovskite film 
from moisture in the air and improve the stability of devices effectively. The protection of 
polymer to perovskite is similar to carbon nanotube/polymer composites enhancing the 
stability of perovskite solar cells [34]. 
Conclusion 
In summary, we proposed a planar perovskite solar cell architecture based on organic network 
via simple, low-cost process. The perovskite film quality and device performance can be 
improved effectively by introducing PCBM/PEG network. More importantly, the long-term 
continuous output of the device is much higher than that of conventional PSCs, which should 
be the foundation of industrial applications. Further investigation reveals that both PCBM and 
PEG play important roles in the PCBM/PEG network perovskite solar cells. PCBM has two 
functions here: passivate charge traps on grain boundaries, and form electron transporting 
channel to TiO2 compact layer. PEG plays the role in improving the morphology of perovskite 
thin film and protecting perovskite from moisture in air. This architecrure provides a solution 
to fabricate uniform perovskite layer and to heal the defects at the same time, by adjusting the 
recipe of the precursor. This recipe can be optimized by choosing other low-cost, more 
effective materials. The organic-network perovskite layer would also reinforces the 
architecture and improves strain tolerance, which might facilitate the production of flexible, 
wearable devices in the future. 
Experimental section  


 
 
11 
 
Device fabrication 
All of the chemicals were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich or J&K Scientific Ltd. unless 
expressly stated. CH3NH3I was purchased from Dyesol. A thin blocking-TiO2 layer is first 
deposited onto fluorine doped tin oxide (FTO) by spin coating titanium diisopropoxide 
bis(acetylacetonate) solution (75% in 2-propanol) diluted in ethanol (1:15, volume ratio) and 
annealed at 450oC for 30 min and then cooling to room temperature naturally. Before use, the 
substrate was preheated to 70°C.  
To get the perovskite solution, CH3NH3I and PbCl2 were dissolved in anhydrous N,N-
Dimethylformamide(DMF) at a 3:1 molar ratio with final concentrations of ~35 wt%. As 
PCBM has very low solubility in DMF, it was firstly dissolved in chlorobenzene at a 
concentration of 50 mg ml-1. For PCBM-perovskite film, PCBM/chlorobenzene solution (90 
l ml-1, 5.4‰ mole ratio to perovskite) was added into the perovskite solution. For 
PCBM/PEG network perovskite film, PEG (molecular weight: 20,000; 20 mg ml-1, 1.1‰ 
mole ratio to perovskite) was firstly added into the perovskite solution under stirring at 60°C 
for 12 h. Then PCBM/chlorobenzene solution was added in perovskite solution.   
Then the as-prepared perovskite solution was spin coated onto the TiO2 substrate to get ~ 
400 nm thick film. The spin coating speed is tuned to 4000 r.p.m for perovskite solution with 
PEG, and is 2500 r.p.m in control sample in order to get the same thickness of perovskite 
films. The film was dried at 50°C for 1 h, and annealed at 100°C for 90 min to form 
perovskite crystal. Then hole transporting materials (HTM) was deposited by spin coating the 
solution of HTM at 3,000 r.p.m. for 60 s. The HTM formulation was prepared by dissolving 
2,2',7,7'-Tetrakis(N,N-p-dimethoxy-phenylamino)-9,9'-spirobifluorene (spiro-MeOTAD, 73 
mg), 4-tert-butylpyridine (tBP, 29.5 μl) and a stock solution of lithium 
bis(trifluoromethylsulphonyl)imide(Li-TFSI, 520 mg ml-1) in acetonitrile (18.5 μl)  in 1 ml 
chlorobenzene. Finally, 80 nm of gold electrodes were deposited on top of the devices by 
evaporation at ~10-6 Torr. 


 
 
12 
 
Device characterization 
J-V Measurement.  
The current−voltage (J−V) characteristics were obtained using an Agilent B2900 Series 
precision source/measure unit, and the cell was illuminated by a solar simulator (Solar IV-
150A, Zolix) under AM1.5 irradiation (100 mW cm−2). For scan test, the J-V curves are tested 
from 1.5 V to -0.1 V and -0.1 V to 1.5 V with a scan velocity of 200 mV s-1. For steady-state 
test, the voltage is fixed on the maximum power point to test the current output for all the test 
time. The masked active area is 9 mm2. The scan test and MPP tracking test were taken in a 
glove box. For stability test, devices were put in the air and the relative humidity is around 
50%~60%. The devices were tested every 12 hours under AM1.5 light irradiation. The 
temperature is around 30oC. 
SEM & EDS.  
The surface morphology and EDS mapping of the perovskite film was characterized by SEM 
(Nano430, FEI). The electron beam is accelerated at 10 kV. Considering that oxygen element 
only exists in PEG and PCBM among the perovskite film, we detect it to stand for PEG and 
PCBM, to see if they distribute homogeneously in the film. 
X-ray diffraction measurement.  
X-ray powder diagrams were recorded on an X’PertMPD PRO from PANalytical equipped 
with a ceramic tube (Cu anode, λ=1.54060A), a secondary graphite (002) monochromator and 
a RTMS X’Celerator detector, and operated in BRAGG-BRENTANO geometry. The samples 
were mounted without further modification, and the automatic divergence slit and beam mask 
were adjusted to the dimensions of the thin films. A step size of 0.008 deg was chosen and an 
acquisition time of up to 7.5 min/deg.  
PL.  


 
 
13 
 
Steady-state photoluminescence spectra were measured using a green laser (514 nm in 
wavelength) guided by a micro-zone confocal Raman spectroscope (Renishaw inVia 
microRaman system) as the laser beam with a spot size diameter of 2 μm. The collected 
duration is ~10 ms. The time-resolved fluorescence spectra were recorded with a high 
resolution streak camera system (Hamamatsu C10910). We used an amplified mode-lock Ti: 
Sapphire femtosecond laser system (Legend, Coherent) and a two-stage optical parametric 
amplifier (OperA Solo, Coherent) to generatethe pump beam with a repetition rate of 1 KHz. 
All the samples were excited by 517 nm at room temperature with ~ 110 nJ cm-2. 
UV–vis.  
The absorbance of the perovskite films on compact TiO2-coated FTO glasses were measured 
on a Carry 300 Bio (Agilent Technologies). 
NMR.  
For NMR measurement, the samples were examined by Bruker 400 UltraShield using pulse 
signal. The MAI, PCBM, PCBM-MAI samples were prepared by dissolving MAI (0.03 mM), 
PCBM (0.03 mM), and MAI (0.02 mM) + PCBM (0.03 mM), in deuterated chlorobenzene 
(PhCl-d5, 500 l) and deuterated N,N-dimethylformamide-d7 (DMF-d7, 30 l) solution, 
respectively. The MAI, PEG, PEG-MAI samples were prepared by dissolving MAI (0.03 
mM), PEG (0.02 mM), and MAI (0.02 mM) + PEG (0.02 mM), in PhCl-d5 (500 l) and 
DMF-d7 (30 l) solution, respectively. 
IS.  
The impedance spectrum and cyclic voltammograms were measured using a 
potentiostat/galvanostat (SP-150, Bio-Logic, France). The frequency can be tuned from 0.1 
Hz to 1 MHz. And the voltage tuned from 0 V to 1.0 V.
