More-\nover, the organic spacers also suppresses ion migration in the\nRPP materials, which signiﬁcantly enhances the thermal and\nphoto stabilities compared to 3D OIHP materials.[10,20–22] Despite\nthe superior environmental stabilities of RPP materials, the RPP-\nbased PSCs still exhibit inferior photovoltaic (PV) performance\ncompared to 3D OIHP-based PSCs.[23] The bulky organic spacers\nof the RPP materials provide strong quantum and dielectric con-\nﬁnement eﬀects, which induces a large exciton binding energy of\nthe RPP materials and causes exciton-exciton annihilation.[24–29]\nIn addition, the RPP materials exhibit in-plane crystal growth,\nand the bulky insulating organic spacer hinders vertical charge\ntransport between the inorganic perovskite sheets.[30–32] There-\nfore, for high PV performance of the RPP-based PSCs, eﬃcient\nvertical charge transport with minimal recombination in the RPP\nmaterials is important.[33]\nPerpendicular crystallographic orientations of RPP materials\nenabling eﬃcient vertical charge transport has been achieved\nwith several strategies, such as additive engineering, hot-solution\ncasting, and post-vacuum processing.[19,34–38] However, pre-\ndominantly solution-based processes inevitably cause structural\nand/or ionic defects during formation of OIHP layers, which in-\nclude 2D and 3D OIHP materials.[39–42] In particular, numerous\ndefect sites exist on the top surfaces of the OIHP layers because\nvolatile species such as small organic cations or halide anions\nexhibit easy migration and escape, hindering interlayer charge\ntransport between the photoactive OIHP layers and the charge–\ntransport layer (CTL).[43–45] Hence, passivation of the top surfaces\nof OIHPs is crucial for achieving high-performance OIHP-based\nPSCs. For ideal top surface engineering, the passivation materi-\nals should 1) not have an adverse eﬀect on the OIHPs; 2) passivate\nboth anion and cation defects; and/or 3) enhance charge carrier\nextraction to the CTLs while minimizing recombination in OIHP\nmaterials.\nIn this study, we demonstrated highly eﬃcient and stable\nRPP-based PSCs by using n-tert-butyl-𝛼-phenylnitrone (PBN) to\npassivate the top surfaces of RPP layers. The PBN passivation\nmolecule leads to a vertical orientation of the RPP crystals and si-\nmultaneously passivates both types of ionic defects, which lead\nto eﬃcient vertical charge transport with suppressed recombi-\nnation in RPP materials. As a result, the optimized PBN-treated\nRPP PSCs exhibited a high PCE of 20.05% (17.53% for the con-\ntrol device) with a high short–circuit current density (JSC) of\n20.71 mA cm−2. More importantly, the PBN passivation material\nstrongly suppressed ion migration in methylammonium (MA)-\nbased RPP materials, and the optimized PSCs showed excel-\nlent operating stability for over 1000 h, maintaining ≈88% of\nthe initial PCE in a nitrogen atmosphere and under continuous\nAM1.5G irradiation (without encapsulation and a UV ﬁlter).\n2. Results and Discussion\nQuasi-2D RPP materials with a stoichiometry of <n> = 5\n(PEA)2MA4Pb5I16 were used in this work, as shown in Fig-\nure 1a. There are two types of charged defects: cation defects\n(halide vacancies, cation interstitials, or uncoordinated Pb atoms)\nand anion defects (cation vacancies, Pb vacancies, or halide\ninterstitials).[46] These ionic defects are the predominant causes\nof charge carrier trapping and recombination loss, leading to\nlower PV performance in PSCs.[47–49] To passivate these defects,\nwe selected nitrone-compound PBN as a top surface passivation\nmaterial. PBN has three diﬀerent kinds of functional groups,\nas shown in Figure 1b: the zwitterionic nitrone (N+–O−) group\ncan passivate both types of charged defect sites via electrostatic\ninteractions (Figure S1, Supporting Information); the tert-butyl\n(–C(CH3)3) group has hydrogen bonding sites that interact with\nthe RPP materials and suppress ion migration; and the aromatic\nring acts as a Lewis base to form acid–base adducts with speciﬁc\nLewis acid-type defects in the RPP materials.[50–52] Therefore, the\nPBN passivation molecule is expected to passivate numerous de-\nfects in the RPP materials eﬀectively.\nTo investigate the interaction between PBN and RPP, we\nconducted Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) analyses of PBN,\npristine RPP, and PBN-treated RPP, as shown in Figure 1c.\nThe stretching vibration modes related to the N–O bonds and\n–C(CH3)3 bonds in PBN appeared at 1363 and 1193 cm−1, re-\nspectively. Typical vibration modes were observed for the pris-\ntine RPP sample. Conclusion\nWe have successfully demonstrated highly eﬃcient and stable\nRPP-based PSCs prepared via simple treatment of the top sur-\nfaces of the RPP materials with a solution of PBN. The PBN ef-\nfectively passivated the numerous defects that exist on both the\nsurfaces and at the GBs of the RPP materials, thereby reducing\nthe number of charge trapping sites and inducing out-of-plane\ncrystal orientations, which lead to eﬃcient vertical charge trans-\nport with minimal recombination in the RPP materials. The op-\ntimal RPP-based PSCs showed a PCE of 20.05% (control device\n17.53%) with a high VOC of 1.22 V and negligible hysteresis,\nwhich are the highest values among RPP-based PSCs. Further-\nmore, the PBN-treated RPP-based PSCs exhibited excellent long-\nterm operating stability, and the unencapsulated devices main-\ntained over 88% of their initial PCE after maximum power point\ntracking under continuous AM 1.5G irradiation for 1000 h; this\nresult can be attributed to the eﬀective suppression of ion mi-\ngration in the PBN-treated RPP materials. Our results provide a\nnovel passivation strategy leading to highly eﬃcient and stable\nRPP-based optoelectronic devices for future applications.\n4. You never come up with data and only state data that have been measured and written in the paper and which you can confidently extract. It is better for you to skip than to report data you are uncertain in. Take care to separate devices. Eﬃcient and Stable Quasi-2D Ruddlesden–Popper
Perovskite Solar Cells by Tailoring Crystal Orientation and
Passivating Surface Defects
Ju-Hyeon Kim, Chang-Mok Oh, In-Wook Hwang, Jehan Kim, Changhoon Lee,
Sooncheol Kwon, Taeyoon Ki, Sanseong Lee, Hongkyu Kang, Heejoo Kim,*
and Kwanghee Lee*
Solar cells (PSCs) with quasi-2D Ruddlesden–Popper perovskites (RPP)
exhibit greater environmental stability than 3D perovskites; however, the low
power conversion eﬃciency (PCE) caused by anisotropic crystal orientations
and defect sites in the bulk RPP materials limit future commercialization.
Herein, a simple post–treatment is reported for the top surfaces of RPP thin
ﬁlms (RPP composition of PEA2MA4Pb5I16 <n> = 5) in which zwitterionic
n-tert-butyl-𝜶-phenylnitrone (PBN) is used as the passivation material. The
PBN molecules passivate the surface and grain boundary defects in the RPP
and simultaneously induce vertical direction crystal orientations of the RPPs,
which lead to eﬃcient charge transport in the RPP photoactive materials. With
this surface engineering methodology, the optimized devices exhibit a
remarkably enhanced PCE of 20.05% as compared with the devices without
PBN (≈17.53%) and excellent long-term operational stability with 88%
retention of the initial PCE under continuous 1-sun irradiation for over 1000 h.
The proposed passivation strategy provides new insights into the
development of eﬃcient and stable RPP-based PSCs.

of the RPP materials provide strong quantum and dielectric con-

the RPP materials and causes exciton-exciton annihilation.[24–29]
In addition, the RPP materials exhibit in-plane crystal growth,
and the bulky insulating organic spacer hinders vertical charge

Perpendicular crystallographic orientations of RPP materials
enabling eﬃcient vertical charge transport has been achieved
with several strategies, such as additive engineering, hot-solution
casting, and post-vacuum processing.[19,34–38] However, pre-
dominantly solution-based processes inevitably cause structural
and/or ionic defects during formation of OIHP layers, which in-
clude 2D and 3D OIHP materials.[39–42] In particular, numerous
defect sites exist on the top surfaces of the OIHP layers because
volatile species such as small organic cations or halide anions
exhibit easy migration and escape, hindering interlayer charge
transport between the photoactive OIHP layers and the charge–
transport layer (CTL).[43–45] Hence, passivation of the top surfaces
of OIHPs is crucial for achieving high-performance OIHP-based
PSCs. For ideal top surface engineering, the passivation materi-
als should 1) not have an adverse eﬀect on the OIHPs; 2) passivate
both anion and cation defects; and/or 3) enhance charge carrier
extraction to the CTLs while minimizing recombination in OIHP
materials.
In this study, we demonstrated highly eﬃcient and stable
RPP-based PSCs by using n-tert-butyl-𝛼-phenylnitrone (PBN) to
passivate the top surfaces of RPP layers. The PBN passivation
molecule leads to a vertical orientation of the RPP crystals and si-
multaneously passivates both types of ionic defects, which lead
to eﬃcient vertical charge transport with suppressed recombi-
nation in RPP materials. As a result, the optimized PBN-treated
RPP PSCs exhibited a high PCE of 20.05% (17.53% for the con-
trol device) with a high short–circuit current density (JSC) of
20.71 mA cm−2. More importantly, the PBN passivation material
strongly suppressed ion migration in methylammonium (MA)-
based RPP materials, and the optimized PSCs showed excel-
lent operating stability for over 1000 h, maintaining ≈88% of
the initial PCE in a nitrogen atmosphere and under continuous
AM1.5G irradiation (without encapsulation and a UV ﬁlter).
2. Results and Discussion
Quasi-2D RPP materials with a stoichiometry of <n> = 5
(PEA)2MA4Pb5I16 were used in this work, as shown in Fig-
ure 1a. There are two types of charged defects: cation defects
(halide vacancies, cation interstitials, or uncoordinated Pb atoms)
and anion defects (cation vacancies, Pb vacancies, or halide
interstitials).[46] These ionic defects are the predominant causes
of charge carrier trapping and recombination loss, leading to
lower PV performance in PSCs.[47–49] To passivate these defects,
we selected nitrone-compound PBN as a top surface passivation
material. PBN has three diﬀerent kinds of functional groups,
as shown in Figure 1b: the zwitterionic nitrone (N+–O−) group
can passivate both types of charged defect sites via electrostatic
interactions (Figure S1, Supporting Information); the tert-butyl
(–C(CH3)3) group has hydrogen bonding sites that interact with
the RPP materials and suppress ion migration; and the aromatic
ring acts as a Lewis base to form acid–base adducts with speciﬁc
Lewis acid-type defects in the RPP materials.[50–52] Therefore, the
PBN passivation molecule is expected to passivate numerous de-
fects in the RPP materials eﬀectively.
To investigate the interaction between PBN and RPP, we
conducted Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) analyses of PBN,
pristine RPP, and PBN-treated RPP, as shown in Figure 1c.
The stretching vibration modes related to the N–O bonds and
–C(CH3)3 bonds in PBN appeared at 1363 and 1193 cm−1, re-
spectively. Typical vibration modes were observed for the pris-
tine RPP sample. After PBN-treatment of the top surface of the
RPP sample, superposition of the FTIR spectra of the PBN and
RPP samples was observed. However, the peaks for the N–O and
–C(CH3)3 vibration modes shifted to lower frequencies, 1361 and
1191 cm−1, respectively. In addition, a broader C─N band for
PBN was present in the spectrum of the PBN-treated RPP, which
implied an interaction between PBN and RPP. To obtain more
detailed information on the eﬀects of PBN on the RPP materi-
als, we performed Raman spectroscopic measurements on the
pristine RPP and the PBN-treated RPP thin ﬁlms and utilized
a 785 nm excitation wavelength to minimize sample degrada-
tion. As shown in Figure 1d, the 𝜋–𝜋vibration mode of the PEA
cation (132.4 cm−1) and the libration/translation mode of the
MA cation (152.4 and 157.8 cm−1) were observed for the control
RPP ﬁlm.[53–55] The PBN-treated RPP ﬁlm showed blueshifted
peaks (133.7, 153.7, and 164.3 cm−1). In particular, the libra-
tion/translation peak of the MA cation peak at 164.3 cm−1 was
prominent, suggesting more clearly deﬁned vibrational states in
the RPP plate and enhanced crystallinity, which was also con-
ﬁrmed by the X-ray diﬀraction (XRD) analysis shown in Figure
S2 (Supporting Information).
In an eﬀort to investigate the distribution of the PBN
molecules inside the RPP materials, we conducted time-of-ﬂight
secondary–ion mass spectrometry (TOF-SIMS) depth proﬁles of
the PBN-treated RPP samples, as shown in Figure 1e. The results
indicate that the MA+ and PEA+ ions show homogeneous distri-
butions in the RPP ﬁlms. However, the intensity of the peak for
the tert-butyl cation (t-butyl+), which corresponds to the fragment
from the PBN molecule, gradually decreases toward the inside of
the RPP materials. This indicates that PBN locates mainly on the
top surfaces of the RPP materials with the formation of gradient
interfaces[56] and passivates the defects present on the RPP top
surface and at the grain boundaries (GBs) of the RPP materials.
To collect additional crystallographic information from the
RPP ﬁlms, we performed grazing–incidence wide-angle X-ray
scattering (GIWAXS) measurements of the control RPP ﬁlm
(Figure 2a) and the PBN-treated RPP ﬁlm (Figure 2b). Both
ﬁlms show discrete Bragg spots at qx,y = 1.0 and 2.0 Å−1, which
correspond to the (111) and (202) planes of the 3D OIHP,

mized RPP-based PSCs without or with PBN treatment are pre-

based PSC showed a PCE of 17.53% with an open-circuit volt-

photon-to-current eﬃciency (IPCE) spectra and corresponding

(Figure 3c and Table 1). The PBN-treated RPP-based PSCs exhibit
higher IPCE values than the control RPP-based PSCs over the
whole wavelength region, which attribute to enhanced absorp-
tion by the RPP ﬁlms (Figure S9a, Supporting Information) and
charge extraction via band bending inside the RPP ﬁlms (Figure
S10b, Supporting Information).[64]
To investigate the enhanced PV performance of the RPP-based
PSCs, we studied the recombination mechanism of the PSCs
with a light intensity (Plight)-dependent PV parameter analysis. As
Figure 3e shows, the PBN-treated devices exhibit lower calculated
slopes for the plots (control device: 1.96 kT/q and PBN-treated de-
vices: 1.58 kT/q, wherein k, T, and q are the Boltzmann constant,
Kelvin temperature, and charge constant, respectively), which in-
dicates suppression of trap-assisted recombination in the RPP-
based PV devices.[65,66] In addition, to quantify the trap densities
in the bulk RPP ﬁlms, we also conducted space-charge limiting
current (SCLC) measurements with each major charge carrier-
only RPP-based devices, as shown in Figure S15 (Supporting In-
formation). The calculated trap densities for the control device
are ≈12.418 × 1015 cm−2 (hole-only device) and 8.511 × 1015 cm−2
(electron-only device), while the PBN-treated device shows re-
duced trap densities of 3.938 × 1015 and 4.077 × 1015 cm−2 for
hole- and electron-only devices, respectively; it also shows higher
charge carrier mobility than the control device (the details are
summarized in the Supporting Information). These results in-
dicate eﬀective defect passivation in the RPP materials by PBN.
Moreover, we also evaluated the Plight dependence of JSC to elu-
cidate the recombination process, as shown in Figure S16 (Sup-
porting Information). The values of the exponential factor (𝛼),
which was derived from the equation: JSC ∝Plight
𝛼, were deter-
mined to be 0.940 (control device) and 0.971 (PBN-treated de-
vice). This indicates that more bimolecular recombination pro-

out transient photocurrent measurements of the PSC, as shown
in Figure 3f. The average decay time (𝜏avg) of the PBN-treated
device (0.48 μs) was much shorter than that of the control device
(0.74 μs), indicating the enhancement of charge carrier extraction
in the PSCs.

We also examined the operating stabilities of nonencapsulated
RPP-based PSCs under continuous AM1.5G irradiation without
a UV ﬁlter (maximum power point tracking and nitrogen atmo-
sphere conditions) in a nitrogen atmosphere to assess the eﬀect
of PBN passivation on the long-term stability of PSCs. As shown
in Figure 5a, the PBN-treated RPP-based PSCs retain ≈88% of
their initial PCE (T88) after 1,000 h, whereas the control device
shows a relatively lower photostability of approximately T80 af-
ter 340 h. In addition, we further checked thermal (temperature
of 85 °C) and humidity (humidity of 65%) stabilities, as shown
in Figure S22 (Supporting Information). The PBN-treated RPP-
based PSCs also exhibit higher thermal and humidity stabilities,
maintaining their initial PCE of 91% and 80%, respectively, af-
ter 400 h. Since migration of iodide ions (I−) or iodine (I2) de-
rived from either the interstitial iodide sites or degradation of the
OIHP material is one of the predominant factors decreasing the
long-term stabilities of PSCs,[71–73] we conducted a UV‒vis ab-
sorption analysis with each solution sample, to investigate iodide
passivation by PBN. As shown in Figure 5b,c, when PBN was
added to an I2 solution, the color of the solution changed from
purple to red, indicating eﬀective passivation of iodide by PBN.
The electrostatic potential (ESP) simulation for interactions be-
tween PBN and I2 (see Figure 5d; Figure S23, Supporting In-
formation) indicated that this passivation can be attributed to
the interaction between all three functional groups (nitrone, t-
butyl, and benzene) in PBN and I2 due to their electron-donating
properties.[46,74]
We also obtained TOF-SIMS depth proﬁles with the control
RPP-based PSCs (Figure 5e) and PBN-treated RPP-based PSCs
(Figure 5f) to gain deeper insight into photoinduced degradation
of the PSCs. The ion distribution, which consisted of RPP compo-
nents (MA+, CsPb+, and CsI+), for the control RPP-based PSCs
is broad, especially near the top (reddish region in Figure 5e)
and bottom (purple region in Figure 5e) surfaces of the RPP lay-
ers after photoaging with 1-sun illumination for 500 h. In con-
trast, the PBN-treated RPP-based PSCs showed negligible diﬀer-
ences in the ion distributions for fresh (upper) and aged sam-
ples (lower). This suggests that the PBN passivation molecule
eﬀectively suppresses ion migration and inhibits photodegra-
dation of the RPP materials, leading to enhanced operating
stability.

3. Conclusion
We have successfully demonstrated highly eﬃcient and stable
RPP-based PSCs prepared via simple treatment of the top sur-
faces of the RPP materials with a solution of PBN. The PBN ef-
fectively passivated the numerous defects that exist on both the
surfaces and at the GBs of the RPP materials, thereby reducing
the number of charge trapping sites and inducing out-of-plane
crystal orientations, which lead to eﬃcient vertical charge trans-
port with minimal recombination in the RPP materials. The op-
timal RPP-based PSCs showed a PCE of 20.05% (control device
17.53%) with a high VOC of 1.22 V and negligible hysteresis,
which are the highest values among RPP-based PSCs. Further-
more, the PBN-treated RPP-based PSCs exhibited excellent long-
term operating stability, and the unencapsulated devices main-
tained over 88% of their initial PCE after maximum power point
tracking under continuous AM 1.5G irradiation for 1000 h; this
result can be attributed to the eﬀective suppression of ion mi-
gration in the PBN-treated RPP materials. Our results provide a
novel passivation strategy leading to highly eﬃcient and stable
RPP-based optoelectronic devices for future applications.
4. Experimental Section
Materials:
[2-(9H-Carbazol-9-yl)ethyl]phosphonic acid (2PACz) was
obtained from Tokyo Chemical Industry (TCI) and diluted with ethanol
(Sigma‒Aldrich) (1 mg mL−1) to prepare the hole–transport layer (HTL)
solution. Lead(II) iodide (PbI2) and lead(II) chloride (PbCl2) were pur-
chased from TCI, and phenethylammonium iodide (PEAI, C8H12IN)
and methylammonium iodide (MAI, CH6IN) were purchased from
Great Cell Solar. A solution of the <n = 5> Ruddlesden–Popper per-
ovskite (RPP) precursor, (PEA)2(MA)4Pb5I16, was obtained by adding
PEAI:MAI:PbI2:PbCl2 at a molar ratio of 0.4:0.9:0.95:0.05 to an anhy-
drous N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF, Sigma‒Aldrich)/dimethyl sulfoxide
(DMSO, Sigma‒Aldrich) mixed solution (9:1 volume ratio).[35] Phenyl-
C61-butyric acid methyl ester (PC60BM, Nanoholdings) and polyethylen-
imine (PEI, Sigma‒Aldrich) were diluted to 20 mg mL−1 (chlorobenzene)

Device Fabrication:
The p–i–n planar structured PSCs were fabri-
cated with the conﬁguration ITO/2PACz/RPP/with or without passiva-
tion/PCBM/PEI/Ag. The 2PACz HTL was deposited on the UV–ozone-
treated ITO substrates by spin-coating at 3000 rpm for 30 s with annealing
at 60 °C for 3 min. Then, the substrates were transferred into a N2-ﬁlled
glove box. The RPP layers were fabricated by spin-casting at 5000 rpm
for 20 s on the preheated substrates (100 °C over 15 min), and then the
ﬁlms were transferred into a low vacuum chamber (−1 bar) for suppressed
nucleation for at least 8 min.[34] After low–vacuum processing, the RPP
ﬁlms were thermally annealed at 100 °C for 10 min. The PBN passivation
solution (various molar ratios in IPA) was spin-cast on the RPP ﬁlm at
5000 rpm for 20 s for top surface passivation without thermal annealing.
Afterward, for fabrication of the electron–transport layer, the PC60BM so-
lution was spin-coated at 2000 rpm for 30 s with a 0.45 μm PTFE ﬁlter, and
then the PEI solution was drop-cast on top of PC60BM ﬁlms at 5000 rpm
for 20 s with annealing at 100 °C for 5 min. Finally, 100 nm–thick silver
electrodes were deposited using the thermal evaporation process under
high-vacuum conditions (1 × 10−6 Torr).
Thin-Film
Characterization:
The
steady-state
photoluminescence
spectra of perovskites in the control and after treatment were measured
with a multichannel spectrophotometer (QEPro, Ocean Insight). In the
PL measurements, ﬁlms of the perovskite control or treated samples were
excited from the active layer side with a 375 nm laser source (PicoQuant
GmbH). The time-resolved ﬂuorescence decays of the control and treated
perovskites were obtained with a time-correlated single photon counting
(TCSPC) system containing a dual grating imaging spectrometer (Acton
SpectraPro SP-2150, Princeton Instrument) with a photomultiplier tube
(Hamamatsu) and a 375 nm laser source (PicoQuant GmbH). The
decay time constants for the ﬁlms were acquired by ﬁtting them to
a sum of multiexponential terms with instrument response function
(IRF) proﬁles, which indicated ≈100 ps for the full peak width at half
maximum. Femtosecond transient absorption (TA) spectra were recorded
using a homemade TA measurement system comprising a femtosecond
Ti:sapphire regenerative ampliﬁer system (Hurricane, Spectra Physics)
with a 1 kHz repetition rate, an optical parametric ampliﬁer (OPA-800CF,
Spectra Physics), and spectrometers (QEPro and NIRQUEST, Ocean
Insight). The pump pulse wavelength was 400 nm, and the power density
was 10 μJ cm−2. Grazing-incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering (GIWAXS)
measurements were performed at the PLS-II 3C SAXS beamline of the
Pohang Accelerator Laboratory in South Korea. For recorded the 2D
GIWAXS patterns, a monochromatic X-ray radiation source operated at
9.8 keV (𝜆= 1.2651 Å) and a 2D charge-coupled detector (CCD) (model
Rayonix 2D SX 165, Rayonix, Evanston, IL, USA) were used. Time-of-ﬂight
secondary–ion mass spectrometry (TOF-SIMS) experiments were con-
ducted with an M6 system (ION-TOF GmbH, Münster, Germany) at the
KBSI Busan Center using a pulsed 30 keV Bi3 primary beam with a current
of 0.34 pA. The analyzed area used in this work was a square measuring
300 μm × 300 μm. Positive ion spectra were internally calibrated with
H+, C+, CH3+, and C2H5+ peaks and normalized to give the respective
secondary total ion yields. The chemical images of the analyzed areas
were recorded with 128 × 128 pixel resolution during data acquisition.
The sputtered area was a square measuring 500 μm × 500 μm and a
Cesium beam (1 keV) and an Ar cluster beam (5 keV) were used for the
depth proﬁle.
UV–vis–NIR absorption spectra were obtained with a UV–vis–NIR spec-
trophotometer (Cary 5000 UV–vis–NIR, Agilent Technologies, Inc.), and IR
transmittance spectra were collected with an FT-IR spectrometer (VERTEX
70, Bruker Co., Ltd.) using potassium bromide (KBr) disks under N2. The
Raman spectra were measured with an inVia Raman microscope (Ren-
ishaw) with a 785 nm diode laser.
High-resolution X-ray diﬀraction patterns were collected with a Smart-
Lab diﬀractometer (Rigaku). SEM images were captured with a Verios 5
UC system (Thermo Fisher Scientiﬁc) under high vacuum conditions. An
FV3000RS (Olympus) confocal laser scanning microscope was used with
an excitation wavelength of 405 nm. Photoelectron spectroscopy was con-
ducted with a NEXSA system (Thermo Fisher Scientiﬁc) with He (I) ra-
diation (21.22 eV) and Al K𝛼radiation for UPS and XPS measurements,
respectively.
Theoretical Calculation:
The molecular geometry and ESP analyses of
the PBN molecule were optimized by ADF with the B3LYP-D functional
and the TZP basis set.[75–78] Since there was no report for crystal struc-
ture of [(PEA)2(MA)4Pb5I16], hypothetical [(PEA)2(MA)4Pb5I16] was con-
structed by replacing the MA molecule of [(BA)2(MA)4Pb5I16] with PEA
molecule. The surface structure of [(PEA)2(MA)4Pb5I16] ≈25 Å vacuum
was also constructed to investigate the PBN passivation and I/Pb atom
vacancy eﬀects. The hypothetical [(PEA)2(MA)4Pb5I16] and surface struc-
ture of [(PEA)2(MA)4Pb5I16] were fully optimized on the basis of GGA cal-
culations. In these DFT calculations, the frozen-core projector augmented
wave method[79,80] encoded in the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package
(VASP)[81] and the generalized-gradient approximation of Perdew, Burke,
and Ernzerhof[82] for the exchange-correlation functional with the plane-
wave-cut-oﬀenergy of 700 eV, the force of 10−2 eV Å−1, and a set of 30
k-point for the irreducible Brillouin zone were employed.
Device Characterization:
The current density–voltages (J–V) of the PV
devices were measured with a solar simulator (Sol 3A, Newport Corp)
and a Keithley 2420 source/meter unit providing AM 1.5G irradiation
with an intensity of 100 mW cm−2. The solar simulator was calibrated
with a certiﬁed reference standard Si photodiode (Newport Corp.). The
incident photon-to-electron conversion eﬃciency (IPCE) measurements
were conducted with a quantum eﬃciency (QE) measurement system
(Quant X-300, Newport Corp.). Calibration was performed with a 603621
calibrated reference detector (Newport Corp.). Transient photocurrents
(TPC) were obtained with an oscilloscope (Waverunner 625Zi, Teledyne
LECROY) coupled with a 470 nm picosecond laser (P-C-470, PicoQuant
GmbH), which acted as the excitation source. For TPC measurements,
the input impedance of the oscilloscope was set to 50 Ω, and then the
sample was exposed to an excitation pulse laser with a repetition rate
of 100 kHz. The TPC decays were recorded by averaging over 20 000
measurements for each sample. Impedance spectra were measured with
a PGSTAT30 system (Metrohm Autolab B.V., Netherlands) over the fre-
quency range 0.01–1 MHz. The density of the trap states was derived from
the angular frequency-dependent capacitance with the following equation:
Nt(Ea) = −(Vbi −Vapp)/qWKT*(dC/df)*f, where Vbi, Vapp, and W are the
built-in potential, applied voltage, and width of the space charge region,
respectively.[61] For the calculation of the energy levels of traps (Ea) via
thermal admittance spectroscopy, the equation Ea = 0.45 −0.025ln(2𝜋f)
was used to give the result in eV at 300 K.

Eﬃcient and Stable Quasi-2D Ruddlesden–Popper
Perovskite Solar Cells by Tailoring Crystal Orientation and
Passivating Surface Defects
Ju-Hyeon Kim, Chang-Mok Oh, In-Wook Hwang, Jehan Kim, Changhoon Lee,
Sooncheol Kwon, Taeyoon Ki, Sanseong Lee, Hongkyu Kang, Heejoo Kim,*
and Kwanghee Lee*
Solar cells (PSCs) with quasi-2D Ruddlesden–Popper perovskites (RPP)
exhibit greater environmental stability than 3D perovskites; however, the low
power conversion eﬃciency (PCE) caused by anisotropic crystal orientations
and defect sites in the bulk RPP materials limit future commercialization.
Herein, a simple post–treatment is reported for the top surfaces of RPP thin
ﬁlms (RPP composition of PEA2MA4Pb5I16 <n> = 5) in which zwitterionic
n-tert-butyl-𝜶-phenylnitrone (PBN) is used as the passivation material. The
PBN molecules passivate the surface and grain boundary defects in the RPP
and simultaneously induce vertical direction crystal orientations of the RPPs,
which lead to eﬃcient charge transport in the RPP photoactive materials. With
this surface engineering methodology, the optimized devices exhibit a
remarkably enhanced PCE of 20.05% as compared with the devices without
PBN (≈17.53%) and excellent long-term operational stability with 88%
retention of the initial PCE under continuous 1-sun irradiation for over 1000 h.
The proposed passivation strategy provides new insights into the
development of eﬃcient and stable RPP-based PSCs.

and form quantum wells.[16–19] This protects the inorganic per-
ovskite from corrosion by external contaminants (e.g., oxygen,
moisture) and ensures long-term environmental stability. More-
over, the organic spacers also suppresses ion migration in the
RPP materials, which signiﬁcantly enhances the thermal and
photo stabilities compared to 3D OIHP materials.[10,20–22] Despite
the superior environmental stabilities of RPP materials, the RPP-
based PSCs still exhibit inferior photovoltaic (PV) performance
compared to 3D OIHP-based PSCs.[23] The bulky organic spacers
of the RPP materials provide strong quantum and dielectric con-
ﬁnement eﬀects, which induces a large exciton binding energy of
the RPP materials and causes exciton-exciton annihilation.[24–29]
In addition, the RPP materials exhibit in-plane crystal growth,
and the bulky insulating organic spacer hinders vertical charge
transport between the inorganic perovskite sheets.[30–32] There-
fore, for high PV performance of the RPP-based PSCs, eﬃcient
vertical charge transport with minimal recombination in the RPP
materials is important.[33]
Perpendicular crystallographic orientations of RPP materials
enabling eﬃcient vertical charge transport has been achieved
with several strategies, such as additive engineering, hot-solution
casting, and post-vacuum processing.[19,34–38] However, pre-
dominantly solution-based processes inevitably cause structural
and/or ionic defects during formation of OIHP layers, which in-
clude 2D and 3D OIHP materials.[39–42] In particular, numerous
defect sites exist on the top surfaces of the OIHP layers because
volatile species such as small organic cations or halide anions
exhibit easy migration and escape, hindering interlayer charge
transport between the photoactive OIHP layers and the charge–
transport layer (CTL).[43–45] Hence, passivation of the top surfaces
of OIHPs is crucial for achieving high-performance OIHP-based
PSCs. For ideal top surface engineering, the passivation materi-
als should 1) not have an adverse eﬀect on the OIHPs; 2) passivate
both anion and cation defects; and/or 3) enhance charge carrier
extraction to the CTLs while minimizing recombination in OIHP
materials.
In this study, we demonstrated highly eﬃcient and stable
RPP-based PSCs by using n-tert-butyl-𝛼-phenylnitrone (PBN) to
passivate the top surfaces of RPP layers. The PBN passivation
molecule leads to a vertical orientation of the RPP crystals and si-
multaneously passivates both types of ionic defects, which lead
to eﬃcient vertical charge transport with suppressed recombi-
nation in RPP materials. As a result, the optimized PBN-treated
RPP PSCs exhibited a high PCE of 20.05% (17.53% for the con-
trol device) with a high short–circuit current density (JSC) of
20.71 mA cm−2. More importantly, the PBN passivation material
strongly suppressed ion migration in methylammonium (MA)-
based RPP materials, and the optimized PSCs showed excel-
lent operating stability for over 1000 h, maintaining ≈88% of
the initial PCE in a nitrogen atmosphere and under continuous
AM1.5G irradiation (without encapsulation and a UV ﬁlter).
2. Results and Discussion
Quasi-2D RPP materials with a stoichiometry of <n> = 5
(PEA)2MA4Pb5I16 were used in this work, as shown in Fig-
ure 1a. There are two types of charged defects: cation defects
(halide vacancies, cation interstitials, or uncoordinated Pb atoms)
and anion defects (cation vacancies, Pb vacancies, or halide
interstitials).[46] These ionic defects are the predominant causes
of charge carrier trapping and recombination loss, leading to
lower PV performance in PSCs.[47–49] To passivate these defects,
we selected nitrone-compound PBN as a top surface passivation
material. PBN has three diﬀerent kinds of functional groups,
as shown in Figure 1b: the zwitterionic nitrone (N+–O−) group
can passivate both types of charged defect sites via electrostatic
interactions (Figure S1, Supporting Information); the tert-butyl
(–C(CH3)3) group has hydrogen bonding sites that interact with
the RPP materials and suppress ion migration; and the aromatic
ring acts as a Lewis base to form acid–base adducts with speciﬁc
Lewis acid-type defects in the RPP materials.[50–52] Therefore, the
PBN passivation molecule is expected to passivate numerous de-
fects in the RPP materials eﬀectively.
To investigate the interaction between PBN and RPP, we
conducted Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) analyses of PBN,
pristine RPP, and PBN-treated RPP, as shown in Figure 1c.
The stretching vibration modes related to the N–O bonds and
–C(CH3)3 bonds in PBN appeared at 1363 and 1193 cm−1, re-
spectively. Typical vibration modes were observed for the pris-
tine RPP sample. After PBN-treatment of the top surface of the
RPP sample, superposition of the FTIR spectra of the PBN and
RPP samples was observed. However, the peaks for the N–O and
–C(CH3)3 vibration modes shifted to lower frequencies, 1361 and
1191 cm−1, respectively. In addition, a broader C─N band for
PBN was present in the spectrum of the PBN-treated RPP, which
implied an interaction between PBN and RPP. To obtain more
detailed information on the eﬀects of PBN on the RPP materi-
als, we performed Raman spectroscopic measurements on the
pristine RPP and the PBN-treated RPP thin ﬁlms and utilized
a 785 nm excitation wavelength to minimize sample degrada-
tion. As shown in Figure 1d, the 𝜋–𝜋vibration mode of the PEA
cation (132.4 cm−1) and the libration/translation mode of the
MA cation (152.4 and 157.8 cm−1) were observed for the control
RPP ﬁlm.[53–55] The PBN-treated RPP ﬁlm showed blueshifted
peaks (133.7, 153.7, and 164.3 cm−1). In particular, the libra-
tion/translation peak of the MA cation peak at 164.3 cm−1 was
prominent, suggesting more clearly deﬁned vibrational states in
the RPP plate and enhanced crystallinity, which was also con-
ﬁrmed by the X-ray diﬀraction (XRD) analysis shown in Figure
S2 (Supporting Information).
In an eﬀort to investigate the distribution of the PBN
molecules inside the RPP materials, we conducted time-of-ﬂight
secondary–ion mass spectrometry (TOF-SIMS) depth proﬁles of
the PBN-treated RPP samples, as shown in Figure 1e. The results
indicate that the MA+ and PEA+ ions show homogeneous distri-
butions in the RPP ﬁlms. However, the intensity of the peak for
the tert-butyl cation (t-butyl+), which corresponds to the fragment
from the PBN molecule, gradually decreases toward the inside of
the RPP materials. This indicates that PBN locates mainly on the
top surfaces of the RPP materials with the formation of gradient
interfaces[56] and passivates the defects present on the RPP top
surface and at the grain boundaries (GBs) of the RPP materials.
To collect additional crystallographic information from the
RPP ﬁlms, we performed grazing–incidence wide-angle X-ray
scattering (GIWAXS) measurements of the control RPP ﬁlm
(Figure 2a) and the PBN-treated RPP ﬁlm (Figure 2b). Both
ﬁlms show discrete Bragg spots at qx,y = 1.0 and 2.0 Å−1, which
correspond to the (111) and (202) planes of the 3D OIHP,

This implies that the PBN passivation method induced more or-
dered vertical orientations of 3D OIHP in RPP materials, which
was also conﬁrmed by an azimuthal angle analysis of the 3D
OIHP (111) plane (Figure S3c, Supporting Information).[59] To
conﬁrm the vertical orientations of the RPP materials, we con-
ducted cross-sectional scanning electron microscopy (SEM) mea-
surements of the RPP thin ﬁlms. As shown in Figure 2c, grain
growth in the vertical direction was more oriented in the PBN-
treated RPP samples (lower image) than in the control RPP sam-
ples (upper image), which agrees well with the GIWAXS analysis.
To investigate the eﬀect of the PBN post-treatment on the
orientation change in the RPP materials, we ﬁrst examined
the impact of PBN concentration on the RPP materials (Fig-
ure S4a, Supporting Information). The isopropyl alcohol (IPA)
solvent did not aﬀect the absorption of the RPP ﬁlms, and the
low-concentration (5.0 mm, optimized condition in this work)
of the PBN-treated RPP sample exhibited enhanced absorption
throughout the visible range, as shown in Figure S4b (Support-
ing Information). However, as the PBN concentration increased
from 0.05 to 1.0 m, the overall absorption of the RPP ﬁlms de-
creased, and PbI2 absorptions remained at ≈390 nm (Figure S4c,
Supporting Information). These results indicate that the PBN
molecules can decompose and dissolve OIHP materials, and we
utilized a low concentration of PBN solution for a top surface
passivation. Furthermore, we conducted atomic force microscopy
(AFM) analysis for the RPP thin ﬁlm samples to observe changes
in the RPP surfaces. As shown in Figure S5 (Supporting Informa-
tion), the control RPP samples had relatively rough surface and
high root-mean-square (RMS) values as compared to the PBN-
treated samples. Additionally, after the PBN treatment, the sur-
face area of the RPP samples was decreased (summarized in
Table S1, Supporting Information). Therefore, a small amount
of PBN caused reconstruction on the RPP crystals, inducing a
change in the RPP crystal orientations toward vertical direction,
as we conﬁrmed it by GIWAXS analysis in Figure 2a,b.
We also used X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) studies
of the control RPP and PBN-treated RPP thin ﬁlms to investi-
gate the defect passivation eﬀects of PBN. Figure 2d shows that
the two distinct peaks for the Pb 4f3/2 (142.8 eV) and Pb 4f5/2
(137.9 eV) binding energies of the control RPP ﬁlm were shifted
to 143.3 and 138.4 eV for the PBN-treated RPP ﬁlm, respectively.

The current density–voltage (J–V) characteristics of the opti-
mized RPP-based PSCs without or with PBN treatment are pre-
sented in Figure 3c. As summarized in Table 1, the control RPP-
based PSC showed a PCE of 17.53% with an open-circuit volt-
age (VOC) of 1.21 V, a JSC of 18.44 mA cm−2, and a ﬁll factor
(FF) of 78.52%. In contrast, a PCE of 20.05% (VOC: 1.22 V, JSC:
20.71 mA cm−2, FF: 79.36%) was determined for a PBN-treated
RPP-based PSC. The statistical analyses of the PV parameters are
described in Figure S12 (Supporting Information), and all PV
parameters were increased by the PBN treatment and showed
negligible hysteresis (Figure S13, Supporting Information). Note
that the PBN-treated RPP-based PSCs exhibits a relatively high
VOC value with over 20% PCE, which is compared with data from
previous reports in Figure S14 and Table S2 (Supporting Infor-
mation). In particular, the enhancement of JSC increases the PV
performance of the RPP-based PSCs. Figure 3d shows incident
photon-to-current eﬃciency (IPCE) spectra and corresponding
integrated JSC values of the PV devices, which are in good agree-
ment with the Jsc values obtained from the J–V measurement
(Figure 3c and Table 1). The PBN-treated RPP-based PSCs exhibit
higher IPCE values than the control RPP-based PSCs over the
whole wavelength region, which attribute to enhanced absorp-
tion by the RPP ﬁlms (Figure S9a, Supporting Information) and
charge extraction via band bending inside the RPP ﬁlms (Figure
S10b, Supporting Information).[64]
To investigate the enhanced PV performance of the RPP-based
PSCs, we studied the recombination mechanism of the PSCs
with a light intensity (Plight)-dependent PV parameter analysis. As
Figure 3e shows, the PBN-treated devices exhibit lower calculated
slopes for the plots (control device: 1.96 kT/q and PBN-treated de-
vices: 1.58 kT/q, wherein k, T, and q are the Boltzmann constant,
Kelvin temperature, and charge constant, respectively), which in-
dicates suppression of trap-assisted recombination in the RPP-
based PV devices.[65,66] In addition, to quantify the trap densities
in the bulk RPP ﬁlms, we also conducted space-charge limiting
current (SCLC) measurements with each major charge carrier-
only RPP-based devices, as shown in Figure S15 (Supporting In-
formation). The calculated trap densities for the control device
are ≈12.418 × 1015 cm−2 (hole-only device) and 8.511 × 1015 cm−2
(electron-only device), while the PBN-treated device shows re-
duced trap densities of 3.938 × 1015 and 4.077 × 1015 cm−2 for
hole- and electron-only devices, respectively; it also shows higher
charge carrier mobility than the control device (the details are
summarized in the Supporting Information). These results in-
dicate eﬀective defect passivation in the RPP materials by PBN.
Moreover, we also evaluated the Plight dependence of JSC to elu-
cidate the recombination process, as shown in Figure S16 (Sup-
porting Information). The values of the exponential factor (𝛼),
which was derived from the equation: JSC ∝Plight
𝛼, were deter-
mined to be 0.940 (control device) and 0.971 (PBN-treated de-
vice). This indicates that more bimolecular recombination pro-
cesses occur in the PBN-treated devices. In addition, we carried
out transient photocurrent measurements of the PSC, as shown
in Figure 3f. The average decay time (𝜏avg) of the PBN-treated
device (0.48 μs) was much shorter than that of the control device
(0.74 μs), indicating the enhancement of charge carrier extraction
in the PSCs.
To clearly elucidate the charge dynamics of the RPP materials,
we performed transient absorption (TA) analyses with the control
RPP neat ﬁlm and a PBN-treated RPP ﬁlm, as shown in Figure
S17 (Supporting Information). Figure 4a,b shows that photoin-
duced absorption (PIA) occurred in the short wavelength region
(500–600 nm), indicating a small n-phase for the RPP materi-
als, while a photobleaching (PB) signal was observed in the long
wavelength region (700–780 nm), which corresponded to RPP

We also examined the operating stabilities of nonencapsulated
RPP-based PSCs under continuous AM1.5G irradiation without

the interaction between all three functional groups (nitrone, t-

RPP-based PSCs (Figure 5e) and PBN-treated RPP-based PSCs

stability.

3. Conclusion
We have successfully demonstrated highly eﬃcient and stable
RPP-based PSCs prepared via simple treatment of the top sur-
faces of the RPP materials with a solution of PBN. The PBN ef-
fectively passivated the numerous defects that exist on both the
surfaces and at the GBs of the RPP materials, thereby reducing
the number of charge trapping sites and inducing out-of-plane
crystal orientations, which lead to eﬃcient vertical charge trans-
port with minimal recombination in the RPP materials. The op-
timal RPP-based PSCs showed a PCE of 20.05% (control device
17.53%) with a high VOC of 1.22 V and negligible hysteresis,
which are the highest values among RPP-based PSCs. Further-
more, the PBN-treated RPP-based PSCs exhibited excellent long-
term operating stability, and the unencapsulated devices main-
tained over 88% of their initial PCE after maximum power point
tracking under continuous AM 1.5G irradiation for 1000 h; this
result can be attributed to the eﬀective suppression of ion mi-
gration in the PBN-treated RPP materials. Our results provide a
novel passivation strategy leading to highly eﬃcient and stable
RPP-based optoelectronic devices for future applications.
4. Experimental Section
Materials:
[2-(9H-Carbazol-9-yl)ethyl]phosphonic acid (2PACz) was
obtained from Tokyo Chemical Industry (TCI) and diluted with ethanol
(Sigma‒Aldrich) (1 mg mL−1) to prepare the hole–transport layer (HTL)
solution. Lead(II) iodide (PbI2) and lead(II) chloride (PbCl2) were pur-
chased from TCI, and phenethylammonium iodide (PEAI, C8H12IN)
and methylammonium iodide (MAI, CH6IN) were purchased from
Great Cell Solar. A solution of the <n = 5> Ruddlesden–Popper per-
ovskite (RPP) precursor, (PEA)2(MA)4Pb5I16, was obtained by adding
PEAI:MAI:PbI2:PbCl2 at a molar ratio of 0.4:0.9:0.95:0.05 to an anhy-
drous N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF, Sigma‒Aldrich)/dimethyl sulfoxide
(DMSO, Sigma‒Aldrich) mixed solution (9:1 volume ratio).[35] Phenyl-
C61-butyric acid methyl ester (PC60BM, Nanoholdings) and polyethylen-
imine (PEI, Sigma‒Aldrich) were diluted to 20 mg mL−1 (chlorobenzene)

Device Fabrication:
The p–i–n planar structured PSCs were fabri-
cated with the conﬁguration ITO/2PACz/RPP/with or without passiva-
tion/PCBM/PEI/Ag. The 2PACz HTL was deposited on the UV–ozone-
treated ITO substrates by spin-coating at 3000 rpm for 30 s with annealing
at 60 °C for 3 min. Then, the substrates were transferred into a N2-ﬁlled
glove box. The RPP layers were fabricated by spin-casting at 5000 rpm
for 20 s on the preheated substrates (100 °C over 15 min), and then the
ﬁlms were transferred into a low vacuum chamber (−1 bar) for suppressed
nucleation for at least 8 min.[34] After low–vacuum processing, the RPP
ﬁlms were thermally annealed at 100 °C for 10 min. The PBN passivation
solution (various molar ratios in IPA) was spin-cast on the RPP ﬁlm at
5000 rpm for 20 s for top surface passivation without thermal annealing.
Afterward, for fabrication of the electron–transport layer, the PC60BM so-
lution was spin-coated at 2000 rpm for 30 s with a 0.45 μm PTFE ﬁlter, and
then the PEI solution was drop-cast on top of PC60BM ﬁlms at 5000 rpm
for 20 s with annealing at 100 °C for 5 min. Finally, 100 nm–thick silver
electrodes were deposited using the thermal evaporation process under
high-vacuum conditions (1 × 10−6 Torr).
Thin-Film
Characterization:
The
steady-state
photoluminescence
spectra of perovskites in the control and after treatment were measured
with a multichannel spectrophotometer (QEPro, Ocean Insight). In the
PL measurements, ﬁlms of the perovskite control or treated samples were
excited from the active layer side with a 375 nm laser source (PicoQuant
GmbH). The time-resolved ﬂuorescence decays of the control and treated
perovskites were obtained with a time-correlated single photon counting
(TCSPC) system containing a dual grating imaging spectrometer (Acton
SpectraPro SP-2150, Princeton Instrument) with a photomultiplier tube
(Hamamatsu) and a 375 nm laser source (PicoQuant GmbH). The
decay time constants for the ﬁlms were acquired by ﬁtting them to
a sum of multiexponential terms with instrument response function
(IRF) proﬁles, which indicated ≈100 ps for the full peak width at half
maximum. Femtosecond transient absorption (TA) spectra were recorded
using a homemade TA measurement system comprising a femtosecond
Ti:sapphire regenerative ampliﬁer system (Hurricane, Spectra Physics)
with a 1 kHz repetition rate, an optical parametric ampliﬁer (OPA-800CF,
Spectra Physics), and spectrometers (QEPro and NIRQUEST, Ocean
Insight). The pump pulse wavelength was 400 nm, and the power density
was 10 μJ cm−2. Grazing-incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering (GIWAXS)
measurements were performed at the PLS-II 3C SAXS beamline of the
Pohang Accelerator Laboratory in South Korea. For recorded the 2D
GIWAXS patterns, a monochromatic X-ray radiation source operated at
9.8 keV (𝜆= 1.2651 Å) and a 2D charge-coupled detector (CCD) (model
Rayonix 2D SX 165, Rayonix, Evanston, IL, USA) were used. Time-of-ﬂight
secondary–ion mass spectrometry (TOF-SIMS) experiments were con-
ducted with an M6 system (ION-TOF GmbH, Münster, Germany) at the
KBSI Busan Center using a pulsed 30 keV Bi3 primary beam with a current
of 0.34 pA. The analyzed area used in this work was a square measuring
300 μm × 300 μm. Positive ion spectra were internally calibrated with
H+, C+, CH3+, and C2H5+ peaks and normalized to give the respective
secondary total ion yields. The chemical images of the analyzed areas
were recorded with 128 × 128 pixel resolution during data acquisition.
The sputtered area was a square measuring 500 μm × 500 μm and a
Cesium beam (1 keV) and an Ar cluster beam (5 keV) were used for the
depth proﬁle.
UV–vis–NIR absorption spectra were obtained with a UV–vis–NIR spec-
trophotometer (Cary 5000 UV–vis–NIR, Agilent Technologies, Inc.), and IR
transmittance spectra were collected with an FT-IR spectrometer (VERTEX
70, Bruker Co., Ltd.) using potassium bromide (KBr) disks under N2. The
Raman spectra were measured with an inVia Raman microscope (Ren-
ishaw) with a 785 nm diode laser.
High-resolution X-ray diﬀraction patterns were collected with a Smart-
Lab diﬀractometer (Rigaku). SEM images were captured with a Verios 5
UC system (Thermo Fisher Scientiﬁc) under high vacuum conditions. An
FV3000RS (Olympus) confocal laser scanning microscope was used with
an excitation wavelength of 405 nm. Photoelectron spectroscopy was con-
ducted with a NEXSA system (Thermo Fisher Scientiﬁc) with He (I) ra-
diation (21.22 eV) and Al K𝛼radiation for UPS and XPS measurements,
respectively.
Theoretical Calculation:
The molecular geometry and ESP analyses of
the PBN molecule were optimized by ADF with the B3LYP-D functional
and the TZP basis set.[75–78] Since there was no report for crystal struc-
ture of [(PEA)2(MA)4Pb5I16], hypothetical [(PEA)2(MA)4Pb5I16] was con-
structed by replacing the MA molecule of [(BA)2(MA)4Pb5I16] with PEA
molecule. The surface structure of [(PEA)2(MA)4Pb5I16] ≈25 Å vacuum
was also constructed to investigate the PBN passivation and I/Pb atom
vacancy eﬀects. The hypothetical [(PEA)2(MA)4Pb5I16] and surface struc-
ture of [(PEA)2(MA)4Pb5I16] were fully optimized on the basis of GGA cal-
culations. In these DFT calculations, the frozen-core projector augmented
wave method[79,80] encoded in the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package
(VASP)[81] and the generalized-gradient approximation of Perdew, Burke,
and Ernzerhof[82] for the exchange-correlation functional with the plane-
wave-cut-oﬀenergy of 700 eV, the force of 10−2 eV Å−1, and a set of 30
k-point for the irreducible Brillouin zone were employed.
Device Characterization:
The current density–voltages (J–V) of the PV
devices were measured with a solar simulator (Sol 3A, Newport Corp)
and a Keithley 2420 source/meter unit providing AM 1.5G irradiation
with an intensity of 100 mW cm−2. The solar simulator was calibrated
with a certiﬁed reference standard Si photodiode (Newport Corp.). The
incident photon-to-electron conversion eﬃciency (IPCE) measurements
were conducted with a quantum eﬃciency (QE) measurement system
(Quant X-300, Newport Corp.). Calibration was performed with a 603621
calibrated reference detector (Newport Corp.). Transient photocurrents
(TPC) were obtained with an oscilloscope (Waverunner 625Zi, Teledyne
LECROY) coupled with a 470 nm picosecond laser (P-C-470, PicoQuant
GmbH), which acted as the excitation source. For TPC measurements,
the input impedance of the oscilloscope was set to 50 Ω, and then the
sample was exposed to an excitation pulse laser with a repetition rate
of 100 kHz. The TPC decays were recorded by averaging over 20 000
measurements for each sample. Impedance spectra were measured with
a PGSTAT30 system (Metrohm Autolab B.V., Netherlands) over the fre-
quency range 0.01–1 MHz. The density of the trap states was derived from
the angular frequency-dependent capacitance with the following equation:
Nt(Ea) = −(Vbi −Vapp)/qWKT*(dC/df)*f, where Vbi, Vapp, and W are the
built-in potential, applied voltage, and width of the space charge region,
respectively.[61] For the calculation of the energy levels of traps (Ea) via
thermal admittance spectroscopy, the equation Ea = 0.45 −0.025ln(2𝜋f)
was used to give the result in eV at 300 K.

Zakeeruddin1, Anders Hagfeldt4,8, Ursula Rothlisberger\n5, Aldo Di Carlo\n3,9✉,\nAram Amassian\n2✉& Michael Grätzel\n1✉\nCost management and toxic waste generation are two key issues that must be addressed\nbefore the commercialization of perovskite optoelectronic devices. We report a ground-\nbreaking strategy for eco-friendly and cost-effective fabrication of highly efﬁcient perovskite\nsolar cells. This strategy involves the usage of a high volatility co-solvent, which dilutes\nperovskite precursors to a lower concentration (<0.5 M) while retaining similar ﬁlm quality\nand device performance as a high concentration (>1.4 M) solution. More than 70% of toxic\nwaste and material cost can be reduced. Mechanistic insights reveal ultra-rapid evaporation\nof the co-solvent together with beneﬁcial alteration of the precursor colloidal chemistry\nupon dilution with co-solvent, which in-situ studies and theoretical simulations conﬁrm.\nThe co-solvent tuned precursor colloidal properties also contribute to the enhancement of\nthe stability of precursor solution, which extends its processing window thus minimizing the\nwaste. This strategy is universally successful across different perovskite compositions, and\nscales from small devices to large-scale modules using industrial spin-coating, potentially\neasing the lab-to-fab translation of perovskite technologies.\nhttps://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-021-27740-4\nOPEN\n1 Laboratory of Photonics and Interfaces, École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne, Lausanne 1015, Switzerland. 2 Department of Materials Science and\nEngineering, and Organic and Carbon Electronics Laboratories (ORaCEL), North Carolina State University, Raleigh, NC 27695, USA. 3 Centre for Hybrid and\nOrganic Solar Energy (CHOSE), University of Rome Tor Vergata, Rome 00133, Italy. 4 Laboratory of Photomolecular Science, Institute of Chemical Sciences\nand Engineering, École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne, Lausanne 1015, Switzerland. 5 Laboratory of Computational Chemistry and Biochemistry, École\nPolytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne, Lausanne 1015, Switzerland. 6 Kimia Solar Research Institute, Kimia Solar Company, Kashan 87137-45868, Iran.\n7 National Synchrotron Light Source II, Brookhaven National Laboratory, Upton, NY 11973, USA. 8 Department of Chemistry – Ångström Laboratory, Uppsala\nUniversity, 751 20 Uppsala, Sweden. 9 ISM-CNR, Institute of Structure of Matter, National Research Council, via del Fosso del Cavaliere 100, 00133\nRome, Italy. 10These authors contributed equally: Hong Zhang, Kasra Darabi, Narges Yaghoobi Nia. ✉email: hong.zhang@epﬂ.ch; aldo.dicarlo@uniroma2.it;\naamassi@ncsu.edu; michael.graetzel@epﬂ.ch\nNATURE COMMUNICATIONS |  (2022) 13:89 | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-021-27740-4 | www.nature.com/naturecommunications\n1\n1234567890():,;\n\n\nS\nolution-processed\nperovskite\nsolar\ncells\n(PSCs)\nhave\nattracted enormous attention due to the prospect of low-\ncost, easy fabrication of high-performance photovoltaic\nthin-ﬁlms1–6. Despite the rapid increase of PSC efﬁciency from\n3.8% in 2009 to 25.5% in 20207, the prospect of commercializa-\ntion remains bleak because of the presence of toxic lead com-\nponents and the generation of toxic waste from the precursor\nsolution during manufacturing8. Several research groups have\ntried to replace or reduce the lead usage with other less toxic\nmetal elements (e.g., tin9, germanium10, and bismuth11), how-\never, the stability and efﬁciency of lead-free or reduced content of\nlead PSCs are still far behind the state-of-the-art lead-based PSCs\nand the solvents used for processing are still toxic in nature.\nOther strategies have recently focused on preventing the leaching\nof toxic lead from solar cells, but these do not address the toxic\nwaste generation12. Therefore, so far, the problem of toxic waste\ngeneration has not been addressed scientiﬁcally despite much of it\nresiding in the formulation, storage, and processing steps. A\nconventional perovskite precursor solution is made of high purity\nlead halide salts, organic or inorganic ammonium salts, dissolved\nin toxic polar aprotic solvents (e.g., dimethylformamide (DMF),\ndimethylacetamide (DMAc), N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP),\netc.)8 and other high-boiling point solvents such as DMSO in\nhigh concentration5,13. Although few green solvents have been\ndeveloped to replace these toxic solvents, the resulting device\nperformance is still not comparable with that of the DMF-based\nprecursor13. In addition, these high purity perovskite raw mate-\nrials (PbI2, formamidinium iodide (FAI), methylammonium\niodide (MAI), etc.) are still very expensive (Supplementary\nTable 1), which increases the fabrication cost, and have a short\nshelf life due to aggregation.\nTypically, a direct correlation between the thickness of the\nperovskite ﬁlm and the precursor solution concentration has\nmeant that fabrication of state-of-the-art PSCs requires a relatively\nhigh concentration (>1.4 M) of lead components14,15 to obtain\nprototypical thin ﬁlms (i.e., thick, compact, highly crystalline, and\npinhole-free) for photovoltaic devices16. Record efﬁciencies are\ncurrently achieved through a combination of spin-coating highly\nconcentrated precursor solutions with an anti-solvent drip\napproach13,17. But one downside of most laboratory-based spin-\ncoating of high concentration solutions is precursor waste gen-\nerated during processing, which cannot be addressed by lowering\nthe concentration of traditional precursors without also lowering\nﬁlm thickness and power conversion efﬁciency (PCE). Such high\nconcentration perovskite solution with high viscosity and low\nevaporation rate create obstacles to typical scalable perovskite\ndeposition methods in industrial applications, e.g., slot-die coat-\ning, spray coating, blade coating, ink-jet printing, roll-to-roll\nprinting as well as industrial-based spin coating, by slowing down\nthe continuous production rate and reducing opportunities for\ncollection and reuse of excess solution. Another downside of\nconcentrated solutions is their short shelf-life due to their pro-\npensity to aggregate and agglomerate, which increases toxic waste.\nTherefore, there is an urgent requirement to develop an eco-\nfriendly strategy that can minimize the consumption of toxic\nmaterials by simultaneously reducing toxic waste during the\nprocessing step and by extending the shelf life of perovskite inks.\nHere, we present a co-solvent dilution strategy that maintains\nhigh-quality perovskite ﬁlms with very low concentration pre-\ncursor solutions. This strategy substantially reduces the quantity\nof expensive raw materials in the perovskite precursor ink and\nreduces the toxic waste production by spin coating through two\nkey routes: minimizing precursor loss during the processing of\nperovskite ﬁlms and enhancing the lifetime and shelf-life of the\ninks by suppressing aggregation of precursor colloids. A PCE of\nover 24% for laboratory PSCs could be achieved with a co-solvent\ndilution to a level as low as 0.5 M. In addition, scalability of the\nco-solvent dilution strategy is tested via fabrication of perovskite\nsolar modules (PSMs) with different sizes using industrial spin\ncoating. The modules fabricated by co-solvent dilution strategy\nshow higher PCEs and far better uniformity and reproducibility\nthan modules prepared with conventional perovskite inks, whilst\nusing a fraction of the precursor. Importantly, more than 70%\ntoxic waste/solvent, perovskite raw material, and fabrication cost\nare projected to be reduced for module fabrication compared to\nthe same modules made using conventional inks by industrial\nspin coating, and in doing so make spin coating a sustainable\ntechnique for medium scale manufacturing, for instance, for\nstandalone modules or Si wafer-scale integration18–21. This work\nshows that through judicious selection of a greener co-solvent, we\ncan signiﬁcantly reduce the usage and waste of toxic solvents and\nperovskite raw materials, while also simplifying fabrication and\ncutting costs of PSCs.\nResults and discussion\nProof of concept. The perovskite precursor solution is prepared\nwith a conventional method16 (denoted as control; C). Then the\njudiciously designed co-solvent THF is added to the as-prepared\nperovskite precursor solution with different dilution ratios\n(denoted as a target; T) as shown in Supplementary Table 2 and\nSupplementary Fig. 1. Precursor solution sta-\nbility is an important issue for reproducible fabrication of PSCs\nwith a wide processing window and for minimizing toxic waste by\nextending shelf-life as well as for the scalable manufacturing of\nperovskite modules20,26,45,46. Inclusion of some additives has\nbeen reported to improve the precursor solution stability26,47,48.\nEncouragingly, we found that our simple co-solvent dilution\nstrategy can signiﬁcantly extend the shelf-life stability of per-\novskite precursor solutions without requiring additives. We\ninvestigated the stability of various precursor inks by storing\nthem in an inert atmosphere and in the dark. First, we investi-\ngated the evolution over time of perovskite precursor colloids of\nthe high-performance double-cation perovskite ((FAPbI3)0.97(-\nMAPbBr3)0.03) by dynamic light scattering measurements. As\nshown in Fig. 6a, a large amount of micron-sized aggregates\nappeared in the high concentration control precursors, which\nindicates the perovskite colloids are unstable in the conventional\nmixtures of DMSO and DMF. In contrast, the co-solvent diluted\nprecursor shows excellent colloidal stability with no change in the\nsize distribution (Fig. 6b). Second, we investigated precursor\ncomposition changes with respect to storage time (Fig. 6c, d). To\nfurther conﬁrm a link between chemical inhomogeneity of the\nsolution (i.e., formation of large aggregates whose composition is\ndifferent from the target) and of the prepared ﬁlm, we checked\nthe XRD of perovskite ﬁlms made from the control and co-\nsolvent diluted precursors that were aged for different durations.\nAs shown in Fig. 6e, the controlled precursor contained large\naggregates after 6 days shows the appearance of impurity phases\nbelow 12°. Interestingly, the co-solvent diluted precursor shows\nsuperior shelf stability, as the high purity photoactive perovskite\nphase still formed even after 12 days of aging (Fig. 6f). The UV-\nVis absorbance of perovskite ﬁlm results also conﬁrmed the\nsimilar tendency in the XRD results (Supplementary Fig. 24).\nImportantly, PSCs fabricated with aged precursor solutions\nexhibit substantially different degradation rates with or without\nco-solvent dilution (Fig. 6g, h). The devices fabricated from the\naged control precursor solutions showed a rapid efﬁciency drop\nfrom 20.35 ± 0.45% (fresh) to 15.54 ± 0.39% (7 days), in agree-\nment with our observation of the ﬁlm absorbance and crystal\nstructure changes. The devices fabricated from the aged co-\nsolvent diluted precursor solution experience much less efﬁciency\ndrop from 20.53 ± 0.32% (fresh) to 18.00 ± 0.28% (7 days). The\nco-solvent dilution strategy can also be employed to enhance the\nprecursor shelf-life of other perovskites (see Supplementary\nFigs. 25 and 26). Therefore, the processing window of perovskite\nprecursors can be signiﬁcantly extended by our co-solvent dilu-\ntion strategy, which also decreases the overall waste of perovskite\nmaterials.\nIn summary, we report a co-solvent dilution strategy for the\nformulation of stable perovskite precursor inks that yields high\nefﬁciency while substantially reducing toxic waste generation\nduring fabrication and through enhanced shelf-life, fabrication\ncost, widening solar cell processing window, thus taking an\nimportant step toward commercialization of small- to medium-\nscale modules via industrial spin-coating, the most widely used\nbatch solution-processing method in the ﬁeld. This strategy\ninvolves the usage of a volatile co-solvent which dilutes perovskite\nprecursor inks to very low concentrations (<0.5 M) while\nretaining similar ﬁlm quality and optoelectronic features as a\nhigh concentration (>1.4 M) precursor when using facile spin\ncoating. A universal co-solvent dilution strategy enables
facile and cost-effective fabrication of perovskite
photovoltaics
Hong Zhang1,10✉, Kasra Darabi2,10, Narges Yaghoobi Nia3,10, Anurag Krishna4, Paramvir Ahlawat
5,
Boyu Guo2, Masaud Hassan S. Almalki1, Tzu-Sen Su1, Dan Ren
1, Viacheslav Bolnykh5,
Luigi Angelo Castriotta
3, Mahmoud Zendehdel
3,6, Linfeng Pan4, Sandy Sanchez Alonso1,4, Ruipeng Li7,
Shaik M. Zakeeruddin1, Anders Hagfeldt4,8, Ursula Rothlisberger

Cost management and toxic waste generation are two key issues that must be addressed
before the commercialization of perovskite optoelectronic devices. We report a ground-
breaking strategy for eco-friendly and cost-effective fabrication of highly efﬁcient perovskite
solar cells. This strategy involves the usage of a high volatility co-solvent, which dilutes
perovskite precursors to a lower concentration (<0.5 M) while retaining similar ﬁlm quality
and device performance as a high concentration (>1.4 M) solution. More than 70% of toxic
waste and material cost can be reduced. Mechanistic insights reveal ultra-rapid evaporation
of the co-solvent together with beneﬁcial alteration of the precursor colloidal chemistry
upon dilution with co-solvent, which in-situ studies and theoretical simulations conﬁrm.
The co-solvent tuned precursor colloidal properties also contribute to the enhancement of
the stability of precursor solution, which extends its processing window thus minimizing the
waste. This strategy is universally successful across different perovskite compositions, and
scales from small devices to large-scale modules using industrial spin-coating, potentially
easing the lab-to-fab translation of perovskite technologies.

S
olution-processed
perovskite
solar
cells
(PSCs)
have
attracted enormous attention due to the prospect of low-
cost, easy fabrication of high-performance photovoltaic
thin-ﬁlms1–6. Despite the rapid increase of PSC efﬁciency from
3.8% in 2009 to 25.5% in 20207, the prospect of commercializa-
tion remains bleak because of the presence of toxic lead com-
ponents and the generation of toxic waste from the precursor
solution during manufacturing8. Several research groups have
tried to replace or reduce the lead usage with other less toxic
metal elements (e.g., tin9, germanium10, and bismuth11), how-
ever, the stability and efﬁciency of lead-free or reduced content of
lead PSCs are still far behind the state-of-the-art lead-based PSCs
and the solvents used for processing are still toxic in nature.
Other strategies have recently focused on preventing the leaching
of toxic lead from solar cells, but these do not address the toxic
waste generation12. Therefore, so far, the problem of toxic waste
generation has not been addressed scientiﬁcally despite much of it
residing in the formulation, storage, and processing steps. A
conventional perovskite precursor solution is made of high purity
lead halide salts, organic or inorganic ammonium salts, dissolved
in toxic polar aprotic solvents (e.g., dimethylformamide (DMF),
dimethylacetamide (DMAc), N-methyl-2-pyrrolidone (NMP),
etc.)8 and other high-boiling point solvents such as DMSO in
high concentration5,13. Although few green solvents have been
developed to replace these toxic solvents, the resulting device
performance is still not comparable with that of the DMF-based
precursor13. In addition, these high purity perovskite raw mate-
rials (PbI2, formamidinium iodide (FAI), methylammonium
iodide (MAI), etc.) are still very expensive (Supplementary
Table 1), which increases the fabrication cost, and have a short
shelf life due to aggregation.
Typically, a direct correlation between the thickness of the
perovskite ﬁlm and the precursor solution concentration has
meant that fabrication of state-of-the-art PSCs requires a relatively
high concentration (>1.4 M) of lead components14,15 to obtain
prototypical thin ﬁlms (i.e., thick, compact, highly crystalline, and
pinhole-free) for photovoltaic devices16. Record efﬁciencies are
currently achieved through a combination of spin-coating highly
concentrated precursor solutions with an anti-solvent drip
approach13,17. But one downside of most laboratory-based spin-
coating of high concentration solutions is precursor waste gen-
erated during processing, which cannot be addressed by lowering
the concentration of traditional precursors without also lowering
ﬁlm thickness and power conversion efﬁciency (PCE). Such high
concentration perovskite solution with high viscosity and low
evaporation rate create obstacles to typical scalable perovskite
deposition methods in industrial applications, e.g., slot-die coat-
ing, spray coating, blade coating, ink-jet printing, roll-to-roll
printing as well as industrial-based spin coating, by slowing down
the continuous production rate and reducing opportunities for
collection and reuse of excess solution. Another downside of
concentrated solutions is their short shelf-life due to their pro-
pensity to aggregate and agglomerate, which increases toxic waste.
Therefore, there is an urgent requirement to develop an eco-
friendly strategy that can minimize the consumption of toxic
materials by simultaneously reducing toxic waste during the
processing step and by extending the shelf life of perovskite inks.
Here, we present a co-solvent dilution strategy that maintains
high-quality perovskite ﬁlms with very low concentration pre-
cursor solutions. This strategy substantially reduces the quantity
of expensive raw materials in the perovskite precursor ink and
reduces the toxic waste production by spin coating through two
key routes: minimizing precursor loss during the processing of
perovskite ﬁlms and enhancing the lifetime and shelf-life of the
inks by suppressing aggregation of precursor colloids. A PCE of
over 24% for laboratory PSCs could be achieved with a co-solvent
dilution to a level as low as 0.5 M. In addition, scalability of the
co-solvent dilution strategy is tested via fabrication of perovskite
solar modules (PSMs) with different sizes using industrial spin
coating. The modules fabricated by co-solvent dilution strategy
show higher PCEs and far better uniformity and reproducibility
than modules prepared with conventional perovskite inks, whilst
using a fraction of the precursor. Importantly, more than 70%
toxic waste/solvent, perovskite raw material, and fabrication cost
are projected to be reduced for module fabrication compared to
the same modules made using conventional inks by industrial
spin coating, and in doing so make spin coating a sustainable
technique for medium scale manufacturing, for instance, for
standalone modules or Si wafer-scale integration18–21. This work
shows that through judicious selection of a greener co-solvent, we
can signiﬁcantly reduce the usage and waste of toxic solvents and
perovskite raw materials, while also simplifying fabrication and
cutting costs of PSCs.
Results and discussion
Proof of concept. The perovskite precursor solution is prepared
with a conventional method16 (denoted as control; C). Then the
judiciously designed co-solvent THF is added to the as-prepared
perovskite precursor solution with different dilution ratios
(denoted as a target; T) as shown in Supplementary Table 2 and
Supplementary Fig. 1. Considering the precursor solubility and
ﬁlm quality (Supplementary Fig. 2), we choose tetrahydrofuran
(THF) as an example of co-solvent to demonstrate our concept in
this work with the following rationale: (i) a greener solvent with
very low disability-adjusted life year (DALYs) per kg of a sub-
stance emitted among typical solvents of PSCs’ fabrication
(Human health characterization factors extracted from USEtox
2.11)22; (ii) low boiling point and a very high vapor pressure (less
energy and time required for drying) (Supplementary Table 3);
(iii) comparatively weak coordination with lead (with respect to
DMSO or DMF, see density functional theory (DFT) calculations
and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations below); (iv) miscible
with the parent solvents (DMF and DMSO) with less environ-
mental impact during air emission of the solvent removed from
the thin ﬁlm22. We note that there are a few studies using THF as
a co-solvent together with methylamine to prepare well-dissolved
MAPbI3 perovskite precursor23,24. However, methylamine has
been widely demonstrated to induce the formation of a non-
perovskite phase upon reacting with FA-based perovskites25,26,
which limits the application of previous strategies towards the
fabrication of high-performance FA-based PSCs.
As a proof of concept, we investigated our co-solvent dilution
strategy with THF on the widely used triple-cation perovskites
(Cs0.05(FA0.9MA0.1)0.95Pb(I0.9Br0.1)3) as illustrated in Fig. 1. The
control precursor solutions were dissolved in DMF/DMSO (4/1,
v/v) mixture with various concentrations viz.,1.40, 0.93, 0.70, and
0.47 M. For our target samples, the high concentration 1.40 M
control precursor solution was diluted with different volumes of
THF (i.e., dilution of 200 v% THF obtains a concentration of
0.47 M). To simplify the labeling, 1.4 M control solution, 200 v%
DMF/DMSO, and 200 v% THF co-solvent diluted solution are
hereafter denoted as C-1.40, C-0.47, and T-0.47 M, respectively.
The perovskite ﬁlms were fabricated with the above-mentioned
precursor solutions using the widely adopted one-step spin-
coating with the antisolvent drip method (see details in Methods).
From scanning electron microscopy (SEM) top-view images in
Fig. 2a, we observe that the morphology in C-1.40 M showed
compact features of large grains. However, the C-0.47 M ﬁlm
morphology is poor containing small grains, poor surface
coverage, and pinholes, whereas in the T-0.47 M sample the
morphology is extremely compact with large and homogeneous

Considering bulk recombination, we derive for the T-0.47 M ﬁlm a
ﬁrst-order rate constant for nonradiative carrier recombination of
k1 = 0.97 × 106 s−1 corresponding to a lifetime of τ = 513.8 ns, while

Co-solvent dilution mechanism. To validate the co-solvent dilu-
tion mechanism, we employ a combination of experimental and
computational methods, including DFT calculations, ab initio MD
simulations as well as in-situ characterization of solution-processing.
We ﬁrst investigated the solvent-solute interaction by DFT calcu-
lations. We calculated the interaction energies of Pb2+ with pure
DMSO, DMF, THF, and their mixtures for prototypical tetra-
coordinates complexes (Supplementary Fig. 9). We ﬁnd that the
interaction energy of Pb2+ with THF is considerably lower than
with DMSO and DMF, as illustrated in Fig. 3a. We also ﬁnd that an
intimate mixture with THF can signiﬁcantly decrease the average
interaction energy of Pb2+ with, solvent molecules which we
anticipate may have implications on the conversion chemistry, that
is, if some THF remains coordinated, the conversion to the per-
ovskite phase might be ameliorated, as will be demonstrated later.
To further understand the ﬁnite temperature solvation effects
at the pre-nucleation stage, we performed ~15 ps ab initio MD
simulations of solute-solvent mixtures without and with THF.
Simulation details are presented in the section of Methods
(Computational methods). To evaluate the effect of co-solvent
dilution on the solvent-solute interaction, we use DMSO as a
model system in the following discussion. As shown in Fig. 3b, we
see that both Pb2+ and monovalent cations (FA+ and MA+) are
highly coordinated with oxygen atoms of DMSO molecules,
forming individual small clusters in the case of perovskite
precursor in pure DMSO. This can be expected due to the high
interaction energies with DMSO (see Fig. 3a). However, in pure
THF, we ﬁnd that the Pb-I edge-sharing clusters start to form
during the MD simulations (Supplementary Fig. 10). This can
also be expected due to the weaker bonding between THF and Pb
ions because of the low donor number (DN) of THF (low-DN
solvents coordinate less strongly with Pb2+)28 and can explain
that precursor complexes are not able to dissolve in pure THF
(see Supplementary Fig. 11). Interestingly, we ﬁnd a mixed
behavior in the DMSO/THF mixed system with the formation of
small mixed Pb-I-solvent clusters and large Pb-I edge-sharing
clusters (Fig. 3c). These smaller solute-solvent clusters can also
act as nucleation centers29. Similar behavior was also observed in
the mixtures of DMSO/DMF/THF (Supplementary Fig. 12). One
of the main insights from these simulations is that the addition of
a co-solvent, like THF, can be used to tune the solvent-solute
interaction strength with a direct impact on the subsequent
conversion and crystallization process of the perovskite phase, as
will be discussed below.
We performed in situ UV–vis transmittance measurements during
spin coating to investigate the evolution of solution thickness, as well
as monitor the metallate precursor (UV absorbance) and perovskite
phase formation (visible spectrum absorbance)30,31. Transmittance
spectra were taken starting 0.5 s after spin coating and show
interference oscillations (Supplementary Fig. 13) indicating a liquid
precursor (sol) ﬁlm whose thickness is rapidly decreasing, as shown
in Fig. 4a. The wet sol ﬁlms thin from ~5 to 8 μm to a steady-state
thickness of ~1.1 μm for C-1.4 M, ~0.7 μm for T-0.47 M, and
~0.15 μm for C-0.47 M by the 20 s mark for anti-solvent drip.
According to these measurements, the choice of co-solvent dilution
strategy clearly dictates the steady-state thickness of the precursor
ﬁlm and strongly inﬂuences the solution thinning dynamics. Next, we
seek to demonstrate the thinning behavior of T-0.47 M vs. C-0.47 M
is due to THF’s rapid evaporation rate. To do so, we cast 20 µl of 200
v% THF-diluted DMF/DMSO mixture, a ~6.67 µl of DMF/DMSO
mixture (volume of DMF/DMSO in 200 v% THF dilution) and 20 µl
of pure THF onto a mass balance, and monitored the mass change
vs. time as shown in Fig. 4b. The solvent mixture appears to follow
Raoult’s law of mixtures whereby THF is removed from the mixture
at the same rate as pure THF. The rapid THF evaporative loss
increases the concentration and viscosity of the precursor solution of
T-0.47 M compared to C-0.47 M, which disrupts its liquid-like
characteristics, including ejection, outﬂow, and related waste during
spin coating.
To further prove this point, we directly monitor the rate of
absorbance decrease of precursor metallates in situ during
solution processing. In Fig. 4c–e, we show the absorbance spectra
