Although aqueous-solution-processed MoO3, GeO2, V2O5
and CrO3 have been used as the anode interfacial layer in

Therefore, further eﬀort into the technological process and the

retained over 50% (62.6% for the PEDOT:PSS–V2O5 based
device) of their initial values in all the PEDOT:PSS–TMO based
devices. In general as the PEDOT:PSS aqueous dispersions are
acidic with a pH value of about 2, they would corrode the ITO
electrode
and
accelerate
the
interface
degradation.
The
aqueous solutions of the MoO3, GeO2, V2O5 and CrO3
materials are almost neutral due to their weak hydrolysis reac-
tions in water. Therefore, the acidity of PEDOT:PSS aqueous
dispersions could be neutralized partly after introducing these
TMO aqueous solutions. The improved stability in the PEDOT:
PSS + V2O5 based device could be reflected from the cross-
sectional SEM images of aged (150 h, exposure to air) devices
(Fig. S8, ESI†). The PEDOT:PSS + V2O5 based device still main-
tained good interface contact at the anode side. In contrast,
the anode interface in the PEDOT:PSS based device was
adversely deteriorated with many large voids. The content ana-
lysis based on the energy-dispersive X-ray (EDX) technique
further confirmed the improved cell stability in the PEDOT:
PSS + V2O5 based device since it still kept a very low oxygen
content even on long time exposure to air.
EDX analysis before and after long time exposure to air is
important to understand the better stability of V2O5 based PS
cell.
In addition, the good hydrophobicity with high contact
angles of these sTMO films (Fig. 3) could restrict the interface
dewetting and delamination partly. Consequently, PEDOT:
PSS–TMO based devices demonstrated long stabilities due to
suppressed interface degradation.
Conclusion
We demonstrated a facile route to deposite aqueous-solution-
processed MoO3, GeO2, V2O5 and CrO3 interfacial layers by
directly dissolving their commercial powders in deionized
water. Due to their higher work functions and stabilities, these
sTMO thin films have great potential application as a hole-
transporting layer in photovoltaic devices, such as organic
solar cells and perovskite solar cells. Among these, the sV2O5
film exhibited the highest work function of 5.2 eV and the best
hydrophobicity with a contact angle of 77.2°. A higher work
function is beneficial not only for enhancing the hole extrac-
tion, which could improve the cell parameter, Jsc but also for
modifying the anode, which could increase the cell parameter,
Voc. As a result, the sV2O5-based organic solar cell and perovs-
kite solar cell presented PCEs of 8.36% and 13.26%, respect-
ively. Furthermore, composite films consisting of PEDOT:PSS
and TMO materials could serve as more eﬃcient HTLs in per-
ovskite solar cells. In particular, the PEDOT:PSS–V2O5 inter-
facial layer based device obtained a maximum PCE of 18.03%

Accepted 18th August 2017

Aqueous-solution-processable metal oxides
for high-performance organic and perovskite
solar cells†
Yan-Hui Loua,b and Zhao-Kui Wang
*a
Poly(3,4-ethylene dioxythiophene):poly(4-styrenesulfonate) (PEDOT:PSS) is a widely utilized hole-trans-
porting material (HTM) in planar photovoltaic devices, such as organic solar cells (OSCs) and perovskite
solar cells (PSCs). However, the hygroscopic nature of PEDOT:PSS aqueous dispersions may restrict their
future application. Therefore, it is necessary to develop other eﬀective and stable HTMs to achieve high-
performance photovoltaic devices. Herein, we demonstrate a facile route to deposit solution-processed
MoO3, GeO2, V2O5 and CrO3 thin ﬁlms as hole-transporting layers by directly dissolving their commercial
powders in deionized water. Among these, the solution-processed V2O5 (sV2O5) ﬁlm exhibited the
highest work function of 5.2 eV, and the best hydrophobicity, with a contact angle of 77.2°. The sV2O5-
based OSCs and PSCs presented power conversion eﬃciencies (PCEs) of 8.36% and 14.13%, respectively.
Notably, the PEDOT:PSS V2O5 composite HTM based device obtained a maximum PCE of 18.03% with a
Voc exceeding 1.0 V. These aqueous-solution-processed HTMs have potential applications in green and
low-cost photovoltaic devices by virtue of their simple and ecofriendly preparations.
Introduction
Low-cost and high-performance photovoltaic cells are currently
studied to solve the global energy issues.1,2 As representative,
organic solar cells (OSCs) based on π-conjugated organic semi-
conductors have attracted more and more attention because of
their advantages, such as light weight, low cost, easy manufac-
turing process and flexibility.3–5 A revolutionary development
in OSCs is the introduction of bulk heterojunctions (BHJ) in
the cell, where the donor and acceptor material are blended
together.6,7 Since there are continuous pathways from the
interface to the respective electrodes through the interfacial
layers, the photon-to-electron conversion eﬃciency is dramati-
cally increased with the power conversion eﬃciency (PCE)
exceeding 10%.8,9 Recently, organometal halide perovskite
solar cells (PSCs) have attracted a lot of attention in the photo-
voltaic community due to their continuous rise in PCE.10–21
For example, the certified PCE of a single-junction perovskite
solar cell reached over 20% recently.19–21
Whether organic solar cells or perovskite solar cells, a
planar device structure is always adopted due to its simple
fabrication
process
and
availability
of
low
temperature
technology.22–26 In a planar structure solar cell, hole- and elec-
tron-interfacial layers are always introduced to manipulate the
carrier transport and extraction.14,22 Clearly, the film pro-
perties of interfacial materials, such as the film conductivity
and the energy levels, could significantly aﬀect the device per-
formance of planar structure solar cells. Poly(3,4-ethylenedioxy-
thiophene):poly(styrenesulfonate)
(PEDOT:PSS)
has
been
widely employed as a hole-transporting layer (HTL) in planar
structure solar cells due to its good film conductivity and solu-
tion processibility. However, the acidic and hygroscopic nature
of PEDOT:PSS may restrict its application in the future.27–29 As
a matter of fact, eﬃcient and stable hole interfacial layers are
still scarce. Some transition metal oxides (TMOs) could act as
HTLs because the hole extraction could be realized eﬃciently
via electron transfer from the conduction band of the TMO
to the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) of the
active
layer.30–32
Recently,
solution-processable
transition
metal oxides (TMOs) such as molybdenum oxide (MoO3),33–35
vanadium oxide (V2O5),36–44 germanium dioxide (GeO2)45 and
nickel oxide (NiO)46–48 have been developed to replace PEDOT:

ations, and device optimization of the perovskite solar cells. See DOI: 10.1039/

Institute of Functional Nano & Soft Materials (FUNSOM), Soochow University,
Suzhou 215123, China. E-mail: zkwang@suda.edu.cn

Optoelectronics and Energy, Soochow University, Suzhou 215123, China

PSS in organic electronic devices. Nevertheless, these TMO
solutions are prepared by the hydration method using oxide
precursors and/or sol–gel based colloidal suspensions with the
aid of diﬀerent organic solvents. This means that the prepa-
ration processes for these TMOs are relatively complicated and
a high annealing temperature is required along with the use of
organic solvents (unfriendly to the environment) during the
precursor preparing process.
Herein, we developed a facile route to deposite aqueous-
solution-processed TMOs (MoO3, GeO2, V2O5 and CrO3) inter-
facial layers by dissolving the commercial TMO powders in de-
ionized water. The sTMOs interfacial layers were fabricated at
room temperature and utilized as HTLs in poly[4,8-bis[(2-ethyl-
hexyl)oxy]benzo[1,2-b:4,5-b′]dithiophene-2,6-diyl][3-fluoro-2-
[(2-ethylhexyl)carbonyl]thieno[3,4-b]thiophenediyl]
(PTB7):
[6,6]-phenyl C71-butyric acid methyl ester (PC71BM) based
organic solar cells and CH3NH3PbIxCl3−x based perovskite
solar cells. The sTMOs-based devices demonstrated compar-
able performance with the PEDOT:PSS-based devices. In par-
ticular, the sV2O5 film exhibited the highest work function of
5.2 eV and the best hydrophobicity, with a contact angle of
77.2° among the four TMO materials. As a result, the sV2O5
based organic solar cell and perovskite solar cell presented a
power conversion eﬃciency (PCE) of 8.36% and 13.2%,
respectively. Furthermore, the composite HTL (by mixing
PEDOT:PSS and TMOs) based perovskite solar cells demon-
strated a significantly improved PCE and cell stability com-
pared with those pristine PEDOT:PSS based ones. Devices
using the optimized composite film (PEDOT:PSS + V2O5)
obtained a maximum PCE of 18.03%, with an open-circuit
voltage (Voc) of 1.02 V, a short-circuit current density (Jsc) of
22.38 mA cm−2, and a fill factor (FF) of 79%. The preparation
process of MoO3, GeO2, V2O5 and CrO3 aqueous solutions is
quite simple and ecofriendly. The developed TMO interfacial
materials
provide
a
diversification
of
hole-transporting
materials in planar perovskite solar cells.
Experimental
TMO solution and perovskite solution preparations
MoO3, GeO2, V2O5 and CrO3 were purchased from Shanghai
Chemical Industry Co., and the corresponding aqueous solu-
tions were prepared by dissolving their powders (∼50 nm in
size) directly in deionized water with stirring for over 24 h in
air at room temperature with an optimized concentration of
1 mg ml−1. When preparing the PEDOT:PSS–TMO composite
precursors with varied mixing ratios, the concentration of
TMO aqueous solution was maintained at 1 mg ml−1. The
PTB7:PC71BM (19 mg mL−1, 1 : 1 by volume) solution was pre-
pared in dichlorobenzene. The perovskite precursor solution
was prepared by mixing CH3NH3I and lead chloride (PbCl2)
powder in anhydrous DMF with a molar ratio of 3 : 1. The
resultant solution was then stirred at 60 °C overnight in a glo-
vebox and then filtered with a 0.45 µm polytetrafluoroethylene
(PTFE) filter before device fabrication.
Device fabrication
Patterned ITO glass substrates were thoroughly cleaned with
acetone, ethanol, and deionized water, in sequence, in an
ultrasonic bath for 15 min. Organic solar cells with a structure
of ITO/HTL/PTB7:PC71BM/LiF/Al and perovskite solar cells
with a structure of ITO/HTL/CH3NH3PbIxCl3−x/PC61BM/Bphen/
Ag were fabricated to investigate the functions of the aqueous-
solution-processed MoO3, GeO2, V2O5 and CrO3 HTLs. PEDOT:
PSS (Baytron PVP Al 4083) based devices were also fabricated
for comparison. After HTL deposition, the substrates were
transferred into a glovebox for active layer coating. In the case
of perovskite solar cell fabrication, PC61BM (20 mg ml−1 in
chloroform) and Bphen (0.5 mg ml−1 in absolute ethanol)
were sequentially deposited by spin coating at 2000 rpm for
40 s and 4000 rpm for 40 s to act as the electron transporting
layer and the cathode interfacial layer, respectively. Finally, the
samples were transferred to a vacuum chamber for Al or Ag
(100 nm) deposition. The active surface area of each device
was 7.25 mm2.
Characterization
Current density–voltage (J–V) characteristics of the organic
solar cells and perovskite solar cells under 1 sun illumination
were performed using a programmable Keithley 2400 source
meter under AM 1.5 G solar irradiation at 100 mW cm−2
(Newport, Class AAA solar simulator, 94023A-U). The incident-
photon-to-current eﬃciency (IPCE) measurements were per-
formed using a system comprising a xenon lamp, a monochro-
mator, a chopper and a lock-in amplifier attached with a cali-
brated silicon photodetector. The absorbance spectra were
measured with a UV/Vis spectrophotometer (PerkinElmer
Lambda 750). Atomic force microscopy (AFM) images were
obtained using a Veeco Multimode V instrument to evaluate
the surface morphology of the sTMO films. The stabilities of
the organic solar cells and perovskite solar cells without encap-
sulation were evaluated under continuous irradiation by an
incandescent lamp (at an intensity of 50 mW cm−2) in air
under ambient conditions. The optical field (|E|2) calculations
in the whole bulk heterojunciton solar cells were carried out
by a classic transfer matrix method.
Results and discussion
In general, the interfacial layer in the planar structure solar
cells is very thin (a few tens of nanometers). Water is easily
accessible and ecofriendly, and thus its known as a green
solvent. Most TMOs have a certain solubility in water, which
provides an opportunity for MoO3, GeO2, V2O5, and CrO3 to
form a thin film via aqueous-solution-processing. Uniform
and transparent MoO3, GeO2, V2O5 and CrO3 aqueous solu-
tions were prepared easily by dissolving these commercial
TMO powders into deionized water with continuous stirring
over 24 h. The sTMO thin films could be deposited by spin-
coating the aqueous solutions onto ITO glass substrates with
annealing (120 °C, 10 min). Then, the sTMO thin films were

utilized as HTLs for fabricating PTB7:PC71BM-based organic
solar cells and CH3NH3PbIxCl3−x based perovskite solar cells.
Fig. 1 presents a flow diagram of the sTMO preparation and
device fabrication process, including the molecule structures
and the device structures.
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) measurements were
first carried out to clarify the components in the aqueous solu-
tion processed MoO3, GeO2, V2O5, and CrO3 films. The peak
positions of all the elements’ core levels were calibrated with
respect to the C 1s peak located at 284.5 eV. As representatives,
Fig. 2(a)–(d) show the Mo 3d, Ge 2p, V 2p and Cr 2p core
levels, respectively. The Mo 3d5/2 and 3d3/2 located at 233.2 eV
and 236.1 eV, the Ge 3d located at 33.7 eV, the V 2p3/2 and 2p1/2
located at 517.8 eV and 523.1 eV, and the Cr 2p3/2 and 2p1/2
located at 579.4 eV and 587.9 eV coincide with the character-
istic peaks in those reported in literature.38,45,49–51 This
suggests that the MoO3, GeO2, V2O5 and CrO3 films could be
easily deposited from their aqueous solutions.
In photovoltaic devices, an interfacial layer between the
electrodes and active layer are determinant for the eﬃciency
improvement. The energy level alignment at the electrode/
active layer by the interfacial layer is one of the main factors
aﬀecting the Voc of the photovoltaic devices. These TMO layers
could act as interfacial layers to modify the ITO substrates.
Ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy (UPS) technique is a
reliable technique for measuring the work function of thin
films.52–54 Fig. 2(e) and (f) present the UPS spectra of spin-
coated PEDOT:PSS, MoO3, GeO2, V2O5 and CrO3 films on ITO
substrates. The work functions estimated from the UPS spectra
are summarized in the inset of Fig. 2(f). Herein, sCrO3 exhibi-

Although aqueous-solution-processed MoO3, GeO2, V2O5
and CrO3 have been used as the anode interfacial layer in
organic solar cells, few studies have been reported on their
application in perovskite solar cells since the critical growth of
the crystal perovskite films. The quality of the perovskite
crystal films, including homogeneity, grain size, and crystal
orientation, strongly depends on the underlayer condition.
Therefore, further eﬀort into the technological process and the
consideration of the surface, interface, and energy levels are
necessary for the layer-by-layer deposition of the perovskite
layer on these TMOs films based on solution processing.
As mentioned, only thin (<10 nm) aqueous-solution-pro-
cessed sMoO3, sGeO2, sV2O5 and sCrO3 films could be pre-
pared since these TMO materials have limited solubility in
water. These TMO layers are discontinuous and exhibit poor
film coverage, which makes it diﬃcult to grow high quality
perovskite films on them. The film thickness and coverage
could be improved by repetitive coating (more than twice).
Under the optimized coating process (three times), uniform
sMoO3, sGeO2, sV2O5 and sCrO3 films could be obtained on
the ITO substrates. The corresponding perovskite solar cells
approached PCE over 12% (ESI, Fig. S4 and Table S1†), which
is comparable to the PEDOT:PSS-based device. Fig. 5(a) shows
the optimized device performances of the perovskite solar cells
incorporating the sMoO3, sGeO2, sV2O5 and sCrO3 HTLs. The
main cell parameters are listed in Table 2.

Similarly, PEDOT:PSS–TMO based perovskite solar cells pre-
sented a stable performance compared with the pristine
PEDOT:PSS based perovskite solar cell. As shown in Fig. 5(f),
the PEDOT:PSS based device exhibited a rapid degradation in
performance, where the PCE decayed to 20.6% of the initial
value after illumination for 360 h in air. In contrast, the PCE
retained over 50% (62.6% for the PEDOT:PSS–V2O5 based
device) of their initial values in all the PEDOT:PSS–TMO based
devices. In general as the PEDOT:PSS aqueous dispersions are
acidic with a pH value of about 2, they would corrode the ITO
electrode
and
accelerate
the
interface
degradation.
The
aqueous solutions of the MoO3, GeO2, V2O5 and CrO3
materials are almost neutral due to their weak hydrolysis reac-
tions in water. Therefore, the acidity of PEDOT:PSS aqueous
dispersions could be neutralized partly after introducing these
TMO aqueous solutions. The improved stability in the PEDOT:
PSS + V2O5 based device could be reflected from the cross-
sectional SEM images of aged (150 h, exposure to air) devices
(Fig. S8, ESI†). The PEDOT:PSS + V2O5 based device still main-
tained good interface contact at the anode side. In contrast,
the anode interface in the PEDOT:PSS based device was
adversely deteriorated with many large voids. The content ana-
lysis based on the energy-dispersive X-ray (EDX) technique
further confirmed the improved cell stability in the PEDOT:
PSS + V2O5 based device since it still kept a very low oxygen
content even on long time exposure to air.
EDX analysis before and after long time exposure to air is
important to understand the better stability of V2O5 based PS
cell.
In addition, the good hydrophobicity with high contact
angles of these sTMO films (Fig. 3) could restrict the interface
dewetting and delamination partly. Consequently, PEDOT:
PSS–TMO based devices demonstrated long stabilities due to
suppressed interface degradation.
Conclusion
We demonstrated a facile route to deposite aqueous-solution-
processed MoO3, GeO2, V2O5 and CrO3 interfacial layers by
directly dissolving their commercial powders in deionized
water. Due to their higher work functions and stabilities, these
sTMO thin films have great potential application as a hole-
transporting layer in photovoltaic devices, such as organic
solar cells and perovskite solar cells. Among these, the sV2O5
film exhibited the highest work function of 5.2 eV and the best
hydrophobicity with a contact angle of 77.2°. A higher work
function is beneficial not only for enhancing the hole extrac-
tion, which could improve the cell parameter, Jsc but also for
modifying the anode, which could increase the cell parameter,
Voc. As a result, the sV2O5-based organic solar cell and perovs-
kite solar cell presented PCEs of 8.36% and 13.26%, respect-
ively. Furthermore, composite films consisting of PEDOT:PSS
and TMO materials could serve as more eﬃcient HTLs in per-
ovskite solar cells. In particular, the PEDOT:PSS–V2O5 inter-
facial layer based device obtained a maximum PCE of 18.03%

Crystallization Kinetics of the Perovskite Films\nTo elucidate the reason of homogeneity improvement in ES, mul-\ntidimensional in situ and ex situ measurements were performed\nto investigate the crystallization mechanism. First, we carried out\nin situ UV–vis absorption measurements on the as-cast ﬁlms\nto track the subsequent crystallization process; we performed\nthe annealing treatment at lower temperatures of 50 °C and/or\n100 °C to guarantee the validity of data. Upon annealing at\n100 °C, the SP-fabricated ﬁlm exhibited obvious change in ab-\nsorption intensity and shift in absorption edge with prolonged\nannealing time, as shown in Figure 2a; Figure S12a, Support-\ning Information. The absorption edge gradually shifted from\nthe initial ≈710 nm to the ﬁnal ≈750 nm, corresponding to\nthe composition transition from bromide-rich perovskite (short\nwavelength) to iodide-rich perovskite (long wavelength).[22] In\ncontrast, the ES-fabricated ﬁlm displayed minimal absorption\nchanges over annealing time, as illustrated in Figure 2b; Figure\nS12b, Supporting Information, and the initial band edge was al-\nready situated at ≈750 nm, with negligible variation during an-\nnealing. This phenomenon indicated that the ES-fabricated ﬁlm\ncould form perovskite ﬁlm with I–Br mixture closed to the de-\ntermined stoichiometry prior to annealing treatment. However,\nthe SP-fabricated ﬁlm tended to form Br-rich-based perovskite\n(large bandgap) initially; and subsequently, transformed into I–\nBr mixed perovskite during annealing. By plotting the absorption\nvalue against annealing time, we found that the SP-fabricated\nﬁlm required ≈10 s to form the perovskite ﬁlm with ﬁnal I–Br\nmixture (as shown in Figure 2a), while the ES-fabricated necessi-\ntated only 1–2 s (Figure 2b). Meanwhile, an additional absorption\nedge at ≈450 nm (present only in SP-fabricated ﬁlm) gradually\ndisappeared after ≈5 s of annealing, as shown in Figure S12a,\nSupporting Information, suggesting that the SP-fabricated ﬁlm\nunderwent a transformation from solvate phase to perovskite\nphase,[23] while ES eﬀectively skipped this step in Figure S12b,\nSupporting Information. These evolution phenomena were fur-\nther ampliﬁed by adjusting the annealing temperature to 50 °C:\nCompared to 100 °C, the window of absorption edge shift (from\n710 to 750 nm) was extended to ≈22 s in the SP-fabricated ﬁlm,\nand it took ≈8 s longer for the disappearance of the solvate phase\n(correlating to the 450 nm absorption edge) (Figure S13, Support-\ning Information). In contrast, the ES process still experienced a\nrapid crystallization within 4 s with well I–Br mixture.\nThe ex situ XRD measurement was also applied to monitor\nthe phase evaluation in the ﬁlms. Remark-\nably, the impressive PCE decay of less than 3% compared to the\nsmall area device suggests that the ES technique is promising for\nscalable fabrication of perovskite photovoltaics. Anion Conﬁnement for Homogeneous Mixed Halide
Perovskite Film Growth by Electrospray
Xiuxiu Niu, Nengxu Li, Zhenhua Cui, Liang Li, Fengtao Pei, Yisha Lan, Qizhen Song,
Yujiang Du, Jing Dou, Zhaoboxun Bao, Lina Wang, Huifen Liu, Kailin Li, Xinran Zhang,
Zijian Huang, Lan Wang, Wentao Zhou, Guizhou Yuan, Yihua Chen, Huanping Zhou,
Cheng Zhu, Guilin Liu, Yang Bai,* and Qi Chen*
Wide-bandgap perovskites are promising absorbers for state-of-the-art
tandem solar cells to feasibly surpass Shockley–Queisser limit with low cost.
However, the commonly used mixed halide perovskites suﬀer from poor
stability; particularly, photoinduced phase segregation. Electrospray
deposition is developed to bridge the gap of growth rate between iodide and
bromide components during ﬁlm growth by spatially conﬁning the anion
diﬀusion and eliminating the kinetic diﬀerence, which universally improves
the initial homogeneity of perovskite ﬁlms regardless of device architectures.
It thus promotes the eﬃciency and stability of corresponding solar cells based
on wide-bandgap (1.68 eV) absorbers. Remarkable power conversion
eﬃciencies (PCEs) of 21.44% and 20.77% are achieved in 0.08 cm2 and 1.0
cm2 devices, respectively. In addition, these devices maintain 90% of their
initial PCE after 1550 h of stabilized power output (SPO) tracking upon one
sun irradiation (LED) at room temperature.
1. Introduction
Recently, perovskite materials have achieved remarkable ad-
vancement in tandem solar cells development, in which the

bromine-based perovskite crystals are formed directly without

perovskites is crucial for improving the phase homogeneity of
mixed halide perovskite ﬁlms.

ﬁlms by improving the annealing temperature[9c,12] or optimizing
the thermal ﬁeld distribution,[9a,b] which suppress the develop-

cursor chemistry to achieve weaker coordination or to lower the
boiling point,[13] and the adopting of anti-solvent[14] have been
attempted to relieve the component inhomogeneity by acceler-
ating nucleation. However, these strategies often impact both

that is beneﬁcial to homogeneity improvement and without sac-

Diﬀerent from blade-coating, slot-die coating, and spin-
coating processes,[15] spray coating techniques have been widely
applied to depositing uniform ﬁlms on various substrates, even
on curved or rough substrates.[16] In comparison, the electro-
spray process involves electrohydrodynamic mechanism by ap-
plying a strong electric ﬁeld between the capillary nozzle and the
substrate; thus, creating uniform charged droplets. The coulomb
ﬁssion enables consistent generation of monodisperse droplets,
allowing reproducible fabrication of uniform and high-quality
thin ﬁlms.[17] Leveraging these advantages, electrospray has been
widely utilized in fabricating organic absorber layers,[18] charge
transport layers,[19] transparent conducting layers,[20] and so on.
However, due to the lack of understanding in perovskites crys-
tallization kinetics in electrospray deposition process, the perfor-
mance of PSCs based on this technique is still far below the state-
of-art (Table S1, Supporting Information).
Here, we used electrospray (ES) to fabricate wide-bandgap
perovskite ﬁlms with improved ion homogeneity. The unique
coulomb explosion and electric polarization eﬀects of ES accel-
erated the crystallization process and balanced the crystallization
kinetics between iodide-based and bromide-based phases. The re-
sulting homogeneous ﬁlm eﬀectively suppressed the phase sep-
aration under light stress, achieving improved eﬃciency and op-
erational stability of PSCs. Based on the ES technique, small-area
devices (0.08 cm2) exhibited a PCE of 21.44% (stabilized power
output of 20.88%) and maintained 90% of their initial PCE after
1550 h of stabilized power output (SPO) tracking. In addition, the
1.0 cm2 PSCs achieved a PCE of 20.77%, demonstrating that the
electrospray is capable for producing high-quality and homoge-
neous wide-bandgap perovskite ﬁlms with scalability. Our ﬁnd-
ings provide a new strategy for the fabrication of large-scale per-
ovskites toward solar cell modules and tandem devices.

Supporting Information) measurements, the ES-based samples
exhibited smaller diﬀerence between these regions and with im-
proved crystallinity (Figure S11, Supporting Information), indi-
cating more homogeneous composition distribution and higher
ﬁlm quality throughout the whole ﬁlm. As is well known, due to
enlarged free energy of I–Br perovskite system, the mixing of I
and Br in the perovskite system becomes thermodynamically un-
favorable with the increase of Br ratio.[2b,21] The inhibited phase
separation in ES perovskites with high Br content may be at-
tributed to the altered crystallization kinetics during ﬁlm growth.
3. Crystallization Kinetics of the Perovskite Films
To elucidate the reason of homogeneity improvement in ES, mul-
tidimensional in situ and ex situ measurements were performed
to investigate the crystallization mechanism. First, we carried out
in situ UV–vis absorption measurements on the as-cast ﬁlms
to track the subsequent crystallization process; we performed
the annealing treatment at lower temperatures of 50 °C and/or
100 °C to guarantee the validity of data. Upon annealing at
100 °C, the SP-fabricated ﬁlm exhibited obvious change in ab-
sorption intensity and shift in absorption edge with prolonged
annealing time, as shown in Figure 2a; Figure S12a, Support-
ing Information. The absorption edge gradually shifted from
the initial ≈710 nm to the ﬁnal ≈750 nm, corresponding to
the composition transition from bromide-rich perovskite (short
wavelength) to iodide-rich perovskite (long wavelength).[22] In
contrast, the ES-fabricated ﬁlm displayed minimal absorption
changes over annealing time, as illustrated in Figure 2b; Figure
S12b, Supporting Information, and the initial band edge was al-
ready situated at ≈750 nm, with negligible variation during an-
nealing. This phenomenon indicated that the ES-fabricated ﬁlm
could form perovskite ﬁlm with I–Br mixture closed to the de-
termined stoichiometry prior to annealing treatment. However,
the SP-fabricated ﬁlm tended to form Br-rich-based perovskite
(large bandgap) initially; and subsequently, transformed into I–
Br mixed perovskite during annealing. By plotting the absorption
value against annealing time, we found that the SP-fabricated
ﬁlm required ≈10 s to form the perovskite ﬁlm with ﬁnal I–Br
mixture (as shown in Figure 2a), while the ES-fabricated necessi-
tated only 1–2 s (Figure 2b). Meanwhile, an additional absorption
edge at ≈450 nm (present only in SP-fabricated ﬁlm) gradually
disappeared after ≈5 s of annealing, as shown in Figure S12a,
Supporting Information, suggesting that the SP-fabricated ﬁlm
underwent a transformation from solvate phase to perovskite
phase,[23] while ES eﬀectively skipped this step in Figure S12b,
Supporting Information. These evolution phenomena were fur-
ther ampliﬁed by adjusting the annealing temperature to 50 °C:
Compared to 100 °C, the window of absorption edge shift (from
710 to 750 nm) was extended to ≈22 s in the SP-fabricated ﬁlm,
and it took ≈8 s longer for the disappearance of the solvate phase
(correlating to the 450 nm absorption edge) (Figure S13, Support-
ing Information). In contrast, the ES process still experienced a
rapid crystallization within 4 s with well I–Br mixture.
The ex situ XRD measurement was also applied to monitor
the phase evaluation in the ﬁlms. In addition to the perovskite
phase at 14.16°, the as-cast SP ﬁlm showed a broad diﬀraction
peak from 6° to 12°, indicating the presence of complicated sol-
vate phases[24] (Figure 2c). The coexistence of perovskite and sol-
vate phases resulted in the yellow color of the ﬁlm from the in-
set photograph. During annealing, the solvate-phase decreased
while the DMSO-based intermediate phase (10.5°) and the 2H
phase (11.5°) appeared. Then, the DMSO-based intermediate
phase disappeared and the 2H phase transformed into the 4H
phase (11.7°). These intermediates were thought to be iodide
dominated, which underwent a smooth and moderate transition
behavior. However, due to the lower formation energy of nucle-
ation, the bromide contents tended to construct the correspond-
ing perovskite (Br-rich) directly and rapidly without intermedi-
ates, maybe resulting in the delayed intercalation of I.[10a,11a,25]

Moreover, the facet of perovskite (001) showed a signiﬁcant
change from 14.16° to 14.08° during annealing (Figure 2e) with
obvious FWHM variation, consistent with our speculation that
the Br-based perovskite was ﬁrst formed in the as-cast ﬁlm, and
then the I gradually entered into the perovskite lattice via the
slower release from intermediates during annealing (accompa-
nied by solvent evaporation) to reach the ﬁnal mixture. As a re-
sult of the diﬀerent crystallization pathways between I-based and
Br-based perovskites, the perovskite ﬁlm exhibited compositional
heterogeneity as shown in Figure 1. In comparison, the as-cast
ﬁlm under the ES process only contained a DMSO-based inter-
mediate phase at 9.7° (Figure 2d), which disappeared immedi-
ately after annealing. In addition, the (001) peak only presented
a slight shift from 14.09° to 14.12° during annealing (Figure 2e)
and with narrow FWHM, indicating that the I and Br mixture
had already formed simultaneously during the residual solvent’s
evaporation in the ES process. By reducing the crystallization dif-
ference between I-based and Br-based perovskites, the more ho-
mogeneous I–Br mixture perovskite was achieved. Finally, after
annealing, the ES-based perovskite exhibited better crystallinity
than the SP-based one (Figure S14, Supporting Information) with
less PbI2 residue. No signiﬁcant diﬀerence in crystallographic
orientation was detected (Figure S15, Supporting Information).
The morphology and color evolution of the perovskite ﬁlms
were also tracked at room temperature in ambient condition. The
SP-based ﬁlm experienced a conspicuous alteration in color, pro-
gressing from light yellow to brown and ultimately to black as pre-
sented in photographs and optical microscopy images (Figures
S16 and S17, Supporting Information). Meanwhile, the ES-based
sample exhibited a consistent black color, with no observable
morphology change over time. This phenomenon was consistent
with the above results and veriﬁed the faster crystallization pro-
cess facilitated by electrospray.
Based on the above results, we have demonstrated that the
electrospray is capable to accelerate the crystallization of per-
ovskite, particularly in the case of I-based one. This strategy
balances the crystallization rate between Br-based and I-based
perovskites, resulting in improved initial phase homogeneity of
the perovskite ﬁlms. Due to the working mechanism of electro-
spray (compared to typical coating methods such as spin-coating,
blade-coating, etc.), we propose that the electrospray modulates
the crystallization of perovskite through two aspects: 1) Electro-
spray is capable to provide a strong electric ﬁeld of ≈625 kV
m−1 during operation (Figure 2f), which is suﬃcient to induce
polarization of the polar solvate intermediate phase. The polar-
ization eﬀect weakens the interaction between solvents and so-
lutes, thereby accelerating the dissociation of solvents.[26] 2) The
perovskite droplet is charged at the spray needle with the same
charge. Coulomb ﬁssion occurs[17a,27] when the coulomb repul-
sion within the droplet exceeds its surface tension, resulting in
the formation of micrometer-level droplet size (≈1 μm in Figure
S18, Supporting Information). On the one hand, the smaller
droplet limits the diﬀusion of ions within a conﬁned domain.
On the other hand, owing to the highly extended speciﬁc surface
area to ≈2.19 m2 g−1 (which is ≈107 times greater than that of
regular solution process), the solvent evaporation is signiﬁcantly
accelerated. Beneﬁting from that, the crystallization rate gap be-
tween iodide and bromide is minimized, leading to the formation
of homogeneous I–Br mixture wide-bandgap perovskite ﬁlms.

(100 mW cm−2) for several hours. As shown in Figure 3a, a
prominent low-energy shoulder peak (≈780 nm) appeared beside
the main emission peak (≈750 nm in Table S4, Supporting Infor-
mation) in the SP-based ﬁlm after 12 h of illumination, indicating
the formation of low-bandgap perovskites (mainly I-rich). Further
extending the illumination duration to 48 h, the primary peak was
signiﬁcantly redshifted by 33 nm (from 750 to 783 nm) compared
to the initial state (Table S4, Supporting Information). A redshift
of the emission peak in the PL spectrum implied the formation of
low-bandgap clusters, which may have promoted carrier recom-
bination due to the “funneling eﬀect”.[28] Then, the peak slightly
broadened after 87 h of light soaking, indicating severe phase sep-
aration. In contrast, ES-based perovskite did not exhibit shoulder
peaks or main peak shift after 48 h of illumination; only a slight
peak broadening was observed (Figure 3b). Finally, the peak posi-
tion red shifted by 11 nm (from 750 to 761 nm) after 87 h of light
soaking (Table S4, Supporting Information), demonstrating the
suppressed phase separation that improved the photostability of
ES-based perovskites.
The formation of I-rich components would result in an in-
crease in lattice constant of the perovskite crystals due to the
larger size of iodine (compared to bromine), which was veriﬁed
by the XRD measurements. As shown in Figure S19a, Support-
ing Information, the (001) peak position of SP-based perovskite
has shifted to lower degree after illumination, indicating the en-
larged lattice constant. Meanwhile, the ES-based perovskite pre-
sented negligible change on the peak positions (Figure S19b and
Table S5, Supporting Information), further conﬁrming that the
light induced halogen separation has been eﬀectively inhibited
in the ES-based perovskite with enhanced initial halides homo-
geneity.
To reveal the mechanisms for inhibited phase segregation,
the activation energies (Ea) of ion migration were probed via
the temperature-dependent conductivity of SP- and ES-based de-
vices under dark condition. As shown in Figure S20, Supporting
Information, the Ea of the SP- and ES-based samples was 0.06
and 0.16 eV, respectively, illustrating ES-fabricated ﬁlm exhibits
a larger energy barrier for ion migration.
The operational stability of PSC devices was ﬁrst evaluated
by tracking the photovoltaic performance evolution under the
open-circuit condition. ES-based p–i–n PSCs (with the device ar-
chitecture of ITO/PTAA/Perovskite/C60/BCP/Au) retained 86%
of their initial PCE (17.87% ± 0.48%) after 1056 h of illumi-
nation (white LED lamp, 100 mW cm−2). In contrast, SP-based
devices only kept 65% of their original PCE (17.51% ± 0.87%)
under the same conditions (Figure 3c). The PL spectra of cor-
responding devices are shown in Figure 3e,f, and a signiﬁcant
red shift (≈38 nm) was observed in SP samples alongside the
broadened FWHM (from 53 to 89 nm in Table S6, Supporting
Information) (Figure 3e). This result indicated the severe phase
separation and poor crystal quality in the aged perovskite layer,

As a result, we demonstrated that the initial homogeneity
of the perovskite ﬁlm is critical in preventing phase separation
under illumination; thus, prolonging the stability of PSC de-
vices. Beneﬁting from the suppressed phase segregation, the ES
method shows advantages in stability improvement with diverse
device architectures, proving the universality of this technique.
5. Devices Eﬃciency
Beneﬁting from the higher crystallinity and larger grain size
in ES-prepared perovskite ﬁlms, the corresponding devices
(p–i–n structure) showed signiﬁcant PCE improvement with
20.14% on average compared to that of SP devices of 19.77%
(Figure 4a; Table S9, Supporting Information). The statistical
analysis showed that both the open-circuit voltage (VOC) and the
short-circuit current density (Jsc) of wide-bandgap (1.68 eV) PSCs
were slightly improved by the ES process (Figure S26, Support-
ing Information). The averaged VOC and Jsc for ES-based devices
were 1.160 V and 21.59 mA cm−2, while for SP-based devices,
these values were 1.153 V and 21.45 mA cm−2 (Table S9, Sup-
porting Information), respectively. The Jsc value was consistent
with the EQE measurement shown in Figure S27, Supporting
Information. A similar trend was also observed in the n–i–p ar-
chitecture with averaged VOC, Jsc, FF, and PCE of ES-based de-
vices of 1.158 V, 21.62 mA cm−2, 79.04%, and 19.79%, respec-
tively, which were slightly higher than those of SP-based devices
(1.136 V, 21.12 mA cm−2, 77.80%, and 18.90%, respectively), as
shown in Figure 4b; Figure S28 and Table S10, Supporting Infor-
mation.
The p–i–n-structured ES-based champion device (aperture
area: 0.08 cm2) showed a reverse scan PCE of 21.44% and
a forward scan PCE of 21% (with a stabilized power output
of 20.88% in Figure S29, Supporting Information), which is
the highest value compared to other reports with ES method
(Figure S30, Supporting Information). In comparison, the best
SP-based device showed a reverse scan PCE of 20.86% and a for-
ward scan PCE of 20.27% (Figure 4c; Table S11, Supporting In-
formation). Further, for the n–i–p structure, the PCE of the cham-
pion ES-based device was 20.90% and 20.41% under reverse-
and forward-scan, respectively, with a stabilized power output
of 20.34% (Figure S31, Supporting Information), signiﬁcantly
higher than that of SP-based device (PCE of 20.36%/19.73% for
reverse/forward-scan, Figure 4d; Table S12, Supporting Informa-
tion).
In addition to its versatility across various device architectures,
the ES technique also holds considerable promise for larger area
devices production beneﬁting from the improved ﬁlm homo-
geneity. As shown in Figure 4e,f, with the aperture area of 1 cm2,
the ES-based device exhibited a PCE of 20.77% from reverse scan
and 20.29% from forward scan (Table S13, Supporting Informa-
tion) for the p–i–n structure, and the n–i–p-structured device also
showed a reverse scan PCE of 20.11% and a forward scan PCE of
19.30% (Figure 4f; Table S14, Supporting Information). Remark-
ably, the impressive PCE decay of less than 3% compared to the
small area device suggests that the ES technique is promising for
scalable fabrication of perovskite photovoltaics. Further, we con-
ducted transient photovoltage (TPV) mapping and transient pho-
tocurrent (TPC) mapping measurements to investigate charge
carrier recombination and transportation properties spatially in
the SP- and ES-based devices, respectively. Figure S32, Support-
ing Information, shows the photovoltage decay time, which is in-
dicative of carrier recombination, and the ES-based device dis-
played a more concentrated distribution of decay times. Simi-
larly, the photocurrent decay results indicate that the ES-based
devices exhibited a more uniform carrier transportation behavior
throughout the entire active area as shown in Figure S33, Sup-
porting Information. These ﬁndings provide further insight into
the enhanced optoelectronic performance of large-area devices
fabricated using the ES process.
6. Conclusion
We have demonstrated that the electrospray is promising for scal-
able fabrication of eﬃcient and stable wide-bandgap PSCs by

Anion Conﬁnement for Homogeneous Mixed Halide
Perovskite Film Growth by Electrospray
Xiuxiu Niu, Nengxu Li, Zhenhua Cui, Liang Li, Fengtao Pei, Yisha Lan, Qizhen Song,
Yujiang Du, Jing Dou, Zhaoboxun Bao, Lina Wang, Huifen Liu, Kailin Li, Xinran Zhang,
Zijian Huang, Lan Wang, Wentao Zhou, Guizhou Yuan, Yihua Chen, Huanping Zhou,
Cheng Zhu, Guilin Liu, Yang Bai,* and Qi Chen*
Wide-bandgap perovskites are promising absorbers for state-of-the-art
tandem solar cells to feasibly surpass Shockley–Queisser limit with low cost.
However, the commonly used mixed halide perovskites suﬀer from poor
stability; particularly, photoinduced phase segregation. Electrospray
deposition is developed to bridge the gap of growth rate between iodide and
bromide components during ﬁlm growth by spatially conﬁning the anion
diﬀusion and eliminating the kinetic diﬀerence, which universally improves
the initial homogeneity of perovskite ﬁlms regardless of device architectures.
It thus promotes the eﬃciency and stability of corresponding solar cells based
on wide-bandgap (1.68 eV) absorbers. Remarkable power conversion
eﬃciencies (PCEs) of 21.44% and 20.77% are achieved in 0.08 cm2 and 1.0
cm2 devices, respectively. In addition, these devices maintain 90% of their
initial PCE after 1550 h of stabilized power output (SPO) tracking upon one
sun irradiation (LED) at room temperature.
1. Introduction
Recently, perovskite materials have achieved remarkable ad-
vancement in tandem solar cells development, in which the

defects,[5] and ion migration driven by

as
composition

defect

have been made to avoid the utilization of
high Br concentration and/or to suppress
the defect-assisted ion migration, which assists the inhabita-
tion of halide separation. However, the initial ion heterogeneity
of perovskite ﬁlms remains a critical issue for large-scale pro-
ductions and hinders the stability development.[9] The ion het-
erogeneity in the as-prepared ﬁlm originates from the diﬀer-
ent crystallization pathways of iodine-based and bromine-based
perovskites. For the iodine-based perovskite, the solvated in-
termediates, that is, (MA)2(DMSO)2Pb3I8 (MA: methylammo-
nium), 𝛿-FAPbI3, (FA)2(DMF)4Pb3I8 (FA: formamidinium), and
PbI2–2DMSO,[10] are ﬁrst formed, which convert into perovskite
crystals during solvent evaporation subsequently. In contrast,
bromine-based perovskite crystals are formed directly without
apparent intermediates.[11] Therefore, minimizing the diﬀerence
on crystallization rate between iodine-based and bromine-based
perovskites is crucial for improving the phase homogeneity of
mixed halide perovskite ﬁlms.
Recently, strategies focus on the thermal treatment of as-cast
ﬁlms by improving the annealing temperature[9c,12] or optimizing
the thermal ﬁeld distribution,[9a,b] which suppress the develop-
ment of heterogeneity domains. Alternatively, manipulating pre-
cursor chemistry to achieve weaker coordination or to lower the
boiling point,[13] and the adopting of anti-solvent[14] have been
attempted to relieve the component inhomogeneity by acceler-
ating nucleation. However, these strategies often impact both

nucleation and crystallization simultaneously, but to diﬀerent ex-
tents. It leads to ﬁlms with reduced grain size and moderate crys-
tallinity. Therefore, it is essential to develop a distinctive approach
that is beneﬁcial to homogeneity improvement and without sac-
riﬁcing ﬁlm crystallinity as well as the grain size.
Diﬀerent from blade-coating, slot-die coating, and spin-
coating processes,[15] spray coating techniques have been widely
applied to depositing uniform ﬁlms on various substrates, even
on curved or rough substrates.[16] In comparison, the electro-
spray process involves electrohydrodynamic mechanism by ap-
plying a strong electric ﬁeld between the capillary nozzle and the
substrate; thus, creating uniform charged droplets. The coulomb
ﬁssion enables consistent generation of monodisperse droplets,
allowing reproducible fabrication of uniform and high-quality
thin ﬁlms.[17] Leveraging these advantages, electrospray has been
widely utilized in fabricating organic absorber layers,[18] charge
transport layers,[19] transparent conducting layers,[20] and so on.
However, due to the lack of understanding in perovskites crys-
tallization kinetics in electrospray deposition process, the perfor-
mance of PSCs based on this technique is still far below the state-
of-art (Table S1, Supporting Information).
Here, we used electrospray (ES) to fabricate wide-bandgap
perovskite ﬁlms with improved ion homogeneity. The unique
coulomb explosion and electric polarization eﬀects of ES accel-
erated the crystallization process and balanced the crystallization
kinetics between iodide-based and bromide-based phases. The re-
sulting homogeneous ﬁlm eﬀectively suppressed the phase sep-
aration under light stress, achieving improved eﬃciency and op-
erational stability of PSCs. Based on the ES technique, small-area
devices (0.08 cm2) exhibited a PCE of 21.44% (stabilized power
output of 20.88%) and maintained 90% of their initial PCE after
1550 h of stabilized power output (SPO) tracking. In addition, the
1.0 cm2 PSCs achieved a PCE of 20.77%, demonstrating that the
electrospray is capable for producing high-quality and homoge-
neous wide-bandgap perovskite ﬁlms with scalability. Our ﬁnd-
ings provide a new strategy for the fabrication of large-scale per-
ovskites toward solar cell modules and tandem devices.
2. Homogeneity of the Initial Perovskite Films
To
estimate
the
quality
of
wide-bandgap
perovskites
Cs0.21FA0.74MA0.05Pb(I0.95−xBrxCl0.05)3 ﬁlms fabricated by the
spin-coating (Figure 1a) and electrospray (Figure 1b; Note S1
for Figure 1b, Supporting Information) techniques, the ﬁlm
homogeneity was ﬁrst probed by the photoluminescence (PL)
mapping measurements. With the ﬁlm composition of x = 0.12
(bandgap of 1.68 eV; Figure S1a,d, Supporting Information), the
ES-based perovskite exhibited a more homogeneous distribution
of PL emission peaks (≈747 nm) in Figure 1d compared to the
spin coated perovskite (SP) in Figure 1c. Statistical analysis

shows that the peak position variation of ES-based perovskite
is ≈3 nm, which is signiﬁcantly smaller than that of SP-based
ﬁlm with ≈8 nm (Figure 1e). The reduction in peak position
variation also indicates that the stoichiometric ratio of halides
and cations remains spatially consistent in ES perovskite ﬁlms.
Further increasing the Br (x) content to x = 0.15, with the
perovskite bandgap up to 1.70 eV (Figure S1b,e, Supporting
Information), the SP perovskite presents obvious inhomoge-
neous regions (with separated peak position distribution at
≈734 and ≈744 nm; Figure S2a,c, Supporting Information). In
contrast, the emission peaks of ES perovskite mainly locate at
≈735 nm with the narrow variation of ≈2 nm (Figure S2b,c,
Supporting Information), indicating the improved homogeneity.
Further, when x is increased to 0.30 (1.79 eV bandgap; Figure
S1c,f, Supporting Information), the ES perovskite still shows a
more homogeneous peak distribution concentrated at ≈702 nm
(Figure 1g,h), compared to that of the SP-based perovskite with
emission peaks ranging from 701 to 710 nm (Figure 1f,h). It is
noteworthy that the main emission peak position of the above
components shows no discernible diﬀerence between ES and
SP ﬁlms in the steady-state PL spectra (Figure S3, Supporting
Information), whereas the ES ﬁlms present narrower full width
at half maximum (FWHM) as shown in Table S2, Supporting
Information, indicating better ﬁlm quality and component
homogeneity.
Moreover, beneﬁting from the improved components homo-
geneity, the uniformity of spatial surface potential distribution
was also enhanced. Consistent with PL mapping results, the ES-
based perovskite exhibited a more concentrated surface poten-
tial distribution with a narrow FWMH of ≈31 mV, while that
of SP was ≈51 mV calculated from the Kelvin probe force mi-
croscopy (KPFM) measurements (Figure 1i–k), indicating a more
continuous optoelectronic property, which could be attributed to
the more concentrated composition distribution and the reduced
grain boundaries in ES ﬁlms (Figure 1i,j). The scanning electron
microscopy (SEM) results of Figures S4 and S5, Supporting In-
formation, showed that the thickness of perovskite ﬁlms fabri-
cated by these two methods was similar. Meanwhile, the time-
resolved photoluminescence (TRPL) analysis showed negligible
diﬀerences, indicating their comparable defect densities (Figure
S6 and Table S3, Supporting Information). Further increasing the
Br content to 0.30, the ES ﬁlm still exhibited a smaller diﬀerence
in surface potential variation as expected (Figure S7, Supporting
Information).
Moreover, the ES showed great advance in larger scale ﬁlms
production. A 5 × 5 cm2 perovskite ﬁlm (x = 0.12) was fabri-
cated and ﬁve selected regions were characterized to probe the
ﬁlm homogeneity (Figure S8, Supporting Information). From the
UV–vis (Figure S9, Supporting Information) and PL (Figure S10,
Supporting Information) measurements, the ES-based samples
exhibited smaller diﬀerence between these regions and with im-
proved crystallinity (Figure S11, Supporting Information), indi-
cating more homogeneous composition distribution and higher
ﬁlm quality throughout the whole ﬁlm. As is well known, due to
enlarged free energy of I–Br perovskite system, the mixing of I
and Br in the perovskite system becomes thermodynamically un-
favorable with the increase of Br ratio.[2b,21] The inhibited phase
separation in ES perovskites with high Br content may be at-
tributed to the altered crystallization kinetics during ﬁlm growth.
3. Crystallization Kinetics of the Perovskite Films
To elucidate the reason of homogeneity improvement in ES, mul-
tidimensional in situ and ex situ measurements were performed
to investigate the crystallization mechanism. First, we carried out
in situ UV–vis absorption measurements on the as-cast ﬁlms
to track the subsequent crystallization process; we performed
the annealing treatment at lower temperatures of 50 °C and/or
100 °C to guarantee the validity of data. Upon annealing at
100 °C, the SP-fabricated ﬁlm exhibited obvious change in ab-
sorption intensity and shift in absorption edge with prolonged
annealing time, as shown in Figure 2a; Figure S12a, Support-
ing Information. The absorption edge gradually shifted from
the initial ≈710 nm to the ﬁnal ≈750 nm, corresponding to
the composition transition from bromide-rich perovskite (short
wavelength) to iodide-rich perovskite (long wavelength).[22] In
contrast, the ES-fabricated ﬁlm displayed minimal absorption
changes over annealing time, as illustrated in Figure 2b; Figure
S12b, Supporting Information, and the initial band edge was al-
ready situated at ≈750 nm, with negligible variation during an-
nealing. This phenomenon indicated that the ES-fabricated ﬁlm
could form perovskite ﬁlm with I–Br mixture closed to the de-
termined stoichiometry prior to annealing treatment. However,
the SP-fabricated ﬁlm tended to form Br-rich-based perovskite
(large bandgap) initially; and subsequently, transformed into I–
Br mixed perovskite during annealing. By plotting the absorption
value against annealing time, we found that the SP-fabricated
ﬁlm required ≈10 s to form the perovskite ﬁlm with ﬁnal I–Br
mixture (as shown in Figure 2a), while the ES-fabricated necessi-
tated only 1–2 s (Figure 2b). Meanwhile, an additional absorption
edge at ≈450 nm (present only in SP-fabricated ﬁlm) gradually
disappeared after ≈5 s of annealing, as shown in Figure S12a,
Supporting Information, suggesting that the SP-fabricated ﬁlm
underwent a transformation from solvate phase to perovskite
phase,[23] while ES eﬀectively skipped this step in Figure S12b,
Supporting Information. These evolution phenomena were fur-
ther ampliﬁed by adjusting the annealing temperature to 50 °C:
Compared to 100 °C, the window of absorption edge shift (from
710 to 750 nm) was extended to ≈22 s in the SP-fabricated ﬁlm,
and it took ≈8 s longer for the disappearance of the solvate phase
(correlating to the 450 nm absorption edge) (Figure S13, Support-
ing Information). In contrast, the ES process still experienced a
rapid crystallization within 4 s with well I–Br mixture.
The ex situ XRD measurement was also applied to monitor
the phase evaluation in the ﬁlms. In addition to the perovskite
phase at 14.16°, the as-cast SP ﬁlm showed a broad diﬀraction
peak from 6° to 12°, indicating the presence of complicated sol-
vate phases[24] (Figure 2c). The coexistence of perovskite and sol-
vate phases resulted in the yellow color of the ﬁlm from the in-
set photograph. During annealing, the solvate-phase decreased
while the DMSO-based intermediate phase (10.5°) and the 2H
phase (11.5°) appeared. Then, the DMSO-based intermediate
phase disappeared and the 2H phase transformed into the 4H
phase (11.7°). These intermediates were thought to be iodide
dominated, which underwent a smooth and moderate transition
behavior. However, due to the lower formation energy of nucle-
ation, the bromide contents tended to construct the correspond-
ing perovskite (Br-rich) directly and rapidly without intermedi-
ates, maybe resulting in the delayed intercalation of I.[10a,11a,25]

Moreover, the facet of perovskite (001) showed a signiﬁcant
change from 14.16° to 14.08° during annealing (Figure 2e) with
obvious FWHM variation, consistent with our speculation that
the Br-based perovskite was ﬁrst formed in the as-cast ﬁlm, and
then the I gradually entered into the perovskite lattice via the
slower release from intermediates during annealing (accompa-
nied by solvent evaporation) to reach the ﬁnal mixture. As a re-
sult of the diﬀerent crystallization pathways between I-based and
Br-based perovskites, the perovskite ﬁlm exhibited compositional
heterogeneity as shown in Figure 1. In comparison, the as-cast
ﬁlm under the ES process only contained a DMSO-based inter-
mediate phase at 9.7° (Figure 2d), which disappeared immedi-
ately after annealing. In addition, the (001) peak only presented
a slight shift from 14.09° to 14.12° during annealing (Figure 2e)
and with narrow FWHM, indicating that the I and Br mixture
had already formed simultaneously during the residual solvent’s
evaporation in the ES process. By reducing the crystallization dif-
ference between I-based and Br-based perovskites, the more ho-
mogeneous I–Br mixture perovskite was achieved. Finally, after
annealing, the ES-based perovskite exhibited better crystallinity
than the SP-based one (Figure S14, Supporting Information) with
less PbI2 residue. No signiﬁcant diﬀerence in crystallographic
orientation was detected (Figure S15, Supporting Information).
The morphology and color evolution of the perovskite ﬁlms
were also tracked at room temperature in ambient condition. The
SP-based ﬁlm experienced a conspicuous alteration in color, pro-
gressing from light yellow to brown and ultimately to black as pre-
sented in photographs and optical microscopy images (Figures
S16 and S17, Supporting Information). Meanwhile, the ES-based
sample exhibited a consistent black color, with no observable
morphology change over time. This phenomenon was consistent
with the above results and veriﬁed the faster crystallization pro-
cess facilitated by electrospray.
Based on the above results, we have demonstrated that the
electrospray is capable to accelerate the crystallization of per-
ovskite, particularly in the case of I-based one. This strategy
balances the crystallization rate between Br-based and I-based
perovskites, resulting in improved initial phase homogeneity of
the perovskite ﬁlms. Due to the working mechanism of electro-
spray (compared to typical coating methods such as spin-coating,
blade-coating, etc.), we propose that the electrospray modulates
the crystallization of perovskite through two aspects: 1) Electro-
spray is capable to provide a strong electric ﬁeld of ≈625 kV
m−1 during operation (Figure 2f), which is suﬃcient to induce
polarization of the polar solvate intermediate phase. The polar-
ization eﬀect weakens the interaction between solvents and so-
lutes, thereby accelerating the dissociation of solvents.[26] 2) The
perovskite droplet is charged at the spray needle with the same
charge. Coulomb ﬁssion occurs[17a,27] when the coulomb repul-
sion within the droplet exceeds its surface tension, resulting in
the formation of micrometer-level droplet size (≈1 μm in Figure
S18, Supporting Information). On the one hand, the smaller
droplet limits the diﬀusion of ions within a conﬁned domain.
On the other hand, owing to the highly extended speciﬁc surface
area to ≈2.19 m2 g−1 (which is ≈107 times greater than that of
regular solution process), the solvent evaporation is signiﬁcantly
accelerated. Beneﬁting from that, the crystallization rate gap be-
tween iodide and bromide is minimized, leading to the formation
of homogeneous I–Br mixture wide-bandgap perovskite ﬁlms.
4. Light Stability of the Perovskite Films and
Devices

ﬁlms with diﬀerent initial homogeneity, the PL spectra of
SP- and ES-based perovskites (x = 0.12) were collected after

exposing the ﬁlms under a white LED lamp illumination
(100 mW cm−2) for several hours. As shown in Figure 3a, a
prominent low-energy shoulder peak (≈780 nm) appeared beside
the main emission peak (≈750 nm in Table S4, Supporting Infor-
mation) in the SP-based ﬁlm after 12 h of illumination, indicating
the formation of low-bandgap perovskites (mainly I-rich). Further
extending the illumination duration to 48 h, the primary peak was
signiﬁcantly redshifted by 33 nm (from 750 to 783 nm) compared
to the initial state (Table S4, Supporting Information). A redshift
of the emission peak in the PL spectrum implied the formation of
low-bandgap clusters, which may have promoted carrier recom-
bination due to the “funneling eﬀect”.[28] Then, the peak slightly
broadened after 87 h of light soaking, indicating severe phase sep-
aration. In contrast, ES-based perovskite did not exhibit shoulder
peaks or main peak shift after 48 h of illumination; only a slight
peak broadening was observed (Figure 3b). Finally, the peak posi-
tion red shifted by 11 nm (from 750 to 761 nm) after 87 h of light
soaking (Table S4, Supporting Information), demonstrating the
suppressed phase separation that improved the photostability of
ES-based perovskites.
The formation of I-rich components would result in an in-
crease in lattice constant of the perovskite crystals due to the
larger size of iodine (compared to bromine), which was veriﬁed
by the XRD measurements. As shown in Figure S19a, Support-
ing Information, the (001) peak position of SP-based perovskite
has shifted to lower degree after illumination, indicating the en-
larged lattice constant. Meanwhile, the ES-based perovskite pre-
sented negligible change on the peak positions (Figure S19b and
Table S5, Supporting Information), further conﬁrming that the
light induced halogen separation has been eﬀectively inhibited
in the ES-based perovskite with enhanced initial halides homo-
geneity.
To reveal the mechanisms for inhibited phase segregation,
the activation energies (Ea) of ion migration were probed via
the temperature-dependent conductivity of SP- and ES-based de-
vices under dark condition. As shown in Figure S20, Supporting
Information, the Ea of the SP- and ES-based samples was 0.06
and 0.16 eV, respectively, illustrating ES-fabricated ﬁlm exhibits
a larger energy barrier for ion migration.
The operational stability of PSC devices was ﬁrst evaluated
by tracking the photovoltaic performance evolution under the
open-circuit condition. ES-based p–i–n PSCs (with the device ar-
chitecture of ITO/PTAA/Perovskite/C60/BCP/Au) retained 86%
of their initial PCE (17.87% ± 0.48%) after 1056 h of illumi-
nation (white LED lamp, 100 mW cm−2). In contrast, SP-based
devices only kept 65% of their original PCE (17.51% ± 0.87%)
under the same conditions (Figure 3c). The PL spectra of cor-
responding devices are shown in Figure 3e,f, and a signiﬁcant
red shift (≈38 nm) was observed in SP samples alongside the
broadened FWHM (from 53 to 89 nm in Table S6, Supporting
Information) (Figure 3e). This result indicated the severe phase
separation and poor crystal quality in the aged perovskite layer,

As a result, we demonstrated that the initial homogeneity
of the perovskite ﬁlm is critical in preventing phase separation
under illumination; thus, prolonging the stability of PSC de-
vices. Beneﬁting from the suppressed phase segregation, the ES
method shows advantages in stability improvement with diverse
device architectures, proving the universality of this technique.
5. Devices Eﬃciency
Beneﬁting from the higher crystallinity and larger grain size
in ES-prepared perovskite ﬁlms, the corresponding devices
(p–i–n structure) showed signiﬁcant PCE improvement with
20.14% on average compared to that of SP devices of 19.77%
(Figure 4a; Table S9, Supporting Information). The statistical
analysis showed that both the open-circuit voltage (VOC) and the
short-circuit current density (Jsc) of wide-bandgap (1.68 eV) PSCs
were slightly improved by the ES process (Figure S26, Support-
ing Information). The averaged VOC and Jsc for ES-based devices
were 1.160 V and 21.59 mA cm−2, while for SP-based devices,
these values were 1.153 V and 21.45 mA cm−2 (Table S9, Sup-
porting Information), respectively. The Jsc value was consistent
with the EQE measurement shown in Figure S27, Supporting
Information. A similar trend was also observed in the n–i–p ar-
chitecture with averaged VOC, Jsc, FF, and PCE of ES-based de-
vices of 1.158 V, 21.62 mA cm−2, 79.04%, and 19.79%, respec-
tively, which were slightly higher than those of SP-based devices
(1.136 V, 21.12 mA cm−2, 77.80%, and 18.90%, respectively), as
shown in Figure 4b; Figure S28 and Table S10, Supporting Infor-
mation.
The p–i–n-structured ES-based champion device (aperture
area: 0.08 cm2) showed a reverse scan PCE of 21.44% and
a forward scan PCE of 21% (with a stabilized power output
of 20.88% in Figure S29, Supporting Information), which is
the highest value compared to other reports with ES method
(Figure S30, Supporting Information). In comparison, the best
SP-based device showed a reverse scan PCE of 20.86% and a for-
ward scan PCE of 20.27% (Figure 4c; Table S11, Supporting In-
formation). Further, for the n–i–p structure, the PCE of the cham-
pion ES-based device was 20.90% and 20.41% under reverse-
and forward-scan, respectively, with a stabilized power output
of 20.34% (Figure S31, Supporting Information), signiﬁcantly
higher than that of SP-based device (PCE of 20.36%/19.73% for
reverse/forward-scan, Figure 4d; Table S12, Supporting Informa-
tion).
In addition to its versatility across various device architectures,
the ES technique also holds considerable promise for larger area
devices production beneﬁting from the improved ﬁlm homo-
geneity. As shown in Figure 4e,f, with the aperture area of 1 cm2,
the ES-based device exhibited a PCE of 20.77% from reverse scan
and 20.29% from forward scan (Table S13, Supporting Informa-
tion) for the p–i–n structure, and the n–i–p-structured device also
showed a reverse scan PCE of 20.11% and a forward scan PCE of
19.30% (Figure 4f; Table S14, Supporting Information). Remark-
ably, the impressive PCE decay of less than 3% compared to the
small area device suggests that the ES technique is promising for
scalable fabrication of perovskite photovoltaics. Further, we con-
ducted transient photovoltage (TPV) mapping and transient pho-
tocurrent (TPC) mapping measurements to investigate charge
carrier recombination and transportation properties spatially in
the SP- and ES-based devices, respectively. Figure S32, Support-
ing Information, shows the photovoltage decay time, which is in-
dicative of carrier recombination, and the ES-based device dis-
played a more concentrated distribution of decay times. Simi-
larly, the photocurrent decay results indicate that the ES-based
devices exhibited a more uniform carrier transportation behavior
throughout the entire active area as shown in Figure S33, Sup-
porting Information. These ﬁndings provide further insight into
the enhanced optoelectronic performance of large-area devices
fabricated using the ES process.
6. Conclusion
We have demonstrated that the electrospray is promising for scal-
able fabrication of eﬃcient and stable wide-bandgap PSCs by

improving the initial ﬁlm homogeneity. The investigation of crys-
tallization kinetics reveals that the transition from intermediates
precursor to perovskites is accelerated by electric polarization
and coulomb explosion during electrospray deposition. More-
over, the spatial conﬁnement of compositional anions by electro-
spray bridges the gap of their crystallization rate to obtain homo-
geneous ﬁlms. As a result of improved ﬁlm homogeneity, the per-
ovskite ﬁlms show continuous and uniform optoelectronic prop-
erty and experience suppressed light-induced phase segregation,
leading to the improvement of device performance and stability.
Overall, our ﬁndings suggest that the electrospray coating tech-
nique is capable for multiple application scenarios and is desir-
able for scalable production for modules and tandem devices.

A steep rise was\nwitnessed in the power conversion eﬃciencies, which currently\npeaks at a certiﬁed value of 22.7%.1 The attractiveness of these\nmaterials resides in their exceptional defect tolerance,2,3\ntunable light absorption and emission properties,4,5 enhanced\ncharge carrier transport and lifetime,4 and cost-eﬀective\npreparation and processability.6 Applications beyond solar\ncells have also been studied, in light emitting diodes,7,8 lasers,8\nphotodetectors,9,10 X-ray detectors,11 γ-detectors,12 and smart\nwindows.13\nSeveral research groups have focused on the synthesis of new\norganic hole-transporting materials (HTMs) for perovskite\nsolar cells (PSCs).14−16 An emerging class of HTMs is the\nfamily of organic polymers, which inherently possesses higher\nhole mobility than dopant-free small molecules.16 Interestingly,\nthis growing interest has not been accompanied by the growth\nin the arsenal of deposition techniques. To date, spin-coating\nremains the preferred choice to deposit such hole conducting\npolymer ﬁlms.\nIn a n−i−p PSC design, hole conducting layers, mainly\nconsisting of polymeric materials (e.g., P3HT17−19 and\nPTAA19) that are soluble in perovskite antisolvents are\nstudied. Although it was demonstrated that PEDOT accepts\nholes as eﬀectively as spiro-OMeTAD,20 its use apart from a\nfew examples,21−23 has been restricted to inverted SC designs\n(p−i−n junction). The direct spin-coating of the aqueous\nPEDOT:PSS solution is not a good option because it is known\nto degrade the perovskite layer. The inverted designs, however,\npose further challenges such as overcoming the energy\nmismatch between FTO/PEDOT and attaining adequate\nsurface coverage of the perovskite layer, which is determined\nby the morphology of the underlying PEDOT.\nAlthough electrochemical deposition of the HTM layer has\nshown promising results in the case of dye-sensitized solar\ncells,24 it remained an elusive task for the n−i−p PSC\narchitecture up to this point. This is mainly because of the\ninstability of MAPbI3 in polar solvents,25 in which most\nelectrochemical syntheses are carried out. Further complica-\ntions arise from the dynamic exchange between the cations and\nhalide ions in the perovskite layer and those present in the\nelectrolyte. Such an exchange of ions can signiﬁcantly alter the\ncomposition of the perovskite layer.26 It has been demon-\nstrated recently that the electrochemical properties of\nMAPbI3\n27−29 and related materials30−34 can be studied in\ndichloromethane based electrolytes. Special care must be\nexercised while conducting electrodeposition, because an\nexternal electrochemical bias can induce unintended side\nreactions (e.g., corrosion of the perovskite layer).29 However,\nby implementing carefully controlled conditions, one can\nemploy electrodeposition as a technique and utilize its superior\ncontrol over several eﬃciency-determining factors (e.g.,\nmorphology, regularity, conductivity, optical absorption, and\nlayer thickness).24\nIn this study, we report the electrochemical deposition of\nPEDOT (HTM layer) directly on the MAPbI3 ﬁlm deposited\non a FTO/TiO2 electrode and its implementation in a\nperovskite solar cell (PSC) with an n−i−p architecture\n(Scheme 1). S Supporting Information
T
he emergence of organic−inorganic metal halide perov-
skites as active components in solar cells has sparked a
great interest in the scientiﬁc community. A steep rise was
witnessed in the power conversion eﬃciencies, which currently
peaks at a certiﬁed value of 22.7%.1 The attractiveness of these
materials resides in their exceptional defect tolerance,2,3
tunable light absorption and emission properties,4,5 enhanced
charge carrier transport and lifetime,4 and cost-eﬀective
preparation and processability.6 Applications beyond solar
cells have also been studied, in light emitting diodes,7,8 lasers,8
photodetectors,9,10 X-ray detectors,11 γ-detectors,12 and smart
windows.13
Several research groups have focused on the synthesis of new
organic hole-transporting materials (HTMs) for perovskite
solar cells (PSCs).14−16 An emerging class of HTMs is the
family of organic polymers, which inherently possesses higher
hole mobility than dopant-free small molecules.16 Interestingly,
this growing interest has not been accompanied by the growth
in the arsenal of deposition techniques. To date, spin-coating
remains the preferred choice to deposit such hole conducting
polymer ﬁlms.
In a n−i−p PSC design, hole conducting layers, mainly
consisting of polymeric materials (e.g., P3HT17−19 and
PTAA19) that are soluble in perovskite antisolvents are
studied. Although it was demonstrated that PEDOT accepts
holes as eﬀectively as spiro-OMeTAD,20 its use apart from a
few examples,21−23 has been restricted to inverted SC designs
(p−i−n junction). The direct spin-coating of the aqueous
PEDOT:PSS solution is not a good option because it is known
to degrade the perovskite layer. The inverted designs, however,
pose further challenges such as overcoming the energy
mismatch between FTO/PEDOT and attaining adequate
surface coverage of the perovskite layer, which is determined
by the morphology of the underlying PEDOT.
Although electrochemical deposition of the HTM layer has
shown promising results in the case of dye-sensitized solar
cells,24 it remained an elusive task for the n−i−p PSC
architecture up to this point. This is mainly because of the
instability of MAPbI3 in polar solvents,25 in which most
electrochemical syntheses are carried out. Further complica-
tions arise from the dynamic exchange between the cations and
halide ions in the perovskite layer and those present in the
electrolyte. Such an exchange of ions can signiﬁcantly alter the
composition of the perovskite layer.26 It has been demon-
strated recently that the electrochemical properties of
MAPbI3
27−29 and related materials30−34 can be studied in
dichloromethane based electrolytes. Special care must be
exercised while conducting electrodeposition, because an
external electrochemical bias can induce unintended side
reactions (e.g., corrosion of the perovskite layer).29 However,
by implementing carefully controlled conditions, one can
employ electrodeposition as a technique and utilize its superior
control over several eﬃciency-determining factors (e.g.,
morphology, regularity, conductivity, optical absorption, and
layer thickness).24
In this study, we report the electrochemical deposition of
PEDOT (HTM layer) directly on the MAPbI3 ﬁlm deposited
on a FTO/TiO2 electrode and its implementation in a
perovskite solar cell (PSC) with an n−i−p architecture
(Scheme 1). The eﬀect of electrochemical post-treatments of
the HTM layer on the performance of PSC has also been
scrutinized.

during the electropolymerization. FTO/TiO2/MAPbI3 electro-

layer, as described in the Supporting Information. The time
frame of the experiment and potential-range of the PEDOT
electrodeposition (in the absence of bis-EDOT monomer) was
established through prolonged immersion of the FTO/TiO2/
MAPbI3 electrode in the solvent and carrying out cyclic
voltammetric experiments. As established in our earlier
methods and protocol work,29 0.1 M Bu4NPF6 in dichloro-
methane oﬀers the best electrochemical condition as no
signiﬁcant change in the overall shape of the optical absorption
of the perovskite ﬁlm is observed after 10 min of exposure

layers were more resistant to oxidation than reduction (Figure
S1B). Top-down and cross-sectional SEM images as well as
XPS studies conﬁrmed the stability of the FTO/TiO2/MAPbI3
electrodes during both immersion in the electrolyte and
oxidative biasing, up to 1.1 V (Figures S2 and S3). However,
EDOT cannot be used as the polymerization precursor,
because its polymerization (oxidation) potential would exceed
the electrochemical stability of MAPbI3 layers. To overcome
this limitation, we employed bis-EDOT as a precursor
(Scheme S1). The use of bis-EDOT, in turn, allowed us to
carry out the (oxidative) electropolymerization and produce
PEDOT ﬁlms without degrading the MAPbI3 layer.35
The electropolymerization process initiated by the electro-
chemical oxidation of bis-EDOT on FTO/TiO2/MAPbI3
electrodes was monitored using in situ spectroelectrochemical
experiments (Figure 1A−C). The gradual growth of PEDOT
during potentiodynamic deposition was evident from the
change in absorption as well as the increasing (pseudo)-
capacitive current in the potential range of 0.0−0.6 V. The
absorption peak at 450 nm was attributed to EDOT oligomers
and the broad absorption in the 500−800 nm region (Figure
1B) was assigned to the polymer product, viz., PEDOT layer.

cycle was plotted along with the absorbance increase at 700 nm
(Figure 1C). A sharp rise in the current at 0.7 V was
accompanied by the absorbance increase at 700 nm, thus
conﬁrming the polymerization of bis-EDOT.
Although polymerization starts at 0.7 V, prolonged exposure
to the electrolyte needs to be avoided. As shown in Figure 1D,
adequate polymerization rate was achieved at potentials above
0.9 V. In addition, by varying the electrochemical charge
density, the thickness of the formed PEDOT layer can be ﬁne-
tuned, as deduced from the absorbance spectra (Figure 1E,F).
The UV−vis absorption features did not indicate any
noticeable changes corresponding to perovskite layer absorp-
tion, thereby conﬁrming the conservation of original MAPbI3
architecture during the electropolymerization process.
Characterization of PEDOT Layer. SEM images captured
the morphological features of the PEDOT layers on the
MAPbI3 ﬁlm following the deposition of PEDOT at 1.0 V with
Qpol = 5 mC cm−2. The top-view images show that the
electropolymerized layer of PEDOT completely covers the
MAPbI3 layer (Figure 2A). The smooth MAPbI3 surface was
not visible anymore, instead a furry polymer coating
developed. These images conﬁrmed the homogeneity of the
PEDOT layer and that the MAPbI3 remained intact during the
electrodeposition. In order to determine the thickness of the
formed PEDOT, cross-sectional FIB-SEM images were
recorded (Figure 2B). The measured PEDOT thickness was
compared with the value, calculated from the charge density
employed during polymerization (Figure 2C). These values fall
in the range of the HTM thicknesses (40−300 nm) employed
in the case of MAPbI3 PSCs using PEDOT.21,22 Raman-
spectroscopic studies (Figure 2D) further conﬁrmed the
characteristics of an electrochemically deposited PEDOT on
top of the MAPbI3 layer.
Post-treatment of PEDOT Layer. The doping level of the
HTL is important for optimization of PSCs. When we
evaluated the photovoltaic performance of the MAPbI3 PSCs
employing the electrochemically deposited PEDOT hole-
transporting layers, without any post-treatment (see Support-
ing Information for detailed analysis (Figure S4)), all of them
exhibited low open circuit voltage (VOC) (Figure 3A) and ﬁll
factor (FF). The inability of PEDOT layer to transport the
holes eﬃciently results in increased charge recombination
(Figure S4). One way to overcome these issues is to modulate
the doping level of PEDOT layer. We employed electro-
chemical post-treatment approach to alter the doping level
(Scheme S2). PEDOT ﬁlms deposited at 1.0 V, with a Qpol =
3−10 mC cm−2 seemed to be optimal to evaluate post-
treatment conditions. This reductive post-treatment method,
however, had an unintended side-eﬀect, as revealed by cross-
sectional SEM images (Figure S5A,B). Though the reduction
of PEDOT is beneﬁcial for its performance, it destroys some of
the MAPbI3 from the underlying layer. Three diﬀerent
strategies were employed to mitigate this eﬀect: (i) rapid
reduction at −0.6 V for 10 s (Figure S6A); (ii) mild reduction
at −0.5 V for 60 s (Figure S6B); and (iii) rapid-mild reduction
at −0.5 V for 20 s (Figure S6C).
There was an improvement in the VOC of the devices
compared to the untreated PEDOT in all cases (Figure S7),
but the JSC and the FF remained low in most cases (Figure
S9A−D). The only exception was the rapid reduction, where
the champion cell had a 5.9% eﬃciency (Figure 3D). Top-
down and cross-sectional SEM images recorded for samples
post-treated with the rapid reduction revealed that the
degradation of the MAPbI3 layers can be avoided using this
strategy (Figure S8).
Transient Absorption Measurements. To probe the
hole accepting ability of PEDOT, transient absorption
spectroscopic measurements were carried out (Figure 4A).
The characteristics of the spectra are in good accordance with
MAPbI3 spectra in the literature.36 The most prominent
