■CONCLUSIONS
The electrochemical deposition of PEDOT oﬀers a convenient
way to deposit a hole-transport layer on a MAPbI3 layer for
designing n−i−p junction perovskite solar cells. By employing
potentiostatically controlled electrodeposition technique, it is
possible to obtain controlled thicknesses of HTM layers. An
electrochemical postreduction step introduced to control the
doping level of the as-deposited PEDOT ﬁlms is an essential
step in achieving better performance of PSCs. Care should be
exercised not to destroy the underlying MAPbI3 layer during
the post-treatment process. The champion device showed a
power conversion eﬃciency of 5.9%. The results presented in
this study open new opportunities to employ electrochemistry
to assemble complex architectures of optically active perov-
skites.

Lead Iodide Film: A Strategy To Assemble Perovskite Solar Cells
Gergely F. Samu,†,‡,⊥Rebecca A. Scheidt,†,∥Gary Zaiats,†,∥Prashant V. Kamat,*,†,∥
and Csaba Janáky*,‡,§,⊥

S Supporting Information
T
he emergence of organic−inorganic metal halide perov-
skites as active components in solar cells has sparked a
great interest in the scientiﬁc community. A steep rise was
witnessed in the power conversion eﬃciencies, which currently
peaks at a certiﬁed value of 22.7%.1 The attractiveness of these
materials resides in their exceptional defect tolerance,2,3
tunable light absorption and emission properties,4,5 enhanced
charge carrier transport and lifetime,4 and cost-eﬀective
preparation and processability.6 Applications beyond solar
cells have also been studied, in light emitting diodes,7,8 lasers,8
photodetectors,9,10 X-ray detectors,11 γ-detectors,12 and smart
windows.13
Several research groups have focused on the synthesis of new
organic hole-transporting materials (HTMs) for perovskite
solar cells (PSCs).14−16 An emerging class of HTMs is the
family of organic polymers, which inherently possesses higher
hole mobility than dopant-free small molecules.16 Interestingly,
this growing interest has not been accompanied by the growth
in the arsenal of deposition techniques. To date, spin-coating
remains the preferred choice to deposit such hole conducting
polymer ﬁlms.
In a n−i−p PSC design, hole conducting layers, mainly
consisting of polymeric materials (e.g., P3HT17−19 and
PTAA19) that are soluble in perovskite antisolvents are
studied. Although it was demonstrated that PEDOT accepts
holes as eﬀectively as spiro-OMeTAD,20 its use apart from a
few examples,21−23 has been restricted to inverted SC designs
(p−i−n junction). The direct spin-coating of the aqueous
PEDOT:PSS solution is not a good option because it is known
to degrade the perovskite layer. The inverted designs, however,
pose further challenges such as overcoming the energy
mismatch between FTO/PEDOT and attaining adequate
surface coverage of the perovskite layer, which is determined
by the morphology of the underlying PEDOT.
Although electrochemical deposition of the HTM layer has
shown promising results in the case of dye-sensitized solar
cells,24 it remained an elusive task for the n−i−p PSC
architecture up to this point. This is mainly because of the
instability of MAPbI3 in polar solvents,25 in which most
electrochemical syntheses are carried out. Further complica-
tions arise from the dynamic exchange between the cations and
halide ions in the perovskite layer and those present in the
electrolyte. Such an exchange of ions can signiﬁcantly alter the
composition of the perovskite layer.26 It has been demon-
strated recently that the electrochemical properties of
MAPbI3
27−29 and related materials30−34 can be studied in
dichloromethane based electrolytes. Special care must be
exercised while conducting electrodeposition, because an
external electrochemical bias can induce unintended side
reactions (e.g., corrosion of the perovskite layer).29 However,
by implementing carefully controlled conditions, one can
employ electrodeposition as a technique and utilize its superior
control over several eﬃciency-determining factors (e.g.,
morphology, regularity, conductivity, optical absorption, and
layer thickness).24
In this study, we report the electrochemical deposition of
PEDOT (HTM layer) directly on the MAPbI3 ﬁlm deposited
on a FTO/TiO2 electrode and its implementation in a
perovskite solar cell (PSC) with an n−i−p architecture
(Scheme 1). The eﬀect of electrochemical post-treatments of
the HTM layer on the performance of PSC has also been
scrutinized.
■RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
Electropolymerization of Hole-Transport Layer. The
ﬁrst step was to ensure that the MAPbI3 layer remains intact
during the electropolymerization. FTO/TiO2/MAPbI3 electro-

optical changes during electrochemical deposition of the HTM
layer, as described in the Supporting Information. The time
frame of the experiment and potential-range of the PEDOT
electrodeposition (in the absence of bis-EDOT monomer) was
established through prolonged immersion of the FTO/TiO2/
MAPbI3 electrode in the solvent and carrying out cyclic
voltammetric experiments. As established in our earlier
methods and protocol work,29 0.1 M Bu4NPF6 in dichloro-
methane oﬀers the best electrochemical condition as no
signiﬁcant change in the overall shape of the optical absorption
of the perovskite ﬁlm is observed after 10 min of exposure
(Figure S1A). As for the electrochemical properties, MAPbI3
layers were more resistant to oxidation than reduction (Figure
S1B). Top-down and cross-sectional SEM images as well as
XPS studies conﬁrmed the stability of the FTO/TiO2/MAPbI3
electrodes during both immersion in the electrolyte and
oxidative biasing, up to 1.1 V (Figures S2 and S3). However,
EDOT cannot be used as the polymerization precursor,
because its polymerization (oxidation) potential would exceed
the electrochemical stability of MAPbI3 layers. To overcome
this limitation, we employed bis-EDOT as a precursor
(Scheme S1). The use of bis-EDOT, in turn, allowed us to
carry out the (oxidative) electropolymerization and produce
PEDOT ﬁlms without degrading the MAPbI3 layer.35
The electropolymerization process initiated by the electro-
chemical oxidation of bis-EDOT on FTO/TiO2/MAPbI3
electrodes was monitored using in situ spectroelectrochemical
experiments (Figure 1A−C). The gradual growth of PEDOT
during potentiodynamic deposition was evident from the
change in absorption as well as the increasing (pseudo)-
capacitive current in the potential range of 0.0−0.6 V. The
absorption peak at 450 nm was attributed to EDOT oligomers
and the broad absorption in the 500−800 nm region (Figure
1B) was assigned to the polymer product, viz., PEDOT layer.
To correlate the polymer formation with the oxidation of bis-

cell by varying the polymerization charge density at diﬀerent applied potentials.

of a PSC, where the PEDOT electrodeposition was carried out at E = 1.0 V with Qpol = 5 mC cm−2. (C) Theoretical and actual PEDOT layer
thicknesses (determined from cross-sectional SEM images). (D) Raman-spectra of a fully assembled FTO/TiO2/MAPbI3/PEDOT architecture

EDOT, the current density of the ﬁrst polymerization half
cycle was plotted along with the absorbance increase at 700 nm
(Figure 1C). A sharp rise in the current at 0.7 V was
accompanied by the absorbance increase at 700 nm, thus
conﬁrming the polymerization of bis-EDOT.
Although polymerization starts at 0.7 V, prolonged exposure
to the electrolyte needs to be avoided. As shown in Figure 1D,
adequate polymerization rate was achieved at potentials above
0.9 V. In addition, by varying the electrochemical charge
density, the thickness of the formed PEDOT layer can be ﬁne-
tuned, as deduced from the absorbance spectra (Figure 1E,F).
The UV−vis absorption features did not indicate any
noticeable changes corresponding to perovskite layer absorp-
tion, thereby conﬁrming the conservation of original MAPbI3
architecture during the electropolymerization process.
Characterization of PEDOT Layer. SEM images captured
the morphological features of the PEDOT layers on the
MAPbI3 ﬁlm following the deposition of PEDOT at 1.0 V with
Qpol = 5 mC cm−2. The top-view images show that the
electropolymerized layer of PEDOT completely covers the
MAPbI3 layer (Figure 2A). The smooth MAPbI3 surface was
not visible anymore, instead a furry polymer coating
developed. These images conﬁrmed the homogeneity of the
PEDOT layer and that the MAPbI3 remained intact during the
electrodeposition. In order to determine the thickness of the
formed PEDOT, cross-sectional FIB-SEM images were
recorded (Figure 2B). The measured PEDOT thickness was
compared with the value, calculated from the charge density
employed during polymerization (Figure 2C). These values fall
in the range of the HTM thicknesses (40−300 nm) employed
in the case of MAPbI3 PSCs using PEDOT.21,22 Raman-
spectroscopic studies (Figure 2D) further conﬁrmed the
characteristics of an electrochemically deposited PEDOT on
top of the MAPbI3 layer.
Post-treatment of PEDOT Layer. The doping level of the
HTL is important for optimization of PSCs. When we
evaluated the photovoltaic performance of the MAPbI3 PSCs
employing the electrochemically deposited PEDOT hole-
transporting layers, without any post-treatment (see Support-
ing Information for detailed analysis (Figure S4)), all of them
exhibited low open circuit voltage (VOC) (Figure 3A) and ﬁll
factor (FF). The inability of PEDOT layer to transport the
holes eﬃciently results in increased charge recombination
(Figure S4). One way to overcome these issues is to modulate
the doping level of PEDOT layer. We employed electro-
chemical post-treatment approach to alter the doping level
(Scheme S2). PEDOT ﬁlms deposited at 1.0 V, with a Qpol =
3−10 mC cm−2 seemed to be optimal to evaluate post-
treatment conditions. This reductive post-treatment method,
however, had an unintended side-eﬀect, as revealed by cross-
sectional SEM images (Figure S5A,B). Though the reduction
of PEDOT is beneﬁcial for its performance, it destroys some of
the MAPbI3 from the underlying layer. Three diﬀerent
strategies were employed to mitigate this eﬀect: (i) rapid
reduction at −0.6 V for 10 s (Figure S6A); (ii) mild reduction
at −0.5 V for 60 s (Figure S6B); and (iii) rapid-mild reduction
at −0.5 V for 20 s (Figure S6C).
There was an improvement in the VOC of the devices
compared to the untreated PEDOT in all cases (Figure S7),
but the JSC and the FF remained low in most cases (Figure
S9A−D). The only exception was the rapid reduction, where
the champion cell had a 5.9% eﬃciency (Figure 3D). Top-
down and cross-sectional SEM images recorded for samples
post-treated with the rapid reduction revealed that the
degradation of the MAPbI3 layers can be avoided using this
strategy (Figure S8).
Transient Absorption Measurements. To probe the
hole accepting ability of PEDOT, transient absorption
spectroscopic measurements were carried out (Figure 4A).
The characteristics of the spectra are in good accordance with
MAPbI3 spectra in the literature.36 The most prominent
feature, the ground state bleach at 760 nm, is caused by charge
separation due to band edge transition in MAPbI3.36
Furthermore, there is no additional bleaching signal present
at ∼500 nm that would arise from PbI2 in the material. The
recovery of the 760 nm bleach follows second-order kinetics
(Figure 4B). Fitting the data to a biexponential decay reveals
that the average lifetime (see Supporting Information for the
calculations and detailed analysis) has the following trend:
reduced PEDOT (tweighed avg = 1280 ps) < as-is PEDOT
(tweighed avg = 1660 ps) < no HTM (tweighed avg = 1750 ps). The
shorter lifetime indicates the transfer of photogenerated holes

properties of the PEDOT ﬁlm.
■CONCLUSIONS
The electrochemical deposition of PEDOT oﬀers a convenient
way to deposit a hole-transport layer on a MAPbI3 layer for
designing n−i−p junction perovskite solar cells. By employing
potentiostatically controlled electrodeposition technique, it is
possible to obtain controlled thicknesses of HTM layers. An
electrochemical postreduction step introduced to control the
doping level of the as-deposited PEDOT ﬁlms is an essential
step in achieving better performance of PSCs. Care should be
exercised not to destroy the underlying MAPbI3 layer during
the post-treatment process. The champion device showed a
power conversion eﬃciency of 5.9%. The results presented in
this study open new opportunities to employ electrochemistry
to assemble complex architectures of optically active perov-
skites.

[ 7–9 ] \n The supercapacitors, also known as \nelectrochemical capacitors, are widely \nrecognized as a new generation of clean \nenergy-storage devices, owing to its high \npower \ndensity, \nfast \ncharge–discharge \nrate, long cycling life, and good opera-\ntional safety. [ 10–13 ] As compared with \nthe supercapacitors fabricated by liquid \nmaterials, the light-weight ﬂ exible super-\ncapacitors fabricated by all solid-state \nmaterials possess the advantages in the \napplications for portable and wearable \ndevices. [ 14–16 ] Numerous efforts have been \ndevoted to develop ﬂ exible solid-state \nsupercapacitors based on nanostructured \ncarbon \nmaterials. [ 17–21 ] \nAmong \nthese \nnanostructured materials, graphene was \nstood out to be one of excellent mate-\nrials due to its excellent electrical con-\nductivity, mechanical ﬂ exibility, large surface area, and good \nchemical stability. [ 22–24 ] Flexible solid-state supercapacitors \nhave been fabricated by using graphene ﬁ lms, [ 25,26 ] graphene \nhydrogels, [ 27,28 ] and graphene ﬁ bers [ 29 ] as the free-standing \nelectrode. In order to fabricate graphene-based supercapaci-\ntors with high charge–discharge rate, graphene ﬁ lms with \n3D structure by chemical vapor deposition (CVD), [ 30 ] facile \nvacuum ﬁ ltration, [ 25,31 ] and hydrothermal method [ 32 ] have been \ndeveloped to produce the graphene ﬁ lms with high surface \narea. [ 33 ] However, 3D graphene ﬁ lms produced by either CVD \nor hydrothermal method need to be further posttreated, which \ngreatly restricts its applications in fabrication of the solid-state \nsupercapacitors. [ 32,34 ] \n In this study, we report the fabrication of ﬂ exible solid-state \nsupercapacitors based on self-stacked solvated graphene (SSG) \nﬁ lms prepared by facile vacuum ﬁ ltration as the free-standing \nelectrode. The ﬂ exible solid-state supercapacitors exhibit \nthe capacitance of 245 F g −1 at the current density of 1 A g −1 \nand maintain 83% original capacitance retention after 10 000 \ncharge–discharge cycles. We further integrate SSG-based ﬂ ex-\nible solid-state supercapacitors with high-performance pero-\nHSCs to build self-powered electronics. It was found that the \nﬂ exible solid-state supercapacitors can be charged by pero-HSCs \nunder the AM 1.5 white light illumination. Liu ,  Peng  Liu ,  Hao-Li  Zhang , * \n and  Xiong  Gong * \n To develop high-capacitance ﬂ exible solid-state supercapacitors and explore \nits application in self-powered electronics is one of ongoing research topics. \nIn this study, self-stacked solvated graphene (SSG) ﬁ lms are reported that \nhave been prepared by a facile vacuum ﬁ ltration method as the free-standing \nelectrode for ﬂ exible solid-state supercapacitors. The highly hydrated SSG \nﬁ lms have low mass loading, high ﬂ exibility, and high electrical conductivity. \nThe ﬂ exible solid-state supercapacitors based on SSG ﬁ lms exhibit excellent \ncapacitive characteristics with a high gravimetric speciﬁ c capacitance of \n245 F g −1 and good cycling stability of 10 000 cycles. Furthermore, the ﬂ exible \nsolid-state supercapacitors are integrated with high performance perovs-\nkite hybrid solar cells (pero-HSCs) to build self-powered electronics. It is \nfound that the solid-state supercapacitors can be charged by pero-HSCs and \ndischarged from 0.75 V. These results demonstrate that the self-powered \nelectronics by integration of the ﬂ exible solid-state supercapacitors with \npero-HSCs have great potential applications in storage of solar energy and in \nﬂ exible electronics, such as portable and wearable personal devices. \nDOI: 10.1002/adfm.201500335\n P. Introduction \n Recently, pervoskite hybrid solar cells (pero-HSCs) as an alter-\nnative to silicon-based photovoltaics have attracted signiﬁ cant \nattention due to their promising high power conversion efﬁ -\nciency (PCE). [ 1–3 ] The PCEs of pero-HSCs have skyrocketed to \nover 19%. [ 4 ] However, pero-HSCs, same as other photovoltaics, \nhave to be applied in sunlight to generate electric energy and \ntheir PCEs are dependent on the time, location, and weather. [ 5 ] \nIn order to alleviate these problems, pero-HSCs would be \nbetter to integrate with energy storage devices, such as super-\ncapacitors, to build self-powered electronics, which can store \nthe electric energy generated by pero-HSCs. Results and Discussion \n As described in the Experimental Section, the free-standing \nSSG ﬁ lms were prepared by chemical converted graphene \n(CCG) dispersion through facile vacuum ﬁ ltration. [ 25,31,35 ] \n Figure  1 a presents the scanning electron microscopy (SEM) \nimages of the freeze-dried SSG ﬁ lms. It is clear that the freeze-\ndried SSG ﬁ lms possess smooth surfaces; however, as shown \nin the cross-section image of the SSG ﬁ lms (Figure  1 b), a \nuniform layer-by-layer structure is observed from entire SSG \nﬁ lms. These results demonstrate that the SSG ﬁ lms formed a \nmicroporous structure between the graphene layers due to layer \naggregation and π–π attractions within graphene. [ 26 ] \n Figure  2 a displays the Fourier transform IR (FT-IR) spectra \nof graphene oxide (GO) powder and CCG powder. The broad \npeak at 3400 cm −1 is attributed to the O–H group, the peak at \n1740 cm −1 is assigned to the C=O stretching vibrations, and \nthe peaks at 1365, 1425, and 1615 cm −1 are associated with \nthe O–H deformations from the C–OH groups and water, \nrespectively. [ 36,37 ] After GO was reduced by hydrazine hydrate \nin ammonia solution, the FT-IR spectrum was signiﬁ cantly \nchanged. The intensity of asymmetric and symmetric C–O \nstretching from the C–O–C group became weak and the C=O \npeaked 1740 cm −1 is almost disappeared. These results indicate \nthat the CCG was successfully prepared from GO. [ 38 ] \n Raman spectroscopy was carried out to further conﬁ rm that \nthe CCG was prepared from GO. As shown in Figure  2 b, the \nGO powder, CCG powder, and the freeze-dried SSG ﬁ lms dis-\nplay both G band at ≈1582 cm −1 and D band at ≈1350 cm −1 . [ 36 ] \nHowever, the ratios of D/G for the CCG powder and the freeze-\ndried SSG ﬁ lms are higher than that of the GO powder, which \nis evidence that the GO powder was converted to the CCG \npowder. \n By measuring the weight, it was found that the as-prepared \nSSG ﬁ lm contains about 94 wt% of water. After freeze-dried \ntreatment, the thickness of the SSG ﬁ lm was decreased to 9 µm \nfrom 80 µm, which indicates that the as-prepared SSG ﬁ lm \nindeed has high hydrated hydrogel with high speciﬁ c area than \nthat of the freeze-dried graphene ﬁ lm. The electrical conductivi-\nties measured by four-probe method are ≈0.38 and ≈1.78 S cm −1 \nfor the as-prepared SSG ﬁ lms and the freeze-dried SSG ﬁ lms, \nrespectively. The electrical conductivity of the as-prepared SSG \nﬁ lms is comparable to that of the dried graphene aerogels with \n3D structure (≈0.87 S cm −1 ). [ 39 ] These results indicate that the \nas-prepared SSG ﬁ lms possess high electrical conductivity. \n Scheme  1 shows the detailed processing steps for fabrication \nof the ﬂ exible solid-state supercapacitors based on SSG ﬁ lms. \n Figure  3 a,b present the capacitance behaviors of SSG ﬁ lms with \na potential range from 0 to 1 V at various scan rates. As shown \nin Figure  3 a, all cyclic voltammetry (CV) curves exhibit a nearly \nrectangular shape with no obvious peaks even at a high scan \nrate 500 mv s −1 , which indicate that the SSG ﬁ lms possess an \nideal electrical double-layer capacitance. [ 40 ] The speciﬁ c capaci-\ntance ( C s ) of the solid-state supercapacitors can be calculated \naccording to the equation of  C s = 4( I Δ t )/( m Δ V ), where  I is the \ndischarge current,  Δt is the one cycle discharge time,  m is the \nmass of the SSG ﬁ lm electrodes, and  ΔV is the potential change \nafter voltage drop during discharge, respectively. Figure  3 c,d \npresent the galvanostatic charge–discharge behaviors of the \nﬂ exible solid-state supercapacitors based on SSG ﬁ lms. Based \non the data presented in Figure  3 c,d, the calculated  C s values \nat different current densities are shown in Figure  3 e. The ﬂ ex-\nible solid-state supercapacitors based on as-prepared SSG ﬁ lms \nexhibit  C s of ≈250 F g −1 at the current density of 0.5 A g −1 . The \n C s remains in 245 F g −1 at the current density of 1 A g −1 , which \nis 98% of its original values. Moreover, the solid-state superca-\npacitors still possess  C s of ≈145 F g −1 , which is 59% of its orig-\ninal value at the current density of 20 A g −1 . The decreased  C s \nat the high current densities is attributed to high internal resist-\nance and slow ion diffusion rate in the solid electrolyte. [ 40 ] On \nthe other hand, the ﬂ exible solid-state super-\ncapacitors based on the freeze-dried SSG \nﬁ lms only possess  C s of ≈181 F g −1 at the cur-\nrent density of 0.5 A g −1 . The  C s is decreased \nto ≈166 and ≈116 F g −1 at the current density \nof 1 and 20 A g −1 , respectively. The small  C s \nobserved from the ﬂ exible solid-state super-\ncapacitors base on the freeze-dried SSG ﬁ lms \nare likely due to the changes of porous struc-\nture and volume in the freeze-dried process, \nwhich hinders the inﬁ ltration of ions. [ 52 ] \n 3.  Conclusions \n In summary, the SSG ﬁ lms prepared by a facile ﬁ ltration \nmethod were used as the free-standing electrode in the ﬂ exible \nsolid-state supercapacitors. The ﬂ exible solid-state supercapaci-\ntors exhibit a high speciﬁ c capacitance of 245 F g −1 at 1 A g −1 \nand retain 83% of its original values up to 10 000 charge–dis-\ncharge cycles. We further integrated the ﬂ exible solid-state \nsupercapacitors with high performance pero-HSCs to build \nself-powered electronics. It was found that the solid-state super-\ncapacitors can be charged by pero-HSCs and discharged from \n0.75 V which is smaller than the open-circuit voltage of pero-\nHSCs. These results demonstrate that the self-powered elec-\ntronics by integration of the ﬂ exible solid-state supercapacitors \nwith pero-HSCs have great potential implications in the appli-\ncations of storing solar energy and ﬂ exible electronics, such as \nportable and wearable personal devices. \n 4. In the second \nprocedure, the acceleration-time was kept at 8 s, but the spin-time was \ntuned from 20 s, with the rotating-speed of 2500 rpm. The wet perovskite \nthin ﬁ lms were placed in petri-dish without cover for 30 min and then \nannealed at 90 °C for 3 h. Next, ≈100 nm of PC 61 BM was spin-coated \non the top of perovskite thin ﬁ lms.  Self-Powered Electronics by Integration of Flexible 
Solid-State Graphene-Based Supercapacitors with High 
Performance Perovskite Hybrid Solar Cells 
 Pengcheng  Du ,  Xiaowen  Hu ,  Chao  Yi ,  Huckleberry C.  Liu ,  Peng  Liu ,  Hao-Li  Zhang , * 
 and  Xiong  Gong * 
 To develop high-capacitance ﬂ exible solid-state supercapacitors and explore 
its application in self-powered electronics is one of ongoing research topics. 
In this study, self-stacked solvated graphene (SSG) ﬁ lms are reported that 
have been prepared by a facile vacuum ﬁ ltration method as the free-standing 
electrode for ﬂ exible solid-state supercapacitors. The highly hydrated SSG 
ﬁ lms have low mass loading, high ﬂ exibility, and high electrical conductivity. 
The ﬂ exible solid-state supercapacitors based on SSG ﬁ lms exhibit excellent 
capacitive characteristics with a high gravimetric speciﬁ c capacitance of 
245 F g −1 and good cycling stability of 10 000 cycles. Furthermore, the ﬂ exible 
solid-state supercapacitors are integrated with high performance perovs-
kite hybrid solar cells (pero-HSCs) to build self-powered electronics. It is 
found that the solid-state supercapacitors can be charged by pero-HSCs and 
discharged from 0.75 V. These results demonstrate that the self-powered 
electronics by integration of the ﬂ exible solid-state supercapacitors with 
pero-HSCs have great potential applications in storage of solar energy and in 
ﬂ exible electronics, such as portable and wearable personal devices.

 1.  Introduction 
 Recently, pervoskite hybrid solar cells (pero-HSCs) as an alter-
native to silicon-based photovoltaics have attracted signiﬁ cant 
attention due to their promising high power conversion efﬁ -
ciency (PCE). [ 1–3 ] The PCEs of pero-HSCs have skyrocketed to 
over 19%. [ 4 ] However, pero-HSCs, same as other photovoltaics, 
have to be applied in sunlight to generate electric energy and 
their PCEs are dependent on the time, location, and weather. [ 5 ] 
In order to alleviate these problems, pero-HSCs would be 
better to integrate with energy storage devices, such as super-
capacitors, to build self-powered electronics, which can store 
the electric energy generated by pero-HSCs. [ 6 ] Moreover, these

 2.  Results and Discussion 
 As described in the Experimental Section, the free-standing 
SSG ﬁ lms were prepared by chemical converted graphene 
(CCG) dispersion through facile vacuum ﬁ ltration. [ 25,31,35 ] 
 Figure  1 a presents the scanning electron microscopy (SEM) 
images of the freeze-dried SSG ﬁ lms. It is clear that the freeze-
dried SSG ﬁ lms possess smooth surfaces; however, as shown 
in the cross-section image of the SSG ﬁ lms (Figure  1 b), a 
uniform layer-by-layer structure is observed from entire SSG 
ﬁ lms. These results demonstrate that the SSG ﬁ lms formed a 
microporous structure between the graphene layers due to layer 
aggregation and π–π attractions within graphene. [ 26 ] 
 Figure  2 a displays the Fourier transform IR (FT-IR) spectra 
of graphene oxide (GO) powder and CCG powder. The broad 
peak at 3400 cm −1 is attributed to the O–H group, the peak at 
1740 cm −1 is assigned to the C=O stretching vibrations, and 
the peaks at 1365, 1425, and 1615 cm −1 are associated with 
the O–H deformations from the C–OH groups and water, 
respectively. [ 36,37 ] After GO was reduced by hydrazine hydrate 
in ammonia solution, the FT-IR spectrum was signiﬁ cantly 
changed. The intensity of asymmetric and symmetric C–O 
stretching from the C–O–C group became weak and the C=O 
peaked 1740 cm −1 is almost disappeared. These results indicate 
that the CCG was successfully prepared from GO. [ 38 ] 
 Raman spectroscopy was carried out to further conﬁ rm that 
the CCG was prepared from GO. As shown in Figure  2 b, the 
GO powder, CCG powder, and the freeze-dried SSG ﬁ lms dis-
play both G band at ≈1582 cm −1 and D band at ≈1350 cm −1 . [ 36 ] 
However, the ratios of D/G for the CCG powder and the freeze-
dried SSG ﬁ lms are higher than that of the GO powder, which 
is evidence that the GO powder was converted to the CCG 
powder. 
 By measuring the weight, it was found that the as-prepared 
SSG ﬁ lm contains about 94 wt% of water. After freeze-dried 
treatment, the thickness of the SSG ﬁ lm was decreased to 9 µm 
from 80 µm, which indicates that the as-prepared SSG ﬁ lm 
indeed has high hydrated hydrogel with high speciﬁ c area than 
that of the freeze-dried graphene ﬁ lm. The electrical conductivi-
ties measured by four-probe method are ≈0.38 and ≈1.78 S cm −1 
for the as-prepared SSG ﬁ lms and the freeze-dried SSG ﬁ lms, 
respectively. The electrical conductivity of the as-prepared SSG 
ﬁ lms is comparable to that of the dried graphene aerogels with 
3D structure (≈0.87 S cm −1 ). [ 39 ] These results indicate that the 
as-prepared SSG ﬁ lms possess high electrical conductivity. 
 Scheme  1 shows the detailed processing steps for fabrication 
of the ﬂ exible solid-state supercapacitors based on SSG ﬁ lms. 
 Figure  3 a,b present the capacitance behaviors of SSG ﬁ lms with 
a potential range from 0 to 1 V at various scan rates. As shown 
in Figure  3 a, all cyclic voltammetry (CV) curves exhibit a nearly 
rectangular shape with no obvious peaks even at a high scan 
rate 500 mv s −1 , which indicate that the SSG ﬁ lms possess an 
ideal electrical double-layer capacitance. [ 40 ] The speciﬁ c capaci-
tance ( C s ) of the solid-state supercapacitors can be calculated 
according to the equation of  C s = 4( I Δ t )/( m Δ V ), where  I is the 
discharge current,  Δt is the one cycle discharge time,  m is the 
mass of the SSG ﬁ lm electrodes, and  ΔV is the potential change 
after voltage drop during discharge, respectively. Figure  3 c,d 
present the galvanostatic charge–discharge behaviors of the 
ﬂ exible solid-state supercapacitors based on SSG ﬁ lms. Based 
on the data presented in Figure  3 c,d, the calculated  C s values 
at different current densities are shown in Figure  3 e. The ﬂ ex-
ible solid-state supercapacitors based on as-prepared SSG ﬁ lms 
exhibit  C s of ≈250 F g −1 at the current density of 0.5 A g −1 . The 
 C s remains in 245 F g −1 at the current density of 1 A g −1 , which 
is 98% of its original values. Moreover, the solid-state superca-
pacitors still possess  C s of ≈145 F g −1 , which is 59% of its orig-
inal value at the current density of 20 A g −1 . The decreased  C s 
at the high current densities is attributed to high internal resist-
ance and slow ion diffusion rate in the solid electrolyte. [ 40 ] On 
the other hand, the ﬂ exible solid-state super-
capacitors based on the freeze-dried SSG 
ﬁ lms only possess  C s of ≈181 F g −1 at the cur-
rent density of 0.5 A g −1 . The  C s is decreased 
to ≈166 and ≈116 F g −1 at the current density 
of 1 and 20 A g −1 , respectively. The small  C s 
observed from the ﬂ exible solid-state super-
capacitors base on the freeze-dried SSG ﬁ lms 
are likely due to the changes of porous struc-
ture and volume in the freeze-dried process, 
which hinders the inﬁ ltration of ions. [ 25 ] 
 In order to understand the underlying 
differences in the above two different super-
capacitors, electrochemical impedance spec-
troscopy (EIS) measurement is carried out to 
investigate the electrical properties of the SSG

 The mechanical property of the ﬂ exible solid-state super-
capacitors based on the as-prepared SSG ﬁ lms was further 
investigated.  Figure  4 a schematically displays how the ﬂ exible 
solid-state supercapacitors were bended. The CV curves of the 
solid-state supercapacitors bent at various angles are shown 
in Figure  4 b. The ﬂ exible solid-state supercapacitors possess 
approximately the same capacitor behaviors and it is even bent 
at 135°, indicating that the solid-state supercapacitors have 
excellent mechanical properties. 
 The CV of the solid-state supercapacitors measured as it was 
prepared, stored for one-week and for one-month are shown in 
 Figure  5 a. It was found that there are improved capacitance for 
the supercapacitors stored after one-week and one-month. Such 
improvement is likely due to the ions that 
were further diffused inside of the SSG ﬁ lms. 
In order to further evaluate the cyclability and 
performance durability of the solid-state super-
capacitors, the galvanostatic charge–discharge 
tests were carried out up to 10 000 cycles 
at the current density of 5 A g −1 . As shown 
in Figure  5 b, the degradation of capacitance 
takes place mainly after 2000 cycles. The 
capacitance keeps 83% of its initial values 
after 10 000 cycles. These results demonstrate 
that the solid-state supercapacitors exhibit 
excellent stability and capacitive performance. 
 The energy density and the power density 
are two important parameters used to evaluate 
the performance of supercapacitors. The energy 
density ( E ) and the power density ( P ) can be 
calculated by  E = 1/2  C s Δ V 2 and  P =  E / t , respec-
tively, [ 38,40 ] where  C s is the speciﬁ c capacitance, 
 ΔV is the potential change during the discharge 
process after voltage drop, and  t is the dis-
charge time of one cycle.  Figure  6 shows the correlation between  E 
and  P , which is termed as the Ragone plot. The ﬂ exible solid-state 
supercapacitors based on the as-prepared SSG ﬁ lms possess  E of 
8.01 Wh kg −1 at  P of 5.97 kW kg −1 . The  P can even reach to 
10.1 kW kg −1 at  E of 4.44 Wh kg −1 . However, the ﬂ exible solid-
state supercapacitors based on the freeze-dried SSG ﬁ lms cannot 
possess such excellent energy density and power density. The 
 E can only reach to 5.87 Wh kg −1 at  P of 3.05 kW kg −1 , and the 
highest  P reaches to 4.25 kW kg −1 at  E of 4.31 Wh kg −1 . Both 
 E and  P from the solid-state supercapacitors based on the as-
prepared SSG ﬁ lms are higher than those from the solid-state 
supercapacitors based on carbon nanotubes and other graphene 
ﬁ lms, [ 18,21,33,40–42 ] indicating that solid-state supercapacitors based 
on the as-prepared SSG ﬁ lms possess excellent performance of 
supercapacitors. 
 In order to explore the potential applications of the ﬂ exible 
solid-state supercapacitors based on the as-prepared SSG ﬁ lms, 
three supercapacitor units were connected in series to make a 
tandem supercapacitor. Each supercapacitor unit has the same 
area (1 × 1 cm 2 ) and same mass loading (≈0.4 mg for one 
electrode) of the SSG ﬁ lm. The CV and galvanostatic charge–
discharge curves of both single supercapacitor and the tandem 
supercapacitors are shown in  Figure  7 a. It is 
clear that the potential windows are 1.0 and 
3.0 V for single supercapacitor and tandem 
supercapacitors, respectively. The CV of the 
tandem supercapacitors almost expresses 
the rectangular structure. These observa-

 3.  Conclusions 
 In summary, the SSG ﬁ lms prepared by a facile ﬁ ltration 
method were used as the free-standing electrode in the ﬂ exible 
solid-state supercapacitors. The ﬂ exible solid-state supercapaci-
tors exhibit a high speciﬁ c capacitance of 245 F g −1 at 1 A g −1 
and retain 83% of its original values up to 10 000 charge–dis-
charge cycles. We further integrated the ﬂ exible solid-state 
supercapacitors with high performance pero-HSCs to build 
self-powered electronics. It was found that the solid-state super-
capacitors can be charged by pero-HSCs and discharged from 
0.75 V which is smaller than the open-circuit voltage of pero-
HSCs. These results demonstrate that the self-powered elec-
tronics by integration of the ﬂ exible solid-state supercapacitors 
with pero-HSCs have great potential implications in the appli-
cations of storing solar energy and ﬂ exible electronics, such as 
portable and wearable personal devices.

procedures for the ﬂ exible solid-state supercapacitors based on SSG

electrolyte was prepared by ﬁ rst diluting 6 g H 2 SO 4 (98%) into 30 mL 
deionized (DI) water and then adding the above H 2 SO 4 solution into 6 g 
PVA with 30 mL DI water. The suspension solution was stirred at 85 °C 
until the solution became clear. After that the SSG ﬁ lm with thickness 
of ≈80 µm (step a) was cut into rectangular strips with an area of 
1 cm × 1 cm and then dried the SSG ﬁ lm to the weight of ≈0.4 mg cm −2 , 
After that, the SSG ﬁ lm was immersed into 1 M H 2 SO 4 solution overnight 
to allow H + protons to be inﬁ ltrated inside of the SSG ﬁ lm (step b). 
The SSG ﬁ lm was carefully assembled on the silver-coated polyimide 
substrate as one electrode (step c). After that, the H 2 SO 4 –PVA gel is

condition to form the SSG ﬁ lm electrode coated with H 2 SO 4 –PVA solid-

 Characterization of Flexible Solid-State Supercapacitors : CV and 
galvanostatic charge–discharge measurement were conducted by using 
Gamry reference 3000 at the potential ranging from 0 to 1 V. EIS was 
measured in the frequency ranging from 10 5 to 10 −2 Hz. 
 Fabrication of the Perovskite Hybrid Solar Cells (Pero-HSCs) : The 
pero-HSCs were fabricated in the device with a conﬁ guration of ITO/
PEDOT:PSS/CH 3 NH 3 PbI 3- x  Cl x /PC 61 BM/Al, where ITO is indium tin 
oxide, CH 3 NH 3 PbI 3- x  Cl x is perovskite materials, and Al is Aluminum. 
Approximately 35 nm of PEDOT:PSS was spin-coated on precleaned ITO 
glass substrates followed by thermal annealing at 150 °C for 10 min. 
The perovskite ﬁ lms were spin-coated on top of ITO/PEDOT:PSS from 
perovskite precursor solution in the glove box with nitrogen atmosphere. 
The perovskite thin ﬁ lms were processed by two-step procedures. In the 
ﬁ rst procedure, the spin-time was kept at 20 s, with the rotating-speed 
of 2500 rpm, but the acceleration-time was 10 s with the rotating-peed 
increased from 0 to 2500 rpm in the acceleration-time. In the second 
procedure, the acceleration-time was kept at 8 s, but the spin-time was 
tuned from 20 s, with the rotating-speed of 2500 rpm. The wet perovskite 
thin ﬁ lms were placed in petri-dish without cover for 30 min and then 
annealed at 90 °C for 3 h. Next, ≈100 nm of PC 61 BM was spin-coated 
on the top of perovskite thin ﬁ lms. Finally, ≈120 nm Al electrode was 
evaporated under high vacuum (2 × 10 6 mbar) through a shade mask. 
The device area is deﬁ ned as 4.5 mm 2 . 
 Characterization of Pero-HSCs : The current densities versus voltage 
( J – V ) characteristics of pero-HSCs were recorded using a Keithley 2400 
Source Meter. The device photocurrent was measured under air mass 
(AM) 1.5 illumination at the light intensity of 100 mW cm −2 . The light 
intensity was accurately calibrated by a standard Si photodiode. The 
Incident photon-to-current efﬁ ciency (IPCE) spectra of pero-HSCs were 
measured through the IPCE measurement setup in use at European 
solar test installation (ESTI) for cells and mini-modules. A 300 W steady-
state xenon lamp provides the source light. Up to 64 ﬁ lters (8–20 nm 
width, range from 300 to 1200 nm) are available on four ﬁ lter-wheels 
to produce the monochromatic input, which is chopped at 75 Hz, 
superimposed on the bias light and measured via the usual lock-in 
technique. 
 Fabrication and Characterization of Self-Powered Electronics : The self-
powered electronics were built by integration of the ﬂ exible solid-state 
supercapacitors with pero-HSCs through two-copper wires. The ﬂ exible 
solid-state supercapacitors were charged by the current generated from 
pero-HSCs under white light illumination. After the ﬂ exible solid-state 
supercapacitors were charged, the electrochemical workstation was 
connected with the copper wires to study the discharge properties of the 
ﬂ exible solid-state supercapacitors.

Among 
these 
nanostructured materials, graphene was 
stood out to be one of excellent mate-
rials due to its excellent electrical con-
ductivity, mechanical ﬂ exibility, large surface area, and good 
chemical stability. [ 22–24 ] Flexible solid-state supercapacitors 
have been fabricated by using graphene ﬁ lms, [ 25,26 ] graphene

developed to produce the graphene ﬁ lms with high surface 
area. [ 33 ] However, 3D graphene ﬁ lms produced by either CVD 
or hydrothermal method need to be further posttreated, which 
greatly restricts its applications in fabrication of the solid-state

 Self-Powered Electronics by Integration of Flexible 
Solid-State Graphene-Based Supercapacitors with High 
Performance Perovskite Hybrid Solar Cells 
 Pengcheng  Du ,  Xiaowen  Hu ,  Chao  Yi ,  Huckleberry C.  Liu ,  Peng  Liu ,  Hao-Li  Zhang , * 
 and  Xiong  Gong * 
 To develop high-capacitance ﬂ exible solid-state supercapacitors and explore 
its application in self-powered electronics is one of ongoing research topics. 
In this study, self-stacked solvated graphene (SSG) ﬁ lms are reported that 
have been prepared by a facile vacuum ﬁ ltration method as the free-standing 
electrode for ﬂ exible solid-state supercapacitors. The highly hydrated SSG 
ﬁ lms have low mass loading, high ﬂ exibility, and high electrical conductivity. 
The ﬂ exible solid-state supercapacitors based on SSG ﬁ lms exhibit excellent 
capacitive characteristics with a high gravimetric speciﬁ c capacitance of 
245 F g −1 and good cycling stability of 10 000 cycles. Furthermore, the ﬂ exible 
solid-state supercapacitors are integrated with high performance perovs-
kite hybrid solar cells (pero-HSCs) to build self-powered electronics. It is 
found that the solid-state supercapacitors can be charged by pero-HSCs and 
discharged from 0.75 V. These results demonstrate that the self-powered 
electronics by integration of the ﬂ exible solid-state supercapacitors with 
pero-HSCs have great potential applications in storage of solar energy and in 
ﬂ exible electronics, such as portable and wearable personal devices.

 1.  Introduction 
 Recently, pervoskite hybrid solar cells (pero-HSCs) as an alter-
native to silicon-based photovoltaics have attracted signiﬁ cant 
attention due to their promising high power conversion efﬁ -
ciency (PCE). [ 1–3 ] The PCEs of pero-HSCs have skyrocketed to 
over 19%. [ 4 ] However, pero-HSCs, same as other photovoltaics, 
have to be applied in sunlight to generate electric energy and 
their PCEs are dependent on the time, location, and weather. [ 5 ] 
In order to alleviate these problems, pero-HSCs would be 
better to integrate with energy storage devices, such as super-
capacitors, to build self-powered electronics, which can store 
the electric energy generated by pero-HSCs. [ 6 ] Moreover, these

implications in the applications of storing solar energy and ﬂ ex-
ible electronics, such as portable and wearable personal devices. 
 2.  Results and Discussion 
 As described in the Experimental Section, the free-standing 
SSG ﬁ lms were prepared by chemical converted graphene 
(CCG) dispersion through facile vacuum ﬁ ltration. [ 25,31,35 ] 
 Figure  1 a presents the scanning electron microscopy (SEM) 
images of the freeze-dried SSG ﬁ lms. It is clear that the freeze-
dried SSG ﬁ lms possess smooth surfaces; however, as shown 
in the cross-section image of the SSG ﬁ lms (Figure  1 b), a 
uniform layer-by-layer structure is observed from entire SSG 
ﬁ lms. These results demonstrate that the SSG ﬁ lms formed a 
microporous structure between the graphene layers due to layer 
aggregation and π–π attractions within graphene. [ 26 ] 
 Figure  2 a displays the Fourier transform IR (FT-IR) spectra 
of graphene oxide (GO) powder and CCG powder. The broad 
peak at 3400 cm −1 is attributed to the O–H group, the peak at 
1740 cm −1 is assigned to the C=O stretching vibrations, and 
the peaks at 1365, 1425, and 1615 cm −1 are associated with 
the O–H deformations from the C–OH groups and water, 
respectively. [ 36,37 ] After GO was reduced by hydrazine hydrate 
in ammonia solution, the FT-IR spectrum was signiﬁ cantly 
changed. The intensity of asymmetric and symmetric C–O 
stretching from the C–O–C group became weak and the C=O 
peaked 1740 cm −1 is almost disappeared. These results indicate 
that the CCG was successfully prepared from GO. [ 38 ] 
 Raman spectroscopy was carried out to further conﬁ rm that 
the CCG was prepared from GO. As shown in Figure  2 b, the 
GO powder, CCG powder, and the freeze-dried SSG ﬁ lms dis-
play both G band at ≈1582 cm −1 and D band at ≈1350 cm −1 . [ 36 ] 
However, the ratios of D/G for the CCG powder and the freeze-
dried SSG ﬁ lms are higher than that of the GO powder, which 
is evidence that the GO powder was converted to the CCG 
powder. 
 By measuring the weight, it was found that the as-prepared 
SSG ﬁ lm contains about 94 wt% of water. After freeze-dried 
treatment, the thickness of the SSG ﬁ lm was decreased to 9 µm 
from 80 µm, which indicates that the as-prepared SSG ﬁ lm 
indeed has high hydrated hydrogel with high speciﬁ c area than 
that of the freeze-dried graphene ﬁ lm. The electrical conductivi-
ties measured by four-probe method are ≈0.38 and ≈1.78 S cm −1 
for the as-prepared SSG ﬁ lms and the freeze-dried SSG ﬁ lms, 
respectively. The electrical conductivity of the as-prepared SSG 
ﬁ lms is comparable to that of the dried graphene aerogels with 
3D structure (≈0.87 S cm −1 ). [ 39 ] These results indicate that the 
as-prepared SSG ﬁ lms possess high electrical conductivity. 
 Scheme  1 shows the detailed processing steps for fabrication 
of the ﬂ exible solid-state supercapacitors based on SSG ﬁ lms. 
 Figure  3 a,b present the capacitance behaviors of SSG ﬁ lms with 
a potential range from 0 to 1 V at various scan rates. As shown 
in Figure  3 a, all cyclic voltammetry (CV) curves exhibit a nearly 
rectangular shape with no obvious peaks even at a high scan 
rate 500 mv s −1 , which indicate that the SSG ﬁ lms possess an 
ideal electrical double-layer capacitance. [ 40 ] The speciﬁ c capaci-
tance ( C s ) of the solid-state supercapacitors can be calculated 
according to the equation of  C s = 4( I Δ t )/( m Δ V ), where  I is the 
discharge current,  Δt is the one cycle discharge time,  m is the 
mass of the SSG ﬁ lm electrodes, and  ΔV is the potential change 
after voltage drop during discharge, respectively. Figure  3 c,d 
present the galvanostatic charge–discharge behaviors of the 
ﬂ exible solid-state supercapacitors based on SSG ﬁ lms. Based 
on the data presented in Figure  3 c,d, the calculated  C s values 
at different current densities are shown in Figure  3 e. The ﬂ ex-
ible solid-state supercapacitors based on as-prepared SSG ﬁ lms 
exhibit  C s of ≈250 F g −1 at the current density of 0.5 A g −1 . The 
 C s remains in 245 F g −1 at the current density of 1 A g −1 , which 
is 98% of its original values. Moreover, the solid-state superca-
pacitors still possess  C s of ≈145 F g −1 , which is 59% of its orig-
inal value at the current density of 20 A g −1 . The decreased  C s 
at the high current densities is attributed to high internal resist-
ance and slow ion diffusion rate in the solid electrolyte. [ 40 ] On 
the other hand, the ﬂ exible solid-state super-
capacitors based on the freeze-dried SSG 
ﬁ lms only possess  C s of ≈181 F g −1 at the cur-
rent density of 0.5 A g −1 . The  C s is decreased 
to ≈166 and ≈116 F g −1 at the current density 
of 1 and 20 A g −1 , respectively. The small  C s 
observed from the ﬂ exible solid-state super-
capacitors base on the freeze-dried SSG ﬁ lms 
are likely due to the changes of porous struc-
ture and volume in the freeze-dried process, 
which hinders the inﬁ ltration of ions. [ 25 ] 
 In order to understand the underlying 
differences in the above two different super-
capacitors, electrochemical impedance spec-
troscopy (EIS) measurement is carried out to 
investigate the electrical properties of the SSG

 The mechanical property of the ﬂ exible solid-state super-
capacitors based on the as-prepared SSG ﬁ lms was further 
investigated.  Figure  4 a schematically displays how the ﬂ exible 
solid-state supercapacitors were bended. The CV curves of the 
solid-state supercapacitors bent at various angles are shown 
in Figure  4 b. The ﬂ exible solid-state supercapacitors possess 
approximately the same capacitor behaviors and it is even bent 
at 135°, indicating that the solid-state supercapacitors have 
excellent mechanical properties. 
 The CV of the solid-state supercapacitors measured as it was 
prepared, stored for one-week and for one-month are shown in 
 Figure  5 a. It was found that there are improved capacitance for 
the supercapacitors stored after one-week and one-month. Such 
improvement is likely due to the ions that 
were further diffused inside of the SSG ﬁ lms. 
In order to further evaluate the cyclability and 
performance durability of the solid-state super-
capacitors, the galvanostatic charge–discharge 
tests were carried out up to 10 000 cycles 
at the current density of 5 A g −1 . As shown 
in Figure  5 b, the degradation of capacitance 
takes place mainly after 2000 cycles. The 
capacitance keeps 83% of its initial values 
after 10 000 cycles. These results demonstrate 
that the solid-state supercapacitors exhibit 
excellent stability and capacitive performance. 
 The energy density and the power density 
are two important parameters used to evaluate 
the performance of supercapacitors. The energy 
density ( E ) and the power density ( P ) can be 
calculated by  E = 1/2  C s Δ V 2 and  P =  E / t , respec-
tively, [ 38,40 ] where  C s is the speciﬁ c capacitance, 
 ΔV is the potential change during the discharge 
process after voltage drop, and  t is the dis-
charge time of one cycle.  Figure  6 shows the correlation between  E 
and  P , which is termed as the Ragone plot. The ﬂ exible solid-state 
supercapacitors based on the as-prepared SSG ﬁ lms possess  E of 
8.01 Wh kg −1 at  P of 5.97 kW kg −1 . The  P can even reach to 
10.1 kW kg −1 at  E of 4.44 Wh kg −1 . However, the ﬂ exible solid-
state supercapacitors based on the freeze-dried SSG ﬁ lms cannot 
possess such excellent energy density and power density. The 
 E can only reach to 5.87 Wh kg −1 at  P of 3.05 kW kg −1 , and the 
highest  P reaches to 4.25 kW kg −1 at  E of 4.31 Wh kg −1 . Both 
 E and  P from the solid-state supercapacitors based on the as-
prepared SSG ﬁ lms are higher than those from the solid-state 
supercapacitors based on carbon nanotubes and other graphene 
ﬁ lms, [ 18,21,33,40–42 ] indicating that solid-state supercapacitors based 
on the as-prepared SSG ﬁ lms possess excellent performance of 
supercapacitors.

solid-state supercapacitors based on the as-prepared SSG ﬁ lms, 
three supercapacitor units were connected in series to make a 
tandem supercapacitor. Each supercapacitor unit has the same 
area (1 × 1 cm 2 ) and same mass loading (≈0.4 mg for one 
electrode) of the SSG ﬁ lm. The CV and galvanostatic charge–
discharge curves of both single supercapacitor and the tandem 
supercapacitors are shown in  Figure  7 a. It is 
clear that the potential windows are 1.0 and 
3.0 V for single supercapacitor and tandem 
supercapacitors, respectively. The CV of the 
tandem supercapacitors almost expresses 
the rectangular structure. These observa-
tions were further conﬁ rmed by galvanostatic 
charge–discharge measurement, as shown in 
Figure  7 b. The potential of the tandem super-
capacitors can increase to 3 V, which is three 
times of that from single supercapacitor. 
Thus, these results indicate that the tandem 
supercapacitors have potentials to be used in 
some devices that need high voltage.

 Figure  8 a presents the  J – V characteristics of pero-HSCs. The 
more details in pero-HSCs fabrication and characterization 
are reported in refs.  [ 43–45 ] . The pero-HSCs exhibits a short-

pero-HSCs fabricated by similar method and with the similar

(IPCE) spectrum of pero-HSCs is presented in Figure  8 b. 
The onset of the photocurrents observed from Figure  8 b is 
at 800 nm, which is in good agreement with the bandgap of 
CH 3 NH 3 PbI 3- x  Cl x observed from absorption spectrum. [ 46,47 ] 
Based on IPCE spectrum, the  J SC of pero-HSCs is estimated 
to be 21.14 mA cm −2 , which is consistent with that observed 
from the  J – V characteristics (Figure  8 a). It was reported that 
the photocurrent hysteresis are originated from the presence 
of traps, ferroelectrically respond in the perovskite materials 
and the ion migration in the perovskite ﬁ lms and interlayers, 
but the devices with negligible photocurrent hysteresis have 
also been reported in the case of perovskite/fullerene planar 
heterojunction solar cells provided that optimized perovs-
kite ﬁ lms. [ 48–51 ] The photocurrent hysteresis of pero-HSCs is 
tested by sweeping the  J – V measurement from both forward 
and reversed directions. The results are shown in Figure  8 c. 
The efﬁ ciency difference between  J – V under forward and 
reversed directions is less than 2%, which is probably attrib-
uted to high quality of perovskite ﬁ lm with high surface cov-

performance. 
 Figure  9 a displays the schematic diagram of integration of 
the ﬂ exible solid-state supercapacitors with pero-HSCs. After

assemble the self-powered electronics, the solid-state superca-
pacitors are charged by pero-HSCs under the white light illu-

solid-state supercapacitors with high performance pero-HSCs

 3.  Conclusions 
 In summary, the SSG ﬁ lms prepared by a facile ﬁ ltration 
method were used as the free-standing electrode in the ﬂ exible 
solid-state supercapacitors. The ﬂ exible solid-state supercapaci-
tors exhibit a high speciﬁ c capacitance of 245 F g −1 at 1 A g −1 
and retain 83% of its original values up to 10 000 charge–dis-
charge cycles. We further integrated the ﬂ exible solid-state 
supercapacitors with high performance pero-HSCs to build 
self-powered electronics. It was found that the solid-state super-
capacitors can be charged by pero-HSCs and discharged from 
0.75 V which is smaller than the open-circuit voltage of pero-
HSCs. These results demonstrate that the self-powered elec-
tronics by integration of the ﬂ exible solid-state supercapacitors 
with pero-HSCs have great potential implications in the appli-
cations of storing solar energy and ﬂ exible electronics, such as 
portable and wearable personal devices.

 Fabrication of Flexible Solid-State Supercapacitors : The fabrication 
procedures for the ﬂ exible solid-state supercapacitors based on SSG 
ﬁ lms are schematically displayed in Scheme  1 . The H 2 SO 4 -PVA gel 
electrolyte was prepared by ﬁ rst diluting 6 g H 2 SO 4 (98%) into 30 mL 
deionized (DI) water and then adding the above H 2 SO 4 solution into 6 g 
PVA with 30 mL DI water. The suspension solution was stirred at 85 °C 
until the solution became clear. After that the SSG ﬁ lm with thickness 
of ≈80 µm (step a) was cut into rectangular strips with an area of 
1 cm × 1 cm and then dried the SSG ﬁ lm to the weight of ≈0.4 mg cm −2 , 
After that, the SSG ﬁ lm was immersed into 1 M H 2 SO 4 solution overnight 
to allow H + protons to be inﬁ ltrated inside of the SSG ﬁ lm (step b). 
The SSG ﬁ lm was carefully assembled on the silver-coated polyimide 
substrate as one electrode (step c). After that, the H 2 SO 4 –PVA gel is 
casted on the top of SSG ﬁ lm from H 2 SO 4 –PVA water solution and then 
evaporated the excess water at room temperature for 12 h in the ambient 
condition to form the SSG ﬁ lm electrode coated with H 2 SO 4 –PVA solid-
state electrolyte (step d). Finally, two SSG ﬁ lm electrodes coated with

 Characterization of Flexible Solid-State Supercapacitors : CV and 
galvanostatic charge–discharge measurement were conducted by using 
Gamry reference 3000 at the potential ranging from 0 to 1 V. EIS was 
measured in the frequency ranging from 10 5 to 10 −2 Hz. 
 Fabrication of the Perovskite Hybrid Solar Cells (Pero-HSCs) : The 
pero-HSCs were fabricated in the device with a conﬁ guration of ITO/
PEDOT:PSS/CH 3 NH 3 PbI 3- x  Cl x /PC 61 BM/Al, where ITO is indium tin 
oxide, CH 3 NH 3 PbI 3- x  Cl x is perovskite materials, and Al is Aluminum. 
Approximately 35 nm of PEDOT:PSS was spin-coated on precleaned ITO 
glass substrates followed by thermal annealing at 150 °C for 10 min. 
The perovskite ﬁ lms were spin-coated on top of ITO/PEDOT:PSS from 
perovskite precursor solution in the glove box with nitrogen atmosphere. 
The perovskite thin ﬁ lms were processed by two-step procedures. In the 
ﬁ rst procedure, the spin-time was kept at 20 s, with the rotating-speed 
of 2500 rpm, but the acceleration-time was 10 s with the rotating-peed 
increased from 0 to 2500 rpm in the acceleration-time. In the second 
procedure, the acceleration-time was kept at 8 s, but the spin-time was 
tuned from 20 s, with the rotating-speed of 2500 rpm. The wet perovskite 
thin ﬁ lms were placed in petri-dish without cover for 30 min and then 
annealed at 90 °C for 3 h. Next, ≈100 nm of PC 61 BM was spin-coated 
on the top of perovskite thin ﬁ lms. Finally, ≈120 nm Al electrode was 
evaporated under high vacuum (2 × 10 6 mbar) through a shade mask. 
The device area is deﬁ ned as 4.5 mm 2 . 
 Characterization of Pero-HSCs : The current densities versus voltage 
( J – V ) characteristics of pero-HSCs were recorded using a Keithley 2400 
Source Meter. The device photocurrent was measured under air mass 
(AM) 1.5 illumination at the light intensity of 100 mW cm −2 . The light 
intensity was accurately calibrated by a standard Si photodiode. The 
Incident photon-to-current efﬁ ciency (IPCE) spectra of pero-HSCs were 
measured through the IPCE measurement setup in use at European 
solar test installation (ESTI) for cells and mini-modules. A 300 W steady-
state xenon lamp provides the source light. Up to 64 ﬁ lters (8–20 nm 
width, range from 300 to 1200 nm) are available on four ﬁ lter-wheels 
to produce the monochromatic input, which is chopped at 75 Hz, 
superimposed on the bias light and measured via the usual lock-in 
technique. 
 Fabrication and Characterization of Self-Powered Electronics : The self-
powered electronics were built by integration of the ﬂ exible solid-state 
supercapacitors with pero-HSCs through two-copper wires. The ﬂ exible 
solid-state supercapacitors were charged by the current generated from 
pero-HSCs under white light illumination. After the ﬂ exible solid-state 
supercapacitors were charged, the electrochemical workstation was 
connected with the copper wires to study the discharge properties of the 
ﬂ exible solid-state supercapacitors.

We report a co-deposited Al2O3-\nperovskite device annealed in under 2.5 seconds with a\nPCE of 10.0% compared to 10.9% for a 45 minute oven-\nannealed device.\nIntroduction\n1\nSolid-state organic-inorganic lead halide perovskite solar cells\n2\nhave recently been the subject of intense study owing to\n3\ntheir low material cost and high performance.1 The path\n4\nto these devices has spanned over two decades, beginning\n5\nwith Gr¨atzel and O’Regan’s work on sensitized colloidal\n6\nTiO2 ﬁlms leading to their widely-cited paper describing\n7\nhigh efﬁciency dye-sensitized solar cells (DSCs) in 1991.2\n8\nSince then, work on improving molecular sensitizers, redox\n9\nelectrolytes and other cell components has seen DSC power\n10\nconversion efﬁciencies (PCEs) increase to 13%.3 In 1998,\n11\nBach et al. published ﬁndings on solid-state hole transport\n12\nmaterials4 as an alternative to the aggressive liquid electrolyte\n13\nused in DSCs. Solid-state dye-sensitized solar cells (ss-DSCs)\n14\nhave since reached PCEs of 7.2%5 using the solid organic\n15\nmolecule 2-7,7-tetrakis(N,N- di-p-methoxyphenylamine)-9,9\n16\n-spirobiﬂuorene (spiro-OMeTAD) as a hole transporter.\n17\nIn 2009, Kojima et al. reported on organic-inorganic lead\n18\nhalide perovskites as a sensitizer akin to the dye in liquid\n19\nDSCs with PCEs of up to 3.81%.6 These CH3NH3PbBr3 and\n20\nCH3NH3PbI3 perovskite absorbers were quickly matched with\n21\nthe spiro-OMeTAD hole transporter in 2012 by Kim et al,7,\n22\nand Lee et al,8, achieving a PCE of over 10%. 2013 saw PCEs\n23\nfor perovskite cells reach 15.4% in a vapour-deposited device\n24\nwith no porous scaffold.9\n25\nUnlike DSCs and s-DSCs where dye molecules are adsorbed\n26\nonto a metal oxide scaffold surface at room temperature, in\n27\nperovskite solar cells the light absorbing material is activated\n28\nby crystallisation upon thermal annealing. Rapid processing of perovskite solar cells in under 2.5 seconds†
Joel Troughton, C´ecile Charbonneau, Matthew J. Carnie, Matthew L. Davies, David A. Worsley, and
Trystan M. Watson
Received Xth XXXXXXXXXX 20XX, Accepted Xth XXXXXXXXX 20XX

DOI: 10.1039/b000000x
A rapid annealing technique for CH3NH3PbI3 perovskite
solar cells is presented. We report a co-deposited Al2O3-
perovskite device annealed in under 2.5 seconds with a
PCE of 10.0% compared to 10.9% for a 45 minute oven-
annealed device.
Introduction
1
Solid-state organic-inorganic lead halide perovskite solar cells
2
have recently been the subject of intense study owing to
3
their low material cost and high performance.1 The path
4
to these devices has spanned over two decades, beginning
5
with Gr¨atzel and O’Regan’s work on sensitized colloidal
6
TiO2 ﬁlms leading to their widely-cited paper describing
7
high efﬁciency dye-sensitized solar cells (DSCs) in 1991.2
8
Since then, work on improving molecular sensitizers, redox
9
electrolytes and other cell components has seen DSC power
10
conversion efﬁciencies (PCEs) increase to 13%.3 In 1998,
11
Bach et al. published ﬁndings on solid-state hole transport
12
materials4 as an alternative to the aggressive liquid electrolyte
13
used in DSCs. Solid-state dye-sensitized solar cells (ss-DSCs)
14
have since reached PCEs of 7.2%5 using the solid organic
15
molecule 2-7,7-tetrakis(N,N- di-p-methoxyphenylamine)-9,9
16
-spirobiﬂuorene (spiro-OMeTAD) as a hole transporter.
17
In 2009, Kojima et al. reported on organic-inorganic lead
18
halide perovskites as a sensitizer akin to the dye in liquid
19
DSCs with PCEs of up to 3.81%.6 These CH3NH3PbBr3 and
20
CH3NH3PbI3 perovskite absorbers were quickly matched with
21
the spiro-OMeTAD hole transporter in 2012 by Kim et al,7,
22
and Lee et al,8, achieving a PCE of over 10%. 2013 saw PCEs
23
for perovskite cells reach 15.4% in a vapour-deposited device
24
with no porous scaffold.9
25
Unlike DSCs and s-DSCs where dye molecules are adsorbed
26
onto a metal oxide scaffold surface at room temperature, in
27
perovskite solar cells the light absorbing material is activated
28
by crystallisation upon thermal annealing. Typically, lab-scale
29

perovskite devices are fabricated onto glass substrates coated
30
with a layer of ﬂuorine-doped tin oxide (FTO) as well as a
31
compact layer of TiO2 (c-TiO2) to act as an electron collection
32
layer.
33
A porous scaffold material may also be sintered to the c-
34
TiO2 to increase surface area and improve charge injection.
35
Historically, this layer consisted of a mesoporous network of
36
anatase TiO2 nanoparticles (m-TiO2). However, Lee et al.
37
demonstrated that a mesoporous network of insulating Al2O3
38
nanoparticles may also yield high PCEs.8 In this case, electron
39
transfer is facilitated entirely through the perovskite material
40
itself, rather than slower transport through the m-TiO2 network.
41
Work by this research group has shown that improvements to
42
device performance can be achieved by simply adding Al2O3
10
43
and SiO2
11 nanoparticles to the perovskite precursor solution.
44
The use of this single step deposition technique can remove the
45
need for a discrete, separately deposited, scaffold layer.
46
Typically for device preparation, a solution containing
47
CH3NH3I and a lead halide salt (PbCl2, PbI2 or PbBr2)
48
dissolved in DMF (N,N-dimethylformamide) is deposited onto
49
the substrate through spin coating, followed by a heat treatment
50
at T >100 ◦C12 to evaporate residual solvent from the ﬁlm,
51
as well as to control the crystallisation of the perovskite
52
material. Typically the annealing process takes between 5
53
to 120 minutes7,8,13–18 to achieve optimal crystallisation and
54
this can be carried out in multiple or ramped stages19,20. This
55
lengthy process poses a potential bottleneck to the large-scale
56
manufacture of perovskite solar cells on an industrial scale
57
and is relatively unpredictable in terms of performance when
58
performed under ambient conditions.
59
In this work, we present an alternative method of post-
60
annealing perovskite ﬁlms which reduces the time required to
61
as little as 2.5 seconds whilst maintaining high PCEs. This was
62
achieved by exposing the freshly deposited perovskite ﬁlm to a
63
short burst of near-infrared (NIR) radiation using commercially
64
available NIR lamps. The NIR region of the electromagnetic
65
spectrum is situated between the visible and the infrared with
66
wavelengths ranging from 700 nm to 2500 nm, peaking at
67
1000 nm. NIR sintering of porous TiO2 ﬁlms has already been
68
demonstrated for use in DSCs21,22 and much like the TiO2
69
precusor paste used to make DSCs the perovskite precursor
70

Conclusions
225
We have demonstrated that it is possible to produce organic-
226
inorganic lead halide perovskite solar cells with PCEs over
227
10% using an annealing process that is orders of magnitude
228
faster than the traditional method widely used in literature.
229
With this faster and less energy-intensive processing method,
230
crystallographic analysis has shown a more preferentially
231
oriented structure. We have also offered possible explanations
232
for differences in VOC, JSC and ﬁll factor in the two processing
233
methods. Further optimisations of NIR annealing parameters
234
will almost certainly improve PCEs and lead to the possibility
235
of rapidly processed and commercially attractive perovskite
236
based photovoltaic products.

Rapid processing of perovskite solar cells in under 2.5 seconds†
Joel Troughton, C´ecile Charbonneau, Matthew J. Carnie, Matthew L. Davies, David A. Worsley, and
Trystan M. Watson
Received Xth XXXXXXXXXX 20XX, Accepted Xth XXXXXXXXX 20XX

A rapid annealing technique for CH3NH3PbI3 perovskite
solar cells is presented. We report a co-deposited Al2O3-
perovskite device annealed in under 2.5 seconds with a
PCE of 10.0% compared to 10.9% for a 45 minute oven-
annealed device.
Introduction
1
Solid-state organic-inorganic lead halide perovskite solar cells
2
have recently been the subject of intense study owing to
3
their low material cost and high performance.1 The path
4
to these devices has spanned over two decades, beginning
5
with Gr¨atzel and O’Regan’s work on sensitized colloidal
6
TiO2 ﬁlms leading to their widely-cited paper describing
7
high efﬁciency dye-sensitized solar cells (DSCs) in 1991.2
8
Since then, work on improving molecular sensitizers, redox
9
electrolytes and other cell components has seen DSC power
10
conversion efﬁciencies (PCEs) increase to 13%.3 In 1998,
11
Bach et al. published ﬁndings on solid-state hole transport
12
materials4 as an alternative to the aggressive liquid electrolyte
13
used in DSCs. Solid-state dye-sensitized solar cells (ss-DSCs)
14
have since reached PCEs of 7.2%5 using the solid organic
15
molecule 2-7,7-tetrakis(N,N- di-p-methoxyphenylamine)-9,9
16
-spirobiﬂuorene (spiro-OMeTAD) as a hole transporter.
17
In 2009, Kojima et al. reported on organic-inorganic lead
18
halide perovskites as a sensitizer akin to the dye in liquid
19
DSCs with PCEs of up to 3.81%.6 These CH3NH3PbBr3 and
20
CH3NH3PbI3 perovskite absorbers were quickly matched with
21
the spiro-OMeTAD hole transporter in 2012 by Kim et al,7,
22
and Lee et al,8, achieving a PCE of over 10%. 2013 saw PCEs
23
for perovskite cells reach 15.4% in a vapour-deposited device
24
with no porous scaffold.9
25
Unlike DSCs and s-DSCs where dye molecules are adsorbed
26
onto a metal oxide scaffold surface at room temperature, in
27
perovskite solar cells the light absorbing material is activated
28
by crystallisation upon thermal annealing. Typically, lab-scale
29
† Electronic Supplementary Information (ESI) available: [details of any

perovskite devices are fabricated onto glass substrates coated
30
with a layer of ﬂuorine-doped tin oxide (FTO) as well as a
31
compact layer of TiO2 (c-TiO2) to act as an electron collection
32
layer.
33
A porous scaffold material may also be sintered to the c-
34
TiO2 to increase surface area and improve charge injection.
35
Historically, this layer consisted of a mesoporous network of
36
anatase TiO2 nanoparticles (m-TiO2). However, Lee et al.
37
demonstrated that a mesoporous network of insulating Al2O3
38
nanoparticles may also yield high PCEs.8 In this case, electron
39
transfer is facilitated entirely through the perovskite material
40
itself, rather than slower transport through the m-TiO2 network.
41
Work by this research group has shown that improvements to
42
device performance can be achieved by simply adding Al2O3
10
43
and SiO2
11 nanoparticles to the perovskite precursor solution.
44
The use of this single step deposition technique can remove the
45
need for a discrete, separately deposited, scaffold layer.
46
Typically for device preparation, a solution containing
47
CH3NH3I and a lead halide salt (PbCl2, PbI2 or PbBr2)
48
dissolved in DMF (N,N-dimethylformamide) is deposited onto
49
the substrate through spin coating, followed by a heat treatment
50
at T >100 ◦C12 to evaporate residual solvent from the ﬁlm,
51
as well as to control the crystallisation of the perovskite
52
material. Typically the annealing process takes between 5
53
to 120 minutes7,8,13–18 to achieve optimal crystallisation and
54
this can be carried out in multiple or ramped stages19,20. This
55
lengthy process poses a potential bottleneck to the large-scale
56
manufacture of perovskite solar cells on an industrial scale
57
and is relatively unpredictable in terms of performance when
58
performed under ambient conditions.
59
In this work, we present an alternative method of post-
60
annealing perovskite ﬁlms which reduces the time required to
61
as little as 2.5 seconds whilst maintaining high PCEs. This was
62
achieved by exposing the freshly deposited perovskite ﬁlm to a
63
short burst of near-infrared (NIR) radiation using commercially
64
available NIR lamps. The NIR region of the electromagnetic
65
spectrum is situated between the visible and the infrared with
66
wavelengths ranging from 700 nm to 2500 nm, peaking at
67
1000 nm. NIR sintering of porous TiO2 ﬁlms has already been
68
demonstrated for use in DSCs21,22 and much like the TiO2
69
precusor paste used to make DSCs the perovskite precursor
70

Conclusions
225
We have demonstrated that it is possible to produce organic-
226
inorganic lead halide perovskite solar cells with PCEs over
227
10% using an annealing process that is orders of magnitude
228
faster than the traditional method widely used in literature.
229
With this faster and less energy-intensive processing method,
230
crystallographic analysis has shown a more preferentially
231
oriented structure. We have also offered possible explanations
232
for differences in VOC, JSC and ﬁll factor in the two processing
233
methods. Further optimisations of NIR annealing parameters
234
will almost certainly improve PCEs and lead to the possibility
235
of rapidly processed and commercially attractive perovskite
236
based photovoltaic products.
237

1. Introduction
The ﬁrst solid-state perovskite solar cell (PSC) was introduced in
2012,[1,2] and since then, organic–inorganic halide perovskites
(OIHPs) have emerged as a major focus of research due to their
immense
potential
for

practical
applications.[3–5]
They offer various advantages, such as an
adjustable bandgap,[6] high light absorp-
tion,[7] long carrier diffusion length,[8,9]
and simple and low-cost solution process-
ing. After a decade of development, PSCs
have achieved a power conversion efﬁ-
ciency (PCE) of 26%.[10] In parallel, the
development of perovskite-silicon tandem
solar cells has also gained widespread inter-
est.[11,12] Combining the high light absorp-
tion and long carrier diffusion length of
perovskite materials with the traditional sil-
icon solar cell structure can improve the
overall PCE and reduce costs. The solution
processing capacity of perovskite materials
also opens up the potential for large-scale
commercial production, allowing for the
realization of low-cost and highly efﬁcient
large-area PSCs.[13,14] Therefore, applying
perovskite materials in optoelectronics is
crucial for the next breakthrough.[15] With
their unique advantages and potential,
PSCs are believed to be the most promising
candidates for the next generation of photovoltaic devices.
Among the various perovskites with the typical 3D structure
of ABX3 (A is the monovalent organic ammonium cation or
cesium (Cs), B is the divalent metal cation, and X stands for
the halide),[16] formamidinium (FAþ) lead iodide (FAPbI3)
perovskites have better application prospects compared to con-
ventional methylammonium (MAþ) lead iodide (MAPbI3) perov-
skites. FAPbI3 perovskites possess a narrower bandgap, which
allows them to absorb light over a broader range of wavelengths
to increase device efﬁciency.[6,17,18] Since FAþ is chemically more
stable than MAþ, FAPbI3 displays higher thermal degradation
activation energy than MAPbI3, making FAPbI3-based perov-
skites possess better thermal stability.[19–22]
The black-phase α-FAPbI3, despite its importance in practical
applications, is highly metastable at room temperature and is
more likely to transform into the yellow δ phase,[23–25] which
poses an obstacle in the commercialization of FAPbI3 perov-
skites. The susceptibility of perovskite to moisture can even accel-
erate this undesirable phase transformation. A signiﬁcant factor
leading to this instability is the large radius of the FAþ, which
results in octahedral deformation, disrupting the α phase stability
of FAPbI3. The high annealing temperature of >160 °C required
to prepare α-FAPbI3 further complicates this process.[26] Thus,
attaining the black phase and maintaining the desired structure
of FAPbI3 ﬁlms is a difﬁcult task. In order to improve the stability

The power conversion efﬁciency (PCE) of organic–inorganic halide perovskite
solar cells (PSCs) has increased rapidly in recent years, with the certiﬁed best
perovskite single-junction photovoltaics reaching an astounding PCE of 26%.
Formamidine (FA)-based perovskites possess excellent photovoltaic properties
and superior thermal stability, establishing them as one of the most promising
perovskite materials for light absorption. However, the issue of the phase
instability of black-phase formamidinium lead iodide (α-FAPbI3) perovskite has
seriously impeded its commercialization process, with the strain found in
perovskite ﬁlms being regarded as a signiﬁcant factor impacting the stability of
PSCs. This article begins by examining the sources of strain and the charac-
terization techniques related to perovskites. Subsequently, it outlines the effects
of strain on FA-based perovskites and presents strategies to modify lattice strain.
Finally, the potential for strain engineering in the future is discussed. This review
aims to clarify the impact of strain on FA-based perovskite, determine potential
methods of strain engineering to enhance device performance, and ultimately
facilitate the commercialization of these materials.

of the black phase, many methods have been proposed to facili-
tate the preparation of α phase FA-based perovskites. Strain engi-
neering is one of the effective methods by which the stability of
the black phase may be improved. Strain refers to a common
physical phenomenon in semiconductors that deﬁnes the varia-
tion of the lattice constant of an ideal crystal caused by intrinsic
deformation (such as point vacancy defects and lattice orientation
expansion) and external conditions (light, electrical bias, and
pressure). Strain in semiconductors can lead to dislocations
and point defects, further promoting the degradation and
destruction of semiconductor ﬁlms. PSCs are even more vulner-
able to strain because of their soft lattice structure. Additionally,
strain in halide perovskite materials, including FAPbI3, can lead
to more defects and nonradiative recombination, adversely affect-
ing device performance.[27,28] Therefore, the instability caused by
strain impedes the commercialization of PSCs. It is of para-
mount importance to adjust lattice strain to enhance the photo-
voltaic performance and intrinsic stability of PSCs.[29]
Several recent studies have suggested that perovskite devices
are more efﬁcient when subjected to compressive strain.[30–32]
Therefore, lattice strain regulation is crucial to achieving long-term,
efﬁcient, and stable PSCs. Although several articles explore strain
engineering topics for PSCs, they are yet to speciﬁcally focus on the
impact of strain engineering on FA-based PSCs.[33–37] Given the
urgent need for a systematic study of FA-based perovskites, this
article summarizes the latest progress in related work, with a spe-
ciﬁc focus on the impact of strain on FA-based perovskite ﬁlms.
Consequently, we present an overview of the strain engineering
strategies for FA-based perovskites to enhance their efﬁciency
and stability, thereby accelerating the commercialization of
PSCs. This review initially outlines the origins and characterization
methods of strain, followed by a discussion of the effect of strain on
FA-based perovskite ﬁlms. We then summarize the strain regula-
tion strategies feasible for FA-based perovskites (Figure 1).
Additionally, we explore the possible future directions in strain
engineering to guide the development of FA-based perovskite.
2. Origin of Strain in Perovskite Films
Crystallization of perovskites typically involves a thermal treatment
to convert the precursor solution into a high-quality ﬁlm. FA-based
perovskite often requires higher annealing temperatures, result-
ing in stress during the cooling process. Strain is the stress applied
to cause changes in lattice parameters. It is frequently quantiﬁed
as the ratio of the change in lattice parameters caused by stress to
the lattice parameter of the strain-free material

where Δa represents the change in lattice constant due to stress,
and a0 represents the lattice constant of strain-free materials.[38]
The tensile strain occurs when the length of the lattice increases
under stress. In contrast, compressive strain is induced by
stress-caused lattice contraction.[39] Another feature of strain is
microstrain, which could be analyzed by Bragg peak width
(Figure 2a).[35] Herein, Figure 2b summarizes the types of lattice
strain in perovskite ﬁlms. Depending on the stress nature, the
strain could be classiﬁed into internal and external strain.
2.1. Internal Strain

by the nonperiodicity of the crystal. Lead iodine octahedral tilt
and nonuniform crystallization usually disrupt crystal symmetry
and cause internal strain.
