of the black phase, many methods have been proposed to facili-
tate the preparation of α phase FA-based perovskites. Strain engi-
neering is one of the effective methods by which the stability of
the black phase may be improved. Strain refers to a common
physical phenomenon in semiconductors that deﬁnes the varia-
tion of the lattice constant of an ideal crystal caused by intrinsic
deformation (such as point vacancy defects and lattice orientation
expansion) and external conditions (light, electrical bias, and
pressure). Strain in semiconductors can lead to dislocations
and point defects, further promoting the degradation and
destruction of semiconductor ﬁlms. PSCs are even more vulner-
able to strain because of their soft lattice structure. Additionally,
strain in halide perovskite materials, including FAPbI3, can lead
to more defects and nonradiative recombination, adversely affect-
ing device performance.[27,28] Therefore, the instability caused by
strain impedes the commercialization of PSCs. It is of para-
mount importance to adjust lattice strain to enhance the photo-
voltaic performance and intrinsic stability of PSCs.[29]
Several recent studies have suggested that perovskite devices
are more efﬁcient when subjected to compressive strain.[30–32]
Therefore, lattice strain regulation is crucial to achieving long-term,
efﬁcient, and stable PSCs. Although several articles explore strain
engineering topics for PSCs, they are yet to speciﬁcally focus on the
impact of strain engineering on FA-based PSCs.[33–37] Given the
urgent need for a systematic study of FA-based perovskites, this
article summarizes the latest progress in related work, with a spe-
ciﬁc focus on the impact of strain on FA-based perovskite ﬁlms.
Consequently, we present an overview of the strain engineering
strategies for FA-based perovskites to enhance their efﬁciency
and stability, thereby accelerating the commercialization of
PSCs. This review initially outlines the origins and characterization
methods of strain, followed by a discussion of the effect of strain on
FA-based perovskite ﬁlms. We then summarize the strain regula-
tion strategies feasible for FA-based perovskites (Figure 1).
Additionally, we explore the possible future directions in strain
engineering to guide the development of FA-based perovskite.
2. Origin of Strain in Perovskite Films
Crystallization of perovskites typically involves a thermal treatment
to convert the precursor solution into a high-quality ﬁlm. FA-based
perovskite often requires higher annealing temperatures, result-
ing in stress during the cooling process. Strain is the stress applied
to cause changes in lattice parameters. It is frequently quantiﬁed
as the ratio of the change in lattice parameters caused by stress to
the lattice parameter of the strain-free material
ε ¼ Δa
a0
(1)
where Δa represents the change in lattice constant due to stress,
and a0 represents the lattice constant of strain-free materials.[38]
The tensile strain occurs when the length of the lattice increases
under stress. In contrast, compressive strain is induced by
stress-caused lattice contraction.[39] Another feature of strain is
microstrain, which could be analyzed by Bragg peak width
(Figure 2a).[35] Herein, Figure 2b summarizes the types of lattice
strain in perovskite ﬁlms. Depending on the stress nature, the
strain could be classiﬁed into internal and external strain.
2.1. Internal Strain
Internal strain is inherent in perovskite crystals, which is caused
by the nonperiodicity of the crystal. Lead iodine octahedral tilt
and nonuniform crystallization usually disrupt crystal symmetry
and cause internal strain.

As shown in Figure 2c, perovskites with the chemical formula of
ABX3 exhibit cubic symmetry, and the stable crystal structure of
the perovskites can be predicted by the reliable empirical index

degree of ½PbI64 octahedral tilt is caused by the formation of
hydrogen bonds, resulting in diverse crystal structures, even
though the ion radius of MAþ and FAþ is relatively similar to each
other.[44]
Since the t of FAPbI3 is very close to 1, it is stabilized in the
cubic perovskite phase at temperatures above 150 °C. However,
it tends to transform to the yellow δ phase at room tempera-
ture.[45] Anisotropic strain lattices present in the (111) plane of
the FAPbI3 crystal structure promote the transition from the α
phase to the δ phase.[46] The δ phase transition is accelerated at
room temperature, especially under humid air. To inhibit the
α-to-δ phase transition by inducing the formation of octahedral
tilt, alloyed perovskites such as MAþ, Csþ, and methylene
diammonium
(MDA2þ)
can
be
added
to
A-position
cations.[28,47–49] Nevertheless, incorporating A-position cations
creates an offset in the bandgap and impairs thermal stability.
Thus, Doherty et al. proposed applying additives (such as ethyl-
enediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA)) that do not incorporate
perovskites to grow pure α-FAPbI3 ﬁlms.[50]
2.1.2. Nonuniform Crystallization
Crystallization involves two main processes: nucleation and
growth.[51] Nucleation can occur uniformly or nonuniformly,
with the latter being preferred at speciﬁc locations such as phase
boundaries and surfaces.[52] During nonuniform nucleation,
molecules deposit onto the surface of their crystalline phase
and the solid, forming the crystalline phase/solid interface.
This process can produce strain sources such as grain bound-
aries (GBs) and twin boundaries (Figure 3c).[35] In addition to
nucleation, the growth process also generates strain due to the
stoichiometric mismatch between the perovskite components
and the different growth conditions during ﬁlm formation. As
a result, the ﬁlm may exhibit inhomogeneity. In a study by
Chen et al., it was found that uneven growth of perovskite ﬁlms
can cause lattice distortion in the crystal structure, which in turn
leads to lattice strain (Figure 3d–g).[53]
Perovskite ﬁlms frequently exhibit localized strain inhomoge-
neity, nonstoichiometric chemical composition at GBs, and high
grain orientation spread (GOS), which can negatively impact
their photovoltaic performance (Figure 3h).[35,54,55] Growing
large perovskite crystals can lead to higher GOS and stronger
nonradiative recombination, further affecting performance.[54]
Researchers have employed various methods to promote the
ordered crystallization of perovskite ﬁlms, including perovskite
crystal arrays (PCA) and precrystallized 2D microcrystallites
(Figure 3i).[56,57] These methods can reduce lattice strain by
controlling the uniform growth of crystallization kinetics and
lead to high-quality perovskite ﬁlms with excellent photovoltaic
properties.
2.2. External Strain
The conditions of external stress periodically deform the lattice,
leading to external strain. This type of strain arises from external
factors such as lattice and thermal expansion mismatch between
ﬁlms and adjacent substrates. External strain is exotic since it
originates from external factors.
2.2.1. Mismatch in the Coefﬁcient of Thermal Expansion
Perovskite ﬁlms are typically crystallized on semiconductor sub-
strates. During the thermal annealing process, the thermal
expansion coefﬁcient mismatch between the perovskites and
substrates results in strain on the ﬁlms (Figure 4a).[58] As the
perovskite ﬁlm created at high temperatures cools to room tem-
perature, the mismatch of the coefﬁcient of thermal expansion
prevents the perovskite ﬁlm from shrinking, causing it to expe-
rience tensile strain in the plane direction while simultaneously
generated compressive strain occurs in the out-of-plane direction
because of the positive Poisson’s ratio in perovskites.[59] The rela-
tionship between residual strain (σ) and thermal expansion mis-
match can be expressed as the following equation
σΔT ¼

and the perovskite layer, respectively.[58,60]
Generally, PSCs require annealing ﬁlms at temperatures over
100 °C to achieve optimal performance. Speciﬁcally, FA-based
perovskites typically require temperatures higher than 150 °C
to enhance crystallinity while reducing defects. However, cooling
the ﬁlms from the annealing temperature to room temperature
causes a larger temperature gradient and increased strain. Thus,
the annealed FA-based perovskite ﬁlms unavoidably experience
some strain. Liu et al. proposed a dynamic liquid-crystal transi-
tion (DLCT) strategy to reduce the stress generated during
annealing. DLCT induces a concentrated LC solid to form during
the annealing process, releasing residual stress.[61]

3. Characterization of Strain
Numerous techniques can be utilized to characterize strain in
perovskites and evaluate its inﬂuence on the photovoltaic perfor-
mance of PSCs.[33] These techniques can be categorized into two
groups: surface strain and interior strain characterization
(Figure 5). It is important to note that surface strain and interior
strain testing methods are not entirely independent. Selecting
the appropriate way should consider the actual measurement
needs and sample characteristics.
3.1. Characterization of Surface Strain
The complex lattice structure of perovskites makes them suscep-
tible to strain-related issues. The surface layer, in particular, is
more sensitive to strain due to the ease with which it is generated
at the interface, which can signiﬁcantly impact the performance
and stability of the perovskite. Therefore, it is crucial to investi-
gate the distribution and patterns of surface strain in perovskite
ﬁlms. Characterization methods for surface strain primarily
encompass photoluminescence (PL), Raman spectroscopy, and
time-resolved photoluminescence (TRPL), which employ distinct
physical signals to characterize surface strain.
When a perovskite ﬁlm is stressed, the lattice distortion results
in a series of phonon spectral lines displacement. Raman spec-
troscopy captures these spectral line changes to measure the
strain. In a study by Torabi et al., the compressive strain was esti-
mated by analyzing the active Raman mode displacement of the
perovskite layer.[78] Similarly, Xu et al. utilized Raman spectros-
copy to investigate the structure of α-FAPbI3 under 0–2.4% com-
pression strain. Their ﬁndings suggest that as the strain
increased, the inorganic skeleton became more tetragonal with
a corresponding increase in Raman signal strength. By the time
the strain reached 1.4%, the Raman peak had split into two,
with the main peak experiencing a blueshift due to the compres-
sion of the Pb─I bond in the plane and the associated Raman
peak undergoing a redshift that reﬂects the stretching of Pb─I
bond outside the plane (Figure 6a).[64] Therefore, Raman spec-
troscopy is a highly effective method for strain measurements,
given its simplicity and sensitivity.
PL spectroscopy is an effective measurement technique for
surface strain in perovskite ﬁlms. Strain and defects have the
potential to reduce the recombination velocity of excitons,
resulting in a variation in PL strength, enabling the characteri-
zation of the distribution of surface strain through PL spectra
measurement (Figure 6b).[54] To directly assess the impact of
strain-related defects on perovskite photovoltaic performance,
Stranks et al. employed PL to investigate the compressively
strained thin ﬁlm and obtained a confocal PL intensity map of
the affected region, ultimately ﬁnding that the local PL distribu-
tion was dominated by strain-induced trap states.[27] TRPL is a
time-resolved measurement method that provides insight into
the surface strain of thin ﬁlms by assessing the lifetime and relax-
ation time of excitons. Stranks and co-workers continued to use
TRPL to assess the ﬁlm’s surface, ﬁnding that regions without
stress had a longer carrier lifetime but that the PL lifetime statisti-
cally declined with an increase in compressive strain (Figure 6c).[27]
Therefore, PL and TRPL possess signiﬁcant potential and

3.3. Simultaneous Characterization of Interior and Surface
Strain
It is essential to analyze strain information on both their surface
and depth to gain comprehensive, accurate, and rapid insight
into the strain of perovskite ﬁlms. The perovskite ﬁlm’s strain
can be better understood by combining interior strain analysis
with the surface strain distribution. Electron backscatter diffrac-
tion (EBSD), grazing-incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering
(GIWAXS), and the aforementioned GIXRD and TEM are all
capable of characterizing both surface and interior strains.
EBSD characterizes the surface of a material through scan-
ning electron microscopy (SEM) while employing dynamic cyclo-
tron
diffraction
to
measure
surface
and
interior
strain
information. Recent advancements in detector technology and
low-vacuum measurement techniques make EBSD mapping
of perovskite ﬁlms feasible (Figure 6g).[54,82–84] For instance,
Ginger et al. employed EBSD to estimate the local strain induced
by crystal orientation errors and assess the strain levels at grains
and GBs of perovskite ﬁlms (Figure 6h).[54] EBSD can also detect
micro- and nanolevel strains, providing valuable insights into the
local lattice strain of perovskite ﬁlms.
As a wide-angle X-ray scattering technology, GIWAXS is
capable of directly obtaining information regarding the global
strain state and distribution in perovskite. It can also accurately
characterize both surface and interior strains.[85,86] Zheng et al.
used GIWAXS to describe the evolution and distribution of
residual strain in perovskite ﬁlms during antisolvent spin
coating (Figure 6i).[85] Using a series of incidence angles ranging
from 0.1° to 2° to investigate the depth-dependent microstructure
of the ﬁlm from the surface to the interior, they were able to
generate a GIWAXS pattern by integrating the orientation in
the in-plane or out-of-plane direction (Figure 6j).[85] Using
GIWAXS signiﬁcantly improves the accuracy of strain analysis
and shows promise as a method for characterizing interior and
surface strains.
4. Strain Effects
It is common for strains to persist during the fabrication of
FA-based perovskite ﬁlms, resulting in notable impacts on their
properties. The strain affects essential properties of perovskites,
such as electron band structure, carrier transport, defect proper-
ties, ion mobility, as well as their overall stability.
4.1. Electronic Band Structure
Lattice distortion is one of the consequences of strain, which
results in crystal deformation in perovskites. Commonly, tilting,
enlarging, or shrinking of the octahedral ½PbI64 skeleton lead to
crystal deformation. The adjustment of bond energy in the lattice
caused by strain-induced lattice distortion leads to changes in the
electronic band structure of FAPbI3 under different strains.
Chen and co-workers discovered that the bandgap slowly
increases during the transition from compressive strain to tensile
strain (Figure 7a).[53] Given the transformation of bandgap under
diverse strains, Ghosh et al. analyzed the structural changes of
perovskites under pressure at the atomic level.[30] They utilized
high-level ab initio simulation techniques to explore the structure
of FA1xCsxPbI3 electron bands under lattice compression. It
was discovered that as compression stress increased, the
bandgap decreased and the absorption sideband showed redshift.
Simultaneously, as the pressure changed, the variation of the
maximum value of the valence band maximum (VBM) compared
to the minimum value of the conduction band maximum (CBM)
became more pronounced (Figure 7b).[30] This different change
in the edge of the band under strain can be explained by the
charge densities of VBM and CBM (Figure 7c).[30] The CBM
in halide lead perovskites is mainly composed of relatively local
Pb-6p orbitals. Accordingly, the VBM is determined by the anti-
bonding between Pb-6s and halide (X)-p orbitals.[87,88] As the
pressure grows, the Pb─I bond length shortens, whichincreases
the inclination of the ½PbI64 octahedron. The shortened Pb─I
bond reinforces the antibond overlap between the Pb-6s and I-5p
orbitals, and the energy of the valence band edge increases
accordingly. Although the tilt of ½PbI64 octahedron leads to a
decrease in the energy of the VBM, the Pb─I bond plays a domi-
nant role during the Pb─I─Pb angle twist, and eventually, the

4.3. Defect Properties
Halide perovskites possess a unique electronic structure that
endows them with high defect tolerance, which is attributable
to the location of their antibond state in VBM. Nonetheless,
surface or GB defects in perovskite ﬁlms tend to create trap states
and
undermine
the
photovoltaic
performance
of
devices
(Figure 8a).[97,98] Defects may be induced when perovskites are sub-
jected to strain. The inherent defects of vacancy and point are usu-
ally related to their formation energy, which can reﬂect the point
defects density of perovskite.[99] Xue et al. applied density func-
tional theory (DFT) to determine how halide vacancy formation
energy varies under different strain conditions. They demonstrated
that tensile strain diminishes halide vacancy formation energy,
while compressive strain ampliﬁes halide hole formation energy
in contrast to strain-free perovskites. As a result, tensile strain cur-
tails nonradiative recombination and elevates device efﬁcacy
(Figure 8b).[58] Islam et al. computed the thermodynamic transition
level of the intrinsic vacancy defect of FA1xCsxPbI3 (x = 0, 0.25)
under external pressure conditions. They detected an alteration in
the transition state energy level of iodide vacancy with more mas-
sive pressure greater than 2 Gpa, leading to a signiﬁcant transition
in iodine vacancy from shallow to deep in FA-based perovskites,
which can act as a nonradiative composition center at pressures
below 0.5 Gpa. However, the transition state energy level of iodine
vacancy defects remains mostly unaltered, and the effect, if any, on
carriers is virtually marginal (Figure 8c).[30] More importantly,
strain favors the formation of FAPbI3 vacancies. Sargent et al. dis-
covered that subbing in Csþ/MAþ and Br for FAþ and I would
alleviate strain and intensify the energy necessary for creating lead
iodide vacancies.[41] In addition, MAPbI3 exhibits the same trend,
meaning that tensile strain increases defect concentration, leading
to nonradiative recombination.[27]
4.4. Device Stability
The strain not only affects the PCE of FA-based PSCs, but it also
signiﬁcantly impacts the stability of devices. The impairment of
perovskite device stability caused by strain poses a signiﬁcant
obstacle to their commercialization.
4.4.1. Structural Stability
Cubic perovskites have shown potential for photovoltaic applica-
tions due to their unique properties. However, α-FAPbI3, a
speciﬁc kind of cubic perovskite, has a critical stability range,
and its cubic perovskite structure is prone to converting to
polygon-shared or edge-shared octahedrons. This impedes the
application of perovskites in photovoltaics.[100] Lattice strain sig-
niﬁcantly affects the structural stability of α-FAPbI3, which is
mainly reﬂected in the phase stability. Many researchers have
discovered that at room temperature, especially in humid air,
the α phase of FAPbI3 easily transitions toward the δ phase.
Zheng et al. demonstrated that lattice tensile strain drives the
transformation of the α phase to the δ phase, while this tensile
strain is alleviated due to the phase transition (Figure 8d).[46]
Chen and co-workers tested the phase stability of FAPbI3 using
XRD, Raman spectroscopy, and PL.[64] Their results showed that
under a compressive strain of 2.4%, the α phase FAPbI3 main-
tains its structural integrity in the XRD pattern even after
360 days. On the other hand, the strain-free FAPbI3 transformed
to the δ phase after only 24 h. Raman and PL analyses also con-
ﬁrmed that compressive strain exhibited better stability for the α
phase of FAPbI3. One signiﬁcant reason that compressive strain
energy stabilizes the α phase is that the compressive stress coun-
teracts the driving force of the α phase to the δ phase, namely the
tensile stress. As a result, the compressive stress restrains the
structural
deformation
caused
by
the
phase
transition
(Figure 8e,f).[64] In addition, Li et al. found that tensile strain
had a different effect on the stability of the black γ phase of
CsPbI3 compared to that of FAPbI3. The tensile strain made
the black γ phase more stable than the yellow δ phase for
CsPbI3
at
room
temperature,
and
it
was
not
so
with
FAPbI3.[101,102]
4.4.2. Material Stability
In FAPbI3, lattice strain promotes the formation of point defect
vacancies. Point defect vacancies in perovskites, especially halide
vacancies, are thought to be the crucial source of instability of
perovskites.[41] The reason for this is that the point defect has
a high afﬁnity for water and oxygen molecules, making it easier
for oxygen and water molecules to penetrate the perovskite lat-
tice. Additionally, strain-induced point defect vacancies can lead
to ion migration, resulting in phase segregation of FA-based per-
ovskites.[103] Zhao et al. investigated the effect of strain on the
stability of perovskite ﬁlms under illumination (Figure 8g).[59]
They found that, after 500 h of light, the unstrained perovskite
ﬁlms remained stable, whereas the ﬁlms under strain degraded
easily.[59] Furthermore, the activation energy of ion migration in
the ﬁlm decreased as the applied strain increased. The activation
energy of ion migration in perovskite ﬁlms can be calculated
utilizing the Nernst–Einstein relationship:

5.1.1. Cation/Anion Doping
FAPbI3 experiences lattice strain due to the weak interaction
between FAþ and the ½PbI64 octahedral backbone, leading to
reduced PSC performance. An effective method to alleviate strain
and adjust the tolerance factor is to alloy small ions. Common
doping ions in the A-position include MAþ, Csþ, MDA2þ, and
Rbþ. Cd2þ and Sr2þ often serve as ions for the incorporation into
the B-position, while halogen ions (e.g., Cl and Br) can be
incorporated into the X-position.

iodine-lead octahedron result from the ion-scale mismatch
between FAþ and lead halide cages, causing local lattice strain
in FAPbI3. Wang et al. found that incorporating different
A-position cations with various molecular properties into FA-rich
mixed perovskite ﬁlms results in divergent crystal growth kinet-

5.1.2. Additive Engineering
Thermodynamically stable FA-based perovskites can be obtained
by regulating strain through component management. However,
precise control of the components of these perovskites is difﬁ-
cult. Additionally, there are numerous defects in the crystal.
Additive engineering is helpful in controlling FA-based perov-
skite crystallization and surface morphology by passivation of
defects on the crystal surface, minimizing lattice strain genera-
tion, and enhancing the phase purity of these perovskites.
Regulating the Uniform Crystallization of Perovskites: The
crystallization process of perovskites can be controlled by the
interaction between additives and precursors, which can also reg-
ulate strain. Wang et al. found that it can form hydrogen bonds
with FAI by adding 2-(2-(2-aminoethoxy)ethoxy)acetic acid
(AEAA) to the precursor solution, which is conducive to the crys-
tallization process and promotes the directed growth of crystals
(Figure 10a).[109] Additionally, multifunctional molecules can be
added to ﬁll vacant defects in the perovskites, subsequently
reducing the strain generated during ﬁlm growth.[110,111] Chen
et al. introduced small molecule ammonium acetate (NH4Ac)
as an additive that interacts strongly with PbI2, FAI via Pb─O
coordination, and N─H···N hydrogen bonding.[111] This interac-
tion results in the vertical orientation of perovskite crystals and
the relaxation of lattice strains. Furthermore, HCOONH4 can be
used as a preburied additive in the electron transport layer (ETL),
enabling the realization of a bottom-up inﬁltration process that
leads to more uniform perovskite crystallization, relaxing
microstrain
and
residual
strain
in
the
perovskite
ﬁlm
(Figure 10b,c).[112]
Construct
Mixed-Dimensional
Perovskites:
Adding
low-
dimensional perovskite molecules to form mixed-dimensional
perovskites on the surface of FAPbI3, part of the lattice strain
can be released. Song and co-workers added 2D perovskite phe-
nylmethyl ammonium lead iodide (PMA2PbI4) to 3D FAPbI3 to
promote uniform crystallization and reduce strain in the ﬁlm.
GIWAXS showed that the surface of perovskite ﬁlms, without
thermal annealing, already contained 58% of α-FAPbI3.[113] It
has been demonstrated that by adding other 2D organic
long-chain spacers, such as phenethylammonium (PEAþ) and
butylammonium (BAþ), 2D/3D perovskites can be constructed
as soft structural subunits on the surface of the ﬁlms,
providing additional ﬂexibility to reduce residual stress.[114,115]
Additionally, the 1D perovskites have also been exploited to reg-
ulate stress (Figure 10d,e).[116,117] Kong et al. added 2-diethylami-
noethylchloride hydrochloride (DEAECCl) to the precursor
solution to form a 1D@3D perovskite structure, and the internal
tensile strain of the 3D perovskite ﬁlms was effectively
alleviated.[116]
Other Mechanisms Compensating for the Strain: During the
preparation of perovskites, the process generates tensile strain,
which can be alleviated by adding polymerizable monomer
molecules to the precursor solution.[118] Chen and co-workers
accomplished this by adding trimethylolpropane triacrylate
(TMTA) into the antisolvent. The in situ crosslinking-enabled
strain-regulating crystallization (CSRC) achieves the limitation
of lattice
expansion and strain
regulation in perovskites
(Figure 10f).[118] Multifunctional additive molecules, such as
adenosine triphosphate, can interact with perovskites and miti-
gate tensile strain by remaining in GBs. These molecules extrude
the lattice due to steric hindrance, which converts the tensile
strain in the perovskites into compressive strain, thereby
improving the stability of the α-FAPbI3 phase.[119] Though many
methods of A-position cationic alloys can obtain FA-rich perov-
skites, the resulting octahedral structures are usually noncubic
and oblique. Doherty et al. introduced EDTA for octahedral sur-
face functionalization, thus templating perovskite growth while
stabilizing α-FAPbI3, inhibiting the transition from angular shar-
ing structure to surface sharing structure and reducing the strain
caused by octahedral tilt.[50] Lattice strain can also occur in per-
ovskites due to inconsistent illumination in the day and night
operating modes. To address this, Jen and co-workers added
SiO2-coated gold nanorods (GNR@SiO2) to perovskite ﬁlm,
utilizing the plasmonic local heating effect to relax the lattice
strain generated during different working modes day and
night.[120] Introducing additives during perovskite substrate
preparation
can

alleviate

within

which is also beneﬁcial in suppressing strain generation.
The performance of PSCs strongly depends on the crystalliza-
tion quality of perovskite ﬁlms, and nonuniform crystallization
leads to strain, which directly affects the quality of the ﬁlm.
Inhomogeneous crystallization during ﬁlm growth can be inhib-
ited by selecting the appropriate precursor solvent or solvent mix-
ture. Adding dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) can help widen the
open layer spacing of lead halides, leading to the formation of
an intermediate phase, which can also eliminate lattice mismatch
with organic components and promote high-quality crystalliza-
tion. According to Yu et al., increasing the amount of DMSO
transforms residual tensile strain into a compressive strain
(Figure 11a).[123] N-methyl pyrrolidone (NMP) is considered
a Lewis base suitable for coordination with FAI. Yang and
co-workers compared the roles of DMSO and NMP in forming
high-quality FAPbI3 ﬁlms, revealing that replacing DMSO with
NMP can form a stable intermediate FAI·PbI2·NMP adduct,
resulting in a more homogeneous FAPbI3 ﬁlm.[124] In addition,
stable PbI2·NMP adduct can inhibit the formation of solvent-
coordinated perovskite intermediate complexes, resulting in
homogeneously crystallized high-quality FA-based perovskite
ﬁlms. The reason is that NMP can react with FAI/CsI in situ
to reduce the formation energy of α phase perovskite and form
α phase FA-based perovskite ﬁlm (FA0.83Cs0.17PbI3) at room tem-
perature (Figure 11b).[125] Recently, the solvent gaming mecha-
nism revealed by Zheng et al. provided a new idea for improving
the uniformity of α-FAPbI3 ﬁlms. They found that in O-donors
with Lewis basic solvents with similar oxygen-containing double
bonds (abbreviated as OXRs), Gutmann donor number (DN) and
Kamlet-Taft β value determine the competitive choice of the sol-
vent intermediate structure. The resulting hydrogen-bond-
favorable intermediates (β ≥DN*) contribute to the preparation
of high-quality and homogeneous α-FAPbI3 ﬁlms.[126] It can be
found that uniform crystallization can reduce the generation of
strain and obtain ﬁlms with high crystallinity.
Adding other solvents to create a mixed solvent is a commonly
used technique to reduce lattice strain and improve the crystalli-
zation of perovskite ﬁlms (Figure 11c).[127,128] Recently, Seok
et al. used a combination of DMSO, alkyl ammonium chloride
(RNH3Cl), and ethanol (EtOH) as mixed solvents to achieve
dense and uniformly crystallized α-FAPbI3 perovskite ﬁlms, with
a device PCE of up to 25.1%.[128] The ratio of FAI and PbI2 in the
precursor can regulate the strain in perovskite ﬁlms.[129,130]
Rothmann et al. discovered that excess PbI2 could exist
seamlessly on the FAPbI3 lattice, forming coherent transition
boundaries and, as a result, reducing lattice strain and lattice
mismatch (Figure 11d).[129] In addition, the aging of precursor
solutions is also considered one of the feasible strain modulation
methods. Hao and co-workers released residual strain in perov-
skite ﬁlms by aging the precursor solution at 130 °C.[131]
5.2. Regulation of External Strain
The incompatibility between the thermal expansion coefﬁcients
of the perovskite layer and the substrate, together with the lattice
mismatch, is typically responsible for inducing external strain.
The perovskite fabrication process (particularly the annealing
step) and interface engineering can provide adjustments to alle-
viate such strains. Alternatively, the imposition of additional
external forces could also be employed as a measure to compen-
sate for part of the remaining external strain.
5.2.1. Manufacturing Process Engineering
Appropriate process engineering methods can reduce strain in
FA-based perovskites. Here, the preparation of ﬁlms at room
temperature, the improvement of the solvent annealing process,
and the vacuum deposition methods in regulating strain are
mainly discussed.
Thermal annealing is an essential step in the preparation of
FAPbI3. The difference in the coefﬁcient of thermal expansion
between the perovskite and the contact layer during annealing
is a signiﬁcant source of strain. Lowering the formation temper-
ature of perovskite ﬁlms is one of the most effective strategies to
reduce the strain during annealing. This is because the annealing
temperature of perovskite is a principal factor in determining lat-
tice strain, as per Equation (3). Many researchers have tried fab-
ricating perovskite ﬁlms at room temperature.[60,132] Dauskardt
et al. experimented with fabricating perovskite ﬁlms at room tem-
perature using a diethyl ether (DEE) bath, which resulted in ﬁlms
with less stress. Bath-converted perovskite ﬁlms formed directly
at room temperature exhibit greatly reduced residual strain. The
strong adhesion between the perovskite layer and the contact
layer after the formation of perovskite ﬁlms is the reason why
bath-converted perovskite ﬁlms formed directly at room temper-
ature are not affected by any post-treatment that requires an ele-
vated temperature (Figure 12a,b).[60,133]
Lowering the annealing temperature for perovskite formation
can alleviate the lattice strain in the ﬁlm. However, the reduction
in device performance resulting from the low-quality perovskite
ﬁlm formed at low temperatures is an issue. Optimization of the
annealing process is another effective approach to alleviate lattice
strain. Chen et al. ﬂipped over the ﬁlm sample during annealing
to create a temperature gradient and obtained FA-based
perovskite ﬁlms with reduced tensile strain.[53] Flash annealing
techniques have been developed to enhance the perovskite tran-
sition and prevent residual strain.[134,135] Dong and co-workers
improved the ﬁlm quality by implementing a ﬂash thermal shock
process, which led to rapid cooling and surface lattice compres-
sion (Figure 12c,d).[135]
Spin coating is the most common method for FAPbI3 ﬁlm
preparation, which can cause inhomogeneity of crystallization
and lattice strain due to the difﬁculty of controlling solvent
volatilization. Vacuum deposition is an ideal method for
preparing perovskite ﬁlms since solvents are not required.
(Figure 12e).[20,59,136] Huang and co-workers prepared strain-free
perovskite ﬁlms by vacuum deposition for three days at room
temperature.[59] Then Liu et al. developed an in-vacuum anneal-
ing process at low temperatures to fabricate the CsI layer on the
surface of the precrystallized ﬁlm, which can relax the lattice
strain and result in a high-quality FA-based perovskite ﬁlm.[136]
In addition, utilizing high-thermal expansion coefﬁcient sub-
strates that match the perovskite, such as polycarbonate (PC) or
polyethylene terephthalate (PET)[58] can reduce the lattice strain
during annealing by reducing the mismatch in thermal

5.2.2. Interface Engineering
Adjusting the perovskite interface can compensate for the inher-
ent tensile strain of the ﬁlm. The thermal expansion coefﬁcient
mismatch and lattice mismatch during ﬁlm growth are the
primary sources of strain, which can be effectively alleviated
by adding functional interlayers. In addition, building a
suitable lattice-matched intermediate interface and top strain
compensation layer is also an effective strategy for strain engi-
neering. Interface engineering can improve the efﬁciency and
stability of PSCs by regulating strain and preventing unwanted
degradation.[137–139]
Inserting a Flexible Interlayer to Release Strain: The relaxation of
lattice strain in perovskite ﬁlms can be achieved by inserting a
material between the perovskite and substrate.[140–142] Meng

not only regulate the interfacial stress but also passivate defects
through the coordination of functional groups, greatly improving
device performance.[144–146] Wang and co-workers employed a

5.2.3. Introduce External Stresses
External forces, such as mechanical force and illumination, can
cause structural deformation of perovskite crystals, leading to
changes in bond length and angle and resulting in strain.
Thus, an effective strategy to regulate the strain of perovskite
ﬁlms is to provide external stress. Islam and co-workers demon-
strated that hydrostatic pressure could be utilized to adjust the
lattice strain of FA-based perovskite and improve photovoltaic
performance.[30] Jia et al. developed a pressure-assisted solution
treatment (PASP) approach that allows strain modulation to
improve ﬁlm growth nucleation. They discovered that PSC
achieved champion
efﬁciency at an external
pressure of
4.9 kPa (Figure 13f).[161] In addition, illumination can release
lattice strain in perovskite ﬁlms. This light-induced lattice expan-
sion leads to the relaxation of the local lattice strain and reduces
the energy barrier at the interface (Figure 13g).[73] Furthermore,
the stresses introduced by mechanical bending and deposition
charge transport layers have been shown to regulate the strain
in ﬁlms of MA-based and inorganic perovskites. This ﬁnding
serves as inspiration for controlling strain in FA-based perovskite
through external force.[58,59]
6. Summary and Perspective
6.1. Summary
FA-based perovskites have been shown to improve the photovol-
taic
performance
of
devices
signiﬁcantly.
However,
nonuniformly distributed lattice tensile strains are often pro-
duced in perovskite ﬁlms, seriously affecting the stability of
PSCs. Several studies have demonstrated that regulating the
strain can produce efﬁcient and stable FA-based PSCs. This arti-
cle comprehensively analyzes the origin, characterization meth-
ods, and effects of strain on FA-based perovskite ﬁlms. The
objective is to gain a deeper understanding of the internal mech-
anisms of strain engineering in enhancing the performance of
FA-based perovskite photovoltaics and identify directions for
future
development in this ﬁeld. Strain in perovskites can originate
from diverse sources, such as internal strain from perovskite
iodine-lead octahedral tilt and heterogeneous nucleation and
external strain induced by lattice mismatch, thermal expansion
coefﬁcient mismatch, electrical bias, temperature ﬂuctuations, or
external pressure. Numerous characterization techniques, such
as PL, TRPL, and Raman spectroscopy, are commonly utilized
to
characterize
the
surface
strain
of
perovskite
ﬁlms.
Additionally, techniques for characterizing interior strains in
ﬁlms include XRD and TEM. There are also methods that can
simultaneously characterize both surface and interior strains,
such as EBSD, GIWAXS, and GIXRD.
Then, we summarize the effects of strain on FA-based perov-
skite ﬁlms, including electronic band structure, carrier transport,
defect properties, and device stability. The following rules have
been obtained. 1) Compressive strain reduces the bandgap in
FA-based perovskite, while tensile strain causes the bandgap
to be blueshifted. 2) VBM is more sensitive than CBM under
strain due to the different compositions of the valence band edge
and conduction band edge. Thus, compressive strain promotes
better alignment of the Fermi energy level and improves carrier
mobility. In contrast, tensile strain reduces charge extraction
capacity. 3) DFT calculations indicate that compression strain
increases the formation energy of halide holes, thereby reducing
nonradiative recombination. In contrast, tensile strain leads to an
increase in the defect concentration and induces nonradiative
recombination. 4) Compressive strain stabilizes the α phase of
FA-based perovskite, limits ion migration, and improves the sta-
bility of ﬁlms. In contrast, tensile strain promotes vacancy forma-
tion and perovskite phase segregation, thereby accelerating the
degradation of ﬁlms.
There have been numerous studies in recent years that focus
on the regulation of strain in FA-based perovskites. This review
paper provides a summary of these investigations, which are clas-
siﬁed into two categories: internal strain regulation and external
strain regulation. Strategies for internal strain regulation include
1) adjusting the tolerance factor via alloy engineering to alleviate
the strain caused by perovskite octahedron inclination and
2) enhancing the crucial crystallization process using additive
and
precursor
engineering
to
minimize
internal
strain.
Additionally, for external strain regulation, strategies include
1) optimizing the preparation process of the ﬁlm to minimize
the generation of strains during the crystalline formation pro-
cess, especially during annealing, 2) reducing the mismatch in
thermal expansion coefﬁcients and lattice between perovskite
and substrate through interface engineering and alleviating
residual strain, and 3) introducing external stress to adjust the
ﬁlm growth process and offset unfavorable strain.

6.2. Perspective
Despite the signiﬁcant progress made in FA-based PSCs, mainly
due to strain strategy advancements, strain engineering chal-
lenges persist and deserve further investigation. The anionic
and cationic alloying can mitigate the lattice strain and enhance
device stability. However, it may alter the physical properties of
the perovskite, thus reducing efﬁciency. Annealing at a lower
temperature can decrease the strain due to thermal expansion
coefﬁcient mismatches, but ﬁlm quality is compromised.
Moreover, there is an insufﬁcient understanding of how resid-
ual/excess PbI2 and its distribution affect lattice strain.[162] An
ongoing debate exists regarding the inﬂuence of light-induced
lattice expansion on the photovoltaic performance of PSCs.
Based on the information obtained in this review, it is proposed
that strain engineering can be investigated in the following direc-
tions in the future: 1) Developing advanced in situ characteriza-
tion techniques to reveal the evolution of nanoscale strains,
promoting
internal
and
surface
strain
characterization
techniques.[163–165]
Tsai
and
co-workers
employed
in situ
GIWAXS to investigate the phenomenon of light-induced lattice
strain relaxation.[73] Using in situ characterization techniques
provides accurate real-time information on lattices and stresses
in perovskites,[73,166] comprehensively and profoundly under-
standing the strain release and regulation mechanisms in perov-
skites and improving the pertinence and effectiveness of strain
engineering for FA-based perovskites. 2) Developing new meth-
ods to fabricate perovskite layers with minimal lattice strain dur-
ing crystal formation produces highly crystalline, homogeneous
ﬁlms at low temperatures. Additionally, these techniques are
expected to exceed the performance of conventional methods
for solution and vacuum deposition. 3) Investigating functional
layers and novel molecules that potentially reduce lattice mis-
matches is critical to enhancing compatibility between perov-
skites and adjacent charge transport layers. For example,
using interfaces that foster atomic intercommunication can
strengthen compatibility between the lattices of the layers.[65]
Attaining the suppression of strains is achievable by implement-
ing these techniques. 4) Utilizing lattice strain to improve device
performance, which has been supported by studies demonstrat-
ing its impact on changing band structure, carrier dynamics, ion
migration, and ﬂexoelectric responses with corresponding pho-
tovoltaic effects.[30,53,58,167] Consequently, there may be converg-
ing approaches to introducing internal and external strains
simultaneously (by adding external pressure and additive mole-
cules, for instance) to signiﬁcantly boost the photovoltaic charac-
teristics of perovskites. Additionally, the comprehensive analysis
of strain regulation may assist PSCs in surmounting their PCE
limitations. 5) Identifying similarities in different strategies,
such as additive engineering, that can both relieve external strain
and regulate internal strain.[168,169] One can also learn from
strain strategies of other perovskite systems, including MA-based
and inorganic perovskites, to achieve strain regulation in
FA-based perovskites.
The
strain
strategy
has
signiﬁcantly
improved
the
performance and stability of FA-based perovskite devices,
enabling PSCs to reach a certiﬁcation efﬁciency of 25.7%.[170]
Nevertheless, despite the signiﬁcant progress, the maximum
efﬁciency of FA-based PSCs is still considerably lower than
the theoretical limit, and the issue of long-term stability persists.
Leveraging strain engineering to improve the efﬁciency and sta-
bility of FA-based PSCs has the potential to substantially boost
the feasibility of the commercial-scale deployment of PSCs.

Yuqin Zhou received his bachelor’s degree from the School of Physics and Optoelectronic Engineering,
Xiangtan University. Currently, he is pursuing his graduate studies at the School of Optoelectronic
Engineering, Chongqing University. His research interests lie in the areas of perovskite solar cells and
energy conversion devices.
Zhiyuan Xu obtained his Ph.D. from Nankai University in 2021. He is currently an assistant research
fellow in Professor Zhigang Zang’s group at Chongqing University. His research concerns organic–
inorganic hybrid perovskite solar cells, ﬂexible electronic and optoelectronic devices, and energy
conversion devices.
Yong Zhou received his Ph.D. in the School of Optoelectronic Information, University of Electronic
Science and Technology of China (UESTC), in 2014. He is now an associate professor in the College of
Optoelectronic Engineering, Chongqing University. His research interests include low-dimensional
materials-based optoelectronic sensors.
Zhigang Zang received his Ph.D. from Kyushu University in 2011. He joined School of Optoelectronic
Engineering, Chongqing University, as a professor in 2014. His research interests mainly focus on the
synthesis of low-dimensional semiconductor materials and their applications in solar cells and light-
emitting diodes.

Introduction  \n15 \nThin-film photovoltaics aim to reduce the cost of electricity \ngenerated from sunlight compared to conventional silicon solar \ncells. Several approaches have been developed for solar cells \nsuch as amorphous and nanocrystalline Si1 , inorganic compound \nsemiconductors 2, 3, quantum dot solar cells (QDSCs) 4-6, dye-\n20 \nsensitized solar cells (DSSCs)7-11, organic solar cells (OSCs) 12, \nand now perovskite-based meso-superstructured solar cells \n(MSSCs) 13. In particular, solid-state perovskite-based solar cells \nhave risen to the forefront of emerging PV research13-18. Evolving \nfrom DSSCs, MSSCs have demonstrated remarkably high power \n25 \nconversion efficiency (PCE) of over 17%, broad light absorption, \nand open-circuit voltages (Voc) of over 1.05V, by employing \nCH3NH3PbI3 perovskite, as the absorber, coated upon the surface \nof a mesoporous TiO2 via two-step liquid sequential method 19. \nAlthough there is potential toxicology issue of lead, a key \n30 \ncomponent in the archetypical material, perovskite absorbers are \nalso desirable by virtue of being easy to solution process at low \ntemperature using low-cost materials and do not rely on the use \nof elements in limited supply, unstable solvents such as hydrazine, \nand high-temperature annealing. \n35 \n \n† School of Materials Science and Engineering, Shijiazhuang Tiedao \nUniversity, 17 Northeast, Second Inner Ring , Shijiazhuang, 050043, \nChina; E-mail: jinjinzhao2012@163.com. \n‡ Hebei Key Lab of Optic-electronic Information and Materials, The \n40 \nCollege of Physics Science and Technology, Hebei University, Baoding \n071002, China, E-mail: yaohuamai@163.com. \n§The Key Laboratory for Health Monitoring and Control of Large \nStructures, Hebei province, 17 Northeast, Second Inner Ring , \nShijiazhuang, 050043, China. \n45 \n† Electronic Supplementary Information (ESI) available: [details of any \nsupplementary information available should be included here]. Experimental Section  \n2.1. Material \nPbI2 and N,N-dimethylformide (DMF) were purchased from \nSigma-Aldrich and Alfa Aesar, respectively. Spiro-MeOTAD \nwas purchased from Shenzhen Feiming Science and Technology \n15 \nCo., Ltd. All materials else were purchased from J&K Scientific \nLtd and used as received. Substrates of the cells are fluorine-\ndoped tin oxide conducting glass (FTO, Pilkington, thickness: \n2.2mm, sheet resistance 14Ω/square). CH3NH3I was synthesized \nas the literature 33.   \n20 \n2.2. Substrate Preparation \nFirst, laser-patterned, FTO-coated glass substrates were \ncleaned by ultrasonication in an alkaline, aqueous washing \nsolution, rinsed with deionized water, ethanol, acetone and 2-\npropanol, respectively. A hole-blocking layer of compact TiO2 \n25 \nwith a thickness of about 50nm was deposited by a dip-coating \nmethod with a TiO2 organic solution 34-35, and then followed by a \nsintering process at 500℃ for 30min. After cooling to room \ntemperature, the substrates were treated in an 40mM aqueous \nsolution of TiCl4 at 70℃ for 30min, rinsed with deionized water \n30 \nand dried at 500℃ for 30min. The mesoporous TiO2 layer with a \nthickness of 180nm was prepared as previously reported 17. The \nmesoporous TiO2 film was immersed in 20m M aqueous TiCl4 \n(>98%, Aldrich) solution at 70, for different time (0min, 5min, \n10min, 20min, 30min, and 60min, respectively) and sintered at \n35 \n500 , for 30min.  \n2.3. Perovskite Solar Cell Fabrication   \nPbI2 was dissolved in DMF at a concentration of 462mg/ml \n(~1M) under stirring. The PbI2 solution was kept at 70, on the \nheating plate. The mesoporous TiO2 films were then infiltrated \n40 \nwith PbI2 by spin coating at 6,500r.p.m. for 5s and dried. The \nfilms were then dipped in a solution of CH3NH3I in 2-propanol \n(10mg/ml) for 120min, rinsed with 2-propanol and dried at 70, \nfor 30min.  \n  The HTM was then deposited by spin coating at 4,000r.p.m. for \n45 \n30s. The notable Jsc of 21.3mA cm-2 and \nefficiency of 14.6% as well as a high Voc of 0.94V have been \n85 \nachieved by the perovskite Solar Cells at 1 sun light intensity. \nThe structure with treatment for 30min exhibits the optimum the \ninterconnectivity of TiO2 grains, and improves the electron-\nextraction and -transport efficiency and charge injection rate, \nwhich contribute significantly to the high Jsc value and PCE for \n90 \nthe perovskite solar cell. Recently, highly efficient solar cells based on organic–inorganic perovskites have been intensively 
reported for developing fabricating methods and device structures. To improve the performance of the 
perovskite film devices, it requires a delicate control of charge transfer materials interconnectivity. Here, 
controlling the mesoporous TiO2 structure improves their charge collection and injection rate, and allows 
substantial enhancement in corresponding device performance. We found that increasing the TiCl4 
10 
processing time deteriorates the device performance by introducing a large amount of excessive large 
perovskite particles, surface roughness and charge recombination. The proper TiCl4 processing 
dramatically improves the charge transport within the electron transfer layer, explaining the efficient 
performances of meso-superstructured solar cells. 
1. Introduction  
15 
Thin-film photovoltaics aim to reduce the cost of electricity 
generated from sunlight compared to conventional silicon solar 
cells. Several approaches have been developed for solar cells 
such as amorphous and nanocrystalline Si1 , inorganic compound 
semiconductors 2, 3, quantum dot solar cells (QDSCs) 4-6, dye-
20 
sensitized solar cells (DSSCs)7-11, organic solar cells (OSCs) 12, 
and now perovskite-based meso-superstructured solar cells 
(MSSCs) 13. In particular, solid-state perovskite-based solar cells 
have risen to the forefront of emerging PV research13-18. Evolving 
from DSSCs, MSSCs have demonstrated remarkably high power 
25 
conversion efficiency (PCE) of over 17%, broad light absorption, 
and open-circuit voltages (Voc) of over 1.05V, by employing 
CH3NH3PbI3 perovskite, as the absorber, coated upon the surface 
of a mesoporous TiO2 via two-step liquid sequential method 19. 
Although there is potential toxicology issue of lead, a key 
30 
component in the archetypical material, perovskite absorbers are 
also desirable by virtue of being easy to solution process at low 
temperature using low-cost materials and do not rely on the use 
of elements in limited supply, unstable solvents such as hydrazine, 
and high-temperature annealing.

2. Experimental Section  
2.1. Material 
PbI2 and N,N-dimethylformide (DMF) were purchased from 
Sigma-Aldrich and Alfa Aesar, respectively. Spiro-MeOTAD 
was purchased from Shenzhen Feiming Science and Technology 
15 
Co., Ltd. All materials else were purchased from J&K Scientific 
Ltd and used as received. Substrates of the cells are fluorine-
doped tin oxide conducting glass (FTO, Pilkington, thickness: 
2.2mm, sheet resistance 14Ω/square). CH3NH3I was synthesized 
as the literature 33.   
20 
2.2. Substrate Preparation 
First, laser-patterned, FTO-coated glass substrates were 
cleaned by ultrasonication in an alkaline, aqueous washing 
solution, rinsed with deionized water, ethanol, acetone and 2-
propanol, respectively. A hole-blocking layer of compact TiO2 
25 
with a thickness of about 50nm was deposited by a dip-coating 
method with a TiO2 organic solution 34-35, and then followed by a 
sintering process at 500℃ for 30min. After cooling to room 
temperature, the substrates were treated in an 40mM aqueous 
solution of TiCl4 at 70℃ for 30min, rinsed with deionized water 
30 
and dried at 500℃ for 30min. The mesoporous TiO2 layer with a 
thickness of 180nm was prepared as previously reported 17. The 
mesoporous TiO2 film was immersed in 20m M aqueous TiCl4 
(>98%, Aldrich) solution at 70, for different time (0min, 5min, 
10min, 20min, 30min, and 60min, respectively) and sintered at 
35 
500 , for 30min.  
2.3. Perovskite Solar Cell Fabrication   
PbI2 was dissolved in DMF at a concentration of 462mg/ml 
(~1M) under stirring. The PbI2 solution was kept at 70, on the 
heating plate. The mesoporous TiO2 films were then infiltrated 
40 
with PbI2 by spin coating at 6,500r.p.m. for 5s and dried. The 
films were then dipped in a solution of CH3NH3I in 2-propanol 
(10mg/ml) for 120min, rinsed with 2-propanol and dried at 70, 
for 30min.  
  The HTM was then deposited by spin coating at 4,000r.p.m. for 
45 
30s. The spin-coating formulation was prepared by dissolving 
72.3mg (2,2',7,7'-tetrakis(N,N-di-p-methoxyphenyl- amine)-9,9-
spirobifluorene) (spiro-MeOTAD), 28.8μl 4-tert-butylpyridine, 
17.5μl of a stock solution of 520mg/ml lithium bis(trifluoro-
methylsulphonyl) imide in acetonitrile in 1 ml chlorobenzene. 
50 
Finally, approximate 200nm Ag (measured by SEM) was 
thermally evaporated under vacuum to act as the cathode. The 
device fabrication was carried out under controlled atmospheric 
conditions and a humidity of <1% in the cleanroom.  
2.4. Characterization  
55 
UV-Vis absorption and TRPL spectra were recorded with a 
Shimadzu UV-2550(300-600nm: xenon lamp, 300W; 600-900nm: 
tungsten-halogen lamp, 150W) and Fls-800 spectrometers, 
respectively. XRD patterns were obtained using D8 Advance 
(Germany) diffractometer with Cu Kα radiation (40kV and 
60 
40mA) with the scanning rate of 4°min-1 for wide angle test 
sincrement over the Bragg angle range of 10-70°. Atomic force 
microscope (AFM) was performed using Bruker Multimode 8 
Scanning Probe Microscope (SPM) in “tapping” mode. SEM 
(Scanning Electron Microscopy) analysis was performed on a 
65 
Hitachi-S-4800 electron microscope. The photocurrent-voltage 
(J-V) characteristics of the solar cells were measured using a 
Keithley 2400 Source under illumination of a simulated sunlight 
(AM 1.5, 100mW/cm2) provided by a solar simulator (Newport 
69907) with an AM 1.5 filter. Light intensity was adjusted with 
70 
an NREL-calibrated Si solar cell with a KG-2 filter for 
approximating 1 sun light intensity. While measuring current and 
voltage, the cell was covered with a black mask with an aperture 
(aperture area is close to the active device area). The incident 
photon-to-current efficiency (IPCE) was measured in DC mode 
75 
with a 1/4 m double monochromator (Crowntech DK242), a 
multi-meter (Keithley 2000), and two light sources depending on 
the wavelength range required (300-600nm: xenon lamp, 300W; 
600-900nm: tungsten-halogen lamp, 150W). The monochromatic 
light intensity for IPCE efficiency was calibrated with a reference 
80 
silicon photodiode. All the measurements of the solar cells were 
performed under ambient atmosphere at room temperature 
without encapsulation.  
3. Results and discussion  
The fabrication of perovskite solar cells with controllable TiCl4 
85 
treatment is described schematically in Fig.1. Firstly, Mesoporous 
TiO2 film (the thickness of ~180nm) was deposited on a thin 
compact TiO2 blocking layer by spin-coating method. Secondly, 
the mesoporous TiO2 film was immersed in 20m M aqueous 
TiCl4 solution at 70℃ for different time (0min, 5min, 10min, 
90 
20min, 30min, and 60min, respectively) and sintered at 500℃ for 
30min, followed by spin-coating PbI2 in N,N-dimethylformamide 
(DMF). Thirdly, the dried PbI2 film was dipped into CH3NH3I 
solution for 120min, heated at 70℃ for 30min to form perovskite. 
Finally, HTM film was spin-coated on the perovskite film 
95 
previous to Ag film evaporated. The present two-step sequential 
deposition method is expected to be more precise than the two-
step dipping method 17, 36, 37, thanks to its uniform reaction 
procedure.

4. Conclusions 
80 
TiCl4 processing on mesoporous TiO2/CH3NH3PbI3 Solar Cells 
for 30min is modified to achieve a uniform and high-coverage 
perovskite absorber layer with a great IPCE performance and 
high UV-visible absorption. The notable Jsc of 21.3mA cm-2 and 
efficiency of 14.6% as well as a high Voc of 0.94V have been 
85 
achieved by the perovskite Solar Cells at 1 sun light intensity. 
The structure with treatment for 30min exhibits the optimum the 
interconnectivity of TiO2 grains, and improves the electron-
extraction and -transport efficiency and charge injection rate, 
which contribute significantly to the high Jsc value and PCE for 
90 
the perovskite solar cell. We believe that the performance of the 
cell can be further improved if more investigations are made on 
materials and interfaces.

perovskite absorber layer with a great IPCE performance and high UV-visible absorption.

Charge-transport efficiently in hybrid lead iodide perovskite solar cells  
Jinjin Zhao,†§* Peng Wang,† Liyu Wei,† Zhenghao Liu, † Xueqian Fang†, Xianglin Liu†, Deliang Ren†‡ and 
Yaohua Mai‡*

5 
Recently, highly efficient solar cells based on organic–inorganic perovskites have been intensively 
reported for developing fabricating methods and device structures. To improve the performance of the 
perovskite film devices, it requires a delicate control of charge transfer materials interconnectivity. Here, 
controlling the mesoporous TiO2 structure improves their charge collection and injection rate, and allows 
substantial enhancement in corresponding device performance. We found that increasing the TiCl4 
10 
processing time deteriorates the device performance by introducing a large amount of excessive large 
perovskite particles, surface roughness and charge recombination. The proper TiCl4 processing 
dramatically improves the charge transport within the electron transfer layer, explaining the efficient 
performances of meso-superstructured solar cells. 
1. Introduction  
15 
Thin-film photovoltaics aim to reduce the cost of electricity 
generated from sunlight compared to conventional silicon solar 
cells. Several approaches have been developed for solar cells 
such as amorphous and nanocrystalline Si1 , inorganic compound 
semiconductors 2, 3, quantum dot solar cells (QDSCs) 4-6, dye-
20 
sensitized solar cells (DSSCs)7-11, organic solar cells (OSCs) 12, 
and now perovskite-based meso-superstructured solar cells 
(MSSCs) 13. In particular, solid-state perovskite-based solar cells 
have risen to the forefront of emerging PV research13-18. Evolving 
from DSSCs, MSSCs have demonstrated remarkably high power 
25 
conversion efficiency (PCE) of over 17%, broad light absorption, 
and open-circuit voltages (Voc) of over 1.05V, by employing 
CH3NH3PbI3 perovskite, as the absorber, coated upon the surface 
of a mesoporous TiO2 via two-step liquid sequential method 19. 
Although there is potential toxicology issue of lead, a key 
30 
component in the archetypical material, perovskite absorbers are 
also desirable by virtue of being easy to solution process at low 
temperature using low-cost materials and do not rely on the use 
of elements in limited supply, unstable solvents such as hydrazine, 
and high-temperature annealing.

So far, the perovskite pigment has been deposited in a single 
50 
step 14, co-evaporation of two precursors (PbCl2 and CH3NH3I) 20, 
vapor assisted solution process21, 22, and two-step sequential 
deposition17,19. Two-step sequential deposition of perovskite 
provides an efficient low-cost route to high performance for 
perovskite solar cells, and better for tolerating I-V hysteresis19. In 
55 
this method, the transformation processing from PbI2 to 
CH3NH3PbI3
23, different PbI2 concentrations24,25, the spin coating 
step of PbI2 
17,26,27, and different solvents for different 
crystallizing processing of PbI2 28 were studied, respectively. In 
addition, 
different 
CH3NH3I 
concentrations19, 
pre-wetting 
60 
processing controlling 24,29, and reaction temperature controlling29 
were used for studying the conversion processing and 
morphology controlling, which are closely related to the 
photovoltaic performance as it should facilitate rapid and efficient 
charge collection and transfer. However, the interconnection of 
65 
TiO2 grains in mesoporous TiO2 film remained experimentally 
unexploited. This would be highly advantageous to the device 
performance 30-32. On one hand, the generated charge will be 
transported fast to electrodes, hence raise charge injection rate, 
and suppress the possibility of recombination. One the other hand, 
70 
easily filling the pores of the mesoporous TiO2 layer with 
perovskite materials and decreasing the roughness of the 
mesoporous TiO2 film surface will form uniform perovskite 
particle size, increase the perovskite coverage and a greater 
fraction of the incoming sunlight to be absorbed. Planar 
75 
perovskite and mesoporous Al2O3-based solar cells both 
transferred electron through perovskites layers, which exhibited 
ambipolar transport of electrons and holes.[57] Whereas using 
mesoporous TiO2 films or MgO ultrathin film coated TiO2 
nanoparticles as electron-transport layer,[58] S. I. Seok fabricated 
80 
MSSCs with maximum PCE greater than 20%. [61]

2. Experimental Section  
2.1. Material 
PbI2 and N,N-dimethylformide (DMF) were purchased from 
Sigma-Aldrich and Alfa Aesar, respectively. Spiro-MeOTAD 
was purchased from Shenzhen Feiming Science and Technology 
15 
Co., Ltd. All materials else were purchased from J&K Scientific 
Ltd and used as received. Substrates of the cells are fluorine-
doped tin oxide conducting glass (FTO, Pilkington, thickness: 
2.2mm, sheet resistance 14Ω/square). CH3NH3I was synthesized 
as the literature 33.   
20 
2.2. Substrate Preparation 
First, laser-patterned, FTO-coated glass substrates were 
cleaned by ultrasonication in an alkaline, aqueous washing 
solution, rinsed with deionized water, ethanol, acetone and 2-
propanol, respectively. A hole-blocking layer of compact TiO2 
25 
with a thickness of about 50nm was deposited by a dip-coating 
method with a TiO2 organic solution 34-35, and then followed by a 
sintering process at 500℃ for 30min. After cooling to room 
temperature, the substrates were treated in an 40mM aqueous 
solution of TiCl4 at 70℃ for 30min, rinsed with deionized water 
30 
and dried at 500℃ for 30min. The mesoporous TiO2 layer with a 
thickness of 180nm was prepared as previously reported 17. The 
mesoporous TiO2 film was immersed in 20m M aqueous TiCl4 
(>98%, Aldrich) solution at 70, for different time (0min, 5min, 
10min, 20min, 30min, and 60min, respectively) and sintered at 
35 
500 , for 30min.  
2.3. Perovskite Solar Cell Fabrication   
PbI2 was dissolved in DMF at a concentration of 462mg/ml 
(~1M) under stirring. The PbI2 solution was kept at 70, on the 
heating plate. The mesoporous TiO2 films were then infiltrated 
40 
with PbI2 by spin coating at 6,500r.p.m. for 5s and dried. The 
films were then dipped in a solution of CH3NH3I in 2-propanol 
(10mg/ml) for 120min, rinsed with 2-propanol and dried at 70, 
for 30min.  
  The HTM was then deposited by spin coating at 4,000r.p.m. for 
45 
30s. The spin-coating formulation was prepared by dissolving 
72.3mg (2,2',7,7'-tetrakis(N,N-di-p-methoxyphenyl- amine)-9,9-
spirobifluorene) (spiro-MeOTAD), 28.8μl 4-tert-butylpyridine, 
17.5μl of a stock solution of 520mg/ml lithium bis(trifluoro-
methylsulphonyl) imide in acetonitrile in 1 ml chlorobenzene. 
50 
Finally, approximate 200nm Ag (measured by SEM) was 
thermally evaporated under vacuum to act as the cathode. The 
device fabrication was carried out under controlled atmospheric 
conditions and a humidity of <1% in the cleanroom.  
2.4. Characterization  
55 
UV-Vis absorption and TRPL spectra were recorded with a 
Shimadzu UV-2550(300-600nm: xenon lamp, 300W; 600-900nm: 
tungsten-halogen lamp, 150W) and Fls-800 spectrometers, 
respectively. XRD patterns were obtained using D8 Advance 
(Germany) diffractometer with Cu Kα radiation (40kV and 
60 
40mA) with the scanning rate of 4°min-1 for wide angle test 
sincrement over the Bragg angle range of 10-70°. Atomic force 
microscope (AFM) was performed using Bruker Multimode 8 
Scanning Probe Microscope (SPM) in “tapping” mode. SEM 
(Scanning Electron Microscopy) analysis was performed on a 
65 
Hitachi-S-4800 electron microscope. The photocurrent-voltage 
(J-V) characteristics of the solar cells were measured using a 
Keithley 2400 Source under illumination of a simulated sunlight 
(AM 1.5, 100mW/cm2) provided by a solar simulator (Newport 
69907) with an AM 1.5 filter. Light intensity was adjusted with 
70 
an NREL-calibrated Si solar cell with a KG-2 filter for 
approximating 1 sun light intensity. While measuring current and 
voltage, the cell was covered with a black mask with an aperture 
(aperture area is close to the active device area). The incident 
photon-to-current efficiency (IPCE) was measured in DC mode 
75 
with a 1/4 m double monochromator (Crowntech DK242), a 
multi-meter (Keithley 2000), and two light sources depending on 
the wavelength range required (300-600nm: xenon lamp, 300W; 
600-900nm: tungsten-halogen lamp, 150W). The monochromatic 
light intensity for IPCE efficiency was calibrated with a reference 
80 
silicon photodiode. All the measurements of the solar cells were 
performed under ambient atmosphere at room temperature 
without encapsulation.  
3. Results and discussion  
The fabrication of perovskite solar cells with controllable TiCl4 
85 
treatment is described schematically in Fig.1. Firstly, Mesoporous 
TiO2 film (the thickness of ~180nm) was deposited on a thin 
compact TiO2 blocking layer by spin-coating method. Secondly, 
the mesoporous TiO2 film was immersed in 20m M aqueous 
TiCl4 solution at 70℃ for different time (0min, 5min, 10min, 
90 
20min, 30min, and 60min, respectively) and sintered at 500℃ for 
30min, followed by spin-coating PbI2 in N,N-dimethylformamide 
(DMF). Thirdly, the dried PbI2 film was dipped into CH3NH3I 
solution for 120min, heated at 70℃ for 30min to form perovskite. 
Finally, HTM film was spin-coated on the perovskite film 
95 
previous to Ag film evaporated. The present two-step sequential 
deposition method is expected to be more precise than the two-
step dipping method 17, 36, 37, thanks to its uniform reaction 
procedure.

4. Conclusions 
80 
TiCl4 processing on mesoporous TiO2/CH3NH3PbI3 Solar Cells 
for 30min is modified to achieve a uniform and high-coverage 
perovskite absorber layer with a great IPCE performance and 
high UV-visible absorption. The notable Jsc of 21.3mA cm-2 and 
efficiency of 14.6% as well as a high Voc of 0.94V have been 
85 
achieved by the perovskite Solar Cells at 1 sun light intensity. 
The structure with treatment for 30min exhibits the optimum the 
interconnectivity of TiO2 grains, and improves the electron-

Graphical Abstract 
 
 
  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
We demonstrate a controllable TiCl4 processing technique for mesoporous TiO2 films, which 
improves their charge collection and injection rate, and allows substantial enhancement in 
corresponding device performance. We find that TiCl4 processing on mesoporous 
TiO2/CH3NH3PbI3 Solar Cells for proper time is modified to achieve a uniform and high-coverage 
perovskite absorber layer with a great IPCE performance and high UV-visible absorption.

However, long-\nterm stability remains one of the critical challenges. This work\ndemonstrates that the introduction of 1,4-phenylenebis-\n(phosphonic acid) (1,4-PBPA) in formamidinium lead triiodide\n(FAPbI3)-based PSCs provides notable enhancements in moisture\nresistance, thermal stability, and power conversion efficiency\n(PCE). The 1,4-PBPA acts as a cross-linker and enables strong\ninteraction between perovskite grains, yielding high-quality films\nwith reduced defects, as evidenced by morphological and structural\nanalyses. The encapsulated FAPbI3 PSC devices with 1,4-PBPA\nretain 100% of the initial PCE even after 2350 h of aging at 95% relative humidity and 40 °C. Notably, the devices exhibit 70% of the\ninitial PCE after 1250 h of thermal stability tests at 85 °C. Compared to carboxylic acids, the phosphonic acid additives demonstrate\nsuperior stability enhancements, highlighting their potential to overcome the key limitations of PSCs.\nKEYWORDS: phosphonic acid, FAPbI3, stability, perovskite solar cell, efficiency, additive, thermal stability, moisture resistance\n1. INTRODUCTION\nSolar energy has emerged as one of the potential solutions to\nmeet the escalating global demand for sustainable and clean\nenergy. Photovoltaic (PV) technologies play a critical role in\nthis regard.1 Since the pioneering discovery of solid-state\nperovskite solar cells (PSCs), the power conversion efficiency\n(PCE) has increased rapidly from 9.7% to a certified PCE of\n26.1%.2−6 This significant improvement has been achieved\nthrough collective approaches, including composition engi-\nneering, surface passivation, doping, interface engineering, and\nmany other techniques. Among perovskite materials, for-\nmamidinium lead triiodide (FAPbI3) stands out for its unique\noptoelectronic properties. Furthermore, FAPbI3 perovskites\nexhibit optimum bandgap that is closer to the Shockley−\nQueisser limit, high absorption coefficient, and prolonged\ncharge carrier lifetime.7−12 However, FAPbI3 is thermodynami-\ncally unstable. The photoactive α-phase is stable above 150 °C,\nbelow which it spontaneously transforms into the less desirable\nwide-bandgap, nonperovskite δ-phase, with moisture accelerat-\ning this transformation.13−17 Despite progress, utilizing FAPbI3\nis still recognized as challenging under real-world conditions.\nComposition engineering has been widely employed to\naddress the limitations of FAPbI3-based SCs.1,18−21 This\nincludes the partial replacement of FA+ ions with smaller\norganic or inorganic cations such as methylammonium\n(MA+),17,20 propyl ammonium (PA+),9 Li+,22 Na+,22 K+,22−24\nRb+,22,25−27 and Cs+,22,26−28 as well as the partial replacement\nof I−ions with Br−ions.29,30 The use of additives results in\nhigh PCEs, improved reproducibility, and enhanced device\nstability compared with pristine FAPbI3. However, their\nincorporation into the crystal lattice reduces α-phase purity,\nleads to bandgap widening, and reduces light absorption.31,32\nAn alternative strategy involves the partial replacement of FA+\nions with bulkier aliphatic alkylammonium cations, which\nimproves moisture resistance by forming lower-dimensional\nperovskite (2D and 2D/3D hybrids) structures, finding use as\nan additive or passivation layer for 3D perovskites.33−36\nNevertheless, this strategy lowers efficiency due to inefficient\ncharge transport and collection at the interfaces.37\nReceived:\nOctober 18, 2024\nRevised:\nJanuary 28, 2025\nAccepted:\nFebruary 5, 2025\nPublished: February 13, 2025\nArticle\nwww.acsaem.org\n© 2025 American Chemical Society\n4962\nhttps://doi.org/10.1021/acsaem.4c02660\nACS Appl. Energy Mater. 2025, 8, 4962−4972\nThis article is licensed under CC-BY-NC-ND 4.0\nDownloaded via 2.215.151.190 on September 1, 2025 at 17:42:11 (UTC).\nSee https://pubs.acs.org/sharingguidelines for options on how to legitimately share published articles.\n\n\nNonradiative recombination in halide perovskites (HPs) is\nmainly associated with the defects at the surface, interface, and\ngrain boundaries where uncoordinated halide ions and Pb2+\nions accumulate.38,39 This heavily influences the operational\nstability and PCE of the PSCs. To overcome these challenges,\nnumerous studies have investigated the use of small organic\nmolecules that promote chemical binding, such as carboxylic\nacids,40 phosphonic acids,41 sulfonic acids,42 and organo-\nammonium halides.9,43,44 The P\x01O, C\x01O, and S\x01O\nbinding modes in these additives passivate lead defect sites\nand control crystallization in HPs.39\nFor instance, the incorporation of 5-ammonium valeric acid\niodide (AVAI) chemically stabilized α-FAPbI3 through\natomic−level interaction, as demonstrated by solid-state\nNMR and density functional theory (DFT) studies.45 Brown\net al. reported that the inclusion of a phosphonic acid-based\nadditive improved surface binding, while carboxylic acids\nimproved electron injection efficiency in SCs.46 Monica and\nco-workers demonstrated enhanced stability of HPs, achieved\nthrough shallow point defect passivation in perovskite layers\nusing a 3-phosphonopropionic acid (H3PP) additive that\ncontains carboxylic acid and phosphonic acid groups. The\nphosphonic acid end forms two types of hydrogen bonding\ninteractions (H···I and O···H) between HP and H3PP, which\nenables extended device stability, while the carboxylic acid\ngroup did not contribute significantly to the stability.39\nPhosphonic acid groups have strong H-donating character\nthat is beneficial for charge injection. However, their utilization\nhas been less popular than those of carboxylic acid and alkyl\nammonium additives. This is attributed to the tetrahedral\nmolecular geometry around the phosphorus atom, which\ndisrupts electron conjugation and reduces charge injection.\nNevertheless, phosphonic acid groups are capable of forming\nstable bonding interactions with metal ions, which could\nsuppress ion migration in PSCs. The strong metal-binding\nability of phosphonic acid groups somewhat counterbalances\nthe disadvantages of tetrahedral phosphorus.47 Furthermore,\nthe Lewis base character of hydroxyl groups contributes to the\nPb−O bond formation with uncoordinated Pb2+ ions\n(passivation effect), thereby reducing lead defect sites in the\nperovskites.48 Although there is acknowledged benefit of the\ninclusion of phosphorus atoms for the thermal resistance of\nfunctional materials, their specific impact on PSCs has been\nrelatively unexplored.\nHerein, we report an effective one-step solution process for\nphase-pure and high-quality α-FAPbI3 perovskite using grain\nbulk cross-linking through a bifunctional phosphonic acid, 1,4-\nphenylenebis(phosphonic acid) (1,4-PBPA), which acts as a\ntemplate to facilitate well-arranged grain development. The\n1,4-PBPA incorporation enhances the quality of the perovskite\nlayer and reduces trap density, resulting in a superior carrier\nlifetime. Consequently, PV devices treated with 1,4-PBPA\nexhibit an enhanced PCE of 21%, which surpasses the\nefficiency of untreated FAPbI3 PSCs. The encapsulated\nFAPbI3 + 1,4-PBPA device retains 100% of their initial PCE\nwhen exposed to 95% relative humidity (RH) at 40 °C for\n2350 h. Additionally, the devices preserve 70% of their initial\nefficiency after the thermal stability assessment performed at\n85 °C, following a 1250 h aging period. NMR and FTIR\nanalyses reveal bulk cross-linking facilitated by atomic-level\ninteractions of phosphonic acid groups with the FAPbI3 grain\nsurface. In contrast, 1,4-PBPA remains unincorporated in the\nbulk lattice, according to X-ray diffraction (XRD). Here, we\ndemonstrate that 1,4-PBPA passivates grain boundaries and\ninterfaces to improve moisture resistance and thermal stability,\nas well as suppresses phase transition to δ-FAPbI3, thus\nimparting high operational stability. Scanning electron\nmicroscopy (SEM) and XRD data confirm the preservation\nof the crystallinity of the FAPbI3 perovskite structure in the\npresence of 1,4-PBPA; in its absence, significant structural\ndeterioration occurred. Overall, this work highlights the\nmultifaceted roles of 1,4-PBPA in improving PCE, moisture\nresistance, and thermal stability of PSCs.\n2. EXPERIMENTAL SECTION\n2.1. Materials.
