RESULTS AND DISCUSSION\nOrganophosphonic acid additives can interact within the\nperovskite layer and with transport layers similarly to\ncarboxylic acid-based additives, which significantly improves\nthe PV performance of PSCs.46,47,55−57 To gain insight into the\nimpact of phosphonic acid functional groups on the efficiency\nand stability of PSCs, organic molecules possessing phosphonic\nacid groups, 1,4-PBPA, 1,4-PBMBPA, 1,6-HDPA, and ATMPA\nwere investigated as additives for PSCs (Figure 1a). The\nadditives used in this study differ in their chain length, number\nof functional groups, and structure. The PSCs were fabricated\nby solution processing using the following architecture: Glass/\nFTO/c-TiO2/m-TiO2/perovskite/OAI/Spiro-OMe-TAD/Au\n(Figure 1b). The reference FAPbI3 PSCs, hereafter denoted as\n“FAPbI3”, were fabricated by a one-step antisolvent deposition\nmethod using a 1.5 M FAPbI3 precursor solution containing\n0.75 M MACl. For the additive-doped FAPbI3 PSCs (denoted\nas “FAPbI3 + name of the additive”), an additional 0.01 M\nadditive was added to the FAPbI3 precursor solution.\nWe first analyzed the PV performance of PSCs, and their\nperformance was compared with the reference FAPbI3 sample\n(Figure 1c,d). Interestingly, the PV performance was improved\nby the incorporation of phosphonic acid additives in FAPbI3\nperovskites compared to the reference sample (PCE of 18.02%,\nFF of 70%, Jsc of 23.10 mA cm−2, and Voc of 1.11 V). The\nadditive screening commenced with 1,4-PBPA, the simplest\naromatic bisphosphonic acid, with phosphonic acid groups\nattached to the phenyl ring. The 1,4-PBPA-treated PSC\nexhibited the highest PCE (20.16%), FF (76%), Jsc (23.60 mA\ncm−2), and Voc (1.13 V) among the tested additives. 1,4-\nPBMBPA, an analogous aromatic bisphosphonic acid with a\nmethylene bridge connected to the phenyl ring and\nphosphonic acid, was introduced as an additive. It exhibited\na PCE of 18.83%, FF of 74%, Jsc of 23.86 mA cm−2, and Voc of\n1.09 V. Despite their structural similarities, the performance of\n1,4-PBMBPA fell behind that of 1,4-PBPA. This can be\nattributed to the presence of a methylene bridge between the\nphenyl ring and the phosphonic acid groups in 1,4-PBMBPA.\nThis could induce differences in electronic properties, steric\neffects, and conformation, affecting grain growth and crystal\nformation, which would subsequently lead to weak interactions\nwith perovskite grains. Next, a bisphosphonic acid with a\nflexible alkyl chain, 1,6-HDPA, was examined in a similar\nmanner. Although the PSC with 1,6-HDPA exhibited a PCE of\n20.01%, FF of 78%, and Jsc of 23.93 mA cm−2, the Voc was\nfound to be low at 1.08 V. Afterward, we explored the PV\nperformance of SCs using ATMPA. This additive has a trigonal\nbipyramidal geometry with a central nitrogen atom inter-\nconnected to three phosphonic acid functional groups through\nmethylene bridges. Therefore, ATMPA is capable of offering\nmultidimensional binding mode through the phosphonic acid\ngroups. The use of ATMPA resulted in a significant\nimprovement in PV performance (PCE of 20.02%, FF of\n77%, Jsc of 23.81 mA cm−2, and Voc of 1.10 V), which is\ncomparable to those observed for the aromatic phosphonic\nacids used in this study. However, Voc was found to be\nrelatively low.\nAn obvious enhancement in the PV performance was\nobserved with the inclusion of the additive in the FAPbI3\nperovskite layer. This can be attributed to the reduction in trap\ndensity and recombination rate and enhanced charge transport\nproperties. The additive screening suggests that aromatic\nbifunctional moieties contribute favorably to the PV properties\nof PSCs. Furthermore, the optimal concentration of the\nadditive was determined to be 0.003 M by using 1,4-PBPA (see\nSupporting Information and Table S1). The champion device\nFigure 2. Figure 5c presents\nthe light soaking durability of encapsulated PSCs recorded\nunder simulated AM 1.5G illumination at 40 °C and 30% RH.\nBoth FAPbI3 and FAPbI3 with 1,4-PBPA demonstrated a\nretention of over 70% of their initial efficiency after 350 h.\nNevertheless, the PCE of FAPbI3 declined drastically to 2%\nafter 1000 h, while the PCE of FAPbI3 + 1,4-PBPA was able to\nsustain over 60% of its initial efficiency for the same period,\ndemonstrating improved light stability.\nFAPbI3 perovskites are sensitive to temperatures, as\nextensive heat can cause decomposition of the perovskite\nstructure and reduce the efficiency of the SCs. To further\nsubstantiate the thermal stability of PSCs, we investigated the\nimpact of 1,4-PBPA on FAPbI3 SCs at higher temperatures\nthrough thermal stability analyses. Figure 5d demonstrates the\nPCE recorded for the encapsulated PSCs stored in the dark at\n85 °C in a thermal incubator in air. Interestingly, the FAPbI3 +\n1,4-PBPA retained over 70% of its original PCE even after\naging for 1250 h, whereas the FAPbI3 retained only 10% of its\noriginal PCE in the same period. This result reveals that 1,4-\nPBPA significantly enhances the thermal stability of the\nFAPbI3 + 1,4-PBPA PSCs.\nNext, we compared the effect of 1,4-PBPA and terephthalic\nacid (TPA), a carboxylic acid variant, in enhancing the thermal\nstability of FAPbI3 PSCs. TPA was incorporated into the\nFAPbI3 layer using the optimized procedure described in the\nExperimental Section to examine its effect. The thermal\nstability of encapsulated FAPbI3 + 1,4-PBPA and FAPbI3 +\nTPA PSCs was monitored in the dark at 85 °C in a thermal\nincubator in air, as presented in Figure 6a. The PCE of FAPbI3\n+ TPA steadily decreased to 25% of its initial efficiency within\n300 h of aging and experienced sudden efficiency loss. In\ncontrast, the FAPbI3 + 1,4-PBPA maintained 86% of its initial\nPCE for the same duration and then gradually decreased to\napproximately 70% of its original PCE after aging over 1250 h,\nas discussed earlier. This result demonstrates the potential of\nphosphonic acid-based additives over carboxylic acid-based\nadditives in enhancing the long-term thermal stability of\nFAPbI3 SCs.\nThe exceptional thermal stability exhibited by FAPbI3 + 1,4-\nPBPA inspired us to investigate the crystal structure and\nmorphological alterations that occur during thermal aging. In\nFigure S1 (refer to the Supporting Information), the cross-\nsection SEM image acquired after the thermal stability test\nconducted on unencapsulated devices at 85 °C under N2\natmosphere for 50 h is presented. Importantly, no interfacial\ndefects, alterations in layer thickness, voids, or changes in\ncrystal size were observed, which underscores the efficacious\nimpact of 1,4-PBPA in mitigating heat-induced morphological\ntransformations. Figure 6b presents XRD patterns of FAPbI3\nand FAPbI3 + 1,4-PBPA SCs subjected to aging for 50 h under\nidentical experimental conditions. Notably, the absence of the\ncharacteristic peak associated with the δ-phase in the FAPbI3 +\n1,4-PBPA sample implies phase stabilization of α-FAPbI3.\nFurthermore, the absence of the diffraction peak of Pb2+ in\nboth samples points to lead defect passivation. Collectively,\nthese results suggest that 1,4-PBPA contributes to phase\nstabilization and lead defect passivation, thereby strengthening\nthe structural integrity and stability of the FAPbI3-based SCs\nunder severe environmental conditions. The robust perform-\nance of the FAPbI3 + 1,4-PBPA is not only due to suppression\nof δ- FAPbI3 formation, improved film quality and grain size,\nand effective bulk cross-linking but also due to the inherent\nproperties of the organophosphorus compound in enhancing\nthermal stability. Organophosphorus molecules are known for\ntheir excellent heat resistance and flame-retardant properties;\nhence, they are widely used as additives in polymers and\nvarious other functional materials for thermal stability\nenhancement. Furthermore, phosphonic acid possesses strong\nH-donating properties, and its two OH groups foster H-\nbonding interactions. Phosphonic acids are excellent chelators\ncompared to carboxylic acids, exhibiting strong affinity toward\nmetal ions and forming strong bonding interactions.61 The 1,4-\nPBPA additive possesses all of these desirable properties,\nmaking it advantageous for integration into FAPbI3 perov-\nskites. The study indicates that structural differences are\namong the key factors that can influence the interaction\nbetween the additives and the perovskite material, thus\nimpacting the stability of the PSCs.\n4. CONCLUSIONS\nIn summary, high-quality FAPbI3 perovskite containing\ninterconnected grains was prepared using rigid 1,4-PBPA by\none-step-solution processing. The unique properties of 1,4-\nPBPA, including the high cohesive energy of the benzene ring\nand the ability to form strong π−π interactions, enable it to\nFigure 6. Con-\nsequently, it acts as a template, affording bulk cross-linked\nperovskite layers and interconnecting perovskite layers with\ntransport layers. The intercalation of the 1,4-PBPA molecule\ninto FAPbI3 significantly enhances the optoelectronic proper-\nties of the resulting PSCs. This leads to a Voc of 1.14 V and a\nPCE of 21%, representing a substantial improvement over the\nefficiency of the reference FAPbI3 PSCs, which achieved an\nefficiency of 18%. The devices treated with 1,4-PBPA exhibit\nremarkable stability, retaining 100% of their initial efficiency\nwhen an encapsulated device was exposed to 95% RH at 40 °C\nfor 2350 h. These devices preserved 70% of their initial\nefficiency after a thermal stability test at 85 °C following a\n1250 h aging period. The NMR and FTIR analyses confirm\nthat bulk cross-linking is facilitated by atomic-level interactions\nof phosphonic acid groups with the FAPbI3 grains. XRD\nanalysis confirms that 1,4-PBPA remains unincorporated in the\nlattice. These interactions passivate grain boundaries and\ninterfaces, enhance moisture resistance and thermal stability,\nand suppress phase transfer to δ-FAPbI3, providing high\noperational stability. The cross-sectional SEM image obtained\nafter the thermal stability test conducted for the unencapsu-\nlated device reveals that the initial morphology of FAPbI3 is\npreserved in the presence of 1,4-PBPA. ABSTRACT: Perovskite solar cells (PSCs) are gaining a lot of
attention in the field of renewable energy as the most promising
photovoltaic technology, owing to their high performance, low-cost
production, and low-temperature processability. However, long-
term stability remains one of the critical challenges. This work
demonstrates that the introduction of 1,4-phenylenebis-
(phosphonic acid) (1,4-PBPA) in formamidinium lead triiodide
(FAPbI3)-based PSCs provides notable enhancements in moisture
resistance, thermal stability, and power conversion efficiency
(PCE). The 1,4-PBPA acts as a cross-linker and enables strong
interaction between perovskite grains, yielding high-quality films
with reduced defects, as evidenced by morphological and structural
analyses. The encapsulated FAPbI3 PSC devices with 1,4-PBPA
retain 100% of the initial PCE even after 2350 h of aging at 95% relative humidity and 40 °C. Notably, the devices exhibit 70% of the
initial PCE after 1250 h of thermal stability tests at 85 °C. Compared to carboxylic acids, the phosphonic acid additives demonstrate
superior stability enhancements, highlighting their potential to overcome the key limitations of PSCs.
KEYWORDS: phosphonic acid, FAPbI3, stability, perovskite solar cell, efficiency, additive, thermal stability, moisture resistance
1. INTRODUCTION
Solar energy has emerged as one of the potential solutions to
meet the escalating global demand for sustainable and clean
energy. Photovoltaic (PV) technologies play a critical role in
this regard.1 Since the pioneering discovery of solid-state
perovskite solar cells (PSCs), the power conversion efficiency
(PCE) has increased rapidly from 9.7% to a certified PCE of
26.1%.2−6 This significant improvement has been achieved
through collective approaches, including composition engi-
neering, surface passivation, doping, interface engineering, and
many other techniques. Among perovskite materials, for-
mamidinium lead triiodide (FAPbI3) stands out for its unique
optoelectronic properties. Furthermore, FAPbI3 perovskites
exhibit optimum bandgap that is closer to the Shockley−
Queisser limit, high absorption coefficient, and prolonged
charge carrier lifetime.7−12 However, FAPbI3 is thermodynami-
cally unstable. The photoactive α-phase is stable above 150 °C,
below which it spontaneously transforms into the less desirable
wide-bandgap, nonperovskite δ-phase, with moisture accelerat-
ing this transformation.13−17 Despite progress, utilizing FAPbI3
is still recognized as challenging under real-world conditions.
Composition engineering has been widely employed to
address the limitations of FAPbI3-based SCs.1,18−21 This
includes the partial replacement of FA+ ions with smaller
organic or inorganic cations such as methylammonium
(MA+),17,20 propyl ammonium (PA+),9 Li+,22 Na+,22 K+,22−24
Rb+,22,25−27 and Cs+,22,26−28 as well as the partial replacement
of I−ions with Br−ions.29,30 The use of additives results in
high PCEs, improved reproducibility, and enhanced device
stability compared with pristine FAPbI3. However, their
incorporation into the crystal lattice reduces α-phase purity,
leads to bandgap widening, and reduces light absorption.31,32
An alternative strategy involves the partial replacement of FA+
ions with bulkier aliphatic alkylammonium cations, which
improves moisture resistance by forming lower-dimensional
perovskite (2D and 2D/3D hybrids) structures, finding use as
an additive or passivation layer for 3D perovskites.33−36
Nevertheless, this strategy lowers efficiency due to inefficient
charge transport and collection at the interfaces.37

Nonradiative recombination in halide perovskites (HPs) is
mainly associated with the defects at the surface, interface, and
grain boundaries where uncoordinated halide ions and Pb2+
ions accumulate.38,39 This heavily influences the operational
stability and PCE of the PSCs. To overcome these challenges,
numerous studies have investigated the use of small organic
molecules that promote chemical binding, such as carboxylic
acids,40 phosphonic acids,41 sulfonic acids,42 and organo-
ammonium halides.9,43,44 The PO, CO, and SO
binding modes in these additives passivate lead defect sites
and control crystallization in HPs.39
For instance, the incorporation of 5-ammonium valeric acid
iodide (AVAI) chemically stabilized α-FAPbI3 through
atomic−level interaction, as demonstrated by solid-state
NMR and density functional theory (DFT) studies.45 Brown
et al. reported that the inclusion of a phosphonic acid-based
additive improved surface binding, while carboxylic acids
improved electron injection efficiency in SCs.46 Monica and
co-workers demonstrated enhanced stability of HPs, achieved
through shallow point defect passivation in perovskite layers
using a 3-phosphonopropionic acid (H3PP) additive that
contains carboxylic acid and phosphonic acid groups. The
phosphonic acid end forms two types of hydrogen bonding
interactions (H···I and O···H) between HP and H3PP, which
enables extended device stability, while the carboxylic acid
group did not contribute significantly to the stability.39
Phosphonic acid groups have strong H-donating character
that is beneficial for charge injection. However, their utilization
has been less popular than those of carboxylic acid and alkyl
ammonium additives. This is attributed to the tetrahedral
molecular geometry around the phosphorus atom, which
disrupts electron conjugation and reduces charge injection.
Nevertheless, phosphonic acid groups are capable of forming
stable bonding interactions with metal ions, which could
suppress ion migration in PSCs. The strong metal-binding
ability of phosphonic acid groups somewhat counterbalances
the disadvantages of tetrahedral phosphorus.47 Furthermore,
the Lewis base character of hydroxyl groups contributes to the
Pb−O bond formation with uncoordinated Pb2+ ions
(passivation effect), thereby reducing lead defect sites in the
perovskites.48 Although there is acknowledged benefit of the
inclusion of phosphorus atoms for the thermal resistance of
functional materials, their specific impact on PSCs has been
relatively unexplored.
Herein, we report an effective one-step solution process for
phase-pure and high-quality α-FAPbI3 perovskite using grain
bulk cross-linking through a bifunctional phosphonic acid, 1,4-
phenylenebis(phosphonic acid) (1,4-PBPA), which acts as a
template to facilitate well-arranged grain development. The
1,4-PBPA incorporation enhances the quality of the perovskite
layer and reduces trap density, resulting in a superior carrier
lifetime. Consequently, PV devices treated with 1,4-PBPA
exhibit an enhanced PCE of 21%, which surpasses the
efficiency of untreated FAPbI3 PSCs. The encapsulated
FAPbI3 + 1,4-PBPA device retains 100% of their initial PCE
when exposed to 95% relative humidity (RH) at 40 °C for
2350 h. Additionally, the devices preserve 70% of their initial
efficiency after the thermal stability assessment performed at
85 °C, following a 1250 h aging period. NMR and FTIR
analyses reveal bulk cross-linking facilitated by atomic-level
interactions of phosphonic acid groups with the FAPbI3 grain
surface. In contrast, 1,4-PBPA remains unincorporated in the
bulk lattice, according to X-ray diffraction (XRD). Here, we
demonstrate that 1,4-PBPA passivates grain boundaries and
interfaces to improve moisture resistance and thermal stability,
as well as suppresses phase transition to δ-FAPbI3, thus
imparting high operational stability. Scanning electron
microscopy (SEM) and XRD data confirm the preservation
of the crystallinity of the FAPbI3 perovskite structure in the
presence of 1,4-PBPA; in its absence, significant structural
deterioration occurred. Overall, this work highlights the
multifaceted roles of 1,4-PBPA in improving PCE, moisture
resistance, and thermal stability of PSCs.

Bis(trifluoromethylsulfonyl)imide lithium salt (Li-TFSI), titanium
diisopropoxide bis(acetylacetonate), diethyl ether, dimethyl sulfoxide
(DMSO), and N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF) were purchased from
Sigma-Aldrich. 2-Methoxyethanol and ethanol were purchased from
WAKO-Chemicals Co., Ltd. Fluorine doped tin oxide (FTO)-coated
transparent glass (thickness: 1.6 mm, sheet resistance ≤10 Ω cm−2)
was purchased from Nippon Sheet Glass.
2.2. Synthesis of FAPbI3 Powder. The FAPbI3 powder was
synthesized in accordance with the previously reported procedure.8 In
brief, an equimolar solution of FAI (0.8 M) and PI2 (0.8 M) in 2-
methoxyethanol was heated to 135 °C for 1 h under stirring. The
black precipitate was collected by filtration and dried over a hot plate
at 150 °C for 3 h. The resulting powder was further dried at 80 °C
under reduced pressure overnight, affording the FAPbI3 precursor
(68%).
2.3. Solar Cell Fabrication. The laser-patterned FTO substrate
was sequentially cleaned in an ultrasonicator using 2% Hellmanex
aqueous solution, deionized water, acetone, and ethanol for 10 min
each. After drying using compressed air, the substrates were cleaned
by ultraviolet-ozone for 20 min.
A compact TiO2 (c-TiO2) layer was coated over the FTO substrate
by spray pyrolysis at 400 °C using a titanium diisopropoxide
bis(acetylacetonate) (75 wt % in isopropanol) precursor solution
diluted in ethanol (1:15.7 v/v). A mesoporous titanium dioxide (m-
TiO2) layer was deposited on the FTO/c-TiO2 substrate by spin
coating using a diluted solution of 30 NR-D paste in ethanol (1:5.5
wt/wt). The substrate was then subjected to a two-step annealing
process in air at 100 °C for 10 min and 120 °C for 15 min.
Subsequently, the substrate was subjected to annealing at 450 °C for a
period of 30 min. Following this, the resulting FTO/c-TiO2/m-TiO2
substrate was transferred to a dry room for the deposition of
perovskite.
FAPbI3-based SCs were fabricated by a one-step antisolvent
deposition method utilizing a 1.5 M FAPbI3 precursor solution, which
was prepared by dissolving FAPbI3 powder and 0.75 M MACl in a
DMF/DMSO (4:1 v/v) mixed solution. For the additive-doped
FAPbI3 PSCs, an additional 0.01 M of additive was added to the
FAPbI3 precursor solution. The FAPbI3 precursor solution was spin
coated over FTO/c-TiO2/m-TiO2 substrate at 6000 rpm for 50 s with
dripping diethyl ether (0.5 mL). The resulting substrate was then
subjected to a rapid annealing process on a hot plate at 150 °C for a
period of 10 min. In order to achieve surface passivation,
octylammonium iodide (15 mM) in isopropyl alcohol (IPA) was
spin coated at 3000 rpm for 30 s and subsequently dried at room
temperature for a period of 24 h. Subsequently, the hole transport

2.4. Device Characterization. The PV performances of SCs were
measured with a digital source meter (Keithley 2400), equipped with
a solar simulator (XB-15T1W1, Wacom Electric Co.) with an AM
1.5G filter, which was adjusted by a calibrated Si reference cell. An
antireflective black metal mask with an aperture of 0.16 cm2 was used
during measurements to eliminate scattered light. A current−voltage
scan was conducted at a constant speed of 100 mV s−1. The PV
properties of the SCs were estimated from an average of 20 samples.
The aging test was conducted in a dry room in the dark at ambient
temperature and RH below 10%. A moisture stability test was
conducted in the dark at 95% RH and 40 °C using a benchtop type
temperature and humidity chamber (SH-242, Espec Co., Ltd.). A
thermal stability test was performed at 85 °C in a thermal incubator
with the unencapsulated cells and the encapsulated devices subjected
to the same conditions. For the encapsulated devices, the experiments
were conducted under a nitrogen atmosphere at 85 °C. The
performance of the devices was periodically measured under
simulated sunlight at room temperature.
Steady-state photoluminescence and time-resolved photolumines-
cence (TRPL) measurements were conducted on perovskite
monolayer samples deposited on a quartz glass substrate. The PL
and PL lifetimes were quantified by a time-correlated single photon
counting system (C12132, Hamamatsu Photonics) at the emission
peak with excitation at 532 nm. The lifetimes were estimated by
double exponential fitting using the origin© software. The incident
photon-to-current conversion efficiency (IPCE) measurement was
conducted with an action spectrum measurement setup (CEP-99W,
Bunkou-Keiki) and a black aperture mask (0.16 cm2) positioned in
front of the incoming light. A SEM image was captured by using a
SEM system (S4800, Hitachi). The experiments were conducted by
using hand-cut samples. The ultraviolet−visible (UV−vis) absorbance
of the perovskite film deposited on the quartz glass was recorded
using a UV−vis spectrophotometer (V-770, JASCO). The impedance
spectra were recorded by using a potentiostat galvanostat (EnergyLab
XM, Ametek Scientific Instruments). The X-ray crystallography of the
perovskite film was acquired by using an X-ray diffractometer
(SmartLab, Rigaku) equipped with a Cu Kα source. The Fourier
transform infrared (FTIR) spectra of the perovskite samples were
recorded by using a Fourier transform infrared spectrometer
(Spectrum One, PerkinElmer Instruments) with optimal resolution
parameters and 32 accumulations in attenuated total reflection (ATR)
mode. A solid-state 31P CP/MAS NMR (cross-polarization/magic
angle spinning nuclear magnetic resonance) spectrum was acquired
using the Bruker AVANCE 400WB spectrometer (B0 = 9.4 T). A 3.2
mm HXY VT-MAS probe was used with a rotor spinning rate of 14
kHz. The contact and duration times were set to 3500 μs and 4 s,
respectively. Both data were accumulated 96 times.
2.5. DFT Calculation. The adsorption/desorption energies were
obtained by using first-principles calculations. Perdew−Burke−
Ernzerhof exchange−correlation density functional revised for solids
(PBEsol)49 approximation to the exchange−correlation interactions
as implemented in the VASP code.50,51 All atom positions were
relaxed. Prerelaxation was conducted using the commercially available
Matlantis package from Preferred Networks with their universal
PreFerred Potential (PFP)52 version 7.0.0, a NNP trained on the PBE
generalized gradient approximation to DFT.53 The lattice parameters
were fixed to those in literature.54

3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
Organophosphonic acid additives can interact within the
perovskite layer and with transport layers similarly to
carboxylic acid-based additives, which significantly improves
the PV performance of PSCs.46,47,55−57 To gain insight into the
impact of phosphonic acid functional groups on the efficiency
and stability of PSCs, organic molecules possessing phosphonic
acid groups, 1,4-PBPA, 1,4-PBMBPA, 1,6-HDPA, and ATMPA
were investigated as additives for PSCs (Figure 1a). The
additives used in this study differ in their chain length, number
of functional groups, and structure. The PSCs were fabricated
by solution processing using the following architecture: Glass/
FTO/c-TiO2/m-TiO2/perovskite/OAI/Spiro-OMe-TAD/Au
(Figure 1b). The reference FAPbI3 PSCs, hereafter denoted as
“FAPbI3”, were fabricated by a one-step antisolvent deposition
method using a 1.5 M FAPbI3 precursor solution containing
0.75 M MACl. For the additive-doped FAPbI3 PSCs (denoted
as “FAPbI3 + name of the additive”), an additional 0.01 M
additive was added to the FAPbI3 precursor solution.
We first analyzed the PV performance of PSCs, and their
performance was compared with the reference FAPbI3 sample
(Figure 1c,d). Interestingly, the PV performance was improved
by the incorporation of phosphonic acid additives in FAPbI3
perovskites compared to the reference sample (PCE of 18.02%,
FF of 70%, Jsc of 23.10 mA cm−2, and Voc of 1.11 V). The
additive screening commenced with 1,4-PBPA, the simplest
aromatic bisphosphonic acid, with phosphonic acid groups
attached to the phenyl ring. The 1,4-PBPA-treated PSC
exhibited the highest PCE (20.16%), FF (76%), Jsc (23.60 mA
cm−2), and Voc (1.13 V) among the tested additives. 1,4-
PBMBPA, an analogous aromatic bisphosphonic acid with a
methylene bridge connected to the phenyl ring and
phosphonic acid, was introduced as an additive. It exhibited
a PCE of 18.83%, FF of 74%, Jsc of 23.86 mA cm−2, and Voc of
1.09 V. Despite their structural similarities, the performance of
1,4-PBMBPA fell behind that of 1,4-PBPA. This can be
attributed to the presence of a methylene bridge between the
phenyl ring and the phosphonic acid groups in 1,4-PBMBPA.
This could induce differences in electronic properties, steric
effects, and conformation, affecting grain growth and crystal
formation, which would subsequently lead to weak interactions
with perovskite grains. Next, a bisphosphonic acid with a
flexible alkyl chain, 1,6-HDPA, was examined in a similar
manner. Although the PSC with 1,6-HDPA exhibited a PCE of
20.01%, FF of 78%, and Jsc of 23.93 mA cm−2, the Voc was
found to be low at 1.08 V. Afterward, we explored the PV
performance of SCs using ATMPA. This additive has a trigonal
bipyramidal geometry with a central nitrogen atom inter-
connected to three phosphonic acid functional groups through
methylene bridges. Therefore, ATMPA is capable of offering
multidimensional binding mode through the phosphonic acid
groups. The use of ATMPA resulted in a significant
improvement in PV performance (PCE of 20.02%, FF of
77%, Jsc of 23.81 mA cm−2, and Voc of 1.10 V), which is
comparable to those observed for the aromatic phosphonic
acids used in this study. However, Voc was found to be
relatively low.
An obvious enhancement in the PV performance was
observed with the inclusion of the additive in the FAPbI3
perovskite layer. This can be attributed to the reduction in trap
density and recombination rate and enhanced charge transport
properties. The additive screening suggests that aromatic
bifunctional moieties contribute favorably to the PV properties
of PSCs. Furthermore, the optimal concentration of the
additive was determined to be 0.003 M by using 1,4-PBPA (see
Supporting Information and Table S1). The champion device

measured by IPCE measurements. Interestingly, the IPCE
spectrum of FAPbI3 + 1,4-PBPA demonstrated higher

to FAPbI3. The enhancement in IPCE can be attributed to

The impact of 1,4-PBPA on the optoelectronic properties of
FAPbI3 perovskites was systematically investigated by using
steady-state UV−vis absorption spectroscopy and PL spec-
troscopy. Figure 3b,c presents the UV−vis absorption and PL
spectra of FAPbI3 films with and without 1,4-PBPA deposited
on a glass substrate. The UV−vis absorption spectra of both
perovskite films were comparable, showing identical band
edges, indicating that the incorporation of 1,4-PBPA did not
alter the fundamental optical bandgap of the perovskite.
However, the PL spectra revealed that the FAPbI3 film
containing 1,4-PBPA exhibited significantly higher emission
intensity compared to the FAPbI3 film without 1,4-PBPA. This
suggests that 1,4-PBPA effectively reduced nonradiative
recombination losses, leading to enhanced luminescence
efficiency and more exciton generation. These improvements
can be attributed to the reduced defect density and improved
crystallinity of the perovskite films, demonstrating the
beneficial role of 1,4-PBPA in enhancing the optoelectronic
properties of FAPbI3 perovskites.
TRPL analysis was performed to investigate the recombina-
tion rate of excitons in FAPbI3 perovskites, both with and
without 1,4-PBPA deposited on a glass film. Figure 3d displays
the TRPL decays of FAPbI3 and FAPbI3 + 1,4-PBPA measured
under pulse excitation at 532 nm. The charge carrier lifetime
was determined by fitting single exponential decay to TRPL
data. The estimated lifetime of FAPbI3 perovskite with 1,4-
PBPA is longer than that of FAPbI3 perovskite without 1,4-
PBPA. This indicates that 1,4-PBPA-treated FAPbI3 perovskite
exhibits efficient exciton generation and delayed nonradiative
recombination compared to untreated FAPbI3 perovskite. This
outcome is facilitated by a reduction in defect or trap density
within the perovskite layer achieved through a bulk cross-
linking mechanism assisted by the phosphonic acid groups in
1,4-PBPA.

Powder XRD was used to analyze the effect of 1,4-PBPA on
the crystallinity of the perovskite film deposited on the FTO/c-
TiO2/m-TiO2 substrate. Both FAPbI3 and FAPbI3 + 1,4-PBPA

presence of the α-phase of the FAPbI3 perovskite (Figure 4a).

induce any noticeable changes in the lattice parameters, thus
eliminating the possibility of 1,4-PBPA additive integration
into the crystal lattice. Instead, 1,4-PBPA acts as a template,
influencing the growing perovskite grains to adopt a specific
crystal packing arrangement.

Solid-state 31P CP/MAS NMR spectroscopy was used to
investigate the interactions between 1,4-PBPA and FAPbI3
perovskite at an atomic level. CP/MAS NMR is a commonly
used characterization technique for analyzing atomic-level
interactions between organic additives and perovskites. Figure
4e illustrates the 31P CP/MAS NMR spectra of both 1,4-PBPA
and FAPbI3 containing 1,4-PBPA. In the 31P CP/MAS NMR
spectra, the phosphorus nucleus of 1,4-PBPA exhibited a
chemical shift at 15.88 ppm. Upon introduction of 1,4-PBPA
into FAPbI3 perovskites, this peak splits into two signals,
observed at 16.16 and 13.60 ppm, respectively. The signal
splitting is due to chemical shift anisotropy, which occurs when
the local electronic environment surrounding the nucleus is
not isotropic. Observations indicate a potential bulk cross-
linking between 1,4-PBPA and the anisotropic FAPbI3
perovskite, leading to changes in the local electronic environ-
ment around the phosphorus nuclei in 1,4-PBPA. Consistent
with previous studies,60 bulk cross-linking between 1,4-PBPA
and FAPbI3 occurs primarily through the PO bond in 1,4-
PBPA. The PO interacts with FA+ ions in the “A” site and
Pb2+ ions in the “B” site of the perovskite structure. The DFT
analysis indicates strong binding interactions at both the FAI-
and PbI2-terminated surfaces. At the FAI-terminated surface,
the oxygen atom bonded to P in 1,4-PBPA forms hydrogen
bonds with two hydrogen atoms from neighboring FA
molecules with a binding energy of 0.99 eV, indicating a
strong surface interaction (Figure S2). At the PbI2-terminated
surface, the oxygen atom bonded to P directly bonds to a
surface Pb atom with a binding energy of 0.95 eV,
demonstrating robust surface binding (Figure S3). The high
binding energy at both surface terminations confirms the
strong surface anchoring of 1,4-PBPA on perovskite. The DFT
results provide quantitative evidence for a strong interaction
between perovskite and 1,4-PBPA, which is consistent with our
experimental observation, including NMR, IR, SEM, and
TRPL decay measurements, supporting the improved material
quality and device performance.

stability of encapsulated FAPbI3 + 1,4-PBPA and FAPbI3 +
TPA PSCs was monitored in the dark at 85 °C in a thermal
incubator in air, as presented in Figure 6a. The PCE of FAPbI3
+ TPA steadily decreased to 25% of its initial efficiency within
300 h of aging and experienced sudden efficiency loss. In
contrast, the FAPbI3 + 1,4-PBPA maintained 86% of its initial
PCE for the same duration and then gradually decreased to
approximately 70% of its original PCE after aging over 1250 h,
as discussed earlier. This result demonstrates the potential of
phosphonic acid-based additives over carboxylic acid-based
additives in enhancing the long-term thermal stability of
FAPbI3 SCs.
The exceptional thermal stability exhibited by FAPbI3 + 1,4-
PBPA inspired us to investigate the crystal structure and
morphological alterations that occur during thermal aging. In
Figure S1 (refer to the Supporting Information), the cross-
section SEM image acquired after the thermal stability test
conducted on unencapsulated devices at 85 °C under N2
atmosphere for 50 h is presented. Importantly, no interfacial
defects, alterations in layer thickness, voids, or changes in
crystal size were observed, which underscores the efficacious
impact of 1,4-PBPA in mitigating heat-induced morphological
transformations. Figure 6b presents XRD patterns of FAPbI3
and FAPbI3 + 1,4-PBPA SCs subjected to aging for 50 h under
identical experimental conditions. Notably, the absence of the
characteristic peak associated with the δ-phase in the FAPbI3 +
1,4-PBPA sample implies phase stabilization of α-FAPbI3.
Furthermore, the absence of the diffraction peak of Pb2+ in
both samples points to lead defect passivation. Collectively,
these results suggest that 1,4-PBPA contributes to phase
stabilization and lead defect passivation, thereby strengthening
the structural integrity and stability of the FAPbI3-based SCs
under severe environmental conditions. The robust perform-
ance of the FAPbI3 + 1,4-PBPA is not only due to suppression
of δ- FAPbI3 formation, improved film quality and grain size,
and effective bulk cross-linking but also due to the inherent
properties of the organophosphorus compound in enhancing
thermal stability. Organophosphorus molecules are known for
their excellent heat resistance and flame-retardant properties;
hence, they are widely used as additives in polymers and
various other functional materials for thermal stability
enhancement. Furthermore, phosphonic acid possesses strong
H-donating properties, and its two OH groups foster H-
bonding interactions. Phosphonic acids are excellent chelators
compared to carboxylic acids, exhibiting strong affinity toward
metal ions and forming strong bonding interactions.61 The 1,4-
PBPA additive possesses all of these desirable properties,
making it advantageous for integration into FAPbI3 perov-
skites. The study indicates that structural differences are
among the key factors that can influence the interaction
between the additives and the perovskite material, thus
impacting the stability of the PSCs.
4. CONCLUSIONS
In summary, high-quality FAPbI3 perovskite containing
interconnected grains was prepared using rigid 1,4-PBPA by
one-step-solution processing. The unique properties of 1,4-
PBPA, including the high cohesive energy of the benzene ring
and the ability to form strong π−π interactions, enable it to

sequently, it acts as a template, affording bulk cross-linked
perovskite layers and interconnecting perovskite layers with
transport layers. The intercalation of the 1,4-PBPA molecule
into FAPbI3 significantly enhances the optoelectronic proper-
ties of the resulting PSCs. This leads to a Voc of 1.14 V and a
PCE of 21%, representing a substantial improvement over the
efficiency of the reference FAPbI3 PSCs, which achieved an
efficiency of 18%. The devices treated with 1,4-PBPA exhibit
remarkable stability, retaining 100% of their initial efficiency
when an encapsulated device was exposed to 95% RH at 40 °C
for 2350 h. These devices preserved 70% of their initial
efficiency after a thermal stability test at 85 °C following a
1250 h aging period. The NMR and FTIR analyses confirm
that bulk cross-linking is facilitated by atomic-level interactions
of phosphonic acid groups with the FAPbI3 grains. XRD
analysis confirms that 1,4-PBPA remains unincorporated in the
lattice. These interactions passivate grain boundaries and
interfaces, enhance moisture resistance and thermal stability,
and suppress phase transfer to δ-FAPbI3, providing high
operational stability. The cross-sectional SEM image obtained
after the thermal stability test conducted for the unencapsu-
lated device reveals that the initial morphology of FAPbI3 is
preserved in the presence of 1,4-PBPA. Overall, our findings
open new opportunities for the development of highly efficient
and stable PSCs, paving the way for the next generation of
sustainable energy solutions.

Enhance Efficiency and High-Temperature Durability in FAPbI3
Perovskite Solar Cells
Siby Mathew,* Naoyuki Nishimura, Atsushi Kogo, Tetsuji Itoh, Kohei Yamamoto, Yoyo Hinuma,
and Takurou N. Murakami*

ABSTRACT: Perovskite solar cells (PSCs) are gaining a lot of
attention in the field of renewable energy as the most promising
photovoltaic technology, owing to their high performance, low-cost
production, and low-temperature processability. However, long-
term stability remains one of the critical challenges. This work
demonstrates that the introduction of 1,4-phenylenebis-
(phosphonic acid) (1,4-PBPA) in formamidinium lead triiodide
(FAPbI3)-based PSCs provides notable enhancements in moisture
resistance, thermal stability, and power conversion efficiency
(PCE). The 1,4-PBPA acts as a cross-linker and enables strong
interaction between perovskite grains, yielding high-quality films
with reduced defects, as evidenced by morphological and structural
analyses. The encapsulated FAPbI3 PSC devices with 1,4-PBPA
retain 100% of the initial PCE even after 2350 h of aging at 95% relative humidity and 40 °C. Notably, the devices exhibit 70% of the
initial PCE after 1250 h of thermal stability tests at 85 °C. Compared to carboxylic acids, the phosphonic acid additives demonstrate
superior stability enhancements, highlighting their potential to overcome the key limitations of PSCs.
KEYWORDS: phosphonic acid, FAPbI3, stability, perovskite solar cell, efficiency, additive, thermal stability, moisture resistance
1. INTRODUCTION
Solar energy has emerged as one of the potential solutions to
meet the escalating global demand for sustainable and clean
energy. Photovoltaic (PV) technologies play a critical role in
this regard.1 Since the pioneering discovery of solid-state
perovskite solar cells (PSCs), the power conversion efficiency
(PCE) has increased rapidly from 9.7% to a certified PCE of
26.1%.2−6 This significant improvement has been achieved
through collective approaches, including composition engi-
neering, surface passivation, doping, interface engineering, and
many other techniques. Among perovskite materials, for-
mamidinium lead triiodide (FAPbI3) stands out for its unique
optoelectronic properties. Furthermore, FAPbI3 perovskites
exhibit optimum bandgap that is closer to the Shockley−
Queisser limit, high absorption coefficient, and prolonged
charge carrier lifetime.7−12 However, FAPbI3 is thermodynami-
cally unstable. The photoactive α-phase is stable above 150 °C,
below which it spontaneously transforms into the less desirable
wide-bandgap, nonperovskite δ-phase, with moisture accelerat-
ing this transformation.13−17 Despite progress, utilizing FAPbI3
is still recognized as challenging under real-world conditions.
Composition engineering has been widely employed to
address the limitations of FAPbI3-based SCs.1,18−21 This
includes the partial replacement of FA+ ions with smaller
organic or inorganic cations such as methylammonium
(MA+),17,20 propyl ammonium (PA+),9 Li+,22 Na+,22 K+,22−24
Rb+,22,25−27 and Cs+,22,26−28 as well as the partial replacement
of I−ions with Br−ions.29,30 The use of additives results in
high PCEs, improved reproducibility, and enhanced device
stability compared with pristine FAPbI3. However, their
incorporation into the crystal lattice reduces α-phase purity,
leads to bandgap widening, and reduces light absorption.31,32
An alternative strategy involves the partial replacement of FA+
ions with bulkier aliphatic alkylammonium cations, which
improves moisture resistance by forming lower-dimensional
perovskite (2D and 2D/3D hybrids) structures, finding use as
an additive or passivation layer for 3D perovskites.33−36
Nevertheless, this strategy lowers efficiency due to inefficient
charge transport and collection at the interfaces.37

Nonradiative recombination in halide perovskites (HPs) is
mainly associated with the defects at the surface, interface, and
grain boundaries where uncoordinated halide ions and Pb2+
ions accumulate.38,39 This heavily influences the operational
stability and PCE of the PSCs. To overcome these challenges,
numerous studies have investigated the use of small organic
molecules that promote chemical binding, such as carboxylic
acids,40 phosphonic acids,41 sulfonic acids,42 and organo-
ammonium halides.9,43,44 The PO, CO, and SO
binding modes in these additives passivate lead defect sites
and control crystallization in HPs.39
For instance, the incorporation of 5-ammonium valeric acid
iodide (AVAI) chemically stabilized α-FAPbI3 through
atomic−level interaction, as demonstrated by solid-state
NMR and density functional theory (DFT) studies.45 Brown
et al. reported that the inclusion of a phosphonic acid-based
additive improved surface binding, while carboxylic acids
improved electron injection efficiency in SCs.46 Monica and
co-workers demonstrated enhanced stability of HPs, achieved
through shallow point defect passivation in perovskite layers
using a 3-phosphonopropionic acid (H3PP) additive that
contains carboxylic acid and phosphonic acid groups. The
phosphonic acid end forms two types of hydrogen bonding
interactions (H···I and O···H) between HP and H3PP, which
enables extended device stability, while the carboxylic acid
group did not contribute significantly to the stability.39
Phosphonic acid groups have strong H-donating character
that is beneficial for charge injection. However, their utilization
has been less popular than those of carboxylic acid and alkyl
ammonium additives. This is attributed to the tetrahedral
molecular geometry around the phosphorus atom, which
disrupts electron conjugation and reduces charge injection.
Nevertheless, phosphonic acid groups are capable of forming
stable bonding interactions with metal ions, which could
suppress ion migration in PSCs. The strong metal-binding
ability of phosphonic acid groups somewhat counterbalances
the disadvantages of tetrahedral phosphorus.47 Furthermore,
the Lewis base character of hydroxyl groups contributes to the
Pb−O bond formation with uncoordinated Pb2+ ions
(passivation effect), thereby reducing lead defect sites in the
perovskites.48 Although there is acknowledged benefit of the
inclusion of phosphorus atoms for the thermal resistance of
functional materials, their specific impact on PSCs has been
relatively unexplored.
Herein, we report an effective one-step solution process for
phase-pure and high-quality α-FAPbI3 perovskite using grain
bulk cross-linking through a bifunctional phosphonic acid, 1,4-
phenylenebis(phosphonic acid) (1,4-PBPA), which acts as a
template to facilitate well-arranged grain development. The
1,4-PBPA incorporation enhances the quality of the perovskite
layer and reduces trap density, resulting in a superior carrier
lifetime. Consequently, PV devices treated with 1,4-PBPA
exhibit an enhanced PCE of 21%, which surpasses the
efficiency of untreated FAPbI3 PSCs. The encapsulated
FAPbI3 + 1,4-PBPA device retains 100% of their initial PCE
when exposed to 95% relative humidity (RH) at 40 °C for
2350 h. Additionally, the devices preserve 70% of their initial
efficiency after the thermal stability assessment performed at
85 °C, following a 1250 h aging period. NMR and FTIR
analyses reveal bulk cross-linking facilitated by atomic-level
interactions of phosphonic acid groups with the FAPbI3 grain
surface. In contrast, 1,4-PBPA remains unincorporated in the
bulk lattice, according to X-ray diffraction (XRD). Here, we
demonstrate that 1,4-PBPA passivates grain boundaries and
interfaces to improve moisture resistance and thermal stability,
as well as suppresses phase transition to δ-FAPbI3, thus
imparting high operational stability. Scanning electron
microscopy (SEM) and XRD data confirm the preservation
of the crystallinity of the FAPbI3 perovskite structure in the
presence of 1,4-PBPA; in its absence, significant structural
deterioration occurred. Overall, this work highlights the
multifaceted roles of 1,4-PBPA in improving PCE, moisture
resistance, and thermal stability of PSCs.
2. EXPERIMENTAL SECTION
2.1. Materials. All chemicals were used as received without further
purification unless otherwise mentioned. 1,4-PBPA, 1,4 phenylenebis-
(methylene)bis(phosphonic acid) (1,4-PBMBPA), 1,6-hexylenediph-
sophonic acid (1,6-HDPA), and aminotris(methylphosphonic acid)
(ATMPA), formamidine hydroiodide (FAI), lead iodide (PbI2),
methylammonium chloride (MACl), n-octyl ammonium iodide
(OAI), and 4-tert-butylpyridine (t-BP) were procured from Tokyo
Chemical Industry Co., Ltd. Mesoporous titanium oxide (m-TiO2;
18NR-D) precursor was purchased from Great Cell Solar. 2,2′,7,7′-
tetrakis(N,N-di-4-methoxyphenylamino)-9,9′-spirobifluorene (Spiro-
OMeTAD) was purchased from Nippon Fine Chemical Co.
Bis(trifluoromethylsulfonyl)imide lithium salt (Li-TFSI), titanium
diisopropoxide bis(acetylacetonate), diethyl ether, dimethyl sulfoxide
(DMSO), and N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF) were purchased from
Sigma-Aldrich. 2-Methoxyethanol and ethanol were purchased from
WAKO-Chemicals Co., Ltd. Fluorine doped tin oxide (FTO)-coated
transparent glass (thickness: 1.6 mm, sheet resistance ≤10 Ω cm−2)
was purchased from Nippon Sheet Glass.
2.2. Synthesis of FAPbI3 Powder. The FAPbI3 powder was
synthesized in accordance with the previously reported procedure.8 In
brief, an equimolar solution of FAI (0.8 M) and PI2 (0.8 M) in 2-
methoxyethanol was heated to 135 °C for 1 h under stirring. The
black precipitate was collected by filtration and dried over a hot plate
at 150 °C for 3 h. The resulting powder was further dried at 80 °C
under reduced pressure overnight, affording the FAPbI3 precursor
(68%).
2.3. Solar Cell Fabrication. The laser-patterned FTO substrate
was sequentially cleaned in an ultrasonicator using 2% Hellmanex
aqueous solution, deionized water, acetone, and ethanol for 10 min
each. After drying using compressed air, the substrates were cleaned
by ultraviolet-ozone for 20 min.
A compact TiO2 (c-TiO2) layer was coated over the FTO substrate
by spray pyrolysis at 400 °C using a titanium diisopropoxide
bis(acetylacetonate) (75 wt % in isopropanol) precursor solution
diluted in ethanol (1:15.7 v/v). A mesoporous titanium dioxide (m-
TiO2) layer was deposited on the FTO/c-TiO2 substrate by spin
coating using a diluted solution of 30 NR-D paste in ethanol (1:5.5
wt/wt). The substrate was then subjected to a two-step annealing
process in air at 100 °C for 10 min and 120 °C for 15 min.
Subsequently, the substrate was subjected to annealing at 450 °C for a
period of 30 min. Following this, the resulting FTO/c-TiO2/m-TiO2
substrate was transferred to a dry room for the deposition of
perovskite.
FAPbI3-based SCs were fabricated by a one-step antisolvent
deposition method utilizing a 1.5 M FAPbI3 precursor solution, which
was prepared by dissolving FAPbI3 powder and 0.75 M MACl in a
DMF/DMSO (4:1 v/v) mixed solution. For the additive-doped
FAPbI3 PSCs, an additional 0.01 M of additive was added to the
FAPbI3 precursor solution. The FAPbI3 precursor solution was spin
coated over FTO/c-TiO2/m-TiO2 substrate at 6000 rpm for 50 s with
dripping diethyl ether (0.5 mL). The resulting substrate was then
subjected to a rapid annealing process on a hot plate at 150 °C for a
period of 10 min. In order to achieve surface passivation,
octylammonium iodide (15 mM) in isopropyl alcohol (IPA) was
spin coated at 3000 rpm for 30 s and subsequently dried at room
temperature for a period of 24 h. Subsequently, the hole transport

layer (HTL) was deposited on the surface of the passivation layer via
spin coating. This involved the use of a solution comprising spiro-
OMeTAD (71 mM), Li-TFSI (49 mM), and t-BP (21 mM) in
chlorobenzene, applied at 3000 rpm for 30 s. Finally, a gold electrode
was deposited on the surface of the HTL via thermal evaporation.
2.4. Device Characterization. The PV performances of SCs were
measured with a digital source meter (Keithley 2400), equipped with
a solar simulator (XB-15T1W1, Wacom Electric Co.) with an AM
1.5G filter, which was adjusted by a calibrated Si reference cell. An
antireflective black metal mask with an aperture of 0.16 cm2 was used
during measurements to eliminate scattered light. A current−voltage
scan was conducted at a constant speed of 100 mV s−1. The PV
properties of the SCs were estimated from an average of 20 samples.
The aging test was conducted in a dry room in the dark at ambient
temperature and RH below 10%. A moisture stability test was
conducted in the dark at 95% RH and 40 °C using a benchtop type
temperature and humidity chamber (SH-242, Espec Co., Ltd.). A
thermal stability test was performed at 85 °C in a thermal incubator
with the unencapsulated cells and the encapsulated devices subjected
to the same conditions. For the encapsulated devices, the experiments
were conducted under a nitrogen atmosphere at 85 °C. The
performance of the devices was periodically measured under
simulated sunlight at room temperature.
Steady-state photoluminescence and time-resolved photolumines-
cence (TRPL) measurements were conducted on perovskite
monolayer samples deposited on a quartz glass substrate. The PL
and PL lifetimes were quantified by a time-correlated single photon
counting system (C12132, Hamamatsu Photonics) at the emission
peak with excitation at 532 nm. The lifetimes were estimated by
double exponential fitting using the origin© software. The incident
photon-to-current conversion efficiency (IPCE) measurement was
conducted with an action spectrum measurement setup (CEP-99W,
Bunkou-Keiki) and a black aperture mask (0.16 cm2) positioned in
front of the incoming light. A SEM image was captured by using a
SEM system (S4800, Hitachi). The experiments were conducted by
using hand-cut samples. The ultraviolet−visible (UV−vis) absorbance
of the perovskite film deposited on the quartz glass was recorded
using a UV−vis spectrophotometer (V-770, JASCO). The impedance
spectra were recorded by using a potentiostat galvanostat (EnergyLab
XM, Ametek Scientific Instruments). The X-ray crystallography of the
perovskite film was acquired by using an X-ray diffractometer
(SmartLab, Rigaku) equipped with a Cu Kα source. The Fourier
transform infrared (FTIR) spectra of the perovskite samples were
recorded by using a Fourier transform infrared spectrometer
(Spectrum One, PerkinElmer Instruments) with optimal resolution
parameters and 32 accumulations in attenuated total reflection (ATR)
mode. A solid-state 31P CP/MAS NMR (cross-polarization/magic
angle spinning nuclear magnetic resonance) spectrum was acquired
using the Bruker AVANCE 400WB spectrometer (B0 = 9.4 T). A 3.2
mm HXY VT-MAS probe was used with a rotor spinning rate of 14
kHz. The contact and duration times were set to 3500 μs and 4 s,
respectively. Both data were accumulated 96 times.
2.5. DFT Calculation. The adsorption/desorption energies were
obtained by using first-principles calculations. Perdew−Burke−
Ernzerhof exchange−correlation density functional revised for solids
(PBEsol)49 approximation to the exchange−correlation interactions
as implemented in the VASP code.50,51 All atom positions were
relaxed. Prerelaxation was conducted using the commercially available
Matlantis package from Preferred Networks with their universal
PreFerred Potential (PFP)52 version 7.0.0, a NNP trained on the PBE
generalized gradient approximation to DFT.53 The lattice parameters
were fixed to those in literature.54
A supercell with 2 × 2 × 8 perovskite blocks was built. In the FAI-
terminated model, atoms were removed to obtain a slab with three
FAI layers and two PbI2 layers. One FA was removed from the top
and bottom surfaces. Such a model is not exactly nonpolar but does
not have a substantial electric field penetrating the slab in the
direction normal to the slab. In the adsorbed state, a 1,4-PBPA
molecule was placed such that the PO3H2 side of the molecule is
positioned at the FA vacancy site. The 1,4-PBPA molecule was moved
10 Å from the slab to obtain the desorbed state. On the other hand, a
PbI2-terminated model containing two FAI layers and three PbI2

3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
Organophosphonic acid additives can interact within the
perovskite layer and with transport layers similarly to
carboxylic acid-based additives, which significantly improves
the PV performance of PSCs.46,47,55−57 To gain insight into the
impact of phosphonic acid functional groups on the efficiency
and stability of PSCs, organic molecules possessing phosphonic
acid groups, 1,4-PBPA, 1,4-PBMBPA, 1,6-HDPA, and ATMPA
were investigated as additives for PSCs (Figure 1a). The
additives used in this study differ in their chain length, number
of functional groups, and structure. The PSCs were fabricated
by solution processing using the following architecture: Glass/
FTO/c-TiO2/m-TiO2/perovskite/OAI/Spiro-OMe-TAD/Au
(Figure 1b). The reference FAPbI3 PSCs, hereafter denoted as
“FAPbI3”, were fabricated by a one-step antisolvent deposition
method using a 1.5 M FAPbI3 precursor solution containing
0.75 M MACl. For the additive-doped FAPbI3 PSCs (denoted
as “FAPbI3 + name of the additive”), an additional 0.01 M
additive was added to the FAPbI3 precursor solution.
We first analyzed the PV performance of PSCs, and their
performance was compared with the reference FAPbI3 sample
(Figure 1c,d). Interestingly, the PV performance was improved
by the incorporation of phosphonic acid additives in FAPbI3
perovskites compared to the reference sample (PCE of 18.02%,
FF of 70%, Jsc of 23.10 mA cm−2, and Voc of 1.11 V). The
additive screening commenced with 1,4-PBPA, the simplest
aromatic bisphosphonic acid, with phosphonic acid groups
attached to the phenyl ring. The 1,4-PBPA-treated PSC
exhibited the highest PCE (20.16%), FF (76%), Jsc (23.60 mA
cm−2), and Voc (1.13 V) among the tested additives. 1,4-
PBMBPA, an analogous aromatic bisphosphonic acid with a
methylene bridge connected to the phenyl ring and
phosphonic acid, was introduced as an additive. It exhibited
a PCE of 18.83%, FF of 74%, Jsc of 23.86 mA cm−2, and Voc of
1.09 V. Despite their structural similarities, the performance of
1,4-PBMBPA fell behind that of 1,4-PBPA. This can be
attributed to the presence of a methylene bridge between the
phenyl ring and the phosphonic acid groups in 1,4-PBMBPA.
This could induce differences in electronic properties, steric
effects, and conformation, affecting grain growth and crystal
formation, which would subsequently lead to weak interactions
with perovskite grains. Next, a bisphosphonic acid with a
flexible alkyl chain, 1,6-HDPA, was examined in a similar
manner. Although the PSC with 1,6-HDPA exhibited a PCE of
20.01%, FF of 78%, and Jsc of 23.93 mA cm−2, the Voc was
found to be low at 1.08 V. Afterward, we explored the PV
performance of SCs using ATMPA. This additive has a trigonal
bipyramidal geometry with a central nitrogen atom inter-
connected to three phosphonic acid functional groups through
methylene bridges. Therefore, ATMPA is capable of offering
multidimensional binding mode through the phosphonic acid
groups. The use of ATMPA resulted in a significant
improvement in PV performance (PCE of 20.02%, FF of
77%, Jsc of 23.81 mA cm−2, and Voc of 1.10 V), which is
comparable to those observed for the aromatic phosphonic
acids used in this study. However, Voc was found to be
relatively low.
An obvious enhancement in the PV performance was
observed with the inclusion of the additive in the FAPbI3
perovskite layer. This can be attributed to the reduction in trap
density and recombination rate and enhanced charge transport
properties. The additive screening suggests that aromatic
bifunctional moieties contribute favorably to the PV properties
of PSCs. Furthermore, the optimal concentration of the
additive was determined to be 0.003 M by using 1,4-PBPA (see
Supporting Information and Table S1). The champion device

and Voc of 1.14 V with a lowest hysteresis index of 0.03%

The spectral response and performance of the SCs were
measured by IPCE measurements. Interestingly, the IPCE
spectrum of FAPbI3 + 1,4-PBPA demonstrated higher
efficiency in the wavelength range of 300−860 nm compared
to FAPbI3. The enhancement in IPCE can be attributed to

PBPA into the FAPbI3 perovskite layer. The integrated current

shown in Figure 3a.
The impact of 1,4-PBPA on the optoelectronic properties of
FAPbI3 perovskites was systematically investigated by using
steady-state UV−vis absorption spectroscopy and PL spec-
troscopy. Figure 3b,c presents the UV−vis absorption and PL
spectra of FAPbI3 films with and without 1,4-PBPA deposited
on a glass substrate. The UV−vis absorption spectra of both

alter the fundamental optical bandgap of the perovskite.
However, the PL spectra revealed that the FAPbI3 film
containing 1,4-PBPA exhibited significantly higher emission
intensity compared to the FAPbI3 film without 1,4-PBPA. This
suggests that 1,4-PBPA effectively reduced nonradiative
recombination losses, leading to enhanced luminescence
efficiency and more exciton generation. These improvements
can be attributed to the reduced defect density and improved
crystallinity of the perovskite films, demonstrating the
beneficial role of 1,4-PBPA in enhancing the optoelectronic
properties of FAPbI3 perovskites.

higher impedance. A larger semicircle (indicating higher

which is generally beneficial for SC efficiency because it allows
more charges to be collected before they recombine. Notably,
despite exhibiting higher resistance compared with the FAPbI3
SC without 1,4-PBPA, the cell with 1,4-PBPA also displayed a
higher Voc. The combination of higher Voc and larger resistance
reveals reduced charge recombination dynamics in the FAPbI3
perovskite when 1,4-PBPA is present. This highlights the
impact of 1,4-PBPA on the electronic properties of FAPbI3
SCs, potentially leading to an improved device performance.
Powder XRD was used to analyze the effect of 1,4-PBPA on
the crystallinity of the perovskite film deposited on the FTO/c-
TiO2/m-TiO2 substrate. Both FAPbI3 and FAPbI3 + 1,4-PBPA
samples exhibited diffraction peaks at 2θ = 14.08° and 28.23°,
corresponding to the (110) and (220) planes, indicating the
presence of the α-phase of the FAPbI3 perovskite (Figure 4a).
The hexagonal, nonperovskite δ-FAPbI3 phase was not present
in either sample. The average crystallite size of the perovskite
layer was estimated by analyzing the full width at half-
maximum (fwhm) of the (110) plane diffraction peak using the
Scherrer equation,58 and the estimated size was 22.01 nm for
FAPbI3 and 24.20 nm for FAPbI3 + 1,4-PBPA perovskite film.
The result signifies that the addition of 1,4-PBPA did not
induce any noticeable changes in the lattice parameters, thus
eliminating the possibility of 1,4-PBPA additive integration
into the crystal lattice. Instead, 1,4-PBPA acts as a template,
influencing the growing perovskite grains to adopt a specific
crystal packing arrangement.
Figure 4b,c shows a top view SEM image of FAPbI3 and
FAPbI3 + 1,4-PBPA perovskite films. Both samples display
polydisperse microsized perovskite grains. Notably, the FAPbI3
yields loosely distributed perovskite islands with grain sizes
ranging from ∼0.25 to ∼1.25 μm on the m-TiO2 layer. Distinct
defects and voids are clearly visible at the grain boundaries in
FAPbI3 (highlighted a few of them by yellow circles in Figure
4b). The analysis suggests that there is insufficient surface
coverage of the perovskite layer on the m-TiO2 layer,
indicating structural imperfections. On the other hand, the
FAPbI3 + 1,4-PBPA film exhibited a densely packed perovskite
layer on the m-TiO2 layer with grain sizes ranging from ∼0.40
to ∼1.35 μm (Figure 4c). A smooth morphology with
continuous and interconnected grains was observed through-
out the perovskite layer. The morphological improvement
reduced defect sites and voids in the FAPbI3 + 1,4-PBPA
perovskites, which is in stark contrast to the uneven and
fractured morphology observed for the FAPbI3 perovskites.

ATR-FTIR spectra of the FAPbI3 perovskite film with and

corresponds to the characteristic stretching vibration bands

Solid-state 31P CP/MAS NMR spectroscopy was used to
investigate the interactions between 1,4-PBPA and FAPbI3
perovskite at an atomic level. CP/MAS NMR is a commonly
used characterization technique for analyzing atomic-level
interactions between organic additives and perovskites. Figure
4e illustrates the 31P CP/MAS NMR spectra of both 1,4-PBPA
and FAPbI3 containing 1,4-PBPA. In the 31P CP/MAS NMR
spectra, the phosphorus nucleus of 1,4-PBPA exhibited a
chemical shift at 15.88 ppm. Upon introduction of 1,4-PBPA
into FAPbI3 perovskites, this peak splits into two signals,
observed at 16.16 and 13.60 ppm, respectively. The signal
splitting is due to chemical shift anisotropy, which occurs when
the local electronic environment surrounding the nucleus is
not isotropic. Observations indicate a potential bulk cross-
linking between 1,4-PBPA and the anisotropic FAPbI3
perovskite, leading to changes in the local electronic environ-
ment around the phosphorus nuclei in 1,4-PBPA. Consistent
with previous studies,60 bulk cross-linking between 1,4-PBPA
and FAPbI3 occurs primarily through the PO bond in 1,4-
PBPA. The PO interacts with FA+ ions in the “A” site and
Pb2+ ions in the “B” site of the perovskite structure. The DFT
analysis indicates strong binding interactions at both the FAI-
and PbI2-terminated surfaces. At the FAI-terminated surface,
the oxygen atom bonded to P in 1,4-PBPA forms hydrogen
bonds with two hydrogen atoms from neighboring FA
molecules with a binding energy of 0.99 eV, indicating a
strong surface interaction (Figure S2). At the PbI2-terminated
surface, the oxygen atom bonded to P directly bonds to a
surface Pb atom with a binding energy of 0.95 eV,
demonstrating robust surface binding (Figure S3). The high
binding energy at both surface terminations confirms the
strong surface anchoring of 1,4-PBPA on perovskite. The DFT
results provide quantitative evidence for a strong interaction
between perovskite and 1,4-PBPA, which is consistent with our
experimental observation, including NMR, IR, SEM, and
TRPL decay measurements, supporting the improved material
quality and device performance.
Figure 5a displays the aging effects observed in the PCE of
unencapsulated FAPbI3 SCs, with and without 1,4-PBPA,
stored in a dry room in the dark at ambient temperature, where
the RH is maintained below 10%. Aging led to a rapid increase
in the PCE of FAPbI3 + 1,4-PBPA SCs during the initial stages
of storage. Following this, the PCE slowly improved, leading to
an overall efficiency boost of around 12% after 2350 h.
Conversely, the reference FAPbI3 exhibited a gradual decline in
performance, with about a 6% efficiency loss observed after
1400 h of testing under the specified conditions. In the case of
PSC with 1,4-PBPA, the average Jsc, Voc, and FF were improved
during the aging process, in line with the previously reported
self-enhancement of the PCE of HPs. The reference FAPbI3
showed a decrease in the average Jsc, Voc, and FF, resulting in
performance loss.

FAPbI3 perovskites are sensitive to temperatures, as
extensive heat can cause decomposition of the perovskite
structure and reduce the efficiency of the SCs. To further
substantiate the thermal stability of PSCs, we investigated the
impact of 1,4-PBPA on FAPbI3 SCs at higher temperatures
through thermal stability analyses. Figure 5d demonstrates the
PCE recorded for the encapsulated PSCs stored in the dark at
85 °C in a thermal incubator in air. Interestingly, the FAPbI3 +
1,4-PBPA retained over 70% of its original PCE even after
aging for 1250 h, whereas the FAPbI3 retained only 10% of its
original PCE in the same period. This result reveals that 1,4-
PBPA significantly enhances the thermal stability of the
FAPbI3 + 1,4-PBPA PSCs.
Next, we compared the effect of 1,4-PBPA and terephthalic
acid (TPA), a carboxylic acid variant, in enhancing the thermal
stability of FAPbI3 PSCs. TPA was incorporated into the
FAPbI3 layer using the optimized procedure described in the
Experimental Section to examine its effect. The thermal
stability of encapsulated FAPbI3 + 1,4-PBPA and FAPbI3 +
TPA PSCs was monitored in the dark at 85 °C in a thermal
incubator in air, as presented in Figure 6a. The PCE of FAPbI3
+ TPA steadily decreased to 25% of its initial efficiency within
300 h of aging and experienced sudden efficiency loss. In
contrast, the FAPbI3 + 1,4-PBPA maintained 86% of its initial
PCE for the same duration and then gradually decreased to
approximately 70% of its original PCE after aging over 1250 h,
as discussed earlier. This result demonstrates the potential of
phosphonic acid-based additives over carboxylic acid-based
additives in enhancing the long-term thermal stability of
FAPbI3 SCs.
The exceptional thermal stability exhibited by FAPbI3 + 1,4-
PBPA inspired us to investigate the crystal structure and
morphological alterations that occur during thermal aging. In
Figure S1 (refer to the Supporting Information), the cross-
section SEM image acquired after the thermal stability test
conducted on unencapsulated devices at 85 °C under N2
atmosphere for 50 h is presented. Importantly, no interfacial
defects, alterations in layer thickness, voids, or changes in
crystal size were observed, which underscores the efficacious
impact of 1,4-PBPA in mitigating heat-induced morphological
transformations. Figure 6b presents XRD patterns of FAPbI3
and FAPbI3 + 1,4-PBPA SCs subjected to aging for 50 h under
identical experimental conditions. Notably, the absence of the
characteristic peak associated with the δ-phase in the FAPbI3 +
1,4-PBPA sample implies phase stabilization of α-FAPbI3.
Furthermore, the absence of the diffraction peak of Pb2+ in
both samples points to lead defect passivation. Collectively,
these results suggest that 1,4-PBPA contributes to phase
stabilization and lead defect passivation, thereby strengthening
the structural integrity and stability of the FAPbI3-based SCs
under severe environmental conditions. The robust perform-
ance of the FAPbI3 + 1,4-PBPA is not only due to suppression
of δ- FAPbI3 formation, improved film quality and grain size,
and effective bulk cross-linking but also due to the inherent
properties of the organophosphorus compound in enhancing
thermal stability. Organophosphorus molecules are known for
their excellent heat resistance and flame-retardant properties;
hence, they are widely used as additives in polymers and
various other functional materials for thermal stability
enhancement. Furthermore, phosphonic acid possesses strong
H-donating properties, and its two OH groups foster H-
bonding interactions. Phosphonic acids are excellent chelators
compared to carboxylic acids, exhibiting strong affinity toward
metal ions and forming strong bonding interactions.61 The 1,4-
PBPA additive possesses all of these desirable properties,
making it advantageous for integration into FAPbI3 perov-
skites. The study indicates that structural differences are
among the key factors that can influence the interaction
between the additives and the perovskite material, thus
impacting the stability of the PSCs.
4. CONCLUSIONS
In summary, high-quality FAPbI3 perovskite containing
interconnected grains was prepared using rigid 1,4-PBPA by
one-step-solution processing. The unique properties of 1,4-
PBPA, including the high cohesive energy of the benzene ring
and the ability to form strong π−π interactions, enable it to

sequently, it acts as a template, affording bulk cross-linked
perovskite layers and interconnecting perovskite layers with
transport layers. The intercalation of the 1,4-PBPA molecule
into FAPbI3 significantly enhances the optoelectronic proper-
ties of the resulting PSCs. This leads to a Voc of 1.14 V and a
PCE of 21%, representing a substantial improvement over the
efficiency of the reference FAPbI3 PSCs, which achieved an
efficiency of 18%. The devices treated with 1,4-PBPA exhibit
remarkable stability, retaining 100% of their initial efficiency
when an encapsulated device was exposed to 95% RH at 40 °C
for 2350 h. These devices preserved 70% of their initial
efficiency after a thermal stability test at 85 °C following a
1250 h aging period. The NMR and FTIR analyses confirm
that bulk cross-linking is facilitated by atomic-level interactions
of phosphonic acid groups with the FAPbI3 grains. XRD
analysis confirms that 1,4-PBPA remains unincorporated in the
lattice. These interactions passivate grain boundaries and
interfaces, enhance moisture resistance and thermal stability,
and suppress phase transfer to δ-FAPbI3, providing high
operational stability. The cross-sectional SEM image obtained
after the thermal stability test conducted for the unencapsu-
lated device reveals that the initial morphology of FAPbI3 is
preserved in the presence of 1,4-PBPA. Overall, our findings
open new opportunities for the development of highly efficient
and stable PSCs, paving the way for the next generation of
sustainable energy solutions.

A widely \naccepted view is that moderate water content induces the formation of hydrate phase which \nenhances the recrystallization of the perovskite. However, the underlying factors which \ninfluence the formation of hydrate phase have yet to be investigated. Herein, by controlling \nthe annealing temperature, it is demonstrated that 60 ℃ is the most suitable temperature for \nthe formation of hydrated perovskite. After further annealing at 120 ℃, the resulting \nperovskite film reveals enhanced crystallinity with a more uniform morphology, contributing \nto device efficiency above 20%. In addition, the water effect on different types of perovskites \nis studied and it is concluded that the formation of hydrated perovskite is mainly determined \nby the cations of the perovskite itself. The findings in this work elucidate the conditions for \nthe formation of hydrated perovskite, contributing to the fabrication of highly efficient \nperovskite solar cells. \n \nAccepted Article\n\n\nThis article is protected by copyright. Introduction \nOrganic-inorganic halide perovskites (OIHP) have attracted significant attention from both \nacademic and industrial communities in recent years.[1] Their unique optoelectronic \nproperties[2-5] have made them an exceptional material class for various applications, such as \nlight-emitting diodes (LED),[6] photodetectors,[7] field effect transistors,[8] and solar cells.[9] In \nphotovoltaics, this new family of materials has proven to be easily solution-processed while \nexhibiting comparable properties with those industrial staples, such as GaAs and Si.[10,11] \nWithin only 10 years, the efficiencies of the perovskite solar cells (PSCs) have rapidly \nincreased from 3.9% to 25.2%.[12-17] Such remarkable progress has made PSCs one of the \nmost promising photovoltaic technologies. \nDespite the simple fabrication, low cost and high efficiency advantages, PSCs suffer from \nseveral drawbacks that need to be overcome before realistic application. Chief among them \nare the sensitivity and instability of the perovskite toward water or moisture.[18,19] To \nunderstand the degradation mechanisms and developing effective solutions to fabricate air \nstable PSCs, tremendous efforts have been devoted. Early studies indicate that water molecule \ntends to induce hydrolysis reactions in which perovskite is degraded into PbI2, and gases, such \nas HI and CH3NH2.[20] Later, Kamat et al.[21] reported that an intermediate perovskite \ndihydrate phase, similar to (MA)4PbI6·2H2O, may be formed before degradation. Shortly \nthereafter, by using time-resolved XRD and ellipsometry method, Barnes and coworkers[22] \ndemonstrated that the perovskite first became monohydrate MAPbI3·H2O before further \nhydration to (MA)4PbI6·2H2O. Benefited from these experimental results and combining with \nsome theoretical studies,[23-25] the moisture-induced degradation mechanism was elucidated by \nHeben et al.[26] Namely, with the presence of water, perovskite first forms monohydrate phase, \nthen further hydrates to dihydrate phase, and finally degrades into PbI2 and other byproducts. \nInterestingly, the formation of monohydrate perovskite was found fully reversible, leading to \nimproved device performance.[27,28] Yang et al.[29] systematically studied the effect of moisture \nAccepted Article\n\n\nThis article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved \n \non the structure and morphology of the perovskite films. They indicated that moderate \nmoisture content led to improved crystallization of the perovskite film by enhancing the \nreconstruction process. More recently, Lunt et al.[30] demonstrated a significant enhancement \nin perovskite crystallinity by directly adding moderate content of water in the perovskite \nprecursor. However, though hydrated perovskite is beneficial in enhancing the crystallinity of \nperovskite, the underlying factors which influence the formation of hydrated perovskite \nremain almost totally unexplored.[31] Besides, the studies of water effect on PSCs thus far \nhave all concentrated on single methylammonium (MA) cation-based perovskite materials. \nWhile in our previous work,[32] triple cation (Cs+, MA+, FA+) based perovskite was studied, \nthe water effect on low dimensional (1D or 2D)[33] and all-inorganic perovskite[34] remains \nunknown. \nHere, we investigate the effect of annealing temperature on the formation of hydrated \nperovskite. The perovskites were deposited using a two-step annealing method, and the phase, \nmorphology, crystallinity as well as optical properties were systematically analyzed. By \nvarying the first annealing (1-A) temperature from 40 to 100 ℃, 60 ℃ is found favorable to \nthe formation of hydrated perovskite which led to a crystal reconstruction in the second \nannealing (2-A) stage, leading to enhanced crystallization of perovskite. As a result, device \nefficiency of above 20% is achieved. In addition, the water effect on different kinds of \nperovskites, such as MAPbI3 (single cation, MA), FA0.85MA0.15PbI2.55Br0.45 (double cation, \nFAMA), guanidinium based GAPbI3 (1D, GA) and CsPbI2Br (all-inorganic, Cs), was studied. \nThe results demonstrate that while water has beneficial impact on improving the crystallinity \nand optoelectronic properties of MA, FAMA and GA perovskites, it has little effect on all-\ninorganic perovskites. Thus, it is concluded that water effect on perovskite is mainly \ndetermined by the cations of the perovskite itself. \n \n2. Effect of Annealing Temperature on the Formation of Hydrated Perovskite \nIt has been reported that water content, pressure and temperature play significant role in \nhydrate formation.[35,36] To ascertain the optimum temperature, water content and pressure are \nwell controlled this study. Conventional FA0.85MA0.15PbI2.55Br0.45 double cation based \nperovskite, abbreviated as FAMA, is adopted as the model system. Water was directly added \nto the perovskite precursor, and the content was controlled at 2% (volume ratio) according to \nprevious studies.[37,38] The post annealing process was divided into two stages: first annealing \n(1-A) stage and second annealing (2-A) stage, as illustrated in Figure 1a. By varying the \ntemperature of the 1-A stage from 40 to 100 ℃, different perovskite films were fabricated and \nnamed as A1 (40 ℃), B1 (60 ℃), C1 (80 ℃) and D1 (100 ℃), respectively. Correspondingly, \nafter the 2-A treatment, the obtained perovskite films were labeled as A, B, C and D. The \ncrystalline structure of the perovskites was evaluated using X-ray diffraction (XRD). For 1-A \nsamples (Figure 1b), almost all diffraction peaks can be assigned to perovskite phase, except \nfor the peak located at around 10.6°. According to previous studies,[23,39,40] this emerging peak \ncorresponds to hydrated perovskite, indicating that the hydrate phase was formed during the \n1-A stage. In contrast, all of the 2-A samples reveal pure perovskite phase, as shown in Figure \n1c. Interestingly, it is noted that sample B shows the strongest and sharpest (110) diffraction \npeak, indicating a highly crystallized perovskite film. Further, UV-vis absorption of the \nperovskites was studied and shown in Figure 1d and e. Consequently, 1-A samples (Figure 1d) \nshow increasing absorption along with the annealing temperature from 40 to 100 ℃. This can \nbe ascribed to enhanced crystallinity with increasing annealing temperature as shown in \nFigure 1b. While, for the 2-A samples (Figure 1e), sample B shows the highest absorption due \nto its highest crystallinity. \nTo evaluate the composition of hydrated perovskite in 1-A samples, X-ray photoelectron \nspectroscopy (XPS) measurement was conducted. The results were fitted using Gaussian-\nLorentzian functions with a Shirley type background as shown in Figure 2. Clearly, for the 1-\nAccepted Article\n\n\nThis article is protected by copyright. Conclusion \nIn summary, we have systematically investigated the influence of annealing temperature on \nthe formation of hydrated perovskite. The results suggest that 60 ℃ is the most favorable \ntemperature for the formation of hydrate phase which leads to a reconstruction process in the \nsecond annealing stage. The resulting films reveal enhanced crystallinity and a more uniform \nmorphology, enabling the fabrication of perovskite solar cells with high efficiency and good \nreproducibility. Moreover, according to the crystalline phase, morphology, and optoelectronic \nproperties results derived from different kinds of perovskites, it is concluded that the water \neffects are mainly determined by the cations of the perovskite itself. Impact of Temperature Dependent Hydration Water on Perovskite Solar Cells
