Keywords: perovskite solar cell, water effect, annealing temperature, cation 
 
Water effect on perovskite solar cells has received growing interest in recent years. A widely 
accepted view is that moderate water content induces the formation of hydrate phase which 
enhances the recrystallization of the perovskite. However, the underlying factors which 
influence the formation of hydrate phase have yet to be investigated. Herein, by controlling 
the annealing temperature, it is demonstrated that 60 ℃ is the most suitable temperature for 
the formation of hydrated perovskite. After further annealing at 120 ℃, the resulting 
perovskite film reveals enhanced crystallinity with a more uniform morphology, contributing 
to device efficiency above 20%. In addition, the water effect on different types of perovskites 
is studied and it is concluded that the formation of hydrated perovskite is mainly determined 
by the cations of the perovskite itself. The findings in this work elucidate the conditions for 
the formation of hydrated perovskite, contributing to the fabrication of highly efficient

1. Introduction 
Organic-inorganic halide perovskites (OIHP) have attracted significant attention from both 
academic and industrial communities in recent years.[1] Their unique optoelectronic 
properties[2-5] have made them an exceptional material class for various applications, such as 
light-emitting diodes (LED),[6] photodetectors,[7] field effect transistors,[8] and solar cells.[9] In 
photovoltaics, this new family of materials has proven to be easily solution-processed while 
exhibiting comparable properties with those industrial staples, such as GaAs and Si.[10,11] 
Within only 10 years, the efficiencies of the perovskite solar cells (PSCs) have rapidly 
increased from 3.9% to 25.2%.[12-17] Such remarkable progress has made PSCs one of the 
most promising photovoltaic technologies. 
Despite the simple fabrication, low cost and high efficiency advantages, PSCs suffer from 
several drawbacks that need to be overcome before realistic application. Chief among them 
are the sensitivity and instability of the perovskite toward water or moisture.[18,19] To 
understand the degradation mechanisms and developing effective solutions to fabricate air 
stable PSCs, tremendous efforts have been devoted. Early studies indicate that water molecule 
tends to induce hydrolysis reactions in which perovskite is degraded into PbI2, and gases, such 
as HI and CH3NH2.[20] Later, Kamat et al.[21] reported that an intermediate perovskite 
dihydrate phase, similar to (MA)4PbI6·2H2O, may be formed before degradation. Shortly 
thereafter, by using time-resolved XRD and ellipsometry method, Barnes and coworkers[22] 
demonstrated that the perovskite first became monohydrate MAPbI3·H2O before further 
hydration to (MA)4PbI6·2H2O. Benefited from these experimental results and combining with 
some theoretical studies,[23-25] the moisture-induced degradation mechanism was elucidated by 
Heben et al.[26] Namely, with the presence of water, perovskite first forms monohydrate phase, 
then further hydrates to dihydrate phase, and finally degrades into PbI2 and other byproducts. 
Interestingly, the formation of monohydrate perovskite was found fully reversible, leading to 
improved device performance.[27,28] Yang et al.[29] systematically studied the effect of moisture

This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved 
 
on the structure and morphology of the perovskite films. They indicated that moderate 
moisture content led to improved crystallization of the perovskite film by enhancing the 
reconstruction process. More recently, Lunt et al.[30] demonstrated a significant enhancement 
in perovskite crystallinity by directly adding moderate content of water in the perovskite 
precursor. However, though hydrated perovskite is beneficial in enhancing the crystallinity of 
perovskite, the underlying factors which influence the formation of hydrated perovskite 
remain almost totally unexplored.[31] Besides, the studies of water effect on PSCs thus far 
have all concentrated on single methylammonium (MA) cation-based perovskite materials. 
While in our previous work,[32] triple cation (Cs+, MA+, FA+) based perovskite was studied, 
the water effect on low dimensional (1D or 2D)[33] and all-inorganic perovskite[34] remains 
unknown. 
Here, we investigate the effect of annealing temperature on the formation of hydrated 
perovskite. The perovskites were deposited using a two-step annealing method, and the phase, 
morphology, crystallinity as well as optical properties were systematically analyzed. By 
varying the first annealing (1-A) temperature from 40 to 100 ℃, 60 ℃ is found favorable to 
the formation of hydrated perovskite which led to a crystal reconstruction in the second 
annealing (2-A) stage, leading to enhanced crystallization of perovskite. As a result, device 
efficiency of above 20% is achieved. In addition, the water effect on different kinds of 
perovskites, such as MAPbI3 (single cation, MA), FA0.85MA0.15PbI2.55Br0.45 (double cation, 
FAMA), guanidinium based GAPbI3 (1D, GA) and CsPbI2Br (all-inorganic, Cs), was studied. 
The results demonstrate that while water has beneficial impact on improving the crystallinity 
and optoelectronic properties of MA, FAMA and GA perovskites, it has little effect on all-
inorganic perovskites. Thus, it is concluded that water effect on perovskite is mainly 
determined by the cations of the perovskite itself.

2.1. Effect of Annealing Temperature on the Formation of Hydrated Perovskite 
It has been reported that water content, pressure and temperature play significant role in 
hydrate formation.[35,36] To ascertain the optimum temperature, water content and pressure are 
well controlled this study. Conventional FA0.85MA0.15PbI2.55Br0.45 double cation based 
perovskite, abbreviated as FAMA, is adopted as the model system. Water was directly added 
to the perovskite precursor, and the content was controlled at 2% (volume ratio) according to 
previous studies.[37,38] The post annealing process was divided into two stages: first annealing 
(1-A) stage and second annealing (2-A) stage, as illustrated in Figure 1a. By varying the 
temperature of the 1-A stage from 40 to 100 ℃, different perovskite films were fabricated and 
named as A1 (40 ℃), B1 (60 ℃), C1 (80 ℃) and D1 (100 ℃), respectively. Correspondingly, 
after the 2-A treatment, the obtained perovskite films were labeled as A, B, C and D. The 
crystalline structure of the perovskites was evaluated using X-ray diffraction (XRD). For 1-A 
samples (Figure 1b), almost all diffraction peaks can be assigned to perovskite phase, except 
for the peak located at around 10.6°. According to previous studies,[23,39,40] this emerging peak 
corresponds to hydrated perovskite, indicating that the hydrate phase was formed during the 
1-A stage. In contrast, all of the 2-A samples reveal pure perovskite phase, as shown in Figure 
1c. Interestingly, it is noted that sample B shows the strongest and sharpest (110) diffraction 
peak, indicating a highly crystallized perovskite film. Further, UV-vis absorption of the 
perovskites was studied and shown in Figure 1d and e. Consequently, 1-A samples (Figure 1d) 
show increasing absorption along with the annealing temperature from 40 to 100 ℃. This can 
be ascribed to enhanced crystallinity with increasing annealing temperature as shown in 
Figure 1b. While, for the 2-A samples (Figure 1e), sample B shows the highest absorption due 
to its highest crystallinity. 
To evaluate the composition of hydrated perovskite in 1-A samples, X-ray photoelectron 
spectroscopy (XPS) measurement was conducted. The results were fitted using Gaussian-
Lorentzian functions with a Shirley type background as shown in Figure 2. Clearly, for the 1-

respectively. While, in the case of samples without water, only one peak at 532.4 eV was

Besides, the composition of hydrated perovskite in 1-A samples was estimated by calculating

storage environment, the area of O 1s peak at 532.4 eV was standardized, and the results are 
summarized in Table S1 (Supporting Information). The largest area of O 1s peak at 531.4 eV 
for sample B1 (Figure 2b) suggests the highest concentration of hydrate phase, indicating that 
60 ℃ is the most suitable temperature for the formation of hydrated perovskite. Further 
increasing the temperature tends to accelerate the crystallization of pure perovskite but not the 
formation of hydrate phase, as suggested by the XRD results (Figure 1b). Earlier studies have 
demonstrated that hydrated perovskite contributes to a recrystallization process, leading to an 
enhancement of crystallinity.[29,32,37] This is the reason why sample B has higher crystallinity 
than A, C and D, as shown in Figure 1c.

compact and pinhole-free morphology with a similar grain size. Combining with atomic force 
microscopy (AFM) images (Figure S1, Supporting Information), it is clear that sample B

2.2. Water Effect on Different Kinds of Perovskites 
To further investigate the impact of perovskite cation on the formation of hydrate phase, 
water effect on different cation-based perovskites, such as MAPbI3 (single cation, MA), 
FA0.85MA0.15PbI2.55Br0.45 (double cation, FAMA), GAPbI3 (low dimensional, GA) and 
CsPbI2Br (all-inorganic, Cs), was studied. The corresponding atomic structure and ionic 
radius of the different cations are shown in Figure 5a. It is clear that guanidinium has an ionic 
radius of 278 pm, which is slightly too large to form a 3D perovskite structure.[43] Analysis of 
the Goldschmidt tolerance factor (t) reveals that pure GAPbI3 has a t value of 1.03, indicating 
a low dimensional perovskite structure.[44] XRD spectra of the perovskites with and without 
(w/o) water are shown in Figure 5b-e. It is noted that all the perovskites show significantly 
enhanced diffraction peak intensity with water introduced, except for all-inorganic Cs 
perovskites (Figure 5e). Further, the full width at half maximum (FWHM) of the diffraction 
peaks was calculated as shown in the corresponding inset. Noticeably, MA, FAMA and GA

Previous studies have demonstrated that water interacts with both the cation ions and lead 
halide framework of the perovskite through hydrogen bonding.[24,25] According to Rappe and 
his coworkers,[53] H2O-MA+ bond in MAPbI3 is mainly derived from the binding between N-
bound hydrogen (HN) and H2O-bound oxygen (OW), while, the H2O-PbI2 bonding represents a 
triaxial phenomenon which consists of one OW-Pb2+ bond and two HW-I- bonds. Computing 
the corresponding binding energy indicated that H2O-MA+ bonding is more favorable while 
the H2O-PbI2 bond is likely to occur under a super-hydrous state (2H2O per MA). In this study, 
the water content was controlled at a low 2% volume ratio, which makes the formation of 
H2O-PbI2 bond unlikely, as indicated by the similar Pb 4f XPS results (Figure S7, Supporting 
Information). Therefore, the effect of water on perovskites is mainly attributed to the

3. Conclusion 
In summary, we have systematically investigated the influence of annealing temperature on 
the formation of hydrated perovskite. The results suggest that 60 ℃ is the most favorable 
temperature for the formation of hydrate phase which leads to a reconstruction process in the 
second annealing stage. The resulting films reveal enhanced crystallinity and a more uniform 
morphology, enabling the fabrication of perovskite solar cells with high efficiency and good 
reproducibility. Moreover, according to the crystalline phase, morphology, and optoelectronic 
properties results derived from different kinds of perovskites, it is concluded that the water 
effects are mainly determined by the cations of the perovskite itself. It is suggested that 
further theoretical and experimental studies should be carried out to verify our assumption 
that water effects are only applicable to perovskite which contains plenty of N-bound 
hydrogen (HN) atoms. 
 
Experimental Section 
Materials: The SnO2 colloid was purchased from Alfa Aesar (tin (IV) oxide). 
Methylammonium iodide (MAI), Methylammonium bromide (MABr), and Cesium bromide 
(CsBr) were purchased from Xi’an Polymer Light Technology Corp. Formamidinium iodide 
(FAI) was purchased from Dyesol Ltd. (Queanbeyan, Australia). Lead iodide (PbI2, 99%), 
Lead bromide (PbBr2, 99.999%), Guanidinium iodide (GAI, 99%), N,N-Dimethylformamide 
(DMF, 99.8%), Dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO, 99.9%), and Chlorobenzene (99.8%) were 
purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. 
Device Fabrication: Devices were fabricated on FTO substrates (15 Ω sq−1) with

dimensions of 20×20 mm. The substrates were thoroughly cleaned and treated with plasma 
for 5 min before usage. Then, a layer of SnO2 was deposited in ambient air as the electron 
transport layer. The MA or GA perovskite films were spin coated from a precursor solution 
containing MAI (1 M) or GAI (1 M) and PbI2 (1 M) in DMF:DMSO 4:1 (v/v). The prepared 
perovskite precursor was dropped on the substrate and spin-coated at 600 rpm for 5 s and then 
at 4000 rpm for 40 s. During the second procedure, 150 μL toluene was dropped on the 
spinning substrate 25 s before program ended. To gain FAMA perovskite films, FAI (1 M), 
PbI2 (1.05 M), MABr (0.2 M), and PbBr2 (0.2 M) were dissolved in DMF:DMSO 4:1 (v/v). A 
same spin protocol was adopted, only the antisolvent dripping time was changed to 15 s 
before program ended. While, for Cs perovskites, CsBr (1 M) and PbI2 (1 M) were dissolved 
in DMSO, and the precursor was spin-coated at 600 rpm for 5 s and then at 3000 rpm for 30 s. 
Importantly, 20 μL (2% volume ratio) of water was directly added in the different kinds of 
perovskite precursor. The resulting FAMA films were annealed at 40, 60, 80, and 100 °C for 5 
min for 1-A samples and then at 120 °C for 10 min for 2-A samples. MA and GA films were 
annealed at 60 °C for 5 min and then at 120 °C for 10 min. Cs perovskite films were annealed 
at 60 °C for 1 min and then at 250 °C for 10 min. After cooling to room temperature, a 
conventional Spiro-OMeTAD layer, which consisted of 72.3 mg spiro-OMeTAD, 28.8 μL 4-
tertbutylpyridine, 17.5 μL lithium-bis (trifluoromethanesulfonyl) imide (Li-TFSI) solution 
(520 mg Li-TFSI in 1 mL acetonitrile), and 1 mL chlorobenzene , was deposited on the 
perovskite films as the hole transport layer. Finally, Au electrode was fabricated using a 
shadow mask under high vacuum by thermal evaporation.

measured using a solar simulator (Newport Oriel Sol 3A Class AAA, 64023A) equipped with 
450 W Xenon lamp (Oriel, USA) and a Keithley 2400 source meter. The light intensity was 
calibrated to AM 1.5G (100 mW cm-2) by using a reference Si solar cell (Newport). The 
devices were masked with a metal aperture of 0.06 cm-2 to define the active area. The J-V

Table of content 
 
A two-step annealing method is developed for studying the water effect on different kinds of 
perovskites. It is demonstrated that 60 ℃ is favorable to the formation of hydrate phase which 
leads to a reconstruction process in the second annealing stage. The corresponding water 
effects highly depend on the cations of the perovskite itself. 
 
Keywords: perovskite solar cells, water effect, annealing temperature, different cations 
 
Weihai Zhang, Juan Xiong, Jinhua Li, Walid A. Daoud*

Impact of Temperature Dependent Hydration Water on Perovskite Solar Cells 
 
Weihai Zhang, Juan Xiong, Jinhua Li, Walid A. Daoud* 
 
W. Zhang, Dr. W. A. Daoud 
School of Energy and Environment, 
City University of Hong Kong, 
Tat Chee Avenue, Hong Kong 
E-mail: wdaoud@cityu.edu.hk 
 
Dr. J. Xiong 
Faculty of Physics & Electronic Sciences, 
Hubei University, 
Wuhan, 430062, China 
 
Dr. J. Li 
School of Materials Science and Engineering, 
Hubei University, 
Wuhan 430062, China 
 
Keywords: perovskite solar cell, water effect, annealing temperature, cation 
 
Water effect on perovskite solar cells has received growing interest in recent years. A widely 
accepted view is that moderate water content induces the formation of hydrate phase which 
enhances the recrystallization of the perovskite. However, the underlying factors which 
influence the formation of hydrate phase have yet to be investigated. Herein, by controlling 
the annealing temperature, it is demonstrated that 60 ℃ is the most suitable temperature for 
the formation of hydrated perovskite. After further annealing at 120 ℃, the resulting 
perovskite film reveals enhanced crystallinity with a more uniform morphology, contributing 
to device efficiency above 20%. In addition, the water effect on different types of perovskites 
is studied and it is concluded that the formation of hydrated perovskite is mainly determined 
by the cations of the perovskite itself. The findings in this work elucidate the conditions for 
the formation of hydrated perovskite, contributing to the fabrication of highly efficient 
perovskite solar cells. 
 
Accepted Article


This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved 
 
1. Introduction 
Organic-inorganic halide perovskites (OIHP) have attracted significant attention from both 
academic and industrial communities in recent years.[1] Their unique optoelectronic 
properties[2-5] have made them an exceptional material class for various applications, such as 
light-emitting diodes (LED),[6] photodetectors,[7] field effect transistors,[8] and solar cells.[9] In 
photovoltaics, this new family of materials has proven to be easily solution-processed while 
exhibiting comparable properties with those industrial staples, such as GaAs and Si.[10,11] 
Within only 10 years, the efficiencies of the perovskite solar cells (PSCs) have rapidly 
increased from 3.9% to 25.2%.[12-17] Such remarkable progress has made PSCs one of the 
most promising photovoltaic technologies. 
Despite the simple fabrication, low cost and high efficiency advantages, PSCs suffer from 
several drawbacks that need to be overcome before realistic application. Chief among them 
are the sensitivity and instability of the perovskite toward water or moisture.[18,19] To 
understand the degradation mechanisms and developing effective solutions to fabricate air 
stable PSCs, tremendous efforts have been devoted. Early studies indicate that water molecule 
tends to induce hydrolysis reactions in which perovskite is degraded into PbI2, and gases, such 
as HI and CH3NH2.[20] Later, Kamat et al.[21] reported that an intermediate perovskite 
dihydrate phase, similar to (MA)4PbI6·2H2O, may be formed before degradation. Shortly 
thereafter, by using time-resolved XRD and ellipsometry method, Barnes and coworkers[22] 
demonstrated that the perovskite first became monohydrate MAPbI3·H2O before further 
hydration to (MA)4PbI6·2H2O. Benefited from these experimental results and combining with 
some theoretical studies,[23-25] the moisture-induced degradation mechanism was elucidated by 
Heben et al.[26] Namely, with the presence of water, perovskite first forms monohydrate phase, 
then further hydrates to dihydrate phase, and finally degrades into PbI2 and other byproducts. 
Interestingly, the formation of monohydrate perovskite was found fully reversible, leading to 
improved device performance.[27,28] Yang et al.[29] systematically studied the effect of moisture 
Accepted Article


This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved 
 
on the structure and morphology of the perovskite films. They indicated that moderate 
moisture content led to improved crystallization of the perovskite film by enhancing the 
reconstruction process. More recently, Lunt et al.[30] demonstrated a significant enhancement 
in perovskite crystallinity by directly adding moderate content of water in the perovskite 
precursor. However, though hydrated perovskite is beneficial in enhancing the crystallinity of 
perovskite, the underlying factors which influence the formation of hydrated perovskite 
remain almost totally unexplored.[31] Besides, the studies of water effect on PSCs thus far 
have all concentrated on single methylammonium (MA) cation-based perovskite materials. 
While in our previous work,[32] triple cation (Cs+, MA+, FA+) based perovskite was studied, 
the water effect on low dimensional (1D or 2D)[33] and all-inorganic perovskite[34] remains 
unknown. 
Here, we investigate the effect of annealing temperature on the formation of hydrated 
perovskite. The perovskites were deposited using a two-step annealing method, and the phase, 
morphology, crystallinity as well as optical properties were systematically analyzed. By 
varying the first annealing (1-A) temperature from 40 to 100 ℃, 60 ℃ is found favorable to 
the formation of hydrated perovskite which led to a crystal reconstruction in the second 
annealing (2-A) stage, leading to enhanced crystallization of perovskite. As a result, device 
efficiency of above 20% is achieved. In addition, the water effect on different kinds of 
perovskites, such as MAPbI3 (single cation, MA), FA0.85MA0.15PbI2.55Br0.45 (double cation, 
FAMA), guanidinium based GAPbI3 (1D, GA) and CsPbI2Br (all-inorganic, Cs), was studied. 
The results demonstrate that while water has beneficial impact on improving the crystallinity 
and optoelectronic properties of MA, FAMA and GA perovskites, it has little effect on all-
inorganic perovskites. Thus, it is concluded that water effect on perovskite is mainly 
determined by the cations of the perovskite itself. 
 
2. Results and Discussion 
Accepted Article


This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved 
 
2.1. Effect of Annealing Temperature on the Formation of Hydrated Perovskite 
It has been reported that water content, pressure and temperature play significant role in 
hydrate formation.[35,36] To ascertain the optimum temperature, water content and pressure are 
well controlled this study. Conventional FA0.85MA0.15PbI2.55Br0.45 double cation based 
perovskite, abbreviated as FAMA, is adopted as the model system. Water was directly added 
to the perovskite precursor, and the content was controlled at 2% (volume ratio) according to 
previous studies.[37,38] The post annealing process was divided into two stages: first annealing 
(1-A) stage and second annealing (2-A) stage, as illustrated in Figure 1a. By varying the 
temperature of the 1-A stage from 40 to 100 ℃, different perovskite films were fabricated and 
named as A1 (40 ℃), B1 (60 ℃), C1 (80 ℃) and D1 (100 ℃), respectively. Correspondingly, 
after the 2-A treatment, the obtained perovskite films were labeled as A, B, C and D. The 
crystalline structure of the perovskites was evaluated using X-ray diffraction (XRD). For 1-A 
samples (Figure 1b), almost all diffraction peaks can be assigned to perovskite phase, except 
for the peak located at around 10.6°. According to previous studies,[23,39,40] this emerging peak 
corresponds to hydrated perovskite, indicating that the hydrate phase was formed during the 
1-A stage. In contrast, all of the 2-A samples reveal pure perovskite phase, as shown in Figure 
1c. Interestingly, it is noted that sample B shows the strongest and sharpest (110) diffraction 
peak, indicating a highly crystallized perovskite film. Further, UV-vis absorption of the 
perovskites was studied and shown in Figure 1d and e. Consequently, 1-A samples (Figure 1d) 
show increasing absorption along with the annealing temperature from 40 to 100 ℃. This can 
be ascribed to enhanced crystallinity with increasing annealing temperature as shown in 
Figure 1b. While, for the 2-A samples (Figure 1e), sample B shows the highest absorption due 
to its highest crystallinity. 
To evaluate the composition of hydrated perovskite in 1-A samples, X-ray photoelectron 
spectroscopy (XPS) measurement was conducted. The results were fitted using Gaussian-
Lorentzian functions with a Shirley type background as shown in Figure 2. Clearly, for the 1-
Accepted Article


This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved 
 
A samples with water, the O 1s data can be fitted to two peaks at 531.4 and 532.4 eV, 
respectively. While, in the case of samples without water, only one peak at 532.4 eV was 
observed. According to our previous work,[32] the peak at 531.4 eV is attributed to the 
hydroxides or organic O, whereas the peak at 532.4 eV corresponds to chemisorbed water or 
oxygen from the environment during storage. Therefore, the presence of O 1s peak at 531.4 
eV for 1-A samples with water further demonstrates the formation of hydrated perovskite. 
Besides, the composition of hydrated perovskite in 1-A samples was estimated by calculating 
the area of the two peaks. Since chemisorbed water or oxygen should be equal for the same 
storage environment, the area of O 1s peak at 532.4 eV was standardized, and the results are 
summarized in Table S1 (Supporting Information). The largest area of O 1s peak at 531.4 eV 
for sample B1 (Figure 2b) suggests the highest concentration of hydrate phase, indicating that 
60 ℃ is the most suitable temperature for the formation of hydrated perovskite. Further 
increasing the temperature tends to accelerate the crystallization of pure perovskite but not the 
formation of hydrate phase, as suggested by the XRD results (Figure 1b). Earlier studies have 
demonstrated that hydrated perovskite contributes to a recrystallization process, leading to an 
enhancement of crystallinity.[29,32,37] This is the reason why sample B has higher crystallinity 
than A, C and D, as shown in Figure 1c. 
Figure 3 shows a comparison of surface scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images of 
1-A and 2-A samples. It can be seen that the grain size of 1-A samples (A1, B1, C1 and D1) 
shows an incremental increase along with annealing temperature. Indicating that higher 
annealing temperature in the 1-A stage tends to induce higher crystallinity, which is in 
agreement with XRD (Figure 1b) and UV-vis (Figure 1d) results. In contrast, little difference 
can be observed from the SEM images for 2-A samples (A, B, C and D), which all show a 
compact and pinhole-free morphology with a similar grain size. Combining with atomic force 
microscopy (AFM) images (Figure S1, Supporting Information), it is clear that sample B 
displays the smallest roughness with a root mean square (RMS) at 12.9 nm. The results 
Accepted Article


This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved 
 
indicate that higher content of hydrate phase (Sample B1) contributes to more uniform 
perovskite film (Sample B). 
For the photovoltaic performance study, a planar device architecture with a configuration 
as FTO/SnO2/Perovskite/Spiro-OMeTAD/Au was adopted. By employing different perovskite 
films (A, B, C and D), a series of devices were fabricated (Device A, B, C and D). The current 
density-voltage (J-V) curves of representative devices under AM 1.5G irradiation (100 mW 
cm-2) were shown in Figure 4a. It is observed that Device B outputs the highest short current 
density (Jsc) and open circuit voltage (Voc) among all devices, with efficiency over 20%. The 
enhancement is mainly derived from its highest crystallinity and most uniform morphology as 
discussed earlier.[41,42] External quantum efficiency (EQE) results reveal that Device B has the 
highest quantum conversion efficiency throughout the effective wavelength range (Figure 4b), 
which is fully consistent with absorption results (Figure 1e). The integrated Jsc based on the 
EQE spectra is in good agreement with the measured value, as summarized in Table 1. 
2.2. Water Effect on Different Kinds of Perovskites 
To further investigate the impact of perovskite cation on the formation of hydrate phase, 
water effect on different cation-based perovskites, such as MAPbI3 (single cation, MA), 
FA0.85MA0.15PbI2.55Br0.45 (double cation, FAMA), GAPbI3 (low dimensional, GA) and 
CsPbI2Br (all-inorganic, Cs), was studied. The corresponding atomic structure and ionic 
radius of the different cations are shown in Figure 5a. It is clear that guanidinium has an ionic 
radius of 278 pm, which is slightly too large to form a 3D perovskite structure.[43] Analysis of 
the Goldschmidt tolerance factor (t) reveals that pure GAPbI3 has a t value of 1.03, indicating 
a low dimensional perovskite structure.[44] XRD spectra of the perovskites with and without 
(w/o) water are shown in Figure 5b-e. It is noted that all the perovskites show significantly 
enhanced diffraction peak intensity with water introduced, except for all-inorganic Cs 
perovskites (Figure 5e). Further, the full width at half maximum (FWHM) of the diffraction 
peaks was calculated as shown in the corresponding inset. Noticeably, MA, FAMA and GA 
Accepted Article


This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved 
 
perovskites with water have dramatically decreased FWHM. According to Scherer equation: 
D=Kλ/βcosθ, where D is grain size, K is a shape factor, λ is X-ray wavelength, β is FWHM, 
and θ is diffraction angle, a smaller FWHM (β) indicates a larger grain size (D). In this case, it 
is concluded that water has a positive effect on fabricating MA, FAMA and GA perovskite 
films with higher crystallinity and larger grain size. It was also found that the addition of 
water influences the light absorption and also the photoluminescence (PL) behavior (Figure 
S2, Supporting Information). Owning to the enhancement of crystallization, MA, FAMA and 
GA perovskite films with water reveals higher absorption than the reference w/o water films 
in the visible region. Besides, the higher PL intensity suggests that the nonradiative 
recombination in MA, FAMA and GA perovskite films with water is effectively suppressed. 
The morphology of the perovskite films with and w/o water was compared as shown in 
Figure 6. It is noteworthy that MA and FAMA perovskite films with water (Figure 6e and f) 
reveal larger grain size when compared with their reference films (Figure 6a and b), which is 
consistent with the FWHM analysis. Further, to estimate the quality of GA perovskite films, 
the number of pinholes was statistically studied (Figure 6k). The much reduced number of 
pinholes suggests that water has positive effect on improving the quality of GA perovskites. 
While, for the Cs perovskite films, almost no difference can be observed from the SEM 
images (Figure 6d and h), indicating that water has little effect on the morphology of 
inorganic Cs perovskites. 
Figure 7a-c and Figure S3 (Supporting Information) show the J-V curves of the devices 
based on different perovskite films. It is found that the devices based on MA, FAMA and GA 
perovskite films with water yield higher Jsc than their reference counterparts, leading to 
increase of PCE from 17.6% to 18.7% for MA, 18.7% to 20.3% for FAMA, and 0.31% to 
0.38% for GA. On the other hand, almost identical J-V curves (Figure 7c) indicate that water 
has no impact on the output of Cs perovskite based devices. The EQE of the devices were 
measured (Figure S4, Supporting Information), and the results are in agreement with UV-vis 
Accepted Article


This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved 
 
absorption results (Figure S2, Supporting Information). In addition, Figure 7d-f shows the 
steady-state Jsc and PCE of the devices biased at maximum power point (MPP). It is clear that 
all devices outputs stable Jsc with PCE close to the value measured from J-V curves.  
Further, the charge dynamics were investigated by conducting time-resolved PL (TRPL) 
and light intensity dependent J-V measurements. The TRPL curves shown in Figure 8a-c 
were fitted using the biexponential equation [45]: Y= Y0 + A1 exp(-t/τ1) + A2 exp(-t/τ2), in 
which a faster decay component (τ1) indicates nonradiative recombination, while a slower 
decay component (τ2) indicates radiative recombination.[46,47] The fitted parameters are 
summarized in Table S2 (Supporting Information). It can be seen that all the perovskites with 
water show significantly prolonged carrier life time, except for all-inorganic Cs perovskites 
(Figure 8c). Figure 8d-f shows the results of Jsc and Voc versus light intensity of the devices 
based on different perovskite films. All devices show a linear correlation with the α value 
close to 1, indicating negligible bimolecular recombination.[48,49] Interestingly, after the 
introduction of water, higher α value for MA and FAMA perovskites based devices was 
observed, suggesting reduced trap density.[50] On the other hand, the Voc versus light intensity 
results reveal that the addition of water tends to induce a smaller slope for MA and FAMA 
perovskite based devices (Figure 8d,e). According to previous studies,[51,52] a deviation 
between slope and 1 KT/q relates to trap-assisted recombination. In this case, the reduced 
slope for MA (from 1.62 to 1.2 KT/q) and FAMA (from 1.54 to 1.21 KT/q) perovskite based 
devices indicates that the trap-assisted recombination process was effectively suppressed. 
However, for Cs perovskite films, the similar α value and slope shown in Figure 8f indicate 
that water has no effect on charge dynamics. 
Figure 9a-c and Figure S5 (Supporting Information) show statistical PCE, Voc, Jsc and FF 
of 40 independent devices derived from different perovskite films with and without water. It 
can be seen that MA and FAMA perovskite based PSCs reveal an enhancement of device 
performance after optimum water content was introduced. Besides, the narrower PCE 
Accepted Article


This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved 
 
distribution (Figure 9a,b) indicates that water improves the reproducibility of MA and FAMA 
perovskite. In comparison, Cs perovskite based devices exhibit similar distribution of 
photovoltaic parameters (Figure 9c and Figure S5c), suggesting that water has no impact on 
the output of Cs perovskite based devices. The stability test results (Figure 9d-f) obtained 
after exposing the unencapsulated devices to ambient environment of 25 ℃ and 25% humidity 
indicate an improvement of long-term stability for devices based on MA and FAMA 
perovskite with water. While, for the Cs perovskite based devices, the similar degradation 
trend (Figure 9f) indicates that water has no effect on device stability. To gain insight into the 
enhanced stability, the crystallinity of the films after storage for two weeks was studied. 
Figure S6 (Supporting Information) exhibits the XRD patterns of the perovskite films, it is 
worth noting that MA and FAMA perovskite with water reveal a suppressed decomposition 
process when compared with their reference counterparts with lower PbI2 peak intensity. It 
has been reported that grain boundaries of perovskite films act as pathways for the diffusion 
of moisture, leading to accelerated degradation of perovskite.[32] In this case, the enhancement 
of stability for MA and FAMA perovskite with water is mainly attributed to their larger grain 
size which contributes to less boundaries, as shown in Figure 6i and j. 
Previous studies have demonstrated that water interacts with both the cation ions and lead 
halide framework of the perovskite through hydrogen bonding.[24,25] According to Rappe and 
his coworkers,[53] H2O-MA+ bond in MAPbI3 is mainly derived from the binding between N-
bound hydrogen (HN) and H2O-bound oxygen (OW), while, the H2O-PbI2 bonding represents a 
triaxial phenomenon which consists of one OW-Pb2+ bond and two HW-I- bonds. Computing 
the corresponding binding energy indicated that H2O-MA+ bonding is more favorable while 
the H2O-PbI2 bond is likely to occur under a super-hydrous state (2H2O per MA). In this study, 
the water content was controlled at a low 2% volume ratio, which makes the formation of 
H2O-PbI2 bond unlikely, as indicated by the similar Pb 4f XPS results (Figure S7, Supporting 
Information). Therefore, the effect of water on perovskites is mainly attributed to the 
Accepted Article


This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved 
 
interaction between water and perovskite cation ions. Accordingly, combining with previous 
theoretical studies,[24,25,53,54] it is concluded that the discussed water effects are only applicable 
to perovskite which contains plenty of N-bound hydrogen (HN) atoms, which could explain 
the reason why water has no effect on all-inorganic Cs perovskites. 
 
3. Conclusion 
In summary, we have systematically investigated the influence of annealing temperature on 
the formation of hydrated perovskite. The results suggest that 60 ℃ is the most favorable 
temperature for the formation of hydrate phase which leads to a reconstruction process in the 
second annealing stage. The resulting films reveal enhanced crystallinity and a more uniform 
morphology, enabling the fabrication of perovskite solar cells with high efficiency and good 
reproducibility. Moreover, according to the crystalline phase, morphology, and optoelectronic 
properties results derived from different kinds of perovskites, it is concluded that the water 
effects are mainly determined by the cations of the perovskite itself. It is suggested that 
further theoretical and experimental studies should be carried out to verify our assumption 
that water effects are only applicable to perovskite which contains plenty of N-bound 
hydrogen (HN) atoms. 
 
Experimental Section 
Materials: The SnO2 colloid was purchased from Alfa Aesar (tin (IV) oxide). 
Methylammonium iodide (MAI), Methylammonium bromide (MABr), and Cesium bromide 
(CsBr) were purchased from Xi’an Polymer Light Technology Corp. Formamidinium iodide 
(FAI) was purchased from Dyesol Ltd. (Queanbeyan, Australia). Lead iodide (PbI2, 99%), 
Lead bromide (PbBr2, 99.999%), Guanidinium iodide (GAI, 99%), N,N-Dimethylformamide 
(DMF, 99.8%), Dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO, 99.9%), and Chlorobenzene (99.8%) were 
purchased from Sigma-Aldrich. 
Device Fabrication: Devices were fabricated on FTO substrates (15 Ω sq−1) with 
Accepted Article


This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved 
 
dimensions of 20×20 mm. The substrates were thoroughly cleaned and treated with plasma 
for 5 min before usage. Then, a layer of SnO2 was deposited in ambient air as the electron 
transport layer. The MA or GA perovskite films were spin coated from a precursor solution 
containing MAI (1 M) or GAI (1 M) and PbI2 (1 M) in DMF:DMSO 4:1 (v/v). The prepared 
perovskite precursor was dropped on the substrate and spin-coated at 600 rpm for 5 s and then 
at 4000 rpm for 40 s. During the second procedure, 150 μL toluene was dropped on the 
spinning substrate 25 s before program ended. To gain FAMA perovskite films, FAI (1 M), 
PbI2 (1.05 M), MABr (0.2 M), and PbBr2 (0.2 M) were dissolved in DMF:DMSO 4:1 (v/v). A 
same spin protocol was adopted, only the antisolvent dripping time was changed to 15 s 
before program ended. While, for Cs perovskites, CsBr (1 M) and PbI2 (1 M) were dissolved 
in DMSO, and the precursor was spin-coated at 600 rpm for 5 s and then at 3000 rpm for 30 s. 
Importantly, 20 μL (2% volume ratio) of water was directly added in the different kinds of 
perovskite precursor. The resulting FAMA films were annealed at 40, 60, 80, and 100 °C for 5 
min for 1-A samples and then at 120 °C for 10 min for 2-A samples. MA and GA films were 
annealed at 60 °C for 5 min and then at 120 °C for 10 min. Cs perovskite films were annealed 
at 60 °C for 1 min and then at 250 °C for 10 min. After cooling to room temperature, a 
conventional Spiro-OMeTAD layer, which consisted of 72.3 mg spiro-OMeTAD, 28.8 μL 4-
tertbutylpyridine, 17.5 μL lithium-bis (trifluoromethanesulfonyl) imide (Li-TFSI) solution 
(520 mg Li-TFSI in 1 mL acetonitrile), and 1 mL chlorobenzene , was deposited on the 
perovskite films as the hole transport layer. Finally, Au electrode was fabricated using a 
shadow mask under high vacuum by thermal evaporation. 
Device Characterization: Current density-voltage (J-V) curves of the devices were 
measured using a solar simulator (Newport Oriel Sol 3A Class AAA, 64023A) equipped with 
450 W Xenon lamp (Oriel, USA) and a Keithley 2400 source meter. The light intensity was 
calibrated to AM 1.5G (100 mW cm-2) by using a reference Si solar cell (Newport). The 
devices were masked with a metal aperture of 0.06 cm-2 to define the active area. The J-V 
Accepted Article


This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved 
 
measurements were all conducted in ambient air with a scanning protocol of 1.2 to -0.05 V 
with a 24 mV voltage step. 
Other characterizations: The XRD patterns (2θ scans) were obtained on Bruker 
Advanced D8 X-ray diffractometer using Cu Kα (λ = 0.154 nm) radiation. The chemical 
environments of the films were analyzed by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (PHI Model 
5802). UV-vis diffuse reflection spectroscopy (UV-vis-DRS, Shimadzu UV-3600) was used to 
collect the absorbance spectra of the perovskite films. Steady state photoluminescence (PL) 
spectra were recorded on Shimadzu RF-5301pc. Surface morphology was studied by field-
emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM, JEOL 7100F) and atomic force microscope 
(AFM, Bruker Dimension Icon). The external quantum efficiency (EQE) spectra were 
measured under a constant white light supplied by an array of white light-emitting diodes. The 
excitation beam from a 300 W xenon lamp was focused through a double-monochromator and 
chopped at 10 Hz. The monochromatic light intensity for the measurement was calibrated 
using a reference silicon photodiode. Time-resolved photoluminescence spectra were 
measured by a PL system (DW-PLE03).

A two-step annealing method is developed for studying the water effect on different kinds of 
perovskites. It is demonstrated that 60 ℃ is favorable to the formation of hydrate phase which 
leads to a reconstruction process in the second annealing stage. The corresponding water 
effects highly depend on the cations of the perovskite itself.

Ho-Baillie \n  2, Han Young Woo \n  3, \nAntonio Facchetti \n  4 \n & Xugang Guo \n  1 \nThe electron-transporting material (ETM) is a key component of perovskite \nsolar cells (PSCs) optimizing electron extraction from perovskite to \ncathode. Fullerenes, specifically C60 and [6,6]-phenyl-C61-butyric acid methyl \nester (PCBM), have been used as the benchmark ETMs for inverted PSCs. \nHowever, C60 is restricted to thermal evaporation, and PCBM suffers from \npoor photothermal stability and suboptimal electron transport, limiting \ntheir PSC applications. Here a solution-processable non-fullerene ETM, \ncyano-functionalized bithiophene imide dimer (CNI2)-based polymer \n(PCNI2-BTI), holds multiple advantages, including excellent photothermal \nstability, efficient electron transport and improved interaction with the \nperovskite layer. Consequently, inverted PSCs incorporating PCNI2-BTI \ndeliver an outstanding power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 26.0% (certified \n25.4%) and remarkable operational stability, with a T80 approaching 1,300 h \nunder ISOS-L-3. Moreover, we synthesize three additional CNI2-based \npolymer ETMs, yielding an average PCE of >25% in PSCs. These findings \ndemonstrate unprecedented potential of non-fullerene ETMs enabling \nhigh-performance and stable PSCs.\nInverted perovskite solar cells (PSCs) have gained considerable \nattention for their simplified architecture, low-temperature solution \nprocessability, small hysteresis and high compatibility with flexible \nsubstrates and all-perovskite tandem devices1–5. Major advances are \ndriven by developing new hole-transporting materials6–8 and interfacial \nlayers9,10, and optimizing perovskite crystallization11,12, recently afford-\ning power conversion efficiencies (PCEs) exceeding 25%1,13,14. However, \nelectron-transporting materials (ETMs) placed on the upper surface \nof the perovskite photoactive layer in inverted cells have received \nlimited attention, despite their critical role in device performance \nand stability15,16. Fullerenes are the benchmark ETMs for inverted PSCs \n(Supplementary Table 1), with C60 and phenyl-C61-butyric acid methyl \nester (PCBM) being the most investigated ones due to their isotropic \ntransport character and good defect passivation effect17–20 (Fig. 1a). \nHowever, C60 processing is limited to thermal evaporation21 and PCBM \nsuffers from several drawbacks, such as high cost due to the existence \nof undesired isomers during fullerene addition reaction, hydrophobic-\nity and poor photothermal stability22–26. Additionally, the spheroidal \nshape of PCBM leads to a film with a low degree of ordering, yielding \nsuboptimal electron transport from perovskite layer to cathode19,27 \nReceived: 23 May 2024\nAccepted: 29 January 2025\nPublished online: 4 March 2025\n Check for updates\n1Department of Materials Science and Engineering, Southern University of Science and Technology (SUSTech), Shenzhen, China. 2School of Physics and \nthe University of Sydney Nano Institute (Sydney Nano), The University of Sydney, Sydney, New South Wales, Australia. 3Department of Chemistry, Korea \nUniversity, Seoul, Republic of Korea. 4School of Materials Science and Engineering, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA, USA. 5These authors \ncontributed equally: Kui Feng, Guoliang Wang. \n e-mail: fengk@sustech.edu.cn; lianq@sustech.edu.cn; afacchetti6@gatech.edu; guoxg@sustech.edu.cn\n\n\nNature Materials | Volume 24 | May 2025 | 770–777\n771\nArticle\nhttps://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-025-02163-4\nLewis acid–base adducts40. Capitalizing on these desirable properties, \nwe propose PCNI2-BTI as a new non-fullerene ETM for inverted PSCs. \nThe non-fullerene cyanated ETM PCNI2-BTI39 and its non-cyanated \nanalogue PBTI2-BTI41 were synthesized and purified following previ-\nously reported procedures (Supplementary Note 1). On the basis of the \nsynthesis cost of PCNI2-BTI as well as the commercial prices of C60 and \nPCBM, the cost of PCNI2-BTI per slice of inverted PSCs is approximately \none-tenth that of PCBM and one-fifth that of C60 (Supplementary Note \n2), demonstrating a significant reduction in material costs of PCNI2-BTI.\nETM characterizations\nUltraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy (UPS) was performed to probe \nthe work function (Φ) and FMOs of the ETMs. The binding-energy cut-\noff (Ecutoff) and onset (Eonset) were used to calculate Φ and the HOMO \nlevel (EHOMO; Supplementary Figs. 3–7). Φ was calculated to be 3.98, \n3.82, 4.15 and 4.32 eV for perovskite, PBTI2-BTI, PCNI2-BTI and PCBM, \nrespectively, on the basis of the equation Φ = hν − Ecutoff, where hν is the \nphoton energy used in the UPS measurement. As shown in Fig. 1d, \nthe EHOMO values are −5.56 and −5.85 eV on the basis of the \nequation EHOMO = 21.22 eV − (Ecutoff – Eonset), and the LUMO levels (ELUMO) \nare −3.57 and −3.95 eV for PBTI2-BTI and PCNI2-BTI, respectively. The \nexperimental trend is consistent with density functional theory \n(DFT)-based calculations (Supplementary Figs. 8 and 9). Compared to \nPCBM, the minimized ΔELUMO between perovskite and PCNI2-BTI should \nfacilitate efficient electron extraction and increase open-circuit voltage \n(VOC). On the basis of the absorption onsets, the optical bandgaps (Eopt\ng ) \nof the films were estimated to be 2.32, 1.88 and 1.90 eV for PCBM, \nPBTI2-BTI and PCNI2-BTI, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 10 and \nSupplementary Table 6).\n(Fig. 1b). Therefore, it is imperative to devise property-optimized ETMs \nto improve the performance and stability of PSCs, which is essential for \ntheir commercialization28,29. A limited number of organic or polymeric \nsemiconductors have been developed as non-fullerene ETMs thus \nfar30,31 (Supplementary Table 2 and Supplementary Fig. 2). Despite \nconsiderable efforts, non-fullerene ETMs have not achieved efficien-\ncies exceeding 21% in PSCs32.\nDesign and synthesis of non-fullerene ETMs\nFigure 1e depicts the key properties of representative non-fullerene \nETMs, such as the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) energy \ndifference (ΔELUMO, eV) between ETM and perovskite (here organo-\nmetal halide perovskite), number of passivation groups (PGs) and \nspace-charge-limited-current (SCLC) electron mobility (µe,SCLC), and the \nPCEs of the resulting devices33–37. Data analysis shows that an optimal \nETM should feature several key properties, including a suitable ΔELUMO, \na large µe,SCLC and multiple PGs. This band \ndownshifts by 7 cm−1 when PCNI2-BTI is deposited atop perovskite, sug-\ngesting increased π conjugation due to backbone planarization caused \nby strong intermolecular interactions (Supplementary Fig. 42). The \nresulting highly planar backbone enhances π conjugation and orbital \noverlap with the perovskite, facilitating efficient electron extraction. \nIn contrast, the Raman spectra of pristine PBTI2-BTI and PBTI2-BTI \non perovskite show negligible variations, indicating weak intermo-\nlecular interactions. This lack of backbone planarization in PBTI2-BTI \nsuggests inferior electron transport characteristics when compared \nwith PCNI2-BTI.\nPhotovoltaic performance and device stability\nTo evaluate the device performance of PCBM, PBTI2-BTI and PCNI2-BTI \nas ETMs, inverted PSCs were fabricated with a device architecture of \nindium tin oxide (ITO)/self-assembled monolayer (SAM)/perovskite \n(Cs0.05FA0.9MA0.05PbI3)/ETM/BCP/Ag (Fig. 5a), in which [4-(3,6-dimet\nhyl-9H-carbazol-9-yl)butyl]phosphonic acid (Me-4PACz) was used as the \nSAM. The current-density–voltage (J–V) curves of the champion cells are \nillustrated in Fig. 5b, and the corresponding device performance param-\neters are summarized in Supplementary Table 8. The best-performing \nPSC based on the benchmark PCBM exhibits a PCE of 24.3% with a VOC \nof 1.156 V, a JSC of 25.25 mA cm−2 and an FF of 83.10%. Notably, the use \nof PCNI2-BTI as the ETM with an optimized thickness of 35 nm (Fig. 5b, \nSupplementary Figs. 43 and 44 and Supplementary Table 9) improves \nthe PCE to 26.0% with a higher VOC of 1.179 V and a remarkable FF of \n86.44%. This PCE is one of the highest values reported for non-fullerene \nETM-based PSCs (Supplementary Table 2 and Fig. 5c). However, when \nPCBM is replaced with PBTI2-BTI, a significantly lower PCE of 14.1% is \nattained, along with a decreased VOC of 0.960 V, a JSC of 24.47 mA cm−2 and \nan FF of 60.30%. The inferior performance of PBTI2-BTI-based devices \ncan be attributed to the mismatched energy level and the reduced \nelectron-transporting capability of this ETM. The integrated JSC val-\nues from external quantum efficiency (EQE) measurements agree well \nwith those from the J–V measurements (Fig. 5d) for all three ETM-based \ndevices. Furthermore, the hysteresis of the PCNI2-BTI-based champion \ndevices (Supplementary Figs. 45–47) is minimal, which is attributed to \neffective suppression of ion migration. Supplementary Table 10 sum-\nmarizes the photovoltaic parameters of PSCs based on different ETMs. \nThe average PCEs of PCBM-, PBTI2-BTI- and PCNI2-BTI-based cells (40 \ndevices) are 24.0 ± 0.3%, 11.6 ± 2.3% and 25.5 ± 0.3% (Fig. 5e and Sup-\nplementary Figs. 48–50), respectively. A certified PCE of 25.4% was \nobtained by an accredited laboratory for the PCNI2-BTI device (Sup-\nplementary Fig. 51). When the device number is increased to 80, the \naverage PCE of PCNI2-BTI is maintained at 25.6 ± 0.2% (Supplementary \nFig. 52). We also synthesized another three batches, and it was found \nthat all batches show comparable number-averaged molecular mass \n(Mn) values (16.2–18.5 kDa) and produce comparable device perfor-\nmances, with all average PCEs exceeding 25.6% (Supplementary Fig. 53 \nand Supplementary Table 11). These results demonstrate the excellent \nreproducibility and reliability of PCNI2-BTI as an ETM for inverted PSCs. \nInspired by the excellent performance of PCNI2-BTI as an ETM, we fur-\nther synthesized three new CNI2-based n-type polymers, PCNI2-DPP, \nPCNI2-BFI and PCNI2-BSeI (Supplementary Fig. 54 and Supplementary \nNote 1). Similar to PBTI2-BTI, these polymers showed a wide range of \ndesirable properties as ETMs (Supplementary Figs. 55–57 and Supple-\nmentary Table 12), thus achieving a champion PCE of 25.2%, 25.6% and \n26.1% for the PCNI2-DPP-, PCNI2-BFI- and PCNI2-BSeI-based devices, \nrespectively (Supplementary Fig. 58 and Supplementary Table 13), all \nhigher than that of the PCBM-based device.\nThe steady-state power output at the maximum power point \nvoltage (Vmax) is shown in Fig. 5f, and the steady-state PCEs align well \nwith the PCEs determined from the J–V scan for all three ETM-based \ndevices. Furthermore, the light-intensity-dependent VOC measure-\nments (Supplementary Fig. 59) exhibit a suppressed ideality factor \n(nid = 1.23 for the PCNI2-BTI device), which is lower than those of the \nPCBM (1.58) and PBTI2-BTI devices (4.29), indicating an excellent \ncharge transfer at the perovskite/PCNI2-BTI interface. When further \napplied in 1.65 eV wide-bandgap PSCs (Supplementary Fig. 60 and \nSupplementary Table 14), the PCNI2-BTI-based device also provided \na PCE (21.5%) higher than that of PCBM (20.2%), demonstrating a wide \napplicability of PCNI2-BTI.\nTo assess the long-term stability of the devices, maximum power \npoint tracking measurements were performed on encapsulated devices \nfollowing the International Summit on Organic Photovoltaic Stabil-\nity (ISOS) protocol. The stability results are collected in Fig. 5g and \nSupplementary Figs. 61 and 62. Here, the PCNI2-BTI-based device exhib-\nited a superior stability, retaining 80% of the original PCE (T80) after \n1,280 h of maximum power point tracking testing, whereas the control \nPCBM-based one only showed a T80 of 759 h. The PBTI2-BTI-based device \nalso experienced a rapid performance decline, with only 60% of the \ninitial efficiency retained after 700 h. By using atomic layer deposition \nSnOx as the inorganic buffer layer instead of BCP, the PCNI2-BTI-based \ndevice retained 100.1% of its initial PCE (25.2%) after continuous heat \ntreatment for over 300 h (Supplementary Fig. 63), which is greater \nthan the retention (97.6%) of the PCBM-based device.\nOutlook\nThis work showcases the successful application of a cyano- \nfunctionalized n-type polymer, PCNI2-BTI, as a non-fullerene ETM in \ninverted PSCs. Devices based on PCNI2-BTI achieve a remarkable PCE \nof 26.0% (certified at 25.4%) and outstanding operational robustness \nunder the ISOS-L-3 protocol (65 °C and 60% ± 10% relative humidity), \nwith a T80 of 1,280 h. Our study established key design principles for \nhigh-performance non-fullerene ETMs, including multiple proper-\nties, such as excellent solubility, good backbone coplanarity, low-lying \nFMOs, outstanding photothermal stability, favourable packing orien-\ntation with close π–π stacking and abundant PGs. Building on these \ninsights, we further developed three new non-fullerene ETMs that \nachieved an average PCE > 25%, with the highest one reaching 26.1% \nin inverted PSCs. This work paves the way for designing and utilizing \nhigh-performance non-fullerene ETMs for PSCs, which will change the \nresearch paradigm of the perovskite-based photovoltaic technology.\nOnline content\nAny methods, additional references, Nature Portfolio reporting sum-\nmaries, source data, extended data, supplementary information, \nacknowledgements, peer review information; details of author contri-\nbutions and competing interests; and statements of data and code avail-\nability are available at https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-025-02163-4.\nReferences\n1.\t\nTan, Q. et al. The electron-transporting material (ETM) is a key component of perovskite 
solar cells (PSCs) optimizing electron extraction from perovskite to 
cathode. Fullerenes, specifically C60 and [6,6]-phenyl-C61-butyric acid methyl 
ester (PCBM), have been used as the benchmark ETMs for inverted PSCs. 
However, C60 is restricted to thermal evaporation, and PCBM suffers from 
poor photothermal stability and suboptimal electron transport, limiting 
their PSC applications. Here a solution-processable non-fullerene ETM, 
cyano-functionalized bithiophene imide dimer (CNI2)-based polymer 
(PCNI2-BTI), holds multiple advantages, including excellent photothermal 
stability, efficient electron transport and improved interaction with the 
perovskite layer. Consequently, inverted PSCs incorporating PCNI2-BTI 
deliver an outstanding power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 26.0% (certified 
25.4%) and remarkable operational stability, with a T80 approaching 1,300 h 
under ISOS-L-3. Moreover, we synthesize three additional CNI2-based 
polymer ETMs, yielding an average PCE of >25% in PSCs. These findings 
demonstrate unprecedented potential of non-fullerene ETMs enabling 
high-performance and stable PSCs.
Inverted perovskite solar cells (PSCs) have gained considerable 
attention for their simplified architecture, low-temperature solution 
processability, small hysteresis and high compatibility with flexible 
substrates and all-perovskite tandem devices1–5. Major advances are 
driven by developing new hole-transporting materials6–8 and interfacial 
layers9,10, and optimizing perovskite crystallization11,12, recently afford-
ing power conversion efficiencies (PCEs) exceeding 25%1,13,14. However, 
electron-transporting materials (ETMs) placed on the upper surface 
of the perovskite photoactive layer in inverted cells have received 
limited attention, despite their critical role in device performance 
and stability15,16. Fullerenes are the benchmark ETMs for inverted PSCs 
(Supplementary Table 1), with C60 and phenyl-C61-butyric acid methyl 
ester (PCBM) being the most investigated ones due to their isotropic 
transport character and good defect passivation effect17–20 (Fig. 1a). 
However, C60 processing is limited to thermal evaporation21 and PCBM 
suffers from several drawbacks, such as high cost due to the existence 
of undesired isomers during fullerene addition reaction, hydrophobic-
ity and poor photothermal stability22–26. Additionally, the spheroidal 
shape of PCBM leads to a film with a low degree of ordering, yielding 
suboptimal electron transport from perovskite layer to cathode19,27

ETM characterizations
Ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy (UPS) was performed to probe 
the work function (Φ) and FMOs of the ETMs. The binding-energy cut-
off (Ecutoff) and onset (Eonset) were used to calculate Φ and the HOMO 
level (EHOMO; Supplementary Figs. 3–7). Φ was calculated to be 3.98, 
3.82, 4.15 and 4.32 eV for perovskite, PBTI2-BTI, PCNI2-BTI and PCBM, 
respectively, on the basis of the equation Φ = hν − Ecutoff, where hν is the 
photon energy used in the UPS measurement. As shown in Fig. 1d, 
the EHOMO values are −5.56 and −5.85 eV on the basis of the 
equation EHOMO = 21.22 eV − (Ecutoff – Eonset), and the LUMO levels (ELUMO) 
are −3.57 and −3.95 eV for PBTI2-BTI and PCNI2-BTI, respectively. The 
experimental trend is consistent with density functional theory 
(DFT)-based calculations (Supplementary Figs. 8 and 9). Compared to 
PCBM, the minimized ΔELUMO between perovskite and PCNI2-BTI should 
facilitate efficient electron extraction and increase open-circuit voltage 
(VOC). On the basis of the absorption onsets, the optical bandgaps (Eopt
g ) 
of the films were estimated to be 2.32, 1.88 and 1.90 eV for PCBM, 
PBTI2-BTI and PCNI2-BTI, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 10 and

Design and synthesis of non-fullerene ETMs
Figure 1e depicts the key properties of representative non-fullerene 
ETMs, such as the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) energy 
difference (ΔELUMO, eV) between ETM and perovskite (here organo-
metal halide perovskite), number of passivation groups (PGs) and 
space-charge-limited-current (SCLC) electron mobility (µe,SCLC), and the 
PCEs of the resulting devices33–37. Data analysis shows that an optimal 
ETM should feature several key properties, including a suitable ΔELUMO, 
a large µe,SCLC and multiple PGs. To attain these properties, we identi-
fied as promising candidates imide-functionalized bithiophene-based 
n-type polymers, which show widely tunable frontier molecular orbitals 
(FMOs), a planar backbone and multiple PGs, thus delivering remark-
able performance in organic electronic devices38. Among them, the 
cyano-functionalized bithiophene imide dimer (CNI2)-based n-type

(OTFTs) and a n-doped conductivity up to 150 S cm−1 (ref. 39). Nota-

Thermogravimetric analysis revealed that PCNI2-BTI has a high 
thermal stability with a decomposition temperature (Td, defined as the 
temperature with a 5% weight loss) above 400 °C, higher than those of 
PCBM (388 °C) and PBTI2-BTI (381 °C) (Fig. 2a). In differential scanning 
calorimetry, PCNI2-BTI and PBTI2-BTI did not show any phase transition 
in the 30–300 °C temperature range (Fig. 2b), while PCBM exhibited 
a distinctive melting peak26. The photothermal stability of the ETM 
films was evaluated by monitoring the changes in ultraviolet–visible 
(UV–Vis) absorption characteristics under thermal ageing (65 °C) and 
illumination conditions for over 200 h (Fig. 2c and Supplementary 
Figs. 11–21). Under continuous thermal stress and/or illumination 
conditions, PCNI2-BTI absorption also showed a minimal variation, 
while PCBM experienced a more notable change25,42. Contact-angle 
measurements using a water droplet (Supplementary Fig. 22) showed 
an increased mean water-droplet contact angle from 83.0° for PCBM 
to 99.7° for PBTI2-BTI and to 106.3° for PCNI2-BTI. These findings 
highlight the distinctive photothermal stability and hydrophobicity 
of PCNI2-BTI as an ETM, which should be beneficial for long-term PSC 
operational stability.
Charge transport characteristics
Electron mobilities of the ETMs were investigated using OTFT and 
SCLC protocols (Fig. 2d–g and Supplementary Figs. 23–25). The 
results revealed that PCNI2-BTI has a higher OTFT electron mobil-
ity (μe,OTFT = 0.17 cm−2 V−1 s−1) and μe,SCLC (1.06 × 10−3 cm−2 V−1 s−1) when 
compared with PBTI2-BTI (μe,OTFT = 0.041 cm−2 V−1 s−1 and μe,SCLC = 8.0
5 × 10−5 cm−2 V−1 s−1) and PCBM (μe,OTFT = 0.052 cm−2 V−1 s−1 and μe,SCLC =  
1.02 × 10−4 cm−2 V−1 s−1)43 (Supplementary Table 7). These findings 
indicate that PCNI2-BTI possesses superior electron-transporting 
properties, making it a promising candidate for enhancing PSC per-
formance when used as the ETM. Two-dimensional grazing-incidence 
wide-angle X-ray scattering (GIWAXS) measurements were carried out

the out-of-plane direction originating from cofacial π–π stacking, 
suggesting a predominant face-on orientation. This orientation leads

Perovskite/ETM surface morphology
The surface morphology of the perovskite/ETM composite layers was 
investigated using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), atomic force 
microscopy (AFM) and Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM). The 
SEM images (Supplementary Fig. 28) reveal that PCBM, PBTI2-BTI and 
PCNI2-BTI layers uniformly cover the perovskite film top without any 
visible large domains or uncovered regions. Further examinations 
using AFM (Supplementary Fig. 29) reveal that the perovskite surface 
has a rough morphology with a root-mean-squared roughness value 
of 22.2 nm. However, after deposition of the ETMs, the upper surface 
becomes substantially smoother, with a root-mean-squared roughness 
value of less than 8.5 nm for the perovskite/PCBM layer, 7.4 nm for the 
perovskite/PBTI2-BTI layer and 7.8 nm for the perovskite/PCNI2-BTI 
layer. The smoother surface of the perovskite/PCNI2-BTI (or PBTI2-BTI) 
composite layers will yield improved contact between the non-fullerene 
ETMs and the perovskite active layer. It is worth noting that some larger 
clusters are observed in certain areas of the perovskite/PCBM layer, 
which could negatively affect device performance24.
In the results of KPFM44,45 (Fig. 3a–c), the spatial distribution of 
contact potential for the perovskite/PCBM layer exhibits noticeable 
undulations, suggesting clustering in line with the AFM results. In con-
trast, a pronounced flattening of the potential distribution is found for 
the perovskite/PBTI2-BTI and perovskite/PCNI2-BTI layers (Supplemen-
tary Fig. 30). The analysis of mean surface potential values indicates a 
relative work function trend of PBTI2-BTI < PCNI2-BTI < PCBM, which 
aligns with the UPS measurements. Notably, the improved energy-level 
alignment between the perovskite and PCNI2-BTI is expected to reduce 
charge carrier accumulation and enhance carrier extraction. The 
favourable morphology of the PCNI2-BTI film is anticipated to facili-
tate efficient electron extraction and transport, thereby improving 
the device performance.

processes. Figure 3f–h presents the colour plot of two-dimensional 
pseudocolour TAS images of the perovskite/ETM stack after photo-

absorption spectra shown in Supplementary Figs. 32 and 33. These 
perovskite/ETM stacks feature a negative ground-state photobleaching 
peak at 780 nm, indicating carrier filling at the bandgap and a reduc-

analysed by fitting with an exponential decay function. It was found 
that the time constant (τ1 = 50 ps; τ1 represents ultrafast charge carrier 
trapping at the perovskite/ETM interface) in the perovskite/PCNI2-BTI 
film is notably smaller than those obtained from perovskite/PCBM 
(τ1 = 111 ps) and perovskite/PBTI2-BTI (τ1 = 120 ps), implying a consider-
ably improved photogenerated electron extraction from the perovskite 
to the cyano-functionalized PCNI2-BTI.
The trap density in perovskite/ETM stacks was evaluated using 
the SCLC method by fabricating electron-only devices. On the basis 
of the SCLC protocol46, the trap density can be correlated with the 
trap-filled limit voltage (VTFL) (Supplementary Figs. 34 and 35). 
The VTFL of perovskite films modified with ETMs was significantly 
decreased, from 0.93 V for pristine film to 0.53 V with PBTI2-BTI, 
to 0.25 V with PCBM and finally to 0.23 V with PCNI2-BTI, reveal-
ing that perovskite/PCNI2-BTI has the smallest charge trap den-
sity. These findings indicate that PCNI2-BTI probably leads to 
enhanced short-circuit current density (JSC) and fill factor (FF) in 
devices when compared with PCBM and non-cyanated PBTI2-BTI 
as the ETMs.
Interfacial interaction and passivation effect
DFT calculations were performed by placing PCBM or a single repeat-
ing unit of PBTI2-BTI (or PCNI2-BTI) on top of the perovskite crystal to 
investigate the passivation effect of the ETMs. As shown in Fig. 4a–d 
and Supplementary Fig. 36, stronger interactions are observed between 
the non-fullerene ETMs and the perovskite than between PCBM and 
the perovskite. In particular, a distinctive Pb−O interaction between 
uncoordinated Pb2+ ions and carbonyl groups is found at the interface 
between the perovskite and PBTI2-BTI, with a bond distance of 2.56 Å. 
At the PCNI2-BTI/perovskite interface, an additional Pb−N interaction 
between the cyano group and Pb2+ is also found. The binding energy 
between PCNI2-BTI and the perovskite surface is −4.02 eV, which is 
substantially higher than that between PBTI2-BTI and the perovskite 
surface (−3.38 eV), indicating a stronger interaction for PCNI2-BTI ena-
bled by the cyano functionality.

Furthermore, at the perovskite/PCNI2-BTI interface (Fig. 4d), a 
hydrogen bond (CN…H) between the cyano group of PCNI2-BTI and 
formamidinium iodide (FAI) is detected, with a distance of 2.01 Å. As 
shown in Fig. 4e,f, perovskite⋯ETM interactions can notably influence 
the electronic properties of perovskite/ETM stacks and fine-tune the 
position of the conduction band (CB) minimum, which in turn impacts 
the electron affinity. In particular, a lower-lying CB (~0.17 eV) is found 
for perovskite when ETM is varied from PBTI2-BTI to PCNI2-BTI, facili-
tating electron extraction at the perovskite/PCNI2-BTI interface. Inter-
estingly, CB topologies reveal an efficient carrier transfer across the 
perovskite/ETM interface for both polymers, but the CB of perovskite/
PCNI2-BTI is fully delocalized over the ETM and a small charge density 
remains localized on the perovskite in the perovskite/PBTI2-BTI system. 
The multiple and strong binding interactions of PCNI2-BTI with the 
perovskite lead to an electron density redistribution along the poly-
mer backbone and a more considerable orbital overlap between the 
ETM and perovskite, which should be beneficial for improving charge 
extraction at the interface.
Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) (Fig. 4g,h and Sup-
plementary Fig. 37) showed that the absorption peaks of neat PCBM 
exhibit a non-discernible shift after blending with PbI2, whereas the 
absorption shoulder shifts from 1,634 to 1,631 cm−1 in the presence of 
PbI2 for PBTI2-BTI, corroborating the presence of Pb−O interactions. 
For neat PCNI2-BTI, two distinctive absorption peaks are observed at 
2,033 and 1,622 cm−1, corresponding to the cyano and carbonyl groups 
(see eigenvectors of Supplementary Fig. 38), respectively. Upon min-
gling with PbI2, the peak shifts from 1,622 to 1,616 cm−1 due to the Pb−O 
interaction. Specifically, the cyano peak exhibits a more notable shift 
(from 2,033 to 2,027 cm−1), suggesting a strong interaction between 
the cyano group and the Pb2+ ion. In X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy 
(Fig. 4i), the uncoordinated Pb2+ shows two pronounced signals at 
138.39 and 143.24 eV, corresponding to the excited electrons of the 4f/7 
and 4f/5 orbitals, respectively. Upon depositing a thin PBTI2-BTI layer, 
both peaks shift to lower binding energies. Interestingly, the shifts are 
more pronounced with the PCNI2-BTI layer, suggesting stronger inter-
actions with Pb2+ than with PBTI2-BTI. The depth X-ray photoelectron 
spectroscopy analysis further confirms the stronger interaction of 
PCNI2-BTI with uncoordinated Pb2+ when compared with PCBM and 
PBTI2-BTI (Supplementary Fig. 39).

Photovoltaic performance and device stability
To evaluate the device performance of PCBM, PBTI2-BTI and PCNI2-BTI 
as ETMs, inverted PSCs were fabricated with a device architecture of 
indium tin oxide (ITO)/self-assembled monolayer (SAM)/perovskite 
(Cs0.05FA0.9MA0.05PbI3)/ETM/BCP/Ag (Fig. 5a), in which [4-(3,6-dimet
hyl-9H-carbazol-9-yl)butyl]phosphonic acid (Me-4PACz) was used as the 
SAM. The current-density–voltage (J–V) curves of the champion cells are 
illustrated in Fig. 5b, and the corresponding device performance param-
eters are summarized in Supplementary Table 8. The best-performing 
PSC based on the benchmark PCBM exhibits a PCE of 24.3% with a VOC 
of 1.156 V, a JSC of 25.25 mA cm−2 and an FF of 83.10%. Notably, the use 
of PCNI2-BTI as the ETM with an optimized thickness of 35 nm (Fig. 5b, 
Supplementary Figs. 43 and 44 and Supplementary Table 9) improves 
the PCE to 26.0% with a higher VOC of 1.179 V and a remarkable FF of 
86.44%. This PCE is one of the highest values reported for non-fullerene 
ETM-based PSCs (Supplementary Table 2 and Fig. 5c). However, when 
PCBM is replaced with PBTI2-BTI, a significantly lower PCE of 14.1% is 
attained, along with a decreased VOC of 0.960 V, a JSC of 24.47 mA cm−2 and 
an FF of 60.30%. The inferior performance of PBTI2-BTI-based devices 
can be attributed to the mismatched energy level and the reduced 
electron-transporting capability of this ETM. The integrated JSC val-
ues from external quantum efficiency (EQE) measurements agree well 
with those from the J–V measurements (Fig. 5d) for all three ETM-based 
devices. Furthermore, the hysteresis of the PCNI2-BTI-based champion 
devices (Supplementary Figs. 45–47) is minimal, which is attributed to 
effective suppression of ion migration. Supplementary Table 10 sum-
marizes the photovoltaic parameters of PSCs based on different ETMs. 
The average PCEs of PCBM-, PBTI2-BTI- and PCNI2-BTI-based cells (40 
devices) are 24.0 ± 0.3%, 11.6 ± 2.3% and 25.5 ± 0.3% (Fig. 5e and Sup-
plementary Figs. 48–50), respectively. A certified PCE of 25.4% was 
obtained by an accredited laboratory for the PCNI2-BTI device (Sup-
plementary Fig. 51). When the device number is increased to 80, the 
average PCE of PCNI2-BTI is maintained at 25.6 ± 0.2% (Supplementary 
Fig. 52). We also synthesized another three batches, and it was found 
that all batches show comparable number-averaged molecular mass 
(Mn) values (16.2–18.5 kDa) and produce comparable device perfor-
mances, with all average PCEs exceeding 25.6% (Supplementary Fig. 53 
and Supplementary Table 11). These results demonstrate the excellent 
reproducibility and reliability of PCNI2-BTI as an ETM for inverted PSCs. 
Inspired by the excellent performance of PCNI2-BTI as an ETM, we fur-
ther synthesized three new CNI2-based n-type polymers, PCNI2-DPP, 
PCNI2-BFI and PCNI2-BSeI (Supplementary Fig. 54 and Supplementary 
Note 1). Similar to PBTI2-BTI, these polymers showed a wide range of 
desirable properties as ETMs (Supplementary Figs. 55–57 and Supple-
mentary Table 12), thus achieving a champion PCE of 25.2%, 25.6% and 
26.1% for the PCNI2-DPP-, PCNI2-BFI- and PCNI2-BSeI-based devices, 
respectively (Supplementary Fig. 58 and Supplementary Table 13), all 
higher than that of the PCBM-based device.
The steady-state power output at the maximum power point 
voltage (Vmax) is shown in Fig. 5f, and the steady-state PCEs align well 
with the PCEs determined from the J–V scan for all three ETM-based 
devices. Furthermore, the light-intensity-dependent VOC measure-
ments (Supplementary Fig. 59) exhibit a suppressed ideality factor 
(nid = 1.23 for the PCNI2-BTI device), which is lower than those of the 
PCBM (1.58) and PBTI2-BTI devices (4.29), indicating an excellent 
charge transfer at the perovskite/PCNI2-BTI interface. When further 
applied in 1.65 eV wide-bandgap PSCs (Supplementary Fig. 60 and 
Supplementary Table 14), the PCNI2-BTI-based device also provided 
a PCE (21.5%) higher than that of PCBM (20.2%), demonstrating a wide 
applicability of PCNI2-BTI.
To assess the long-term stability of the devices, maximum power 
point tracking measurements were performed on encapsulated devices 
following the International Summit on Organic Photovoltaic Stabil-
ity (ISOS) protocol. The stability results are collected in Fig. 5g and 
Supplementary Figs. 61 and 62. Here, the PCNI2-BTI-based device exhib-
ited a superior stability, retaining 80% of the original PCE (T80) after 
1,280 h of maximum power point tracking testing, whereas the control 
PCBM-based one only showed a T80 of 759 h. The PBTI2-BTI-based device 
also experienced a rapid performance decline, with only 60% of the 
initial efficiency retained after 700 h. By using atomic layer deposition 
SnOx as the inorganic buffer layer instead of BCP, the PCNI2-BTI-based 
device retained 100.1% of its initial PCE (25.2%) after continuous heat 
treatment for over 300 h (Supplementary Fig. 63), which is greater 
than the retention (97.6%) of the PCBM-based device.
Outlook
This work showcases the successful application of a cyano- 
functionalized n-type polymer, PCNI2-BTI, as a non-fullerene ETM in 
inverted PSCs. Devices based on PCNI2-BTI achieve a remarkable PCE 
of 26.0% (certified at 25.4%) and outstanding operational robustness 
under the ISOS-L-3 protocol (65 °C and 60% ± 10% relative humidity), 
with a T80 of 1,280 h. Our study established key design principles for 
high-performance non-fullerene ETMs, including multiple proper-
ties, such as excellent solubility, good backbone coplanarity, low-lying 
FMOs, outstanding photothermal stability, favourable packing orien-
tation with close π–π stacking and abundant PGs. Building on these 
insights, we further developed three new non-fullerene ETMs that 
achieved an average PCE > 25%, with the highest one reaching 26.1% 
in inverted PSCs. This work paves the way for designing and utilizing 
high-performance non-fullerene ETMs for PSCs, which will change the 
research paradigm of the perovskite-based photovoltaic technology.
