Methods
Materials
Me-4PACz and piperazinium diiodide were purchased from TCI. FAI 
(99.9%), methylammonium chloride (99.9%), methylammonium iodide 
(99.9%) and lead iodide (PbI2, 99.999%) were bought from Advanced 
Election Technology Co., Ltd. BCP (99.99%), N,N-dimethylformamide 
(anhydrous, 99.8%), dimethylsulfoxide (anhydrous, 99.9%), 2-propanol 
(anhydrous, 99.5%) and ethyl acetate (anhydrous, 99.8%) were pur-
chased from Sigma-Aldrich.
Measurements and characteristics
Gel permeation chromatography was performed on a Polymer Labora-
tories GPC-PL220 high-temperature gel permeation chromatography/
size-exclusion chromatography system at 150 °C using polystyrene 
as the standard and trichlorobenzene as the eluent. Ultraviolet−vis-
ible−near-infrared absorption spectra were recorded on a Shimadzu 
UV-3600 UV–Vis–NIR spectrophotometer. UPS and X-ray photoelec-
tron spectroscopy are measured using a Thermo ESCALAB 250Xi, 
the X-ray excitation source is monochromatic Al Kα (hν = 1,486.6 eV), 
150 W, and the X-ray spot is 500 μm. FTIR spectral data for the devices 
were collected over the 500–3,000 cm−1 range using a Nicolet NEXUS 
870 FTIR spectrometer. Two-dimensional GIWAXS measurements 
were performed at the beamline PLS-II 9A small-angle X-ray scatter-
ing instrument of Pohang Accelerator Laboratory, Republic of Korea. 
Resonance Raman spectra with 532 nm laser excitations were recorded 
for thin-film samples using a HORIBA LabRAM HR Evolution laser 
microscopy confocal Raman spectrometer equipped with a mono-
chromator of focal length 800 mm, a confocal microscope with a 
×100 objective and a high-performance CCD (charge-coupled device) 
detector. This set-up has a spectral resolution lower than 1 cm−1. SEM 
mapping images were characterized using a Helios NanoLab 600i 
focused ion beam. Steady-state PL and time-resolved PL spectra were 
recorded on an Edinburgh Instruments FLS 1000. TAS was carried out 
on a TA100 (Time-tech Spectra). KPFM measurements were performed 
in a single-pass frequency-modulation mode using a Cypher ES (Asy-
lum Research) and HF2LI lock-in amplifier (Zurich Instruments) with 
PtIr-coated tips (PPP-EFM, NANOSENSORS).
Perovskite-film and solar-cell fabrication
ITO glass substrates were washed with soapy water, acetone and isopro-
panol in sequence for 30 min each and then treated with UV–ozone for a 
time period of 45 min. Me-4PACz (0.5 mg ml−1) solution was spin-coated 
on fresh ITO at 4,000 r.p.m. (4 s acceleration) for 30 s, followed by 
heating on a hot plate at 100 °C for 5 min. Then Al2O3/isopropyl alcohol 
(1:150; v:v) was spin-coated on SAMs and annealed at 100 °C for 5 min. 
The Cs0.05FA0.9MA0.05PbI3 perovskite precursor was prepared by dissolv-
ing 746.8 mg PbI2, 238 mg FAI, 19.8 mg CsI, 11.5 mg methylammonium 
iodide and 12 mg methylammonium chloride in a mixed solvent of N, 
N-dimethylformamide and dimethylsulfoxide (5/1; v/v) and filtered 
with a 0.22 μm polytetrafluoroethylene filter. The perovskite precur-
sor solution was spin-coated on the top at 100 r.p.m. for 10 s and 5,000 
r.p.m. for 30 s, then treated with 150 μl ethyl acetate dropping onto the 
substrate over 25 s and further annealed at 60 °C for 5 min and 100 °C 
for 20 min. Subsequently, the PCBM (20 mg ml−1 in chlorobenzene; 
1,200 r.p.m. for 60 s and 6,000 r.p.m. for 10 s), PBTI2-BTI (7 mg ml−1 
in chloroform:dichlorobenzene = 1:1; 1,200 r.p.m. for 60 s and 6,000 
r.p.m. for 10 s) or PCNI2-BTI (7 mg ml−1 in chloroform:dichlorobenzen
e = 1:1; 1,000, 1,200, 1,500 or 2,000 r.p.m. for 60 s and 6,000 r.p.m. for 
10 s) solution was deposited (thickness ~35 nm) and the resulting films 
were annealed at 100 °C for 5 min. Finally, 7 nm BCP and 150 nm Ag were 
thermally evaporated on ETM to finish the device fabrication with an 
active area of 15 mm2. For the stability test, the device was encapsulated 
with UV glue and polyisobutylene sealant.
For wide-bandgap PSCs, 2PACz (0.5 mg ml−1) solution was 
spin-coated on fresh ITO at 4,000 r.p.m. (4 s acceleration) for 30 s, 
followed by heating on a hot plate at 100 °C for 5 min. Then Al2O3/
isopropyl alcohol (1/150; v/v) was spin-coated on SAMs and annealed 
at 100 °C for 5 min. Caesium formamidinium perovskite was deposited 
from a stoichiometric solution containing CsI, FAI, PbI2 and PbBr2 in 
a mixture of N, N-dimethylformamide and dimethylsulfoxide. The 
solution was deposited through a 0.2 μm polytetrafluoroethylene 
filter and spun at 1,000 r.p.m. for 10 s, followed by 6,000 r.p.m. for 
30 s. During spin-coating, chlorobenzene was quickly dispensed 5 s 
before the end of the spin process as an antisolvent to assist perovskite 
crystallization. The films were annealed on a hot plate at 100 °C for 
20 min. Next, saturated piperazinium diiodide/isopropyl alcohol solu-
tion was spin-coated on the perovskite layer at 6,000 r.p.m. for 30 s, 
and annealed at 100 oC for 2 min. After that, PCBM (20 mg dissolved 
in chlorobenzene, 1,200 r.p.m. for 60 s and 6,000 r.p.m. for 10 s) or 
PCNI2-BTI (7 mg ml−1 in chloroform:dichlorobenzene = 1:1, 1,200 r.p.m. 
for 60 s and 6,000 r.p.m. for 10 s) was deposited on top of the samples 
and then annealed at 100 °C for 5 min. Then, 8 nm BCP and 100 nm Ag 
were deposited by thermal evaporation.
Device characterization
J–V measurements were carried out using a Keithley 2400 source meter 
under AM 1.5G irradiation (checked with a calibrated reference solar 
cell from Newport) in a N2 glovebox with a solar simulator (Enlitech 
with a 300 W Xenon lamp). A 0.085 cm2 metal mask was used for all 
J–V measurements. EQE measurements for devices were conducted 
on an Enlitech EQE measurement system. For the operational stability 
test, an encapsulated device was placed on a 65 ± 1 °C hot plate under 
irradiation with a 1 sun equivalent light-emitting diode lamp in ambient 
conditions with a humidity of 60 ± 10%.

nature materials
Article
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-025-02163-4
Non-fullerene electron-transporting 
materials for high-performance and stable 
perovskite solar cells
 
Kui Feng 
  1,5 
, Guoliang Wang 
  2,5, Qing Lian 
  1 
, Sergio Gámez-Valenzuela1, 
Bolin Li1, Riqing Ding1, Wanli Yang1, Keli Wang1, Jie Zeng1, Yong Zhang 
  1, 
Sang Young Jeong3, Baomin Xu 
  1, Anita Ho-Baillie 
  2, Han Young Woo 
  3, 
Antonio Facchetti 
  4 
 & Xugang Guo 
  1 
The electron-transporting material (ETM) is a key component of perovskite 
solar cells (PSCs) optimizing electron extraction from perovskite to 
cathode. Fullerenes, specifically C60 and [6,6]-phenyl-C61-butyric acid methyl 
ester (PCBM), have been used as the benchmark ETMs for inverted PSCs. 
However, C60 is restricted to thermal evaporation, and PCBM suffers from 
poor photothermal stability and suboptimal electron transport, limiting 
their PSC applications. Here a solution-processable non-fullerene ETM, 
cyano-functionalized bithiophene imide dimer (CNI2)-based polymer 
(PCNI2-BTI), holds multiple advantages, including excellent photothermal 
stability, efficient electron transport and improved interaction with the 
perovskite layer. Consequently, inverted PSCs incorporating PCNI2-BTI 
deliver an outstanding power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 26.0% (certified 
25.4%) and remarkable operational stability, with a T80 approaching 1,300 h 
under ISOS-L-3. Moreover, we synthesize three additional CNI2-based 
polymer ETMs, yielding an average PCE of >25% in PSCs. These findings 
demonstrate unprecedented potential of non-fullerene ETMs enabling 
high-performance and stable PSCs.
Inverted perovskite solar cells (PSCs) have gained considerable 
attention for their simplified architecture, low-temperature solution 
processability, small hysteresis and high compatibility with flexible 
substrates and all-perovskite tandem devices1–5. Major advances are 
driven by developing new hole-transporting materials6–8 and interfacial 
layers9,10, and optimizing perovskite crystallization11,12, recently afford-
ing power conversion efficiencies (PCEs) exceeding 25%1,13,14. However, 
electron-transporting materials (ETMs) placed on the upper surface 
of the perovskite photoactive layer in inverted cells have received 
limited attention, despite their critical role in device performance 
and stability15,16. Fullerenes are the benchmark ETMs for inverted PSCs 
(Supplementary Table 1), with C60 and phenyl-C61-butyric acid methyl 
ester (PCBM) being the most investigated ones due to their isotropic 
transport character and good defect passivation effect17–20 (Fig. 1a). 
However, C60 processing is limited to thermal evaporation21 and PCBM 
suffers from several drawbacks, such as high cost due to the existence 
of undesired isomers during fullerene addition reaction, hydrophobic-
ity and poor photothermal stability22–26. Additionally, the spheroidal 
shape of PCBM leads to a film with a low degree of ordering, yielding 
suboptimal electron transport from perovskite layer to cathode19,27

ETM characterizations
Ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy (UPS) was performed to probe 
the work function (Φ) and FMOs of the ETMs. The binding-energy cut-
off (Ecutoff) and onset (Eonset) were used to calculate Φ and the HOMO 
level (EHOMO; Supplementary Figs. 3–7). Φ was calculated to be 3.98, 
3.82, 4.15 and 4.32 eV for perovskite, PBTI2-BTI, PCNI2-BTI and PCBM, 
respectively, on the basis of the equation Φ = hν − Ecutoff, where hν is the 
photon energy used in the UPS measurement. As shown in Fig. 1d, 
the EHOMO values are −5.56 and −5.85 eV on the basis of the 
equation EHOMO = 21.22 eV − (Ecutoff – Eonset), and the LUMO levels (ELUMO) 
are −3.57 and −3.95 eV for PBTI2-BTI and PCNI2-BTI, respectively. The 
experimental trend is consistent with density functional theory 
(DFT)-based calculations (Supplementary Figs. 8 and 9). Compared to 
PCBM, the minimized ΔELUMO between perovskite and PCNI2-BTI should 
facilitate efficient electron extraction and increase open-circuit voltage 
(VOC). On the basis of the absorption onsets, the optical bandgaps (Eopt
g ) 
of the films were estimated to be 2.32, 1.88 and 1.90 eV for PCBM, 
PBTI2-BTI and PCNI2-BTI, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 10 and 
Supplementary Table 6).

to improve the performance and stability of PSCs, which is essential for

Design and synthesis of non-fullerene ETMs
Figure 1e depicts the key properties of representative non-fullerene 
ETMs, such as the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) energy 
difference (ΔELUMO, eV) between ETM and perovskite (here organo-
metal halide perovskite), number of passivation groups (PGs) and 
space-charge-limited-current (SCLC) electron mobility (µe,SCLC), and the 
PCEs of the resulting devices33–37. Data analysis shows that an optimal 
ETM should feature several key properties, including a suitable ΔELUMO, 
a large µe,SCLC and multiple PGs. To attain these properties, we identi-
fied as promising candidates imide-functionalized bithiophene-based 
n-type polymers, which show widely tunable frontier molecular orbitals 
(FMOs), a planar backbone and multiple PGs, thus delivering remark-
able performance in organic electronic devices38. Among them, the 
cyano-functionalized bithiophene imide dimer (CNI2)-based n-type 
polymer PCNI2-BTI exhibits excellent solubility, good backbone copla-
narity, high crystallinity with a predominant face-on orientation (Fig. 1c) 
and a deep-lying LUMO level below −3.90 eV, yielding a high electron 
mobility exceeding 0.2 cm2 V−1 s−1 in organic thin-film transistors 
(OTFTs) and a n-doped conductivity up to 150 S cm−1 (ref. 39). Nota-
bly, PCNI2-BTI features multiple PGs that could effectively passivate

Thermogravimetric analysis revealed that PCNI2-BTI has a high 
thermal stability with a decomposition temperature (Td, defined as the 
temperature with a 5% weight loss) above 400 °C, higher than those of 
PCBM (388 °C) and PBTI2-BTI (381 °C) (Fig. 2a). In differential scanning 
calorimetry, PCNI2-BTI and PBTI2-BTI did not show any phase transition 
in the 30–300 °C temperature range (Fig. 2b), while PCBM exhibited 
a distinctive melting peak26. The photothermal stability of the ETM 
films was evaluated by monitoring the changes in ultraviolet–visible 
(UV–Vis) absorption characteristics under thermal ageing (65 °C) and 
illumination conditions for over 200 h (Fig. 2c and Supplementary 
Figs. 11–21). Under continuous thermal stress and/or illumination 
conditions, PCNI2-BTI absorption also showed a minimal variation, 
while PCBM experienced a more notable change25,42. Contact-angle 
measurements using a water droplet (Supplementary Fig. 22) showed 
an increased mean water-droplet contact angle from 83.0° for PCBM 
to 99.7° for PBTI2-BTI and to 106.3° for PCNI2-BTI. These findings 
highlight the distinctive photothermal stability and hydrophobicity 
of PCNI2-BTI as an ETM, which should be beneficial for long-term PSC 
operational stability.
Charge transport characteristics
Electron mobilities of the ETMs were investigated using OTFT and 
SCLC protocols (Fig. 2d–g and Supplementary Figs. 23–25). The 
results revealed that PCNI2-BTI has a higher OTFT electron mobil-
ity (μe,OTFT = 0.17 cm−2 V−1 s−1) and μe,SCLC (1.06 × 10−3 cm−2 V−1 s−1) when 
compared with PBTI2-BTI (μe,OTFT = 0.041 cm−2 V−1 s−1 and μe,SCLC = 8.0
5 × 10−5 cm−2 V−1 s−1) and PCBM (μe,OTFT = 0.052 cm−2 V−1 s−1 and μe,SCLC =  
1.02 × 10−4 cm−2 V−1 s−1)43 (Supplementary Table 7). These findings 
indicate that PCNI2-BTI possesses superior electron-transporting 
properties, making it a promising candidate for enhancing PSC per-

orientated crystallites. In contrast, both neat PBTI2-BTI and PCNI2-BTI 
films exhibit a pronounced hump-shaped (010) diffraction peak along 
the out-of-plane direction originating from cofacial π–π stacking, 
suggesting a predominant face-on orientation. This orientation leads

Perovskite/ETM surface morphology
The surface morphology of the perovskite/ETM composite layers was 
investigated using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), atomic force 
microscopy (AFM) and Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM). The 
SEM images (Supplementary Fig. 28) reveal that PCBM, PBTI2-BTI and 
PCNI2-BTI layers uniformly cover the perovskite film top without any 
visible large domains or uncovered regions. Further examinations 
using AFM (Supplementary Fig. 29) reveal that the perovskite surface 
has a rough morphology with a root-mean-squared roughness value 
of 22.2 nm. However, after deposition of the ETMs, the upper surface 
becomes substantially smoother, with a root-mean-squared roughness 
value of less than 8.5 nm for the perovskite/PCBM layer, 7.4 nm for the 
perovskite/PBTI2-BTI layer and 7.8 nm for the perovskite/PCNI2-BTI 
layer. The smoother surface of the perovskite/PCNI2-BTI (or PBTI2-BTI) 
composite layers will yield improved contact between the non-fullerene 
ETMs and the perovskite active layer. It is worth noting that some larger 
clusters are observed in certain areas of the perovskite/PCBM layer, 
which could negatively affect device performance24.
In the results of KPFM44,45 (Fig. 3a–c), the spatial distribution of 
contact potential for the perovskite/PCBM layer exhibits noticeable 
undulations, suggesting clustering in line with the AFM results. In con-
trast, a pronounced flattening of the potential distribution is found for 
the perovskite/PBTI2-BTI and perovskite/PCNI2-BTI layers (Supplemen-
tary Fig. 30). The analysis of mean surface potential values indicates a 
relative work function trend of PBTI2-BTI < PCNI2-BTI < PCBM, which 
aligns with the UPS measurements. Notably, the improved energy-level 
alignment between the perovskite and PCNI2-BTI is expected to reduce 
charge carrier accumulation and enhance carrier extraction. The 
favourable morphology of the PCNI2-BTI film is anticipated to facili-
tate efficient electron extraction and transport, thereby improving 
the device performance.

that the time constant (τ1 = 50 ps; τ1 represents ultrafast charge carrier 
trapping at the perovskite/ETM interface) in the perovskite/PCNI2-BTI 
film is notably smaller than those obtained from perovskite/PCBM 
(τ1 = 111 ps) and perovskite/PBTI2-BTI (τ1 = 120 ps), implying a consider-
ably improved photogenerated electron extraction from the perovskite 
to the cyano-functionalized PCNI2-BTI.
The trap density in perovskite/ETM stacks was evaluated using 
the SCLC method by fabricating electron-only devices. On the basis 
of the SCLC protocol46, the trap density can be correlated with the 
trap-filled limit voltage (VTFL) (Supplementary Figs. 34 and 35). 
The VTFL of perovskite films modified with ETMs was significantly 
decreased, from 0.93 V for pristine film to 0.53 V with PBTI2-BTI, 
to 0.25 V with PCBM and finally to 0.23 V with PCNI2-BTI, reveal-
ing that perovskite/PCNI2-BTI has the smallest charge trap den-
sity. These findings indicate that PCNI2-BTI probably leads to 
enhanced short-circuit current density (JSC) and fill factor (FF) in 
devices when compared with PCBM and non-cyanated PBTI2-BTI 
as the ETMs.
Interfacial interaction and passivation effect
DFT calculations were performed by placing PCBM or a single repeat-
ing unit of PBTI2-BTI (or PCNI2-BTI) on top of the perovskite crystal to 
investigate the passivation effect of the ETMs. As shown in Fig. 4a–d 
and Supplementary Fig. 36, stronger interactions are observed between 
the non-fullerene ETMs and the perovskite than between PCBM and 
the perovskite. In particular, a distinctive Pb−O interaction between 
uncoordinated Pb2+ ions and carbonyl groups is found at the interface 
between the perovskite and PBTI2-BTI, with a bond distance of 2.56 Å. 
At the PCNI2-BTI/perovskite interface, an additional Pb−N interaction 
between the cyano group and Pb2+ is also found. The binding energy 
between PCNI2-BTI and the perovskite surface is −4.02 eV, which is 
substantially higher than that between PBTI2-BTI and the perovskite 
surface (−3.38 eV), indicating a stronger interaction for PCNI2-BTI ena-
bled by the cyano functionality.

Furthermore, at the perovskite/PCNI2-BTI interface (Fig. 4d), a 
hydrogen bond (CN…H) between the cyano group of PCNI2-BTI and 
formamidinium iodide (FAI) is detected, with a distance of 2.01 Å. As 
shown in Fig. 4e,f, perovskite⋯ETM interactions can notably influence 
the electronic properties of perovskite/ETM stacks and fine-tune the 
position of the conduction band (CB) minimum, which in turn impacts 
the electron affinity. In particular, a lower-lying CB (~0.17 eV) is found 
for perovskite when ETM is varied from PBTI2-BTI to PCNI2-BTI, facili-
tating electron extraction at the perovskite/PCNI2-BTI interface. Inter-
estingly, CB topologies reveal an efficient carrier transfer across the 
perovskite/ETM interface for both polymers, but the CB of perovskite/
PCNI2-BTI is fully delocalized over the ETM and a small charge density 
remains localized on the perovskite in the perovskite/PBTI2-BTI system. 
The multiple and strong binding interactions of PCNI2-BTI with the 
perovskite lead to an electron density redistribution along the poly-
mer backbone and a more considerable orbital overlap between the 
ETM and perovskite, which should be beneficial for improving charge 
extraction at the interface.
Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) (Fig. 4g,h and Sup-
plementary Fig. 37) showed that the absorption peaks of neat PCBM 
exhibit a non-discernible shift after blending with PbI2, whereas the 
absorption shoulder shifts from 1,634 to 1,631 cm−1 in the presence of 
PbI2 for PBTI2-BTI, corroborating the presence of Pb−O interactions. 
For neat PCNI2-BTI, two distinctive absorption peaks are observed at 
2,033 and 1,622 cm−1, corresponding to the cyano and carbonyl groups 
(see eigenvectors of Supplementary Fig. 38), respectively. Upon min-
gling with PbI2, the peak shifts from 1,622 to 1,616 cm−1 due to the Pb−O 
interaction. Specifically, the cyano peak exhibits a more notable shift 
(from 2,033 to 2,027 cm−1), suggesting a strong interaction between 
the cyano group and the Pb2+ ion. In X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy 
(Fig. 4i), the uncoordinated Pb2+ shows two pronounced signals at 
138.39 and 143.24 eV, corresponding to the excited electrons of the 4f/7

Photovoltaic performance and device stability
To evaluate the device performance of PCBM, PBTI2-BTI and PCNI2-BTI 
as ETMs, inverted PSCs were fabricated with a device architecture of 
indium tin oxide (ITO)/self-assembled monolayer (SAM)/perovskite 
(Cs0.05FA0.9MA0.05PbI3)/ETM/BCP/Ag (Fig. 5a), in which [4-(3,6-dimet
hyl-9H-carbazol-9-yl)butyl]phosphonic acid (Me-4PACz) was used as the 
SAM. The current-density–voltage (J–V) curves of the champion cells are 
illustrated in Fig. 5b, and the corresponding device performance param-
eters are summarized in Supplementary Table 8. The best-performing 
PSC based on the benchmark PCBM exhibits a PCE of 24.3% with a VOC 
of 1.156 V, a JSC of 25.25 mA cm−2 and an FF of 83.10%. Notably, the use 
of PCNI2-BTI as the ETM with an optimized thickness of 35 nm (Fig. 5b, 
Supplementary Figs. 43 and 44 and Supplementary Table 9) improves 
the PCE to 26.0% with a higher VOC of 1.179 V and a remarkable FF of 
86.44%. This PCE is one of the highest values reported for non-fullerene 
ETM-based PSCs (Supplementary Table 2 and Fig. 5c). However, when 
PCBM is replaced with PBTI2-BTI, a significantly lower PCE of 14.1% is 
attained, along with a decreased VOC of 0.960 V, a JSC of 24.47 mA cm−2 and 
an FF of 60.30%. The inferior performance of PBTI2-BTI-based devices 
can be attributed to the mismatched energy level and the reduced 
electron-transporting capability of this ETM. The integrated JSC val-
ues from external quantum efficiency (EQE) measurements agree well 
with those from the J–V measurements (Fig. 5d) for all three ETM-based 
devices. Furthermore, the hysteresis of the PCNI2-BTI-based champion 
devices (Supplementary Figs. 45–47) is minimal, which is attributed to 
effective suppression of ion migration. Supplementary Table 10 sum-
marizes the photovoltaic parameters of PSCs based on different ETMs. 
The average PCEs of PCBM-, PBTI2-BTI- and PCNI2-BTI-based cells (40 
devices) are 24.0 ± 0.3%, 11.6 ± 2.3% and 25.5 ± 0.3% (Fig. 5e and Sup-
plementary Figs. 48–50), respectively. A certified PCE of 25.4% was 
obtained by an accredited laboratory for the PCNI2-BTI device (Sup-
plementary Fig. 51). When the device number is increased to 80, the 
average PCE of PCNI2-BTI is maintained at 25.6 ± 0.2% (Supplementary 
Fig. 52). We also synthesized another three batches, and it was found 
that all batches show comparable number-averaged molecular mass 
(Mn) values (16.2–18.5 kDa) and produce comparable device perfor-
mances, with all average PCEs exceeding 25.6% (Supplementary Fig. 53 
and Supplementary Table 11). These results demonstrate the excellent 
reproducibility and reliability of PCNI2-BTI as an ETM for inverted PSCs. 
Inspired by the excellent performance of PCNI2-BTI as an ETM, we fur-
ther synthesized three new CNI2-based n-type polymers, PCNI2-DPP, 
PCNI2-BFI and PCNI2-BSeI (Supplementary Fig. 54 and Supplementary 
Note 1). Similar to PBTI2-BTI, these polymers showed a wide range of 
desirable properties as ETMs (Supplementary Figs. 55–57 and Supple-
mentary Table 12), thus achieving a champion PCE of 25.2%, 25.6% and 
26.1% for the PCNI2-DPP-, PCNI2-BFI- and PCNI2-BSeI-based devices, 
respectively (Supplementary Fig. 58 and Supplementary Table 13), all 
higher than that of the PCBM-based device.
The steady-state power output at the maximum power point 
voltage (Vmax) is shown in Fig. 5f, and the steady-state PCEs align well 
with the PCEs determined from the J–V scan for all three ETM-based 
devices. Furthermore, the light-intensity-dependent VOC measure-
ments (Supplementary Fig. 59) exhibit a suppressed ideality factor 
(nid = 1.23 for the PCNI2-BTI device), which is lower than those of the 
PCBM (1.58) and PBTI2-BTI devices (4.29), indicating an excellent 
charge transfer at the perovskite/PCNI2-BTI interface. When further 
applied in 1.65 eV wide-bandgap PSCs (Supplementary Fig. 60 and 
Supplementary Table 14), the PCNI2-BTI-based device also provided 
a PCE (21.5%) higher than that of PCBM (20.2%), demonstrating a wide 
applicability of PCNI2-BTI.
To assess the long-term stability of the devices, maximum power 
point tracking measurements were performed on encapsulated devices 
following the International Summit on Organic Photovoltaic Stabil-
ity (ISOS) protocol. The stability results are collected in Fig. 5g and 
Supplementary Figs. 61 and 62. Here, the PCNI2-BTI-based device exhib-
ited a superior stability, retaining 80% of the original PCE (T80) after 
1,280 h of maximum power point tracking testing, whereas the control 
PCBM-based one only showed a T80 of 759 h. The PBTI2-BTI-based device 
also experienced a rapid performance decline, with only 60% of the 
initial efficiency retained after 700 h. By using atomic layer deposition 
SnOx as the inorganic buffer layer instead of BCP, the PCNI2-BTI-based 
device retained 100.1% of its initial PCE (25.2%) after continuous heat 
treatment for over 300 h (Supplementary Fig. 63), which is greater 
than the retention (97.6%) of the PCBM-based device.
Outlook
This work showcases the successful application of a cyano- 
functionalized n-type polymer, PCNI2-BTI, as a non-fullerene ETM in 
inverted PSCs. Devices based on PCNI2-BTI achieve a remarkable PCE 
of 26.0% (certified at 25.4%) and outstanding operational robustness 
under the ISOS-L-3 protocol (65 °C and 60% ± 10% relative humidity), 
with a T80 of 1,280 h. Our study established key design principles for 
high-performance non-fullerene ETMs, including multiple proper-
ties, such as excellent solubility, good backbone coplanarity, low-lying 
FMOs, outstanding photothermal stability, favourable packing orien-
tation with close π–π stacking and abundant PGs. Building on these 
insights, we further developed three new non-fullerene ETMs that 
achieved an average PCE > 25%, with the highest one reaching 26.1% 
in inverted PSCs. This work paves the way for designing and utilizing 
high-performance non-fullerene ETMs for PSCs, which will change the 
research paradigm of the perovskite-based photovoltaic technology.

Methods
Materials
Me-4PACz and piperazinium diiodide were purchased from TCI. FAI 
(99.9%), methylammonium chloride (99.9%), methylammonium iodide 
(99.9%) and lead iodide (PbI2, 99.999%) were bought from Advanced 
Election Technology Co., Ltd. BCP (99.99%), N,N-dimethylformamide 
(anhydrous, 99.8%), dimethylsulfoxide (anhydrous, 99.9%), 2-propanol 
(anhydrous, 99.5%) and ethyl acetate (anhydrous, 99.8%) were pur-
chased from Sigma-Aldrich.
Measurements and characteristics
Gel permeation chromatography was performed on a Polymer Labora-
tories GPC-PL220 high-temperature gel permeation chromatography/
size-exclusion chromatography system at 150 °C using polystyrene 
as the standard and trichlorobenzene as the eluent. Ultraviolet−vis-
ible−near-infrared absorption spectra were recorded on a Shimadzu 
UV-3600 UV–Vis–NIR spectrophotometer. UPS and X-ray photoelec-
tron spectroscopy are measured using a Thermo ESCALAB 250Xi, 
the X-ray excitation source is monochromatic Al Kα (hν = 1,486.6 eV), 
150 W, and the X-ray spot is 500 μm. FTIR spectral data for the devices 
were collected over the 500–3,000 cm−1 range using a Nicolet NEXUS 
870 FTIR spectrometer. Two-dimensional GIWAXS measurements 
were performed at the beamline PLS-II 9A small-angle X-ray scatter-
ing instrument of Pohang Accelerator Laboratory, Republic of Korea. 
Resonance Raman spectra with 532 nm laser excitations were recorded 
for thin-film samples using a HORIBA LabRAM HR Evolution laser 
microscopy confocal Raman spectrometer equipped with a mono-
chromator of focal length 800 mm, a confocal microscope with a 
×100 objective and a high-performance CCD (charge-coupled device) 
detector. This set-up has a spectral resolution lower than 1 cm−1. SEM 
mapping images were characterized using a Helios NanoLab 600i 
focused ion beam. Steady-state PL and time-resolved PL spectra were 
recorded on an Edinburgh Instruments FLS 1000. TAS was carried out 
on a TA100 (Time-tech Spectra). KPFM measurements were performed 
in a single-pass frequency-modulation mode using a Cypher ES (Asy-
lum Research) and HF2LI lock-in amplifier (Zurich Instruments) with 
PtIr-coated tips (PPP-EFM, NANOSENSORS).
Perovskite-film and solar-cell fabrication
ITO glass substrates were washed with soapy water, acetone and isopro-
panol in sequence for 30 min each and then treated with UV–ozone for a 
time period of 45 min. Me-4PACz (0.5 mg ml−1) solution was spin-coated 
on fresh ITO at 4,000 r.p.m. (4 s acceleration) for 30 s, followed by 
heating on a hot plate at 100 °C for 5 min. Then Al2O3/isopropyl alcohol 
(1:150; v:v) was spin-coated on SAMs and annealed at 100 °C for 5 min. 
The Cs0.05FA0.9MA0.05PbI3 perovskite precursor was prepared by dissolv-
ing 746.8 mg PbI2, 238 mg FAI, 19.8 mg CsI, 11.5 mg methylammonium 
iodide and 12 mg methylammonium chloride in a mixed solvent of N, 
N-dimethylformamide and dimethylsulfoxide (5/1; v/v) and filtered 
with a 0.22 μm polytetrafluoroethylene filter. The perovskite precur-
sor solution was spin-coated on the top at 100 r.p.m. for 10 s and 5,000 
r.p.m. for 30 s, then treated with 150 μl ethyl acetate dropping onto the 
substrate over 25 s and further annealed at 60 °C for 5 min and 100 °C 
for 20 min. Subsequently, the PCBM (20 mg ml−1 in chlorobenzene; 
1,200 r.p.m. for 60 s and 6,000 r.p.m. for 10 s), PBTI2-BTI (7 mg ml−1 
in chloroform:dichlorobenzene = 1:1; 1,200 r.p.m. for 60 s and 6,000 
r.p.m. for 10 s) or PCNI2-BTI (7 mg ml−1 in chloroform:dichlorobenzen
e = 1:1; 1,000, 1,200, 1,500 or 2,000 r.p.m. for 60 s and 6,000 r.p.m. for 
10 s) solution was deposited (thickness ~35 nm) and the resulting films 
were annealed at 100 °C for 5 min. Finally, 7 nm BCP and 150 nm Ag were 
thermally evaporated on ETM to finish the device fabrication with an 
active area of 15 mm2. For the stability test, the device was encapsulated 
with UV glue and polyisobutylene sealant.
For wide-bandgap PSCs, 2PACz (0.5 mg ml−1) solution was 
spin-coated on fresh ITO at 4,000 r.p.m. (4 s acceleration) for 30 s, 
followed by heating on a hot plate at 100 °C for 5 min. Then Al2O3/
isopropyl alcohol (1/150; v/v) was spin-coated on SAMs and annealed 
at 100 °C for 5 min. Caesium formamidinium perovskite was deposited 
from a stoichiometric solution containing CsI, FAI, PbI2 and PbBr2 in 
a mixture of N, N-dimethylformamide and dimethylsulfoxide. The 
solution was deposited through a 0.2 μm polytetrafluoroethylene 
filter and spun at 1,000 r.p.m. for 10 s, followed by 6,000 r.p.m. for 
30 s. During spin-coating, chlorobenzene was quickly dispensed 5 s 
before the end of the spin process as an antisolvent to assist perovskite 
crystallization. The films were annealed on a hot plate at 100 °C for 
20 min. Next, saturated piperazinium diiodide/isopropyl alcohol solu-
tion was spin-coated on the perovskite layer at 6,000 r.p.m. for 30 s, 
and annealed at 100 oC for 2 min. After that, PCBM (20 mg dissolved 
in chlorobenzene, 1,200 r.p.m. for 60 s and 6,000 r.p.m. for 10 s) or 
PCNI2-BTI (7 mg ml−1 in chloroform:dichlorobenzene = 1:1, 1,200 r.p.m. 
for 60 s and 6,000 r.p.m. for 10 s) was deposited on top of the samples 
and then annealed at 100 °C for 5 min. Then, 8 nm BCP and 100 nm Ag 
were deposited by thermal evaporation.
Device characterization
J–V measurements were carried out using a Keithley 2400 source meter 
under AM 1.5G irradiation (checked with a calibrated reference solar 
cell from Newport) in a N2 glovebox with a solar simulator (Enlitech 
with a 300 W Xenon lamp). A 0.085 cm2 metal mask was used for all 
J–V measurements. EQE measurements for devices were conducted 
on an Enlitech EQE measurement system. For the operational stability 
test, an encapsulated device was placed on a 65 ± 1 °C hot plate under 
irradiation with a 1 sun equivalent light-emitting diode lamp in ambient 
conditions with a humidity of 60 ± 10%.

engineering for high-performance\ninorganic–organic hybrid perovskite solar cells\nNam Joong Jeon1†, Jun Hong Noh1†, Young Chan Kim1, Woon Seok Yang1, Seungchan Ryu1\nand Sang Il Seok1,2*\nOrganolead trihalide perovskite materials have been successfully used as light absorbers in eﬃcient photovoltaic cells. Two\ndiﬀerent cell structures, based on mesoscopic metal oxides and planar heterojunctions have already demonstrated very\nimpressive advances in performance. Here, we report a bilayer architecture comprising the key features of mesoscopic and\nplanar structures obtained by a fully solution-based process. We used CH3NH3 Pb(I1−xBrx)3 (x=0.1–0.15) as the absorbing layer\nand poly(triarylamine) as a hole-transporting material. The use of a mixed solvent of γ-butyrolactone and dimethylsulphoxide\n(DMSO) followed by toluene drop-casting leads to extremely uniform and dense perovskite layers via a CH3NH3I–PbI2–DMSO\nintermediate phase, and enables the fabrication of remarkably improved solar cells with a certiﬁed power-conversion eﬃciency\nof 16.2% and no hysteresis. These results provide important progress towards the understanding of the role of solution-\nprocessing in the realization of low-cost and highly eﬃcient perovskite solar cells.\nT\noday, crystalline silicon dominates the solar panel industry\nbut remains relatively expensive to manufacture. If devices\ncould be fabricated from cheap materials by a simple solution\nprocess without annealing at high temperature, their costs could\nbe considerably reduced through mass production. Although\ndye-sensitized1, quantum dot2,3, organic4,5, and inorganic–organic\nheterojunction solar cells6,7 can be fabricated by multiple or single\nsolution processes, the cells still suﬀer from problems such as a\nlack of long-term stability and low conversion eﬃciency due to\nfundamental energy losses associated with the extensive interface\nfor charge separation. Recently, methylammonium lead halide\n(MAPbX3, where MA is methylammonium CH3NH3 and X is a\nhalogen) perovskites8–16 have oﬀered the promise of a breakthrough\nfor next-generation solar devices. The use of perovskites aﬀords\nseveral advantages: excellent optical properties that are tunable by\nmanaging chemical compositions13; ambipolar charge transport10;\nand very long electron–hole diﬀusion lengths17,18. Perovskite\nmaterials have been applied as light absorbers to thin or thick\nmesoscopic metal oxides and planar heterojunction solar devices.\nFor example, when MAPbI3 was loaded on a mesoporous\n(mp)-TiO2 electrode by the sequential deposition of PbI2 and\nmethylammonium iodide (MAI), a 15.0% power-conversion\neﬃciency (PCE) was achieved under 1 sun illumination11. The\nauthors of ref. 12 reported a maximum performance of 15.4%\neﬃciency with an open-circuit voltage (Voc) of 1.07 V and short-\ncircuit current density (Jsc) of 21.5 mA cm−2, based on uniform\nMAPbI3−xClx planar thin layers deposited by the vacuum thermal\nevaporation method without the mp-TiO2 electrode. Several other\ngroups also reported eﬃcient planar solar cells, based on normal\norganic photovoltaic structure12,19. Although very impressive cell\neﬃciencies have been achieved, the cell architecture, use of vacuum,\nor the two-step deposition process should be modified to improve\neﬃciency and reduce fabrication cost.\nSpin-coating, one of the cheapest film production methods,\nis widely used in solution-processed perovskite solar cells.\nEvaporation and the convective self-assembly process during\nspinning immediately induce the formation of well-crystallized\nperovskite materials due to strong ionic interactions between the\nmetal cations and halogen anions. Generally, γ-butyrolactone\n(GBL),\nN,N-dimethylformamide,\nDMSO\nand\nN-methyl-2-\npyrrolidone are used as eﬀective solvents for lead halides and\nMAI. However, simple spin-coating did not yield a homogeneous\nperovskite layer having uniform thickness over a large area20,\nalthough the convective spreading flow due to centrifugal force was\napplied to the slowly evaporating solvents. Previously, we reported\nthe formation of a pillared structure with an island-type upper\nlayer10, and proposed the importance of a homogeneous upper\nlayer on the mp-TiO2 base; however, we were unable to deposit\nuniform thin films by the solution process. Furthermore, it was\nreported that the uniformity of the perovskite films depended on\nthe thickness of the TiO2 compact layer, and modification of the\nspinning conditions could not achieve 100% surface coverage20.\nThis limited the applicability of the solution process.\nHere, we report the solution-process fabrication of eﬃcient\nperovskite solar cells comprising a bilayer architecture and\nMAPb(I1−xBrx)3 perovskites formed by a solvent-engineering\ntechnology. The MAPb(I1−xBrx)3 perovskite composition was used\nbecause the substitution of 10–15 mol% Br−for I−in MAPbI3\ngreatly improved the stability in ambient atmosphere, and the\ndual halide material demonstrated similar performance over the\ncompositional range13. When the perovskite was deposited using\na mixture of GBL and DMSO, followed by a toluene drip while\nspinning, extremely uniform and dense layers were formed. This\nsolvent-engineering technology enabled a fully solution-processed\nperovskite solar cell with a certified 16.2% power-conversion\neﬃciency under standard reporting conditions.\nFigure 1 presents a schematic diagram of the cell architecture and\ndeposition of perovskite materials by the solvent-engineering tech-\nnology by means of spin-coating, as well as X-ray diﬀraction (XRD)\npatterns of the resulting coatings. PUBLISHED ONLINE: 6 JULY 2014 | DOI: 10.1038/NMAT4014
Solvent engineering for high-performance
inorganic–organic hybrid perovskite solar cells
Nam Joong Jeon1†, Jun Hong Noh1†, Young Chan Kim1, Woon Seok Yang1, Seungchan Ryu1
and Sang Il Seok1,2*
Organolead trihalide perovskite materials have been successfully used as light absorbers in eﬃcient photovoltaic cells. Two
diﬀerent cell structures, based on mesoscopic metal oxides and planar heterojunctions have already demonstrated very
impressive advances in performance. Here, we report a bilayer architecture comprising the key features of mesoscopic and
planar structures obtained by a fully solution-based process. We used CH3NH3 Pb(I1−xBrx)3 (x=0.1–0.15) as the absorbing layer
and poly(triarylamine) as a hole-transporting material. The use of a mixed solvent of γ-butyrolactone and dimethylsulphoxide
(DMSO) followed by toluene drop-casting leads to extremely uniform and dense perovskite layers via a CH3NH3I–PbI2–DMSO
intermediate phase, and enables the fabrication of remarkably improved solar cells with a certiﬁed power-conversion eﬃciency
of 16.2% and no hysteresis. These results provide important progress towards the understanding of the role of solution-
processing in the realization of low-cost and highly eﬃcient perovskite solar cells.
T
oday, crystalline silicon dominates the solar panel industry
but remains relatively expensive to manufacture. If devices
could be fabricated from cheap materials by a simple solution
process without annealing at high temperature, their costs could
be considerably reduced through mass production. Although
dye-sensitized1, quantum dot2,3, organic4,5, and inorganic–organic
heterojunction solar cells6,7 can be fabricated by multiple or single
solution processes, the cells still suﬀer from problems such as a
lack of long-term stability and low conversion eﬃciency due to
fundamental energy losses associated with the extensive interface
for charge separation. Recently, methylammonium lead halide
(MAPbX3, where MA is methylammonium CH3NH3 and X is a
halogen) perovskites8–16 have oﬀered the promise of a breakthrough
for next-generation solar devices. The use of perovskites aﬀords
several advantages: excellent optical properties that are tunable by
managing chemical compositions13; ambipolar charge transport10;
and very long electron–hole diﬀusion lengths17,18. Perovskite
materials have been applied as light absorbers to thin or thick
mesoscopic metal oxides and planar heterojunction solar devices.
For example, when MAPbI3 was loaded on a mesoporous
(mp)-TiO2 electrode by the sequential deposition of PbI2 and
methylammonium iodide (MAI), a 15.0% power-conversion
eﬃciency (PCE) was achieved under 1 sun illumination11. The
authors of ref. 12 reported a maximum performance of 15.4%
eﬃciency with an open-circuit voltage (Voc) of 1.07 V and short-
circuit current density (Jsc) of 21.5 mA cm−2, based on uniform
MAPbI3−xClx planar thin layers deposited by the vacuum thermal
evaporation method without the mp-TiO2 electrode. Several other
groups also reported eﬃcient planar solar cells, based on normal
organic photovoltaic structure12,19. Although very impressive cell
eﬃciencies have been achieved, the cell architecture, use of vacuum,
or the two-step deposition process should be modified to improve
eﬃciency and reduce fabrication cost.
Spin-coating, one of the cheapest film production methods,
is widely used in solution-processed perovskite solar cells.
Evaporation and the convective self-assembly process during
spinning immediately induce the formation of well-crystallized
perovskite materials due to strong ionic interactions between the
metal cations and halogen anions. Generally, γ-butyrolactone
(GBL),
N,N-dimethylformamide,
DMSO
and
N-methyl-2-
pyrrolidone are used as eﬀective solvents for lead halides and
MAI. However, simple spin-coating did not yield a homogeneous
perovskite layer having uniform thickness over a large area20,
although the convective spreading flow due to centrifugal force was
applied to the slowly evaporating solvents. Previously, we reported
the formation of a pillared structure with an island-type upper
layer10, and proposed the importance of a homogeneous upper
layer on the mp-TiO2 base; however, we were unable to deposit
uniform thin films by the solution process. Furthermore, it was
reported that the uniformity of the perovskite films depended on
the thickness of the TiO2 compact layer, and modification of the
spinning conditions could not achieve 100% surface coverage20.
This limited the applicability of the solution process.
Here, we report the solution-process fabrication of eﬃcient
perovskite solar cells comprising a bilayer architecture and
MAPb(I1−xBrx)3 perovskites formed by a solvent-engineering
technology. The MAPb(I1−xBrx)3 perovskite composition was used
because the substitution of 10–15 mol% Br−for I−in MAPbI3
greatly improved the stability in ambient atmosphere, and the
dual halide material demonstrated similar performance over the
compositional range13. When the perovskite was deposited using
a mixture of GBL and DMSO, followed by a toluene drip while
spinning, extremely uniform and dense layers were formed. This
solvent-engineering technology enabled a fully solution-processed
perovskite solar cell with a certified 16.2% power-conversion
eﬃciency under standard reporting conditions.

deposition of perovskite materials by the solvent-engineering tech-
nology by means of spin-coating, as well as X-ray diﬀraction (XRD)

reveals a bilayer structure comprising mesoscopic and planar struc-
tures, and is eﬀective for suﬃciently absorbing light and collecting
charges. Atop the mp-TiO2 layer lies a highly uniform perovskite
active layer (100–300 nm thick). Poly(triarylamine) (PTAA) and Au
metal were next deposited on the active layer as a hole-transporting
material and photocathode, respectively. For this architecture, the
formation of a homogeneous thin perovskite layer is extremely
important, and we developed our solvent-engineering technology as
an eﬀective tool for creating such a layer. The process involves five
stages, as depicted in Fig. 1c. First, a mixture of MAI, MABr, PbI2,
PbBr2, GBL and DMSO in the appropriate ratio is spread over the
entire surface of the substrate. Second, the spin-coater is accelerated
to the desired rotational speed and maintained there for several
tens of seconds to evaporate the solvent. Third, a solvent that does
not dissolve the perovskite materials and is miscible with DMSO
and GBL (for example, toluene or chloroform) is dripped on the
substrate during spinning. Fourth, all constituents are frozen into
a uniform layer on the removal of the residual DMSO and then
a new complex as an intermediate phase is formed (see below).
Finally, the complex is converted into highly uniform and crystalline
perovskite on annealing at 100 ◦C for 10 min (Fig. 1b). As is apparent
from Supplementary Fig. 1, the morphology of the perovskite thin
layer is markedly changed by this solvent-engineering process, as
compared with model systems on quartz substrate. In pure GBL,
the perovskite crystals formed immediately, and the colour of the
film on the substrate changed to dark hazy brown during rotation
at 5,000 r.p.m, regardless of the application of the toluene drip. The
resulting morphology appears as inhomogeneous islands with low
coverage on the substrate (Supplementary Fig. 1a). In contrast, in
the DMSO and GBL mixed solvent, the colour change to dark brown
is not observed during spin-coating, even after 5 min rotation. The
spin-coated layer formed with the solvent mixture followed by the
toluene drip is extremely uniform and transparent, and covers the
full surface with low surface roughness. Without the toluene drip
treatment, the resulting material adopts a textile-like inhomoge-
neous layer that does not fully cover the substrate, and perovskite
crystals are formed from the coating after annealing at 100 ◦C
(Supplementary Fig. 1b). Here, the crystallinity of the perovskite
films is almost the same regardless of the toluene drop-casting, as
can be seen in values of full-width at half-maximum of (110) XRD
peaks of Supplementary Fig. 2. Therefore, the solvent-engineering
technique is critically important for this process.
To gain further insight into the mixed-solvent application and
subsequent toluene drip treatment, we isolated the intermediate
phase formed by pouring MAI and PbI2 dissolved in GBL and
DMSO into toluene. In this experiment, we excluded the doping
of MABr and PbBr2 to simplify our analysis. The XRD profiles
shown in Fig. 2a imply that the resultant intermediate phase is self-
organized and highly crystalline in nature. Therefore, we think that
the phase formed on toluene drop-casting in step 3 of Fig. 1c has
a well-developed crystalline form. To get further information for
the phase, we compared it with the XRD patterns for PbI2, MAI
and PbI2(DMSO)2, because the constituents in the mixed solvent
can be simply precipitated in the non-dissolving solvent. Here, PbI2
as a layered semiconductor material contains a plane of Pb ions
sandwiched between adjacent layers of hexagonally arranged iodide
ions. The interlayer spaces allow rapid intercalation of diﬀerent
guest molecules owing to the weak bonding between the two planes
by van der Waals-type interactions, leading to the expansion of the
interlayer distance along the c axis21. It was known that the DMSO
used as a solvent in this work can coordinate with lead halide to
form a PbI2(DMSO)2 complex22. However, as can be seen in the
figure, the isolated powder is a new and unreported compound
that cannot be assigned to reported materials, and is related to
the intermediate phase formed during perovskite deposition from
DMSO and GBL. Thus, we considered a MAI–PbI2–DMSO complex
as a possible crystalline compound that can be formed from

On the basis of the above observations, we propose a plausible
mechanism for the formation of the uniform and dense perovskite
layer during spin-coating from MAI, PbI2 and DMSO with a toluene
drip treatment. As shown in Fig. 2d, at the initial stage during
spinning, the film is composed of MAI and PbI2 dissolved in the
DMSO/GBL solvent mixture, whereas in the intermediate stage,
the composition of the film is concentrated by the evaporation of
GBL. Then the toluene droplets lead to the immediate freezing of
the constituents on spinning via the quick removal of the excess
DMSO solvent and the rapid formation of the MAI–PbI2–DMSO
phase, leaving a uniform and transparent thin layer (Supplementary
Fig. 1d). The role of DMSO in the MAI–PbI2–DMSO phase is
to retard the rapid reaction between PbI2 and MAI during the
evaporation of solvent in the spin-coating process. Finally, the
extremely homogeneous flat film (shown in Fig. 3a) is converted
into a pure crystalline MAPbI3 perovskite layer after annealing at
100 ◦C. In this process, the key material is the flat film consisting
of MAI–PbI2–DMSO. These behaviours do not change by using the
mixed-halide materials, MAPb(I1−xBrx)3 (x =0.1–0.15).
Accordingly, the formation of the intermediate phase is a critical
factor for smoothing the surface via dropwise toluene application,
which finally results in compact and uniform thin layers. Figure 3
illustrates images obtained by atomic force microscopy (AFM)
for the intermediate film and the perovskite film on fused silica
substrate, and field-emission scanning electron microscopy (SEM)
images of the surface of the perovskite upper layer and the cross-
section of a representative cell formed by our solvent-engineering
technology. As can be seen in the three-dimensional AFM images
and topography of Fig. 3a,b, the root mean square roughness
values for the intermediate phase and crystalline perovskite layer
are 6.0 and 8.3 nm, respectively, even though the formation of
the perovskite from the intermediate layer gave slightly increased
roughness. In Fig. 3c, we can observe that the surface exhibits a
dense-grained uniform morphology with grain sizes in the range
100–500 nm. The entire film is composed of a homogeneous, well-
crystallized perovskite layer. In addition, from a typical cross-
sectional SEM image of a real device, we can see two uniform
layers consisting of a TiO2/perovskite nanocomposite and the pure
perovskite (Fig. 3d); the perovskite materials are fully infiltrated into
the pores of the mp-TiO2 film, and also deposited in a very uniform
thick film with 100% surface coverage atop the mp-TiO2, compared
with the conventional method10,11.

harvester must be thick enough to absorb suﬃcient incident
light. Fortunately, the high absorption coeﬃcient (Supplementary
Fig. 4) of a perovskite light absorber film allows the use of
very thin layers (∼330 nm thick) to absorb the entire range
of visible light. Indeed, the authors of ref. 12 fabricated a
highly eﬃcient thin solar cell exceeding 15% eﬃciency with a
perovskite absorber (MAPbI1−xClx) of ∼300 nm without mp-TiO2,
and reported that the MAPbI1−xClx perovskite had a long diﬀusion

time was long. Furthermore, the average eﬃciency from the reverse
and forward scans continued to decline with increasing delay time.

are 15.8 and 15.9% with an average of 15.85%, clearly showing the
reliability of the I–V measurements. Generally, the average value
of the eﬃciency, determined from the forward and reverse scans
should be widely accepted when the scanning delay time is longer
than 40 ms (ref. 23), because an excessively long time to complete
the measurement is impractical.

parameters on both scan directions, we investigated the diﬀerence
between the forward and reverse scans for a 40 ms scan time
as a function of the thickness of the mp-TiO2 layer. As the
layer thickness increased to ∼200 nm, the diﬀerence in eﬃciency
between the forward and reverse scans reached a minimum, and
then again deviated slightly with continuing mp-TiO2 thickness

reproducibility. a, J–V curves for the best cell measured by forward and
reverse scans, fabricated using a 200-nm-thick mp-TiO2 layer. The average

reverse scan did not vary greatly with the mp-TiO2 thickness,
whereas the forward scan yielded a pronounced variation, resulting
in a large discrepancy between the two scan directions. Such
a strong dependence of the measured eﬃciency on the scan
direction with mp-TiO2 thickness suggests that solar cells fabricated
from MAPbX3 perovskite materials operate diﬀerently than other
types of cells such as organic, dye-sensitized, and conventional Si
solar cells. The stepwise increase or decrease in the bias voltage,
corresponding to a reverse or forward scan, respectively, requires
a charge redistribution to reach a new equilibrium state. These
characteristics of perovskite solar cells may be related to the large
diﬀusion capacitance of such cells operating under reverse or
forward biases24. The large capacitance is assumed to be related to
the underestimation in the forward scan and overestimation in the
reverse scan by charging and discharging during the voltage sweep
in the solar cells. In other words, the generated charge (electrons
or holes) may persist in the perovskite owing to the slow charge
collection in the thick perovskite layer, and require significant time
for charge distribution. This would impede a quick response to the
rapid scanning of the applied voltage for the I–V measurements.
Therefore, the slow charge collection via the perovskite material
itself must be improved to eliminate the large discrepancy with scan
direction, and an optimally thick mp-TiO2 layer must be introduced
for eﬃcient charge collection from the perovskite via the large TiO2
interface. Eventually, it will be very important to impart eﬀective
charge collection and light absorption properties through a balance
in the ratios between the perovskite-infiltrated TiO2 layer and the
thin upper layers. Of course, the tendency for discrepancy according
to scan direction can be related to the perovskite composition,
because the exciton diﬀusion length was markedly changed by
doping Cl ions into MAPbI3 (ref. 17).
To further enhance the performance of our cells fabricated
by solvent engineering, we repeated the fabrication procedure
using mp-TiO2 with a thickness of ∼200 nm. The J–V curves
and incident photon-to-current eﬃciency (IPCE) spectrum of the
best performing solar cell are presented in Fig. 5. The average
values from the J–V curves from the reverse and forward scans
(Fig. 5a) exhibited a Jsc of 19.58 mA cm−2, Voc of 1.105 V, and
FF of 76.2%, corresponding to a PCE of 16.5% under standard
AM 1.5 G conditions. The best device also showed a very broad
IPCE plateau of over 80% between 420 and 700 nm, as shown in
Fig. 5b. The Jsc value integrated from the IPCE agreed well with that
measured by I–V. In Fig. 5c a histogram of the average PCEs for
all of the independently fabricated cells contributing to our study is
presented. Around 80% of the cells made using our process exhibited
an overall eﬃciency exceeding of 15% under 1 sun conditions,
proving the conceptual validity of a balanced thickness between
the TiO2 and thin upper layers. In addition, an evaluation of the
available results allows us to conclude that this solvent-engineering
approach provides a simple and eﬀective means for realizing high-
eﬃciency and low-cost perovskite-based solar cells. One of these
devices was certified by the standardized method in a photovoltaics
calibration laboratory, confirming a PCE of 16.2% under AM 1.5 G
full sun (Supplementary Fig. 6).
In summary, we developed a solvent-engineering technology
for the deposition of extremely uniform perovskite layers, and
demonstrated a solution-processed perovskite solar cell with
16.5% PCE under standard conditions (AM 1.5 G radiation,
100 mW cm−2). We proposed a plausible mechanism for the
formation of uniform and dense perovskite layers during the
solvent-engineering process. The formation of a stable MAI(Br)–
PbI2–DMSO phase via an intercalation process during the dropwise
application of a non-dissolving solvent was a decisive factor in
retarding the rapid reaction between MAI(Br) and PbI(Br)2, which
enabled the formation of a highly uniform and dense surface.
Furthermore, we found that thick perovskite cells fabricated without
mp-TiO2 showed a large hysteresis and distortion between reverse
and forward scans, and raised arguments about the estimation
of conversion eﬃciencies for perovskite cells. Hence, the ratio of
the thicknesses of the perovskite-infiltrated mp-TiO2 and the pure
perovskite should be optimized to fabricate eﬃcient perovskite cells
with coincident reverse and forward scans. These results will provide
an eﬀective strategy for forming uniform PbI2-based perovskite
layers through intercalation, and lead to more eﬃcient and cost-
eﬀective inorganic–organic hybrid heterojunction solar cells in
the future.
Methods
Solar cell fabrication. A dense blocking layer of TiO2 (bl-TiO2, ∼70 nm in
thickness) was deposited onto a F-doped SnO2 (FTO, Pilkington, TEC8) substrate
by spray pyrolysis, using a 20 mM titanium diisopropoxide bis(acetylacetonate)
solution (Aldrich) at 450 ◦C to prevent direct contact between the FTO and the
hole-conducting layer. A 200–300-nm-thick mesoporous TiO2 (particle size:
about 50 nm, crystalline phase: anatase) film was spin-coated onto the
bl-TiO2/FTO substrate using home-made pastes14 and calcining at 500 ◦C for 1 h
in air to remove organic components. CH3NH3I (MAI) and CH3NH3Br (MABr)
were first synthesized by reacting 27.86 ml CH3NH2 (40% in methanol, Junsei
Chemical) and 30 ml HI (57 wt% in water, Aldrich) or 44 ml HBr (48 wt% in
water, Aldrich) in a 250 ml round-bottom flask at 0 ◦C for 4 h with stirring,
respectively. The precipitate was recovered by evaporation at 55 ◦C for 1 h. MAI
and MABr were dissolved in ethanol, recrystallized from diethyl ether, and dried
at 60 ◦C in a vacuum oven for 24 h. The prepared MAI and MABr powders, PbI2
(Aldrich) and PbBr2 (Aldrich) for 0.8 M MAPb(I1−xBrx)3 (x =0.1–0.15) solution
were stirred in a mixture of GBL and DMSO (7:3 v/v) at 60 ◦C for 12 h. The
resulting solution was coated onto the mp-TiO2/bl-TiO2/FTO substrate by a
consecutive two-step spin-coating process at 1,000 and 5,000 r.p.m for 10 and
20 s, respectively. During the second spin-coating step, the substrate (around 1 cm
× 1 cm) was treated with toluene drop-casting. A detailed time-rotation profile
for the spin-coating is represented in Supplementary Fig. 1c. The substrate was
dried on a hot plate at 100 ◦C for 10 min. A solution of poly(triarylamine) (15 mg,
PTAA, EM Index, Mw =17,500 g mol−1) in toluene (1.5 ml) was mixed with 15 µl
of a solution of lithium bistrifluoromethanesulphonimidate (170 mg) in

Characterization. The XRD spectra of the prepared films were measured using a
Rigaku SmartLab X-ray diﬀractometer, and in situ XRD experiments of the
powder isolated as an intermediate phase were performed using a Rigaku Ultima
IV with an X-ray tube (Cu Kα, λ=1.5406Å). The elemental analysis (C, H, N
and S) of the complex was performed using a FISONS EA–1108 CHN analyser.
The FTIR spectra (4,000–500 cm−1) were recorded on a Bruker EQUINOX 55
spectrophotometer with samples prepared by the KBr pellet method.
Ultraviolet–visible absorption spectra were recorded on a Shimadzu UV 2550
spectrophotometer in the 200–800 nm wavelength range at room temperature.
AFM was performed using Bruker multimode 8 in ‘tapping’ mode. The IPCE was
measured using a power source (Newport 300 W xenon lamp, 66920) with a
monochromator (Newport Cornerstone 260) and a multimeter (Keithley 2001).
J–V curves were measured using a solar simulator (Newport, Oriel Class A,
91195A) with a source meter (Keithley 2420) at 100 mW cm−2, AM 1.5 G
illumination, and a calibrated Si-reference cell certified by the NREL. The J–V
curves were measured by reverse (forward bias (1.2 V) →short circuit (0 V)) or
forward (short circuit (0 V) →forward bias (1.2 V)) scan. The step voltage was
fixed at 10 mV and the delay time, which is a set delay at each voltage step before
measuring each current, was modulated. J–V curves for all devices were
measured by masking the active area with a metal mask 0.094 cm−2 in area.

engineering for high-performance\ninorganic–organic hybrid perovskite solar cells\nNam Joong Jeon1†, Jun Hong Noh1†, Young Chan Kim1, Woon Seok Yang1, Seungchan Ryu1\nand Sang Il Seok1,2*\nOrganolead trihalide perovskite materials have been successfully used as light absorbers in eﬃcient photovoltaic cells. Two\ndiﬀerent cell structures, based on mesoscopic metal oxides and planar heterojunctions have already demonstrated very\nimpressive advances in performance. Here, we report a bilayer architecture comprising the key features of mesoscopic and\nplanar structures obtained by a fully solution-based process. We used CH3NH3 Pb(I1−xBrx)3 (x=0.1–0.15) as the absorbing layer\nand poly(triarylamine) as a hole-transporting material. The use of a mixed solvent of γ-butyrolactone and dimethylsulphoxide\n(DMSO) followed by toluene drop-casting leads to extremely uniform and dense perovskite layers via a CH3NH3I–PbI2–DMSO\nintermediate phase, and enables the fabrication of remarkably improved solar cells with a certiﬁed power-conversion eﬃciency\nof 16.2% and no hysteresis. These results provide important progress towards the understanding of the role of solution-\nprocessing in the realization of low-cost and highly eﬃcient perovskite solar cells.\nT\noday, crystalline silicon dominates the solar panel industry\nbut remains relatively expensive to manufacture. If devices\ncould be fabricated from cheap materials by a simple solution\nprocess without annealing at high temperature, their costs could\nbe considerably reduced through mass production. Although\ndye-sensitized1, quantum dot2,3, organic4,5, and inorganic–organic\nheterojunction solar cells6,7 can be fabricated by multiple or single\nsolution processes, the cells still suﬀer from problems such as a\nlack of long-term stability and low conversion eﬃciency due to\nfundamental energy losses associated with the extensive interface\nfor charge separation. Recently, methylammonium lead halide\n(MAPbX3, where MA is methylammonium CH3NH3 and X is a\nhalogen) perovskites8–16 have oﬀered the promise of a breakthrough\nfor next-generation solar devices. The use of perovskites aﬀords\nseveral advantages: excellent optical properties that are tunable by\nmanaging chemical compositions13; ambipolar charge transport10;\nand very long electron–hole diﬀusion lengths17,18. Perovskite\nmaterials have been applied as light absorbers to thin or thick\nmesoscopic metal oxides and planar heterojunction solar devices.\nFor example, when MAPbI3 was loaded on a mesoporous\n(mp)-TiO2 electrode by the sequential deposition of PbI2 and\nmethylammonium iodide (MAI), a 15.0% power-conversion\neﬃciency (PCE) was achieved under 1 sun illumination11. The\nauthors of ref. 12 reported a maximum performance of 15.4%\neﬃciency with an open-circuit voltage (Voc) of 1.07 V and short-\ncircuit current density (Jsc) of 21.5 mA cm−2, based on uniform\nMAPbI3−xClx planar thin layers deposited by the vacuum thermal\nevaporation method without the mp-TiO2 electrode. Several other\ngroups also reported eﬃcient planar solar cells, based on normal\norganic photovoltaic structure12,19. Although very impressive cell\neﬃciencies have been achieved, the cell architecture, use of vacuum,\nor the two-step deposition process should be modified to improve\neﬃciency and reduce fabrication cost.\nSpin-coating, one of the cheapest film production methods,\nis widely used in solution-processed perovskite solar cells.\nEvaporation and the convective self-assembly process during\nspinning immediately induce the formation of well-crystallized\nperovskite materials due to strong ionic interactions between the\nmetal cations and halogen anions. Generally, γ-butyrolactone\n(GBL),\nN,N-dimethylformamide,\nDMSO\nand\nN-methyl-2-\npyrrolidone are used as eﬀective solvents for lead halides and\nMAI. However, simple spin-coating did not yield a homogeneous\nperovskite layer having uniform thickness over a large area20,\nalthough the convective spreading flow due to centrifugal force was\napplied to the slowly evaporating solvents. Previously, we reported\nthe formation of a pillared structure with an island-type upper\nlayer10, and proposed the importance of a homogeneous upper\nlayer on the mp-TiO2 base; however, we were unable to deposit\nuniform thin films by the solution process. Furthermore, it was\nreported that the uniformity of the perovskite films depended on\nthe thickness of the TiO2 compact layer, and modification of the\nspinning conditions could not achieve 100% surface coverage20.\nThis limited the applicability of the solution process.\nHere, we report the solution-process fabrication of eﬃcient\nperovskite solar cells comprising a bilayer architecture and\nMAPb(I1−xBrx)3 perovskites formed by a solvent-engineering\ntechnology. The MAPb(I1−xBrx)3 perovskite composition was used\nbecause the substitution of 10–15 mol% Br−for I−in MAPbI3\ngreatly improved the stability in ambient atmosphere, and the\ndual halide material demonstrated similar performance over the\ncompositional range13. When the perovskite was deposited using\na mixture of GBL and DMSO, followed by a toluene drip while\nspinning, extremely uniform and dense layers were formed. This\nsolvent-engineering technology enabled a fully solution-processed\nperovskite solar cell with a certified 16.2% power-conversion\neﬃciency under standard reporting conditions.\nFigure 1 presents a schematic diagram of the cell architecture and\ndeposition of perovskite materials by the solvent-engineering tech-\nnology by means of spin-coating, as well as X-ray diﬀraction (XRD)\npatterns of the resulting coatings. ARTICLES
PUBLISHED ONLINE: 6 JULY 2014 | DOI: 10.1038/NMAT4014
Solvent engineering for high-performance
inorganic–organic hybrid perovskite solar cells
Nam Joong Jeon1†, Jun Hong Noh1†, Young Chan Kim1, Woon Seok Yang1, Seungchan Ryu1
and Sang Il Seok1,2*
Organolead trihalide perovskite materials have been successfully used as light absorbers in eﬃcient photovoltaic cells. Two
diﬀerent cell structures, based on mesoscopic metal oxides and planar heterojunctions have already demonstrated very
impressive advances in performance. Here, we report a bilayer architecture comprising the key features of mesoscopic and
planar structures obtained by a fully solution-based process. We used CH3NH3 Pb(I1−xBrx)3 (x=0.1–0.15) as the absorbing layer
and poly(triarylamine) as a hole-transporting material. The use of a mixed solvent of γ-butyrolactone and dimethylsulphoxide
(DMSO) followed by toluene drop-casting leads to extremely uniform and dense perovskite layers via a CH3NH3I–PbI2–DMSO
intermediate phase, and enables the fabrication of remarkably improved solar cells with a certiﬁed power-conversion eﬃciency
of 16.2% and no hysteresis. These results provide important progress towards the understanding of the role of solution-
processing in the realization of low-cost and highly eﬃcient perovskite solar cells.
T
oday, crystalline silicon dominates the solar panel industry
but remains relatively expensive to manufacture. If devices
could be fabricated from cheap materials by a simple solution
process without annealing at high temperature, their costs could
be considerably reduced through mass production. Although
dye-sensitized1, quantum dot2,3, organic4,5, and inorganic–organic
heterojunction solar cells6,7 can be fabricated by multiple or single
solution processes, the cells still suﬀer from problems such as a
lack of long-term stability and low conversion eﬃciency due to
fundamental energy losses associated with the extensive interface
for charge separation. Recently, methylammonium lead halide
(MAPbX3, where MA is methylammonium CH3NH3 and X is a
halogen) perovskites8–16 have oﬀered the promise of a breakthrough
for next-generation solar devices. The use of perovskites aﬀords
several advantages: excellent optical properties that are tunable by
managing chemical compositions13; ambipolar charge transport10;
and very long electron–hole diﬀusion lengths17,18. Perovskite
materials have been applied as light absorbers to thin or thick
mesoscopic metal oxides and planar heterojunction solar devices.
For example, when MAPbI3 was loaded on a mesoporous
(mp)-TiO2 electrode by the sequential deposition of PbI2 and
methylammonium iodide (MAI), a 15.0% power-conversion
eﬃciency (PCE) was achieved under 1 sun illumination11. The
authors of ref. 12 reported a maximum performance of 15.4%
eﬃciency with an open-circuit voltage (Voc) of 1.07 V and short-
circuit current density (Jsc) of 21.5 mA cm−2, based on uniform
MAPbI3−xClx planar thin layers deposited by the vacuum thermal
evaporation method without the mp-TiO2 electrode. Several other
groups also reported eﬃcient planar solar cells, based on normal
organic photovoltaic structure12,19. Although very impressive cell
eﬃciencies have been achieved, the cell architecture, use of vacuum,
or the two-step deposition process should be modified to improve
eﬃciency and reduce fabrication cost.
Spin-coating, one of the cheapest film production methods,
is widely used in solution-processed perovskite solar cells.
Evaporation and the convective self-assembly process during
spinning immediately induce the formation of well-crystallized
perovskite materials due to strong ionic interactions between the
metal cations and halogen anions. Generally, γ-butyrolactone
(GBL),
N,N-dimethylformamide,
DMSO
and
N-methyl-2-
pyrrolidone are used as eﬀective solvents for lead halides and
MAI. However, simple spin-coating did not yield a homogeneous
perovskite layer having uniform thickness over a large area20,
although the convective spreading flow due to centrifugal force was
applied to the slowly evaporating solvents. Previously, we reported
the formation of a pillared structure with an island-type upper
layer10, and proposed the importance of a homogeneous upper
layer on the mp-TiO2 base; however, we were unable to deposit
uniform thin films by the solution process. Furthermore, it was
reported that the uniformity of the perovskite films depended on
the thickness of the TiO2 compact layer, and modification of the
spinning conditions could not achieve 100% surface coverage20.
This limited the applicability of the solution process.
Here, we report the solution-process fabrication of eﬃcient
perovskite solar cells comprising a bilayer architecture and
MAPb(I1−xBrx)3 perovskites formed by a solvent-engineering
technology. The MAPb(I1−xBrx)3 perovskite composition was used
because the substitution of 10–15 mol% Br−for I−in MAPbI3
greatly improved the stability in ambient atmosphere, and the
dual halide material demonstrated similar performance over the
compositional range13. When the perovskite was deposited using
a mixture of GBL and DMSO, followed by a toluene drip while
spinning, extremely uniform and dense layers were formed. This
solvent-engineering technology enabled a fully solution-processed
perovskite solar cell with a certified 16.2% power-conversion
eﬃciency under standard reporting conditions.

tures, and is eﬀective for suﬃciently absorbing light and collecting
charges. Atop the mp-TiO2 layer lies a highly uniform perovskite
active layer (100–300 nm thick). Poly(triarylamine) (PTAA) and Au
metal were next deposited on the active layer as a hole-transporting
material and photocathode, respectively. For this architecture, the
formation of a homogeneous thin perovskite layer is extremely
important, and we developed our solvent-engineering technology as
an eﬀective tool for creating such a layer. The process involves five
stages, as depicted in Fig. 1c. First, a mixture of MAI, MABr, PbI2,
PbBr2, GBL and DMSO in the appropriate ratio is spread over the
entire surface of the substrate. Second, the spin-coater is accelerated
to the desired rotational speed and maintained there for several
tens of seconds to evaporate the solvent. Third, a solvent that does
not dissolve the perovskite materials and is miscible with DMSO
and GBL (for example, toluene or chloroform) is dripped on the
substrate during spinning. Fourth, all constituents are frozen into
a uniform layer on the removal of the residual DMSO and then
a new complex as an intermediate phase is formed (see below).
Finally, the complex is converted into highly uniform and crystalline
perovskite on annealing at 100 ◦C for 10 min (Fig. 1b). As is apparent
from Supplementary Fig. 1, the morphology of the perovskite thin
layer is markedly changed by this solvent-engineering process, as
compared with model systems on quartz substrate. In pure GBL,
the perovskite crystals formed immediately, and the colour of the
film on the substrate changed to dark hazy brown during rotation
at 5,000 r.p.m, regardless of the application of the toluene drip. The
resulting morphology appears as inhomogeneous islands with low
coverage on the substrate (Supplementary Fig. 1a). In contrast, in
the DMSO and GBL mixed solvent, the colour change to dark brown
is not observed during spin-coating, even after 5 min rotation. The
spin-coated layer formed with the solvent mixture followed by the
toluene drip is extremely uniform and transparent, and covers the
full surface with low surface roughness. Without the toluene drip
treatment, the resulting material adopts a textile-like inhomoge-
neous layer that does not fully cover the substrate, and perovskite
crystals are formed from the coating after annealing at 100 ◦C
(Supplementary Fig. 1b). Here, the crystallinity of the perovskite
films is almost the same regardless of the toluene drop-casting, as
can be seen in values of full-width at half-maximum of (110) XRD
peaks of Supplementary Fig. 2. Therefore, the solvent-engineering
technique is critically important for this process.

On the basis of the above observations, we propose a plausible
mechanism for the formation of the uniform and dense perovskite
layer during spin-coating from MAI, PbI2 and DMSO with a toluene
drip treatment. As shown in Fig. 2d, at the initial stage during
spinning, the film is composed of MAI and PbI2 dissolved in the
DMSO/GBL solvent mixture, whereas in the intermediate stage,
the composition of the film is concentrated by the evaporation of
GBL. Then the toluene droplets lead to the immediate freezing of
the constituents on spinning via the quick removal of the excess
DMSO solvent and the rapid formation of the MAI–PbI2–DMSO
phase, leaving a uniform and transparent thin layer (Supplementary
Fig. 1d). The role of DMSO in the MAI–PbI2–DMSO phase is
to retard the rapid reaction between PbI2 and MAI during the
evaporation of solvent in the spin-coating process. Finally, the
extremely homogeneous flat film (shown in Fig. 3a) is converted
into a pure crystalline MAPbI3 perovskite layer after annealing at
100 ◦C. In this process, the key material is the flat film consisting
of MAI–PbI2–DMSO. These behaviours do not change by using the
mixed-halide materials, MAPb(I1−xBrx)3 (x =0.1–0.15).
Accordingly, the formation of the intermediate phase is a critical
factor for smoothing the surface via dropwise toluene application,
which finally results in compact and uniform thin layers. Figure 3
illustrates images obtained by atomic force microscopy (AFM)
for the intermediate film and the perovskite film on fused silica
substrate, and field-emission scanning electron microscopy (SEM)
images of the surface of the perovskite upper layer and the cross-
section of a representative cell formed by our solvent-engineering
technology. As can be seen in the three-dimensional AFM images
and topography of Fig. 3a,b, the root mean square roughness
values for the intermediate phase and crystalline perovskite layer
are 6.0 and 8.3 nm, respectively, even though the formation of
the perovskite from the intermediate layer gave slightly increased
roughness. In Fig. 3c, we can observe that the surface exhibits a
dense-grained uniform morphology with grain sizes in the range
100–500 nm. The entire film is composed of a homogeneous, well-
crystallized perovskite layer. In addition, from a typical cross-
sectional SEM image of a real device, we can see two uniform
layers consisting of a TiO2/perovskite nanocomposite and the pure
perovskite (Fig. 3d); the perovskite materials are fully infiltrated into
the pores of the mp-TiO2 film, and also deposited in a very uniform
thick film with 100% surface coverage atop the mp-TiO2, compared
with the conventional method10,11.

whereas the forward scan yielded a pronounced variation, resulting
in a large discrepancy between the two scan directions. Such
a strong dependence of the measured eﬃciency on the scan

types of cells such as organic, dye-sensitized, and conventional Si
