corresponding to a reverse or forward scan, respectively, requires
a charge redistribution to reach a new equilibrium state. These
characteristics of perovskite solar cells may be related to the large
diﬀusion capacitance of such cells operating under reverse or
forward biases24. The large capacitance is assumed to be related to
the underestimation in the forward scan and overestimation in the
reverse scan by charging and discharging during the voltage sweep
in the solar cells. In other words, the generated charge (electrons
or holes) may persist in the perovskite owing to the slow charge
collection in the thick perovskite layer, and require significant time
for charge distribution. This would impede a quick response to the
rapid scanning of the applied voltage for the I–V measurements.
Therefore, the slow charge collection via the perovskite material
itself must be improved to eliminate the large discrepancy with scan
direction, and an optimally thick mp-TiO2 layer must be introduced
for eﬃcient charge collection from the perovskite via the large TiO2
interface. Eventually, it will be very important to impart eﬀective
charge collection and light absorption properties through a balance
in the ratios between the perovskite-infiltrated TiO2 layer and the
thin upper layers. Of course, the tendency for discrepancy according
to scan direction can be related to the perovskite composition,
because the exciton diﬀusion length was markedly changed by
doping Cl ions into MAPbI3 (ref. 17).
To further enhance the performance of our cells fabricated
by solvent engineering, we repeated the fabrication procedure
using mp-TiO2 with a thickness of ∼200 nm. The J–V curves
and incident photon-to-current eﬃciency (IPCE) spectrum of the
best performing solar cell are presented in Fig. 5. The average
values from the J–V curves from the reverse and forward scans
(Fig. 5a) exhibited a Jsc of 19.58 mA cm−2, Voc of 1.105 V, and
FF of 76.2%, corresponding to a PCE of 16.5% under standard
AM 1.5 G conditions. The best device also showed a very broad
IPCE plateau of over 80% between 420 and 700 nm, as shown in
Fig. 5b. The Jsc value integrated from the IPCE agreed well with that
measured by I–V. In Fig. 5c a histogram of the average PCEs for
all of the independently fabricated cells contributing to our study is
presented. Around 80% of the cells made using our process exhibited
an overall eﬃciency exceeding of 15% under 1 sun conditions,
proving the conceptual validity of a balanced thickness between
the TiO2 and thin upper layers. In addition, an evaluation of the
available results allows us to conclude that this solvent-engineering
approach provides a simple and eﬀective means for realizing high-
eﬃciency and low-cost perovskite-based solar cells. One of these
devices was certified by the standardized method in a photovoltaics
calibration laboratory, confirming a PCE of 16.2% under AM 1.5 G
full sun (Supplementary Fig. 6).
In summary, we developed a solvent-engineering technology
for the deposition of extremely uniform perovskite layers, and
demonstrated a solution-processed perovskite solar cell with
16.5% PCE under standard conditions (AM 1.5 G radiation,
100 mW cm−2). We proposed a plausible mechanism for the
formation of uniform and dense perovskite layers during the
solvent-engineering process. The formation of a stable MAI(Br)–
PbI2–DMSO phase via an intercalation process during the dropwise
application of a non-dissolving solvent was a decisive factor in
retarding the rapid reaction between MAI(Br) and PbI(Br)2, which
enabled the formation of a highly uniform and dense surface.
Furthermore, we found that thick perovskite cells fabricated without
mp-TiO2 showed a large hysteresis and distortion between reverse
and forward scans, and raised arguments about the estimation
of conversion eﬃciencies for perovskite cells. Hence, the ratio of
the thicknesses of the perovskite-infiltrated mp-TiO2 and the pure
perovskite should be optimized to fabricate eﬃcient perovskite cells
with coincident reverse and forward scans. These results will provide
an eﬀective strategy for forming uniform PbI2-based perovskite
layers through intercalation, and lead to more eﬃcient and cost-
eﬀective inorganic–organic hybrid heterojunction solar cells in
the future.
Methods
Solar cell fabrication. A dense blocking layer of TiO2 (bl-TiO2, ∼70 nm in
thickness) was deposited onto a F-doped SnO2 (FTO, Pilkington, TEC8) substrate
by spray pyrolysis, using a 20 mM titanium diisopropoxide bis(acetylacetonate)
solution (Aldrich) at 450 ◦C to prevent direct contact between the FTO and the
hole-conducting layer. A 200–300-nm-thick mesoporous TiO2 (particle size:
about 50 nm, crystalline phase: anatase) film was spin-coated onto the
bl-TiO2/FTO substrate using home-made pastes14 and calcining at 500 ◦C for 1 h
in air to remove organic components. CH3NH3I (MAI) and CH3NH3Br (MABr)
were first synthesized by reacting 27.86 ml CH3NH2 (40% in methanol, Junsei
Chemical) and 30 ml HI (57 wt% in water, Aldrich) or 44 ml HBr (48 wt% in
water, Aldrich) in a 250 ml round-bottom flask at 0 ◦C for 4 h with stirring,
respectively. The precipitate was recovered by evaporation at 55 ◦C for 1 h. MAI
and MABr were dissolved in ethanol, recrystallized from diethyl ether, and dried
at 60 ◦C in a vacuum oven for 24 h. The prepared MAI and MABr powders, PbI2
(Aldrich) and PbBr2 (Aldrich) for 0.8 M MAPb(I1−xBrx)3 (x =0.1–0.15) solution
were stirred in a mixture of GBL and DMSO (7:3 v/v) at 60 ◦C for 12 h. The
resulting solution was coated onto the mp-TiO2/bl-TiO2/FTO substrate by a
consecutive two-step spin-coating process at 1,000 and 5,000 r.p.m for 10 and
20 s, respectively. During the second spin-coating step, the substrate (around 1 cm
× 1 cm) was treated with toluene drop-casting. A detailed time-rotation profile
for the spin-coating is represented in Supplementary Fig. 1c. The substrate was
dried on a hot plate at 100 ◦C for 10 min. A solution of poly(triarylamine) (15 mg,
PTAA, EM Index, Mw =17,500 g mol−1) in toluene (1.5 ml) was mixed with 15 µl
of a solution of lithium bistrifluoromethanesulphonimidate (170 mg) in

Characterization. The XRD spectra of the prepared films were measured using a
Rigaku SmartLab X-ray diﬀractometer, and in situ XRD experiments of the
powder isolated as an intermediate phase were performed using a Rigaku Ultima
IV with an X-ray tube (Cu Kα, λ=1.5406Å). The elemental analysis (C, H, N
and S) of the complex was performed using a FISONS EA–1108 CHN analyser.
The FTIR spectra (4,000–500 cm−1) were recorded on a Bruker EQUINOX 55
spectrophotometer with samples prepared by the KBr pellet method.
Ultraviolet–visible absorption spectra were recorded on a Shimadzu UV 2550
spectrophotometer in the 200–800 nm wavelength range at room temperature.
AFM was performed using Bruker multimode 8 in ‘tapping’ mode. The IPCE was
measured using a power source (Newport 300 W xenon lamp, 66920) with a
monochromator (Newport Cornerstone 260) and a multimeter (Keithley 2001).
J–V curves were measured using a solar simulator (Newport, Oriel Class A,
91195A) with a source meter (Keithley 2420) at 100 mW cm−2, AM 1.5 G
illumination, and a calibrated Si-reference cell certified by the NREL. The J–V
curves were measured by reverse (forward bias (1.2 V) →short circuit (0 V)) or
forward (short circuit (0 V) →forward bias (1.2 V)) scan. The step voltage was
fixed at 10 mV and the delay time, which is a set delay at each voltage step before
measuring each current, was modulated. J–V curves for all devices were
measured by masking the active area with a metal mask 0.094 cm−2 in area.

PUBLISHED ONLINE: 6 JULY 2014 | DOI: 10.1038/NMAT4014
Solvent engineering for high-performance
inorganic–organic hybrid perovskite solar cells
Nam Joong Jeon1†, Jun Hong Noh1†, Young Chan Kim1, Woon Seok Yang1, Seungchan Ryu1
and Sang Il Seok1,2*
Organolead trihalide perovskite materials have been successfully used as light absorbers in eﬃcient photovoltaic cells. Two
diﬀerent cell structures, based on mesoscopic metal oxides and planar heterojunctions have already demonstrated very
impressive advances in performance. Here, we report a bilayer architecture comprising the key features of mesoscopic and
planar structures obtained by a fully solution-based process. We used CH3NH3 Pb(I1−xBrx)3 (x=0.1–0.15) as the absorbing layer
and poly(triarylamine) as a hole-transporting material. The use of a mixed solvent of γ-butyrolactone and dimethylsulphoxide
(DMSO) followed by toluene drop-casting leads to extremely uniform and dense perovskite layers via a CH3NH3I–PbI2–DMSO
intermediate phase, and enables the fabrication of remarkably improved solar cells with a certiﬁed power-conversion eﬃciency
of 16.2% and no hysteresis. These results provide important progress towards the understanding of the role of solution-
processing in the realization of low-cost and highly eﬃcient perovskite solar cells.
T
oday, crystalline silicon dominates the solar panel industry
but remains relatively expensive to manufacture. If devices
could be fabricated from cheap materials by a simple solution
process without annealing at high temperature, their costs could
be considerably reduced through mass production. Although
dye-sensitized1, quantum dot2,3, organic4,5, and inorganic–organic
heterojunction solar cells6,7 can be fabricated by multiple or single
solution processes, the cells still suﬀer from problems such as a
lack of long-term stability and low conversion eﬃciency due to
fundamental energy losses associated with the extensive interface
for charge separation. Recently, methylammonium lead halide
(MAPbX3, where MA is methylammonium CH3NH3 and X is a
halogen) perovskites8–16 have oﬀered the promise of a breakthrough
for next-generation solar devices. The use of perovskites aﬀords
several advantages: excellent optical properties that are tunable by
managing chemical compositions13; ambipolar charge transport10;
and very long electron–hole diﬀusion lengths17,18. Perovskite
materials have been applied as light absorbers to thin or thick
mesoscopic metal oxides and planar heterojunction solar devices.
For example, when MAPbI3 was loaded on a mesoporous
(mp)-TiO2 electrode by the sequential deposition of PbI2 and
methylammonium iodide (MAI), a 15.0% power-conversion
eﬃciency (PCE) was achieved under 1 sun illumination11. The
authors of ref. 12 reported a maximum performance of 15.4%
eﬃciency with an open-circuit voltage (Voc) of 1.07 V and short-
circuit current density (Jsc) of 21.5 mA cm−2, based on uniform
MAPbI3−xClx planar thin layers deposited by the vacuum thermal
evaporation method without the mp-TiO2 electrode. Several other
groups also reported eﬃcient planar solar cells, based on normal
organic photovoltaic structure12,19. Although very impressive cell
eﬃciencies have been achieved, the cell architecture, use of vacuum,
or the two-step deposition process should be modified to improve
eﬃciency and reduce fabrication cost.
Spin-coating, one of the cheapest film production methods,
is widely used in solution-processed perovskite solar cells.
Evaporation and the convective self-assembly process during
spinning immediately induce the formation of well-crystallized
perovskite materials due to strong ionic interactions between the
metal cations and halogen anions. Generally, γ-butyrolactone
(GBL),
N,N-dimethylformamide,
DMSO
and
N-methyl-2-
pyrrolidone are used as eﬀective solvents for lead halides and
MAI. However, simple spin-coating did not yield a homogeneous
perovskite layer having uniform thickness over a large area20,
although the convective spreading flow due to centrifugal force was
applied to the slowly evaporating solvents. Previously, we reported
the formation of a pillared structure with an island-type upper
layer10, and proposed the importance of a homogeneous upper
layer on the mp-TiO2 base; however, we were unable to deposit
uniform thin films by the solution process. Furthermore, it was
reported that the uniformity of the perovskite films depended on
the thickness of the TiO2 compact layer, and modification of the
spinning conditions could not achieve 100% surface coverage20.
This limited the applicability of the solution process.
Here, we report the solution-process fabrication of eﬃcient
perovskite solar cells comprising a bilayer architecture and
MAPb(I1−xBrx)3 perovskites formed by a solvent-engineering
technology. The MAPb(I1−xBrx)3 perovskite composition was used
because the substitution of 10–15 mol% Br−for I−in MAPbI3
greatly improved the stability in ambient atmosphere, and the
dual halide material demonstrated similar performance over the
compositional range13. When the perovskite was deposited using
a mixture of GBL and DMSO, followed by a toluene drip while
spinning, extremely uniform and dense layers were formed. This
solvent-engineering technology enabled a fully solution-processed
perovskite solar cell with a certified 16.2% power-conversion
eﬃciency under standard reporting conditions.
Figure 1 presents a schematic diagram of the cell architecture and
deposition of perovskite materials by the solvent-engineering tech-
nology by means of spin-coating, as well as X-ray diﬀraction (XRD)
patterns of the resulting coatings. The cell architecture (Fig. 1a)

Figure 1 | Device architecture, scheme of solvent engineering process, and XRD of perovskite layer. a, Device architecture of the bilayered perovskite
solar cell (glass/FTO/bl-TiO2/mp-TiO2-perovskite nanocomposite layer/perovskite upper layer/PTAA/Au). b, XRD pattern of the annealed perovskite
coating on fused silica substrate. The inset shows a SEM image of a surface consisting of a glass/FTO/bl-TiO2/mp-TiO2-perovskite nanocomposite
layer/perovskite upper layer. c, Solvent engineering procedure for preparing the uniform and dense perovskite ﬁlm.
reveals a bilayer structure comprising mesoscopic and planar struc-
tures, and is eﬀective for suﬃciently absorbing light and collecting
charges. Atop the mp-TiO2 layer lies a highly uniform perovskite
active layer (100–300 nm thick). Poly(triarylamine) (PTAA) and Au
metal were next deposited on the active layer as a hole-transporting
material and photocathode, respectively. For this architecture, the
formation of a homogeneous thin perovskite layer is extremely
important, and we developed our solvent-engineering technology as
an eﬀective tool for creating such a layer. The process involves five
stages, as depicted in Fig. 1c. First, a mixture of MAI, MABr, PbI2,
PbBr2, GBL and DMSO in the appropriate ratio is spread over the
entire surface of the substrate. Second, the spin-coater is accelerated
to the desired rotational speed and maintained there for several
tens of seconds to evaporate the solvent. Third, a solvent that does
not dissolve the perovskite materials and is miscible with DMSO
and GBL (for example, toluene or chloroform) is dripped on the
substrate during spinning. Fourth, all constituents are frozen into
a uniform layer on the removal of the residual DMSO and then
a new complex as an intermediate phase is formed (see below).
Finally, the complex is converted into highly uniform and crystalline
perovskite on annealing at 100 ◦C for 10 min (Fig. 1b). As is apparent
from Supplementary Fig. 1, the morphology of the perovskite thin
layer is markedly changed by this solvent-engineering process, as
compared with model systems on quartz substrate. In pure GBL,
the perovskite crystals formed immediately, and the colour of the
film on the substrate changed to dark hazy brown during rotation
at 5,000 r.p.m, regardless of the application of the toluene drip. The
resulting morphology appears as inhomogeneous islands with low
coverage on the substrate (Supplementary Fig. 1a). In contrast, in
the DMSO and GBL mixed solvent, the colour change to dark brown
is not observed during spin-coating, even after 5 min rotation. The
spin-coated layer formed with the solvent mixture followed by the
toluene drip is extremely uniform and transparent, and covers the
full surface with low surface roughness. Without the toluene drip
treatment, the resulting material adopts a textile-like inhomoge-
neous layer that does not fully cover the substrate, and perovskite
crystals are formed from the coating after annealing at 100 ◦C
(Supplementary Fig. 1b). Here, the crystallinity of the perovskite
films is almost the same regardless of the toluene drop-casting, as
can be seen in values of full-width at half-maximum of (110) XRD
peaks of Supplementary Fig. 2. Therefore, the solvent-engineering
technique is critically important for this process.
To gain further insight into the mixed-solvent application and
subsequent toluene drip treatment, we isolated the intermediate
phase formed by pouring MAI and PbI2 dissolved in GBL and
DMSO into toluene. In this experiment, we excluded the doping
of MABr and PbBr2 to simplify our analysis. The XRD profiles
shown in Fig. 2a imply that the resultant intermediate phase is self-
organized and highly crystalline in nature. Therefore, we think that
the phase formed on toluene drop-casting in step 3 of Fig. 1c has
a well-developed crystalline form. To get further information for
the phase, we compared it with the XRD patterns for PbI2, MAI
and PbI2(DMSO)2, because the constituents in the mixed solvent
can be simply precipitated in the non-dissolving solvent. Here, PbI2
as a layered semiconductor material contains a plane of Pb ions
sandwiched between adjacent layers of hexagonally arranged iodide
ions. The interlayer spaces allow rapid intercalation of diﬀerent
guest molecules owing to the weak bonding between the two planes
by van der Waals-type interactions, leading to the expansion of the
interlayer distance along the c axis21. It was known that the DMSO
used as a solvent in this work can coordinate with lead halide to
form a PbI2(DMSO)2 complex22. However, as can be seen in the
figure, the isolated powder is a new and unreported compound
that cannot be assigned to reported materials, and is related to
the intermediate phase formed during perovskite deposition from
DMSO and GBL. Thus, we considered a MAI–PbI2–DMSO complex
as a possible crystalline compound that can be formed from
the solution mixture. In the DMSO and GBL solution mixture,

On the basis of the above observations, we propose a plausible
mechanism for the formation of the uniform and dense perovskite
layer during spin-coating from MAI, PbI2 and DMSO with a toluene
drip treatment. As shown in Fig. 2d, at the initial stage during
spinning, the film is composed of MAI and PbI2 dissolved in the
DMSO/GBL solvent mixture, whereas in the intermediate stage,
the composition of the film is concentrated by the evaporation of
GBL. Then the toluene droplets lead to the immediate freezing of
the constituents on spinning via the quick removal of the excess
DMSO solvent and the rapid formation of the MAI–PbI2–DMSO
phase, leaving a uniform and transparent thin layer (Supplementary
Fig. 1d). The role of DMSO in the MAI–PbI2–DMSO phase is
to retard the rapid reaction between PbI2 and MAI during the
evaporation of solvent in the spin-coating process. Finally, the
extremely homogeneous flat film (shown in Fig. 3a) is converted
into a pure crystalline MAPbI3 perovskite layer after annealing at
100 ◦C. In this process, the key material is the flat film consisting
of MAI–PbI2–DMSO. These behaviours do not change by using the
mixed-halide materials, MAPb(I1−xBrx)3 (x =0.1–0.15).
Accordingly, the formation of the intermediate phase is a critical
factor for smoothing the surface via dropwise toluene application,
which finally results in compact and uniform thin layers. Figure 3
illustrates images obtained by atomic force microscopy (AFM)
for the intermediate film and the perovskite film on fused silica
substrate, and field-emission scanning electron microscopy (SEM)
images of the surface of the perovskite upper layer and the cross-
section of a representative cell formed by our solvent-engineering
technology. As can be seen in the three-dimensional AFM images
and topography of Fig. 3a,b, the root mean square roughness
values for the intermediate phase and crystalline perovskite layer
are 6.0 and 8.3 nm, respectively, even though the formation of
the perovskite from the intermediate layer gave slightly increased
roughness. In Fig. 3c, we can observe that the surface exhibits a
dense-grained uniform morphology with grain sizes in the range
100–500 nm. The entire film is composed of a homogeneous, well-
crystallized perovskite layer. In addition, from a typical cross-
sectional SEM image of a real device, we can see two uniform
layers consisting of a TiO2/perovskite nanocomposite and the pure
perovskite (Fig. 3d); the perovskite materials are fully infiltrated into
the pores of the mp-TiO2 film, and also deposited in a very uniform
thick film with 100% surface coverage atop the mp-TiO2, compared
with the conventional method10,11.

reverse scan did not vary greatly with the mp-TiO2 thickness,
whereas the forward scan yielded a pronounced variation, resulting
in a large discrepancy between the two scan directions. Such
a strong dependence of the measured eﬃciency on the scan
direction with mp-TiO2 thickness suggests that solar cells fabricated
from MAPbX3 perovskite materials operate diﬀerently than other
types of cells such as organic, dye-sensitized, and conventional Si
solar cells. The stepwise increase or decrease in the bias voltage,
corresponding to a reverse or forward scan, respectively, requires
a charge redistribution to reach a new equilibrium state. These
characteristics of perovskite solar cells may be related to the large
diﬀusion capacitance of such cells operating under reverse or
forward biases24. The large capacitance is assumed to be related to
the underestimation in the forward scan and overestimation in the
reverse scan by charging and discharging during the voltage sweep
in the solar cells. In other words, the generated charge (electrons
or holes) may persist in the perovskite owing to the slow charge
collection in the thick perovskite layer, and require significant time
for charge distribution. This would impede a quick response to the
rapid scanning of the applied voltage for the I–V measurements.
Therefore, the slow charge collection via the perovskite material
itself must be improved to eliminate the large discrepancy with scan
direction, and an optimally thick mp-TiO2 layer must be introduced
for eﬃcient charge collection from the perovskite via the large TiO2
interface. Eventually, it will be very important to impart eﬀective
charge collection and light absorption properties through a balance
in the ratios between the perovskite-infiltrated TiO2 layer and the
thin upper layers. Of course, the tendency for discrepancy according
to scan direction can be related to the perovskite composition,
because the exciton diﬀusion length was markedly changed by
doping Cl ions into MAPbI3 (ref. 17).
To further enhance the performance of our cells fabricated
by solvent engineering, we repeated the fabrication procedure
using mp-TiO2 with a thickness of ∼200 nm. The J–V curves
and incident photon-to-current eﬃciency (IPCE) spectrum of the
best performing solar cell are presented in Fig. 5. The average
values from the J–V curves from the reverse and forward scans
(Fig. 5a) exhibited a Jsc of 19.58 mA cm−2, Voc of 1.105 V, and
FF of 76.2%, corresponding to a PCE of 16.5% under standard
AM 1.5 G conditions. The best device also showed a very broad
IPCE plateau of over 80% between 420 and 700 nm, as shown in
Fig. 5b. The Jsc value integrated from the IPCE agreed well with that
measured by I–V. In Fig. 5c a histogram of the average PCEs for
all of the independently fabricated cells contributing to our study is
presented. Around 80% of the cells made using our process exhibited
an overall eﬃciency exceeding of 15% under 1 sun conditions,
proving the conceptual validity of a balanced thickness between
the TiO2 and thin upper layers. In addition, an evaluation of the
available results allows us to conclude that this solvent-engineering
approach provides a simple and eﬀective means for realizing high-
eﬃciency and low-cost perovskite-based solar cells. One of these
devices was certified by the standardized method in a photovoltaics
calibration laboratory, confirming a PCE of 16.2% under AM 1.5 G
full sun (Supplementary Fig. 6).
In summary, we developed a solvent-engineering technology
for the deposition of extremely uniform perovskite layers, and
demonstrated a solution-processed perovskite solar cell with
16.5% PCE under standard conditions (AM 1.5 G radiation,
100 mW cm−2). We proposed a plausible mechanism for the
formation of uniform and dense perovskite layers during the
solvent-engineering process. The formation of a stable MAI(Br)–
PbI2–DMSO phase via an intercalation process during the dropwise
application of a non-dissolving solvent was a decisive factor in
retarding the rapid reaction between MAI(Br) and PbI(Br)2, which
enabled the formation of a highly uniform and dense surface.
Furthermore, we found that thick perovskite cells fabricated without
mp-TiO2 showed a large hysteresis and distortion between reverse
and forward scans, and raised arguments about the estimation
of conversion eﬃciencies for perovskite cells. Hence, the ratio of
the thicknesses of the perovskite-infiltrated mp-TiO2 and the pure
perovskite should be optimized to fabricate eﬃcient perovskite cells
with coincident reverse and forward scans. These results will provide
an eﬀective strategy for forming uniform PbI2-based perovskite
layers through intercalation, and lead to more eﬃcient and cost-
eﬀective inorganic–organic hybrid heterojunction solar cells in
the future.
Methods
Solar cell fabrication. A dense blocking layer of TiO2 (bl-TiO2, ∼70 nm in
thickness) was deposited onto a F-doped SnO2 (FTO, Pilkington, TEC8) substrate
by spray pyrolysis, using a 20 mM titanium diisopropoxide bis(acetylacetonate)
solution (Aldrich) at 450 ◦C to prevent direct contact between the FTO and the
hole-conducting layer. A 200–300-nm-thick mesoporous TiO2 (particle size:
about 50 nm, crystalline phase: anatase) film was spin-coated onto the
bl-TiO2/FTO substrate using home-made pastes14 and calcining at 500 ◦C for 1 h
in air to remove organic components. CH3NH3I (MAI) and CH3NH3Br (MABr)
were first synthesized by reacting 27.86 ml CH3NH2 (40% in methanol, Junsei
Chemical) and 30 ml HI (57 wt% in water, Aldrich) or 44 ml HBr (48 wt% in
water, Aldrich) in a 250 ml round-bottom flask at 0 ◦C for 4 h with stirring,
respectively. The precipitate was recovered by evaporation at 55 ◦C for 1 h. MAI
and MABr were dissolved in ethanol, recrystallized from diethyl ether, and dried
at 60 ◦C in a vacuum oven for 24 h. The prepared MAI and MABr powders, PbI2
(Aldrich) and PbBr2 (Aldrich) for 0.8 M MAPb(I1−xBrx)3 (x =0.1–0.15) solution
were stirred in a mixture of GBL and DMSO (7:3 v/v) at 60 ◦C for 12 h. The
resulting solution was coated onto the mp-TiO2/bl-TiO2/FTO substrate by a
consecutive two-step spin-coating process at 1,000 and 5,000 r.p.m for 10 and
20 s, respectively. During the second spin-coating step, the substrate (around 1 cm
× 1 cm) was treated with toluene drop-casting. A detailed time-rotation profile
for the spin-coating is represented in Supplementary Fig. 1c. The substrate was
dried on a hot plate at 100 ◦C for 10 min. A solution of poly(triarylamine) (15 mg,
PTAA, EM Index, Mw =17,500 g mol−1) in toluene (1.5 ml) was mixed with 15 µl
of a solution of lithium bistrifluoromethanesulphonimidate (170 mg) in

Characterization. The XRD spectra of the prepared films were measured using a
Rigaku SmartLab X-ray diﬀractometer, and in situ XRD experiments of the
powder isolated as an intermediate phase were performed using a Rigaku Ultima
IV with an X-ray tube (Cu Kα, λ=1.5406Å). The elemental analysis (C, H, N
and S) of the complex was performed using a FISONS EA–1108 CHN analyser.
The FTIR spectra (4,000–500 cm−1) were recorded on a Bruker EQUINOX 55
spectrophotometer with samples prepared by the KBr pellet method.
Ultraviolet–visible absorption spectra were recorded on a Shimadzu UV 2550
spectrophotometer in the 200–800 nm wavelength range at room temperature.
AFM was performed using Bruker multimode 8 in ‘tapping’ mode. The IPCE was
measured using a power source (Newport 300 W xenon lamp, 66920) with a
monochromator (Newport Cornerstone 260) and a multimeter (Keithley 2001).
J–V curves were measured using a solar simulator (Newport, Oriel Class A,
91195A) with a source meter (Keithley 2420) at 100 mW cm−2, AM 1.5 G
illumination, and a calibrated Si-reference cell certified by the NREL. The J–V
curves were measured by reverse (forward bias (1.2 V) →short circuit (0 V)) or
forward (short circuit (0 V) →forward bias (1.2 V)) scan. The step voltage was
fixed at 10 mV and the delay time, which is a set delay at each voltage step before
measuring each current, was modulated. J–V curves for all devices were
measured by masking the active area with a metal mask 0.094 cm−2 in area.

All rights reserved.\nSuppressing the formation of tin vacancy yields efficient lead-free \nperovskite solar cells \nShurong Wang a, Luo Yan b, Weike Zhu a, Zhiyuan Cao a, Liujiang Zhou b,c,**, Liming Ding d,*, \nFeng Hao a,* \na School of Materials and Energy, University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, Chengdu 611731, China \nb School of Physics, University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, Chengdu 610054, China \nc Yangtze Delta Region Institute (Huzhou), University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, Huzhou 313001, China \nd Center for Excellence in Nanoscience (CAS), Key Laboratory of Nanosystem and Hierarchical Fabrication (CAS), National Center for Nanoscience and Technology, \nBeijing 100190, China   \nA R T I C L E  I N F O   \nKeywords: \nResidual strain \nDefect passivation \nHigh voltage output \nStructural stability \nNon-radiative recombination \nA B S T R A C T   \nTin hybrid perovskite solar cells (TPSCs) have emerged as the most promising candidate to the lead counterparts \nfor the low toxicity and high theoretical efficiency. However, the easy Sn2+ oxidation and related defects hinder \nfurther efficiency and stability improvement. Therefore, a facile Lewis base molecule of 4-amino-3-hydroxyben\xad\nzoic acid (4A3HA) is employed in the perovskite precursor to coordinate with the under-coordinated Sn2+ ions \nand passivate the Sn defects. The effective suppression of the formation of Sn vacancy also has been verified from \nthe density functional theory calculations. The 4A3HA modification significantly suppresses the trap-mediated \nrecombination of Sn perovskite film. Accordingly, these benefits deliver a high power conversion efficiency \n(PCE) of 13.43% for TPSCs with notably improved on-shelf and thermal stability.   \n1. Introduction \nTin (Sn) hybrid perovskites act as the most promising lead-free \nalternative with a record power conversion efficiency (PCE) over 14% \nnow, [1,2] though the PCE is still far below those of lead (Pb) hybrid \nperovskite solar cells with a current PCE record of 25.7% [3]. Compared \nto Pb2+, Sn2+ has a similar outer shell electron configuration with lower \ntoxicity and superior semiconductor properties such as nearly ideal band \ngap (~1.3 eV) for single-junction photovoltaic devices, long diffusion \nlength, small excitation energy, and high carrier mobility [4–8]. How\xad\never, the structural stability of Sn perovskites lag significantly behind Pb \nanalogs due to the low defect formation energies. The easy oxidation of \nSn2+ and p-type self-doping characteristics result in severe non-radiative \nrecombination and therefore causes poor device performance, especially \nthe deficit in open-circuit voltage (Voc) [9,10]. \nTo remedy these issues, from the initial attempt of SnF2 to \ncompensate the Sn2+ stoichiometry, to the development of other SnX2 \n(such as SnCl2, SnBr2, SnI2) and then to tin(II) acetylacetonate that could \nsuppress the self-oxidation of Sn2+, various approaches have been \nexplored [11–15]. Meanwhile, the introduction of large organic cations \nto form Dion-Jacobson (DJ) or Ruddlesden-Popper (RP) phases further \nretarded external H2O or O2 ingression and suppressed the formation of \nSn defects for reduced charge carrier non-radiative recombination [16, \n17]. To overcome the Sn2+ oxidation, some functional additives also can \nmanipulate the perovskite thermodynamics and direct the orientation \nduring the film formation. \nReducing agents such as hydrazine, hydrazinium tin iodide, and \nother Lewis-acid type additives have been reported to protect the Sn2+\noxidation and suppress defects in Sn perovskites [18–21]. Thereinto, the \nreducing agents containing Lewis-base groups (e.g., N-donor, O-donor, \nS-donor, and P-donor) not only mitigate the formation of Sn vacancy \n(VSn) in perovskites by coordinating with Sn2+ but also suppress the \nphase segregation of SnX2 [22–25]. Yan et al. introduced gallic acid (GA) \nto interact with SnCl2 by forming Lewis acid-base adduct and main\xad\ntained 80% of the original PCE for 1000 h in ambient air [14]. The C––O \ngroup, owing to the two lone electron pairs, could coordinate with Sn2+\nto passivate trap states and suppress the surface defects. Recently, Li \net al. enabled the modulation of perovskite crystallization and obtained \ncompact morphology through strong O⋅⋅⋅Sn chelation by adding \nn-butylammonium acetate [26]. The full elucidation and modulation of the defect \npassivation, as well as non-radiative recombination channel for Sn \nperovskite, are needed to address the bottleneck of efficiency and sta\xad\nbility of TPSCs. \nHere, 4-amino-3-hydroxybenzoic acid (4A3HA) was employed in the \nSn perovskite precursor to modulate the defect and micro-strain. The \nC––O group acts as the additional Lewis-base source, which could \nreinforce the coordination with Sn2+ to reduce the Sn2+ oxidation and \nself p-doping level defects. This approach was beneficial to increase the \nformation energy of Sn vacancy, as revealed by the density functional \ntheory (DFT) calculations. Conclusion \nIn this work, we developed a novel Lewis base to alleviate the \nstructural disorder and under-coordinated Sn2+ defects in the Sn pe\xad\nrovskites. The reduced VSn defect by Lewis acid-base strategy rendered \nslow Sn2+ oxidation and long-term structural stability of the Sn perov\xad\nskites. We achieved a high PCE up to 13.43% in inverted TPSCs through \nsubstantially suppressed charge carrier non-radiative carrier recombi\xad\nnation. Meanwhile, the target devices retained over 80% of the initial \nPCE for 1000 h after 85 ◦C thermal heating and showed almost no \nchange of the initial PCE for 2000 h in N2 atmosphere. Therefore, our \nwork provides an effective protocol for approaching the theoretical Voc \nlimit in TPSCs through tin vacancy regulation. \nCRediT authorship contribution statement \nShurong Wang: Conceptualization, Methodology, Data curation, \nFig. 5. perovskite solar cells

A R T I C L E  I N F O   
Keywords: 
Residual strain 
Defect passivation 
High voltage output 
Structural stability 
Non-radiative recombination 
A B S T R A C T   
Tin hybrid perovskite solar cells (TPSCs) have emerged as the most promising candidate to the lead counterparts 
for the low toxicity and high theoretical efficiency. However, the easy Sn2+ oxidation and related defects hinder 
further efficiency and stability improvement. Therefore, a facile Lewis base molecule of 4-amino-3-hydroxyben­
zoic acid (4A3HA) is employed in the perovskite precursor to coordinate with the under-coordinated Sn2+ ions 
and passivate the Sn defects. The effective suppression of the formation of Sn vacancy also has been verified from 
the density functional theory calculations. The 4A3HA modification significantly suppresses the trap-mediated 
recombination of Sn perovskite film. Accordingly, these benefits deliver a high power conversion efficiency 
(PCE) of 13.43% for TPSCs with notably improved on-shelf and thermal stability.   
1. Introduction 
Tin (Sn) hybrid perovskites act as the most promising lead-free 
alternative with a record power conversion efficiency (PCE) over 14% 
now, [1,2] though the PCE is still far below those of lead (Pb) hybrid 
perovskite solar cells with a current PCE record of 25.7% [3]. Compared 
to Pb2+, Sn2+ has a similar outer shell electron configuration with lower 
toxicity and superior semiconductor properties such as nearly ideal band 
gap (~1.3 eV) for single-junction photovoltaic devices, long diffusion 
length, small excitation energy, and high carrier mobility [4–8]. How­
ever, the structural stability of Sn perovskites lag significantly behind Pb 
analogs due to the low defect formation energies. The easy oxidation of 
Sn2+ and p-type self-doping characteristics result in severe non-radiative 
recombination and therefore causes poor device performance, especially 
the deficit in open-circuit voltage (Voc) [9,10]. 
To remedy these issues, from the initial attempt of SnF2 to 
compensate the Sn2+ stoichiometry, to the development of other SnX2 
(such as SnCl2, SnBr2, SnI2) and then to tin(II) acetylacetonate that could 
suppress the self-oxidation of Sn2+, various approaches have been 
explored [11–15]. Meanwhile, the introduction of large organic cations 
to form Dion-Jacobson (DJ) or Ruddlesden-Popper (RP) phases further 
retarded external H2O or O2 ingression and suppressed the formation of 
Sn defects for reduced charge carrier non-radiative recombination [16, 
17]. To overcome the Sn2+ oxidation, some functional additives also can 
manipulate the perovskite thermodynamics and direct the orientation 
during the film formation. 
Reducing agents such as hydrazine, hydrazinium tin iodide, and 
other Lewis-acid type additives have been reported to protect the Sn2+
oxidation and suppress defects in Sn perovskites [18–21]. Thereinto, the 
reducing agents containing Lewis-base groups (e.g., N-donor, O-donor, 
S-donor, and P-donor) not only mitigate the formation of Sn vacancy 
(VSn) in perovskites by coordinating with Sn2+ but also suppress the 
phase segregation of SnX2 [22–25]. Yan et al. introduced gallic acid (GA) 
to interact with SnCl2 by forming Lewis acid-base adduct and main­
tained 80% of the original PCE for 1000 h in ambient air [14]. The C––O 
group, owing to the two lone electron pairs, could coordinate with Sn2+
to passivate trap states and suppress the surface defects. Recently, Li 
et al. enabled the modulation of perovskite crystallization and obtained 
compact morphology through strong O⋅⋅⋅Sn chelation by adding 
n-butylammonium acetate [26]. However, these implementations also

have a large Voc deficit according to the theoretical Shockley-Queisser 
(S-Q) limit [27]. The full elucidation and modulation of the defect 
passivation, as well as non-radiative recombination channel for Sn 
perovskite, are needed to address the bottleneck of efficiency and sta­
bility of TPSCs. 
Here, 4-amino-3-hydroxybenzoic acid (4A3HA) was employed in the 
Sn perovskite precursor to modulate the defect and micro-strain. The 
C––O group acts as the additional Lewis-base source, which could 
reinforce the coordination with Sn2+ to reduce the Sn2+ oxidation and 
self p-doping level defects. This approach was beneficial to increase the 
formation energy of Sn vacancy, as revealed by the density functional 
theory (DFT) calculations. Moreover, the target perovskite film showed 
almost no phase segregation after continuously heating at 85 ◦C in the 
N2 atmosphere. As a result, the utilization of 4A3HA significantly sup­
pressed the non-radiative recombination by carrier dynamic analysis. 
Owing to the passivation effect, the PCE of inverted TPSCs was improved 
from 9.44% to 13.43%, together with a Voc improved from 0.84 V to 
0.90 V. More importantly, the devices exhibited almost no PCE decay 
over 2000 h in the N2 atmosphere and maintained over 80% of the initial 
PCE after 85 ◦C aging over 1000 h. 
2. Results and discussion 
The Sn perovskite films were prepared using a spin-coating process 
using FA0.75MA0.25SnI2.75Br0.25 precursor with 10 mol% SnF2, 10% PEAI 
and 5 mg mL–1 Sn0 powder in a mixed solvent of DMF and DMSO. We 
first investigated the film morphology of perovskite films by scanning 
electron microscope (SEM) measurements (Figs. 1a and 1b). In the 
following, the 4A3HA-added perovskite was termed the target sample. 
The target film exhibited less SnI2 compared to the control film, as 
indicated by the white dots [28]. The Fourier transform infrared spectra 
(FTIR) was used to evaluate the possible interaction between the 4A3HA 
and perovskites (Figs. 1c-1d and S1). Two infrared signals of the 4A3HA 
at 1666.20 cm–1 and 1608.34 cm–1, belonging to of C––O stretching 
vibration, shifted toward the lower wavenumber from 1664.46 cm–1 
(–1.74 cm–1) to 1602.73 cm–1 (–5.61 cm–1). The C––O stretching 
from a higher wave number position attributed to quinones derivatives 
due to the reducing hydroxyl group [14,29,30]. The typical O–H 
stretching around 3350–3200 cm–1 showed negligible change (Fig. S1) 
Due to the electron-acceptor nature of the empty orbital in the valence 
shell of SnI2, the down-shifted of C––O stretch from carboxyl group from 
a lower wave number position indicated a strong interaction between 
SnI2 and C––O by forming a Lewis acid-base adduct. Meanwhile, the 
high-resolution X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) of N 1 s and C 1 
s were performed in Fig. S2 and S3. In N 1 s and C 1 s spectrum, the 
characteristic peak of C––NH2
+ (401.6 eV and 286.3 eV, respectively) 
showed a visible increase after 4A3HA treatment, which indicates the 
successful introduction of 4A3HA. However, there was no peak shift of 
C-N bonds after 4A3HA treatment in N 1 s spectrum, which helps to 
explain the tiny interaction of –NH2 group. In the C 1 s spectrum, the

C––N/C––O, respectively. The oxidized C species in control film would 
originate from the inevitable decay when exposed to air [31]. Due to the 
FA+ is constant, the C––N peak in control film did not change. The 
increased peak at 288.3 eV in C 1 s spectrum was contributed to the 
C––O bonds after 4A3HA treatment. Furthermore, the C––O peak shifted 
to lower binding energy around 0.3 eV after 4A3HA treatment, 
demonstrating the strong interaction of C––O group [26]. 
The absorption enhancement of target film in Fig. 1e was noticed by 
ultraviolet-visible (UV-Vis) absorbance spectroscopy. To probe the 
crystal structure, X-ray diffraction (XRD) was measured for control and 
target film (Fig. 1f and S4-S5). Three dominant peaks are located at 
14.3◦, 28.6◦, and 43.4◦, which can be indexed to the characteristic 
(100), (200), and (300) crystal planes. The calculated crystallinity was 
89.99% and 93.26%, respectively. Meanwhile, the target film showed a 
smaller full-width half maxima (FWHM) value and higher peak in­
tensity, demonstrating an enhanced crystallinity. Generally, the residual 
strain increased the non-radiative recombination and defect concen­
tration in perovskite films. To determine the lattice strain of the Sn 
perovskite layer after 4A3HA treatment, we deposited the perovskite 
films onto PEDOT:PSS substrates and estimated the micro-strain from 
XRD in Fig. 1f. The micro-strain decreased in the target film along the 
(100), (200), and (300) planes (Fig. 1g and Table S1, calculation method 
was shown in supporting information). Thus, the strain relaxation 
minimized the defect/trap centers and lattice distortion [32–34]. 
To further verify the passivation effect of 4A3HA, the absorption 
energies of C––O were explored by density functional theory (DFT) 
calculations at the atomic level. To simplify the calculated perovskite 
process, the simplified perovskite structure of FASnI3 was used instead 
of FA0.75MA0.25SnI2.75Br0.25. The side view in Figs. 2a-2d showed the 
total energy. The most stable configuration was reflected in the planar 
structure (Fig. 2a and Table S2). We further simulated the total density 
of states (DOS) of control and target films to evaluate the energy levels 
contribution (Fig. 2e). The DOS of 4A3HA was located near the band 
edge states and affected the Fermi level (Ef), which is consistent with the 
ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy (UPS) results (Fig. S6). The par­
tial density of states (PDOS) in Figs. 2f and 2h confirmed that the ex­
istence of 4A3HA at the Sn-I terminated surface enhanced the energy of 
Sn 5p states, therefore reducing the possible non-radiative recombina­
tion. The detailed electron localization function (ELF) analysis (Figs. 2g 
and 2i) further indicated the obvious variation of the electron cloud 
around the Sn atoms and transferred local charge from Sn atoms to O 
atoms. Hence, the coordinated interaction between Sn2+ and 4A3HA 
could stabilize the [SnI6]4– octahedra near the surface and eliminate the 
under-coordinated Sn defects, which would further suppress the non- 
radiative recombination from the defects. 
Given the enhancements in crystallization and defect passivation, the 
perovskite films with 4A3HA were fabricated to investigate how coor­
dination interaction affects the photovoltaic performance (Fig. 3a). The 
target device delivered a champion PCE of 13.43% with a high Voc of 
0.90 V (Fig. 3b), and a fill factor (FF) of 71.22% under AM 1.5 G light 
illumination with a scan speed of 200 mV/s and 20 ms setting time 
(Fig. S7), while the control device showed a champion PCE of 9.44% 
with a Voc of 0.84 V, and a FF of 68.53% (Other devices with different 
ratio of 4A3HA can be seen in Table S3). The energy loss (Eloss) (Eloss

hydroxyl group is attached to the benzene ring, which can scavenge 
oxygen by donating hydrogen atoms and electrons. Moreover, the 
4A3HA molecule shows a strong conjugation effect than other additives 
like glycine and S4A2HA. 
The changes of PCE in the N2 atmosphere were tracked over 2000 h 
to test the long-term stability (Fig. 3f). The results showed almost un­
changed PCE after 2000 h, whereas the control devices decreased over 
60% of the original PCE during this time. Also, as shown in Fig. 3g, the 
thermal stability at 85 ◦C of the target devices was noticeably improved, 
maintaining over 80% of the original PCE after 1000 h heating. In 
contrast, the control devices lost near 70% of the initial efficiency. 
Meanwhile, the contact angle of water drops (Fig. S11) was 53.8◦and

encapsulation (Fig. S12).

According to the theoretical analysis, the Vsn is the dominant defect 
in Sn perovskites [43]. The high concentration of Vsn in perovskites leads 
to a high level of p-type doping effect [44]. The formation energy of Vsn 
was calculated for the control and target devices (Fig. 5a and Fig. S17). 
The increase of Vsn indicates the suppressed self-doping by 4A3HA, 
leading to reduced Voc deficit in the target device [45]. To verify the 
enhanced structural stability, XPS spectrum was measured to under­
stand the Sn2+ oxidation retardation ability (Fig. 5b). The samples were 
stored overnight in a vacuum chamber and then tested. The corre­
sponding peak of Sn2+ 3d 5/2 and Sn2+ 3d 3/2 located at 486.4 and 
494.8 eV, respectively (Table S8). The Sn2+ peaks shifted to lower 
binding energy (~ 0.3 eV) after 4A3HA treatment, which indicated the 
strong Lewis acid-base interaction between SnI2 and C––O group. This 
result also consistent with the C 1 s spectrum of C––O peak. Sn4+ region 
exhibited two divided peaks at 487.0 and 495.4 eV, which are attributed 
to Sn4+ 3d 5/2 and Sn4+ 3d 3/2, respectively. The calculated fractions of 
Sn4+ in the target film means that the presence of 4A3HA prevent the 
Sn2+ oxidation during the film formation process, which is consistent 
with previous report [21,46]. To confirm the long-term Sn2+ protection, 
the crystallographic data under 85 ◦C heating in N2 atmosphere over 26 
days were collected (Figs. 5c-5d). The heated films exposed to the air for 
about 20 min to check the structural variation by XRD spectra. The 
characteristic peaks of vacancy-ordered double perovskite derivative 
A2SnI6 at 24.8◦and 27.4◦appeared under 85 ◦C heating after 16 days 
and increased quickly for the control film, while the target film did not 
appear the A2SnI6 peak at 24.8◦and showed negligible peak at 27.4◦. 
Those results further confirmed the better structural stability under 
thermal environment, which is consistent with the long-term 85 ◦C 
stability test. Meanwhile, we observed a slightly blue-shifted peak of 
(100) and SnI2 around 0.1◦after heating for 16 days and then stabilized 
(Figs. 5c-5e and Fig. S18-S19), indicative of a slight lattice expansion 
after 16 days heating [47]. These phenomenon occurred by the high 
coefficients of volumetric thermal expansion for Sn perovskites [48,49]. 
3. Conclusion 
In this work, we developed a novel Lewis base to alleviate the 
structural disorder and under-coordinated Sn2+ defects in the Sn pe­
rovskites. The reduced VSn defect by Lewis acid-base strategy rendered 
slow Sn2+ oxidation and long-term structural stability of the Sn perov­
skites. We achieved a high PCE up to 13.43% in inverted TPSCs through 
substantially suppressed charge carrier non-radiative carrier recombi­
nation. Meanwhile, the target devices retained over 80% of the initial 
PCE for 1000 h after 85 ◦C thermal heating and showed almost no 
change of the initial PCE for 2000 h in N2 atmosphere. Therefore, our 
work provides an effective protocol for approaching the theoretical Voc 
limit in TPSCs through tin vacancy regulation.

All rights reserved.\nSuppressing the formation of tin vacancy yields efficient lead-free \nperovskite solar cells \nShurong Wang a, Luo Yan b, Weike Zhu a, Zhiyuan Cao a, Liujiang Zhou b,c,**, Liming Ding d,*, \nFeng Hao a,* \na School of Materials and Energy, University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, Chengdu 611731, China \nb School of Physics, University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, Chengdu 610054, China \nc Yangtze Delta Region Institute (Huzhou), University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, Huzhou 313001, China \nd Center for Excellence in Nanoscience (CAS), Key Laboratory of Nanosystem and Hierarchical Fabrication (CAS), National Center for Nanoscience and Technology, \nBeijing 100190, China   \nA R T I C L E  I N F O   \nKeywords: \nResidual strain \nDefect passivation \nHigh voltage output \nStructural stability \nNon-radiative recombination \nA B S T R A C T   \nTin hybrid perovskite solar cells (TPSCs) have emerged as the most promising candidate to the lead counterparts \nfor the low toxicity and high theoretical efficiency. However, the easy Sn2+ oxidation and related defects hinder \nfurther efficiency and stability improvement. Therefore, a facile Lewis base molecule of 4-amino-3-hydroxyben\xad\nzoic acid (4A3HA) is employed in the perovskite precursor to coordinate with the under-coordinated Sn2+ ions \nand passivate the Sn defects. The effective suppression of the formation of Sn vacancy also has been verified from \nthe density functional theory calculations. The 4A3HA modification significantly suppresses the trap-mediated \nrecombination of Sn perovskite film. Accordingly, these benefits deliver a high power conversion efficiency \n(PCE) of 13.43% for TPSCs with notably improved on-shelf and thermal stability.   \n1. Introduction \nTin (Sn) hybrid perovskites act as the most promising lead-free \nalternative with a record power conversion efficiency (PCE) over 14% \nnow, [1,2] though the PCE is still far below those of lead (Pb) hybrid \nperovskite solar cells with a current PCE record of 25.7% [3]. Compared \nto Pb2+, Sn2+ has a similar outer shell electron configuration with lower \ntoxicity and superior semiconductor properties such as nearly ideal band \ngap (~1.3 eV) for single-junction photovoltaic devices, long diffusion \nlength, small excitation energy, and high carrier mobility [4–8]. How\xad\never, the structural stability of Sn perovskites lag significantly behind Pb \nanalogs due to the low defect formation energies. The easy oxidation of \nSn2+ and p-type self-doping characteristics result in severe non-radiative \nrecombination and therefore causes poor device performance, especially \nthe deficit in open-circuit voltage (Voc) [9,10]. \nTo remedy these issues, from the initial attempt of SnF2 to \ncompensate the Sn2+ stoichiometry, to the development of other SnX2 \n(such as SnCl2, SnBr2, SnI2) and then to tin(II) acetylacetonate that could \nsuppress the self-oxidation of Sn2+, various approaches have been \nexplored [11–15]. Meanwhile, the introduction of large organic cations \nto form Dion-Jacobson (DJ) or Ruddlesden-Popper (RP) phases further \nretarded external H2O or O2 ingression and suppressed the formation of \nSn defects for reduced charge carrier non-radiative recombination [16, \n17]. To overcome the Sn2+ oxidation, some functional additives also can \nmanipulate the perovskite thermodynamics and direct the orientation \nduring the film formation. \nReducing agents such as hydrazine, hydrazinium tin iodide, and \nother Lewis-acid type additives have been reported to protect the Sn2+\noxidation and suppress defects in Sn perovskites [18–21]. Thereinto, the \nreducing agents containing Lewis-base groups (e.g., N-donor, O-donor, \nS-donor, and P-donor) not only mitigate the formation of Sn vacancy \n(VSn) in perovskites by coordinating with Sn2+ but also suppress the \nphase segregation of SnX2 [22–25]. Yan et al. introduced gallic acid (GA) \nto interact with SnCl2 by forming Lewis acid-base adduct and main\xad\ntained 80% of the original PCE for 1000 h in ambient air [14]. The C––O \ngroup, owing to the two lone electron pairs, could coordinate with Sn2+\nto passivate trap states and suppress the surface defects. Recently, Li \net al. enabled the modulation of perovskite crystallization and obtained \ncompact morphology through strong O⋅⋅⋅Sn chelation by adding \nn-butylammonium acetate [26]. The full elucidation and modulation of the defect \npassivation, as well as non-radiative recombination channel for Sn \nperovskite, are needed to address the bottleneck of efficiency and sta\xad\nbility of TPSCs. \nHere, 4-amino-3-hydroxybenzoic acid (4A3HA) was employed in the \nSn perovskite precursor to modulate the defect and micro-strain. The \nC––O group acts as the additional Lewis-base source, which could \nreinforce the coordination with Sn2+ to reduce the Sn2+ oxidation and \nself p-doping level defects. This approach was beneficial to increase the \nformation energy of Sn vacancy, as revealed by the density functional \ntheory (DFT) calculations. Moreover, the target perovskite film showed \nalmost no phase segregation after continuously heating at 85 ◦C in the \nN2 atmosphere. As a result, the utilization of 4A3HA significantly sup\xad\npressed the non-radiative recombination by carrier dynamic analysis. \nOwing to the passivation effect, the PCE of inverted TPSCs was improved \nfrom 9.44% to 13.43%, together with a Voc improved from 0.84 V to \n0.90 V. More importantly, the devices exhibited almost no PCE decay \nover 2000 h in the N2 atmosphere and maintained over 80% of the initial \nPCE after 85 ◦C aging over 1000 h. \n2. We \nfirst investigated the film morphology of perovskite films by scanning \nelectron microscope (SEM) measurements (Figs. 1a and 1b). In the \nfollowing, the 4A3HA-added perovskite was termed the target sample. \nThe target film exhibited less SnI2 compared to the control film, as \nindicated by the white dots [28]. The Fourier transform infrared spectra \n(FTIR) was used to evaluate the possible interaction between the 4A3HA \nand perovskites (Figs. 1c-1d and S1). The DOS of 4A3HA was located near the band \nedge states and affected the Fermi level (Ef), which is consistent with the \nultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy (UPS) results (Fig. S6). Conclusion \nIn this work, we developed a novel Lewis base to alleviate the \nstructural disorder and under-coordinated Sn2+ defects in the Sn pe\xad\nrovskites. The reduced VSn defect by Lewis acid-base strategy rendered \nslow Sn2+ oxidation and long-term structural stability of the Sn perov\xad\nskites. We achieved a high PCE up to 13.43% in inverted TPSCs through \nsubstantially suppressed charge carrier non-radiative carrier recombi\xad\nnation. Meanwhile, the target devices retained over 80% of the initial \nPCE for 1000 h after 85 ◦C thermal heating and showed almost no \nchange of the initial PCE for 2000 h in N2 atmosphere. Therefore, our \nwork provides an effective protocol for approaching the theoretical Voc \nlimit in TPSCs through tin vacancy regulation. \nCRediT authorship contribution statement \nShurong Wang: Conceptualization, Methodology, Data curation, \nFig. 5. A B S T R A C T   
Tin hybrid perovskite solar cells (TPSCs) have emerged as the most promising candidate to the lead counterparts 
for the low toxicity and high theoretical efficiency. However, the easy Sn2+ oxidation and related defects hinder 
further efficiency and stability improvement. Therefore, a facile Lewis base molecule of 4-amino-3-hydroxyben­
zoic acid (4A3HA) is employed in the perovskite precursor to coordinate with the under-coordinated Sn2+ ions 
and passivate the Sn defects. The effective suppression of the formation of Sn vacancy also has been verified from 
the density functional theory calculations. The 4A3HA modification significantly suppresses the trap-mediated 
recombination of Sn perovskite film. Accordingly, these benefits deliver a high power conversion efficiency 
(PCE) of 13.43% for TPSCs with notably improved on-shelf and thermal stability.   
1. Introduction 
Tin (Sn) hybrid perovskites act as the most promising lead-free 
alternative with a record power conversion efficiency (PCE) over 14% 
now, [1,2] though the PCE is still far below those of lead (Pb) hybrid 
perovskite solar cells with a current PCE record of 25.7% [3]. Compared 
to Pb2+, Sn2+ has a similar outer shell electron configuration with lower 
toxicity and superior semiconductor properties such as nearly ideal band 
gap (~1.3 eV) for single-junction photovoltaic devices, long diffusion 
length, small excitation energy, and high carrier mobility [4–8]. How­
ever, the structural stability of Sn perovskites lag significantly behind Pb 
analogs due to the low defect formation energies. The easy oxidation of 
Sn2+ and p-type self-doping characteristics result in severe non-radiative 
recombination and therefore causes poor device performance, especially 
the deficit in open-circuit voltage (Voc) [9,10]. 
To remedy these issues, from the initial attempt of SnF2 to 
compensate the Sn2+ stoichiometry, to the development of other SnX2 
(such as SnCl2, SnBr2, SnI2) and then to tin(II) acetylacetonate that could 
suppress the self-oxidation of Sn2+, various approaches have been 
explored [11–15]. Meanwhile, the introduction of large organic cations 
to form Dion-Jacobson (DJ) or Ruddlesden-Popper (RP) phases further 
retarded external H2O or O2 ingression and suppressed the formation of 
Sn defects for reduced charge carrier non-radiative recombination [16, 
17]. To overcome the Sn2+ oxidation, some functional additives also can 
manipulate the perovskite thermodynamics and direct the orientation 
during the film formation. 
Reducing agents such as hydrazine, hydrazinium tin iodide, and 
other Lewis-acid type additives have been reported to protect the Sn2+
oxidation and suppress defects in Sn perovskites [18–21]. Thereinto, the 
reducing agents containing Lewis-base groups (e.g., N-donor, O-donor, 
S-donor, and P-donor) not only mitigate the formation of Sn vacancy 
(VSn) in perovskites by coordinating with Sn2+ but also suppress the 
phase segregation of SnX2 [22–25]. Yan et al. introduced gallic acid (GA) 
to interact with SnCl2 by forming Lewis acid-base adduct and main­
tained 80% of the original PCE for 1000 h in ambient air [14]. The C––O 
group, owing to the two lone electron pairs, could coordinate with Sn2+
to passivate trap states and suppress the surface defects. Recently, Li 
et al. enabled the modulation of perovskite crystallization and obtained 
compact morphology through strong O⋅⋅⋅Sn chelation by adding 
n-butylammonium acetate [26]. However, these implementations also

have a large Voc deficit according to the theoretical Shockley-Queisser 
(S-Q) limit [27]. The full elucidation and modulation of the defect 
passivation, as well as non-radiative recombination channel for Sn 
perovskite, are needed to address the bottleneck of efficiency and sta­
bility of TPSCs. 
Here, 4-amino-3-hydroxybenzoic acid (4A3HA) was employed in the 
Sn perovskite precursor to modulate the defect and micro-strain. The 
C––O group acts as the additional Lewis-base source, which could 
reinforce the coordination with Sn2+ to reduce the Sn2+ oxidation and 
self p-doping level defects. This approach was beneficial to increase the 
formation energy of Sn vacancy, as revealed by the density functional 
theory (DFT) calculations. Moreover, the target perovskite film showed 
almost no phase segregation after continuously heating at 85 ◦C in the 
N2 atmosphere. As a result, the utilization of 4A3HA significantly sup­
pressed the non-radiative recombination by carrier dynamic analysis. 
Owing to the passivation effect, the PCE of inverted TPSCs was improved 
from 9.44% to 13.43%, together with a Voc improved from 0.84 V to 
0.90 V. More importantly, the devices exhibited almost no PCE decay 
over 2000 h in the N2 atmosphere and maintained over 80% of the initial 
PCE after 85 ◦C aging over 1000 h. 
2. Results and discussion 
The Sn perovskite films were prepared using a spin-coating process 
using FA0.75MA0.25SnI2.75Br0.25 precursor with 10 mol% SnF2, 10% PEAI 
and 5 mg mL–1 Sn0 powder in a mixed solvent of DMF and DMSO. We 
first investigated the film morphology of perovskite films by scanning 
electron microscope (SEM) measurements (Figs. 1a and 1b). In the 
following, the 4A3HA-added perovskite was termed the target sample. 
The target film exhibited less SnI2 compared to the control film, as 
indicated by the white dots [28]. The Fourier transform infrared spectra 
(FTIR) was used to evaluate the possible interaction between the 4A3HA 
and perovskites (Figs. 1c-1d and S1). Two infrared signals of the 4A3HA 
at 1666.20 cm–1 and 1608.34 cm–1, belonging to of C––O stretching 
vibration, shifted toward the lower wavenumber from 1664.46 cm–1 
(–1.74 cm–1) to 1602.73 cm–1 (–5.61 cm–1). The C––O stretching 
from a higher wave number position attributed to quinones derivatives 
due to the reducing hydroxyl group [14,29,30]. The typical O–H 
stretching around 3350–3200 cm–1 showed negligible change (Fig. S1) 
Due to the electron-acceptor nature of the empty orbital in the valence 
shell of SnI2, the down-shifted of C––O stretch from carboxyl group from 
a lower wave number position indicated a strong interaction between 
SnI2 and C––O by forming a Lewis acid-base adduct. Meanwhile, the 
high-resolution X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) of N 1 s and C 1 
s were performed in Fig. S2 and S3. In N 1 s and C 1 s spectrum, the 
characteristic peak of C––NH2

successful introduction of 4A3HA. However, there was no peak shift of 
C-N bonds after 4A3HA treatment in N 1 s spectrum, which helps to 
explain the tiny interaction of –NH2 group. In the C 1 s spectrum, the

The absorption enhancement of target film in Fig. 1e was noticed by 
ultraviolet-visible (UV-Vis) absorbance spectroscopy. To probe the 
crystal structure, X-ray diffraction (XRD) was measured for control and 
target film (Fig. 1f and S4-S5). Three dominant peaks are located at 
14.3◦, 28.6◦, and 43.4◦, which can be indexed to the characteristic 
(100), (200), and (300) crystal planes. The calculated crystallinity was 
89.99% and 93.26%, respectively. Meanwhile, the target film showed a 
smaller full-width half maxima (FWHM) value and higher peak in­
tensity, demonstrating an enhanced crystallinity. Generally, the residual 
strain increased the non-radiative recombination and defect concen­
tration in perovskite films. To determine the lattice strain of the Sn 
perovskite layer after 4A3HA treatment, we deposited the perovskite 
films onto PEDOT:PSS substrates and estimated the micro-strain from 
XRD in Fig. 1f. The micro-strain decreased in the target film along the 
(100), (200), and (300) planes (Fig. 1g and Table S1, calculation method 
was shown in supporting information). Thus, the strain relaxation 
minimized the defect/trap centers and lattice distortion [32–34]. 
To further verify the passivation effect of 4A3HA, the absorption 
energies of C––O were explored by density functional theory (DFT) 
calculations at the atomic level. To simplify the calculated perovskite 
process, the simplified perovskite structure of FASnI3 was used instead 
of FA0.75MA0.25SnI2.75Br0.25. The side view in Figs. 2a-2d showed the 
total energy. The most stable configuration was reflected in the planar 
structure (Fig. 2a and Table S2). We further simulated the total density 
of states (DOS) of control and target films to evaluate the energy levels 
contribution (Fig. 2e). The DOS of 4A3HA was located near the band 
edge states and affected the Fermi level (Ef), which is consistent with the 
ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy (UPS) results (Fig. S6). The par­
tial density of states (PDOS) in Figs. 2f and 2h confirmed that the ex­
istence of 4A3HA at the Sn-I terminated surface enhanced the energy of 
Sn 5p states, therefore reducing the possible non-radiative recombina­
tion. The detailed electron localization function (ELF) analysis (Figs. 2g 
and 2i) further indicated the obvious variation of the electron cloud 
around the Sn atoms and transferred local charge from Sn atoms to O 
atoms. Hence, the coordinated interaction between Sn2+ and 4A3HA 
could stabilize the [SnI6]4– octahedra near the surface and eliminate the 
under-coordinated Sn defects, which would further suppress the non- 
radiative recombination from the defects. 
Given the enhancements in crystallization and defect passivation, the 
perovskite films with 4A3HA were fabricated to investigate how coor­
dination interaction affects the photovoltaic performance (Fig. 3a). The 
target device delivered a champion PCE of 13.43% with a high Voc of 
0.90 V (Fig. 3b), and a fill factor (FF) of 71.22% under AM 1.5 G light 
illumination with a scan speed of 200 mV/s and 20 ms setting time 
(Fig. S7), while the control device showed a champion PCE of 9.44% 
with a Voc of 0.84 V, and a FF of 68.53% (Other devices with different 
ratio of 4A3HA can be seen in Table S3). The energy loss (Eloss) (Eloss 
= Eg-qVoc) decreased from 0.55 eV to 0.48 eV in our devices after 
4A3HA modification. External quantum efficiency (EQE) spectrum in

hydroxyl group is attached to the benzene ring, which can scavenge 
oxygen by donating hydrogen atoms and electrons. Moreover, the 
4A3HA molecule shows a strong conjugation effect than other additives 
like glycine and S4A2HA. 
The changes of PCE in the N2 atmosphere were tracked over 2000 h 
to test the long-term stability (Fig. 3f). The results showed almost un­
changed PCE after 2000 h, whereas the control devices decreased over 
60% of the original PCE during this time. Also, as shown in Fig. 3g, the 
thermal stability at 85 ◦C of the target devices was noticeably improved, 
maintaining over 80% of the original PCE after 1000 h heating. In 
contrast, the control devices lost near 70% of the initial efficiency. 
Meanwhile, the contact angle of water drops (Fig. S11) was 53.8◦and 
62.7◦for control and target films, respectively, indicating enhanced 
hydrophobicity due to the effect of the hydrophobic benzene group after 
4A3HA treatment. The air stability also improved after 4A3HA treat­
ment, along with 80% retain after 133 h storage in air without any 
encapsulation (Fig. S12).

coefficients of volumetric thermal expansion for Sn perovskites [48,49]. 
3. Conclusion 
In this work, we developed a novel Lewis base to alleviate the 
structural disorder and under-coordinated Sn2+ defects in the Sn pe­
rovskites. The reduced VSn defect by Lewis acid-base strategy rendered 
slow Sn2+ oxidation and long-term structural stability of the Sn perov­
skites. We achieved a high PCE up to 13.43% in inverted TPSCs through 
substantially suppressed charge carrier non-radiative carrier recombi­
nation. Meanwhile, the target devices retained over 80% of the initial 
PCE for 1000 h after 85 ◦C thermal heating and showed almost no 
change of the initial PCE for 2000 h in N2 atmosphere. Therefore, our 
work provides an effective protocol for approaching the theoretical Voc 
limit in TPSCs through tin vacancy regulation.

full professor. His research focuses on innovative materials and 
devices. He is RSC Fellow, the nominator for Xplorer Prize, and

Suppressing the formation of tin vacancy yields efficient lead-free 
perovskite solar cells 
Shurong Wang a, Luo Yan b, Weike Zhu a, Zhiyuan Cao a, Liujiang Zhou b,c,**, Liming Ding d,*, 
Feng Hao a,* 
a School of Materials and Energy, University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, Chengdu 611731, China 
b School of Physics, University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, Chengdu 610054, China 
c Yangtze Delta Region Institute (Huzhou), University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, Huzhou 313001, China 
d Center for Excellence in Nanoscience (CAS), Key Laboratory of Nanosystem and Hierarchical Fabrication (CAS), National Center for Nanoscience and Technology, 
Beijing 100190, China   
A R T I C L E  I N F O   
Keywords: 
Residual strain 
Defect passivation 
High voltage output 
Structural stability 
Non-radiative recombination 
A B S T R A C T   
Tin hybrid perovskite solar cells (TPSCs) have emerged as the most promising candidate to the lead counterparts 
for the low toxicity and high theoretical efficiency. However, the easy Sn2+ oxidation and related defects hinder 
further efficiency and stability improvement. Therefore, a facile Lewis base molecule of 4-amino-3-hydroxyben­
zoic acid (4A3HA) is employed in the perovskite precursor to coordinate with the under-coordinated Sn2+ ions 
and passivate the Sn defects. The effective suppression of the formation of Sn vacancy also has been verified from 
the density functional theory calculations. The 4A3HA modification significantly suppresses the trap-mediated 
recombination of Sn perovskite film. Accordingly, these benefits deliver a high power conversion efficiency 
(PCE) of 13.43% for TPSCs with notably improved on-shelf and thermal stability.   
1. Introduction 
Tin (Sn) hybrid perovskites act as the most promising lead-free 
alternative with a record power conversion efficiency (PCE) over 14% 
now, [1,2] though the PCE is still far below those of lead (Pb) hybrid 
perovskite solar cells with a current PCE record of 25.7% [3]. Compared 
to Pb2+, Sn2+ has a similar outer shell electron configuration with lower 
toxicity and superior semiconductor properties such as nearly ideal band 
gap (~1.3 eV) for single-junction photovoltaic devices, long diffusion 
length, small excitation energy, and high carrier mobility [4–8]. How­
ever, the structural stability of Sn perovskites lag significantly behind Pb 
analogs due to the low defect formation energies. The easy oxidation of 
Sn2+ and p-type self-doping characteristics result in severe non-radiative 
recombination and therefore causes poor device performance, especially 
the deficit in open-circuit voltage (Voc) [9,10]. 
To remedy these issues, from the initial attempt of SnF2 to 
compensate the Sn2+ stoichiometry, to the development of other SnX2 
(such as SnCl2, SnBr2, SnI2) and then to tin(II) acetylacetonate that could 
suppress the self-oxidation of Sn2+, various approaches have been 
explored [11–15]. Meanwhile, the introduction of large organic cations 
to form Dion-Jacobson (DJ) or Ruddlesden-Popper (RP) phases further 
retarded external H2O or O2 ingression and suppressed the formation of 
Sn defects for reduced charge carrier non-radiative recombination [16, 
17]. To overcome the Sn2+ oxidation, some functional additives also can 
manipulate the perovskite thermodynamics and direct the orientation 
during the film formation. 
Reducing agents such as hydrazine, hydrazinium tin iodide, and 
other Lewis-acid type additives have been reported to protect the Sn2+
oxidation and suppress defects in Sn perovskites [18–21]. Thereinto, the 
reducing agents containing Lewis-base groups (e.g., N-donor, O-donor, 
S-donor, and P-donor) not only mitigate the formation of Sn vacancy 
(VSn) in perovskites by coordinating with Sn2+ but also suppress the 
phase segregation of SnX2 [22–25]. Yan et al. introduced gallic acid (GA) 
to interact with SnCl2 by forming Lewis acid-base adduct and main­
tained 80% of the original PCE for 1000 h in ambient air [14]. The C––O 
group, owing to the two lone electron pairs, could coordinate with Sn2+
to passivate trap states and suppress the surface defects. Recently, Li 
et al. enabled the modulation of perovskite crystallization and obtained 
compact morphology through strong O⋅⋅⋅Sn chelation by adding 
n-butylammonium acetate [26]. However, these implementations also
