have a large Voc deficit according to the theoretical Shockley-Queisser 
(S-Q) limit [27]. The full elucidation and modulation of the defect 
passivation, as well as non-radiative recombination channel for Sn 
perovskite, are needed to address the bottleneck of efficiency and sta­
bility of TPSCs. 
Here, 4-amino-3-hydroxybenzoic acid (4A3HA) was employed in the 
Sn perovskite precursor to modulate the defect and micro-strain. The 
C––O group acts as the additional Lewis-base source, which could 
reinforce the coordination with Sn2+ to reduce the Sn2+ oxidation and 
self p-doping level defects. This approach was beneficial to increase the 
formation energy of Sn vacancy, as revealed by the density functional 
theory (DFT) calculations. Moreover, the target perovskite film showed 
almost no phase segregation after continuously heating at 85 ◦C in the 
N2 atmosphere. As a result, the utilization of 4A3HA significantly sup­
pressed the non-radiative recombination by carrier dynamic analysis. 
Owing to the passivation effect, the PCE of inverted TPSCs was improved 
from 9.44% to 13.43%, together with a Voc improved from 0.84 V to 
0.90 V. More importantly, the devices exhibited almost no PCE decay 
over 2000 h in the N2 atmosphere and maintained over 80% of the initial 
PCE after 85 ◦C aging over 1000 h. 
2. Results and discussion 
The Sn perovskite films were prepared using a spin-coating process 
using FA0.75MA0.25SnI2.75Br0.25 precursor with 10 mol% SnF2, 10% PEAI 
and 5 mg mL–1 Sn0 powder in a mixed solvent of DMF and DMSO. We 
first investigated the film morphology of perovskite films by scanning 
electron microscope (SEM) measurements (Figs. 1a and 1b). In the 
following, the 4A3HA-added perovskite was termed the target sample. 
The target film exhibited less SnI2 compared to the control film, as 
indicated by the white dots [28]. The Fourier transform infrared spectra 
(FTIR) was used to evaluate the possible interaction between the 4A3HA 
and perovskites (Figs. 1c-1d and S1). Two infrared signals of the 4A3HA 
at 1666.20 cm–1 and 1608.34 cm–1, belonging to of C––O stretching 
vibration, shifted toward the lower wavenumber from 1664.46 cm–1 
(–1.74 cm–1) to 1602.73 cm–1 (–5.61 cm–1). The C––O stretching 
from a higher wave number position attributed to quinones derivatives 
due to the reducing hydroxyl group [14,29,30]. The typical O–H 
stretching around 3350–3200 cm–1 showed negligible change (Fig. S1) 
Due to the electron-acceptor nature of the empty orbital in the valence 
shell of SnI2, the down-shifted of C––O stretch from carboxyl group from 
a lower wave number position indicated a strong interaction between 
SnI2 and C––O by forming a Lewis acid-base adduct. Meanwhile, the 
high-resolution X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) of N 1 s and C 1 
s were performed in Fig. S2 and S3. In N 1 s and C 1 s spectrum, the 
characteristic peak of C––NH2
+ (401.6 eV and 286.3 eV, respectively) 
showed a visible increase after 4A3HA treatment, which indicates the 
successful introduction of 4A3HA. However, there was no peak shift of 
C-N bonds after 4A3HA treatment in N 1 s spectrum, which helps to 
explain the tiny interaction of –NH2 group. In the C 1 s spectrum, the 
Fig. 1. (a-b) SEM images of perovskite films without/with 4A3HA additives. (c-d) FTIR spectra of SnI2 with/without 4A3HA. (e) UV-Vis images of the control and 
target films. (f) XRD patterns of perovskite films. (g) Micro-strain distribution for (100), (200), and (300) planes. 
S. Wang et al.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   


Nano Energy 99 (2022) 107416
3
peak at 284.8, 286.3, and 288.3 eV were assigned to C-C, C––NH2
+, and 
C––N/C––O, respectively. The oxidized C species in control film would 
originate from the inevitable decay when exposed to air [31]. Due to the 
FA+ is constant, the C––N peak in control film did not change. The 
increased peak at 288.3 eV in C 1 s spectrum was contributed to the 
C––O bonds after 4A3HA treatment. Furthermore, the C––O peak shifted 
to lower binding energy around 0.3 eV after 4A3HA treatment, 
demonstrating the strong interaction of C––O group [26]. 
The absorption enhancement of target film in Fig. 1e was noticed by 
ultraviolet-visible (UV-Vis) absorbance spectroscopy. To probe the 
crystal structure, X-ray diffraction (XRD) was measured for control and 
target film (Fig. 1f and S4-S5). Three dominant peaks are located at 
14.3◦, 28.6◦, and 43.4◦, which can be indexed to the characteristic 
(100), (200), and (300) crystal planes. The calculated crystallinity was 
89.99% and 93.26%, respectively. Meanwhile, the target film showed a 
smaller full-width half maxima (FWHM) value and higher peak in­
tensity, demonstrating an enhanced crystallinity. Generally, the residual 
strain increased the non-radiative recombination and defect concen­
tration in perovskite films. To determine the lattice strain of the Sn 
perovskite layer after 4A3HA treatment, we deposited the perovskite 
films onto PEDOT:PSS substrates and estimated the micro-strain from 
XRD in Fig. 1f. The micro-strain decreased in the target film along the 
(100), (200), and (300) planes (Fig. 1g and Table S1, calculation method 
was shown in supporting information). Thus, the strain relaxation 
minimized the defect/trap centers and lattice distortion [32–34]. 
To further verify the passivation effect of 4A3HA, the absorption 
energies of C––O were explored by density functional theory (DFT) 
calculations at the atomic level. To simplify the calculated perovskite 
process, the simplified perovskite structure of FASnI3 was used instead 
of FA0.75MA0.25SnI2.75Br0.25. The side view in Figs. 2a-2d showed the 
total energy. The most stable configuration was reflected in the planar 
structure (Fig. 2a and Table S2). We further simulated the total density 
of states (DOS) of control and target films to evaluate the energy levels 
contribution (Fig. 2e). The DOS of 4A3HA was located near the band 
edge states and affected the Fermi level (Ef), which is consistent with the 
ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy (UPS) results (Fig. S6). The par­
tial density of states (PDOS) in Figs. 2f and 2h confirmed that the ex­
istence of 4A3HA at the Sn-I terminated surface enhanced the energy of 
Sn 5p states, therefore reducing the possible non-radiative recombina­
tion. The detailed electron localization function (ELF) analysis (Figs. 2g 
and 2i) further indicated the obvious variation of the electron cloud 
around the Sn atoms and transferred local charge from Sn atoms to O 
atoms. Hence, the coordinated interaction between Sn2+ and 4A3HA 
could stabilize the [SnI6]4– octahedra near the surface and eliminate the 
under-coordinated Sn defects, which would further suppress the non- 
radiative recombination from the defects. 
Given the enhancements in crystallization and defect passivation, the 
perovskite films with 4A3HA were fabricated to investigate how coor­
dination interaction affects the photovoltaic performance (Fig. 3a). The 
target device delivered a champion PCE of 13.43% with a high Voc of 
0.90 V (Fig. 3b), and a fill factor (FF) of 71.22% under AM 1.5 G light 
illumination with a scan speed of 200 mV/s and 20 ms setting time 
(Fig. S7), while the control device showed a champion PCE of 9.44% 
with a Voc of 0.84 V, and a FF of 68.53% (Other devices with different 
ratio of 4A3HA can be seen in Table S3). The energy loss (Eloss) (Eloss 
= Eg-qVoc) decreased from 0.55 eV to 0.48 eV in our devices after 
4A3HA modification. External quantum efficiency (EQE) spectrum in 
Fig. 3c showed an integrated short-current density (Jint) of 
Fig. 2. The total energy of 4A3HA-treated perovskites with (a) planar, (b) vertical, (c) standing, and (d) oblique structures. (e) The total density of states (DOS) of 
FASnI3, 4A3HA-treated FASnI3, and the distribution of 4A3HA in FASnI3. Partial density of states (PDOS) of (f) control and (h) 4A3HA-treated perovskite films. 
Electron localization function (ELF) results of (g) control and (i) 4A3HA-treated perovskite films. 
S. Wang et al.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   


Nano Energy 99 (2022) 107416
4
20.98 mA cm–2 from the target device, well-matched with the short- 
current density (Jsc) from the current density-voltage (J-V) curves, 
whereas the control device obtained a Jint of 16.33 mA cm–2
. 
A higher 
and more stable PCE of the target device was achieved when compared 
to the control device (Fig. 3d). The box charts in Fig. 3e and S8 for 20 
devices exhibited the distribution of PCE, Voc, Jsc, and FF, respectively, 
thus confirming the good reproducibility. Therefore, our approach 
achieved a superior PCE with high Voc output, compared to other Lewis- 
acid-base strategies (Fig. S9). The other additives like glycine, benzoic 
acid, (S)-(-)−4-amino-2-hydroxybutyric acid (S4A2HA), and 4-amino­
benzoic acid (4AA) were also investigated (Fig. S10). When compared 
to the control device, the glycine-modified device had a slight increase 
of Voc and FF. The benzoic acid and 4AA-modified device had an overall 
improvement in efficiency. The adding of S4A2HA showed almost no 
significant improvement. In this case, the other functional groups along 
with the carbonyl group have a synergistic effect. The interaction be­
tween the hydroxyl group and benzene ring in phenol makes its chem­
ical properties more active than alcohol and benzene. The reducing 
hydroxyl group is attached to the benzene ring, which can scavenge 
oxygen by donating hydrogen atoms and electrons. Moreover, the 
4A3HA molecule shows a strong conjugation effect than other additives 
like glycine and S4A2HA. 
The changes of PCE in the N2 atmosphere were tracked over 2000 h 
to test the long-term stability (Fig. 3f). The results showed almost un­
changed PCE after 2000 h, whereas the control devices decreased over 
60% of the original PCE during this time. Also, as shown in Fig. 3g, the 
thermal stability at 85 ◦C of the target devices was noticeably improved, 
maintaining over 80% of the original PCE after 1000 h heating. In 
contrast, the control devices lost near 70% of the initial efficiency. 
Meanwhile, the contact angle of water drops (Fig. S11) was 53.8◦and 
62.7◦for control and target films, respectively, indicating enhanced 
hydrophobicity due to the effect of the hydrophobic benzene group after 
4A3HA treatment. The air stability also improved after 4A3HA treat­
ment, along with 80% retain after 133 h storage in air without any 
encapsulation (Fig. S12). 
To elucidate the carrier dynamics of devices, we further investigated 
the charge carrier transport properties by photo-induced charge 
extraction by linearly increasing voltage (Photo-CELIV) method with a 
structure of ITO/SnO2/perovskite/ICBA/Ag (Figs. 4a-4b, and Fig. S13). 
The electron mobility (μe) could be studied using the following equation:

whereas the target device showed a smaller △j than the control device.

target device, higher than the control device (1.88 ×10–6 cm–2 V–1 
s–1) under 100 mW cm–2 light intensity (Table S4). In addition, the 
steady-state photoluminescence (PL) peak intensity of the target film 
showed 2.5 times higher compared with the control film (Fig. 4c and 
S14). Meanwhile, the PL decay (Fig. 4d and Table S5) showed a pro­
longed decay time for the target film (8.24 ns vs. 4.18 ns), which implied 
reduced non-radiative recombination. 
To understand the charge extraction and carrier lifetime dynamics, 
the transient photocurrent (TPC) and transient photovoltage (TPV) 
measurements were carried in Figs. 4e and 4f. The target device showed 
faster TPC decay than the control device, which can contribute to more 
effective electron transport. The recombination lifetime extracted from 
TPV results showed a decay value of 127.86 μs for the target device and 
41.57 μs for the control device, further demonstrating reduced trap 
density after 4A3HA treatment. Fig. 4g provided the electrical imped­
ance spectroscopy (EIS) spectra to extract the value of series resistance 
(Rs) and charge-recombination resistance (Rrec) for both devices. 
Compared to the control device, the lower Rs and higher Rrec value were 
derived for the target device (Table S6), which means suppressed charge 
recombination in the target device [37]. We also considered the dark J-V 
analysis to reveal intrinsic characteristics of the devices (Fig. S15). It is 
clear that the target device displayed much decreased leakage current in 
the reverse direction, which indicates a charge-carrier channel with less 
direct shunting. 
The electron-only device with a structure of ITO/SnO2/perovskite/ 
ICBA/Ag and hole-only device with a structure of ITO/PEDOT:PSS/ 
perovskite/Au were fabricated to check the electron/hole trap density 
(Fig. 4h and Fig. S16) [38,39]. The trap-state density could be detected 
by the trap-filled limit voltage (VTFL) using the following equation: [40] 
VTFL = qntL2

where q, L, ε, and ε0 denote the elemental charge, film thickness 
(~170 nm), the relative dielectric constant of the perovskite film (35), 
and permittivity of a vacuum, respectively. A lower VTFL was obtained 
with the target devices (from 0.504 V to 0.262 V for electron-only de­
vices, and from 0.448 V to 0.335 V for hole-only devices. The trap 
density decreased from 7.80 ×1015 cm–3 to 4.05 ×1015 cm–3 for the 
electron-only device in the target film (all data can be seen in Table S7), 
which was attributed to the efficient defect passivation effect by 4A3HA. 
The charge-carrier density was also estimated by capacitance-voltage 
(C-V) measurements with Mott-Schottky analysis (Fig. 4i) using the 
following equation: [41]

where A, C, Vbi, V, Nd corresponds to the active electrode area, capaci­
tance, the flat band potential, the applied voltage, and charge-carrier 
density, respectively. The Vbi of target device was enhanced compared 
with a the control device, which was in agreement with the improved FF 
and Voc [42]. A reduced Nd from 5.27 × 1015 cm–3 to 4.72 × 1015 cm–3 
with the addition of 4A3HA implied the effectiveness in suppressing 
Sn2+ oxidation in perovskite film. 
According to the theoretical analysis, the Vsn is the dominant defect 
in Sn perovskites [43]. The high concentration of Vsn in perovskites leads 
to a high level of p-type doping effect [44]. The formation energy of Vsn 
was calculated for the control and target devices (Fig. 5a and Fig. S17). 
The increase of Vsn indicates the suppressed self-doping by 4A3HA, 
leading to reduced Voc deficit in the target device [45]. To verify the 
enhanced structural stability, XPS spectrum was measured to under­
stand the Sn2+ oxidation retardation ability (Fig. 5b). The samples were 
stored overnight in a vacuum chamber and then tested. The corre­
sponding peak of Sn2+ 3d 5/2 and Sn2+ 3d 3/2 located at 486.4 and 
494.8 eV, respectively (Table S8). The Sn2+ peaks shifted to lower 
binding energy (~ 0.3 eV) after 4A3HA treatment, which indicated the 
strong Lewis acid-base interaction between SnI2 and C––O group. This 
result also consistent with the C 1 s spectrum of C––O peak. Sn4+ region 
exhibited two divided peaks at 487.0 and 495.4 eV, which are attributed 
to Sn4+ 3d 5/2 and Sn4+ 3d 3/2, respectively. The calculated fractions of 
Sn4+ in the target film means that the presence of 4A3HA prevent the 
Sn2+ oxidation during the film formation process, which is consistent 
with previous report [21,46]. To confirm the long-term Sn2+ protection, 
the crystallographic data under 85 ◦C heating in N2 atmosphere over 26 
days were collected (Figs. 5c-5d). The heated films exposed to the air for 
about 20 min to check the structural variation by XRD spectra. The 
characteristic peaks of vacancy-ordered double perovskite derivative 
A2SnI6 at 24.8◦and 27.4◦appeared under 85 ◦C heating after 16 days 
and increased quickly for the control film, while the target film did not 
appear the A2SnI6 peak at 24.8◦and showed negligible peak at 27.4◦. 
Those results further confirmed the better structural stability under 
thermal environment, which is consistent with the long-term 85 ◦C 
stability test. Meanwhile, we observed a slightly blue-shifted peak of 
(100) and SnI2 around 0.1◦after heating for 16 days and then stabilized 
(Figs. 5c-5e and Fig. S18-S19), indicative of a slight lattice expansion 
after 16 days heating [47]. These phenomenon occurred by the high 
coefficients of volumetric thermal expansion for Sn perovskites [48,49]. 
3. Conclusion 
In this work, we developed a novel Lewis base to alleviate the 
structural disorder and under-coordinated Sn2+ defects in the Sn pe­
rovskites. The reduced VSn defect by Lewis acid-base strategy rendered 
slow Sn2+ oxidation and long-term structural stability of the Sn perov­
skites. We achieved a high PCE up to 13.43% in inverted TPSCs through 
substantially suppressed charge carrier non-radiative carrier recombi­
nation. Meanwhile, the target devices retained over 80% of the initial 
PCE for 1000 h after 85 ◦C thermal heating and showed almost no 
change of the initial PCE for 2000 h in N2 atmosphere. Therefore, our 
work provides an effective protocol for approaching the theoretical Voc 
limit in TPSCs through tin vacancy regulation.

joined National Center for Nanoscience and Technology as a 
full professor. His research focuses on innovative materials and 
devices. He is RSC Fellow, the nominator for Xplorer Prize, and 
the Associate Editor for Journal of Semiconductors.

perovskite solar cells\nA solution-processable semiconducting polymer with remarkable ﬁlm-forming and\nhole transport properties is synthesized to fabricate perovskite solar cells with\n\x0125% efﬁciency. The exceptional mechanical properties endow the cells with\nexcellent thermal durability at 85\x03C and operational stability.\nLifei He, Yuyan Zhang, Yuefang\nWei, Yaohang Cai, Jing Zhang,\nPeng Wang\npw2015@zju.edu.cn\nHighlights\nA helicene-based polymer with\nextraordinary Tg is prepared in\nhigh yield\nThe polymer efﬁciently extracts\nand transports holes from\nphotoexcited perovskites\nThe uniform and compact\npolymer ﬁlm exhibits exceptional\nnanomechanical properties\nPerovskite solar cells with this\npolymer display high efﬁciency\nand thermostability\nHe et al., Matter 6, 4013–4031\nNovember 1, 2023 ª 2023 Elsevier Inc.\nhttps://doi.org/10.1016/j.matt.2023.09.006\nll\n\n\nArticle\nA helicene-based semiconducting polymer\nfor stable and efﬁcient perovskite solar cells\nLifei He,1,2 Yuyan Zhang,1,2 Yuefang Wei,1 Yaohang Cai,1 Jing Zhang,1 and Peng Wang1,3,*\nSUMMARY\nThe relentless pursuit of higher efﬁciencies in perovskite solar cells\nrelies on the use of spiro-OMeTAD as a hole transport material, re-\nsulting in an impressive efﬁciency record of 25.7%. However, these\nhigh-efﬁciency cells have proven vulnerable to harsh heat conditions\nat 85\x01C. Here, we employed direct arylation polycondensation to\nefﬁciently synthesize a semiconducting polymer (p-O5H-E-POZ-E),\nthe main chain of which consists of a strategic alternation of oxa[5]\nhelicene, 3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene, phenoxazine, and 3,4-ethyl-\nenedioxythiophene. The air-doped composite of p-O5H-E-POZ-E\nand lithium bis(triﬂuoromethanesulfonyl)imide exhibits a room tem-\nperature conductivity of 75 mS cm\x031 and an exceptional glass-transi-\ntion temperature of 187\x01C. Compared to spiro-OMeTAD, p-O5H-E-\nPOZ-E demonstrates a comparable highest occupied molecular\norbital energy level for efﬁcient hole extraction while exhibiting\nenhanced elastic modulus and fracture strength and reduced water\npermeation in its composite ﬁlm. Using p-O5H-E-POZ-E in the hole\ntransport layer, we demonstrate perovskite solar cells with an\naverage efﬁciency of 24.9% and thermostability at 85\x01C.\nINTRODUCTION\nSolution-processed thin ﬁlms of organic-inorganic hybrid lead halide perovskites\nexhibit remarkable properties, including tunable light absorption, extended charge\ncarrier lifetime, and high charge mobility.1 These perovskites have attracted sub-\nstantial attention in the academic and industrial communities as promising light-\nabsorbing layers for heterojunction solar cells. In fact, perovskite solar cells (PSCs)\nhave achieved an impressive power conversion efﬁciency (PCE) record of 26.1%.2\nThe fabrication of efﬁcient and stable PSCs relies not only on achieving high-quality\ndeposition of perovskite ﬁlms but also on judiciously selecting superior interlayers\nand charge-transport layers.\nAmong various organic semiconductors (OSCs), the small-molecule OSC spiro-\nOMeTAD3 (Figure 1) is commonly employed as the main component of the hole\ntransport layer (HTL) in n-i-p-type PSCs due to its relatively shallow highest occupied\nmolecular orbital (HOMO) energy level. This characteristic enables effective air\ndoping, resulting in a proper hole density and desirable conductivity. Interestingly,\nthe pristine regioregular poly(3-hexylthiophene) (P3HT) with a higher HOMO energy\nlevel actually exhibits a considerably high hole density and conductivity (10\x0330 mS\ncm\x031) due to unintentional air doping. However, prolonged exposure to elevated\ntemperatures of 85\x01C causes signiﬁcant morphological degradation in amorphous\nspiro-OMeTAD composite ﬁlms, leading to reduced device efﬁciency.4–6 The ther-\nmal stability of PSCs with P3HT has not yet been reported due to its pretty low\nglass-transition temperature of 38\x01C.7 Another frequently used material in PSCs’\nPROGRESS AND POTENTIAL\nSolar cells should endure\nscorching summer heat. This\npresents a signiﬁcant challenge in\ndeveloping organic charge-\ntransport layers suitable for\nperovskite solar cells. Charge\ntransport in the organic\nsemiconductor thin ﬁlms occurs\nthrough a hopping mechanism,\nnecessitating doping to achieve\nsufﬁciently high carrier density,\nmobility, and conductivity. We\nreport a high-performance\nsemiconducting polymer by\nintegrating helicene into the main\nchain. This polymer exhibits high\nsolubility, favorable ﬁlm\nmorphology, matched energy\nlevels, and efﬁcient hole\nconduction. Notably, it showcases\nexceptional resistance to water\npenetration and a high elastic\nmodulus. Leveraging this polymer\nin the hole transport layer, we\nfabricated highly efﬁcient and\nthermally stable perovskite solar\ncells. Our research will stimulate\nthe exploration of\nsemiconducting polymers,\nemphasizing mechanical\nperformance, for practical\noptoelectronic devices.\nMatter 6, 4013–4031, November 1, 2023 ª 2023 Elsevier Inc. 4013\nll\n\n\nHTLs is the polymeric OSC PTAA (Figure 1),8 which faces challenges in achieving suf-\nﬁcient conductivity through air doping and swift hole extraction due to its deeper\nHOMO energy level, resulting in lower PCEs compared to spiro-OMeTAD.\nFor PSCs utilizing oxide electron transport layers such as TiO2 or SnO2, designing\nOSCs with sufﬁciently high HOMO energy levels is crucial to ensure efﬁcient hole\nextraction within the devices. Ideal HTLs should also possess favorable characteris-\ntics, including good ﬁlm-forming ability, hole conduction, resistance to morpholog-\nical degradation under heating, and effective mitigation of internal and external spe-\ncies diffusion. Compared with small-molecule OSCs, the molecular weight of\npolymeric OSCs ranges from 104 to 107. The elongated main chain of polymers\nadopts a random coil conformation and becomes entangled with other chains. In\naddition to displaying typical elastic deformation, polymer materials also exhibit\nhigh elastic deformation when heated above their glass-transition temperatures, re-\nsulting in thin ﬁlms with enhanced mechanical strength and improved fracture resis-\ntance. Despite exhaustive experimentation with diverse semiconducting polymers in\nPSCs, to date, none have exhibited simultaneous achievements of PCEs surpassing\n24% and endurance at 85\x01C.9–36\nRecently, nonconventional small-molecule OSCs derived from nonplanar conju-\ngated polycycles have attracted signiﬁcant interest.37,38 Helicenes, a notable subset\nof contorted molecules composed of ortho-fused aromatic rings, exhibit chirality\ndue to steric repulsion of terminal rings.39–41 While helicenes offer improved solu-\ntion processibility compared with their planar counterparts, their utilization in\norganic electronic devices emerged only in 2009.42 In 2013, Yang et al. demon-\nstrated the fabrication of organic ﬁeld-effect transistors capable of measuring circu-\nlarly polarized light using optically pure aza[6]helicene.43 In the same year, Nakahara\nFigure 1. Chemical structures of two helicene-based semiconducting polymers and the reference\ncopolymer, alongside state-of-the-art hole transport materials employed in perovskite solar cells\n1State Key Laboratory of Silicon and Advanced\nSemiconductor Materials, Department of\nChemistry, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou\n310030, China\n2These authors contributed equally\n3Lead contact\n*Correspondence: pw2015@zju.edu.cn\nhttps://doi.org/10.1016/j.matt.2023.09.006\nll\n4014 Matter 6, 4013–4031, November 1, 2023\nArticle\n\n\net al. achieved an impressive hole mobility of 1 cm2 V\x031 s\x031 in a single-crystal tran-\nsistor of oxa[5]helicene (O5H).44 However, the deep HOMO energy level of\nextremely cost-effective O5H poses a challenge when being used as the HTL in\nPSCs. By derivatizing O5H with an electron-rich diphenylamine, some hole transport\nmaterials for n-i-p-type PSCs with \x0421% efﬁciency have been developed.45,46 How-\never, these cells struggle to withstand the extreme heat of 85\x01C. Very recently, Vai-\nlassery and Sun made a detailed review on the physical properties and device per-\nformance of helicene-based small-molecule OSCs for PSCs.47 Among various\nhelicene-based molecular semiconductors, TBPC-611 achieved the best efﬁ-\nciencies, ranging from 23.5% to 24.8%.48\nInterestingly, our accidental experiment reveals that the copolymer p-O5H-E (Fig-\nure 1) with a number-average molecular weight (Mn) of 49 kDa, comprising the\nalternating monomers of O5H and 3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene (EDOT), exhibits\na remarkable room temperature solubility of >10 mg mL\x031 in chlorobenzene.\nAdditionally, p-O5H-E demonstrates a theoretical glass-transition temperature as\nhigh as 323\x01C. It is valuable to point out that polymers posting such a high\nglass-transition temperature and solubility have been rarely reported.49,50 Unfortu-\nnately, theoretical calculations using the density functional theory (DFT) method\nreveal that the HOMO energy level of p-O5H-E is deeper by 450 and 200 meV\ncompared to spiro-OMeTAD and PTAA, respectively (Table S1). To solve this\nissue, we attempted to substitute half of O5H with 10-(2-octyldodecyl)-10H-phe-\nnoxazine, resulting in a quaternary alternating copolymer named p-O5H-3,7-\nbis(2,3-dihydrothieno[3,4-b][1,4]dioxin-5-yl)-10-(2-octyldodecyl)-10H-phenoxazine\n(E-POZ-E) (Figure 1). Theoretical calculations suggest that the HOMO energy level\nof p-O5H-E-POZ-E is comparable to that of spiro-OMeTAD, while its glass-transi-\ntion temperature signiﬁcantly exceeds those of spiro-OMeTAD (153\x01C) and PTAA\n(118\x01C) at 268\x01C. In order to gain a systematic understanding of the structure-\nproperty relationship, a reference alternating copolymer, p-POZ-E, was synthe-\nsized, as illustrated in Figure 1.\nIt was found that the highly soluble p-O5H-E-POZ-E can codeposit with the air-\ndoping auxiliary reagent lithium bis(triﬂuoromethanesulfonyl)imide (LiTFSI), forming\nuniform and compact thin ﬁlms on various substrates with excellent hole conduction.\nBy incorporating p-O5H-E-POZ-E as an essential component of the HTL, we success-\nfully fabricated PSCs with an average initial PCE of 24.9%, surpassing those of the\ncontrol cells with spiro-OMeTAD (24.0%) and PTAA (21.6%). Importantly, the\np-O5H-E-POZ-E-based solar cells demonstrated signiﬁcantly improved operational\nstability and thermal stability at 85\x01C. Comprehensive device degradation analysis\nhas revealed the crucial importance of a high elastic modulus, fracture strength,\nand minimal water permeation within the HTL, thereby conferring thermal stability\nto PSCs.\nRESULTS AND DISCUSSION\nSynthesis\nFor details on the synthesis, puriﬁcation, and structural characterization of p-O5H-E,\np-O5H-E-POZ-E, and p-POZ-E, please refer to the supplemental information. In\nbrief, the synthesis involved a 2-fold Suzuki-Miyaura cross-coupling reaction be-\ntween 3,7-dibromo-10-(2-octyldodecyl)-10H-phenoxazine (2Br-POZ) and 2-(3,4-\nethylenedioxythiophen-5-yl)-4,4,5,5-tetramethyl-1,3,2-dioxaborolane, resulting in\nthe formation of the monomer E-POZ-E with an 86% yield. Subsequently,\na palladium-catalyzed direct arylation polycondensation was performed between\nll\nMatter 6, 4013–4031, November 1, 2023 4015\nArticle\n\n\n5,9-dibromodinaphtho[2,1-b:10,20-d]furan (2Br-O5H) and E-POZ-E, leading to the\nformation of p-O5H-E-POZ-E with a yield of 90%. Similarly, p-O5H-E and p-POZ-E\nwere synthesized by copolymerizing EDOT with 2Br-O5H and 2Br-POZ, respec-\ntively. High-temperature gel permeation chromatography, using polystyrene as a\nstandard, revealed Mn values of 49 kDa for p-O5H-E, 401 kDa for p-O5H-E-POZ-\nE, and 178 kDa for p-POZ-E, with polymer dispersity indexes of 1.7, 1.6, and 2.2,\nrespectively. Article
A helicene-based semiconducting polymer for
stable and efﬁcient perovskite solar cells
A solution-processable semiconducting polymer with remarkable ﬁlm-forming and
hole transport properties is synthesized to fabricate perovskite solar cells with
25% efﬁciency. The exceptional mechanical properties endow the cells with
excellent thermal durability at 85C and operational stability.
Lifei He, Yuyan Zhang, Yuefang
Wei, Yaohang Cai, Jing Zhang,
Peng Wang
pw2015@zju.edu.cn
Highlights
A helicene-based polymer with
extraordinary Tg is prepared in
high yield
The polymer efﬁciently extracts
and transports holes from
photoexcited perovskites
The uniform and compact
polymer ﬁlm exhibits exceptional
nanomechanical properties
Perovskite solar cells with this
polymer display high efﬁciency
and thermostability
He et al., Matter 6, 4013–4031

INTRODUCTION
Solution-processed thin ﬁlms of organic-inorganic hybrid lead halide perovskites
exhibit remarkable properties, including tunable light absorption, extended charge
carrier lifetime, and high charge mobility.1 These perovskites have attracted sub-
stantial attention in the academic and industrial communities as promising light-
absorbing layers for heterojunction solar cells. In fact, perovskite solar cells (PSCs)
have achieved an impressive power conversion efﬁciency (PCE) record of 26.1%.2
The fabrication of efﬁcient and stable PSCs relies not only on achieving high-quality
deposition of perovskite ﬁlms but also on judiciously selecting superior interlayers
and charge-transport layers.
Among various organic semiconductors (OSCs), the small-molecule OSC spiro-
OMeTAD3 (Figure 1) is commonly employed as the main component of the hole
transport layer (HTL) in n-i-p-type PSCs due to its relatively shallow highest occupied
molecular orbital (HOMO) energy level. This characteristic enables effective air
doping, resulting in a proper hole density and desirable conductivity. Interestingly,
the pristine regioregular poly(3-hexylthiophene) (P3HT) with a higher HOMO energy
level actually exhibits a considerably high hole density and conductivity (1030 mS
cm1) due to unintentional air doping. However, prolonged exposure to elevated
temperatures of 85C causes signiﬁcant morphological degradation in amorphous
spiro-OMeTAD composite ﬁlms, leading to reduced device efﬁciency.4–6 The ther-
mal stability of PSCs with P3HT has not yet been reported due to its pretty low
glass-transition temperature of 38C.7 Another frequently used material in PSCs’

addition to displaying typical elastic deformation, polymer materials also exhibit

It was found that the highly soluble p-O5H-E-POZ-E can codeposit with the air-
doping auxiliary reagent lithium bis(triﬂuoromethanesulfonyl)imide (LiTFSI), forming
uniform and compact thin ﬁlms on various substrates with excellent hole conduction.
By incorporating p-O5H-E-POZ-E as an essential component of the HTL, we success-
fully fabricated PSCs with an average initial PCE of 24.9%, surpassing those of the
control cells with spiro-OMeTAD (24.0%) and PTAA (21.6%). Importantly, the
p-O5H-E-POZ-E-based solar cells demonstrated signiﬁcantly improved operational
stability and thermal stability at 85C. Comprehensive device degradation analysis
has revealed the crucial importance of a high elastic modulus, fracture strength,
and minimal water permeation within the HTL, thereby conferring thermal stability
to PSCs.

Electron paramagnetic resonance spectra and hole density, conductivity, and
mobility
An OSC in its intrinsic state relies on a thermally activated disproportionation mech-
anism to generate charge carriers. However, for OSCs with an Eg larger than 1.5 eV,
the density of charge carriers produced through disproportionation remains below
104 cm3 at room temperature. Even with high electron and hole mobilities of up to
10 cm2 V1 s1, the resulting electrical conductivity (s) calculated using the equation
s = mnqn + mpqp remains below 107 mS cm1. Here, q represents the elementary
charge, mn is the electron mobility, mp is the hole mobility, n is the electron density,
and p is the hole density. These ﬁndings clearly indicate the insulating nature of
intrinsic OSCs.

Stability at 85C and device degradation analysis
The p-O5H-E and p-POZ-E cells exhibited low PCEs below 21%; therefore, long-term
thermal stability tests were conducted solely on the p-O5H-E-POZ-E, PTAA, and
spiro-OMeTAD cells. Six cells of each type were subjected to an 85C oven for a speciﬁc
duration, followed by J-V measurements under AM1.5G conditions at room tempera-
ture. The temporal evolution of the average PCE was analyzed using a biexponential
decay function (Figure 5A). After 1,000 h, the PCE of the p-O5H-E-POZ-E cells
decreased from an initial 24.9% to a ﬁnal 23.2%, retaining 93% of its initial value. In com-
parison, the PTAA cells retained 78% of their initial PCE, while the spiro-OMeTAD cells
only retained 25%. The small PCE drop of the p-O5H-E-POZ-E cell can be partly
ascribed to the slow evaporation of residual TBP. A better doping procedure could
further enhance the 85C stability of the p-O5H-E-POZ-E cell.
Representative J-V curves of the cells after 1,000 h of aging, along with the corre-
sponding photovoltaic parameters listed in Table 1, are shown in Figure 5B. Analysis
revealed that the decrease in PCE of the p-O5H-E-POZ-E cells primarily resulted
from a 4.3% decrease in FF, with minor reductions in JSC and VOC of 1.5% and
1.3%, respectively. In contrast, the PTAA cells exhibited a signiﬁcant decay rate in
FF of 15.3%, accompanied by decay rates in JSC and VOC of 5.0% and 3.6%, respec-
tively. Notably, the spiro-OMeTAD cells experienced substantial decay rates in FF,
JSC, and VOC, with values of 34%, 47%, and 30%, respectively.

85C for 1,000 h resulted in a 43% reduction in the EQE maximum of the spiro-OMe-
TAD cell, decreasing from 94% to 51%. In contrast, the PTAA cell exhibited a minor
decrease in the EQE maximum, dropping only from 93% to 89%. Similarly, the p-
O5H-E-POZ-E cell displayed a marginal decrease in the EQE maximum, declining

Operational stability
Finally, we conducted operational stability assessments on solar cells employing p-
O5H-E-POZ-E and spiro-OMeTAD under simulated AM1.5G sunlight in a nitrogen
atmosphere at 40C. The tracking of maximum power points (MPPs) was performed
using the standard perturb and observe method. The temporal evolutions of PCE
(PCEMPP), photocurrent density (JMPP), and photovoltage (VMPP) at MPPs are pre-
sented in Figures 7A–7C. Over a duration of 500 h, the spiro-OMeTAD cell exhibited
a signiﬁcant decline of 25% in PCEMPP, attributed to a 21% decrease in JMPP and a 5%
reduction in VMPP. In contrast, after 500 h of tracking, the p-O5H-E-POZ-E cell’s
PCEMPP decreased from 24.3% to 23.9%, indicating an excellent retention rate of
98%, due to a 2% decline in JMPP.
We also intermittently recorded J-V data during MPP tracking and employed
Shockley diode ﬁtting to extract two pivotal physical parameters: series resistance
(Rs) and shunt resistance (Rsh). Figures 7D and 7E demonstrate the progressive in-
crease in Rs and decrease in Rsh for the spiro-OMeTAD cell during MPP tracking. In
contrast, the p-O5H-E-POZ-E cell exhibited a slight increase in Rs, while Rsh re-
mained unchanged. The decrease in Rsh indicates accelerated charge recombina-
tion, potentially linked to an augmentation of defects within the perovskite layer.
Simultaneously, the rise in Rs can be attributed to the presence of additional

Article
A helicene-based semiconducting polymer
for stable and efﬁcient perovskite solar cells
Lifei He,1,2 Yuyan Zhang,1,2 Yuefang Wei,1 Yaohang Cai,1 Jing Zhang,1 and Peng Wang1,3,*
SUMMARY
The relentless pursuit of higher efﬁciencies in perovskite solar cells
relies on the use of spiro-OMeTAD as a hole transport material, re-
sulting in an impressive efﬁciency record of 25.7%. However, these
high-efﬁciency cells have proven vulnerable to harsh heat conditions
at 85C. Here, we employed direct arylation polycondensation to
efﬁciently synthesize a semiconducting polymer (p-O5H-E-POZ-E),
the main chain of which consists of a strategic alternation of oxa[5]
helicene, 3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene, phenoxazine, and 3,4-ethyl-
enedioxythiophene. The air-doped composite of p-O5H-E-POZ-E
and lithium bis(triﬂuoromethanesulfonyl)imide exhibits a room tem-
perature conductivity of 75 mS cm1 and an exceptional glass-transi-
tion temperature of 187C. Compared to spiro-OMeTAD, p-O5H-E-
POZ-E demonstrates a comparable highest occupied molecular
orbital energy level for efﬁcient hole extraction while exhibiting
enhanced elastic modulus and fracture strength and reduced water
permeation in its composite ﬁlm. Using p-O5H-E-POZ-E in the hole
transport layer, we demonstrate perovskite solar cells with an
average efﬁciency of 24.9% and thermostability at 85C.
INTRODUCTION
Solution-processed thin ﬁlms of organic-inorganic hybrid lead halide perovskites
exhibit remarkable properties, including tunable light absorption, extended charge
carrier lifetime, and high charge mobility.1 These perovskites have attracted sub-
stantial attention in the academic and industrial communities as promising light-
absorbing layers for heterojunction solar cells. In fact, perovskite solar cells (PSCs)
have achieved an impressive power conversion efﬁciency (PCE) record of 26.1%.2
The fabrication of efﬁcient and stable PSCs relies not only on achieving high-quality
deposition of perovskite ﬁlms but also on judiciously selecting superior interlayers
and charge-transport layers.
Among various organic semiconductors (OSCs), the small-molecule OSC spiro-
OMeTAD3 (Figure 1) is commonly employed as the main component of the hole
transport layer (HTL) in n-i-p-type PSCs due to its relatively shallow highest occupied
molecular orbital (HOMO) energy level. This characteristic enables effective air
doping, resulting in a proper hole density and desirable conductivity. Interestingly,
the pristine regioregular poly(3-hexylthiophene) (P3HT) with a higher HOMO energy
level actually exhibits a considerably high hole density and conductivity (1030 mS
cm1) due to unintentional air doping. However, prolonged exposure to elevated
temperatures of 85C causes signiﬁcant morphological degradation in amorphous
spiro-OMeTAD composite ﬁlms, leading to reduced device efﬁciency.4–6 The ther-
mal stability of PSCs with P3HT has not yet been reported due to its pretty low
glass-transition temperature of 38C.7 Another frequently used material in PSCs’
PROGRESS AND POTENTIAL
Solar cells should endure
scorching summer heat. This
presents a signiﬁcant challenge in
developing organic charge-
transport layers suitable for
perovskite solar cells. Charge
transport in the organic
semiconductor thin ﬁlms occurs
through a hopping mechanism,
necessitating doping to achieve
sufﬁciently high carrier density,
mobility, and conductivity. We
report a high-performance
semiconducting polymer by
integrating helicene into the main
chain. This polymer exhibits high
solubility, favorable ﬁlm
morphology, matched energy
levels, and efﬁcient hole
conduction. Notably, it showcases
exceptional resistance to water
penetration and a high elastic
modulus. Leveraging this polymer
in the hole transport layer, we
fabricated highly efﬁcient and
thermally stable perovskite solar
cells. Our research will stimulate
the exploration of
semiconducting polymers,
emphasizing mechanical
performance, for practical
optoelectronic devices.
Matter 6, 4013–4031, November 1, 2023 ª 2023 Elsevier Inc. 4013

HTLs is the polymeric OSC PTAA (Figure 1),8 which faces challenges in achieving suf-
ﬁcient conductivity through air doping and swift hole extraction due to its deeper
HOMO energy level, resulting in lower PCEs compared to spiro-OMeTAD.
For PSCs utilizing oxide electron transport layers such as TiO2 or SnO2, designing
OSCs with sufﬁciently high HOMO energy levels is crucial to ensure efﬁcient hole
extraction within the devices. Ideal HTLs should also possess favorable characteris-
tics, including good ﬁlm-forming ability, hole conduction, resistance to morpholog-
ical degradation under heating, and effective mitigation of internal and external spe-
cies diffusion. Compared with small-molecule OSCs, the molecular weight of
polymeric OSCs ranges from 104 to 107. The elongated main chain of polymers
adopts a random coil conformation and becomes entangled with other chains. In
addition to displaying typical elastic deformation, polymer materials also exhibit
high elastic deformation when heated above their glass-transition temperatures, re-
sulting in thin ﬁlms with enhanced mechanical strength and improved fracture resis-
tance. Despite exhaustive experimentation with diverse semiconducting polymers in
PSCs, to date, none have exhibited simultaneous achievements of PCEs surpassing
24% and endurance at 85C.9–36
Recently, nonconventional small-molecule OSCs derived from nonplanar conju-
gated polycycles have attracted signiﬁcant interest.37,38 Helicenes, a notable subset
of contorted molecules composed of ortho-fused aromatic rings, exhibit chirality
due to steric repulsion of terminal rings.39–41 While helicenes offer improved solu-
tion processibility compared with their planar counterparts, their utilization in
organic electronic devices emerged only in 2009.42 In 2013, Yang et al. demon-
strated the fabrication of organic ﬁeld-effect transistors capable of measuring circu-
larly polarized light using optically pure aza[6]helicene.43 In the same year, Nakahara

Electron paramagnetic resonance spectra and hole density, conductivity, and
mobility
An OSC in its intrinsic state relies on a thermally activated disproportionation mech-
anism to generate charge carriers. However, for OSCs with an Eg larger than 1.5 eV,
the density of charge carriers produced through disproportionation remains below
104 cm3 at room temperature. Even with high electron and hole mobilities of up to
10 cm2 V1 s1, the resulting electrical conductivity (s) calculated using the equation
s = mnqn + mpqp remains below 107 mS cm1. Here, q represents the elementary
charge, mn is the electron mobility, mp is the hole mobility, n is the electron density,
and p is the hole density. These ﬁndings clearly indicate the insulating nature of
intrinsic OSCs.
Next, we incorporated LiTFSI to enhance the p value in air-doped OSC thin ﬁlms.
Notably, in this context, atmospheric oxygen acts as a p-dopant, while LiTFSI func-
tions as an auxiliary reagent for oxygen doping. For the electron paramagnetic reso-
nance (EPR) measurements, we fabricated composite thin ﬁlms by codepositing
LiTFSI with each OSC onto glass slides. As presented in Figures 3A and S4, the in-
tensity of the EPR signal from cationic radicals within the OSC-based ﬁlms increased
as the weight percentage of LiTFSI was raised. The quadratic integral intensity of the

for OSC ﬁlms incorporating varying weight percentages of LiTFSI. At a speciﬁc

p-O5H-E < PTAA < p-O5H-E-POZ-E < spiro-OMeTAD < p-POZ-E.

Stability at 85C and device degradation analysis
The p-O5H-E and p-POZ-E cells exhibited low PCEs below 21%; therefore, long-term
thermal stability tests were conducted solely on the p-O5H-E-POZ-E, PTAA, and
spiro-OMeTAD cells. Six cells of each type were subjected to an 85C oven for a speciﬁc
duration, followed by J-V measurements under AM1.5G conditions at room tempera-
ture. The temporal evolution of the average PCE was analyzed using a biexponential
decay function (Figure 5A). After 1,000 h, the PCE of the p-O5H-E-POZ-E cells
decreased from an initial 24.9% to a ﬁnal 23.2%, retaining 93% of its initial value. In com-
parison, the PTAA cells retained 78% of their initial PCE, while the spiro-OMeTAD cells
only retained 25%. The small PCE drop of the p-O5H-E-POZ-E cell can be partly
ascribed to the slow evaporation of residual TBP. A better doping procedure could
further enhance the 85C stability of the p-O5H-E-POZ-E cell.
Representative J-V curves of the cells after 1,000 h of aging, along with the corre-
sponding photovoltaic parameters listed in Table 1, are shown in Figure 5B. Analysis
revealed that the decrease in PCE of the p-O5H-E-POZ-E cells primarily resulted
from a 4.3% decrease in FF, with minor reductions in JSC and VOC of 1.5% and
1.3%, respectively. In contrast, the PTAA cells exhibited a signiﬁcant decay rate in
FF of 15.3%, accompanied by decay rates in JSC and VOC of 5.0% and 3.6%, respec-
tively. Notably, the spiro-OMeTAD cells experienced substantial decay rates in FF,
JSC, and VOC, with values of 34%, 47%, and 30%, respectively.

decrease in the EQE maximum, dropping only from 93% to 89%. Similarly, the p-
O5H-E-POZ-E cell displayed a marginal decrease in the EQE maximum, declining

O5H-E-POZ-E, instead of either PTAA or spiro-OMeTAD, not only preserved the

Operational stability
Finally, we conducted operational stability assessments on solar cells employing p-
O5H-E-POZ-E and spiro-OMeTAD under simulated AM1.5G sunlight in a nitrogen
atmosphere at 40C. The tracking of maximum power points (MPPs) was performed
using the standard perturb and observe method. The temporal evolutions of PCE
(PCEMPP), photocurrent density (JMPP), and photovoltage (VMPP) at MPPs are pre-
sented in Figures 7A–7C. Over a duration of 500 h, the spiro-OMeTAD cell exhibited
a signiﬁcant decline of 25% in PCEMPP, attributed to a 21% decrease in JMPP and a 5%
reduction in VMPP. In contrast, after 500 h of tracking, the p-O5H-E-POZ-E cell’s
PCEMPP decreased from 24.3% to 23.9%, indicating an excellent retention rate of
98%, due to a 2% decline in JMPP.
We also intermittently recorded J-V data during MPP tracking and employed
Shockley diode ﬁtting to extract two pivotal physical parameters: series resistance
(Rs) and shunt resistance (Rsh). Figures 7D and 7E demonstrate the progressive in-
crease in Rs and decrease in Rsh for the spiro-OMeTAD cell during MPP tracking. In
contrast, the p-O5H-E-POZ-E cell exhibited a slight increase in Rs, while Rsh re-
mained unchanged. The decrease in Rsh indicates accelerated charge recombina-
tion, potentially linked to an augmentation of defects within the perovskite layer.
Simultaneously, the rise in Rs can be attributed to the presence of additional
